title: Mor Çatı’nın uluslararası konferansında kadın dayanışması öne çıktı
content:
Mor Çatı Kadın Sığınağı Vakfı, İstanbul Beyoğlu’nda “Kadına Yönelik Şiddetle Mücadelede Dayanışma Merkezleri - Uluslararası Deneyimler” başlıklı bir konferans düzenledi.




MA'nın haberine göre, Konferansın “Dayanışma Merkezleri: Kadına Yönelik Şiddetle Mücadelede Nasıl Bir Dönüşüm Yaşanıyor?” başlıklı ilk oturumunda Avrupa Şiddete Karşı Kadınlar Ağı (WAVE) temsilcisi Elena Floriani, Danimarka’daki Danner kadın örgütünden Ditte Specht ve Mor Çatı’dan Leyla Soydiç konuştu. Oturumu Mor Çatı gönüllüsü Elif Ege yönetti.




“Kadın örgütleri değişimin aktörleri”




WAVE temsilcisi Elena Floriani, kadınlara ve kız çocuklarına yönelik şiddetle mücadelede uzman destek hizmetlerinin önemine dikkat çekti. Bu hizmetlerin kadınların ihtiyaçlarını merkeze aldığını ve kendi yaşamlarına ilişkin kararlarını desteklediğini söyledi.




Kadın örgütlerinin tarihsel mücadelesine değinen Floriani, 1970’lerde feminist aktivistlerin ilk kadın sığınaklarını açarak şiddeti siyasi gündeme taşıdığını hatırlattı.




Kadın örgütlerinin yalnızca destek hizmeti sunmadığını, toplumsal değişime de öncülük ettiğini belirten Floriani, şöyle konuştu:




“Kadın örgütlerinin kadına yönelik şiddetle mücadele politikalarının oluşmasında en önemli itici güç olduğunu araştırmalar gösteriyor. Bu nedenle kadınlara yönelik uzman destek hizmetlerini yalnızca hizmet sağlayıcılar olarak değil, değişimin aktörleri olarak ele alıyoruz.”




WAVE’nin bu yıl yayımladığı 

Değişimin Aktörleri

 (Agents of Change) başlıklı raporun bulgularını da paylaşan Floriani, kadın örgütlerinin kadınların güçlenmesinden yasal düzenlemelere ve kurumlar arası işbirliğine kadar birçok alanda etkili olduğunu söyledi.




Şiddete maruz bırakılan kadınlara destek vermenin yalnızca sığınakta bir yatak sağlamaktan ibaret olmadığını vurgulayan Floriani, “Kadınlara özgü bir yaklaşımı olmayan genel hizmetler, uzman destek hizmetlerinin yerini alamaz. Kadına ve kız çocuklarına yönelik şiddetle anlamlı bir mücadele için bu hizmetler vazgeçilmezdir” dedi.




Kadın haklarına yönelik tepkilerin, toplumsal cinsiyet karşıtı hareketlerin ve finansman kısıtlamalarının kadın örgütlerinin çalışmalarını zorlaştırdığını belirten Floriani, uzman destek hizmetlerinin korunması ve güçlendirilmesi çağrısı yaptı.




“Sığınaktan ayrılmakla mücadele sona ermiyor”




Danimarka’daki Danner kadın örgütünden Ditte Specht, kadına yönelik şiddetle mücadelede farklı sektörlerin ve meslek gruplarının işbirliği yapması gerektiğini söyledi.




Kadın sığınaklarında sunulan desteğin, kadınların sığınaktan ayrılmasıyla sona ermediğini vurgulayan Specht, şiddetten uzak bir yaşam kurmanın uzun bir süreç olduğunu belirtti.




Specht, “Kadın sığınaktan ayrıldığında da desteğimiz sona ermiyor; şiddetten uzak bir yaşama giden yol sığınaktan çıkmakla tamamlanmıyor. Hatta gerçek mücadelenin o zaman başladığını söyleyebiliriz” diye konuştu.




“Kadınlar kendi hayatlarının uzmanıdır”




Mor Çatı gönüllüsü Leyla Soydiç, şiddetin kadınların yaşamında uzun yıllar süren sosyal, ekonomik ve ruhsal sonuçlar yarattığını belirterek dayanışma merkezlerinin bu süreçte kadınlara eşlik ettiğini söyledi.




Erkek şiddetini yalnızca bireysel sorunlarla açıklamanın patriyarkayı ve güç ilişkilerini görünmez kıldığını ifade eden Soydiç, kadınların kendi yaşamlarına ilişkin kararları kendilerinin alması gerektiğini vurguladı.




“Zehirli ilişki” şiddeti görünmez kılıyor




Konferansın “Dayanışma Merkezlerini Çeşitlilikle Sürdürmek” başlıklı ikinci oturumunda Fransa, İspanya ve İtalya’dan kadın örgütlerinin temsilcileri deneyimlerini paylaştı. Oturumu Mor Çatı gönüllüsü Selime Büyükgöze yönetti.




Fransa Ulusal Kadın Dayanışma Federasyonu (FNSF) İletişim Birimi Sorumlusu Camille Lextray, kadınların maruz bırakıldığı şiddetin resmi istatistiklere bütünüyle yansımadığına dikkat çekti. Federasyonun Fransa genelinde 80’den fazla derneği bir araya getirdiğini belirten Lextray, yardım hatlarına başvuran kadınların ortalama üç farklı şiddet biçimi bildirdiğini, psikolojik şiddetin yüzde 85 ile ilk sırada yer aldığını söyledi.




Fransa’da aile içi şiddetin giderek “zehirli ilişki” olarak tanımlanmasına karşı çıkan Lextray, bu ifadenin şiddet uygulayan kişinin sorumluluğunu ve ilişkideki tahakkümü görünmez kıldığını belirtti.




Lextray, “Resmi istatistikler yaşananların yalnızca bir bölümünü gösteriyor. Biz resmi kayıtlarda görünmeyenleri ortaya çıkarmak istiyoruz” dedi.




Göçmen kadınlarla dayanışma




İtalya’daki Casa della Donna bünyesinde faaliyet gösteren Şiddet Karşıtı Merkez’in koordinatörü Dr. Francesca Pidone, örgütün gönüllülerin çalışmalarıyla ayakta durduğunu ve ayrım gözetmeden tüm kadınlara destek sunduğunu anlattı. Pidone, kadınlar tarafından kamusal bir alana dönüştürülen mekânlarında feminist çalışmalar yürüttüklerini söyledi.




İspanya’nın Valencia kentindeki Senin İçin Kadın Derneği (Asociación Por Ti Mujer) temsilcisi ve insan hakları avukatı Dr. Lucía Ávila Carrillo ise göçmen kadınların haklara erişimi ve şiddetle mücadele alanındaki çalışmalarını aktardı.




Derneğin 2009’da göçmen kadınlar tarafından kurulduğunu belirten Carrillo, kadınlara vatandaşlık, yasal statü ve insan haklarından yararlanma süreçlerinde destek verdiklerini söyledi. Carrillo, çalışmalarında kesişimsel toplumsal cinsiyet, insan hakları ve kültürlerarası yaklaşımı esas aldıklarını ifade etti.




Konferans, ikinci oturumun soru-cevap bölümünün ardından sona erdi.



















Erkek Şiddeti Çetelesi




12 Aralık 2024










(EMK)

author: Corey Larocque
title: Minority government outcome stalls PQ referendum pledge
content:
It’s hard to believe Nunavik is a hotbed of Quebec separatist sentiment, but there you have it.




The region’s newly elected member of the Quebec national assembly is Sonia Caron, of the separatist Parti Québécois that won a minority government in Monday’s provincial election.




Fortunately, the PQ’s failure to form a majority government means it will be much harder for the its leaders to deliver on their key promise to hold a referendum on Quebec’s future within Canada during its first term.




Just two days after the election, Caron was cagey about talking about a referendum.




“I can’t comment on that at this point,” she said in an 

interview

 with Nunatsiaq News on Wednesday.




Nunavik is better off in a united Canada, so it should come as a relief the PQ’s ability to hold a sovereignty referendum will be tempered.




On the campaign trail, party Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said a PQ government would hold a referendum on separating from Canada in its first term. But there’s one condition — the referendum would only be held after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office. Presumably, that would put any vote off until 2029, when Trump’s second term ends.
















Having lost two referendums — in 1980 and 1995 — many PQ supporters are reluctant to hold a third referendum if it looks like they will lose again. A lot of Parti Québécois supporters only want to hold a referendum if there are winning conditions.




It’s hard to imagine that the winning conditions will exist by 2029. Will Quebecers be more inclined to look for independence after four years of a trade war with the U.S.? Will national unity be galvanized because Canadians have stood together to respond to the Trump-imposed economic challenges?




The PQ’s election as a minority government (it won 59 of the national assembly’s 127 seats) likely dampens St-Pierre Plamondon’s ability to deliver on his pledge to hold a referendum. The federalist Liberal and Conservative parties won 40 and 19 seats, respectively, leaving the Québec solidaire’s with the balance of power.




National unity is facing another — more immediate — challenge in the form of a referendum taking place in Alberta on Oct. 19.




Albertans will go to the polls to answer a question about whether the provincial government should hold a binding referendum about whether the province should remain in Canada.




If there’s a silver lining in the election of a separatist party in Quebec, it could be that the Ungava riding’s representative will be sitting in the government benches.
















It’s similar to the idea that Nunavut MP Lori Idlout is better able to get the federal government’s attention on northern issues by sitting as a Liberal than she could while sitting in the House of Commons as a New Democrat.




Over the past eight years, Ungava’s MNA was Denis Lamothe, who was also a member of the Coalition Avenir Québec government. The Coalition party paid attention to the massive northern Quebec riding. Ministers like Ian Lafrenière, who held the Indigenous affairs and public security portfolios, visited the riding from time to time.




Northern Quebec was on the Coalition Avenir Québec’s radar.




Hopefully, that will continue as Caron takes over as the riding’s new representative in a new PQ government.

author: Dalia Abu Ramadan
title: A Shadow of Fear Hangs Over Gazans Amid Israeli Defense Minister’s Threats
content:
Israel Katz says Israel will forcibly displace 1 million Gazans if “even one Israeli soldier” is abducted.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

We are about to close out three years and enter another since Israel invaded Gaza, but we are not leaving the war behind to begin a new life. We are entering yet another year without knowing when this war will end — or whether it will end at all.

The fear remains. The destruction remains. The threats remain. It feels as though each passing year does not bring us closer to an end, but closer to the possibility of another war.

Despite everything we are living through in Gaza, we understand what it means to live one day at a time — to hold on to every simple moment we can still have. Imagine planning for another morning, perhaps for the simplest of things: going out with the friends you still have, or taking your family to the sea in the morning, amid all this destruction, simply to experience a moment that feels like life.

Then, as you are planning that ordinary morning, you hear a statement from Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, who said on September 22: “If even one Israeli soldier or civilian is abducted, the city of Gaza — with its homes and terrorist towers — will be evacuated southward of its one million residents.”

Words like these are enough not only to disrupt your day, but to shake your entire future. The first question we asked ourselves was: Where would we go? Is there anywhere left for us to go?

“Everyone is talking about how the possibility of an Israeli soldier being captured has become impossible, that it will not happen, and that it could be an excuse to provoke people in Gaza and pave the way for the war to return,” Haneen Salem, a photographer in Gaza City, told me. “I am certain something will happen. No one knows what, but there is a shadow of fear hanging over Gaza’s civilians.”

Even my father said, “Expect it to happen at any moment,” warning that we could be forcibly displaced yet again, especially because we are living through another difficult period in Gaza. The intensity of Israeli bombardment had increased in the weeks leading up to Katz’s statement, and warplanes had not stopped flying overhead at night.

Words like these are enough not only to disrupt your day, but to shake your entire future. The first question we asked ourselves was: Where would we go? Is there anywhere left for us to go?

We are being asked to imagine another war while we are still living inside the aftermath of the one that was supposed to have ended.

The so-called ceasefire took effect at noon local time on October 10, 2025. A year has passed since that announcement, but the war has not ended. It is true that the intensity of the escalation and displacement has eased compared to the height of Israel’s war, but the bombardment and destruction have continued. So, what does it mean to hear threats of the war returning with the same ferocity when we have not even begun to recover from what has already happened?

When the “ceasefire” was announced, I believed the war would end as the wars of 2021, 2014, and previous years had ended — with a clear conclusion, a moment when we would know that the war was truly over. I expected that, immediately after the announcement, we would begin clearing the rubble, rebuilding what had been destroyed and slowly putting our lives back together.

Instead, it felt as though the war continued in another form, behind the scenes — a reality visible only to the people of Gaza who have been living through its consequences every day. Today, we still have not recovered. Even the most basic medical necessities remain unavailable, the siege is tightening, and the consequences of the war continue to surround every part of our lives.

The collapse of the Al-Sadah building in Tal al-Hawa is one example of what this unfinished recovery looks like. The building had been home to approximately 80 displaced Palestinians. In the early hours of September 16, it collapsed, with parts of the structure also falling onto nearby buildings and tents that were sheltering other displaced families. Rescue teams initially estimated that around 100 people, including at least 50 children, were trapped beneath the rubble. After rescue operations ended, Civil Defense teams confirmed that 21 people had been killed, including 12 children and five women, while 45 injured people were taken to hospitals.

With rubble left uncleared and too little being done to address the dangers left behind by the destruction, many partially damaged buildings across Gaza have been left standing in a fragile state, at risk of collapsing at any moment.

The Al-Sadah building had sustained structural damage from Israeli bombardment during the war and was struck several times in 2024 and again in March 2025. Civil defense teams had warned residents not to return to the building. Yet some had no other choice but to live there. With tents and homes unavailable, displaced Palestinians have been forced to shelter in cracked and damaged buildings, despite the risk that they could collapse around them.

But the danger does not end when people are pulled from the rubble. Those who survive still face a health system struggling to meet even the most basic needs. As World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on September 24, “Essential medicines, diagnostics, equipment and fuel remain in critically short supply.”

These shortages are not limited to life-saving medicines and hospital equipment; they reach into the most ordinary forms of care, turning even a visit to the dentist into a struggle.

It may be one of the most basic forms of health care, but anyone who has experienced severe tooth pain knows how unbearable it can be — especially as poor nutrition and the effects of prolonged hunger have taken a toll on people’s dental health.

Fear has become part of the way we respond to every sound. We can even find ourselves startled by the sound of a chair moving.

“Getting dental supplies and materials into Gaza has become extremely difficult,” dentist Dr. Ghalib Zimmo told me. “And when they do enter, they are prohibitively expensive. The cost of dental materials has risen to 10 times what it was before the war.”

The consequences are painful. “Many patients come to us needing root canal treatment, which can involve unbearable pain,” Dr. Ghalib said. “But because of the cost, they choose to have the tooth extracted instead of treating it.”

“Before the war, a root canal cost around $40,” he explained. “Now, it can cost as much as $250.”

Imagine how deeply exhausted we have become. We search for medicine, and it is not there. We search for wheelchairs for those who have lost limbs in the war, and they are not there. We search for the simplest things that make life possible, and they are not there.

Fear has become part of the way we respond to every sound. Sometimes, when we hear a sudden noise, we immediately think it is the sound of a missile just before it strikes. We can even find ourselves startled by the sound of a chair moving.

We are living with a trauma that no one can truly feel the way we do. Three years of relentless bombardment have left their mark on us. We search for life itself, and we cannot find it.

The administration is pursuing numerous strategies to manipulate data, neutralize safeguards, and disenfranchise voters.

The upcoming midterm elections seem destined to serve as a bellwether for the state of democracy in this deeply fraught period of U.S. electoral history. The results will be interpreted as a referendum on the catastrophically unpopular second Trump administration and will determine much of the legislative landscape over the next two years. Substantial Democratic victories could significantly constrain Trump’s powers or even place his presidency in jeopardy, and the Election Day performance of crucial structures and procedures could attest to either a resilient democracy — insofar as the country’s very flawed but still-vital electoral institutions are worthy of the name — or, conversely, a system that has at last been compromised by years of right-wing attacks, leaving the integrity and legitimacy of future votes in serious question.

The Trump administration, keenly aware of the stakes, has gone to unprecedented lengths to exert undue influence on electoral procedures. Having mobilized the Department of Justice (DOJ), the FBI, and other arms of the federal government now radically subservient to Trump, the administration is pursuing numerous strategies, legal and extralegal, to bludgeon its way into sensitive databases, neutralize electoral safeguards, and disenfranchise legitimate voters, with the intent of negating the wishes of the U.S. public and illicitly enshrining their own power.

In reality, states are fully capable of maintaining their own rolls without the DOJ’s intervention (removing individuals who have died or moved out of state, for instance). And, more to the point, cases of “illegal voting” are extraordinary rarities, and have collectively had less-than-negligible — zero — impact on any real election results. Since the DOJ’s rationales are utterly fictitious, it’s not hard to imagine that there may be other motives underlying their aggressive nationwide efforts to access voter rolls, given that these initiatives originate from an administration led by and filled with election deniers.

Obtaining unredacted state rolls has not always been a simple matter, and the Trump Justice Department has in many cases resorted to strongarming, undermining, or otherwise attempting to manipulate state governments and other agencies to further its aims. Any plan to wrest election operations away from the states must inevitably find ways to circumvent the fundamental obstacle to federal control — Article 1, Section 4 of the Constitution, according to which elections are to be overseen solely by the states. Of course, questions of constitutionality have never burdened Trump’s conscience, and he has openly announced his desire to “nationalize” elections and place them under federal (i.e., his) jurisdiction. Were that to someday occur, unfettered voter roll access would be a boon for election manipulators.

Still — in court, at least — the Trump administration’s efforts to attain that level of nationwide control have been less than fruitful. The Trump DOJ has initiated numerous lawsuits that seek to force states to sign data-handover agreements: no fewer than 31 to date, with one of those filed against Washington, D.C., and the rest against states, most of them governed by Democrats. Of the remaining 20 states not sued, 16, all Republican-led, dutifully volunteered to submit their voters’ crucial personal data to Trump’s feds without a fight. Back in December 2025, the DOJ sent Republican governors a confidential deal to sign; it gave the federal government unprecedented roll access and also allowed the DOJ to share that highly sensitive personal data with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The text of those confidential agreements, Eileen O’Connor wrote in a Brennan Center report, “reveals both the DOJ’s plans to interfere with the states’ authority to run elections and how dangerously insecure the sensitive data will be in the department’s hands.”

The administration is pursuing numerous strategies, legal and extralegal, to bludgeon its way into sensitive databases, neutralize electoral safeguards, and disenfranchise legitimate voters.

O’Connor then cited an especially troubling case in which a “Department of Government Efficiency,” or DOGE, employee working at the Social Security Administration (SSA) at the time of the former agency’s ransacking of the latter was found to have signed an agreement to illicitly funnel voter data to an external entity. The incident came to light in the course of a union lawsuit against the SSA and its DOJ counsel, which were forced to admit in court that this employee was contacted by, and voluntarily contracted with, a “political advocacy group,” which goes unnamed in the filing, but which had the “stated aim … to find evidence of voter fraud and to overturn election results in certain States.”

Doing its part, the Trump DHS, a whistleblower report alleges, has ordered immigration officers to break various laws in pursuit of its “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” a hunt for — again, non-existent —“illegal” votes; the department directed subordinates to lie to gain data access and enforced unmeetable quotas, which effectively guaranteed high error rates, translating to high rates of erroneous/illicit disenfranchisement of legal voters.

The end goal seems to be, if possible, to subject all 50 states’ confidential voter data to the same fate. However, at least in some legal arenas, Trump’s DOJ has been decisively thwarted: nearly all of these lawsuits against the states plus D.C. — out of a total of 31 cases, 26 and counting — have already failed spectacularly in the legal system. The overwhelming extent of these defeats hints at the lawsuits’ farcical baselessness and unconstitutionality.

Chris Diaz is the director of legislative tracking at Voting Rights Lab, a non-partisan, non-profit voter advocacy group that provides expert analysis of the shifting dynamics within U.S. electoral systems and democratic institutions. “Judges have consistently found,” Diaz wrote in an email to Truthout, “that the Department of Justice’s demands for unredacted state voter rolls overstep constitutional bounds and violate state privacy laws.” Still, Diaz pointed out, this failure could be spun into further justifications for denying legitimate outcomes, as in all likelihood, “we can expect the administration to use its inability to get this information as a reason to challenge, or undermine, election results it doesn’t like in those states that have refused to give them the unredacted lists.”

Unlike the lower and lesser courts, the Supreme Court, highest in the land, purports to represent timeless principles that transcend petty partisanship; currently dominated by Republicans, it just happens to accede to the president’s wishes far more often than not. Recently, the Supreme Court overruled a lower court’s stay, ruling 6-3 (along partisan lines) to allow the administration’s use of a tool called the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system, clearing the way for both federal and state governments to use the system to identify “non-citizen voters.”

Initially built to review the citizenship status of state-benefits applicants, the SAVE system has been adapted (with dubious efficacy) to trawl voter data, in part by enabling it to compare voter information against Social Security databases. SAVE is notoriously unreliable, routinely returning errors, as Diaz told Truthout, especially false positives that misidentify real citizens as ineligible non-citizens. “This has caused problems in states that have relied on it for voter list maintenance purposes.” In September, he noted, “Nevada officials found that every individual on a list of 185 purported non-citizens provided by the federal government was in fact a citizen.”

Experts at CISA, in the last election, were able to debunk Trump’s lies about rigged voting machines at a critical juncture. Today, many of the overseers involved in that series of events have been fired.

Beyond the system’s usefulness in carrying out purges, experts also believe that the Trump administration is so intent on using SAVE because the software can dredge through data and generate results — whether they are accurate is a different question — to promote false claims of large-scale illegal voting. In addition, SAVE plays a role in the federal government’s plan to compile lists of vote-eligible citizens in each state, as Trump sought to do with his anti-democratic executive order in March of 2025. However, as Diaz told Truthout, the “primary risk here is last-minute attempts to push states to use [SAVE’s] unreliable federal data to pursue aggressive voter roll purges.”

There is, Diaz explained, an existing safeguard against late-game disenfranchisement, in that “federal law prohibits systematic list maintenance within 90 days of a federal election.” Nevertheless, “some states may be willing to push the limits of the law to pursue aggressive hunts for purported non-citizens,” he added — and given what we’ve seen from Trump’s election-denying state allies, it would not be surprising. Indeed, Republicans have set about attempting to undermine that prohibition: NPR reported that the Supreme Court, once again, has already “agreed to the Republican National Committee’s request to take up an Arizona-based case that could narrow the [90-day] quiet period’s scope.”

There is likewise a precedent for “quiet period” extension in the form of, per the same NPR article: “a brief, unexplained ruling the Supreme Court’s conservative majority made before the 2024 election, allowing a Virginia program for removing suspected noncitizens to continue during that year’s quiet period.” The latter decision ended up allowing Virginia to purge eligible citizens and deny them the vote.

The administration and its most powerful agencies have gone to great lengths to test out pressure tactics. In one unnerving gesture, polling locations in the midterms will be surveilled by an unprecedented number of federal “election observers” who will “ensure polling locations are complying with federal law,” as the DOJ told CNN. Observers are not new, but deploying a thousand of them is. Perhaps even more egregiously, in July of 2026, DHS took steps to condition the provision of counterterrorism funding upon states’ compliance with certain demands — what DHS called “common-sense election security measures.” The measures they were pressing to impose involved supplying voter roll data to the SAVE system. Unless states complied with its demands for data, DHS would freeze 20 percent of their funds. On September 28, a federal judge blocked that particular power play.

The repurposing of federal police to attack the president’s opponents may in some respects be the most concerning development of all.

Such tactics have increasingly approached the mafia-esque. In the course of ordering states to both share their voter rolls and to preserve older data from the 2024 election (presumably to scrape more data and challenge those results as well), the Trump Justice Department went so far as to level clear threats at state officials. The Associated Press (AP) obtained one of the DOJ’s demand letters, in which “a Justice Department official told Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican, that she is ‘under investigation’ and subject to ongoing litigation over the state’s failure to turn over statewide voter registration lists.” Similarly, as an article from the Campaign Legal Center relates, “The DOJ even sent a letter to Minnesota Governor Tim Walz at the start of 2026 with several demands, including access to the state’s unredacted voter rolls, and suggested that compliance with the demand was a condition of removing federal immigration law enforcement officers from the Minneapolis area.”

An especially chilling investigation by ProPublica documented the administration’s behind-the-scenes undermining or outright eradication of federal agencies and experts at the Foreign Malign Influence Center (FMIC), the FBI’s public corruption team, the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and others. Experts at CISA, in the last election, were able to debunk Trump’s lies about rigged voting machines at a critical juncture that halted the false narrative. Today, many of the overseers involved in that series of events have been fired, and experts and officials throughout the system are being replaced with toadies.

Across several federal agencies, ProPublica’s investigation identified 75 fired experts who have been replaced with “roughly two dozen people” now installed in high-level oversight positions “that could affect elections. Ten of them actively worked to reverse the 2020 vote, and the rest are associates of such people. In some cases, ProPublica found, officials have been hired from activist groups that are pillars of the election denial movement.” Relatedly, Voting Rights Lab has tracked and reported on numerous worrisome instances of infiltration and abuse of power in state entities like election boards, including the many state-level election-denying officials who have refused to certify results. Trump also forced out the administrators of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission.

The downfall of the democratic vote is not yet a foregone conclusion. We can be certain, however, that the current administration will do everything in its power to put its thumb on the scales.

The repurposing of federal police to attack the president’s opponents may in some respects be the most concerning development of all. In an appalling decision (reminiscent of the Bureau’s longstanding propensity for political meddling, from the Palmer Raids to COINTELPRO), FBI director, Trump devotee, and children’s book author Kash Patel requisitioned 100 federal agents in June of 2026 to raid the offices of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a pro-democracy social justice non-profit and the leading voter-registration organization in the swing state. In February of the same year, the FBI had raided Georgia state election offices and actually seized official election records, citing a pretense of “investigating” purported voter fraud in 2020 — Trump’s pet grievance.

The salience of the illegal-voting narrative among Trump’s base (an overwhelming 86 percent of Republicans polled in 2024 believed, against all evidence, that non-eligible voter participation was a concern) shows no sign of abating, and those kinds of narratives, according to Diaz, “could build momentum for enacting more restrictive laws.” Diaz told Truthout:

False and misleading claims about ineligible voters lay the groundwork to undermine public trust and manufacture pretexts to contest election outcomes as demonstrated by the months-long legal battle following the 2024 North Carolina Supreme Court race, where the losing candidate challenged thousands of ballots after the election, [and] bad-faith actors could leverage flawed data to launch targeted voter challenges and try to manipulate results in close races.

The Trump administration’s efforts to overturn democratic elections make for frightening times, especially as they arrive amid all the other crises and abuses of power that have characterized the nascent fascism that increasingly shadows the United States. Even short of Trump’s extremist dreams of total federalization, there remain weaknesses in U.S. electoral institutions that are cause for severe concern — from the now-compromised election oversight agencies to the deniers among state election officials to the weaponized transformation of the DOJ from a civil rights and voting rights adjudicator (however flawed) into a rabidly Trumpist attack dog. But despite the looming threats, there is still every reason to believe that the downfall of the democratic vote is not yet a foregone conclusion. We can be certain, however, that the current administration will do everything in its power to put its thumb on the scales.

Truthout is funded almost entirely by readers — that’s why we can speak truth to power and cut against the mainstream narrative. But independent journalists at Truthout face mounting political repression under Trump.

title: Sustam: Those who sow insecurity reap revolt in France - Part One
content:
Student protests that began in high schools in France over educational conditions, staff shortages and deepening inequalities have spread to universities. The protests, which are continuing in many cities, particularly Paris and its suburbs, have brought into view not only discontent with the education system but also young people’s anger over a lack of prospects, poverty and social inequality.




Police interventions and far-right rhetoric criminalizing students have also reignited debates in France over security policies, racism and hostility towards migrants.




ANF spoke to Associate Professor Engin Sustam, a sociologist at Paris 8 University, about the causes of the student protests in France, their connection to the tradition of struggle stretching from 1968 to the present, and their potential to develop into a broader social opposition movement.




How do you assess the student protests that have spread from high schools to universities across France in recent weeks? What are the main social and political dynamics behind this movement?




For several months now, students across France, particularly high school students, have significantly expanded their protests and taken part in blockades, especially in Paris and its major suburbs, as well as in Bordeaux, Lyon and many other areas. High school students have even confronted the police much more forcefully, perhaps more forcefully than ever before in France’s history. According to today’s reports, the government has detained around 5,000 people.




You know the Seine-Saint-Denis area in particular. This is already a pilot area. Especially since La France Insoumise (LFI) won the municipality, policies have emerged that have turned the area into a place where, from the perspective of the police, the government or the security system, many things can be treated as terrorism or suppressed. But this, of course, affects the entire student movement.




Why did the students, particularly high school students, begin protesting? The movement started in Creil, outside Paris. Students said their needs had to be met and staff shortages addressed. There is a shortage of teachers for classes, while educational resources in classrooms are also inadequate. They have also raised many other issues, including lowering cafeteria prices and renovating school buildings.




‘The education system has become a tool of discrimination’




As the protests began to spread, however, they also reached the universities. University students then began raising issues such as Parcoursup, which, as you know, is a very important issue in France, as well as the Mon Master programme. There is a competitive system here. This is an issue that has emerged through the liberal policies that have increasingly taken hold in France, particularly under the Macron government.




Students are ranked according to their grades, placed on waiting lists and, after receiving a yes or no, can ultimately be rejected from those lists. This is more or less how Parcoursup creates discrimination. The education system has become a tool of discrimination.




The French National Student Assemblies also raised this issue during a Senate session in 2026, pointing to Parcoursup and similar systems. If you do not obtain the bac (baccalauréat) in high school, you cannot enter university in France. All of these mechanisms create discrimination in one way or another, and because students encounter this discrimination from high school onwards, I think they have now reached a breaking point.




The issue has also begun to go beyond students’ everyday needs. At universities, student meals are provided through student restaurants known as CROUS, but high school students do not have the same system.




There has also been a serious increase in sexual violence, gender-based violence and violence within high schools. There is also a very significant divide between central high schools, particularly those in central Paris and schools attended by students from more privileged classes, and high schools in the suburbs.




The protests have brought issues such as inadequate resources and staffing in education, student poverty, inequality and insecurity about the future to the fore. Do you think young people in France today are primarily protesting against the education system, or against the broader economic and political order?




At first, the students were focused entirely on the education system and, at the local level, even solely on shortcomings in their own high schools. But as you know, high school and university student movements can change over time by connecting with different sectors and develop into a social movement.




Of course, it is still too early to say that this has happened. But as of today, trade unions, university unions, university students, educators and academics have issued declarations saying that they will take to the streets and stand in solidarity with high school students. We are part of this as well. For example, I had a class at Paris 8 University yesterday. When I arrived, there was a blockade, and I joined it with the students. We did not hold the class; instead, we took part in the blockade. There was a banner there that, in my view, summed up the whole situation very well: ‘Those who sow insecurity reap revolt.’




That phrase actually sums up the situation high school students find themselves in. We are facing a generation of young people who have been deprived of a future. We are talking in particular about a generation that has completely lost its sense of belonging to the education system.




Deteriorating living and educational conditions, social inequalities, racism, violence, the rise of the far right and inadequate resources in education are all interconnected issues.




‘Those who sow insecurity reap revolt’




There is also a process of militarization that began with the war in Ukraine and has intensified particularly over the past two years. Amid the militarization of Europe and France, Iran, Ukraine, Russia and a culture of conflict, the country’s internal dynamics have been forgotten. By internal dynamics, I mean social inequalities, social assistance and schools in the suburbs being left to fend for themselves. All of this is leading high school students to position themselves along a new political line.




There is also an issue that Pierre Bourdieu emphasized: inequality in cultural capital. This divide, which already existed in France, has become much more starkly visible over roughly the past twelve years. People cannot find jobs after graduating. Depending on the high schools they graduate from and their rankings within the Parcoursup system, students can be directed not to the university or department they want, but to the places they supposedly ‘deserve’ based on their grades.




This creates serious social demoralization, particularly about the future. People feel abandoned. Schools have been left neglected, there is police violence, there is a lack of prospects for the future, and there is no strong political mobilization against any of this. All of these factors therefore directly affect high school students.

title: Mother tongue, identity and collective memory
content:
The mother tongue is more than the first language through which a person begins to discover the world. It is a bridge through which identity takes shape, a sense of belonging is established and collective memory is passed down through generations. From the language in which a child begins their education to the language in which a person can express themselves when receiving healthcare, the mother tongue encompasses far more than a purely cultural debate. Restricting the use of a language, excluding it from education or denying it a place in public life undoubtedly affects an individual's relationship with themselves and society.




People first learn to make sense of the world through the relationships around them. Alongside family and social relationships, language becomes part of this initial process of understanding. Sometimes, the first word a person learns is more than a means of communication; it becomes part of their connection to their family, their past and the community to which they belong.




Psychologist Siyabend Aslan defines the mother tongue as “the first home into which a person is born when they open their eyes to the world.” Aslan spoke to ANF about the place of language in human life, saying, “Rather than simply being an ordinary tool for communicating with the outside world, it lies at the very heart of our identity, our past and our sense of belonging.”




Identity and collective memory




The mother tongue is one of the foundations on which identity is formed. Much of a person's connection to family, society, culture and the past is carried through language. Restricting the use of a language can therefore also affect a person's relationship with the community to which they feel they belong.




Aslan explained the impact of restricting a community's use of its mother tongue on individual and collective psychological well-being: “Restricting a community's use of its own mother tongue is tantamount to telling its members directly, ‘You, your ancestors and your feelings are worthless.’”




Aslan described the psychological impact of this as “linguistic trauma,” adding: “It is a profound wound that causes people to feel ashamed of their own roots and to experience a deep sense of worthlessness.”




Alienation from one's roots




Researcher and linguist Zana Farqînî placed the issue within a broader social context. Farqînî said, “Assimilation is not merely about banning a language or excluding it from everyday life, education and the public sphere,” and explaining that distancing different communities from their own roots is also part of this process.




Farqînî drew attention to the relationship between language and identity, saying, “Assimilated individuals tend to assimilate into the dominant identity imposed through the dominant language and, over time, begin to feel that they belong to that identity.”




Collective memory, in turn, gives identity its social dimension. Farqînî explained this relationship: “Language is not merely a means of communication. It is the creator, carrier and transmitter of a culture. It is the raw material of all verbal arts and forms of expression. It is the memory of society.”




In short, the weakening of a language affects both the possibilities for communication today and the ways in which the past is passed on.




Passing memory down through generations




The continuity of collective memory depends on the transmission of language between generations. A language known by older family members but difficult for children to understand or speak can gradually disappear from everyday family life. As children become a generation that hears the language but does not use it, passing it on to the next generation becomes even more difficult.




This situation is also clearly evident in the case of Kurdish. Farqînî said, “Today, Kurdish is being lost between generations. The proportion of children and young people who speak Kurdish is quite low, and this proportion is declining with each passing day.”




Farqînî said language use also varies according to age and education level: “Kurdish is spoken more frequently among older and middle-aged Kurds and those with lower levels of education. As education levels rise and age decreases, we see the opposite trend.”




The ability to pass a language on to the next generation is just as important as knowing it. Farqînî said, “A language that is not passed on to children has no future and is condemned to die,” and stressing the importance of using the language within the family: “Kurdish parents should at least use their own language within their families and homes.”




The divide that begins at the school gate




The most visible aspect of the mother tongue debate is education. For a child, school is the most important social environment after the family. The language used there affects not only whether the child understands the lessons, but also whether the world they know is recognised within the educational environment.




A child who grows up speaking one language at home but begins their education in a completely different language may face an additional burden in the learning process. The child must simultaneously try to understand the language of instruction and learn the information being taught.




UNICEF's assessments of multilingual education also emphasise the importance of children building a strong foundation for learning through a language they already know.




Aslan described this process from the perspective of a child's psychological world: “The first day of school is critically important in a child's life. It is their first major encounter with the world after leaving the safety of home.”




He explained the linguistic divide between home and school: “Imagine a child whose mother and father have spoken to them in their mother tongue at home and introduced them to the world through those words. But when the child enters the classroom, they encounter an unfamiliar language. In a child's world, this is nothing short of a shock.”




Aslan said that while trying to learn the language of instruction, children also spend some of the mental energy they would otherwise devote to academic content on understanding the language itself. Aslan also said, “Instead of experiencing the joy of learning new things and playing games, the child spends all their mental energy trying to understand that unfamiliar language.” He stressing that fear of making mistakes and being ridiculed can also cause children to withdraw into silence.




The fundamental issue, therefore, is the place given to a child's first language within the educational process.




Education and the sense of belonging




When the language a child learns at home is also recognised at school, the distance between the family and the educational institution is reduced. Recognition of the child's language in the educational environment also increases the public visibility of that language and the community that speaks it.




Farqînî stressed that using a language only at home and within one's immediate social circle is no longer sufficient under today's conditions. He said, “In this digital age, when formal education in the dominant language has spread to even the most remote areas, it is impossible for a language to survive solely as a spoken language.”




Farqînî also expressed his views on the position of Kurdish in education and public life: “Kurdish must have official status, gain official recognition and be used in education, teaching, the public sphere and, in short, every area of life. This is essential for a language to survive.”




This assessment of Kurdish also raises a broader question: How long can a language survive if it is spoken only at home? The more a language is used in education and public life, the more it encounters new concepts, develops and finds a place in the lives of future generations.




The importance of language in mental health




The influence of the mother tongue is not limited to education. People also need language to describe their most difficult experiences. Fear, trauma, grief and anger are all experiences whose meanings in a person's mind and emotional world are closely connected to language.




Psychologist Siyabend Aslan said there is a significant difference between expressing traumatic experiences in another language and expressing them in one's mother tongue. Aslan said, “Our emotions are imprinted without any filter on the language through which we first came to know the world, our mother tongue.”




Aslan said that a second language can sometimes create distance between a person and the pain they have experienced. “Severe abuse, grief or trauma experienced in the past can be described in a second language using detached, mechanical words, as though the suffering had been experienced by someone entirely different.”




For this reason, Aslan stressed the importance of people being able to express themselves in their mother tongue during psychotherapy. He said, “If we want to achieve lasting healing through psychotherapy, if we truly want to clean and heal that wound, we have to reach the person's emotional core.”




Aslan made his position clear: “This is precisely why mental health services in one's mother tongue are not a luxury or a privilege. They are an indisputable and fundamental human right.”




Being understood in public services




The importance of the mother tongue in everyday life becomes even more apparent in public services. When a person needs to explain their symptoms at a hospital, make a request at school, describe an experience at a judicial institution or communicate their needs to any public institution, language once again becomes a fundamental issue. Here, the mother tongue is no longer simply a marker of identity but a direct necessity of everyday life.




Aslan particularly emphasised this point in relation to mental health: “No one should be forced to heal the intimate wounds of their soul through interpreters, using borrowed words.”




The mother tongue as a collective right




Speaking a language at home, producing literary and artistic works, publishing and conducting academic research are important for keeping it alive. However, the ability to use a language in education and public life depends on broader social conditions.




Zana Farqînî therefore viewed language rights as something that goes beyond individual choice: “A language cannot fully overcome its current situation through individual efforts and personal struggle alone. Language is a cultural and collective right.”




Farqînî also stressed the importance of individual efforts: “Of course, individual efforts and initiatives are not insignificant. Their work, contributions and struggles pave the way, generating both energy and synergy.”




His main emphasis, however, was on collective action: “What matters most is that this issue becomes a social concern and that the struggle is carried forward through the organised strength of society.”




This approach takes the mother tongue issue beyond the question of which language an individual chooses to speak. The ability to use a language in education, culture, science and public life requires not only individual choice but also social and institutional conditions.




The language of future generations




All these issues ultimately converge on the same point: children. A language that is not spoken at home, taught at school, recognised in public life or used in academic work gradually occupies a smaller place in children's lives.




As Farqînî put it, “Just as children are the future of a people, children are also the future of a language.” Intergenerational transmission is therefore not the final element of the mother tongue debate, but the fundamental factor connecting all its dimensions.




Children acquire a language at home, develop it at school, use it with friends, encounter it in books and enrich it with new concepts in the digital world. When they can also use that language to access public services, it becomes a natural part of everyday life. If any link in this chain is broken, the space in which the language is used becomes narrower.




Where does a language live?




Ultimately, the mother tongue issue cannot be reduced to the question, “Which language do we speak?” The more fundamental questions are broader: Which language can we live in? Which language do we receive our education in? Which language can we express ourselves in? Which language can we access public services in? Which language can we pass on to our children?




These questions are interconnected. Language is tied to identity, and identity is connected to collective memory. Memory is passed down from generation to generation. Education can either strengthen or weaken this transmission. In mental health, language becomes one of the means through which individuals can access their own experiences. In public services, it becomes one of the fundamental conditions for being understood.

title: PYD calls for unity and restraint amid tensions in Hesekê
content:
The Democratic Union Party (PYD) issued a written statement about the provocations in Hesekê. The statement noted that Syria is going through a sensitive transitional period and called on all political and social forces to engage in dialogue, show solidarity and work to build trust.




The PYD stressed that the rise in hate speech and provocations in the region threatens internal peace, emphasising the need to clarify the circumstances surrounding the incidents and hold those responsible to account.




Syria needs a democratic and pluralistic system




The statement noted that Syria is passing through a sensitive and important transitional period. It said that all political and social forces must fulfil their national and historical responsibilities, strengthen dialogue among all of Syria’s communities and work to build trust.




The statement also stressed that steps had recently been taken to make progress on implementing the 29 January Agreement. It said these steps would contribute to strengthening stability, unifying efforts and building a democratic Syria.




‘Hate speech and provocations threaten internal peace’




The statement drew attention to recent security incidents and tensions in the region. It said the developments began with the death of a member of the Foca officers’ unit in Qamişlo, followed by an attack on a vehicle belonging to the security forces, the killing of Sîpan Hiznî, and incidents in Kobanê and other areas.




The statement said that hate speech and provocations on digital platforms had increased alongside these developments. It noted that this situation threatens internal peace, fuels tensions and creates conditions for divisions within society.




The PYD said it was following developments with concern and stressed the need to approach the incidents responsibly and calmly, avoiding hasty reactions.




‘The constitutional rights of Kurds must not be defended’




The statement said that escalating tension between Syria’s communities not only threatens internal peace and the social fabric, but could also be exploited to return Syria to a centralised, uniform system.




It stated that such efforts could be aimed at obstructing the constitutional rights and legal protections of the Kurdish people, preventing all communities, particularly Kurds, from participating meaningfully in building the new Syria, and undermining the gains made under the stated objective of establishing state authority and legitimacy.




The statement emphasised that any attempt to impose exclusion and domination would result in losses for all Syrians. It added that such efforts would also undermine the stability and coexistence that are intended to be established.




Call to identify and hold those responsible to account




The PYD called on the public not to be influenced by hate speech. The statement urged all administrative and security institutions within the Hesekê Governorate, as well as the relevant parties, to fulfil their responsibilities.




It said action must be taken to uncover the truth about the incidents and hold those responsible to account. It also called for measures to protect the public and maintain security and stability.




The PYD further called on political, social and media circles to help defuse the situation, reject provocations and put the public interest first.




‘Preserving coexistence is a shared responsibility’




The statement stressed that preserving internal peace and coexistence among the region’s communities is a shared responsibility. It said that common sense, solidarity and dialogue are essential to achieving this.




It concluded by stating that efforts must be made to build a democratic and pluralistic Syria that respects the rights of all its citizens and guarantees their meaningful participation, enabling them to live with dignity and equality.

title: Memorial in Argentina for Martyr Lêgerîn Çiya
content:
A meeting was held on Friday at 

Espacio de Alina

, in the mountains near Córdoba in Argentina. The space was established to keep the memory of Martyr Lêgerîn Çiya (Alina Sánchez) alive and strengthen solidarity among women.




The meeting was attended by feminist groups, indigenous women and comrades from the Kurdish women’s movement. Participants discussed political developments in Abya Yala and the dangers posed by the spread of fascism.







 








Through her struggle and resistance, Martyr Legerin Ciya succeeded in building bridges between Abya Yala, where she grew up, and the Kurdish movement she chose to join, said participants, adding that "she serves as an example and a guide not only within the Kurdish liberation movement but also within many feminist movements in Latin America, particularly in Argentina. The Alina Space, built in the mountains near the city of Córdoba in her memory, aims to become one of the physical places where this connection is forged. Various feminist and women’s collectives participated in the construction—including the physical building—of this space, using natural and traditional materials and methods."




Participants developed a shared analysis of the situation in Abya Yala and the dangers posed by the spread of fascism, and they shared methods of struggle. Together, they participated in rituals that combined the ancestral spirituality of the indigenous peoples represented by the women present with a struggle for survival in the face of the extractivist and capitalist system.




Patrizia, Legerin Ciya’s mother, also attended the event.




Claudia Corol, a feminist activist, popular educator, and journalist, remembered Legerin Ciya with these words: “We want to honor our comrade and sister Alina Sanchez, to whom this space is dedicated. Born in southern Argentina, in Patagonia, she came here, near Córdoba, with her mother Patricia, and as a child she used to run and play in these places.




She then decided to study medicine in Cuba and learned about the struggle in Kurdistan. She was a determined person who did what she loved and desired. She also helped us in the field of popular education to understand what health truly means."




Corol continued: "In Kurdistan, she was helping to establish a healthcare system amid a war with many wounded. We discussed about this by comparing various systems, to understand how to build a healthcare system in Abya Yala, given the military attacks we are currently experiencing. When she returned to Kurdistan, she fell as a martyr: on the one hand, our hearts were broken; on the other, we told ourselves, 'We must continue her struggle.'




In this context, her mother, Patricia, during a meeting of the network of popular educators, proposed that we build this space for popular education and community health right here, in the backyard of the house where she lives. We didn’t know how to do it, yet here we are, doing it. For us, it’s a commitment to remember her at all times, along with the work we’re carrying out in this space—work that has never stopped."





Corol explained that "the goal is for this to become a space for political, feminist, and health education—a place where we can take care of our sisters and comrades and carry on the struggle. Several comrades from the Kurdistan women’s movement have come here, leaving their mark as we built these walls together. We want to make the women’s revolution—which is so important to us—present here as well. I’d like to conclude by sharing an anecdote.




When Alina went to the mountains of Kurdistan, the first thing she said was, 'I have to offer you some criticism!' 'What criticism?' the comrades asked. 'The criticism is,' Alina replied, 'that you, as a revolutionary women’s movement, know very little about the revolutionary women of Abya Yala. But I also have to offer some self-criticism,' she continued, 'and that is that we, as women of Abya Yala, know very little about the women’s movement in Kurdistan and the struggle it is waging. That is why we are here today building bridges, as best we can; and that is why Alina is the pillar of these bridges,' she said."

title: Lawyer Çimen: Public power used to cover up Gülistan Doku case
content:
New developments have emerged in recent months in the investigation into the disappearance of Munzur University student Gülistan Doku, who went missing in Dersim on 5 January 2020. Numerous suspects have been detained or arrested as part of the investigation, while new digital records, witness statements and evidence have been added to the case file.




The number of people arrested in the investigation reached 38 in September, but questions surrounding Gülistan Doku's disappearance remain unanswered, and her family's pursuit of justice continues.




Ali Çimen, one of the lawyers representing Gülistan Doku's family, spoke to ANF about the latest developments in the investigation.




‘The case was systematically covered up’




Lawyer Ali Çimen said six waves of operations had been carried out in the Gülistan Doku case, with legal action taken against approximately 78 people and 38 arrested.




Çimen said the investigation had been ongoing for nearly seven years and that organised efforts had been made to cover up the case from the outset. He explained that they had faced serious difficulties in obtaining certain evidence, particularly because digital data had been deleted over time.




Çimen described the problems surrounding digital evidence and said: “Six waves of operations have been carried out in the Gülistan Doku case. So far, legal action has been taken against nearly 78 people, and 38 people have been arrested. Of course, since this is an investigation that has been ongoing for seven years, and one that has been systematically covered up, we face difficulties in obtaining certain evidence, particularly because data has been deleted.




For example, footage from the City Security Management System (KGYS) is deleted after three months, while records from the Licence Plate Recognition System (PTS) are deleted after two years. Requests have therefore been sent to the central servers to determine whether these records can be recovered. These are the kinds of difficulties we face. The most significant missing element in our case is that we have still not found Gülistan. However, I believe that the Erzurum and Tunceli Chief Public Prosecutors' Offices will eventually return Gülistan to her family as a result of the investigation.”




‘They tried to cover it up, but the truth came to light’




Çimen stressed that the investigation should not be limited to the existing suspects and said: “The case must be investigated from different angles. We expect another operation involving the seizure of assets. We also expect the investigation to be expanded. As you know, the provincial police chief was suspended from duty, although he appeared to be outside the scope of the investigation. We expect investigative proceedings concerning him to continue and expand.




Even after all the years that have passed since Gülistan disappeared, her family has not even been granted the right to mourn.




I believe Gülistan's body will be found. The Erzurum and Tunceli governor's offices will return her body to her family. They failed to protect Gülistan, failed to protect her life, and now they are not even returning her body. Her family is being denied the right to mourn. An organised cover-up was carried out for six years.”




‘Tuncay Sonel’s phone is like a crime machine’




Ali Çimen said an organised cover-up had been carried out in the Gülistan Doku case for six years, with public authority used as an instrument in the process.




Çimen concluded: “The phone of Tuncay Sonel, who was the governor of Tunceli at the time, must be examined as part of the investigation. Tuncay Sonel's phone is like a crime machine. More information will emerge. I do not believe these matters constitute state secrets. Details relating to the crimes must be shared with the public. There are very serious allegations. The necessary investigation must be carried out. The investigation into Tuncay Sonel must also examine the assets involved. Those assets should be handed over to the public.”

title: Internationalist youth delegation applies to meet Öcalan
content:
Members of the Diplomacy Commission of the Youth Assembly of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), together with an internationalist youth delegation from eight countries, submitted an application to the Ministry of Justice to meet with Abdullah Öcalan. The delegation made a statement at DEM Party headquarters following the application, expressing support for the Peace and Democratic Society Process and stressing the importance of Öcalan's freedom.




The delegation included representatives of Contre-Attaque & Autonomie from Switzerland, Sindacato Unione Democrazia Dignità Cobas from Italy, the Prosfygika Squatted Houses Community on Alexandras Avenue from Greece, La Saó from Catalonia, Mala Zêrîn from Austria, Jeunesse Internationaliste Française from France, Cumann Saol Saor from Ireland, and the Democratic Youth Union (YUNA) from Germany.




The statement was read in English by YUNA member Isabelle Marie Whittenberg and in Turkish by DEM Party Youth Assembly member Jiyan Bahadır.




‘The Peace and Democratic Society Process is a historic opportunity’




Isabelle Marie Whittenberg said the delegation had come from European countries to support the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She said Abdullah Öcalan had been targeted by an international conspiracy 27 years ago and had been held on Imrali Island ever since.




Whittenberg said the peace and democracy process was launched in February 2025 following a proposal by Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement. She stressed that the process represented an important opportunity not only for the Kurdish and Turkish peoples but also for all peoples around the world who seek to live in peace, autonomy and with the right to self-determination.




‘Our struggle is shared’




Isabelle Marie Whittenberg drew attention to the importance of international solidarity in the development of societies and social movements, stressing the need to unite struggles in different countries around common goals.




Whittenberg said local struggles shared feminist, anti-capitalist, anti-imperialist, anti-fascist and anti-racist foundations, adding that internationalists had a responsibility to connect these struggles and unite them on a confederal basis. She said the struggle to live in peace and dignity was a common struggle for all humanity.




‘Women’s freedom and solidarity will lead the way’




Isabelle Marie Whittenberg said a free society is founded on democratic values such as communal life, equality, ecology and solidarity, stressing that these values can only be put into practice through organised struggle based on women’s freedom and democracy.




Whittenberg said state and capital domination sought to suppress peoples’ efforts to organise themselves and govern their own affairs. She added that international women’s solidarity would play a leading role in building peace and a democratic communal society.




‘Resolving the Kurdish question will pave the way for the democratisation of the Middle East’




Isabelle Marie Whittenberg drew attention to the historical responsibility of European states for the partition of Kurdistan and the denial of the Kurdish people, saying that internationalists from Europe regarded solidarity with the Kurdish and Turkish peoples as their responsibility.




Whittenberg said a political solution to the Kurdish question that includes the freedom of the Kurdish people would pave the way for the democratisation of the Middle East and, subsequently, the world. She expressed solidarity with the Kurdish Freedom Movement.




‘We demand Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom’




Isabelle Marie Whittenberg called for Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom to ensure the continuation of the peace process, drawing attention to his political position within Kurdish society and its collective consciousness.




Whittenberg said Öcalan had developed theoretical and practical approaches to a political solution to the Kurdish question in recent years, despite harsh prison conditions. She stressed that his freedom was necessary for the continued progress and lasting success of the peace process.




Whittenberg said, “It is impossible to imprison hope, but it is possible to open the cell doors that restrict the creativity and goodwill needed for society to learn to live in peace.”




Call for Abdullah Öcalan’s release




Isabelle Marie Whittenberg explained the reasons behind the delegation’s application to visit Imrali Prison and called on the Turkish state to respect the Peace and Democratic Society Process and take steps consistent with its objectives.




Whittenberg said a political solution to the Kurdish question was important for ending the conflicts that the peoples of the region had endured for so long and ushering in a new era in the Middle East.




She called for Abdullah Öcalan’s release and for him to be allowed to establish diplomatic relations with domestic and international actors.

title: Xerîb Hiso: Attempts are being made to provoke conflict between Kurds and Arabs in Hesekê
content:
As steps are being taken to implement the agreement signed on January 29 between the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria and the Syrian Interim Government, security incidents and provocations continue in the region. The incidents began with the killing of a member of the Internal Security Forces in Qamishlo and continued with an attack on a vehicle of security forces, the killing of Sîpan Hiznî, and developments in various areas, particularly Kobanê.




Most recently, groups gathered in the Xiwêran neighborhood of Hesekê and marched toward Kurdish neighborhoods and engaged in provocations. One member of the Internal Security Forces and three civilians were injured in the ensuing incidents.




PYD co-chair Xerîb Hiso spoke to ANF about the provocation in Hesekê.




'The racist mentality that denies the Kurds is active on the ground'




Recalling the January 29 Agreement signed between the Autonomous Administration and the Syrian Interim Government, which came to power in Damascus following the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, Hiso said: “Significant progress is being made on the integration of the security, defense and autonomous administration institutions. Although there are obstacles, these provocations can be overcome when the focus is on dialogue, a common solution and genuine partnership. However, these provocations are spreading with each passing day. This racist mentality that previously denied the Kurds is now active on the ground. They want to attack, and they do not want integration to move forward. They do not want dialogue. They constantly seek to target us through conspiracies and provocations and to undermine the January 29 Agreement and the integration process.”




‘They want to provoke a war between Kurds and Arabs’




Hiso stated that certain groups were organizing these provocations through digital media and encouraging groups from other areas to gather in Hesekê, saying: “They want to provoke major unrest in Hesekê. They want to drag the Kurds into a conflict and provoke a war between Kurds and Arabs. They are trying to undermine relations between Kurds and Arabs. They want to destroy the will to coexist. But Kurds and Arabs are stronger than these provocations.”




‘Provocations pose a risk of conflict’




Stating that the provocations are spreading across an increasingly wider area, Hiso said that similar attempts have taken place in different neighborhoods of Hesekê. Pointing out that attacks on Kurdish symbols and rhetoric of revenge were heightening the danger, Hiso warned that the incidents could escalate into conflict.




The PYD co-chair noted that the Interim Government had yet to issue a statement and criticized those who described the actions as “peaceful demonstrations.” He said: “Those who view these as peaceful actions are actually destroying peace. If the government has a genuine position on this, it must hold those responsible accountable. Those who support these provocations are also complicit in the crime.”




‘ISIS could exploit the situation’




Hiso stated that the communities in the Cizîr region had taken a strong stance against the provocations and recalled that one member of the Internal Security Forces and three civilians were injured in the incidents. Noting that the Interior Ministry had yet to issue a statement, Hiso warned: “Racist and religious extremist incidents must be prevented. The US withdrawal has also reopened the way for ISIS. ISIS is present here as well, and it will exploit this as an opportunity.”




‘The Kurdish people do not want war’




Hiso stated that the situation in Hesekê had calmed down and that the population was remaining vigilant in order to defend the city. He stressed that the Kurds have the right to legitimate self-defense but do not want to be drawn into a war.




The PYD co-chair pointed out that the groups behind the provocations had been brought in from Shaddadi, Deir ez-Zor and Til Berak, and said that the Syrian national flag was being used as a pretext. Stating that the real objective was to deny the Kurds’ language, identity, symbols and will, he said: “The Kurdish people want peace, dialogue, coexistence and domestic peace. But others are trying to provoke conflict and discord.”




Finally, Hiso called on Kurds in Hesekê, across Rojava and in other regions to remain vigilant and not fall for the provocations of racist groups. Stating that the Kurdish people have the right to defend their existence, language, geography and rights, Hiso emphasized the need to preserve coexistence with different communities and maintain a peaceful stance.

title: Jineolojî to determine roadmap for the new period
content:
The European Jineolojî Conference will be held in the Netherlands from October 16 to 18 under the slogan “Building a Communal and Free Life with Jineolojî.” Organized by members of the Jineolojî Academy and the European Jineolojî Committee, the conference will take place under the main theme “The Role of Jineolojî in Building a Democratic and Communal Life.”




The conference will assess the experience accumulated through more than a decade of Jineolojî work in Europe in the fields of women’s liberation struggle, alternative knowledge production, collective living practices, democratic education and communal solidarity. It also aims to further develop the role of Jineolojî in social construction and determine a roadmap for the period ahead.




The organizers said that the goal is to develop a shared perspective on the future of Jineolojî, which has generated significant knowledge and opened up new avenues in Europe and around the world over the past decade.




Jineolojî’s role in social construction to be discussed




As part of the conference, the ten years of experience accumulated through Jineolojî work in Europe will be assessed from historical, sociological and organizational perspectives. The role of Jineolojî in social construction and the organizational model for the new period will be discussed within the framework of a democratic and communal society.




Developing a shared approach to how the perspective of democratic modernity centered on women’s freedom can become embedded in society under European conditions is also among the conference’s objectives. In this context, methods for developing concrete expressions of Jineolojî in everyday life, education, culture, art and organizing will be addressed.




Alongside efforts to free knowledge from colonial influences and to develop and enrich alternative methods of knowledge production, the conference will also explore opportunities for dialogue and collaboration with different women’s struggles, feminist experiences and democratic social movements in Europe.




Three main sessions and workshops over three days




Aimed at discussing strategic objectives and adopting joint decisions, the conference program will be structured around three main sessions and seven workshops. Following the opening speech and the reading of messages, the first day of the conference will feature a session titled “Jineolojî: The Science of Building Women’s Identity on the Basis of Freedom.” The session will address ten years of experience in Europe, the achievements made and perspectives for the new period.




In the afternoon, seven separate workshops will be held to discuss questions concerning the socialization and organization of Jineolojî and its role as a foundational force in building a democratic and communal society.




The workshop topics are as follows:




- Jineolojî’s organizational model in Europe




- The pedagogy of Jineolojî




- Family, social transformation and the transformation of men




- Women’s memory and cultural resistance




- Young women and Jineolojî




- Ecologically based social life and Jineolojî




- The importance and organization of media and publishing work




Liberation of knowledge to be addressed




On the second day of the conference, two main sessions will be held under the titles “Building a Communal Democratic Society” and “Socializing Knowledge and Freeing Science from Colonial Influences.”




The second session will discuss the role of Jineolojî in the transition from the Ideology of Women’s Liberation to the Political Empowerment of Women’s Liberation. The third session will focus on the results of the alternative pedagogical methods developed by Jineolojî over more than a decade and how these methods can be further developed.




Within the framework of liberation of knowledge, Jineolojî’s research objectives and methods, as well as the social role of Jineolojî academies from the perspective of democratic modernity, will be assessed.




Workshop outcomes to be finalized




In the final part of the conference, the outcomes of the work carried out in the seven workshops will be shared and joint decisions will be adopted. The conference will conclude with the discussions and decisions reached over the three days being reflected in a final declaration.
