author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Sonia Caron, du PQ, va prendre les rênes de la plus grande circonscription du Québec
content:
Après 12 ans, Sonia Caron, du Parti québécois, a repris la circonscription d’Ungava, dans le Nord-du-Québec, ramenant celle-ci dans le giron du PQ lors de l’élection du 5 octobre.




Sonia Caron est née à Chibougamau, où elle réside toujours, près de la Nation crie de Mistissini. Dans une entrevue accordée à APTN Nouvelles nationales, elle a indiqué qu’elle souhaite devenir une porte-parole de l’ensemble des personnes vivant dans le Nord.




« Moi, je représente le Parti québécois, évidemment, parce que ça reflète mes valeurs », a-t-elle déclaré à APTN Nouvelles nationales, « mais mon intérêt est avant tout un intérêt pour parler du Nord à Québec et être la meilleure voie possible, justement, pour les gens avec qui je travaille. C’est important de traduire nos besoins à l’État, puis qu’on comprenne de part et d’autre avec quoi on peut avancer ensemble pour être plus efficace, puis répondre à quels besoins en priorité. »




S’étendant sur 855 164 km

2

, la circonscription québécoise d’Ungava figure parmi les plus grandes au pays. Sa superficie n’est surpassée que par celles des circonscriptions fédérales du Nunavut et des Territoires du Nord-Ouest, qui englobent chacune un territoire entier.




Ungava est plus vaste que l’ensemble de la France. Pourtant, selon Élections Québec, sa population ne compte que 45 740 personnes, dont 30 773 sont admissibles au vote. La population est dispersée aux quatre coins de cette immense circonscription, qui englobe les 14 communautés du Nunavik, où vivent quelque 13 000 Inuit, ainsi que les neuf communautés de la Nation crie d’Eeyou Istchee, qui compte environ 20 000 membres. La circonscription englobe aussi plusieurs localités non autochtones, dont Chibougamau, Lebel-sur-Quévillon, Matagami et Chapais, qui comptent ensemble quelque 14 000 personnes.




Le 5 octobre, 8 516 personnes se sont prévalus de leur droit de vote dans Ungava, pour un taux de participation de 27,61 %. Sonia Caron a obtenu le plus grand nombre de voix, soit 3 272.




Enseignante et directrice d’école ayant amorcé sa carrière à Inukjuak avant de retourner à Chibougamau pour y fonder une famille, Sonia Caron affirme vouloir mieux cerner les enjeux du Nord qui sont mal compris à Québec et qui nécessitent une représentation plus soutenue. Elle souhaite également collaborer avec les dirigeants cris et inuit afin de répondre aux besoins de leurs communautés.




« Je suis très consciente que je représente trois entités différentes sur un même territoire », a-t-elle dit. « Que ce soit pour les services aux aînés, la santé mentale, l’accès à une éducation de qualité, tout est là. Pour moi, c’est seulement de mettre tout le monde ensemble à la même table. »




Expérience et priorités




Après avoir enseigné et travaillé dans des écoles primaires et secondaires, Sonia Caron dirige un centre de formation professionnelle depuis les dix dernières années. Elle affirme également avoir siégé, au cours de la dernière décennie, à plusieurs conseils d’administration, dont ceux de l’Institut national des mines du Québec, de l’Assemblée des partenaires de la Société du Plan Nord et du Conseil régional des partenaires du marché du travail. Dans ce dernier cas, elle a notamment travaillé aux côtés de représentants des nations crie et inuit.




« J’ai touché beaucoup à la main-d’œuvre, à la santé, à l’éducation, au secteur minier, forestier, de par les formations qu’on donne à notre centre », a-t-elle dit. “Donc, je me suis dit pourquoi ne pas aller faire écouter la voix que tu portes depuis dix ans sur tous ces comités-là pour faire comprendre et connaître les réels enjeux du nord. »




Après des décennies passées dans le milieu de l’éducation, tout en collaborant avec des organismes gouvernementaux et des sociétés d’État, Sonia Caron estime avoir acquis une bonne compréhension du fonctionnement de l’appareil gouvernemental et des moyens de le rendre plus efficace.




« Mon bagage en éducation et en direction m’amène aussi à analyser toujours les causes d’une problématique », a-t-elle dit, « ou aller en profondeur pour intervenir à la source. C’est sûr que des fois, c’est plus long, mais quand on intervient sur les bons facteurs de changement, ça peut faire beaucoup de belles choses. »




Selon elle, cette expérience lui a donné les outils nécessaires pour travailler efficacement dans un territoire aussi grand qu’Ungava.




« Souvent, on est enclavé par soit l’avion, les voies maritimes ou les routes qui sont parfois hasardeuses l’hiver », dit-elle. « Mais depuis toujours, même nous à la Bay James, au Centre de services scolaires, on a toujours travaillé à distance. Avoir un bureau physique, c’est important, mais je vais être une députée de terrain que les gens vont pouvoir interpeller de façon régulière pour me tenir au courant des enjeux et de l’évolution de ces enjeux-là. »




Sonia Caron rejette l’idée selon laquelle « nous sommes peu nombreux sur un vaste territoire ». Elle soutient plutôt que les personnes qui vivent dans la région sont celles qui la connaissent le mieux.




« Ma vision va être déterminée avec celle des Premières Nations et des Inuit, tout comme avec les Jamésiens », a-t-elle dit. « Le Québec ne peut pas fonctionner sans le Nord. Donc, je veux donner au Nord l’importance qu’il y a, et pas juste une importance historique et symbolique. »




L’enjeu de la souveraineté




Le Parti québécois défend avant tout l’idée d’un Québec indépendant. Cependant, les nations crie et inuit ont, au fil des décennies, clairement manifesté leur rejet de la souveraineté du Québec.




Sonia Caron reconnaît l’existence de ces différences de points de vue, mais affirme que l’essentiel est d’abord de rencontrer les personnes vivant dans la circonscription et d’entendre ce qu’elles ont à dire.




« Je pense qu’il faut se comprendre », dit-elle, « et que les Cris et les Inuit comprennent l’intention du Parti québécois et que nous, au Parti québécois, on comprenne la nécessité d’une application juste des ententes antérieures.




« Les Québécois et Québécoises veulent exactement ce que les Communautés Cris et Inuit revendiquent par les différentes ententes, qu’on soit pas juste consultés, mais qu’on soit impliqués dans les décisions, qu’on puisse décorer notre maison comme on veut et qu’on la bâtisse ensemble, notre maison. »




Selon elle, il est encore trop tôt pour déterminer comment cet objectif pourrait être réalisé dans les faits. Elle affirme néanmoins avoir confiance en Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, qui souhaite, selon elle, construire le projet souverainiste québécois à partir des accords déjà signés entre le Québec et les Premières Nations et les Inuit.




Sonia Caron rappelle également que l’histoire du Parti québécois est marquée par d’importantes ententes avec les peuples autochtones. Elle mentionne notamment la Paix des Braves, signée en 2002 par le premier ministre Bernard Landry et le grand chef cri Ted Moses.




« Pour moi, systématiquement, je prends en compte la spécificité des Inuit, des Cris, la spécificité de la gouvernance aussi », a-t-elle dit. « Puis, mon chef l’a dit depuis le début, on veut développer, on veut revenir à ces relations de confiance-là constructives que Lévesque et Landry ont eues avec les Premières Nations et les Inuit. »




Elle explique que toute évolution des relations entre un gouvernement péquiste et les Premières Nations et les Inuit devrait s’inscrire dans la continuité des engagements prévus par la Convention de la Baie‑James et du Nord québécois et par la Paix des Braves.




« Il y a nécessité de se rassoir pour faire le portrait de tout ça puis envisager la suite », a-t-elle dit, en référence au « Livre bleu » du PQ sur la souveraineté, qui aborde brièvement la question des Premières Nations et des Inuit, mais qui ne contient pas encore le chapitre prévu sur les relations entre ces peuples et l’État québécois.




« En ce sens qu’on est une région où il y a plusieurs ressources naturelles, la protection du territoire, et cetera. », a-t-elle dit. « Ce qu’on veut faire, c’est de remettre vivante ces instances de gouvernance-là puis s’assurer que la politique future entre Québec et les nations vont être abordées directement de nation à nation, comme c’est prévu dans les différentes ententes. »




Confiance




Sonia Caron a également reconnu l’ampleur de certains défis dans le Nord, notamment en matière de santé au Nunavik, où les cas de tuberculose sont en hausse, ainsi que les enjeux de racisme systémique au sein d’institutions comme le réseau de la santé et le système correctionnel. Toutefois, l’entrevue ayant été réalisée moins de trois jours après son élection, elle a précisé qu’elle était encore en train de constituer son bureau et son équipe et qu’elle devait d’abord prendre connaissance des dossiers.




« Je suis au fait de l’augmentation des cas de tuberculose depuis 2018. Je suis au fait de plusieurs statistiques ou plusieurs situations qui fragilisent la santé et le bien-être des habitants de l’ensemble du territoire, incluant le Nunavik », dit-elle. « Les solutions, je pense qu’il faut les définir avec les gens sur le terrain qui sont à même de nous aider à comprendre davantage pour mieux intervenir. Pour moi, c’est bien au-delà de juste une question financière. C’est une question de coordination mentale pour régler les problématiques en amont. »




Elle a aussi reconnu qu’un nombre grandissant de Québécois semblent éprouver des préoccupations ou un certain malaise à l’égard des systèmes publics auxquels ils ont recours.




« Je pense qu’à tous les points de vue au Québec, les Québécois et les Québécoises ont perdu un peu confiance envers l’État et les services publics », dit-elle. « Donc, pour moi, c’est primordial de revenir à ça. Puis, à partir des études qui sont là, on va s’assurer d’avoir un portrait juste de la situation pour pouvoir poser les bonnes actions. »




Pour l’heure, Sonia Caron affirme devoir d’abord se familiariser avec les dossiers qui serviront à orienter les futures décisions politiques. Selon elle, cette nécessité concerne à la fois les questions propres aux peuples autochtones et les enjeux touchant les systèmes publics auxquels ont accès tous les citoyens du Québec.




« Puis on va d’abord apprendre à connaître nos organes de gouvernance, parce que le gouvernement de la Nation Crie, c’est un palier supplémentaire de gouvernance », a-t-elle dit, en soulignant que tous les Québécois n’ont pas le même rapport avec Makivvik ou le KRG que les habitants du Nord, ni même ne comprennent forcément ces organismes. « Pour moi, ce qui est important, c’est que tout le monde connaisse les paramètres, les contraintes de chacun de ces entités-là pour qu’on puisse ensemble déterminer où on va et qu’est-ce qui va être le mieux pour les habitants du Nord et la protection de l’environnement. »




Sonia Caron explique que, même sur un territoire aussi vaste, il est essentiel que la population puisse être entendue. Elle entend donc favoriser les échanges en personne, par téléphone et par voie électronique.




« La distance que je vais avoir avec les gens, c’est celle qu’ils voudront que j’aille avec eux », dit-elle. « Donc, plus je suis terrain, plus je suis sur place, que ce soit virtuellement, physiquement, plus les gens m’envoient de l’info, plus je vais être en même de bien connaître mes dossiers pour porter les bons argumentaires pour répondre aux besoins. Je vais être la députée de tous les citoyens d’Ungava, les quarante-quelques-mille sont tous très importants pour moi. »




Elle prêtera serment lorsque l’Assemblée nationale du Québec reprendra ses travaux le 17 novembre.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Supreme Court delivers landmark decision on Indigenous offenders and victims
content:
A Supreme Court of Canada decision on Friday has clarified the factors that judges should account for when a defendant and victim are both Indigenous.




The landmark case, 

R. v. Cope

, concerns Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaw man from Nova Scotia who pleaded guilty to assaulting his partner, a Mi’kmaw woman, in 2021.




The Supreme Court weighed in on a trial judge’s decision to sentence Cope to five years in prison and the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s decision to reduce that sentence to three years.




On Friday, the Supreme Court upheld the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s ruling, which accounted for Cope’s mental illness and substance use.




“The sentencing judge should have linked the mental health factor to the offender’s moral blameworthiness on the aggravated assault offence, but failed to do so,” wrote Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin, writing for the majority of the judges. “The court of appeal was therefore correct to intervene and it arrived at a just and appropriate sentence.”




Four of nine judges sided with the Nova Scotia provincial court’s original ruling, which dismissed recommendations from community members who proposed no further jail time and opted for a treatment program instead.




Anne Crawford, an Iqaluit lawyer who handles family and domestic violence cases, said the Supreme Court judgement uplifts the role that Indigenous victims, their families and their community should play in criminal sentencing.
















“It provides emphasis on the value of women, mothers and partners,” said Crawford, who has previously worked as a defence lawyer. “I think it’s part of a broader shift in Canadian society towards accountability for offenders.”




That shift includes changes to the Criminal Code that came into effect in June, she said. The law now defines murders “that occur within a pattern of coercive” behaviour toward an intimate partner as first-degree murders, and it asks courts to consider life imprisonment when somenone commits manslaughter within such a pattern.




“I don’t think our courts come anywhere near addressing what victims need,” Crawford added about the landmark judgement. “(But) I do think it comes closer to holding offenders to account.”




Twenty intervenors, including provincial and community prosecutorial services, legal aid centres, and organizations representing lawyers and Indigenous women, all participated in the hearings, held Dec. 11 and 12 at the Supreme Court in Ottawa.




Philippe Boucher, a doctoral candidate in legal studies at Carleton University, serves as a Gladue report writer, which provides judges with a portrait of an Indigenous offender before they decide the length and severity of a sentence.




He said the court’s message is that condemning violence doesn’t always require longer prison sentences.
















The Supreme Court judgement also provides guidance on how judges should balance their responsibility to avoid imprisonment when offenders are Indigenous with protecting Indigenous women and girls, Boucher said.




O’Bonsawin proposed a three-step test. Judges must first assess the gravity of the offence and responsibility of the offender in light of the Indigeneity of both the offender and the victim.




Second, they must identify what the sentence is meant to achieve while considering denunciation and deterrence, a key addition to the Criminal Code after the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls.




Third, they must chose a proportionate sentence with everything in context.




“What the Supreme Court said this morning is that denunciation and deterrence doesn’t automatically mean a custodial sentence, it doesn’t mean prison, and it can also be another alternative to detention,” he said.

author: Unknown
title: "Katiller yargılanana kadar mücadelemiz bitmeyecek"
content:
Irmak Su Timur [email protected] Özlem Songül Abayoğlu [email protected]

Ankara Garı’nın önünde 2015 yılında; emek, barış ve demokrasi güçlerinin “barış ve demokrasi” talebiyle bir araya geldiği mitinge düzenlenen saldırıda 103 kişi hayatını kaybetti. Katliamın üzerinden 11 yıl geçmesine rağmen hayatını kaybedenlerin aileleri, yoldaşları, arkadaşları adalet mücadelesini sürdürüyor. İl dışında olan aileler; her davaya gelmeye, bulundukları illerde çocuklarının, yoldaşlarının mücadelesini, “barış ve demokrasi” talebini yükseltmeye, onların isimlerini yaşatmaya devam ediyor.

Katliamın 11 yılında Evrensel’e konuşan aileler her davada, her 10 Ekim’de söyledikleri gibi kamu görevlilerinin sorumluluğuna, katliama nasıl yol verildiğine dikkat çekiyor. Aileler, sorumluları ortaya çıkarmayanlara, “Mücadelemizden vazgeçmeyeceğiz” diye sesleniyor.

Katliamda hayatını kaybeden Cemal Avşar’ın eşi Gülşen Avşar, mücadeleye devam ettiğini ve ısrarla adalet talep ettiğini anlatıyor. “Çok yorulduk ama devam edeceğiz” diyen Gülşen Avşar yaşadıklarından şöyle bahsediyor: “11 yıldır mücadele ediyoruz. Onlar bizi yıldırmaya çalışıyorlar ama yılmıyoruz. Hem yollar hem mahkemeler bizi yoruyor. Her davadan döndüğümde çocuklarımın başının bükülmesi bizi yoruyor. 11 sene oldu, hiçbir şekilde sesimizi duyuramadık. O zaman kızım 11 yaşındaydı, şimdi işe başladı. Torunlarım dedelerini göremedi. Ben ağlayamadım bile. İşe gitmek zorunda kaldım. Çocuklarıma anne, baba, abi olacağım diye sağlığım gitti. Artık adalet istiyoruz.”

Şebnem Yurtman’ın annesi Şafak Yurtman da kızının mücadelesinden ne kadar gurur duyduğunu anlatarak başlıyor sözlerine. Katliamın ardından eşine karakolda, “Kızınızın oraya gittiğinden haberiniz var mıydı?” diye sorulduğunu anlatan Yurtman, “Kızım 23 yaşındaydı, izin mi alacaktı? Zaten işim olmasaydı ben de gidecektim. Beraber o alanda olacaktık. Barışı beraber talep edecektik. 11 senedir davalara gidip geliyoruz. Küçücük bir ilerleme olmaz mı? İnsan ‘adalet varmış’ demez mi? Biz diyemiyoruz. Sözüm var Şebnem’e. Ömrüm yettiği sürece mücadeleye devam edeceğim. Tüm ailelere sesleniyorum. Bu hepimizin mücadelesi” diyor. Yurtman, “Elimizden bütün renklerimizi aldılar. Ben rengarenk bir insandım. Şebnem’in sevdiği yemekler evde pişmiyor. İnternette gezinirken Şebnem’in yoldaşlarının, onun resimlerini paylaştığını görüyorum. Bazıları benim bile bilmediğim resimler. Mutlu oluyorum” diye noktalıyor sözlerini.

Korkmaz Tedik’in annesi Zöhre Tedik de o gün barış talep etmek için ailecek mitinge gittiklerini anlatıyor: “Biz ailecek gittik alana. Ben gidemeyecektim. Korkmaz, ‘Anne gelmen lazım, sen gelmezsen barış olmaz. Bak parti çağırıyor’ demişti de ikna etmişti beni. O gün hepimiz alandaydık. Bir ara Korkmaz yanımızdan ayrıldı, sonra bomba patladı. Ancak öğrendik ki bomba patladığında Korkmaz hayattaymış. Onunla ilgilenen arkadaşına, ‘Ben iyiyim, sen diğerlerine bak’ demiş. Korkmaz’ın ölümüne neden olan, bombanın ardından polis tarafından sıkılan biber gazı olmuş.”

O günden itibaren avukatlarla, Korkmaz’ın yoldaşlarıyla, katledilenlerin aileleriyle mücadeleyi sürdürdüklerine vurgu yapan Zöhre Tedik, “İçimiz kan ağlarken katillerden hesap sormak için mücadele ettik. Başta Korkmaz’ın yoldaşları, partisi, avukatlar, sendikalar birleşti. Bugüne kadar da mücadeleyi sürdürdük. Avukatlarımız bize cesaret verdi. İl il, ilçe ilçe gezip delil topladılar. Davanın heyeti 4 kere değişti, hepsine dosyayı baştan anlattılar. Biz de olduğumuz her yerde bu katliam unutulmasın diye mücadele etmeye devam ediyoruz. Dönemin başbakanının sözlerini ve sorumluluğunu, bakanlarının sözlerini ve sorumluluklarını da unutmadık, unutmayacağız. Dünya alem bilsin ki katillerden hesap soracağız. Vasiyetimdir, benden sonra da Korkmaz’ın ve diğer 102 insanın mücadelesi unutulmasın” diye konuşuyor.

Güney Doğan’ın annesi Derman Doğan da “11 yılı yaşayan bilir. 11 yıldır hem onun yokluğu hem de mahkemeler yıpratıyor bizi” diye söz ediyor mücadelesinden. Mahkemeden olumlu bir ilerleme görememenin, sürekli heyet değişmesinin, her heyete tüm dosyanın tekrar anlatılmasının yorucu olduğunu söyleyen Doğan, “Mahkeme heyetinin bize karşı tavırları, ‘Çok konuşursan dışarı atarım’ demelerine mi göğüs gerelim, acıya mı göğüs gerelim bilmiyorum” diye soruyor.

“Benim çocuğum sadece barış istediği için katledildi” diyen Doğan, “Katledilenlerin suçları barış, özgürlük, demokrasi istemekti” diye tepkisini anlatıyor. Doğan, “Bombanın ardından yaralıların üstüne zehirli gaz sıkıldığını mahkemede öğrendim. Bunları duymak beni kahrediyor. Benim çocuğum öğrenciydi. Talebim bir an önce katillerin cezalandırılması. Çocuğumun katilleri dışarıda” diye tepki gösteriyor. Doğan, sözlerini şöyle noktalıyor: “Benim çocuğum yaşayamadı, bundan sonraki çocuklar barış içinde yaşasın. Başka anneler üzülmesin”

Dilan Sarıkaya’nın annesi Nesligül Sarıkaya, “Bu düzen değişmezse, yargı baskılanmaya devam ederse bu dava uzayacak” diyerek başlıyor sözlerine. İnsanlığa karşı suçtan yargılama yapılmamasına değinen Sarıkaya, “Davalar bizim ağzımıza bir parmak bal çalmaktan ibaret. Avukatlarımızın talepleri karşılanmıyor. Mahkeme ailelere zorluk çıkarıyor” diye tepki gösteriyor. Tüm bunlara karşı birlik olma çağrısı yapan Sarıkaya, siyasi partilere, sendikalara, konfederasyonlara, ailelere, “Mahkemelere katılın, salonları dolduralım” diye sesleniyor.

Dava sürecinde bir sürü yeni insanla tanıştığını anlatan Sarıkaya, “Dava sürecinde tanıştıklarımla aile gibi olduk. İki ayda bir, üç ayda bir görüştüğümüzde sanki aileden birini görmüşüz gibi sarılıyoruz. Orada birbirimize destek veriyoruz” diye anlatıyor. Avukatların mücadelesinin davayı bugünlere getiren temel şeylerden biri olduğunu vurgulayan Sarıkaya, “Avukatlarımızın çok büyük gayretleriyle, inatlarıyla bu dava buraya kadar geldi. Yoksa çoktan bitirmeyi düşünüyorlardı. En umutsuz olduğumuz zamanda bile avukatlarımız bizlere umut verdi” diye anlatıyor.

Uygar Çoşgun’un annesi Nuray Çoşgun da geçen sürede acılarının azalmadığını vurguluyor. Mahkemelerde kendilerine izleyici gibi muamele edilmesine tepki gösteren Coşgun, “Biz seyirci değiliz, biz bir müştekiyiz. Acımızı görmeyen bir karşı taraf var. Sanki sanık biriz, öbür taraf müşteki gibi. ‘Mahkemenin huzurunu bozma’ diyorlar bize. Bu katliamın arkasında bir sürü insan var. Hepsinin yakalanmasını istiyoruz. Dava insanlığa karşı suçtan görülmeli. Ancak sanıklar tam olarak bundan beraat ettiler” diyor.

Hâlâ barış istediklerinin altını çizen Coşgun, sözlerini şöyle tamamlıyor: “Biz kavgadan yana olanlar değiliz. Biz insanların ölmesinden yana olanlar değiliz. Biz sadece barış için mücadele eden insanlarız. Herkes oraya barış için gitti. Kimse ölmesin, barış olsun, huzur olsun, mutluluk olsun.”

10 Ekim Ankara Gar Katliamı’nda hayatını kaybeden Elif Kanlıoğlu’nun ardından “Bum” isimli şarkıyı besteleyen ve seslendiren Beliz İtiş, katliamın 11. yılında duygularını Evrensel’e anlattı:

“Ben Elif’i kalbinden tanıdım; gözündeki ışıltıdan, gülüşündeki umuttan…

Aynı köyün çocuklarıydık biz, onun annesiyle benim babam süt kardeş olmasına rağmen ne hikmetse Elif’le hiç yüz yüze gelememiştik. Onu, kaybettikten sonra, tanışmadan tanıdım.

İnsan genç yaşlardayken bir yaşıtını kaybetmeyi pek kabullenemiyor, hele ki söz konusu barış ve iyilik uğrunda yitirilmiş bir hayat ise etkisi bir ömür sürüyor sanırım. Şimdi, bu yaşımızda Elif nasıl biri olurdu, neler yapardı diye merak etmekten kendimi alıkoyamıyor, anneciğinin gülüşündeki hüznü gördükçe insanlık adına utanıyorum.

Ankara Garındaki o patlamanın haberlerini okuduğum günden bu yana kendimce Elif yerine de yaşıyorum; umudumu sırtlanıp iyiliğin peşinden gidiyor, zorlandığım zamanlarda sanki beni duyarmışçasına onunla dertleşiyorum. Bu dertleşmelerden biri zaman içinde “Bum” isminde bir şarkıya evrilmişti; şimdi her 10 Ekim dönümünde göğe bakıp şarkımı söylüyor, Elif’e ve o gün kaybettiğimiz onlarca cana selam uçuruyorum.

Canım Elif; kalbi gözünde, umudu göğsümde…”

Hâlâ yıkık, boynu bükük aileler

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Daron Letts
title: Elder van project could hit the streets in 2027, premier says
content:
Five accessible elders vans that were purchased with $1 million in public money remain off the roads one year after a 

pilot project

 affirmed the need for such a service.




While he wouldn’t provide a specific timeline for the vans’ rollout, Premier John Main said it’s his “desire” to see the vans back in operation in 2027 — three years after they were purchased.




“The update is, as of right now, they’re still not operating,” he said in a phone interview Friday. “But, our government does want to follow through on this.”




The project stalled in 2025, at the end of the previous government’s term, due to a lack of an operating budget.




That changed in spring 2026 when MLAs in the current legislative assembly approved $1.25 million in additional funding,

 Main said.




When the bus service was first announced, it was a partnership among Northern Future Skills Development, Arctic Training Ltd., and Caribou Cabs.




There is one van in each of five communities: 

Iqaluit, Cambridge Bay, Rankin Inlet, Coral Harbour and Pangnirtung. 

Northern Future Skills Development, a private company, bought them with funding it got from the GN.



















Representatives of Arctic Training Ltd. and Caribou Cabs were not available to comment on this story.




Kopa Mike stands next to the elders bus operated by the Pairiniit Society at Iqaluit’s Elders’ Qammaq on Friday. (Photo by Daron Letts)




Policy is being developed behind the scenes and, once complete, the government plans to issue a call for proposals before the end of 2026, Main said.




It remains to be decided whether that call will be public or “by invitation,” he added.




Arctic Training Ltd. ran a self-funded, month-long 

short-term soft launch

 of the service in Iqaluit a year ago, in October 2025. The company responded to approximately 200 service calls each weekend.




Kopa Mike, a board member with the Pairijiit Tigummiaqtikkut Iqaluit Elders Society, used the new van three times that month to travel between the Elders Qammaq, food bank, and grocery store, she said.
















The new van’s ramp was a bit challenging with her bad leg, she said, but an assistant on the bus made it easy to climb until she could reach the handrails inside the bus while she boarded, she said.




“It was great having help,” she said.




The elders society itself runs three vehicles, including an elder bus. But that bus’ accessibility ramp has been broken for a long time, said fellow board member Ainiak Korgak.




”We got tired of waiting for the new bus so we forgot about it,” Mike added.




“I realize it’s been some time since these vans were originally purchased, and there is some anticipation and frustration around the fact that they’re still not operating,” Main said. “The next step is to see a policy established, which would govern that funding and see it flow across Nunavut to folks who will be running this type of service.”

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Dene Nation establishes water council as leaders warn of tar sands tailings risks
content:
The Dene Nation unanimously passed a resolution to establish a Dene Water Council at its 56th national assembly, in Kátł’odeeche First Nation, Northwest Territories.




The resolution referred to water as “a sacred gift from the Creator” and called for greater Dene-led oversight of water quality, industrial activity and contamination across the North.




The conversation led by Gerry Cheezie, co-chair of Keepers of the Water and a former chief of the Tthebatthie Denesųłiné Nation, comes as Indigenous leaders raise concerns about proposed plans to treat and release oilsands tailings water into the Athabasca River, which flows north into the Mackenzie River basin.




The resolution states that Dene waters are facing increasing pressures from industrial development, resource extraction, climate change, contamination and cumulative effects.




Cheezie, who recently attended Suncor Energy Inc.’s engagement sessions on its plans to treat and release tailings, said the water issue has never been more urgent.




”We’re impacted and we don’t want to see our waters polluted,” Cheezie said.




The Dene Nation Assembly building in Kátł’odeeche First Nation, N.W.T., where delegates gathered for the 56th Dene National Assembly. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.







Industrial development in northern Alberta has already affected the environment and the exercise of Treaty 8 rights, which include an agreement to protect Indigenous inherent rights to fish, hunt, trap and pursue traditional ways of life.




Cheezie took issue with Alberta’s regulatory response to industrial contamination.




“They [Suncor]  were fined $50,000 by the Alberta Energy Regulators for the Carle Lake plant, in which they released millions of litres of tailings into the Atabasca and they got a slap on the wrist,” Cheezie said. “The province of Alberta’s regulations aren’t being enforced and the federal government is silent on this, so we have to rely on ourselves.”




Cheezie said oversight and advocacy groups he works with are exploring possible legal action over cumulative impacts on treaty rights and traditional ways of life.


He said the evidence, costs and next steps would need to be considered by leadership which is why he is asking the Dene Nation to join as an intervener.




“When we talk about water, it’s at the 11th hour right now,” Cheezie said. “Industry, the oil industry is trying to poison our water and we have to step up and stop it.”




Cheezie warned that the contamination threat extends far beyond any single community.




“If you live in the community of Hay River, what are you gonna do? Where are you gonna go to get your water?” he said. “Great Slave Lake will be polluted; there will be toxins, heavy metals and other all kinds of forever chemicals in the water that are all going to impact your health.”




Chief Allan Adam, on the right, of the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation calling on chiefs across the North to speak up about the threats posed by oil-sands tailings releases.







The N.W.T. and Alberta relies strictly on a trans-boundary water agreement, which Indigenous governments are not a party to, and it’s agreement Cheezie said hasn’t helped Indigenous groups when they have tried to negotiate with oil industry and governments in the past.




“We pull out the trans-boundary agreement and say this is supposed to protect our rights in the territories, and all they [GNWT and Albertan provincial government] do is communicate with us,” he said. “They’re approving projects, approving environmental issues that could affect us without telling us.




In July, 2026, the Dene Nation and Treaty 8 First Nations in Alberta signed a memorandum of understanding to work together on protecting shared waters in the Mackenzie River basin.




“We want to work together supporting each other legally, scientifically, environmentally, to protect the water because we’re not moving anywhere,” he said.




Cheezie, who was born in Fort Chipewyan, said the resolution passed at the assembly represents a step toward protecting the water that sustains communities and traditional practices.




“We have to haul water when we’re going out on the land and that’s beyond anybody’s imagination back in 1899 that we would have to do that when we signed the treaty,” he said.




Chief Allan Adam of the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation, a guest presenter at the assembly, also addressed delegates, delivering a passionate call to action to the large gathering about the urgency of the crisis.




Adam challenged chiefs along the Peace, Slave and Mackenzie rivers to use their voices.




“Everyone along the Peace, Slave and Mackenzie River; you guys ought to start speaking up,” Adam said. “Because if you don’t, what’s going on in our community [Fort Chipewyan] is going to be here 20 years from now.”




Adam addressed the need for Suncor to engage directly with northern communities.




“If Suncor wants to treat and release the tailings pond issue, they better start talking to the people that are going to be affected by it,” Adam said. “So they’ve talked to us in the community of Fort Chip and I’m requesting them to come up north and start speaking with the northern communities.”




The Dehcho (Mackenzie River) connects winds through several Indigenous communities in Denendeh. The Dene Nation have passed resolution to create a Dene Water Council to monitor contamination and industrial activity in the watershed. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.







He stressed that all Indigenous communities need to understand the potential impacts before they can support any proposals from industry.




Adam said his nation has already developed its own water policy,  one that neither Canada nor Alberta has been willing to recognize.




“Nobody wants to take it into consideration because if they do, it would hold them accountable to make sure that they reach the benchmark that is safe drinking water for our community,” Adam said.




According to the resolution the Dene Water council will develop and implement a Dene Water Policy, a Dene Water Protection Strategy, a Dene water-monitoring program, a Dene Water Atlas, and water emergency response procedures.




It will provide the Dene Nation and Dene governments with independent scientific, technical, legal, policy, mapping and water-monitoring capacity, and will monitor and assess water quality, water quantity, contamination, industrial activities and cumulative effects.




The post 

Dene Nation establishes water council as leaders warn of tar sands tailings risks

 appeared first on 

APTN News

.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Supreme Court decision balances Gladue factors against concern for Indigenous women
content:
The Supreme Court of Canada upheld a reduced sentence in the case of a Mi’kmaw man convicted of brutally assaulting his Mi’kmaw partner in 2021 in a decision expected to have significant effect on the way judges consider Indigenous men who commit violent crimes against Indigenous women.




In 

a five-four split decision

, the court found the initial five-year sentence fell short in factoring for both the convicted man’s mental health issues and Indigenous considerations, and upheld an appeals court judgement that reduced the sentence to three years plus two years probation after release, minus time served on remand.




The case turned on two serious considerations for Indigenous people in the legal system.




One was guidance written into the criminal code following the 1999 decision in R. v. Gladue, which instructs courts to consider systemic and background factors that affect the “moral blameworthiness” of an Indigenous offender, and to consider the sentencing and sanctions appropriate to an Indigenous offender’s specific circumstances.




The second consideration was of guidance in the criminal code that resulted from the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG), in which a judge must prioritize objectives of “denunciation and deterrence” in sentencing someone who abused “a person who is vulnerable, including because they are an Indigenous woman or girl.”




“The legislative history of these provisions is clear that they were introduced with the goal of addressing violence against Indigenous women and girls and other vulnerable victims that has been overlooked for far too long,” writes Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin in the majority decision, which was supported by Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Sheilah Martin, Nicholas Kasirer and Mary Moreau.




A dissenting opinion was written by Justices Malcolm Rowe and Mahmud Jamal, supported by Justice Suzanne Côté and Chief Justice Richard Wagner. It argued the original sentence should be restored, because the sentencing judge properly weighed all relevant factors, while the Court of Appeal’s reduced sentence “did not reflect denunciation, deterrence, the victim’s vulnerability, or the sentencing judge’s conclusion that the offender poses a continuing danger to society.”




Yet O’Bonsawin’s decision stresses the considerations of both Indigenous offenders and Indigenous women and girls who are victims of violence should not be seen at odds with each other.




“Viewing these provisions as conflicting misrepresents their goals,” she writes. “The sentencing judge’s task is to impose a proportionate and individualized sentence that gives due consideration to both the needs of Indigenous offenders and Indigenous victims. Reconciliation must serve as an important lodestar in applying these provisions together.”




Supreme Court Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.







The crime and the conviction




The case centres on Harry Arthur Cope, who pled guilty to attacking his occasional partner, a woman from Sipekne’katik First Nation, in a 2021 assault. The judgment described the attack as “horrendous” and “brutal,” in which “the victim’s head was repeatedly punched, kicked and smashed against the sidewalk, leaving her with significant injuries.”




At the time of the assault, Cope — whom the decision describes as having “severe mental health challenges” — had been off his medication for just over a year, and had instead been consuming illicit drugs.




The court ordered an Indigenous Background Report and a sentencing circle consider the case. That circle found community members felt further incarceration would not help Cope, whom they recommended receive holistic care, including in-patient treatment.




Nova Scotia Provincial Court Judge Christine Driscoll recognized that because of Cope’s “Gladue factors” (those elements in which his background as an Indigenous person affected his circumstances), as well as his mental health problems and major addictions issues, he was less morally culpable of the crime than a person that did not carry those burdens. She also acknowledged the community’s lack of recommendation of further jail time.




However, Driscoll found intimate-partner violence against an Indigenous woman was an aggravating factor, and handed down a five-year sentence.




A majority in the Court of Appeal revised that decision, arguing Driscoll failed to accurately emphasize the connections between Cope’s mental illness, drug abuse and his Gladue factors, and consequently sentenced Cope disproportionately to his moral culpability. That court reduced Cope’s sentence to three years, less 18 months credit for time served on remand.




Subsequently, Nova Scotia Crown Attorney Erica Koresawa challenged the Court of Appeal, leading to the Supreme Court of Canada considering the case.




Gladue factors




Anishinabek/Mohawk lawyer Christa Big Canoe, from Georgina Island First Nation, has been the legal director of Ontario-based Aboriginal Legal Services since 2011. She has also been lead commission counsel to the MMIWG inquiry and earlier this year, was lead prosecutor in the Permanent Peoples Tribunal on Missing and Disappeared Indigenous Children and Unmarked Graves in Canada.




In a press release following the judgment, Aboriginal Legal Services — which was an intervener both at the Supreme Court and in the original Nova Scotia Court of Appeals cases — praised the court finding that each Indigenous person before the criminal justice system, whether as offender or as victim, has “been uniquely shaped by the experiences of colonialism.”




Attorney Christa Big Canoe speaks to witnesses during the Permanent People’s Tribunal in Montreal in May, 2026. Photo: Jesse Staniforth/APTN







Speaking to APTN News, Big Canoe talked about the crucial role Gladue considerations play in attempting to address the phenomenon of mass-incarceration of Indigenous people.




“Historically and even continuously, Indigenous people will get stricter sentences for similar offenses as [non-Indigenous] individuals who have a similar criminal record,” she said, explaining that was due to “false assumptions and discrimination and colonialism.”


At the criminal level, she said, Gladue requires the judge sentencing an Indigenous offender convicted of a crime to engage directly with the offender’s circumstances.




Gladue “is not a list,” she said. “It requires a judge to take into account those circumstances, and then it requires a judge to find a ‘fit and appropriate’ sentence. [That] may be one thing, like you have to do jail time, or it may be you have a community justice program, you have all the resources in place and we know that you can be supported in a way that will help actually rehabilitate you. The fit and appropriate sentence is always based on the circumstance of the individual and the case.”




Case-by-case basis




During her time at the MMIWG inquiry, Big Canoe said she heard victims’ family members say they felt as though Gladue allowed Indigenous offenders leniency. But she argued it’s important to recognize the factors that prevent Indigenous people being heard fairly before the courts — whether offenders’ unique backgrounds are discounted, as Gladue attempts to correct, or the complexity of victims’ experiences is unheard, as the MMIWG inquiry sought to address.




Each piece of sentencing guidance aims to remedy historical injustices Indigenous people have faced before the courts, and consequently Big Canoe said each decision considering either or both is a careful balancing act.




“This particular circumstance [in R. v. Cope], it was an Indigenous community that actually held the sentencing circle, that actually put into place a plan for a fit and appropriate sentence. And the lower court just completely ignored it. They said on the record, ‘We read what the sentencing circle said.’ And then they said nothing else. So they didn’t.”




She noted that an Indigenous person is not automatically eligible for Gladue factors, but the court must consider and explain why Gladue applies.




Similarly, she said, “in this case, it’s not enough to say, ‘There was a sentencing circle, and this is what they said, but here’s what we’re going to do.’”




Big Canoe said the lack of deference to the sentencing circle in the initial decision was something the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal underlined as a concern.




“You have to talk about a fit and appropriate sentence,” she said. “And you have to seriously look at what the resources and options are and the outcome of rehabilitation, as opposed to simply mass-incarceration. Because people don’t become better citizens in jail. They don’t go back to their First Nations or their Métis or their Inuit communities healed or resolved. In fact, they often come back a lot more damaged and often a lot more violent.”




The goal, Big Canoe said, is to make Indigenous communities safer, and tough-on-crime policies often fail to make offenders safe members of communities.




“Jail’s not working,” she said. “It’s producing more violent offenders, bringing less safety to our communities. So, what are ways that we know to reduce violence within communities? And why does it matter when an Indigenous community is finding paths or trying to achieve fit and appropriate sentences, which is different than producing more violent people returning to our communities?”




Paramount protections for Indigenous women




Cree lawyer Donald Worme, from the Kawacatoose First Nation in Saskatchewan, is a founding member of the Indigenous Bar Association of Canada, and a member of the Saskatchewan Human Rights Tribunal.




Saskatchewan attorney Donald Worme. Photo: APTN file







Speaking to APTN, he noted that it has been nearly 30 years since the Gladue case, which was intended to direct courts to consider alternatives to incarceration.




“We know that since Gladue, the statistics with respect to Aboriginal incarceration didn’t improve,” Worme explained. “In fact, they got worse, if one could imagine that.”




He agreed with the aims behind Gladue, noting, “Indigenous people have long suffered at the hands of court decisions that simply did not consider the background, the history of colonialism in this country, and that has been to the detriment of Indigenous populations generally.”




At the same time, Worme said he has lost his mother and three of his sisters to murder, and that it was incumbent upon him to underline the scale of the crisis of violence against Indigenous women and girls.




“It is clear that there must be denunciation of violence against Indigenous women in this country,” he told APTN. “If that balance runs against Indigenous men who have Gladue factors, then I think that that balance has to come down in favor of protecting Indigenous women as vulnerable, and particularly the most vulnerable, in this country. And in this particular instance, notwithstanding his Gladue factors, his mental illness and his addictions, it’s clear that denunciation has to figure prominently in Mr. Cope’s sentencing.”




Justice O’Bonsawin addressed this matter in her opinion, noting that “Engaging with Indigenous perspectives does not hinder the denunciation and deterrence of crime, nor does primary consideration given to those objectives, and to the vulnerability of Indigenous women in intimate partnerships, preclude proper application of Indigenous background principles.”




Big Canoe, meanwhile, also agrees with the emphasis on the specific circumstances of Indigenous women who’ve been victims of violence. In fact, she noted, while intimate violence affecting people of many ethnic groups in Canada often comes from other members of the same ethnic group, Indigenous women face a higher rate of violence from non-Indigenous people.




“Where the judicial or justice system has also failed Indigenous, MMIW, Two-Spirited people, is men don’t get prosecuted to the full extent of law when they’re non-Indigenous and they harm an Indigenous woman,” she explained.




“Police services and enforcement and judicial systems actually doing what they say they need to do in terms of sentencing, punishment, denouncement — that doesn’t happen with regularity when an Indigenous woman is harmed by a non-Indigenous person.”




View from the bench of the Supreme Court of Canada. Photo: Supreme Court of Canada Collection







Sentencing circles and Indigenous perspectives




In the Aboriginal Legal Services’ press release following the verdict, Big Canoe said, “We are pleased that the majority of the Supreme Court recognized the important contribution sentencing circles can make to ensure that Indigenous perspectives are considered in cases involving Indigenous people.”




The release underlined paragraph 107 of the decision, that sentencing circles “should be treated as a bridge between the criminal justice system and Indigenous models of justice, not an exercise in performative tokenism, which will only erode trust, set back reconciliation and exacerbate the challenges Indigenous people face with the criminal justice system.”




Speaking with APTN, Big Canoe noted there’s no Criminal Code obligation for courts to give deference to Indigenous Circles, communities or processes. Meanwhile, she noted, two per cent of the Ontario Bar is Indigenous, and while that appears to meet parity with two per cent of the Ontario population being Indigenous, it fails to respond to judicial districts like Kenora, where Indigenous people represent some 87 per cent of those on criminal dockets. It’s not uncommon for an offender, or a victim, to be the only Indigenous person in the courtroom.




Big Canoe praised the increased diversity of judges — including the presence of Abenaki justice O’Bonsawin —in recent years.




“For many years, we didn’t have a very diverse bench like we do now,” she said. “A lot of judges would be disconnected from a lot of different communities or groups — not understanding a Black background, not understanding an immigrant background.”




Yet the judge’s job, she said, was to recognize all such factors and take them into consideration, and to both understand and apply however many facts as are relevant to the case.




“The entire judicial system is obviously not designed with looking at rehabilitative justice in the same way Indigenous perspectives would.”




Ivstitia, justice in latin, is one of two statues that stand outside the Supreme Court just a block away from Parliament Hill. Photo: APTN.







These perspectives are broad, she said, and a great number of Indigenous people in the justice system have been affected by systems that do not include them.




“There’s no work that we do that’s not connected to the genocide and the harm that’s been caused to Indigenous people from things like Indian residential school,” she said. “But at the end of the day, you’ve got to think about what’s helping. If it’s just continuing to create more violence and harm, it’s clearly not working.




“When something happens like that, what do you do? In our traditional societies, we wouldn’t just keep doing the same thing if it was having a bad result. But that’s what we do in this system because it’s an entire system, and how do you break an entire system?”




Binding Case Law




In the nearly 30 years since the Gladue case in 1999, various courts have tried and failed to implement its directions properly, while others have had some successes. Big Canoe said she hopes the Supreme Court decision in R. v. Cope helps clarify the process.




“I hope the decision helps courts understand not only how they have to apply Gladue, but how they have to balance between the harm, the newer provisions that say that you must treat it as aggravating, and what does that balance look like? It’s not going to look the same every time because that’s the whole point of the balancing exercise.”




Big Canoe noted that Gladue applies to Indigenous women who have been accused or convicted of a crime as well, and that Indigenous mass-incarceration likewise exists in women’s prisons. Nearly 50 per cent of women in prison in Canada are Indigenous.




“As long as people aren’t applying Gladue or as long as people aren’t taking into consideration as an aggravating factor the harm it causes an Indigenous woman, then we’re going to continue to see increased victimization of Indigenous women or further mass incarceration of Indigenous people.”




And while she says courts are notoriously slow-moving, Big Canoe noted a Supreme Court decision means there is now a standard by which other cases can be measured.




“If the court doesn’t follow the test or doesn’t follow whatever the Supreme Court lays out, then at least it’s appealable,” she said. “And someone can make an appeal. It takes a long time. It’s a hard system to go through. But then at least there’s an opportunity if someone’s not following the law for you to have recourse.”




 




The post 

Supreme Court decision balances Gladue factors against concern for Indigenous women

 appeared first on 

APTN News

.

author: Maira Escardovelli
title: Terror das feministas: radicais, deputadas conservadoras disputam poder na extrema direita
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando 

aqui

.













O terror das feministas. É como se autointitulam Ana Caroline Campagnolo e Eduarda Campopiano, as deputadas estaduais mais votadas em Santa Catarina e São Paulo. Ambas do Partido Liberal (PL), elas se apresentam como amigas em posts nas redes sociais e se dizem admiradoras  de Olavo de Carvalho. Juntas, as duas somaram mais de 2,3 milhões de votos na eleição de 2026. Ao lado delas, ocupando o posto de deputada estadual mais votada do Estado, está Índia Armelau, também do PL, que conquistou 248.504 votos para a Assembleia Legislativa do Rio de Janeiro. 




São 

mulheres que se unem ao clã de Michelle Bolsonaro (PL-DF), Damares Alves (Republicanos-DF), Bia Kicis (PL-DF) e Celina Leão (PP-DF) pela pauta anti-identitária e antiaborto

, mas que, segundo especialistas ouvidas pela 

Agência Pública

, não pertencem ao mesmo grupo de suas antecessoras, inclusive considerando a construção de narrativas para o eleitorado. 




Na visão de Lívia Reis, coordenadora de Religião e Política no Instituto de Estudos da Religião (ISER), a extrema-direita conquistou uma pluralidade de candidaturas femininas nesta eleição, o que pode criar uma disputa pelo poder de influência entre as próprias eleitas. 




“O Valdemar [Costa Neto, presidente do PL] não está preocupado com o alinhamento ideológico de uma influenciadora, ele quer que ela seja eleita e vote com ele”, argumenta a antropóloga em referência a eleição de Eduarda Campopiano, atualmente com mais de 2,5 milhões de seguidores do Instagram.

 “Vejo que talvez isso seja também um dos atritos que a própria Michelle vai ter com ele, porque ela quer centralizar o PL Mulheres

 e as candidaturas femininas, mas o próprio PL vai apostar em quem quiser”, explica Reis. 




Vereadora de Praia Grande, no litoral paulista, Eduarda Campopiano foi eleita para a Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo como uma espécie de discípula de Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG), deputado federal mais votado da história do país, com mais de 22 milhões de seguidores no Instagram. Outro aliado é o vereador paulistano Lucas Pavanato (PL), que detém mais de 5 milhões de seguidores na rede social da Meta e foi eleito para deputado federal com mais de 3 milhões de votos. 




“O PL sabe o poder das redes sociais. Todas as candidaturas se forjam ali, eles estão elegendo influenciadores há muito tempo e agora chegaram ao ápice dos candidatos mais votados serem os influenciadores. Por isso, eu diria que a Eduarda chega [ao partido] com tanto poder quanto a Michelle. E vai disputar isso”, explica Reis. 




A esposa do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, preso por tentativa de golpe de Estado, protagonizou em junho deste ano o seu primeiro embate público com o Partido. Após a rejeição da sigla ao nome indicado por ela ao Senado pelo Ceará, o da deputada Priscila Costa (PL-CE), Michelle publicou um vídeo contando que Flávio Bolsonaro a havia desrespeitado durante a formação dos arranjos partidários nos estados. “Ele disse que seria melhor eu ficar fora das decisões do partido. Disse que eu havia chegado ontem e não entendia nada de política”, afirmou a ex-primeira dama.




No vídeo, ela exaltou sua atuação à frente do PL Mulher, ala de mulheres conservadoras do partido: “[em 2024] elegemos 45,8% mais mulheres que em 2020. Foram 1.005 mulheres eleitas”, disse. Com a instauração da crise, que abalou a campanha à presidência de Flávio Bolsonaro, e após se reunir com Costa Neto, Michelle anunciou sua saída da presidência do PL Mulher. 




Na visão de parlamentares próximos ao PL, Campopiano representa um discurso mais radical da extrema-direita, capitaneado por Olavo de Carvalho

, conhecido como o “guru” do bolsonarismo. “Eu acho que ela [Eduarda] vem muito daquela linha do Olavo de Carvalho, que é essa juventude conservadora formada. Mas creio que com a maturidade ela vai entender que a pauta feminina não é uma pauta feminista. A gente vai ter ainda um tempo para fazer esse convencimento”, disse à 

Pública

 a senadora Damares Alves, que também afirmou que irá dialogar nesse sentido com a deputada Índia Armelau.   




A pesquisadora do Centro Brasileiro de Análise e Planejamento (CEBRAP) Jacqueline Teixeira aponta que o discurso de Campopiano pode ser entendido a partir dos efeitos produzidos por políticas que começaram, entre 2014 a 2016, a proibir gênero nos parâmetros curriculares. Segundo a antropóloga, que realiza pesquisas na área de gênero, raça, sexualidade e religião, trata-se de uma geração jovem que cresceu em uma “escuta mais próxima do antifeminismo” e que, portanto, se apresenta como “mais refratária” às conquistas do movimento. 




“Estamos falando de coisas que aconteceram no cenário político e que produziram efeitos direto nas escolas nos últimos 12 anos. Então, é a chegada desse grupo muito jovem no cenário democrático, com uma série de entendimentos, sem necessariamente terem conseguido produzir um repertório de várias dessas heranças e da importância delas. 

Eles acabam se engajando mais numa proposta disruptiva de política, que vai, consequentemente, levar a um lugar mais conservador para pensar as políticas públicas”

, analisa Teixeira. 




Uma das professoras de Campopiano nesse aspecto é a deputada estadual Ana Carolina Campagnolo, eleita, pela segunda vez, como a mais votada no estado de Santa Catarina. Em sua biografia no Instagram, a parlamentar se classifica como “conservadora, cristã e antifeminista”, e frequentemente se refere a Olavo de Carvalho para basear suas propostas e conteúdos publicados na rede social. Ela é autora do livro “Feminismo: perversão e subversão”. 




“Em São Paulo, a sua deputada estadual é Eduarda Campopiano, que eu tenho orgulho em dizer que é minha amiga, minha leitora (…) Se você quer ter a sua deputada que parece com a Ana Campagnolo aí em São Paulo, tenho certeza que essa pessoa é a Eduarda Campopiano”, afirma Campagnolo em vídeo no Instagram ao lado de Eduarda. “Ana, a nossa intenção é barrar os avanços da extrema esquerda no estado de São Paulo assim como você consegue fazer tão bem”, completa Campopiano na publicação. 




Defensora da pauta anti-identitária e do homeschooling, Campagnolo chegou a pedir em maio deste ano apoio na Assembleia Legislativa do Estado de Santa Catarina ao Projeto de Lei 2.577/2026 apresentado na Câmara dos Deputados, que “concede anistia a pais ou responsáveis que tenham sido investigados, processados, condenados ou penalizados administrativa, civil ou criminalmente pela prática de educação domiciliar”. 




A proposta é de autoria da deputada federal Caroline de Toni (PL-SC), eleita agora para o Senado com 2.694.918 votos. Também é dela o PL 4.213/2020, que altera a Lei nº 9.504/97 para extinguir a reserva mínima de 30% das vagas para mulheres nas candidaturas para mandatos eletivos preenchidos pelo sistema proporcional (deputadas federais, estaduais e vereadores).




Ao lado delas, está a deputada federal Júlia Zanatta (PL-SC), reeleita com 560.223 votos. Em comemoração, no último domingo, 4 de outubro, a parlamentar caminhou entre seu apartamento e o comitê de campanha, em Florianópolis, dando chicotadas na rua. Uma de suas principais referências também é Olavo de Carvalho, de quem foi aluna e até visitou em Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos. Em 2024, Zanatta apresentou na Câmara o PL 3.338/2024, que “assegura aos pais e responsáveis o direito de vedar a participação de seus filhos em atividades pedagógicas de gênero em âmbito nacional”. 




Já em 2025, a parlamentar apresentou um projeto de lei para alterar a Lei Maria da Penha, para prever punições a mulheres que fizerem falsas acusações de violência ou utilizarem de maneira “indevida” as medidas protetivas de violência doméstica. Zanatta também é contra o 

PL da Misoginia

. 







Negação do feminicídio




Em uma das postagens de Campopiano mais republicadas nas redes sociais, a vereadora afirma que “feminicídio não existe”. A questão, no entanto, é reconhecida por parlamentares que buscam encabeçar o movimento de mulheres da direita na política, caso da própria senadora Damares e de Celina Leão, também amiga de Michelle Bolsonaro, e atual candidata ao governo do Distrito Federal. 




“Eu acho um erro isso [a ideia de que feminicídio não existe], 

é um erro, é um reforço. Como é que a gente saberia quantas mulheres são assassinadas se você não tivesse a tipificação desse crime?”

, afirmou Celina Leão à 

Pública.

 À frente do governo Distrito Federal, após o então governador Ibaneis Rocha renunciar ao cargo em março de 2026, Celina disputa no segundo turno, à reeleição, contra o candidato Leandro Grass, do PT.  




Ela terminou o pleito com 825.530 votos, o que representa 49,93% do total de votos válidos. Fortemente apoiada por Michelle, que adotou a estratégia do voto casado ao Senado para ela e Bia Kicis, Celina disse a jornalistas na última terça-feira,  6 de outubro, que acredita não ter sido eleita no primeiro turno devido à “confusão” dos eleitores ao escolherem o número na urna. No domingo, mais de 26 mil pessoas no Distrito Federal digitaram 22, o número do PL, ao votarem para governador, apesar de não haver um candidato ao posto com essa identificação. 




“Claro que existe uma concentração de coisas mais à direita, mas essas mulheres acabam sendo levadas a defender pautas e determinadas políticas públicas que as puxam mais para o centro do que para a extrema-direita. Pode acontecer com a Damares, por exemplo, no Senado. 

Você vê que a Damares ali é bem mais centro-direita do que era, por exemplo, quando ela estava no governo Bolsonaro”

, avalia Jacqueline Teixeira. 




Questionada pela reportagem sobre a expectativa em relação às pautas que serão tratadas por Michelle no Senado, Damares afirmou, inclusive, que não haverá “retrocesso de direitos”, uma das principais críticas de eleitoras contrárias ao movimento de mulheres conservadoras na política. 




“A Michelle é uma mulher conservadora, mas de um coração voltado para o social. Então está todo mundo preocupado ‘vai ter retrocesso de direitos’. Não vai, nós teremos sentinelas aqui dentro”, afirmou Alves. Sem detalhar possíveis ações da ex-primeira dama, a senadora afirmou que Michelle vai se dedicar a pautas ligadas à proteção de mães atípicas e das crianças. “Nenhum retrocesso, nenhum direito a menos, e nada sobre nós sem nós, com a presença deles o tempo todo aqui dentro”, disse a senadora. 




Na visão de Lívia Reis, do ISER, o que une essa heterogeneidade de candidaturas de mulheres da extrema-direita é, sobretudo, a agenda anti-identitária, mobilizada por elas mesmas. “Quando a Michelle fala naquele vídeo, de crítica ao Flávio, que estava sofrendo violência de gênero, ela está nomeando a violência que ela sofre a partir de uma identidade. Isso é histórico na direita, eles mobilizam pautas identitárias, acusando o outro de identitários, mas eles nunca deixaram de mobilizar suas identidades para atuar politicamente, e não está sendo diferente agora”, conclui.

author: infolibre
title: Οι κινητοποιήσεις συνεχίζονται παντού στη Γαλλία
content:
Παρίσι – Ανταπόκριση: Ηρώ Σιαφλιάκη




Η

 πλατεία της Βαστίλης γέμισε σήμερα ασφυκτικά με χαρούμενους νέους και νέες. Αποφασισμένους, από ότι φαίνεται, να δείξουν πως η παρούσα εξέγερση δεν είναι ένα εφηβικό ξέσπασμα, αλλά μια πολιτική πράξη ριζοσπαστικής χειραφέτησης και μια ρήξη με την σημερινή τάξη πραγμάτων. Αυτό που ήδη κατάφεραν είναι να έχουν μια ξεκάθαρα αντιφασιστική (και αντι-εξουσιαστική) παρουσία : το ρυθμό έδιναν και σήμερα σλόγκαν κατά της ακροδεξιάς και κατά της αστυνομίας. 




500 οι ιδιαίτερα βάναυσες προσαγωγές, ήταν αργά το απόγευμα. Συνολικά 6.500 συλλήψεις ανηλίκων σε δέκα μέρες. Μια τέτοια καταστολή είναι πρωτοφανής όχι μόνο για τη Γαλλία. Επίσης, από την αρχή των κινητοποιήσεων, στις 17 Σεπτέμβρη, 215 μαθητές και 85 μέλη του εκπαιδευτικού προσωπικού έχουν τραυματιστεί βαριά.




Τις 

τελευταίες μέρες στις πόλεις 

Bourgoin

–

Jallieu

, 

Troyes

 και 

Dunkerque

 αυτόπτες μάρτυρες φίλμαραν αυτοκίνητα της αστυνομίας να ορμούν μέσα στο πλήθος των διαδηλωτών. 




Οι μαθητές στη Γαλλία έδωσαν ήδη νέα μέρα διαδήλωσης την επόμενη Τρίτη (13/10). Ταυτόχρονα σημειώνονται μαθητικές κινητοποιήσεις στο Βέλγιο, στην Ιταλία, στη Γερμανία, στην Ισπανία, στη Χιλή, ακόμα και στην Αργεντινή του Μιλέι.

 




ΑΙΤΙΑ ΑΠΟΥΣΙΑΣ

 

: Πολλοί απασχολημένοι να αγωνιζόμαστε για το μέλλον μας !




Η νεολαία θυμωμένη (

FACHEE

) όχι φασιστική (

FACHO

)







Σήμερα δεν είμαι 

vegan

, το μενού έχει κοτόπουλο (κοτόπουλο/

poulet

 : στην αργκό ο αστυνομικός)







Δεν ξέρω πια για ποιον λόγο διαδηλώνω, υπάρχουν τόσοι πολλοί λόγοι










Αβράκωτος (γλωσσοπαίγνιο: ξεβράκωτος, χωρίς προστασία, και οι ριζοσπαστικές λαϊκές τάξεις κατά τη διάρκεια της

 

Γαλλικής Επανάστασης

) κατά Ρομποκόπ







Χωρίς μπάτσους το Παρίσι είναι μαγικό




Η εξέγερση των μαθητών ήταν μια έκπληξη. Ξεκίνησε από προάστια του Παρισιού κι εξαπλώθηκε γρήγορα παντού. Οι νέοι εμφανίστηκαν στο προσκήνιο καταγγέλλοντας την έλλειψη μέσων στην εκπαίδευση. Αναπάντεχα, αυτοοργανώθηκαν και έθεσαν ζητήματα που ξεπερνούσαν την έλλειψη καθηγητών ή τις ακατάλληλες αίθουσες. Στην πλατεία της Βαστίλης, στο «

 

δάσος

 

» των πανκαρτ μπορούμε να διαβάσουμε 

Δεν ξέρω πια για πιο λόγο διαδηλώνω, υπάρχουν τόσοι πολλοί

. 




Το μέλλον που διακρίνουν μπροστά τους, μεταξύ ανεργίας και πολεμικής απειλής δεν φαίνεται επιθυμητό. Και η πρώτη αντίδραση ήρθε, αυτή τη φορά, από μαθητές των λαικών περιοχών στην περιφέρεια της πόλης, όπου οι κοινωνικές διακρίσεις είναι περισσότερο από φανερές, κι η αστυνομική παρουσία είναι εδώ και καιρό απαράδεκτη. Είναι γι αυτό ίσως που η καταστολή ήρθε τόσο άμεσα και είναι τόσο βίαιη; 




Η κυβερνητική δημοσιογραφία, αφού σιώπησε τις πρώτες μέρες την αστυνομική βία, χρησιμοποίησε γι άλλη μια φορά τα γνωστά επιχειρήματα, της καταστροφής της πόλης, την διάκριση μεταξύ «

 

κάποιων μπαχαλάκιδων

 

» μαθητών και των «

 

πολλών άλλων

 

» που προσδοκούν να ξεκινήσουν επιτέλους τα μαθήματα τους, μεταδίδοντας συστηματικά τους αριθμούς των καμένων κάδων σκουπιδιών. Νεαρός μαθητής , παρέλασε μάλιστα ως «

 

εκπρόσωπος

 

» των μαθητών, σε πολλά κανάλια, ώσπου αποκαλύφθηκε πως ήταν βοηθός βουλευτού του 

Attal

, εφήμερου πρωθυπουργού του Μακρόν, και φυσικά ούτε καν μαθητής. Ενώ στο 

Belfort

, νεαρός «

 

διαδηλωτής

 

» που αρχικά κατηγορήθηκε για απόπειρα δολοφονίας αστυνομικών αποδείχθηκε … αστυνομικός, μεταμφιεσμένος σε 

black bloc

. 




Πάντως οι ιδιαίτερα έξυπνες και ποιητικές φράσεις που γράφονται, τα φανερά αντι-εξουσιαστικά σλόγκαν, όπως και αυτά υπέρ της ματωμένης Παλαιστίνης, η αυτοοργάνωση χωρίς ηγετίσκους και τα τραγούδια θυμίζουν Κίτρινα Γιλέκα. Θα εξαπλωθεί άραγε η εξέγερση, ίσως και σε άλλους χώρους, ή με άλλες πρακτικές; Σίγουρα την ώρα που όλοι περίμεναν τις ερχόμενες εκλογές τις άνοιξης, οι ανήλικοι μαθητές, που δεν μετρούν ούτε καν σαν ψηφοφόροι, ανοίγουν μια πολύ πιο σημαντική κι ενδιαφέρουσα σελίδα. 




Μετά μια σειρά κινητοποιήσεων των Πανεπιστημίων τις τελευταίες ημέρες σε

 

ένδειξη αλληλεγγύης προς το μαθητικό κίνημα

 

(χτες το 

Sciences Po

 και το 

Dauphine

 στο Παρίσι, το Πανεπιστήμιο στη Νάντη με 2.000 φοιτητές να το καταλαμβάνουν), 

πραγματοποιήθηκε σήμερα ιστορικός αποκλεισμός (

blocus

)

 

στο Πανεπιστήμιο

 

Paris

–

Panth

é

on

–

Assas

, 

πρωτοφανές γεγονός

 

για τη συγκεκριμένη σχολή, η οποία θεωρείται παραδοσιακά συντηρητική και σπάνια συμμετέχει σε φοιτητικές κινητοποιήσεις.




Ανάμεσα σε άλλες πρωτοβουλίες, αυτές τις μέρες οι αγρότες βρέθηκαν δίπλα στους μαθητές είτε προσφέροντας πρωινό έξω από τα μπλοκαρισμένα σχολεία (στο Μπορντό), είτε προστατεύοντας τα λύκεια με τρακτέρ (

Ard

è

che

), μοιράζοντας ζεστές σούπες και λαχανικά στους μαθητές που διαδήλωναν (

Reims

) ή στηρίζοντας τον αποκλεισμό ενός αγροτικού λυκείου και προμήθευοντας τους νέους με βιολογικά και τοπικά προϊόντα (το συνδικάτο 

Conf

é

d

é

ration Paysanne

 στο 

Deux

–

S

è

vres

).




The post 

Οι κινητοποιήσεις συνεχίζονται παντού στη Γαλλία

 first appeared on 

infolibre

.
