title: Berlin Twinning Association visits partner city Dêrik
content:
A delegation from the Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg–Dêrik Twinning Association has been visiting its partner city of Dêrik in Rojava since September 28. During meetings with the city’s new leadership and visits to schools, healthcare facilities and water projects, the focus has been both on political and administrative changes and on continuing the long-standing partnership.




At the beginning of the visit, the delegation met Dêrik’s new mayor, Mihemed, and her deputy, Carlos Kori. The discussions focused on the current integration process in Syria, changes to municipal structures and future cooperation with Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg. During an official reception, the delegation also met Şero Şero, who holds an important regional role as district governor.




“Reliable relationships at the municipal level are particularly important at a time when political and administrative structures are undergoing fundamental change,” said Janosch Tries, a board member of the Twinning Association.







Featured image © Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg–Dêrik Twinning Association e.V.










Economic crisis weighs on daily life




The political changes are unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing severe economic crisis. Sharp increases in fuel prices are driving up the cost of daily life. Numerous public-sector employees, including doctors at state hospitals, are still waiting to receive their salaries. At the same time, many internally displaced people continue to live in camps in the greater Dêrik area. Healthcare is also shaped by the long-term consequences of the war that has continued since 2011. Thousands of doctors have left Syria, and access to medical care remains limited, particularly in rural areas.




Mobile clinic serves 19 villages




The Berlin delegation accompanied several visits by the Mobile Clinic, which has been operating with support from the Twinning Association since 2020. Established jointly with the Foundation of Free Women in Syria (SJAS), the project is aimed particularly at women and children in remote communities, where the nearest healthcare facility is often far away. The Mobile Clinic visits 19 villages in the surrounding area of Dêrik every month. Last year, more than 1,000 women received medical care through the project. In addition to examinations and treatment, its services include first-aid courses and medical information sessions.




Schools face switch to Arabic




The political changes are currently particularly evident in the education sector. The delegation visited four schools that had been renovated with support from the Twinning Association and its partner organizations. In recent weeks, Kurdish students and families in various parts of Rojava have protested against restrictions on Kurdish-language education. “Our language is Kurdish—and we have a right to it,” was one of their central demands.




Teachers at the schools visited by the delegation also reported sudden changes. Instructions from Damascus require most teaching to be switched to Arabic. For many children, this poses a significant challenge, as they have grown up speaking Kurdish in their daily lives. “This abrupt transition is extremely difficult for the children. But what are we supposed to do? If we don’t follow the Arabic curricula, they won’t receive a school-leaving certificate,” one teacher said.




According to teachers, there have also been changes to religious education. Whereas lessons previously covered different religions and shared ethical values, the new curricula have a markedly more conservative Islamic orientation.




Further water projects planned




Another focus of the visit is water supply. During a meeting with the responsible water authority, the delegation discussed the continuation of joint projects. These efforts build on the solar-powered well completed in the Şehîd Xebat neighborhood in 2024. The facility supplies around 5,000 people with drinking water. The talks are intended to identify areas in which cooperation on water supply can be continued and expanded through additional projects.

author: Unknown
title: Satellite images document ecological destruction in Southern Kurdistan
content:
Satellite images from twenty areas in the Duhok province in Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq)  document the extent of ecological destruction linked to the Turkish occupation. Comparisons of the images show how formerly forested mountain slopes were extensively cleared within just a few years and opened up by new roads. The regions of Zaxo and Amêdî, where the Turkish army has been expanding its military infrastructure for years, have been particularly affected, according to a report by the Mezopotamya News Agency (MA).




Particularly since the intensification of Turkish incursions into Zap, Avaşîn and Metîna in 2017, numerous roads and military bases have been constructed in the mountainous regions. Forest areas are cleared for their construction, fragmenting previously contiguous landscapes. At the same time, large quantities of timber have been transported from the affected areas to Turkey for years.




Deforestation in the mountainous regions of Behdînan




The Behdînan region, particularly the areas of Zaxo, Duhok, Berwarî Bala and Amêdî, has been especially severely affected. Deforestation there has once again intensified recently. According to research conducted on the ground, the companies involved are stepping up their operations ahead of winter. The felled trees are loaded onto trucks under military supervision and transported across the border into Turkey.




According to the research, Turkish companies are involved in logging operations. Hundreds of thousands of trees are reported to have been felled in the affected areas in recent years. Among the locations where logging is currently particularly intensive are the villages of Mîska, Qumri, Hirûrê, Kêste, Tirwaniş and Nizdûrê in Berwarî Bala.







Çiyayê Basêr / Barzan / Amêdî, 2017-2022


​​​​







The continued destruction of the forests has met with resistance from the local population. Residents of the affected areas are calling on both the Iraqi federal government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) to take action against the deforestation.




Ali Teter, governor of the KDP-run Duhok province, rejected reports of the logging. He claimed that the published images had been taken in Turkey and did not show deforestation within the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Journalists on the ground disputed this account and confirmed that the trees are being felled in Southern Kurdistan and subsequently transported to Turkey.




Twenty sites examined over several years




The scale of the environmental damage is evident from comparisons of satellite images from twenty areas in Duhok province. The images cover different periods between 2013 and 2023 and show both the loss of extensive tree cover and the construction of new roads and access routes.




The changes are particularly striking north of the village of Dêreşîş in the Zaxo region. While an image from 2018 still shows largely contiguous forest cover on Mount Celde, by 2023 the area had been extensively deforested. Numerous roads and tracks cut across the slopes, with only scattered patches of the former tree cover remaining.







Dêreşîş, 2018-2023








The landscape northeast of the village of Êkmale in the Zaxo-Batîfa region also changed considerably within a short period. Between 2017 and 2019, a large proportion of the vegetation disappeared from one of the areas examined. The previously predominantly forested slope was replaced by extensive barren areas and a branching network of roads and tracks.







Êkmale, 2017-2019








Another example can be found in the Amêdî region, around two kilometers northeast of the Gilalte stream near the former settlement of Horkî. A comparison of images from 2015 and 2021 shows a significant decline in vegetation. The more recent image reveals largely barren mountain slopes crisscrossed by numerous roads and tracks.







Horkî, 2015-2021








Other areas examined are located west and east of the town of Gelûk, around Senat, and on the slopes of the Gurvil and Girê Heşkî mountains. These also include areas near Kûxkê and Barzan in Amêdî. The comparisons demonstrate that the environmental damage is not confined to individual military sites but extends across large parts of the mountainous Behdînan region.







Çiyayê Qîra / Gelûk, 2018-2020










The scale of the destruction extends beyond satellite imagery




The satellite images analyzed extend through 2023. The deforestation and expansion of military infrastructure in the years that followed are therefore not yet reflected in these image comparisons. In particular, the recently reported intensification of logging falls outside the documented period.




At the same time, the images clearly show how closely the loss of tree cover at numerous locations is linked to the construction of new transport routes. Roads, military bases and access routes extend deep into the mountainous landscape and fragment contiguous forest areas.




As the Turkish army has continued to expand its presence in Southern Kurdistan, the ecological consequences of these developments remain directly felt by the affected population. Residents are calling on the governments in Baghdad and Hewlêr (Erbil) to halt the ongoing deforestation and protect the region’s natural resources and livelihoods.

author: Unknown
title: KHRN reports enforced disappearances of five Kurdish opposition figures in Iran
content:
The security agencies of the Islamic Republic of Iran, specifically the Ministry of Intelligence and the Intelligence Organization of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have increasingly deployed enforced disappearance against members of Kurdish opposition groups since June 2025, following the outbreak of the 12-day Israel-Iran conflict, which also involved US military strikes.




At least five Kurdish political activists have since been subjected to enforced disappearance: Mohsen Ghaderi, Sara Rashidi Kachlanlou, Zahra Pirdehghan, Parvin (Akhtar) Rasegh Qizilbash and Sirwan Habibi. They were arrested in Baneh, Paveh, Orumiyeh, and Kamyaran, and subsequently subjected to enforced disappearance.




Despite credible eyewitness testimonies and evidence confirming their detention by Iranian government security forces, Iran’s judicial authorities have not formally registered their detention. Security agencies also continue to deny their families information about their whereabouts or custody status.




This situation places the detainees outside the protection of the law, depriving them of access to legal counsel, communication with their families and necessary medical care.




These enforced disappearances have emerged amid a shift in detention practices following the recent regional hostilities and the bombardment of several security facilities.




The emerging pattern involves the relocation of detainees to unofficial detention facilities, denial of due process and restrictions on communication with legal representatives and family members.




Previously, individuals arrested in the Kurdish region were generally transferred to designated intelligence detention centres in provincial capitals. Security agencies are now increasingly holding detainees in secret facilities or relocating them to detention facilities in neighbouring provinces, including Hamadan and East Azerbaijan.




In all five documented cases, state agencies have refused to acknowledge responsibility for the arrests. Relevant local courts have consistently refused to provide information, effectively blocking families from pursuing legal avenues to establish the fate and whereabouts of their relatives.




As a result, all five detainees have been completely cut off from the outside world, with their current whereabouts and conditions remaining unknown.




The following section documents the circumstances surrounding the arrests and subsequent enforced disappearances of the five Kurdish political activists.




Mohsen Ghaderi




Political affiliation: Free Life Party of Kurdistan (PJAK)




Date of arrest: 22 June 2025




Location: Hangeh-Zhal border area, Baneh




Detaining agency: IRGC Intelligence Organization




Mohsen Ghaderi was arrested alongside a local border worker (kolbar) in the Hangeh-Zhal border area of Baneh on 22 June 2025.




Following their arrest, both men were taken to an IRGC facility in Baneh before being transferred to the IRGC Intelligence Organization’s Shahramfar detention centre in Sanandaj.




The kolbar, who was released on bail after three months, confirmed that no military engagement had taken place at the time of their arrest.




However, the IRGC Intelligence Organization twice summoned Ghaderi’s family in mid-2025, claiming that he had been killed during a military confrontation and prohibiting the family from holding a funeral service.




Local inquiries and accounts from residents contradict the Iranian authorities’ narrative, indicating that both individuals were taken into custody without any armed confrontation.




Ghaderi was last seen at the Shahramfar detention facility in September 2025. Unconfirmed reports indicate that he may subsequently have been transferred to an IRGC intelligence detention facility in Orumiyeh.




The Iranian authorities had previously made false claims regarding Ghaderi’s death following a July 2021 ambush in Bukan. Ghaderi later publicly rejected those claims in a video message.




Despite evidence of his detention, the authorities have not acknowledged his current custody status or disclosed his whereabouts.




Sara Rashidi Kachlanlou




Political affiliation: A Kurdish opposition party




Date of arrest: 11 January 2026




Location: Kermanshah–Paveh Road, near Paveh




Detaining agency: IRGC Intelligence Organization




Sara Rashidi Kachlanlou was arrested without a court warrant while travelling in a civilian vehicle on the Kermanshah–Paveh road during the January 2026 protests.




Following her arrest, she was transferred to the IRGC Intelligence Organization’s Nabi Akram detention centre in Meydan Naft, Kermanshah.




Despite repeated inquiries by her family, security and judicial authorities in Kermanshah have refused to provide any information regarding her custody status or whereabouts.




The authorities have not formally acknowledged her detention, leaving her family without information about her fate or access to legal procedures to establish her whereabouts.




Zahra Pirdehghan and Parvin (Akhtar) Rasegh Qizilbash




Political affiliation: Society of Free Women of Eastern Kurdistan (KJAR)




Dates of arrest: 25 June 2026 (Pirdehghan) and 28 June 2026 (Rasegh Qizilbash)




Location: Orumiyeh




Detaining agency: IRGC Intelligence Organization




Zahra Pirdehghan, 32, and Parvin (Akhtar) Rasegh Qizilbash, 33, were arrested by the IRGC Intelligence Organization while engaging in political activities in Orumiyeh.




Pirdehghan was arrested on 25 June 2026, followed by Rasegh Qizilbash on 28 June 2026.




Reports indicate that Pirdehghan was initially held at an IRGC intelligence detention facility in Tabriz before being transferred to an undisclosed detention facility in Orumiyeh.




Their families have repeatedly approached local courts, the Ministry of Intelligence, and the IRGC Intelligence Organization seeking information about their detention and whereabouts.




However, these inquiries have yielded no official acknowledgment of their detention, and the authorities continue to withhold information about their fate and custody status.




Both women remain subjected to enforced disappearance, without confirmed access to their families or legal representatives.




Sirwan Habibi (also known as Aram Sine)




Political affiliation: Free Life Party of Kurdistan (PJAK)




Date of arrest: 9 September 2026




Location: Baath town, Kamyaran




Detaining agency: Ministry of Intelligence




Sirwan Habibi, also known by his PJAK code name Aram Sine, was arrested by Ministry of Intelligence operatives during a security operation in Baath town, Kamyaran, in the early hours of 9 September 2026.




According to eyewitness accounts, Ministry of Intelligence operatives in unmarked vehicles surrounded several streets in the area before carrying out the arrest.




At approximately 01:00 local time, intelligence agents intentionally struck Habibi’s motorcycle with a vehicle that moved at high speed. This had severely injured Habibi.




Eyewitnesses reported that Habibi was unarmed but the intelligence agents continued to beat him despite his injuries. They then covered his head and took him away in a civilian vehicle.




Plainclothes agents also fired live ammunition into the air to disperse bystanders, some of whom had attempted to administer first aid to the injured man.




Local police patrols (Emergency 110) were called to the scene by intelligence agents who, according to eyewitnesses, had described the incident as a “security matter”.




Despite eyewitness testimonies confirming Habibi’s arrest by Ministry of Intelligence operatives, judicial and intelligence authorities in Kamyaran and Sanandaj continue to deny knowledge of his detention.




No official court case has been registered, and the authorities have refused to disclose his whereabouts or provide information about his physical condition.




Given the severe injuries he sustained during the arrest, the continued denial of information regarding his detention raises serious concerns about his health and access to necessary medical treatment.




Other documented cases of enforced disappearance




These five cases are not isolated incidents of state-enforced disappearance in Iran’s Kurdish region.




Other Kurdish political activists documented by the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN), including Idris Faqhi and Osman Mame, remain forcibly disappeared years after being taken into custody by Iranian security forces.




Despite repeated efforts to establish their fate and whereabouts, the Iranian authorities have continued to refuse to clarify what happened to them or acknowledge responsibility for their detention.




The five recent cases, alongside those long-standing disappearances, indicate a continuing pattern in which Iranian security agencies detain Kurdish opposition figures while refusing to acknowledge their custody or disclose their whereabouts.




The relocation of detainees to undisclosed facilities, denial of communication with families and legal representatives, and refusal by judicial authorities to register their detention have further restricted the ability of families to pursue legal avenues.




These practices leave detainees outside the protection of the law and raise serious concerns about their physical safety, access to medical care, as well as exposure to torture and other forms of ill-treatment.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Admits He Wants to Privatize Social Security
content:
“I wanted to do it so badly,” Trump said of his desire to privatize Social Security in his first year in office.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In remarks to reporters at the White House on Wednesday, President Donald Trump admitted that he wanted to push for privatizing Social Security in his first term in office, contradicting campaign promises he made in 2016 and earlier that he wouldn’t touch the popular social safety net program.

“I wanted to ride with Social Security being fully invested in the stock market, in the first month of my first year, so 2016,” Trump said, errantly conflating the year he was elected to the year he was inaugurated.

Trump complained that he wasn’t able to do so due to “tremendous criticism from the Democrats and some Republicans.”

Trump: I wanted to ride with Social Security being fully invested in the stock market. But I was met with opposition from Democrats and Republicans. pic.twitter.com/wv15WCI7Ze

Trump then reiterated his desire to privatize the program. “I wanted to do it so badly,” he said.

Trump described so-called “Trump Accounts,” investment accounts for children in the U.S., as “a version” of what Social Security privatization could look like — confirming observers’ fears that the accounts were a means to eventually overhaul the program.

At many points during his 2016 presidential campaign — and in the years prior to announcing a run — Trump denounced the idea of cutting Social Security as a way to reduce costs for the program, using his stance to differentiate himself from GOP rivals. But budget proposals he has sent to Congress as president have included deep cuts to Social Security.

A 2025 analysis published by Edward Lane, a professor at the Levy Economics Institute of Bard College, argued against the idea of privatization, noting that the privatization of similar retirement and social safety net programs around the world has failed.

“It is financially impossible to replace the scope of current Social Security benefits in the private market without a substantial increase in cost,” Lane noted, adding that there is also an increased financial risk in tying Social Security to the markets, as privatization “would subject retirement savings to stock market volatility, potentially leaving retirees with significantly reduced benefits during economic downturns.”

“The bottom line is that privatizing Social Security programs has not worked elsewhere, as benefits for many groups have been curtailed where it has been implemented. There is no reason to expect a different result in the U.S.,” Lane explained.

Social Security remains extremely popular among most Americans. An AARP poll published in August found that 95 percent of respondents view the program as important. Furthermore, 91 percent of Americans want Congress to enact legislation to protect Social Security so that it remains available to future generations, the survey found.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: As French Police Teargas Students, Trump Blames Protests on “Mass Migration”
content:
Over 200 students have been injured as police fired teargas and used batons against the youth protestors.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On Tuesday, Trump took to his social media platform, Truth Social, to smear the student mobilizations spreading across France as caused by “out of control mass migration” and “Islam wanting to take over.”

Other right-wing politicians and commentators echoed these spurious claims.

“This will come to America if the Democrats take power again,” claimed right-wing commentator Dave Rubin on X.

Their comments came as France’s weeks-long student movement transformed into a nationwide revolt on Tuesday, with organizers and trade unions estimating some 450,000 people protesting in 40 cities across the country.

The movement began on September 21, with high school students organizing demonstrations against poor school conditions, a neglected public education system, and dilapidated buildings. The protests began in the suburbs of Paris and quickly spread, with students blockading their schools to force them to shut.

Since the movement’s start, French police have arrested some 6,000 students — a majority of them minors. Over 200 students have been injured, as police have fired teargas and used batons against the youth protestors.

On Tuesday, France’s General Confederation of Labor (CGT) — one of the country’s largest and most powerful trade unions, representing teachers and civil servants, among other workers — joined the nationwide protests.

One of the participants in Tuesday’s demonstration, a teacher named Manel ben Boubaker, told Truthout that the mobilization was “a massive success.”

“What struck me most is that it really shows the emergence of a new generation of young people in France who are refusing the world as it has been built for them — the way the education system is organized, neoliberal policies, racism, the way our society is structured,” she said.

Manel added that 90 percent of universities in France were blockaded and shut down on Tuesday, largely by left-wing university student unions acting in solidarity with the high school protestors.

Contrary to the claims of Trump and right-wing commentators in the U.S. and internationally, Manel asserted that the student movement “is extremely organized and serious. The students have clear demands and clear slogans. They know exactly what they are fighting for.”

Manel outlined the students’ demands: more resources for public education; renovation of school buildings; free school meals; and more teachers, nurses, psychologists and social workers in their schools.

The student movement is also demanding the abolition of the university selection process and the Parcoursup platform introduced by French President Emmanuel Macron — which has restricted access to higher education, as previously high school graduates who passed their exit exam could enroll automatically in local public universities.

Manel explained that the high school student protests originated in Seine-Saint-Denis, a working-class neighborhood, in a high school largely attended by students of color. Manel works in this neighborhood.

The students, she said, “are making connections very explicitly” between the negligence at their schools, Palestinian liberation, and racism and Islamophobia.

“There are slogans about racist violence in schools, about the banning of abayas and the wearing of the hijab — in other words, about Islamophobia. We also see many Palestinian flags and Congolese flags,” she said.

“These students are part of a generation that is becoming politically conscious around questions of genocide and mass violence around the world. They are deeply outraged by what they are witnessing.”

But they are also building on a long tradition of mass protest and revolt in France, including by students and youth, dating back to May 1968, when student protests against grievances at French universities eventually grew into a general strike that paralyzed the national economy. Student movements in France have become commonplace — though today’s are being described as the most powerful student-led movement since May 1968.

“The students are mobilizing around issues that I have also fought over for many years,” Manel explained. “I personally took part in major education struggles in 2018, 2019 and 2020, as well as in the 2024 emergency plan mobilization in Seine-Saint-Denis. We went on strike for three months to demand more resources, and we got nothing.”

“We have seen a steady deterioration in the conditions of public education in France, while successive governments have pursued policies that increasingly favor the private sector.”

Manel also explained that the student movement “illustrates the failure of Macronism” — in other words, privatization and free market policies under the veneer of progress. Macron “began his presidency with the Yellow Vest movement, and he is ending it with a high school student movement. After nine years of Macronist education policies, the consequences are now impossible to ignore,” she said.

The student movement is demonstrating its rejection of Macron’s policies, but also demanding “a real break with the current system” ahead of elections that threaten to bring to power a growing far right political party.

“Yes, this movement is against Macron, but it goes beyond Macron. It is also a rejection of all those political and media leaders, all those elites, who would be willing to give us another five years of Macronism — or something even worse, potentially the Rassemblement National [the National Rally, France’s far right political party] coming to power,” Manel concluded.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: UK Terrorism Arrests up 1,553% Since Palestine Action Ban
content:
Terror arrests in the UK have increased by 1,553% and hit a record high, with the overwhelming majority linked to support for Palestine Action, new Home Office statistics show. 




3,867 arrests were made for terrorism-related activity in the year ending June 2026, compared to 234 arrests in the year ending June 2025, according to 

data released by the Home Office

 on Thursday. 




Of those arrests, a whopping 3,630 – 94% – were linked to support for Palestine Action following the group’s proscription. 




The Labour government under Keir Starmer proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group in July 2025, making it the first direct action group to be banned under the Terrorism Act in British history.




Protests against Palestine Action’s proscription, organised by campaign group Defend Our Juries (DOJ), have seen elderly and disabled people arrested and carried away by police after holding up paper signs with the words “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.” 




Since the ban, terrorism-related arrests are up 1,525% on the historical ten-year median of 238 arrests.




The Home Office’s report also confirmed that 704 arrests had so far resulted in a charge, with 634 of those charges made under Section 12 or Section 13 of the Terrorism Act 2000 and linked to supporting Palestine Action. 




A spokesperson for DOJ told Novara Media: “History shows that unjust laws become unenforceable when they are met with mass opposition, until governments are eventually forced to abandon them. The statistics released today are a clear indication of just how unpopular and unenforceable the government’s ban on Palestine Action is.




“Over a year on, and hundreds of regular people are still prepared to be arrested as ‘terrorists’ to demand that the new Labour leadership to do the only sensible thing and lift the ban on Palestine Action.”




In a statement, Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director Tom Southernden said: “The vast majority of the enormous increase in terrorism arrests are of grandparents, teenagers and everyone in between for peacefully holding placards. 




“We are seeing a shameful attack on our right to protest. It’s past time to end the proscription of Palestine Action and with it the use of counter terrorism power to punish direct action protests.”




Dozens of peaceful protesters 

opposing Israel’s genocide and the ban on Palestine Action – including 

a 94-year-old Jewish human rights lawyer

 – were arrested outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool at the end of September. 




The next day, foreign secretary Ed Miliband replied to a question about the proscription 

from Andrew Marr on LBC 

about “all those elderly people and vicars and grannies and so on” by saying: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised.” 




Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori has been granted permission to challenge the ban in the Supreme Court.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: New Poll Finds Voters Concerned about Rights and Democracy Ahead of 2026 Midterms
content:
A new national poll from The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights finds that voters are increasingly concerned about threats to their rights, democracy, and the 2026 elections. The 2026 Civil Rights Monitor found that 82% of voters are concerned that rights and freedoms are being taken away or rolled back, the highest level recorded in the five-year history of the poll.

The poll, conducted by Brilliant Corners Research, surveyed 1,000 likely voters by phone between August 23 and September 6. It found that concerns about democracy are also at a series high, with 76% of voters saying they believe democracy is under a major threat. At the same time, voters report high motivation to participate in the upcoming midterm elections, with 84% saying they plan to definitely vote in November.

Protecting the freedom to vote was rated as the top civil rights priority, receiving the highest importance rating among white, Black, Hispanic, and Asian American voters as well as among Democrats and Republicans. Overall, 14% of voters identified voting rights as their top issue, tying it with border security and ranking ahead of abortion rights, which 10% selected.

The findings come as voters express potential concerns surrounding potential interference with the midterm elections. Seventy seven percent said they are concerned that political leaders could pressure election officials to change election outcomes, while 65% are concerned the federal government could attempt to stop elections by declaring a state of emergency.

Voters also expressed concerns relating to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). In fact, 62% are concerned that ICE could appear at polling places to intimidate or interfere with voters. Opposition to ICE is particularly strong when voters are asked about the budget increase from $10 billion to $85 billion by cutting programs such as Medicare and SNAP. In fact, 71% oppose using those programs to fund the increase, including 61% who strongly oppose it.

Black voters reported particularly high levels of concern with 83% said they are very concerned about their rights being taken away. Black voters were also the group most likely to say race relations are getting worse, and 81% said their heritage, traditions, and cultural identity are under attack in the United States.

Despite widespread concerns about the state of race relations, the poll found broad agreement on the value of a diverse society. Ninety-two percent of voters said that diversity makes the country stronger, including most Republican voters.

As the 2026 midterms approach, the poll indicates that protecting voting rights remains a priority for voters across racial and partisan lines. Students have an important role to play in making sure those rights are protected. Make sure you are registered to vote at your current address and have a voting plan! Find more information at vote411.org/feminist.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Informe reveló el alto nivel de endeudamiento y atraso en los pagos en barrios populares
content:
De acuerdo a un relevamiento realizado por el Centro para la Integración Socio Urbana (CISUR) casi ocho de cada diez hogares de los barrios populares están endeudados y casi la mitad de esas familias tomó deuda para comprar alimentos.







Escuchar el reporte de Gabriel Robledo desde Radio Futura de La Plata







El informe se realizó sobre unos 420 hogares de 119 barrios populares en 15 provincias y  muestra que tres de cada diez hogares endeudados están en mora, con más de 90 días de atraso.




Fernanda García Monticelli, directora del CISUR, dijo que casi la mitad de las deudas de las familias son para comprar alimentos, “las familias están en una situación muy complicada, tienen muchos trabajos, trabajan en general más de 45 horas semanales, solamente el 15% de los encuestados tiene trabajo registrado”.




El relevamiento muestra además que la deuda promedio por hogar supera los 2 millones de pesos, mientras que el ingreso promedio ronda el millón de pesos. Es decir que las familias acumulan deudas que superan ampliamente lo que ganan en un mes.




Fernanda García Monticelli explicó que las deudas tienen tasas de intereses muy altas y las familias no llegan a pagar. “Esta situación genera mucha angustia, fue una realidad muy difícil porque muchas cuestiones de salud mental, las familias se levantan a la mañana y no saben cómo van a terminar el día y cómo van a hacer para afrontar estas deudas que se van multiplicando día a día”, relató Monticelli.




Según el relevamiento, las aplicaciones y billeteras virtuales son la principal fuente de endeudamiento. También aparecen los prestamistas del barrio y el fiado en comercios.




La directora del Centro de Integración Socio Urbana adelantó que estos datos fueron enviados a los legisladores para que lo tengan en cuenta en el debate sobre el endeudamiento de las familias que se discute en el Congreso la semana que viene.

author: Sarah Lane
title: Where you’ll find Equality Now at the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) in Dakar, Senegal
content:
8th October 2026










Where you’ll find Equality Now at the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) in Dakar, Senegal
















7 min read



















News and Insights




Africa






































































The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) is a key institution within the African Union responsible for promoting and protecting human rights across the African continent. Its Ordinary Sessions, held biannually,  play a crucial role in advancing the human rights agenda in Africa.




During the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) in Dakar, Senegal, Equality Now will host side events, read our statement, engage in submitted shadow reports review, and host side events.




Here is where you can find us.


























































Events






































                                        Monday, 12 October 2026                                    













Defining a Positive Cultural Context: Women’s Rights and the Rise of Anti-Rights Movements in Africa




Article 17 of the Maputo Protocol provides for women’s right to live in a positive cultural context and the right to participate in the determination of cultural policies, moving beyond seeing women as merely beneficiaries of cultural protection and recognising them as individuals who contribute to the creation, interpretation, and transformation of culture.




The Centre for Human Rights (University of Pretoria), Equality Now and SOAWR will convene a panel discussion, bringing together experts and practitioners to discuss the impact of regressive women’s rights movements on Article 17, in light of the growing prevalence of anti-rights movements, and the pivotal role of Article 17.




Date: 12th October 2026




Time: 13:00 – 15:00 GMT




Location: King Fahd Palace Hôtel (Dakar, Senegal)




















                                                                             













Strengthening CSO Resilience in the Face of Rising Anti-Rights and Anti-Gender Pushback to End Harmful Practices




Convened by 

Equality Now, Amref Health Africa and End FGM/C Network Africa

, this side event will examine the growing anti-rights and anti-gender backlash threatening progress towards ending harmful practices such as FGM/C and child, early and forced marriage.




The discussion will bring together civil society, human rights defenders and other stakeholders to share practical strategies for strengthening resilience, countering backlash and advancing accountability through strategic litigation, digital advocacy, coalition-building and regional and continental mechanisms.




Date: 12th October 2026




Time: 12:30 – 14:00 GMT




Location: 

Sama Hotel (Salle Casamance

), Dakar, Senegal






































                                        Tuesday, 13 October 2026                                    













Analysis of the gender responsiveness of the AU Nationality Protocol




Convened by Equality Now and the SOAWR Coalition on the margins of the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, this side event will present findings on an analysis of the gender responsiveness of the  AU Nationality Protocol.




The AU Nationality Protocol provides for equality in acquiring, transmitting, changing, and retaining nationality for men and women, embedding gender equality within a broader non-discrimination and statelessness-prevention framework. However,  it has some limitations on gender responsiveness, such as clawback clauses on the grounds of national legislation, national security, public order, and an explicit provision on conferment of nationality to foreign spouses on an equal basis for both men and women.  




Date: 13th October 2026




Time: 13:00 – 15:00 GMT




Location: Sama Hotel (Dakar, Senegal)




Transportation will be provided from King Fahd to Sama Hotel and back. Transportation will leave King Fahd at 1:00 pm (GMT). Lunch will be provided.




















                                        Wednesday, 14 October 2026                                    













Promising Practices in Ensuring and Strengthening Access to Justice for Survivors of Sexual and Gender-Based Violence in Africa




This side event during the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights showcases promising practices and specialised mechanisms drawn from ten African countries to close the gap between progressive legal frameworks and effective, survivor-centred access to justice for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence. Building on 




Equality Now’s research (

Barriers to Justice: Rape in Africa, law, practice and access to justice

), the Nairobi Principles on specialised courts and mechanisms, the Africa Political Statement, and alignment with the Maputo Protocol and Niamey Guidelines, the event engages ACHPR Commissioners, the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Women in Africa, states, and practitioners to share lessons, address barriers (including technology-facilitated GBV), and advance domestication, implementation, and monitoring of regional standards.

author: Gustavo Faleiros
title: Com Flávio, o Brasil pode virar um grande garimpo
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Ligando os pontos, enviada toda quinta-feira. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui

.







O amor da família Bolsonaro pelo garimpo não é novidade.

 Ficou famosa a frase de Jair Bolsonaro de que ele mesmo gostava de “faiscar”, de pegar uma bateia e sair em busca de pepitas de ouro. Porém, essa visão romântica de como funciona a mineração não ajudou a esconder os enormes danos causados pela ilegalidade garimpeira nos quatro anos de sua gestão.




Dados da plataforma independente 

Amazon Mining Watch revelam que, durante o governo Bolsonaro

, a velocidade de crescimento dos garimpos foi exorbitante. 

No início de 2019, quando se tornou presidente, o monitoramento por imagens de satélite mostrava que existiam 201,5 mil hectares de áreas de mineração de ouro na Amazônia. Quatro anos depois, já eram 401,5 mil hectares, uma área igual a 3,3 vezes a cidade do Rio de Janeiro e 92% maior que no início do governo.




Para fins de comparação, a mesma ferramenta, que utiliza inteligência artificial para analisar imagens Sentinel-2 com resolução de 10 metros, indica que, 

durante o governo de Lula 3, a taxa de crescimento foi bem menor – 24,3%

, elevando o total de áreas de garimpo na Amazônia a 499 mil hectares até a metade desde ano. 

Este resultado coincide com o aumento de ações de fiscalização durante a gestão petista.

 A repressão ocorreu principalmente em áreas de mineração nas terras indígenas e pela apreensão de máquinas usadas pelos criminosos ambientais.




Durante o governo de Bolsonaro, foram muitas as evidências de que os garimpeiros ilegais tinham portas abertas nos gabinetes de Brasília.

 Uma investigação do The Intercept 

revelou gravações nas quais Eduardo Bim, então presidente do Ibama

, órgão que deve zelar pela proteção ao meio ambiente, pedia para fiscais aliviarem a barra de uma empresa investigada por falsificar lavras de extração de ouro. 




Essas evidências, de que os interesses escusos estão intimamente conectados ao clã Bolsonaro, foram reforçadas na semana passada com uma 

reportagem da Agência Pública

 

mostrando que um dos chefões dos garimpos na Terra Indígena Yanomami, em Roraima, foi um dos articuladores da fuga para os Estados Unidos de Alexandre Ramagem, o diretor da Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin) durante a gestão Bolsonaro. Foragido da justiça

, Ramagem está condenado a 16 anos de prisão por participação na trama golpista. 




Já faz mais de uma década que os arautos da extrema direita gostam de “lacrar” dizendo que o Brasil governado pelos candidatos de esquerda, como Lula e Dilma, estava a um passo de se tornar a Venezuela. Uma grande fake news: nada do que ocorreu aqui nas últimas duas décadas se compara com os sofrimentos causados pelos erros do chavismo no país vizinho. Aqui não houve mudança na Constituição para acabar com o limite de mandatos presidenciais. As eleições foram respeitadas e sempre aferidas por observadores transparentes. A autonomia entre os poderes segue preservada.




Mas é no tema da soberania sobre seus recursos naturais onde, infelizmente, Brasil e Venezuela estão se aproximando cada vez mais.

 A invasão promovida na Venezuela por Trump para impor um governo subserviente aos interesses dos Estados Unidos gerou uma nova corrida pelo ouro e minérios daquele país. 

A atual presidente, Delcy Rodríguez, tem se mostrado pródiga em deixar a exploração de petróleo e ouro nas mãos do governo norte-americano

 – em 18 de setembro, por exemplo, 

o Financial Times noticiou que  31 toneladas em barras de ouro

 estavam sendo negociadas para serem transferidas da Venezuela para o Banco Central dos EUA.




Isso ocorre exatamente no momento em que operações do exército venezuelano, com ajuda militar norte-americana, tentam dominar a atuação de grupos ilegais no 

Arco Mineral do Orinoco,

 uma grande zona mineira criada em 2016 por Nicolás Maduro com o objetivo de gerar novas receitas para seu regime autoritário. Nunca deu certo, pois as minas de ouro foram sempre controladas pelos chamados “sindicatos”, organizações infra-legais atuando em conluio com militares corruptos.




Até o momento, as ações de repressão também não estão funcionando. Como mostrou o site de notícias Armando.info, 

os grupos criminais continuam hackeando o sistema

 e contrabandeando ouro ilegal para dentro do mercado norte-americano. Na verdade, mais do que isso: 

a Venezuela se tornou um hub de lavagem de ouro ilegal. Os garimpos que ainda continuam operando em territórios indígenas no Brasil têm usado a estrutura clandestina do país vizinho para exportar ouro à Índia, Oriente Médio, EUA e Europa.




Assim como a venezuelana Delcy Rodríguez, Flávio Bolsonaro mostrou-se disposto a sacrificar a soberania de seu país.

 Já deu muitos sinais de que vai abrir portas para uma intervenção norte-americana para combater o crime organizado, caso eleito. Em todos os países da América Latina onde isso ocorreu, os resultados têm sido desastrosos. 

A presença dos Estados Unidos na Colômbia, no Peru, no México e na Venezuela não alterou o quadro de ilegalidade generalizada. Apenas levou a uma valorização dos produtos ilícitos, intensificação da violência e impulsionou a reorganização dos grupos criminosos.




Talvez o leitor menos conhecedor das agruras geradas pela mineração ilegal na Amazônia possa perguntar porque afinal não deveria o Brasil aproveitar a oportunidade e lucrar com as altas cotações do ouro. A questão é que, por detrás dos garimpos, há uma cadeia de danos ambientais e sociais. 

Se aqui, como na Venezuela, o caminho for fazer um acordo com os Estados Unidos, é muito provável que eles fiquem com os ganhos e nós com a contaminação dos rios e matas.

content:
Da una settimana in Calabria si susseguono blocchi autostradali, pichetti e mobilitazioni: gli agricoltori chiedono certezze da parte del governo per affrontare il caro gasolio.




Da Radio Blackout




Anche in campania, Sicilia e Piemonte sono avvenute mobilitazioni e blocchi dei “trattori”.




La misura tetto del governo, che ha già preso 

2,5 miliardi dalle casse

 dello stato è irrisoria a fronte di un aumento del carburante che è già costato alla popolazione Italiana 4,7 miliardi in più in rifornimento, dall’aggressione statunitenste all’Iran. Basti pensare che il pieno di una macchina agricola può costare più di 1.500 euro. 




I trattori, ci racconta Gianluca di “Agricoltori brutti”, sono già fermi e il danno dai campi fino al prezzo sugli scaffali è già reale. 




Il caro dei carburanti è particolarmente impattante a fronte dell’inflazione, che in Calabria si aggiunge a salati cronicamente bassi, part-time involontari che dimezzano gli stipendi e all’alta disoccupazione. Secondo i 

dati istat

 del 2025 sono 300 mila le persone, ovvero il 20% della popolazione, in Calabria che vivono in condizione di grave deprivazione materiale e sociale, mentre tra i 20-65 anni il tasso di occupazione è sotto al 48,5%.

 a Cosenza, ore 14:00 – Piazza Europa, la popolazione scende in piazza a fianco degli agricoltori per dire “Ora basta: Non riusciamo più a campare […] Non vogliamo pagare il prezzo delle guerre del governo e dei suoi sporchi affari!”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Melchor Romero: ordenan el cierre de las celdas de aislamiento
content:
En cumplimiento de la resolución de la Sala III del Tribunal de Casación Penal bonaerense, el Juzgado de Ejecución Penal N° 1 de La Plata resolvió una serie de medidas y prohibiciones tendientes a garantizar abordajes terapéuticos, tratamientos y regímenes de vida respetuosos de los derechos de las personas con padecimientos de salud mental privadas de la libertad en las Unidades Penitenciarias Ns° 34 y 45 del Servicio Penitenciario Bonaerense (SPB) ubicadas en La Plata. Entre las medidas se dispuso la clausura inmediata de las celdas de aislamiento de ambas Unidades que habían sido reabiertas. La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM), en su carácter de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura (MLPT), estuvo presente en la constatación judicial llevada a cabo el marco de este Habeas Corpus Colectivo iniciado por las unidades mencionadas. Allí relevó un conjunto de irregularidades vinculadas al aislamiento prolongado y la falta de asistencia de profesionales, entre otras falencias.







El fallo del Juzgado de Ejecución Penal N° 1 de La Plata –a cargo del juez Juan José Ruiz– ordena una serie de medidas tendientes a hacer cesar las vulneraciones de derechos padecidas por las personas con padecimientos de salud mental privadas de su libertad en las unidades penitenciarias 34 y 45 de Melchor Romero.




El inicio de esta acción judicial se remonta al año 2018 mediante la presentación de un habeas corpus colectivo del cual la CPM es parte actora. En ese marco, el Tribunal de Casación Penal de la provincia ya había dispuesto un conjunto de medidas que apuntaban a abordar las mismas problemáticas de falta o deficiente atención de la salud mental en el encierro. Luego de varios años de trámite, a fines del año pasado, el Tribunal ordenó el archivo de dicho expediente por considerar que la sentencia estaba cumplida.




Sin embargo, transcurrido un breve tiempo, la CPM constató una grave regresión en términos de derechos humanos de las personas alojadas en la UP 34. Particularmente, denunció la creación de nuevos espacios de aislamiento que funcionaban ya sin un control judicial pormenorizado, motivo por el cual se requirió el desarchivo de la acción. El máximo tribunal penal bonaerense ordenó reabrir aquel expediente y encomendó al Juzgado de Ejecución Penal N° 1 de La Plata que retomara el seguimiento del cumplimiento de lo resuelto oportunamente.




En este marco, se realizó una constatación judicial junto con representantes del órgano judicial, la Asesoría Pericial, Salud Penitenciaria, el Servicio Penitenciario Bonaerense (SPB) y la CPM. En la misma se comprobaron una serie de violaciones a los derechos humanos que fueron descritas en un informe presentado por la Comisión, donde se denunciaron deficiencias en la atención de profesionales, irregularidades o inexistencia de tratamientos acordes y regímenes de vida justificados únicamente por criterios de seguridad.




Como mayor agravante se destacó la creación de un nuevo espacio para someter a aislamiento a personas que presentan descompensaciones en sus cuadros de salud mental. El sometimiento a este régimen está expresamente prohibido tanto por la normativa nacional como por la internacional, y llega a constituirse como tortura y tratos crueles, inhumanos o degradantes.




A partir del informe, y luego de la celebración de una audiencia en la cual la CPM reiteró el pedido de clausura, el titular del juzgado resolvió la clausura inmediata de la celda de separación y aislamiento del sector sanidad de la UP 34 en la cual se encontró alojada a una persona en condiciones indignas e inhumanas.




Asimismo, la resolución prohíbe el aislamiento de cualquiera de las personas alojadas en esa unidad penal, como también en el anexo femenino de la UP 45. En los casos de descompensación o crisis subjetiva, el juez dispuso que se deben implementar protocolos especiales para su estabilización y atención de forma inmediata.




El fallo destaca textualmente que “en la atención recibida por parte del interno que se encuentre en crisis se deberá abordar la situación primando la perspectiva médica por encima de la perspectiva de seguridad, instando a las autoridades del Ministerio de Justicia y DDHH y del Servicio Penitenciario Bonaerense a capacitar a los agentes penitenciarios que prestan funciones en estos establecimientos respecto de la actuación que deberán llevar adelante en las situaciones antes mencionadas”.




Por otra parte, la Justicia prohibió el ingreso de personas que no se encuentren bajo algún tipo de medida de coerción penal y requirió a las autoridades un informe completo sobre las personas privadas de la libertad en la UP 34 y el anexo de la 45 que no cuenten con criterio médico para su alojamiento allí. También se ordenó al área de salud mental una actualización urgente de las historias clínicas y se exigió examinar y resolver las deficientes condiciones materiales de infraestructura e higiene que agravan el alojamiento.




En su carácter de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura, la CPM relevó un total de 22 personas alojadas en las UP 34 y 45 sin criterio de permanencia. En las inspecciones se identificó la primacía del criterio de seguridad por sobre el abordaje sanitario, el uso del aislamiento como forma de control de personas descompensadas, sobrepoblación y graves faltas de higiene. Todos estos factores fueron notificados al juzgado y considerados para el dictado de las medidas.




Este fallo es un paso importante para no retroceder en los avances que se habían logrado en estas unidades penales, las cuales alojan a personas con padecimientos de salud mental en conflicto con la ley penal, y que deben ser controladas exhaustivamente debido a la particular situación de vulnerabilidad en la que se encuentran.

title: KNK condemns the 9 October conspiracy, calls for freedom for Öcalan
content:
The Foreign Affairs Commission of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) released a statement condemning the international conspiracy that led to Abdullah Öcalan’s imprisonment, and once again expressing its support for his call for ‘peace and democratic society’.




The international conspiracy began on October 9, 1998, when Abdullah Öcalan was forced to leave Syria amid intense political and military pressure on the country. This was followed by a months-long odyssey through various countries, ending on February 15, 1999, with his abduction from the Kenyan capital Nairobi to Turkey. The Kurdish leader has been held on the prison island of Imrali ever since.




The KNK statement on Thursday reads as follows:




“With the end of the Cold War, the United States adopted a new strategy on the world stage. This approach, known as the “New World Order,” aimed to consolidate global dominance. In the early 1990s, the U.S. launched a large-scale military intervention in the Middle East. Its aim was to reshape the region in line with its own interests. Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait on August 2, 1990, was the pretext the U.S. needed to rapidly increase its military presence in the region.




At the heart of the US master plan was the neutralisation of what they perceived as threats in Iran, Iraq and Syria. To achieve this, the U.S. planned to enlist the support of the Turkish government as a NATO ally. In turn, Turkey insisted on eliminating the PKK (Kurdistan Workers Party), which had increased its influence in the Middle East and become a key player by 1998.




The U.S. rejected any alternative in the region that did not serve its own interests. Under the leadership of Abdullah Öcalan, the PKK was implementing a strategy aimed at achieving democracy by resolving the Kurdish issue in Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria. For this reason, Abdullah Öcalan was targeted in an effort to neutralise the PKK. His strategic goal was to end the denial of the Kurdish people in these states through dialogue and negotiation, thereby paving the way for their democratisation and the creation of a democratic Middle East. Öcalan pursued this goal from 1979 to 1998 while living in Syria.




The pretext for the war in Syria was the presence of Öcalan in Damascus. However, Öcalan left Damascus on 9 October 1998 and went to Europe with the aim of preventing the war. The goal in Europe was to persuade the states responsible for the Kurdish issue to find a solution through political and diplomatic efforts. Unfortunately, however, the European states were also unwilling to resolve the Kurdish issue. Consequently, they did not want Öcalan to remain in Europe. Following his departure from Damascus, the Kurdish movement came under increased international pressure.




Between 9 October 1998 and 15 February 1999, Öcalan was under constant threat. On 15 February 1999, he was abducted and handed over by CIA and MOSSAD to the Turkish state. Imprisoned on Imralı Island for the last 27 years, he has been subjected to severe isolation, injustice and lawlessness.




This massive operation targeting Öcalan, the leader of the Kurdish people, was later exposed by evidence that came to light. In summary, it was characterised by lawlessness, immorality, hypocrisy, false friendship, and a web of vested interests among those in positions of power.




Yet Öcalan—who has never compromised his belief in peace under any circumstances—continues to strive for peace in the region. On 27 February 2025, he initiated negotiations with the Turkish state, opening a new opportunity for peace. In the 18 months since then, Öcalan has continued to take historic steps to turn his vision of peace into reality.




Öcalan, who was sentenced to death in 1999, is now sitting at the negotiating table with those who once demanded his execution, seeking a solution to the Kurdish issue. What makes Öcalan remarkable is his unwavering commitment to peace and his determination to pursue it, together with the Kurdish people, who have never abandoned him.




Despite these peace initiatives and the ongoing negotiations, Abdullah Öcalan remains imprisoned. For peace to be achieved and the resolution process to succeed, he must be free.




We once again strongly condemn those who carried out and supported the October 9 plot.”

author: Unknown
title: The memory of the future
content:
Almost five hundred years ago, the eighteen-year-old Étienne de La Boétie wrote his 

Discourse on Voluntary Servitude

. This text, which asks how freedom is lost and how people can become accustomed to submission, is today assigned as reading to secondary school students in France.




Why do people submit?




La Boétie’s answer, which continues to preoccupy us to this day, is not solely about tyranny. The first generation may still be subjugated by force. But subsequent generations, born under the yoke and having never known freedom, may begin to regard the order into which they were born as the natural condition of life. Habit, La Boétie argues, teaches people to “swallow the poison of servitude without finding it bitter.” It is then no longer merely a matter of submitting, but of drinking the poison and, after a while, no longer even realizing that it is poison.




An order established through violence can, over time, become a matter of habit. But another question makes La Boétie even more relevant to us today: Do people become accustomed only to their own subjugation, or can they also become accustomed to the injustice inflicted on the person right beside them? When we apply this question to Turkey and Kurdistan, we are confronted with a deeply burdensome history.




Violence is often narrated to us not from the point at which it begins, but from the point at which it becomes visible. When a shot is fired, we see the violence. But what happens before the shot is fired?




What do we call it when a mother spends twenty years searching for her son’s grave?




Despite her advanced age and illness, Fatime Ülüş traveled from Strasbourg to Cudi to find the grave of her son, for which she had been searching for years. Aysel Tuğluk was in prison when her mother died. After being granted permission to attend the funeral, the family was forced, because of threats and attacks at the cemetery, to exhume the body of the mother they had only just buried.




What do we call it when a person cannot bury their mother?




These are not merely the stories of two individuals. In the memory of almost every Kurd reading these lines, another name, another village, another prison, another grave is likely to emerge. The question, therefore, is not simply: “Did all of this happen?”




How did a society become accustomed to living with all of this?




Under what concept of violence do we place displacement from one’s own village, years of uncertainty about the fate of a loved one, the inability to bury one’s own dead, or being forced to continually prove the legitimacy of one’s own language and identity? If we allow violence to begin only at the moment a shot is fired, we render invisible an entire life that preceded that moment. If we separate a reaction from the conditions that produced it, we not only condemn the act but also strip it of its political meaning.




The durability of domination does not arise solely from the ability to exercise coercion; as La Boétie describes, it rests on a web of ties and interests. The state must therefore be examined not only in terms of what it does to Kurds, but also in terms of how it shapes the concepts through which Turkish society views them. For many years, the Kurdish language was treated less as a matter of language and rights than as part of a security issue. Kurdish demands concerning identity, language and a political future of their own were defined not as a question of rights, but as a threat. The repression exercised in response was, in turn, legitimized through concepts such as “protecting public order” and “preserving the state.”




The document concerning a “crackdown plan,” reportedly dated September 2014, became the subject of parliamentary deliberations in late 2015. The curfews, deaths and displacement that followed in Cizre, Sur and Nusaybin were documented in international human rights reports. Kurdistan experienced this as a historic rupture and inscribed it as such into its collective memory.




But what did Turkey see?




Why did the destruction experienced by Kurdistan not also become a social and moral rupture for large sections of Turkish society? How could what one people experienced as a catastrophe remain merely a security issue in the eyes of another society?




When does the language of the state become the language of society?




And perhaps the even more serious question is this: Why did the injustice experienced by Kurds not produce a social rupture in western Turkey to the same extent and with the same continuity? Why did trade unions, academia, the press, left-wing, socialist and secular circles, as well as the legal and human rights community, fail to make this one of their central concerns?




At first, an event shocks people. Then it becomes news, then a number, and finally a statistic. In the end, the state of exception experienced by one people can become merely the backdrop to the ordinary life of their neighbors.




People can become accustomed not only to their own subjugation, but also to the injustice inflicted on others.




This is precisely why İsmail Beşikçi must be remembered. He crossed the boundaries of the official order of knowledge; he examined the “Reform Plan for the East” (Şark Islahat Planı), forced resettlement and Dersim, addressed the Kurdish question through the conceptual framework of colonialism, and paid a price for doing so. He showed both academia and Turkish society that it was possible to see things differently. If one person was able to see, it is not enough simply to say: “We did not know.”




Why did so many people fail to see?




Living together also means being able to recognize the violence inflicted on one’s neighbor as violence.




Today, there is talk of a new political phase in Turkey. The state describes it as a “terror-free Turkey,” while within the Kurdish political movement the concepts of “peace and a democratic society” have come to the fore. The fact that the guns have fallen silent is significant. But no political process can mean erasing the Kurds’ historical memory and their visions of the future and starting from zero.




For beneath all these debates lies a deeper question: the self-confidence of a people.




When a people are told across generations which futures are not possible for them, when thinking about their own destiny is branded as a crime, a threat or separatism, what risks being lost is not merely a particular political demand, but the collective confidence that another future is possible. The most enduring form of domination that can be imposed on a people is not to tell them what they cannot do, but eventually to make them cease believing that they could act differently at all. What coercion cannot achieve, habit can complete.




Yet the history of Kurdistan points to another continuity. Uprisings were suppressed, organizations dismantled, people killed and driven into exile. Despite all this, the Kurdish demand to have a say in determining their own future has repeatedly resurfaced at different times, through different generations and by different means.




The current process may succeed or it may fail. Wanting peace and making the entire future of a people dependent on the success of any particular political process are not the same thing. But if a people relinquishes the right to think about its own future, this is not a change of strategy.




It is a historic rupture.




The current phase carries another risk. Symbols of resistance, concepts and historical meanings that have become deeply embedded in the collective memory of Kurdish society over the past fifty years may be redefined within a new political language. Of course, every generation rereads its past; forms of struggle, concepts and political means can change. The danger does not lie in change itself.




The danger lies in the boundary becoming blurred between rethinking the past and altering its meaning to suit the needs of the present. For the memory of a people preserves not only what it has experienced, but also the meaning it has given to those experiences.




If what meant resistance to one generation is conveyed to the next merely as a mistake, and what people paid a price for in one era comes to be seen in another merely as a burden to be overcome, this does not make the past disappear. It does something quieter: it leaves the past in place but changes its meaning.




That is why glorifying the past and preserving the meaning of the past are not the same thing. We do not need to leave future generations the answers of today. But if they are to find their own answers, we must ensure that they know what happened, what was resisted, what was defended and what futures were envisioned.




This is precisely why we must think fifty years ahead, to the year 2075.




A Kurdish child who will be of school age in 2075 has not yet been born. Many of today’s actors and witnesses, ourselves included, will no longer be here. We do not know which organizations, regimes and borders will still exist. But we can influence today what that child will one day possess:




Will Kurds in 2075 still have to ask others for the right to live in their own language?




Will they still have to read their own history in the archives of others?




Through whose memory will they learn about Şêx Seîd, Dersim, August 15, the village evacuations and Cizre?




Will they merely know the price paid by the generations before them, or will they also know why those generations resisted, what they defended and what kind of future they envisioned?




This is not a political prescription, but an assessment of what we will leave behind.




The Kurds of 2075 may not organize themselves within the organizations of today or use the concepts of today. The point is not to instill the answers of the present in them, but to leave them the means with which they can ask their own questions: a language, an archive, institutions, historical memory and collective self-confidence.




Almost five hundred years ago, a young man of just eighteen posed a question that still reaches us today.




Will a Kurdish child who will be of school age in 2075 be able to read about what is happening today in their own language and in their own archive? Will they know not only what we experienced, but also what we defended and what kind of future we wanted?




One of the most effective ways to cut a people off from its future is to break its collective confidence that another future is possible.




To destroy its very ability to imagine a future of its own.




That is precisely what the memory of the future means: not forgetting the past, but equally refusing to leave the future to the definitions, interests and attempts at direction imposed by others.

title: MSD on incidents in Heseke: The issues must be addressed through political and legal dialogue
content:
Following a demonstration featuring anti-Kurdish demands in Heseke, the Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) expressed deep concern over the recent developments and the growing tensions in the city.




At a rally in the predominantly Arab neighborhood of Xiwêran (Ghweiran) last Friday, around 200 people called, among other things, for Kurds to be removed from institutions in Hesekê province. During the demonstration, in which a particularly large number of children and young people participated, slogans were also chanted against Kurdish national symbols and flags. Kurdish flags were also reportedly burned following Friday prayers. 




“Statements and positions that could deepen ethnic and social divisions are particularly troubling in an area known for its diversity and the close ties among its communities, “MSD said in a statement on Thursday.




The MSD recognizes that residents of Heseke Governorate, regardless of their background, have legitimate concerns, demands, and rights, and they have the right to express them peacefully. These include calls for security, public services, effective state institutions, and political and administrative rights. Such concerns should be addressed through the law, dialogue, and the political process, not through accusations, exclusion, or incitement.




At the same time, the MSD warns against turning any political or security disagreement into a conflict between communities, saying: “Incidents, symbols, or ethnic and religious identities must not be used to provoke hostility or hatred among the people of the region. Heseke has long been home to Kurds, Arabs, Syriac-Assyrians, and other communities who have lived alongside one another for generations. Their relationships have been built through neighborhood ties, work, marriage, shared interests, and a common future. After years of war, suffering, and displacement, what they share should serve as the foundation for building a common future, not be used to deepen division and conflict.”




Accordingly, the MSD:




1. Warns against any inciting language or conduct based on generalizations, exclusion, or holding an entire community responsible for the position, actions, or behavior of an individual. Political disagreements must not be allowed to turn into conflict among members of the same society.




2. Rejects any attack on symbols associated with any community within Syrian society. It also rejects the use of ethnic or religious symbols and identities to spread hatred or encourage retaliation. Respecting the symbols of others is part of respecting one another and is essential to living together peacefully.




3. Calls on Kurds, Arabs, Syriac-Assyrians, and all other residents of Heseke not to be drawn into calls for confrontation, revenge, or accusations of betrayal. No incident, however painful or provocative, should be allowed to become a trigger for wider social conflict.




4. Holds the responsible authorities and security forces accountable for protecting civilians and maintaining security and civil peace. They must prevent any attack, incitement, or threat and hold anyone found responsible for acts of violence or incitement accountable under the law, without selective enforcement or collective blame.




5. At the same time, the MSD calls on all political forces and parties, tribal and religious leaders, cultural and media figures, community leaders, civil society organizations, women, and youth to fulfill their national and moral responsibilities. They should play an active role in calming tensions, preventing the spread of hate speech and rumors, and discouraging incitement.




Protecting civil peace is not the responsibility of the state alone, although the state has the primary responsibility to protect citizens and enforce the law. It is a shared responsibility of everyone with political, social, cultural, or media influence, as well as every citizen who cares about the future of their community and country.




6. Calls on all sides not to use the current circumstances to settle political scores, impose changes through force, or revive ethnic and social divisions. The outstanding issues between the people of the region and state institutions must be addressed through political and legal dialogue, within the framework of existing understandings and the process of building a united and democratic Syrian state.




MSD underlined that: “The Syria we want to create cannot be based on one community defeating another or one identity being erased in favor of another. It must be based on a state that protects all its citizens and safeguards their rights, freedoms, and dignity. This state must also recognize diversity as a source of strength rather than a cause of conflict.”




At this critical time, MSD conveyed the following message to the people of Heseke:




– Do not allow anyone to turn your political differences into hostility among you.




– Do not let a single incident destroy a long history of living together.




– Do not allow those who seek division to find supporters among you.




“Preserving civil peace is not about choosing a side. It is about protecting the people of Heseke and safeguarding the future of Syria as a whole,” the statement concluded.
