author: EDRi
title: The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) represents everything that’s wrong with Europe’s approach to digital sovereignty
content:
The EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package is supposed to jump-start Europe’s “sovereign AI” ambitions. But due to fundamental misunderstandings about the technology behind ‘AI’ and the blind trust in Big Tech’s AI doomer and boomer narratives, it is more likely to instead hurt digital rights and the environment instead, and waste valuable public resources that should have been invested in actually increasing Europe’s digital resilience. The Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, adds up to an aggressive policy push to impose “European AI”.

Published on 3 June, the European Commission’s Tech Sovereignty Package—comprising the Chips Act 2.0, the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA), the EU Open Source Strategy, and a Strategic Roadmap for Energy Digitalisation—is portrayed as a significant shift in the EU’s digital governance strategy. It signals that the EU is no longer content to rely on regulatory frameworks like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Digital Services Act (DSA), Digital Markets Act (DMA) and the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act. The EU now seeks to artificially inflate both the supply of and demand for AI data centres, as well as to expand the material infrastructures underpinning them.

Yet, as the rhetoric of “strategic autonomy” echoes through the policymaking corridors of Brussels, the Package is fractured by internal contradictions. It conflates the fraught competitiveness agenda with the goal of genuine digital self-determination, mistakes building AI data centres on EU soil for structural tech independence, and engages in what can only be described as “sovereignty-washing”—repackaging the deregulation of fundamental rights and environmental protection as an industrial win. This aggressive industrial policy also embraces the EU’s securitisation and militarisation agenda, as Europe’s loss of competitiveness is perceived as a security threat.

The Commission’s AI policy is almost entirely based on the highly speculative assumption that ‘AI’ is the inevitable future of tech and everybody needs it now or they will lose out on global markets. It claims—without evidence—that “the Union’s limited data centre capacity poses a significant threat to its ability to benefit from the digital transformation” towards AI.

The CADA proposal specifically aims at “regaining and retaining control over data and cloud computing services” and “expanding domestic computational capacity” in order to push for broad AI adoption.

In order to achieve that, the Regulation proposes the massive funding of “research and innovation” projects through public funds and private investment. These projects—called “Cloud and AI Leadership Initiatives”—are supposed to develop, test and deploy “advanced AI technologies,” including autonomous cars, drones and robots (“physical AI”) and AI models for specific industrial sectors (“industrial AI”), notably in healthcare, defence, and in the public sector. CADA is thus supposed to provide the material conditions to implement the EU’s Apply AI strategy principle of “AI first,” forcing the use of more ‘AI’ on public administrations across the continent.

Moreover, CADA would require Member States to establish national “experience and acceleration centres for AI” meant to secure the widespread adoption of AI in private and public sectors. EU countries are also expected to adopt national strategies, mandating the application of the “AI first” principle by all private and public organisations.

On the infrastructure side, Member States would be required to designate so-called “Data Centres Acceleration Zones” on their territory, in which permit-granting procedures are sped up, energy supply is guaranteed, and environmental assessments are fast-tracked, an approach that can put some Member States in a tight spot and risks increasing popular discontent with such imposed infrastructural build-out in their communities.

The inherent flaw of the EU’s “digital sovereignty” policy, illustrated by CADA, is to focus its effort on territorial control over data, infrastructure, and supply chains, instead of the ability to control vendor dependencies and the technology itself. “Building tech in Europe” becomes a goal in itself, one that shifts public resources and attention towards an unproven technology that is currently developed in wildly overvalued markets full of highly indebted companies that may fail at any moment. But it buries a much more important question: What kind of tech should we be building? Who owns it, and whom does it serve?

There is no reason to believe that large, EU-based AI and data centre corporations are going to treat people’s personal data any better, respect the environment more, or not undermine democracy, than their US counterparts. Digital sovereignty is not about the sovereignty of nations, it is about the sovereignty of people to be in control of the technology they depend on.

What is more, this package cannot be read in isolation from the Commission’s broader deregulation agenda, notably the so-called “Digital Omnibus”. While CADA proposes to redirect significant amounts of public funding to private enterprises, the Omnibus strips away hard-won rights protections by weakening the AI Act and GDPR.

When our fundamental rights are stripped away in the name of European tech sovereignty, we need to ask the question: Whose digital sovereignty is this policy supposed to serve? True digital self-determination is not a goal desired only by Europeans, but by people around the world. By misunderstanding digital sovereignty for self-sufficiency and by attempting to build an insular, defensive digital Fortress Europe, the EU misses a crucial opportunity to support other countries as a leader for sovereign digital ecosystems that do not depend on Big Tech.

Data centres are not neutral infrastructure. They can serve and support specific political goals such as military operations. For example, until a year ago, Israeli military intelligence relied until a year ago on Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform in the Netherlands to store its mass surveillance data. Google and Amazon Web Services also entered into a $1.2 billion contract with Israel’s armed forces, called “Project Nimbus”, which included the construction of multiple data centres in Israel to provide cloud computing services. OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI models have been used by the US government for military planning and analysis, and the latter has infamously almost led to a military confrontation with China. Hence, the EU’s industrial push for ‘AI’ and compute cannot be divorced from its own broader militarisation agenda, the main objective of which is to unlock EU and Member States’ defence spending, including military AI.

CADA contributes to this agenda by vowing to fund “highly secured” computing infrastructures for the training, testing and deployment of defence-related AI models. Its “sovereignty framework” to assess “cloud and AI independence” will also influence national public procurement policies for the defence sector.

The Commission’s objective to force the massive build-out of new AI data centres comes at a time where Europeans are already acutely experiencing the dangerous effects of the climate crisis. The EU is already overshooting its internationally agreed emissions budget and with CADA as it is proposed, this could get much worse.

The CADA proposal aims to “triple EU capacity (…) and reach the needed capacity by 2035.” Estimates put the current European data centre market at a total energy consumption of about 13 Gigawatt (GW) by the end of 2026. Tripling that capacity would require 39 GW of electricity to be produced and transported to those AI data centres. For perspective: a typical nuclear reactor has a capacity of about 1 GW. 39 GW is the annually averaged power consumption of over 70 million people.

While the Commission promises the promotion of “clean energy” and “sustainable” data centres in “Data Acceleration Zones,” studies show this will not be sufficient to prevent a dramatic rise in overall greenhouse gas emissions. The direction accelerated by CADA will certainly not address the wider environmental and social problems generated by data centres, such as carbon emissions, excessive water demands, extraction of raw materials and e-waste, displacement of people and wildlife, and public health issues.

The Commission seems to be well aware of those risks and the public opposition against Europe’s data centre boom, as local communities increasingly mobilise to safeguard their living conditions and protest rising electricity prices, water and land use, as well as the unchecked power of Big Tech. As part of CADA, it therefore proposes that Member States create “single information points” to inform the public, “with the aim of increasing public acceptance of the data centre project.”

One of the Commission’s justifications for CADA is that without it European AI companies depend on foreign (read: US)-based “hyperscaler” infrastructure, which can pose a threat to people’s fundamental rights and to data protection due to “third-country jurisdictions” with “laws mandating data access and transfer.” Yet this is a wholly unconvincing argument from an institution that enacts, maintains, and expands exactly those data transfers via agreements like the 2022 “EU-US Data Privacy Framework”, and the new biometric data-sharing arrangement negotiated with the Trump administration.

In reality, with CADA, current and future data centres in the EU will continue to rely on US investors and tech companies, who will capture most of the wealth and entrench their power on European critical infrastructures while outsourcing the negative external effects on people and the environment onto communities in the EU.

First, the EU must acknowledge that fundamental rights are not an obstacle to the EU’s technological independence; they are a precondition. Europe’s rights-based order is what makes the continent attractive and helps working towards a world in which the economy works for everyone.

Second, instead of losing its head in the ‘AI’ cloud, the EU should focus on the key properties of any technology that fosters digital self-determination:

Does it avoid problematic dependencies and vendor lock-in?

Does it protect data security and user privacy?

Does it prevent market concentration and contribute to fair competition in the EU?

Is the technology interoperable with open standards and is the code open for inspection and re-use (open source)? Can it contribute to the digital commons?

Are the technology’s governance and business models compatible with democracy and human rights?

The jurisdiction and geographic location of any given vendor may play a part in this calculation—for instance to avoid service providers that are subject to authoritarian rule or pressure by hostile foreign governments—but it is not a sufficient sovereignty metric. CADA’s assumption that there is an absolute necessity for Europe to invest in its own polluting ‘AI’ data centres in order to become digitally sovereign, seems therefore fraught with contradictions at best, and plain wrong at worst.

Interestingly, the European Commission has already spelled out some of the things Europe should do to increase people’s digital self-determination in the accompanying EU Open Source Strategy:

Strengthen and promote a vibrant open source ecosystem, with a particular focus on public interest, non-profit digital infrastructure and their governing bodies;

Promote and support open and interoperable digital ecosystems for public administrations, including EU institutions, and become a real anchor customer for them;

In particular, strengthen the open source social media space by supporting open and decentralised social media solutions and platforms;

Build out the EU’s Open Source Programme Office (OSPO); and

Reinforce digital standards and international outreach.

While this list is by no means complete, it is a better start than CADA to start this conversation. Such an approach to a decentralised, open source, public interest-oriented tech ecosystem would provide Europe and its people with better digital resilience and a renewed sense of digital self-determination, rather than trying to win an imaginary “AI race” against the US and China, with little to no consideration for the environmental, societal, and financial risks it creates.

This blog post will be followed by a deeper policy analysis and EDRi is committed to constructively engaging with lawmakers.

author: EDRi
title: No human required: Austria’s plan for AI-only government decisions
content:
A sweeping change to Austria's administrative law would let authorities issue binding decisions using AI systems with no human ever reviewing the outcome. EDRi member epicenter.works has sent an open letter to parliament, and is looking for input from readers elsewhere in Europe about how other countries are handling, or planning to handle, the same issue.

By epicenter.works (guest author) · October 8, 2026

Austria is about to find out what happens when a member state lets large language models write legally binding government decisions, with no human required to review them.

This autumn, the Constitutional Affairs Committee of Austria’s parliament will debate a sweeping change to the country’s General Administrative Procedure Act (AVG). The AVG is the default procedural code for essentially all administrative proceedings in Austria, covering everything from social assistance and building permits to business licensing and public subsidies. A single change to the general code can therefore affect how decisions get made across almost the entire administration, not just in one sector. According to the draft law, authorities would for the first time be allowed to issue fully automated administrative decisions: legally binding rulings with direct effect on a person’s rights, comparable to what other jurisdictions might call an administrative act or order, without a human ever reviewing the specific outcome before it goes out.

Ahead of this autumn’s debate, epicenter.works has written to the Constitutional Affairs Committee, sending an open letter laying out exactly why fully automated decisions with no human review are incompatible with fundamental rights.

Let’s be precise about what’s actually being automated, because the draft treats generative AI the same way previous automation laws treated simple rule-based software.

Classic automated administrative systems are deterministic: same input, same output, traceable logic. A system built on a large language model works fundamentally differently in three ways that each map directly onto a legal guarantee:

Hallucination. LLMs generate outputs that sound plausible but can be flatly wrong or entirely invented. Even specialised legal AI systems show hallucination rates of roughly 17 to 33%, and errors are often impossible for the affected person to spot. Hallucinated facts underpinning a binding decision affect the right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights: a person can’t meaningfully exercise that right when the decision against them is built on evidence that doesn’t exist.

Black box. How the system arrived at a given output is structurally not fully explainable. This is not simply “not yet documented” but not explainable even in principle with current models. That sits uneasily with a basic rule-of-law demand: that the exercise of state power be transparent and reviewable, not just efficient.

Bias. Systematic distortions like race, income level, migration status etc. are baked into how these models are trained and can’t be engineered away by picking a “better” vendor. Left unchecked, this risks group-based unequal treatment that no one notices, because the system doesn’t expose it, touching the principle of non-discrimination, which both EU law and the Austrian constitution guarantee explicitly.

These aren’t implementation flaws. They’re inherent to how current LLMs work, and every legal objection below follows directly from this technical reality.

Weeks before this autumn’s parliamentary debate, Austria’s own state-run AI assistant “ida” supplied a preview of the problem: it falsely described a sitting vice-chancellor as a former government member and invented a government minister who doesn’t exist.

A more serious example came out of the UK in July 2026. An Upper Tribunal judge found that the Home Office had refused an asylum claim, from a woman who had fled forced child marriage and severe violence, by citing a policy document that, on inspection, appears never to have existed. The judge noted the refusal letter bore the hallmarks of AI-generated content, and suggested the reference was likely an AI hallucination, warning that this would represent an extremely serious failing on the department’s part if confirmed.

Read together, these two cases show an escalation from a chatbot inventing a minister’s name in Austria to a fabricated document underpinning an actual refusal of protection in the UK, in exactly the kind of fundamental-rights-sensitive, factually complex proceeding that should never be handed to a system with no reliable way of checking its own claims.

The draft bill (89/ME) gives authorities two new powers that are each individually contentious:

Chatbots (§§ 13, 13a AVG) that don’t just inform citizens but can treat what someone tells the system as a formal submission in a proceeding.

Fully automated decisions (§ 18a AVG) with real legal effect, and no human involved in the individual case. Which types of proceedings actually qualify for this is largely left to secondary legislation, a regulation, rather than being written into the law itself.

The second point runs into a structural problem that goes beyond AI risk management: under Austrian constitutional law, decisions this consequential are supposed to be made by parliament, through a law, not delegated to the administration to decide for itself. The draft hands that call to whichever “top authority” is materially responsible for the matter at hand, and that’s a far more scattered group than it sounds. Depending on the subject, it could be a federal minister, a state government, or, since Austria’s roughly 2,092 municipalities each administer their own local affairs, a municipal council. There is no single or small set of bodies deciding this: the power to define the scope of automation is spread across potentially thousands of separate decision-makers, each authorising the use of a technology whose risks they may have little capacity to assess, and each one also responsible for making sure their own system meets the AI Act’s sector-specific requirements. Relying on thousands of potential decision-makers to each verify their own compliance is an inadequate safeguard. There’s no exclusion in the law itself for sensitive areas like asylum or social welfare, either. That’s left entirely to secondary legislation, case by case.

Austrian courts have long required that a human official retain what’s known as “decisive influence” over an automated decision for it to count as a genuine act of the state at all, a standard built for simple, rule-based systems decades ago. Nobody has a workable answer for what that standard even means applied to a model that cannot fully explain its own output. The draft’s four safeguards, traceability, a testing phase, the ability to intervene, and ongoing checks, are standard IT governance measures for any public-sector deployment. They don’t actually test whether “decisive influence” exists; they sidestep the question.

The draft also shifts risk onto the people affected by it. Citizens get two weeks to challenge an automated decision, a tight window when errors from an LLM are often invisible without close scrutiny, while the authority itself can revoke the same decision on its own initiative for up to two months, in some cases even without pointing to a specific error, simply citing a “systemic” one. The government keeps the option to fix its own mistakes later; the person on the receiving end carries the uncertainty in the meantime. Moreover, Austria still has no independent AI oversight body, despite the EU AI Act calling for exactly that.

The organisation’s position is straightforward:

A human must make the final call in administrative decisions as the rule, not the exception.

No blank check for complex or sensitive cases. The draft must contain a statutory exclusion for proceedings involving particularly complex facts or that are especially sensitive from a fundamental-rights perspective, such as asylum or social assistance.

Parliament, not future regulation, must decide. Whether these areas ever get automated should be settled in the law itself from the outset, not left to a regulation decided later by the same authority that would benefit from automating them.

In March 2026, the ministry sent the draft bill out for consultation. For months, the debate stayed confined to the 35 submissions filed during that process, a technical, insider affair. The draft has since been tabled in parliament as a government bill, and parliamentary debate is scheduled for this autumn and winter.

epicenter.works still hopes the process produces changes before it’s finalised, which is part of why it published its open letter to the Constitutional Affairs Committee at the start of September 2026. Within days, Austria’s national broadcaster ORF covered the bill on television and online, and public radio interviewed the president of Austria’s judges’ association. This is no longer a niche debate confined to legal-tech circles.

As far as epicenter.works is aware, Austria is currently an absolute outlier in planning to allow fully automated decisions across such a broad range of administrative matters, with the scope largely left open to future regulation. But the organisation holds that claim loosely: there is no coherent, up-to-date evidence base on where other European countries stand, and gaps in its own knowledge are likely.

Has a comparable law been discussed, proposed, or is it even considered feasible in your country? If you know of anything, or can confirm that nothing like it exists, epicenter.works would genuinely like to hear from you.

Contribution by: EDRi member, epicenter.works

author: EDRi
title: Your data, their decision: the hidden surveillance infrastructure behind Europe’s digital borders
content:
A new report by ARTICLE 19 examines how the European Union is presiding over the most significant expansion of border surveillance in its history. Much of this development is being outsourced to private companies – with profound consequences for privacy and freedom of expression.

By ARTICLE 19 (guest author) · October 8, 2026

In October 2025, the EU began systematically collecting and storing fingerprints and facial images of every third-country national crossing its external border, under the Entry/Exit System (EES). By late 2026, the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) will expand this approach by pre-screening visa-exempt travellers before they arrive at EU borders.

Together, the two systems are capable of processing more than 1.4 billion travellers, integrating biometric, migration, visa, and law-enforcement data into searchable profiles.

The new report by ARTICLE 19, examining how the EU is significantly expanding border surveillance, focuses on the agency at the heart of the system: EU-LISA (EU Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems in the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice). This little-scrutinised entity plays a key role in building and maintaining the large-scale digital infrastructure projects that underpin EU migration and border management.

ARTICLE 19 analysed EUR 1.99 billion in contracts awarded by EU-LISA between 2019-2025. The analysis shows how private companies, including IDEMIA, Sopra Steria, IBM, and Leonardo SpA, have gained unprecedented power to shape how the systems operate.

Because of the way EU-LISA procurement works, private companies are gaining real influence over what the systems can do and recommend, through large building blocks of biometrics, engineering, and operations. In practice, this means that surveillance capacities within EES and ETIAS could be expanded through ‘technical adjustments’ decided by companies rather than accountable political decisions.

Those same companies are part of a growing industry that spans global digital IDs, defence and security projects worldwide. IDEMIA, for instance, develops and implements national biometric identification systems in countries including Morocco, Chile, and Colombia, as well as election management technologies in Kenya.

How these technologies travel across contexts deserves further scrutiny.

This scale of digitalisation at the border has real-life consequences for the people subjected to it.

For migrants and people on the move, participation in these systems is not optional: biometric registration and automated risk-scoring are conditions for mobility or legal status, not choices people can opt out of.

This is deeply concerning because interconnected systems mean a single database error can cascade across the entire network, leading to delayed or denied entry or visa refusals – often with little transparency about how a decision was made or how to challenge it. Many migrants lack the linguistic, legal, and financial resources needed to exercise rights they formally have.

The long-term picture remains uncertain: how exactly will these systems classify people, what further changes might be introduced, and what mechanisms can people use to question decisions or access their own data.

One thing is clear: accountability mechanisms are lagging further behind the pace of deployment of these surveillance tools.

Individuals’ rights and freedoms should not be subordinated to commercial interests. Strengthening rights mechanisms and transparency for migrant populations requires protective frameworks designed for the conditions they face.

Existing legal frameworks cannot simply apply to EES and ETIAS on paper. They need to be enforced without the broad exceptions for migration and law enforcement that currently undermine both the GDPR and the AI Act. EDRi and its members have already documented how the AI Act fails migrants and people on the move.

We need binding transparency obligations around EU-LISA’s procurement processes and its relationships with private contractors. Decisions that expand surveillance capacities should require the same level of public scrutiny and political accountability as any other major policy change. They cannot be left to commercial and engineering considerations alone.

More broadly, the design, development, and deployment of digital border infrastructure must not be allowed to proceed without open public debate and meaningful participation of those most affected. Migrant-led organisations, refugee rights groups, and digital rights networks should be included at every stage of design and evaluation, not just after systems are already operational.

As the report shows, surveillance infrastructures too often operate in the dark. We need to make them visible and open to sustained public scrutiny.

Right now, Europe seems to be running in the opposite direction: toward systems that grow more powerful and more opaque, while the people most affected by them have the least insight into how they operate.

This can and must be reversed. Democratic oversight of border infrastructure is urgent and cannot be optional. ARTICLE 19 will keep monitoring developments at EU-LISA and within the EES/ETIAS framework, and continue pushing for the transparency these systems currently lack.

Infrastructure currently operating in the dark, must be brought back into the scope of democratic accountability.

Contribution by: EDRi member, ARTICLE 19

author: EDRi
title: D3 brings class actions on addictive design against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube
content:
The Portuguese digital rights organisation and EDRi member D3 announces that it has brought four class actions lawsuits against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube over the use of addictive design practices. The cases challenge design practices that can encourage compulsive use of online platforms and seek to hold platforms accountable for the way their services affect users. Similar initiatives might come up in other EU Member States as part of a broader European response.

By D3 – Defesa dos Direitos Digitais & NOVA School of Law (guest author) · October 8, 2026

In April and May 2026, D3 brought four cases before the Portuguese civil courts against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. The proceedings took the form of a “popular action”, that is, a specific legal mechanism for collective redress provided for in the Portuguese Constitution in which D3 acts as a collective representative of the rights of people in Portugal.

The cases concern the business models of major platforms and the incentives created by the attention economy. D3 argues that the platforms’ business models should not depend on design mechanisms that undermine users’ ability to exercise control over their own use of digital services.

The purpose of the actions is to seek greater accountability from platforms and to ensure that users can have a safer experience online.

The actions were brought by a team of lawyers led by Miguel Miranda and Efigénia Marabuto Tavares, from Andersen Tax & Legal Iberia. Academic experts Fabrizio Esposito and Cecília Isola, from NOVA School of Law, also supported the cases.

Online platforms have access to large amounts of information about users’ behaviour and interactions. Such concentration of information gives a small number of companies significant power to shape how people interact with their services.

The actions focus on design practices commonly described as dark patterns, including infinite scrolling, automatic playback, persistent notifications, personalised recommendation systems and gamification. Together, these features act as a powerful force that makes people spend more time on platforms and interact with them more frequently.

The case argues that such practices draw on knowledge of human behaviour and psychology, combined with information about users’ preferences, vulnerabilities and interests. The resulting systems can make it more difficult for users to stop using a service voluntarily and can reduce the scope for independent decision-making.

Research across fields including medicine, psychology, sociology and technology has examined the relationship between digital design and compulsive patterns of use. The issue has also received attention from the European Parliament and the European Commission, as well as in legal proceedings in the United States and by EDRi member Bits of Freedom in the Netherlands.

One of the groups of people most vulnerable to deceptive and manipulative design of platforms are young people. So far, the EU’s response to calls for protecting them has unfortunately been limited to age gates and restrictions, putting the responsibility on the individual rather than the platforms.

D3 argues that restricting access to social media for people under 16 should not be treated as a substitute for addressing potentially harmful design practices. Social media platforms have become important means of communication and interaction, making it necessary to address the design of these services rather than simply excluding particular groups from them.

As D3 president Ricardo Lafuente explains, platforms can provide a healthier online environment if effective rules are properly enforced and responsibility is placed on platforms that fail to comply with them.

The Portuguese cases contribute to a growing European debate about platform design, user autonomy and platform accountability. D3’s approach focuses on the responsibilities of platforms and the conditions under which digital services are designed and operated.

With similar initiatives potentially being prepared in other EU Member States, cooperation between digital rights organisations and legal initiatives could help develop a coordinated European response to addictive design.

The objective is not to prevent people from using social media, rather to support an online environment in which users retain meaningful control over their digital experiences.

People should not have to choose between access to essential online services and the ability to use those services without being subjected to design practices that encourage compulsive use.

Contribution by: Eduardo Santos, D3 – Defesa dos Direitos Digitais, EDRi member; Fabrizio Esposito, NOVA School of Law

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Bukidnon Lumad’s fight for ancestral land remains uncertain
content:
Representatives of the Gulinsao and Maranding clans join a dialogue held at Provincial Tulugan Hall, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, on September 7, 2026. Photo from Bukidnon Provincial IPMR Datu Makayuba Renato Sumbongan’s Facebook page

CAGAYAN DE ORO — After the fifth dialogue aiming to settle the land dispute between Indigenous peoples and a government agency in Barangay Dalwangan, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, Lumad are still deprived of their ancestral land.

“They should return the land they borrowed,” Datu Aldren Gulinsao told Bulatlat in the vernacular following the dialogue last month.

Since 2017, the Gulinsao clan belonging to the Talaandig tribe has been reclaiming over 600 hectares of ancestral land, while their relative, the Maranding clan, has been claiming over 400 hectares. These form part of the more than 1,000 hectares of land under the title they obtained during the Philippine Commonwealth owned by their ancestor Maximo Gulinsao.

The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), on the other hand, said the subject land has been a titled property of the Department of Agriculture (DA) since the 1930s.

To assert their rights, in February, a few members of the Gulinsao clan forcibly entered the land, which resulted in the arrest of three individuals.

CONTEXT: Uncertainty forces Lumad to enter disputed ancestral land in Bukidnon

In a dialogue launched in December 2021, lawyer Heinz Villanueva, then legal officer of the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), told the Lumad claimants that they needed to file a case to cancel DA’s title before they could proceed in filing an ancestral domain claim.

Gulinsao opposed the suggestion, saying that DA possessed the same title that they have. During the September 7, 2026 dialogue, he asked the DA representative if they have a Deed of Sale. The representative could not provide a definite answer as it still needed to be checked.

The Lumad leader said they are in the process of completing their certificate of ancestral domain claim (CADC) before the NCIP.

The concerned Lumad clans, however, were told that they could be beneficiaries of the government’s agrarian reform program after 358 hectares of the subject land—also within the claim of the Gulinsao clan—has been subject to Executive Order No. 75-2019, an order directing all government agencies to identify state-owned lands suitable for agriculture for distribution to qualified agrarian reform beneficiaries.

Datu Ornan Lesion, a representative of the Maranding clan, said in the September 7, 2026, dialogue that there were more than 200 of them who wanted to become beneficiaries. The Gulinsao clan has almost the same number of members. Both clans welcomed the offer because of their eagerness to have a land to till. But this also remains a challenge.

Gulinsao said they already made repeated requests to the municipal and provincial agrarian reform offices, but they were told to also submit a request to the DA, which allegedly did not respond despite follow-ups.

Marvin Calleja, DAR Malaybalay representative, said that Task Force Dalwangan was already created in 2023, but the status of the 358 hectares of land remains pending. He said he would forward the dialogue discussion to their provincial office to clarify the matter.

“With our process now, we have lost hope on our government agencies,” Gulinsao said in the vernacular when asked for their future plans.

He said there are clan members currently living in Barangay Dalwangan, but outside their ancestral land. Other members are living in the neighboring town of Impasug-ong. He said they want to resolve the matter through a sala, a Lumad customary practice of settling disputes, as their final resort.

The month of October serves as the Indigenous Peoples’ Month. (RVO)

Disclosure: All of the dialogue discussions cited in this article were based on the minutes of meetings obtained by the Gulinsao clan from the Office of the City and Provincial Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representatives and forwarded to Bulatlat.

title: Festival-themed protest underscores teachers’ economic demands
content:
MANILA – On World Teachers’ Day, members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) held a protest near Malacañang Palace billed as “Pistang Protesta: Dagdag Sweldo, Hindi Dagdag Trabaho.”

Teachers from different public and private schools all over Metro Manila, as well as students and supporters marched Padre Noval Street corner España Boulevard toward Mendiola, October 5, 2026.

Carrying bunting flags and surrounded by ice cream carts, protesters called for a reduced and humane workload, allocation of six percent of GDP to education, P5,000 (approximately US$79.68) economic relief allowance and P50,000 (approximately US$796.81) entry-level salary for all teachers.

The current starting basic pay of a Teacher is pegged at P31,705 (approximately US$505.26) while the economic relief allowance is only P2,000 (approximately US$31.87)

Hogier Villarias, secretary general of Alliance of Concerned Teachers NCR, said that their call for salary hike is timely considering the increase in the country’s Gross Domestic Product.

“Our primary call remains a salary increase since our GDP grew by four percent, so we are expecting that wages should also be increased,” said Villarias, who joined the protest along with his fellow teachers from Andres Bonifacio Elementary School.

According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the GDP of the country grew by 4.4 percent in 2025. However, progressive groups argued that economic growth is meaningless if it does not translate to higher wages and better working conditions.

Katrina Ortega, president of All UP Academic Employees Union Diliman, meanwhile, pointed out wrong priorities of the Marcos Jr. administration.

“We cannot accept that funds are diverted to confidential funds and flood control projects while we lack teachers and classrooms. The children suffer — they have no learning materials, and even basic school needs like water and comfort rooms are lacking. All of these affect the children,” Ortega stated.

In the proposed P7.2-trillion (approximately US$114.74 billion) national budget for 2027, P1.326 trillion (approximately US$21.13 billion) is allotted for the education sector — P975.96 billion (approximately US$15.56 billion) for the Department of Education and P176.5 billion (approximately US$2.81 billion) for higher education. This is around 1.41 percent lower than the P1.345 trillion (approximately US$21.43 billion) allocated in 2026.

The proposed P1.467 trillion (approximately US$23.38 billion) fund for the government-wide infrastructure program is still 10.6 percent higher than the budget proposed for education. Moreover, there is also a roughly 13.8 percent increase in infrastructure budget from the P1.29 trillion (approximately US$20.56 billion) allocated in 2026.

Infrastructure projects are vulnerable to political patronage, according to the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC). In fact, the coalition identified P970 billion (approximately US$15.46 billion) worth of potential ‘pork’ from the proposed 2027 budget as they observed patterns of alleged political influence particularly in flood-control projects.

Concerns over potential misuse and abuse of these funds fueled protesters’ calls for a different direction in government spending. Progressive groups are urging the administration to stop feeding political interests and instead pour more funds toward public welfare programs.

During the protest, former ACT Teachers Party-list Representative France Castro amplified her condemnation of corruption and demand for greater funding for social services, including education.

“From the passage of the budget to its signing into law, the budget is full of corruption — this is what we are opposing. What we are demanding is funding for social services, education, housing, and others,” Castro said.

Protesters said their fight doesn’t end with the dispersal, pledging to carry the fight beyond the streets and continue pushing for urgent education reforms. (RVO)

author: Lance Selfa
title: What’s up with Jacobin’s “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”?
content:
Every few months, 

Jacobin 

magazine announces what it purports to be a secret to win working-class voters based on a finding from its associated Center for Working Class Politics (CWCP). Its 14 September editorial “

Report: The Working Class Vote is Not Lost

” was the latest in this series.

CWCP’s latest innovation is the “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”, which Jacobin describes as “a data-driven road map for winning back working-class voters”. It purports to demonstrate the optimal combination of social and political appeals to move working-class voters to vote for a hypothetical Democratic candidate.

Two points should be made at the outset. When

 Jacobin

 and CWCP talk about “winning working class voters,” they don’t mean winning the working class to socialism. They mean “winning” the working class to vote for Democrats. And they define the “working class” as non-college-educated people with family incomes of between $30,000 and $150,000.

This supposedly groundbreaking survey and analysis is an exercise in political message-testing for Democratic candidates. It uses the definition of “working-class” that is the standard in lazy polling and media commentary, and thus adds no new insights. Attaching the labels of “socialist” and “working-class” doesn’t change the fact that what

 Jacobin

 and CWCP are engaged in is a completely conventional activity that regularly earns millions for Democratic Party consultants.

Without digressing into a long discussion of the inadequacies of the study’s understanding of class, it’s worth pondering why, under its definition, a non-college educated small business owner is “working class” but a college-educated nurse or K-12 teacher who is a union activist is not considered working-class. It’s the same sort of logic that 

had Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-adjacent consultants and 

Jacobin

 fawning over

 working-class avatar “oyster farmer” Graham Platner as a US Senate candidate in Maine before Platner’s campaign imploded.

The study’s key findings include “lead with working-class economics” and “adopt culture and climate positions that resonate with working-class voters”. These takeaways are supposed to increase the hypothetical Democratic candidate’s support over what it calls a “Kamala Harris-2024 style Democrat.”

For working-class economics or economic populist policies, the winning positions come from a list of ordinary policies from tuition-free community college to protecting Social Security from cuts to capping prescription-drug prices. There is nothing wrong with these proposals. But they are hardly bold. In fact, many of them are the same poll-tested offerings that Democratic Party politicians have included in their campaigns for years.

The fact that they are repackaged here as keys to victory should emphasise how little the Democrats have done to implement these when they have held power in the past. And it’s noteworthy that “Medicare for All,” the signature proposal that social democrats like 

Jacobin

 and DSA have championed for more than a decade, didn’t make the list.

But what really gives the game away are the “culture and climate” positions the analysis considers 

losing

 messages for Democratic politicians. For anyone who is familiar with 

Jacobin’s

 antipathy to 

“subcultural leftism”

, the losing positions won’t surprise: reducing funding for police, “abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),” and letting “trans girls play in girls’ sports.” Other so-called “social issues,” such as defence of abortion rights, don’t significantly move the needle toward the Democrats, CWCP finds.

Mainstream Democratic Party campaigns in the midterm electoral cycle are following this script without even dialling up the “Win-o-Meter”. It’s an article of faith that serious Democratic candidates run on “kitchen-table issues” like the price of groceries and gasoline, and “don’t take the bait” by engaging with Republicans over “silly culture war” issues. Or they try to get ahead of the Republican attacks by pre-emptively jumping to the conservative side. For example, Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico said he too 

opposes trans girls in girls’ sports

. As the liberal journalist 

Perry Bacon

 explained:

“‘Economic issues not cultural wars’ produces a party that both loses elections and abandons moral causes and vulnerable people. That’s not a theoretical argument—it’s the story of the Democratic Party of my entire adulthood. The reality is that there are no silly culture wars happening in America. There are equality wars and justice wars and fairness wars. Democrats should try to win those wars—and the elections that involve them.”

When

 Jacobin

 argues for Democratic candidates to express their positions in the language of “working-class values,” it explicitly cites “loyalty to community and country, pride in hard work, respect for traditional institutions and for playing by the rules, personal security, and anti-elitism.”

A Democratic politics stressing “it’s the economy, stupid” and supporting people who “work hard and play by the rules” isn’t some new formula that 

Jacobin

 discovered. In fact, these were two catchphrases of Bill Clinton’s first run for president in 1992! Daniel Goulden’s takedown of the “Win-O-Meter” asked a pertinent question: “

Why Does Jacobin Sound Like Third Way?”

 Third Way is the corporate-funded DC think tank that pushes warmed-over Clintonism and that recently announced a 

McCarthyite campaign against “democratic socialists”

 in the Democratic Party.

Why would a “socialist” initiative end up echoing some of the worst Democratic Party conventional wisdom? The conventional wisdom that opened the door to Trump, no less.

At a base level, this is where you end up if you accept the DSA perspective that the most important form 

of “mass politics” is electoral and focused on the bosses’ Democratic Party

. The DSA may have built an impressive canvassing operation for Mayor Mamdani’s election in New York City, 

but that mass element has mostly dissipated since

. Moreover, since Bernie Sanders’ unsuccessful run for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016, prominent supporters of his have gone on 

to form consultancies for Democratic candidates

 that reflect just the sort of politics CWCP espouses.

When you play in Democratic politics, you adopt its norms and tropes. This is not a new problem, as the Democrats have historically absorbed challenges from the left and disarmed them. In his 

Communists in Harlem During the Depression

, historian Mark Naison shows how, during the 1930s Popular Front era, the Communists transformed themselves from radical organisers of community protests into deal-making operatives whose efforts helped propel the career of the Harlem Democratic machine politician, the reverend Adam Clayton Powell, Jr.

A fundamental principle of socialism, going back to Marx and Engels, is 

the commitment to build a working-class political organisation independent of capitalist politics

. Histories of U.S. communism in the 1920s and 1930s demonstrate how the CP abandoned that principle as it transformed itself into the left wing of the New Deal. But where the CP once had what you might call a “heroic period” of working-class radical activism to abandon, the DSA can’t claim that. It has always been an electoral organisation focused on transforming the Democratic Party, abandoning instead calls for breaks 

(“dirty” or otherwise) from the liberal capitalist party

.

Even though DSA, 

Jacobin

, CWCP and the rest aren’t in practice committed to a fundamental goal of nineteenth century social democracy—that is, building a social democratic or labour party—they operate on a theory of working-class politics and consciousness very much in line with their social democratic forebears.

In 

Party and Class

,

 the late British revolutionary socialist Chris Harman distinguished between the social-democratic party, that purports to organise the “whole” working class, and the Leninist revolutionary party that organises the most politically conscious and active members of that class. Unlike the social-democratic party, which caters to the lowest common denominator of an electoral coalition, the revolutionary party carries out “continual agitation and propaganda among more [politically] backward elements of the class so as to raise their self-consciousness and self-reliance” to fight for socialism.

From these conceptions of political organisation and working-class consciousness, it’s entirely understandable why Jacobin and friends would workshop ways to attract support of voters (even Trumpy ones) with “kitchen-table issues” while accommodating their conservatism on other issues. It’s the direct counterposition to Lenin’s view that socialists should be “tribunes of the people” who champion the rights of the oppressed in the broader class struggle.

A socialist focus on “kitchen-table issues” is entirely inadequate, not only because wide swathes of working-class people are activated

 because

 they oppose Trump’s racist, xenophobic, sexist and homophobic policies, but because there is no hope to build a working-class opposition to Trumpism unless it confronts its racist, far-right core. As Lenin noted in another context:

“There are two sorts of independent [working-class] activity. There is the independent activity of a proletariat that possesses revolutionary initiative, and there is the independent activity of a proletariat that is undeveloped and held in leading strings … There are Social Democrats to this day who contemplate with reverence the second kind of activity, who believe they can evade a direct reply to pressing questions of the day by repeating the word ‘class’ over and over again ...”

Lenin wrote those words more than a century ago. But they could have been written about 

Jacobin 

and the “Win-o-Meter” today.

First published at the 

International Socialism Project

. Lance Selfa is the author of 

The Democrats: A Critical History

 and editor of 

U.S. Politics in an Age of Uncertainty: Essays on a New Reality

.

author: Jonathan Strauss
title: Qld NTEU members rally against wage cuts
content:
More than 500 university workers, members of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU), struck from 11am on October 8 before rallying at Queens Gardens in the city.

They came from Magan-djin/Brisbane’s three universities: Griffith; Queensland University of Technology (QUT); and the University of Queensland (UQ). The rally was joined by students and other unionists.

Members of the NTEU branches at all three universities are bargaining on pay and conditions with their universities’ managements. The latter have made either below-inflation pay offers or none at all. Both QUT and UQ managements are trying to have the Fair Work Commission intervene on their behalf, while Griffith’s bosses are saying they will not negotiate until next year.

NTEU members repeatedly said the workers were the ones creating the valuable things universities provide, but are being continually squeezed for money and time by management.

They contrasted this with the recent surpluses declared by UQ and QUT managements, and the spending on buildings by Griffith, including $67 million to purchase a building, opposite the rally site, that did not have the offices needed for university activities.

NTEU members said a fair pay rise would at least maintain the value of their pay against cost-of-living rises.

They are also looking to win equity in superannuation payments for casualised staff and an end to the job cuts and spiralling workloads, including among administrative, other professional and technical staff whose work underpins academics’ teaching and research.

The range of speakers from the union’s three branches — local office bearers, casually-employed activists and others — reflected the on-the-ground activism the bargaining campaigns are achieving.

This rally was larger than a similar one during bargaining four years ago, as the development of workplace organising by the union has started to take hold.

National NTEU president Alison Barnes was the lead speaker, alongside NSW Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi and two student union representatives. Barnes noted that the cross-campus action is inspiring.

author: Unknown
title: Karasu: Once Öcalan’s freedom is secured, the conspiracy will be completely defeated
content:
In the second part of this interview with 

Medya Haber

, KCK Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu said that the aim of the conspiracy against Abdullah Öcalan on 9 October 1998, was to completely dismantle the Freedom Movement. He said that the political approach pursued by Leader Apo, and the prospect of resolving the Kurdish question on a democratic basis, would weaken the collaborative foundations on which the United States and other external powers relied, and that the International Conspiracy was therefore carried out by the United States and Israel.




The first part of this in-depth interview can be read 

here

.




We are approaching the 28th anniversary of the international conspiracy against Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan, which started on 9 October 1998, and concluded on 15 February 1999. What kind of approach and stance towards the international conspiracy, given the current political juncture, do you see as appropriate?




Before answering these questions, I must mention our very dear comrades who were martyred in October. They were pioneered by the comrades Gurbetelli Ersöz (8 October 1997), Nagihan Akarsel (4 October 2022), and Bêrîtan (25 October 1992), who fell as martyrs in the month of October. I knew comrade Gurbetelli Ersöz personally. While we were in prison, she would regularly attend our meetings. Later, she was assigned to work in the press, and we maintained contact during her time in Europe. She was a good friend, and I knew her well. Truly a conscious comrade. She had strong patriotic feelings and was a person who had a good understanding of Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] and the movement. When she first came to prison, she hadn’t yet fully joined the movement as a cadre. At that time, she was still in college, but she was already actively involved. She had actually decided to join but still had academic work to complete at the university. Later, she took on responsibilities in the press and truly shaped the press work.




During the 1990s, when our movement was developing, the role of the press was extremely important. The press’s coverage of our struggle truly made significant contributions to the development of the struggle. Particularly in this regard, our comrade Gurbetelli played a very important role. She laid the foundation for our press, shaped its spirit, and defined its perspective. Gurbetelli Ersöz is a pioneer of the press within the freedom movement. It is therefore that our press academy today is named the ‘Gurbetelli Ersöz Academy.’ Press activities, the academy, and the training programs are all conducted in the name of our comrade Gurbetelli. She holds a truly vital place in our struggle, and still today her stance is of great importance to us. After her work for the press in Europe, she came to the guerrillas. Her participation in the struggle in the mountains was truly enthusiastic and meaningful. Her transition from the press to the guerrilla ranks – joining the guerrillas with such a level of consciousness – naturally represented an important stance from the guerrillas’ perspective in terms of guerrilla training, organization, and the struggle. I commemorate her with respect and gratitude.




Nagihan Akarsel was also an important journalist. She was a force of thought. As is known, she was assassinated in Sulaymaniyah. The Turkish state bears great guilt in this murder. The Turkish state has murdered many of our comrades, particularly our journalists, with their UCAVs. Many of our comrades working in the media in Sulaymaniyah, the Medya Defense Zones, and in Southern Kurdistan in general have been murdered by the Turkish state’s airstrikes and UCAV attacks. I commemorate all of them with gratitude and respect.




Comrade Nagihan Akarsel was not only a journalist but also made very important contributions to Jineolojî, the science of women’s liberation. She is one of the pioneers of the science of women’s liberation. And Jineolojî is the mother of all sciences. It is the mother of the social sciences. Without understanding the science of women’s liberation, the social sciences cannot be properly understood. The social sciences cannot be properly addressed. And the contributions of Nagihan Akarsel to Jineolojî have truly been immense. I also remember her with gratitude and respect.




Comrade Bêrîtan’s stance is of the utmost importance. She is a symbol of the stance for women’s freedom. Indeed, Rêber Apo defined the character and identity of our cadres as embodying the character and identity of Bêrîtan and Kemal Pir. It established that their stance represents the PKK line and that their stance is the line of freedom. This is extremely important. Because the line of women’s freedom is the defining characteristic of our movement. It is its most fundamental characteristic. It is its most fundamental defining characteristic. It is the line of women’s freedom that gives meaning to and adds value to all other dimensions. Comrade Bêrîtan has taken the lead. She has made immense contributions to the struggle for women’s freedom. What does a stance for women’s freedom look like? What does a woman’s stance look like? She demonstrated this in every moment of her life. I also remember her with gratitude and respect.




On its anniversary, I once again condemn all the countries and individuals involved in the international conspiracy against Rêber Apo. Through this conspiracy, they have committed a crime against humanity. I want to emphasize this in particular. Why did this conspiracy take place? Why was Rêber Apo targeted? This was not merely the Turkish state’s targeting. Indeed, on February 15, 1999, after Rêber Apo was handed over to Turkey, Bülent Ecevit said that he couldn’t understand why Rêber Apo was handed over to them. The United States and Israel were the primary architects of the international conspiracy. They carried out this conspiracy, and Europe was also complicit. But primarily, the US viewed our freedom struggle – led by Rêber Apo – as a threat to its own interests in the Middle East. They believed our struggle was hindering those interests, and that is why they carried out the conspiracy. In this regard, it is essential to recognize this reality.




The Turkish state occasionally accuses the US of supporting the PKK. Do they really think that the people are so forgetful or stupid? The US carried out the conspiracy against Rêber Apo and against our movement. They even dragged Russia into it and used Greece for this purpose. It was about the creation of a new order in the Middle East. The Middle East was a region where peoples were pitted against one another, turned into enemies, and where ethnic and sectarian wars were fueled. Rêber Apo wanted to change this Middle East. He was pursuing a policy of resolution based on the brotherhood of peoples in the Middle East. He argued that the unresolved Kurdish issue was harming all the peoples of the Middle East. Based on the resolution of the Kurdish issue – and on a democratic solution – he wanted to create a new order in the Middle East founded on the brotherhood of peoples.




This order would have shaken the US-backed order reliant on collaborators. Because the policy pursued by our movement – the resolution of the Kurdish issue on a democratic basis – would have weakened the collaborative foundation upon which the US and other external powers relied. In 1924, with the Treaty of Lausanne, Kurdistan was divided into four parts. It used to be two parts, but with the inclusion of Mosul, it was divided into four parts. This was such a system that they sought to create a conflict of interests in the Middle East through the Kurds and to bind all countries to themselves. Driven by fear of the Kurds, Turkey tied itself to foreign powers. Iraq tied itself to differing foreign powers. Also in Syria and Iran, due to fear of the Kurds, collaboration was taking root. The unresolved Kurdish issue had become a shackle on the peoples of the Middle East. Rêber Apo wanted to resolve this. He wanted to resolve it on the basis of the Kurdish people’s freedom and on the basis of democracy.




Rêber Apo did not wage the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom within a framework of hostility toward the other peoples of the region. On the contrary, he aimed to free all the peoples of the region – including those in Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran – from this burden. This is precisely why Rêber Apo and our movement were targeted. Because our struggle was gaining momentum and continuing to grow. Had it continued to develop, a new order would have emerged in the Middle East. The forces of collaboration would have weakened. This, in turn, would have shaken the dominance of international powers in the region. That is why the conspiracy was carried out. This aspect is important to be understood. Together with our people, we waged a great struggle against this conspiracy. The aim of the conspiracy was to liquidate our movement through the imprisonment of our leader. It was to sever the people from their leader, to sever the movement from Rêber Apo, and to liquidate the struggle. But we stood by our leader, and so did our people. We waged the struggle on the basis of Rêber Apo’s freedom. We continued this struggle based on his perspectives. Because Rêber Apo was the leader that enabled and ensured the development of this struggle. It was the leader that advanced the free and democratic life of the Kurdish people. Our people were very well aware of this. And since we knew Rêber Apo so well, we fought against the international conspiracy’s policy of neutralizing our movement by imprisoning him and limiting the Kurdish people’s freedom struggle – by standing by Rêber Apo with the according strategy and by analyzing the true character of the conspiracy – and we have brought the struggle to where it is today. How should this conspiracy be approached today? In terms of its objectives, this conspiracy has been largely thwarted. But Rêber Apo is still in captivity.




The objectives the conspiracy aimed for have not been realized. There is certainly a failure in this regard. We have thwarted the conspiracy, but of course, since Rêber Apo is still in captivity, the struggle against the conspiracy must continue today as a struggle for Rêber Apo’s freedom. Once Rêber Apo’s freedom is secured, the conspiracy will be completely thwarted. Then the conspiracy will be entirely defeated. We have waged this struggle so far, and we will continue to wage it from here on out. The struggle against the conspiracy must be the struggle to secure the freedom of Rêber Apo. Both the Kurdish people and our friends should focus on the freedom of Rêber Apo. Therefore, awareness of the conspiracy is very important. Bringing this conspiracy to light comes by posing questions like: What is the Kurdish question? What is the Kurdish reality? What is the correct struggle?




It is possible to both push back against the conspiracy and advance our struggle. Raising awareness of the conspiracy is extremely important. Without raising awareness of the international conspiracy against the Kurds, the Kurdish people cannot wage a proper struggle for freedom. Therefore, we are constantly striving to raise awareness of this conspiracy. Rêber Apo has continuously assessed the conspiracy, thereby enlightening our movement and our people. We know what this conspiracy is and what the conspirators’ aims are. The conspiratorial approach continues today. Especially after Rêber Apo introduced the new paradigm, the conspiracy remained on the agenda. The conspiratorial mindset persists. This is because, under Rêber Apo’s leadership, the conspirators view the Kurdish people’s quest for a democratic solution and a democratic Middle East as a threat to their own interests. Not only the Kurdish people but all the peoples of the Middle East should see this. The peoples of the Middle East should clearly understand the implications of the attacks launched against us by international powers and various other forces. This is not merely an attack against us, nor is it an attack against the Kurdish people; it is an attack against all the peoples of the Middle East and against all the democratic and freedom-striving forces in the entire region. In this regard, while fighting against the international conspiracy, not only the Kurdish people but all the peoples of the region should see what this conspiracy is and what the conspiracy waged against us signifies. Everyone must recognize and play their own roles in the struggle against the conspiracy. Because the conspiracy targeting our movement is a conspiracy targeting the entire Middle East.




Many say that through the international conspiracy, an entire people – represented by the people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan – was sought to be erased from history. Yet today, we are witnessing the Peace and Democratic Society Process. How was it possible to get from one such extreme point to the other?




Yes, that assessment is definitely true. Rêber Apo – as the Kurds’ greatest will and greatest power in the Middle East – was targeted, and the aim was annihilation. But through 28 years of struggle – the struggle spearheaded by Rêber Apo – it wasn’t just Rêber Apo himself who grew. Today, Rêber Apo is a great leader. He is a leader of humanity. He is a leader that has put forth the call for humanity’s liberation. And our movement has grown too. Our movement has become very influential. It has become influential in all four parts of Kurdistan. And it has become an influential force in the Middle East. Despite all the attacks, it has maintained this strength. The Kurdish presence has demonstrated its influence even more over these 28 years. The level the Kurdish presence has reached today reveals just how strongly and on a grand scale the struggle against the conspiracy has been waged.




And now, today, the Peace and Democratic Society Process is underway. Rêber Apo is spearheading this effort. Undoubtedly, there are dangers involved, but it must be emphasized that the Kurds’ presence, strength, influence, and capacity to fight against any dangers have decisively grown. When an effective struggle is waged against these dangers through organized strength – encompassing the four parts of Kurdistan and the organized strength of Kurds worldwide – and with the level of consciousness that has been achieved, any and all dangers can be neutralized. Today, there are about 60 million Kurds. Within it lay a strong potential of force. Today, there is a Kurdish force that everyone must take into account. The international conspiracy aimed to liquidate our movement and Rêber Apo. They wanted to break the will of the Kurds. But the very fact that we’re speaking about 60 million Kurds being active in the Middle East today shows not only that the international conspiracy has failed but also that it is the result of the struggle of Rêber Apo and the Kurdish freedom movement. Anyone with a conscience and integrity can assess it this way. If Kurds are alive and dynamic today in the four parts of Kurdistan, the existence of our freedom movement and the struggle it has waged play a decisive role in this. Without recognizing this reality, no one can pursue the correct Kurdish policy. No one can wage an effective struggle.




Still dangers persist, because in the Middle East, concepts of hegemony based on the genocide of the Kurds and the elimination of the Kurds have not yet been abandoned. A complete shift in this mindset has not yet taken place. Yes, the Kurdish presence has emerged in a vibrant way and has asserted itself. But the powers that still exercise hegemony over the Kurds – the reactionary forces in the region – are still waging an attack against the Kurdish presence. They are still making efforts to neutralize the Kurdish influence. That is a reality that needs to be acknowledged. But a Kurdish force has emerged, and as a result of decades of struggle, this Kurdish presence and this Kurdish force, when the right policies are implemented, when an organized struggle is waged, and when this reality is organized, the Kurdish people will undoubtedly achieve a free and democratic life everywhere.
