{1} It is this element of relationship which leads me to speak of gift exchange as an “erotic” commerce, opposing eros (the principle of attraction, union, involvement which binds together) to logos (reason and logic in general, the principle of differentiation in particular). A market economy is an emanation of logos.

{2} This story illustrates almost all the main characteristics of a gift, so I shall be referring back to it. As an aside, therefore, I want to take a stab at its meaning. It says, I think, that if a girl without a father is going to get along in the world, she’d better have a good connection to her mother. The birds are the mother’s spirit, what we’d now call the girls’ psychological mother. The girl who gives the gift back to the spirit-mother has, as a result, her mother-wits about her for the rest of the tale. Nothing in the tale links the dead man with the girls’ father, but the mother seems to be a widow, or at any rate the absence of a father at the start of the story is a hint that the problem may have to do with men. It’s not clear, but when the first man she meets is not only dead but difficult, we are permitted to raise our eyebrows. The man is dead, but not dead enough. When she hits him with the stick, we see that she is in fact attached to him. So here’s the issue: when a fatherless woman leaves home, she’ll have to deal with the fact that she’s stuck on a dead man. It’s a risky situation—the two elder daughters end up dead. Not much happens in the wild run through the forest, except that both parties get bruised. The girl manages to stay awake the whole time, however. This is a power she probably got from the birds, for they are night birds. The connection to the mother cannot spare her the ordeal, but it allows her to survive. When it’s all over she’s unstuck, and we may assume that the problem won’t arise again. Though the dilemma of the story is not related to gift, all the psychological work is accomplished through gift exchange.

{3} Folk tales are the only proof I shall be able to offer for these assertions. The point is more spiritual than social: in the spiritual world, new life comes to those who give up.

{4} In the fall of 1980 a group of Australian aborigines asked the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva to help them protect their lands from commercial exploitation. According to a wire service report, “one of the group’s major concerns is the violation of the sacred home of the aboriginal lizard god, Great Goanna, by Amax, an American petroleum company that is under contract to the state government of Western Australia to drill there. The Yungnara tribe on the Noonkanbah pastoral station believes that if Goanna is disturbed he will order the six-foot monitor lizards, which are a source of food for the aborigines, to stop mating and thus eventually cause a food shortage.” There may be no necessary link between scarcity and exploitation, but the connection is not unknown, either. In the North Pacific, salmon stocks actually did decline as soon as European settlers began to treat the fish as a commodity to be sold for a profit. By the end of the nineteenth century a salmon cannery sat at the mouth of every major river on the Alaskan coast; many overfished the runs and drove themselves out of business. On the East Coast the salmon essentially disappeared, although they were once so plentiful as to have been the dietary staple of the textile workers in the mill towns along the Merrimac River. (In the summer of 1974 a salmon was found in the Connecticut River; it was dead, but it was the first to appear in those waters in 150 years.)

{5} To say that coppers are images of zoë-life would explain why their exchange is accompanied by recitations of history and genealogy. Like the Kula articles, the passage of these gifts keeps history alive so that individuals may witness and affirm their participation in nonindividual life. Note as well the mortuary potlatch’s connection to my opening story, the first salmon rite, which also has the bones of the dead, their imagined reassembly, and a sense of increase.

{6} A confusion between organic liveliness and cultural or spiritual liveliness is inherent in a discussion of gift exchange. As Mauss first pointed out, in an exchange of gifts, “things…are to some extent parts of persons, and persons…behave in some measure as if they were things.” In the case of the mortuary potlatch, a material thing symbolizes a biological fact, the survival of the group despite the death of the individual. But it may be that the group would not survive as a group (and individual life would not survive, then, either) if these “biological” facts could not be expressed symbolically. We are social and spiritual beings; at some level biological, social, and spiritual life cannot be differentiated.

{7} In a typical example from a book of Russian folk tales, a woman walking in the woods found a baby wood-demon “lying naked on the ground and crying bitterly. So she covered it up with her cloak, and after a time came her mother, a female wood-demon, and rewarded the woman with a potful of burning coals, which afterward turned into bright golden ducats.” The woman covers the baby because she’s moved to do so, a gratuitous, social act. Then the gift comes to her. It increases solely by its passage from the realm of wood-demons to her cottage.

{8} Barnett’s language, the language of gift exchange, has procreation at its root. Generosity comes from genere (Old Latin: beget, produce), and the generations are its consequence, as are the gens, the clans. At its source in both Greek and Sanskrit, liberality is desire; libido is its modern cousin. Virtue’s root is a sex (vir, the man), and virility is its action. Virtue, like the gift, moves through a person, and has a procreative or healing power (as in the Bible story about the woman who touched the hem of Jesus’s garment in the faith that it would heal her: “And Jesus, immediately knowing in himself that virtue had gone out of him turned about in the press and said, ‘Who touched my clothes?’ ”).

{9} Capitalism is the ideology that asks that we remove surplus wealth from circulation and lay it aside to produce more wealth. To move away from capitalism is not to change the form of ownership from the few to the many, but to cease turning so much surplus into capital, that is, to treat most increase as a gift. It is quite possible to have the state own everything and still convert all gifts to capital, as Stalin demonstrated. When he decided in favor of the “production mode”—an intensive investment in capital goods—he acted as a capitalist, the locus of ownership having nothing to do with it.

{10} Separation often involves a “cutting” ceremony rather than a gift (see Van Gennep’s remarks on divorce, for example). Going-away presents are given at the time of separation, but as the Scottish tale well illustrated, such farewells attempt to overcome the physical departure, rather than facilitate it. “My spirit goes with you,” they say. Going-away presents are gifts of spiritual incorporation.

{11} Those who write on gift exchange usually mention at this point that the German word Gift means “poison.” The connection is more accidental than significant, however. The French etymologist Benveniste writes: “There is a…medical usage in which [the Greek word] dósis denotes the act of giving, whence develops the sense of the amount of medicine given, a ‘dose’…This sense passed by loan translation into German, where Gift, like Gr.-Lat. dósis, was used as a substitute for ven˜enum, ‘poison’…”

{12} Few modern therapies present their teachings as gifts the way AA does. You can pay almost any amount for spiritual advice, psychotherapy, or “self-help” lessons. Despite my obvious bias, I don’t maintain that fees for such services are inappropriate. Therapists, meditation instructors, and so forth work at what they do, and they deserve to earn their keep. A lot depends on the spirit of the exchange, too; gifts will sometimes circulate above the cash. The AA example indicates, however, that the fee is not always a necessary part of the transaction as it is often made out to be. Further, the size of the fee is sometimes the clearest indication that the proffered teaching may not in fact lead to transformation, as when the minimum initial “donation” to the Church of Scientology is $2,700 for a 12½-hour “intensive.”

{13} That the helpers are in a sort of bondage is clearer in other tales with the same motif. Several examples are cited in the notes at the end of the book.

{14} As those who must worry about the livelihood of artists are fond of saying, “You cannot play ‘The Minute Waltz’ in less than a minute.” Worse (or perhaps better) you cannot write “The Minute Waltz” in less than…what? A day, a week, a year?—however long it takes. There is no technology, no time-saving device that can alter the rhythms of creative labor. When the worth of labor is expressed in terms of exchange value, therefore, creativity is automatically devalued every time there is an advance in the technology of work.

{15} To atone and to forgive are complementary acts. In forgiving a sin, he who has been sinned against initiates the exchange that reestablishes the bond. We forgive once we give up attachment to our wounds.

{16} I use “value” and “worth” when I want to mark this distinction. I was therefore delighted to find the following footnote in Marx: “In the seventeenth century, many English authors continued to write ‘worth’ for ‘use-value’ and ‘value’ for ‘exchange-value,’ this being accordant with the genius of a language which prefers an Anglo-Saxon word for an actual thing, and a Romance word for its reflexion.”

{17} The prohibition on gifts to public servants has always been a problem because our expectations are conflicting: we want such people to become a part of their community, but we do not want them to be beholden to one particular element. Is a policeman who accepts an apple from the greengrocer an extortionist? Is he a lackey of the grocery trade, or is he merely accepting and expressing his connection to the group he serves?

{18} Alcoholics who get sober in AA tend to become very attached to the group, at least to begin with. Their involvement seems, in part, a consequence of the fact that AA’s program is a gift. In the case of alcoholism, the attachment may be a necessary part of the healing process. Alcoholism is an affliction whose relief seems to require that the sufferer be bound up in something larger than the ego-of-one (in a “higher power,” be it only the power of the group). Healings that call for differentiation, on the other hand, may be more aptly delivered through the market.

{19} Schizophrenia occurs at about the same rate throughout the world with two exceptions: it is more common in one area of northern Sweden and in all of Ireland. This tale is Gaelic. The strained relations between fairies and mortals in Gaelic tales seem appropriate to a land where commerce with the spirits is unusually risky.

{20} A third alternative, besides sharing and separation, is deceit. In Mexican peasant communities, which are marked by similar networks of mutual aid, one finds the opposite of “conspicuous consumption”: a family that has become rich will maintain the shabbiest of adobe walls around the house so that their wealth will not be apparent. Magnolia and Calvin could have squirreled away the money, leaving the rent unpaid, the dead unburied, and the children unclothed.

{21} Magnolia could have turned her inheritance into commodity-money by loaning it out at interest. In the long run she would have needed loan collectors, police, and so forth to pull it off, however—the conflicts with the spirit of a kin network should be obvious.

{22} A gift economy allows its own form of individualism: to be able to say “I gave that.” After he had lived with the Sioux Indians for a while, Erik Erikson commented about their treatment of children: “A parent…would not touch a child’s possessions, because the value of possessions lay in the owner’s right to let go of them when he was moved to do so—i.e., when it added prestige to himself and to the person in whose name he might decide to give it away.” Individualism in a gift economy inheres in the right to decide when and how to give the gift. The individual controls the flow of property away from him (rather than toward him, a different individualism).

{23} A patent differs from a trade secret in a significant way. Historically a guild or trade could keep its secret for as long as it was able to. Some were kept for centuries. But patents are granted for a limited term (seventeen years in the United States), and as such they are a mechanism for rewarding private invention while slowly moving it into the public domain. Patents belong to a group of property rights, including copyright and usufruct, which grant the right to limited exclusive exploitation. Property rights of this kind are a wise middle ground between gift and commodity; they manage to honor the desire for individual enrichment and at the same time recognize the needs of the community.

{24} An exception that seems to prove the rule is the case of the “academic” scientist installed in an industrial research facility. “Industrial research organizations whose goals are only in the area of applied research,” Hagstrom notes, “often appoint distinguished men to do basic research, give a small amount of time to other scientists for this purpose, and publicize their research results, solely to make themselves attractive to superior scientists. If they do not permit pure research, their applied research and development efforts suffer.”

{25} Weitling adds the abolition of money to the older abolition of contract and debt instruments. The idea became a standard part of the program of European anarchists, who usually, like Weitling, called for cash exchange to be replaced by barter (not gift).

{26} The exceptions to this rule are those communities which, like the community of science, are organized around quite specific concerns. The group that does not pretend to support the wider social life of its members—feeding them, healing them, getting them married, and so forth—can be connected through gift exchange and still be quite large.

{27} Marcel Mauss’s essay is one of the first syntheses of true ethnography. It follows the established tradition of seeking the roots of the modern in the archaic, and its conclusions are a mixture of Hobbes and Kropotkin. On the one hand, Mauss’s explication of the spirit of the gift (the hau) makes it clear that gift contract requires the spirit, and that the spirit of the gift is not well reproduced in law or derived from reason. On the other hand, like Hobbes, Mauss is not at ease with emotion as a social force, and in a pinch, he will submit it to reason. Thus he can write that “by opposing reason to emotion…peoples succeed in substituting alliance, gift and commerce for war, isolation and stagnation.” Or he will speak of “total presentation”—by which he means constant, large-scale gift exchanges—saying, “although [they] take place under a voluntary guise they are in essence strictly obligatory, and their sanction is private or open warfare.” As with his phrase “the obligation to return,” the emphasis falls on “oblige” and the motive is fear, not desire. Pure Hobbes. Obviously many gift exchanges in practice are a mixture of fear (or guilt) and desire, but we should at least note that it is just as logical to invert Mauss’s premises and say, “It is by opposing eros to reason…that peoples succeed in substituting gift for war,” or that “wars are undertaken in seemingly voluntary guise…but really out of fear of private or open friendship.” Otherwise the ground emotions are fear and self-interest, the hau is lost, and we are back with reason suggesting law and authority.

{28} In 1980 a New Jersey couple tried to exchange their baby for a secondhand Corvette worth $8,800. The used-car dealer (who had been tempted into the deal after the loss of his own family in a fire) later told the newspapers why he changed his mind: “My first impression was to swap the car for the kid. I knew moments later that it would be wrong—not so much wrong for me or the expense of it, but what would this baby do when he’s not a baby anymore? How could this boy cope with life knowing he was traded for a car?”

{29} I assume this historical asymmetry derives from the fact that while both parents contribute to conception, the mother must carry the child, give it birth, and suckle it. Even in a matriarchy her contribution is greater.

{30} In the modern world the rights that adults have in their children—male or female—normally pass slowly from parent to child during adolescence and become fully vested in the child when he or she is ready to leave home. If our lives are gifts to begin with, however, in some sense they are not “ours” even when we become adults. Or perhaps they are, but only until such time as we find a way to bestow them. The belief that life is a gift carries with it the corollary feeling that the gift should not be hoarded. As we mature, and particularly as we come into the isolation of being “on our own,” we begin to feel the desire to give ourselves away—in love, in marriage, to our work, to the gods, to politics, to our children. And adolescence is marked by that restless, erotic, disturbing inquisition: Is this person, this nation, this work, worthy of the life I have to give?

{31} The examples of male life given as a gift are usually stories of sacrifice. It may be that so long as no gift institution recognizes the contribution to conception—and as the male body cannot in fact give birth—when male life is treated as a gift, the tendency is to give the body itself. In the chapter on the gift bond I spoke of compassionate deities who give their bodies to join man to a higher spiritual plane. These deities are generally male.

{32} For a case illustrating the “stability”side, see Wendy James’s article, “Sister-Exchange Marriage,”Scientific American (December 1975).

{33} It would have been interesting to see the results had the government instituted groomwealth or childwealth, for it is really the Uduk husband who gives children to the wife’s kin.

{34} Abandoning the bestowal of the bride in favor of her autonomy is one way to rearrange the pattern of this institution. Because the woman given in marriage does assume the functions of the gift, the group loses something even as the woman gains. When someone other than the couple being married is allowed to stand up at a wedding and say “I do,” then marriage is understood to be a social event; the ceremony recognizes that we sometimes have rights in the lives of our friends and relations, and that the union occurs within an “ego” wider than the couple’s “ego-of-two.” For the feminist wary of the father’s right to bestow his daughter, but wary as well of what I earlier called the perfect freedom of strangers—that pure individualism which is corrosive to social life—we might, rather than drop all sense of persons as gifts, extend a “female” submersion in the group to the groom, instead of a “male” indivudualism to the bride. We could, in other words, add the bestowal of the man to the ceremony and—a necessary corollary—recognize that mothers share in the donation of their offspring. In fact, if Freud is right that the most difficult attachment to resolve is the one we have to the parent of the opposite sex, it might be useful for the mother of the groom to stand and declare that she, too, is willing to allow her interest in the life of her son to pass to another woman; that she, like the father of the bride, is letting go of a gift.

{35} Gift exchange is not aboriginally, nor yet universally, a “female” commerce. There have always been times and there are still places where both men and women are sensitive to the functions of gift exchange, and where a man in particular may acquire his masculinity, or affirm it, through the bestowal of gifts. For a fascinating discussion of gender and exchange in a tribal group, see Annette Weiner’s recent book on the Trobriand Islands, Women of Value, Men of Renown.

{36} Philip Drucker provides an example from the tribes of the North Pacific coast. Loans were not uncommon there, but most were in the nature of a gift, returned with voluntary increase to indicate gratitude. “However,” Drucker tells us, “loans at interest were strictly commercial transactions, the rate being agreed upon at the time of the loan. The ruinous 100 percent rate was usual for a long-term loan, that is, for several years…There are no exact data on the origin of the custom, but there is reason to suspect that it may not be aboriginal in origin…It is probably significant that loans at interest consisted of trade blankets or money, not of aboriginal value items.” Here, as I surmise must be the general case, the appearance of interest on loans coincides with the introduction of market exchange with foreigners.

{37} I am not fond of arguments that depend upon declaring something “natural” or “unnatural”; they tend not only to cut off debate but to assume a division between man and nature. Usury may be justly hated, but since men invented it, we must either accept it as a part of nature or say that men are not. To give Aristotle his due, however, we might change the terms to “organic” and “inorganic.” Organic wealth was the original context for most of our economic language. In The Origins of European Thought Richard Onians makes an interesting observation in regard to the word “capital.” For both the Greeks and the Romans, the human head was regarded not as the seat of consciousness but as the container of procreative powers, the seeds of life. A Roman metaphor for kissing was “to diminish the head,” according to Onians; sexual intercourse also “diminished the head,” the point being that erotic or generative activity draws the life-stuff out of its container. In this way it was understood that caput (head, but also capital) produced offspring. Onians tells of a Roman cult, the Templars, who worshiped a divine head “as the source of wealth, as making trees bloom and earth to germinate.” Aboriginally “capital” was a strictly organic wealth that quite literally bore tokos, and in this context Aristotle is right: it is unnatural, it is not true to nature, to speak and act as if inorganic capital could possibly do the same.

{38} Such a double economy is hardly unique to the Jews; it occurs wherever there is a strong sense of an in-group. In fact, if ancient usury was not the exorbitant rate to which the term now refers but something closer to “rent” or “interest,” then the Jewish law is comparatively mild. An ethnologist writes as follows of a Solomon Island society: “Native moralists assert that neighbors should be friendly and mutually trustful, whereas people from far-off are dangerous and unworthy of morally just consideration. For example, natives lay great stress on honesty involving neighbors while holding that trade with strangers may be guided by caveat emptor.”

{39} This remarkable piece of scholarship first appeared in 1949 and has now been reprinted, with addenda, by the University of Chicago Press. Nelson was a historian of religion who, touched by Max Weber’s similar work, fixed on the usury debate as a way to trace moral and economic conscience through the history of the Church. I am indebted to his guidance.

{40} “The law was our custodian until Christ came, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a custodian.”—Gal. 3:24–25. Luther reinstates the law in civil affairs where faith may not be assumed, but risk may. His is an Old Testament spirit.

{41} It may be time to add a note on the Islamic parallel to this story. As we noted at the outset, the Koran clearly forbids charging interest on a loan. The history of that prohibition is essentially the same as that of the Mosaic law, but without the back-and-forth dialectic, as Muhammad makes no distinction between brothers and others, faithful and infidel. During and after the Middle Ages, Muslims accepted a practical modification of the Koranic prohibition by allowing a return on capital provided the creditor had taken a risk. A man was still forbidden to take interest in the sense of a guaranteed percentage return, but he could share in a profit if he had taken a risk. Nowadays some Muslims, like some Orthodox Jews, still refuse to charge interest on a loan, but most allow a reasonable rate of return. The debate between these two factions was one of the minor dramas to be played out in Iran after the fall of the Shah in 1979. The stated intent of the followers of Ayatollah Ruhallah Khomeini was to organize an “Islamic republic” rooted in the precepts of the Koran. Even a man not closely aligned with the clergy, former president Abolhassen Bani-Sadr, reportedly maintained an elaborate microfilm library with Koranic codes cross-referenced to economic issues. But, as Calvin told us, a modern state cannot operate on the ethics of an ancient tribe. Soon after the fall of the Shah, the new head of the state-owned oil company—a devout Muslim, a radical lawyer, an enemy of the Shah—declared himself perplexed as to how to proceed, finding it “neither possible nor beneficial…to put all political, economic and judicial problems into an Islamic mold.” A state whose wealth derives from selling fossil fuel to foreigners cannot operate without interest on capital. When this drama is resolved, I imagine that, as was the case in Europe, the merchant princes will emerge with the power. And the clergy will have to produce a Luther or a Calvin if they wish to share that power.

{42} In the trajectory of Whitman’s life one can discern a tendency toward a more disincarnate spirituality. As an old man he wrote that Leaves of Grass was a collection of songs of the body and that he had thought of writing a second book to indicate that “the unseen Soul govern[s] absolutely at last.” And yet, he says, “It is beyond my powers,” adding that “the physical and the sensuous…retain holds upon me which I think are never entirely releas’d…”

{43} When Whitman later tried to raise money for his work in the Civil War hospitals, a friend wrote to him from Boston: “There is a prejudice against you here among the ‘fine’ ladies and gentlemen of the transcendental School. It is believed that you are not ashamed of your reproductive organs and, somehow, it would seem to be the result of their logic—that eunuchs only are fit for nurses.”

{44} The quahaug is the same one that appeared in the fantasy of the hungry soul: “Now do I talk of mine and his?—Has my heart no more passion than a squid or clam shell has?”

{45} The poem from which these lines are taken is the one about which D. H. Lawrence made his perceptive comment, “Whitman is a very great poet, of the end of life.” The remark is often quoted without its context so as to imply that Whitman is only a poet of death. But the context is the same as the one I am setting up here. “…Of the end of life,” says Lawrence, and he adds, “But we have all got to die, and disintegrate. We have got to die in life, too, and disintegrate while we live…Something else will come. ‘Out of the cradle endlessly rocking.’ ”

{46} To speak of procreation as a bestowal, Whitman is forced to abandon his habitual evenhandedness toward the sexes. The male self ejaculates sperm, the female gives birth to babies.

{47} There are other “speech centers” in the self besides what Whitman is calling the soul. The intellect can speak—it can describe the known world, it can draw logical conclusions. But it cannot create speech for the mute. It is a gesture of the wakened soul to offer articulation to the speechless content of the self. “The talkers…talking the talk of the beginning and the end” cannot do it; only soul, imagination, muse, genius can do it.

{48} When I speak of celebration, I do not mean that all our art must be a cheery affirmation. To utter sorrow and loss is also a responsive speech, and a form of celebration. I use the term broadly, of course, as when we speak of “celebrating” the anniversary of someone’s death. “Sadness, in order to sing, / Will have to drink black water,” says the Spanish poet José Luis Hidalgo. No one welcomes the black water of grief, but it too, when it comes, may be accepted and articulated. Spoken sorrow—or despair, or longing—descries the shape of the lost. We keep alive through speech the spirit of what we do not have; we survive, spiritually, by uttering the names of the dead and the names of what we need but cannot find. (There is little of this in Whitman, by the way. Only in Calamus and in some of the old-age poems do we feel him trying to name what he could not find. He is primarily a poet of praise, “I keep no account with lamentation,” he wrote early on. By that same token, however, some of his sorrow remained mute and some of his intensity never came to life.)

{49} In an account of a center serving the Jewish elderly in California, the anthropologist Barbara Myerhoff offers the following observation about storytelling; “Stories are a renewal of the word, made alive by being spoken, passed from one to another, released from considerations of correctness and law…Rabbi Nechman of Bratzlav ordered that all written records of his teachings be destroyed. His words must be passed from mouth to mouth, learned by and in heart. ‘My words have no clothes,’ he said. ‘When one speaks to one’s fellows, there arises a simple light and a returning light.’ ” The oral tradition—stories, songs, poems passed from mouth to mouth—keeps the gift of speech alive. The poet Gary Snyder, asked in an interview why the oral tradition is so weak in the United States, answered: “Because of the stress on individual names and the emphasis on keeping a text pure.” Each of these preoccupations—the one a concern of the market, the other a concern of the academy—treats our art as proprietary works, not gifts.

{50} This is one reason we cannot read an artist’s work by his life. We learn something when we read the life, of course, but the true artist leaves us with the uncanny sense that the experience fails to explain the creation.

{51} As it is, for example, in Mao Tse-tung’s political aesthetic where “work in literature and art…is subordinated to the revolutionary tasks set by the Party…”

{52} Justin Kaplan, Whitman’s most recent biographer, says that Whitman’s symptoms suggest severe hypertension and, perhaps, mercury poisoning from overdoses of calomel.

{53} “But this /…is entertaining.”

{54} All cultures seem to find a slightly alien local population to carry the Hermes projection. For the Vietnamese it is the Chinese, and for the Chinese it is the Japanese. For the Hindu it is the Muslim; for the North Pacific tribes it was the Chinook; in Latin America and in the American South it is the Yankee. In Uganda it is the East Indians and Pakistanis. In French Quebec it is the English. In Spain the Catalans are “the Jews of Spain.” On Cyprus it is the Turks, and in Turkey it is the Armenians. Lawrence Durrell says that when he lived in Cyprus he was friends with the Greeks, but that when he wanted to buy some land they sent him to a Turk, saying that a Turk was what you needed for trade, though of course he couldn’t be trusted. This figure who is good with money but a little tricky is always treated as a foreigner even if his family has been around for centuries. Often he actually is a foreigner, of course. He is invited in when the nation needs trade and he is driven out—or murdered—when nationalism begins to flourish: the Chinese out of Vietnam in 1978, the Japanese out of China in 1949, the Yankees out of South America and Iran, the East Indians out of Uganda under Idi Amin, and the Armenians out of Turkey in 1915–16. The “outsider” is always used as a catalyst to arouse nationalism, and when times are hard he will always be its victim as well.

{55} Here we have another reason why Hermes is both the god of trade and of thieves. A commerce in commodities involves the trick of symbolic exchange.

{56} If we ask what’s to keep tricky financiers from getting themselves appointed as price commissioners, Pound replies: “No part or function of government should be under closer surveillance, and in no part or cranny of government should higher moral criteria be ASSURED.” Men of super goodwill will watch the men of goodwill who set the just price. Pound was very sharp when it came to spotting crooks in the banking business, but he was a little dull when it came to crimes of power, order, and efficiency.

{57} His repeated call for state sovereignty and his prohibition on foreign money in the homeland both seem tribal to me. (If you begin with such tribal nationalism, however, you soon must have either complete isolation or a double standard for dealing with strangers. With what can only be called the wisdom of Moses, Pound arrives at the latter solution: “A country CAN have one currency for internal use, and another for home and foreign use.”)

{58} In formulating a modified permission to practice usury, the reformers revived the Mosaic law, and in that sense they brought the Jew into the Church. That, at any rate, was how Pound saw it; he was of the opinion, for example, that Calvin was really a Jew: “that heretical scoundrel Calvin (the alias of Cauein, or Cohen, philo-usurer).”

{59} One of Pound’s last pieces of writing was a clarification: “Re USURY. I was out of focus, taking a symptom for a cause. The cause is AVARICE.”

{60} Artists who sell their work commonly take on an agent as a way of organizing this double economy: the artist labors with his gift and his agent works the market.

{61} An amusing echo of this debacle was heard many years later: in 1948 one of the tour’s “surplus” paintings, Stuart Davis’s Still Life with Flowers, was bought for a high school in Chicago by one of its art teachers. The price was $62.50. In 2006 the school sold the painting at auction for $3.1 million.

{62} Actually, wit may not be the key ingredient; power helps. It was the American Federation of Musicians that got the Music Performance Fund started as part of their collective bargaining with the recording industry. The loss of union power is another chapter of the recent saga of market triumphalism.

{63} Our original artist contracts formalized the give-back provision of our grants. Some years later, however, having learned that artist budgets are almost impossible to quantify, we made it clear that any return gifts are entirely voluntary. True generosity is not, after all, a contractual matter.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Lizzie O’Shea: ‘Surveillance technology is a threat to democracy’
content:
Lizzie O’Shea, a writer, lawyer and founder of Digital Rights Watch, told the New South Wales Council for Civil Liberties’ (NSWCCL) annual fundraising dinner and journalism awards on October 1 that rapidly developing surveillance technology is throwing up many challenges.

Digital technology and democracy are in a “significant amount of tension”, O’Shea said. She added that defending civil liberties is not about “clever people working to impose civil liberties on everybody else”, but that campaigners “have to convince a critical mass that they have to defend their own rights”.

Referencing the origins of professional policing in London in the late 18th century, she described it as “a period of immense technological disruption”, as the Industrial Revolution was reshaping society.

The new police force, O’Shea said, was used to “monitor, enforce and impose the new conditions of social order”. Specifically, it ensured merchants’ profits and prevented dockworkers from supplementing their wages by pilfering stock. The idea was to get the state and industry to collaborate, with a “form of surveillance of everyday people”.

“Policing was talked about as a new science in the detection and prevention of crime,” she said. The spectacle of force “offered an economical and effective way of maintaining order”.

O’Shea said it helps explain the state’s decisions in the digital age. “Like their historical counterparts, modern police understand the power of surveillance in enforcing a form of discipline.

“‘Safety’ is about preserving social order, rather than reducing harm. By allowing law enforcement and intelligence agencies to tell us what is safe, we allow them to use technology in increasingly oppressive ways.

“Rapid technological advances have been accompanied by disruptive transformations in social relations, and an acceleration of policing has often been a response.”

O’Shea described advances in technology in the 21st century as being “a fundamental threat” to democracy. She said more than 100 “security” bills have been passed over the past two decades, connected to surveillance, national intelligence agencies and law enforcement, and 875 new offences have been created.

Many have sought to repurpose existing systems of corporate surveillance for state surveillance, while surveillance technology companies receive lucrative government contracts.

O’Shea also said Labor has “effectively abandoned” regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and facial recognition technology.

“Less than 10% of Australians think it’s reasonable for a retailer to ask for your biometric information to access their services, but on an almost daily basis they will experience this.

“Everyone is telling us that AI is fundamentally important — politicians, the financial markets, a media that takes industry sources as truth — but a study by the University of Melbourne found that Australians are among the least optimistic in the world about artificial intelligence.

“More people are concerned about the negative outcomes than the benefits … 87% would be more inclined to trust and use AI products if international standards were in place to protect them.”

O’Shea pointed to the campaign to remove Palantir from Coles stores and the defeat of a data centre proposal in Lane Cove as examples of where most people’s attitudes lie.

“The hand of power is seeking to crush us, but we have the capacity to land a counterpunch,” she said. “This is the time for organisers, agitators, lawyers, ratbags and policy nerds to work together to build an alternative future where civil liberties are protected and our democracy can flourish.”

NSWCCL president Timothy Roberts told the gathering that the NSWCCL aimed to be an “ever-watchful guardian” of civil liberties, noting the huge challenges. He referenced last year’s March for Humanity, across the Sydney Harbour Bridge, when 300,000 people marched to protest Israel’s genocide in Gaza and demand that Labor act.

“It felt like the flame of liberty could not burn brighter or stronger — we must continue to celebrate that occasion as an example of the collective exercise of our human rights,” Roberts said.

The NSWCCL’s journalism awards went to Guardian journalists Ariel Bogle and Nino Bucci for uncovering the use of “less-lethal” weapons by police. Star Observer journalist Jacques Nieuwoudt won the young journalist award for his coverage of police raids of LGBTIQ spaces on Oxford Street.

[Isaac Nellist was able to attend the fundraiser after being given an activist ticket, generously funded by others.]

NSW Council for Civil Liberties (NSWCCL)

author: Isaac Nellist
title: University of Sydney threatens to throttle student body for being pro-Palestine
content:
University of Sydney (USyd) management is pursuing its anti-democratic practices, with a threat to defund the main student representative body and take over its election process.

It comes as NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the recent Student Representative Council (SRC) elections, describing a pro-Palestine “Globalise the Intifada” ticket as antisemitic.

It appears that they lent on Usyd management, which is now threatening to defund and take over the SRC elections.

Honi Soit reported on September 28 that a source, “privy to proceedings of the University Senate”, said that Vice-Chancellor Mark Scott “raised the possibility of the university taking over responsibility for SRC elections”. It was an un-minuted segment of the meeting.

The recent SRC elections returned incumbent president Grace Street, who led the Grassroots ticket, which is also pro-Palestine. A referendum on the university cutting ties with Israel and weapons companies complicit in genocide was held at the same time and passed with about 90% of the vote.

Scott and Chancellor David Thodey released a statement claiming that the phrase “Globalise the intifada” is “hate speech” and “incit[es] violence”.

“We reject the contention that this phrase is innocuous,” Scott and Thodey said. “The deliberately provocative use of this slogan has caused — and continues to cause — overwhelming distress to members of our University community. These hateful campaigns must stop.” They also threatened to report students to “police, federal intelligence and counter terrorism agencies”.

USyd management has threatened and shut down anti-genocide activism on campus, including in May sending disciplinary letters to students for displaying the Handala symbol, a symbol of Palestinians’ struggle for freedom and self-determination.

It appointed pro-Israel academic Michael Abrahams-Sprod as its special advisor on antisemitism. Abrahams-Sprod is a leading member of the pro-Israel Australian Academic Alliance Against Antisemitism (5A), which considers any pro-Palestine activism to be antisemitic.

The university has form. In 2024, it introduced its Campus Access Policy, curtailing freedom of speech and the right to protest on campus, following the successful Palestine solidarity encampment.

Management’s new threats have prompted the USyd SRC to publish an open letter; it quickly drew hundreds of signatories from students, staff, alumni, community members and several Palestine solidarity and student organisations.

It said management’s proposal contradicts a 2019 Model Code for the Protection of Freedom of Speech and Academic Freedom that USyd had adopted, which states that free speech — even when controversial, offensive, or challenging — “should not be subject to university penalties”.

It said management’s concerns are being “manufactured and weaponised to justify the vilification, defunding, and removal of the independence of the SRC once and for all”, and is another example of the university trying to “silence progressive voices”.

Further, the letter said ticket names that are “racist, sexist, ableist, homophobic, transphobic or classist” are already prohibited. “Globalise the Intifada” is not a discriminatory phrase. “There is no room for doubt in understanding this phrase and campaign as one [which is] calling for justice and an end to violence.”

Timothy Roberts, president of the NSW Council for Civil Liberties, told Honi Soit that USyd’s proposal would create a “massive conflict of interest” if management writes the rules for the student representatives, “whose job it is to voice student concerns and to hold management accountable”.

The open letter calls for Usyd management to respect the independence of the SRC and that any review of its funding be conducted by an independent body.

It also calls for freedom of speech and political freedom on campus, for the Campus Access Policy to be scrapped and for management to act on the referendum that called on the university to cut ties with Israeli institutions and weapons companies.

[Sign the open letter here. Isaac Nellist is a student at the University of Sydney and is running for Socialist Alliance in Balmain in the March 2027 election.]

author: Unknown
title: Namık Tan: TBMM onayına sunulmayan Mekke Anlaşması'nın hukuksal zemini nedir?
content:
Yeni Parti İstanbul Milletvekili Namık Tan, sosyal medya hesabından "Mekke Ortak Savunma Anlaşması"na ilişkin yaptığı açıklamada TBMM onayına sunulmamış anlaşmanın hukuksal zeminini sordu.

Tan'ın açıklaması şöyle: "Sözü uzatmadan tekrar tekrar soralım: Var olduğu iddia edilen 'Mekke Ortak Savunma Anlaşması' TBMM onayına sunulmadan nasıl geçerli olur, nasıl uygulanabilir? Eğer ortada bir 'ortak savunma anlaşması' değil de bir 'mutabakat muhtırası' veya 'mutabakat zabtı' hatta o bile değil yalnızca bir 'ortak basın açıklaması' varsa bu atılan adımların hukuksal zemini nedir? Yineliyoruz ve uyarıyoruz bu yapılanlar anayasal suçtur. Dış politika açısından ise hele bu ortam ve bağlamda sözkonusu gözükara girişimler, tek adam rejimlerine özgü bir kıyamet günü senaryosu saplantısını ortaya koymaktadır. Yemen'e askerî kuvvet ve/veya yetenek sevki iddiası doğruysa bu saplantının apaçık bir dışavurumu, kanıtıdır."

Pazartesi günü Riyad'da düzenlenen toplantıda Türkiye ve Pakistan, Mekke Anlaşması uyarınca Suudi Arabistan'a "askeri kuvvet ve kabiliyetlerin sağlanması ve hızla konuşlandırılması" kararı almıştı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: London Conference's conclusions: Peace must be guaranteed by rule of law and democratic institutions
content:
Following the Peace and Democratic Integration Conference, held in London on September 29–30, the Centre for Kurdish Affairs published its conclusions from the conference discussions, along with recommendations for the period ahead.




During the two-day conference, representatives of Kurdish political and civil society organizations, as well as figures involved in peace processes in different parts of the world, academics, politicians, and experts came together. They discussed a wide range of topics, from the democratic resolution of the Kurdish issue in Turkey to international experiences of peacebuilding; from legal guarantees and local democracy to the role of women, as well as developments in Syria and the wider region.




The Centre for Kurdish Affairs stressed that "this communiqué presents the Centre’s analysis of the conference discussions. The views, interpretations and conclusions contained herein should not be understood as a collective statement on behalf of every speaker, participant or supporting institution."




The text said: "The Centre for Kurdish Affairs convened a two-day international conference in London, bringing together peace practitioners, academics, political representatives, policymakers and civil society representatives to examine comparative experiences of conflict resolution, peacebuilding, constitutional accommodation, power-sharing and self-government, and to consider their relevance to contemporary discussions concerning the Kurdish question.




For the purposes of this communiqué, democratic integration refers to rights-based and voluntary participation within a plural democratic order and should not be understood as cultural, linguistic or political assimilation. Furthermore, the phrase ‘the Kurdish question’ is employed to encompass the full spectrum of legal, political, cultural, economic, and social issues impacting Kurdish populations."




Summarizing the two-day conference, the text said: "The first day focused on comparative international experiences through three panels: ‘Why Peace Processes Succeed or Fail’; ‘Peace, Power-Sharing and Constitutional Accommodation: Lessons from the UK’; and ‘Autonomy, Devolution and Self-Government’. Drawing on a range of conflict-resolution and constitutional experiences, the discussions considered the political and institutional conditions under which negotiations can be sustained, settlements can acquire legitimacy and durability, and differing territorial and political claims can be accommodated within democratic frameworks.




The second day turned more directly to the Kurdish question through three panels: ‘Post-Conflict Kurdish Democratic Politics’; ‘The Kurdish Question Across Borders’; and ‘Inclusive Peace: Women, Minorities, and Systems of Justice’. The discussions examined the possible evolution of Kurdish politics in a post-conflict environment, the regional and transnational dimensions of the Kurdish question across Türkiye, Syria, Iraq and Iran, as well as within the diaspora, and the role of women, minorities and the media in broadening participation and embedding peace within democratic political life."




Conference Context and International Engagement




The text continued: "London offered a particularly resonant setting for these discussions. The United Kingdom’s constitutional tradition has evolved over many centuries, with Magna Carta of 1215 among its historic reference points in the development of law, political authority, representation and consent.




Its more recent experience of devolution, power-sharing and negotiated settlement provides a further point of reference for considering how established political systems can adapt to diverse identities and political aspirations. In this context, PDIC provided a forum for diplomatic and policy discussion in which Kurdish perspectives could be considered alongside wider international experience on conflict resolution, democratic accommodation and the prospects for a durable political settlement.




The conference received expressions of support and engagement from Catherine West MP, Bambos Charalambous MP and the Rt Hon David Lammy MP, underscoring the importance of sustained engagement between Kurdish perspectives and the United Kingdom’s political and policy community at a time when questions of peace, democratic participation and regional stability are assuming renewed significance.




The conference also received messages of encouragement from academics, intellectuals, civil society figures, peace practitioners and institutions internationally. We are grateful for this wider engagement, which reflects a broad international interest. International engagement of this kind can help sustain dialogue, widen the space for constructive political debate and support the conditions in which a credible political process can develop."




The conference also received a letter from Mr Abdullah Öcalan, who is imprisoned on İmralı Island, expressing support for the conference and its objectives. The Centre regards this message as a contribution to the wider discussion concerning the prospects for a peaceful and democratic settlement.




The text added: "In this context, and in light of the role attributed to Mr Öcalan by relevant actors and his capacity to communicate with significant constituencies within the Kurdish movement, the Centre considers it important that he be able to participate in any meaningful negotiation process under conditions conducive to effective and direct dialogue. A credible process requires that those who may bear responsibility for negotiation and implementation are able to communicate, consult and engage with relevant parties."




Key Conclusions




Below are the conclusions by the Kurdish Centre: 




"1. The cessation of armed violence may mark the beginning of peace; it is not peace itself.




The end of armed conflict creates a historic opportunity for a lasting and democratic settlement. The ceasefire, however, should not be equated with resolving the political, legal, social, cultural and economic issues associated with the origins and persistence of the conflict.




Sustainable peace is more likely to take root where democratic politics, credible legal safeguards, institutional reform and meaningful societal participation are strengthened, and democratic mechanisms through which political disagreements can be addressed without recourse to violence.




Peace will therefore depend not only on disarmament, but also on ensuring that democratic politics, the rule of law, dialogue and accountable institutions become the principal means through which political disagreements are addressed.




2. Democratic integration does not mean assimilation.




The Conference discussions strongly highlighted that democratic integration should not be understood as the assimilation of distinct identities or the incorporation of historically marginalised communities and organisations into an existing political and social order on unequal terms.




Genuine democratic integration should be based not on the elimination of difference, but on enabling different identities to become constituent elements of a shared political life, protected by legal and political guarantees.




The ability of Kurdish communities to participate in a shared political future while preserving and developing their identities, languages and cultures, and exercising political agency through democratic institutions is an essential component of meaningful democratic integration.




Democratic integration may therefore be understood not simply as incorporation into existing structures, but as a reciprocal process of democratic adaptation involving state–society relations, representation, citizenship and relations between central and local government.




3. The transition from armed struggle to democratic politics requires credible legal safeguards.




Comparative international experience indicates that processes of disarmament, demobilisation, and reintegration cannot be treated solely as technical security matters.




Clear, predictable, and credible mechanisms are needed to enable individuals leaving armed organisations to participate lawfully and peacefully in civilian life, society and democratic politics.




Overcoming mistrust arising from previous peace initiatives will require verifiable steps, appropriate legal arrangements, and durable institutional safeguards.




Uncertainty regarding the legal status and future of those who respond to calls for peace may undermine public confidence in any renewed peace process.




4. As the space for arms recedes, the space for democratic politics should expand.




A transition away from armed struggle should not be understood as requiring individuals or communities to abandon their political aspirations, identities or languages, or lawful forms of social and political mobilisation.




On the contrary, as armed violence recedes from political life, the space available for peaceful democratic politics should expand accordingly.




Freedom of political and civic organisation, freedom of expression, democratic representation and lawful social activity should increasingly be protected and regulated through democratic law rather than approached primarily as security matters. This is an essential condition for sustainable peace.




5. Peace should rest on law and institutions, not on governments alone.




One of the clearest lessons emerging from international experience suggests that peace processes are more durable when they do not depend solely on the political will of governments.




Governments may change, and regional circumstances may shift. For peace to withstand such changes, agreed arrangements need to be embedded in law and supported by resilient democratic institutions.




Safeguards concerning political representation, power-sharing, local governance, oversight mechanisms, linguistic and cultural rights, and democratic participation can help ensure that peace becomes institutionally grounded and is not dependent on the political will of particular office-holders.




6. Local democracy and self-government are central to discussions of a democratic settlement.




The international experiences considered at the Conference illustrate the variety of arrangements involving devolution, autonomy, power-sharing and self-government in response to different historical, regional, political, and linguistic circumstances.




None of these models can simply be transplanted wholesale to the Kurdish context.




They do, however, offer valuable lessons regarding the distribution of political and administrative authority between central and local government; the participation of local communities in decisions affecting their lives; the allocation of financial resources; and the protection of linguistic and cultural rights.




Local democracy, central–local relations, fiscal and administrative authority, democratic representation, and legal guarantees for local government should therefore form substantive elements of future discussions on a democratic settlement rather than as secondary considerations.




7. Truth and justice should not be postponed until after peace.




A lasting societal peace is difficult to sustain if serious alleged or documented violations and the legacies of past conflict remain unaddressed.




Disappearances, unresolved killings, forced displacement, village evacuations, allegations of torture, experiences of detention and imprisonment, and the broader consequences of conflict for society may require investigation, documentation and appropriate preservation of the historical record and collective memory.




Efforts to establish truth and advance transitional justice need not wait for a final peace agreement.




Work can begin now to facilitate access to relevant archives, hear from victims and witnesses, investigate disappearances, document past violations and ensure that the experiences of those affected are recognised.




Peace concerns not only the future that is to be built, but also the manner in which society addresses and comes to terms with its past.




8. Women should be recognised not merely as participants in peace, but as constituent actors in shaping it.




One of the strongest themes to emerge from the Conference was that the role of women in peace processes should not be limited to symbolic representation or consultative mechanisms.




Women have been directly affected by the consequences of war and conflict. At the same time, over many decades, women have developed substantial political, social and community-based organisational capacity, including women-led institutions.




Women should not be approached merely as participants to be invited once the terms of a peace process have already been defined. They should be recognised from the outset as substantive actors in shaping the peace agenda, its institutions and the future democratic order.




Women’s equal and effective participation in decision-making mechanisms should be ensured, while women-led political and social institutions should be recognised as important components of the democratic foundations of peace.




The meaningful participation of women should be assessed not simply in terms of numerical representation, but also by their ability to shape the substance of decisions and influence the character of future institutions.




9. Societal peace requires broad and inclusive participation.




The legitimacy and sustainability of any peace process depend upon genuine and meaningful participation by society.




Women, young people, those affected by conflict, prisoners and detainees connected to the conflict, where relevant to the peace process, local communities, diverse ethnic, cultural and faith communities, civil society organisations, the diaspora, political actors, and the direct parties to the conflict should all have meaningful opportunities to contribute at different stages of the peace process.




Participation should extend beyond consultation to include appropriate roles in implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and democratic decision-making mechanisms.




An armed conflict may be brought to an end through agreement between its direct parties; durable societal peace depends on broad participation across society.




10. The different geographical dimensions of the Kurdish question are interconnected, while each must be understood in its own specific context.




The political, legal and institutional circumstances affecting Kurdish communities in Türkiye, Syria, Iraq and Iran differ significantly.




A settlement developed in one context cannot simply be transferred to another.




At the same time, the cross-border character of the Kurdish question means that political and regional developments in one context can have significant implications for neighbouring contexts.




A regional perspective is therefore important, one that recognises the distinct circumstances of different Kurdish communities while also taking account of the political and societal interactions between them.




In the context of Syria in particular, the Conference discussions highlighted the importance of assessing future political and administrative arrangements in light of the rights and freedoms of all communities, democratic representation, local institutions, women’s participation and institutional gains, and linguistic and cultural guarantees. Any such arrangements should be considered within an inclusive Syrian-led political process and in accordance with applicable international law.




11. The social and economic dimensions of peace must not be overlooked.




Political and constitutional transformation alone cannot guarantee societal peace.




For peace to be tangible in people’s everyday lives, it must also address regional inequalities, fair access to public resources, equitable access to economic opportunities, stronger local institutions, and the social and economic consequences of past conflict.




A democratic settlement should therefore be understood not only as a constitutional or security matter, but also as a question of social justice, economic inclusion and equitable opportunity, and democratic governance.




12. International experience should inform the process, but ready-made models should not be imported.




The experiences of Northern Ireland, Colombia, South Africa, the Basque Country and different European arrangements concerning autonomy, power-sharing, and devolution offer important lessons.




At the same time, every conflict has its own history, political structure, and societal context.




The purpose of drawing on international experience should therefore not be to import a ready-made settlement, but to help identify the relevant questions, consider different institutional options, learn from both the achievements and shortcomings of previous processes, and contribute to the development of democratic arrangements appropriate to the particular historical and political circumstances of the Kurdish question."




Call for the Way Forward




The text continued: "In light of the framework that emerged from the Conference discussions, the Conference underscores the importance of:




- Transforming the current opportunities for ending armed conflict into a lasting, democratic and societal peace process.




- Reviewing and, where appropriate, addressing legal and political barriers to democratic participation, while broadening channels for meaningful political engagement.




- Establishing credible legal mechanisms to support the transition from armed struggle to civilian and democratic life.




- Ensuring that the linguistic, cultural, political and social rights of Kurdish individuals and communities are protected within a democratic legal framework, alongside the equal rights and freedoms of all communities.




- Addressing local democracy, local government, the distribution of authority and central–local relations as integral components of democratic integration.




- Ensuring that women participate at every stage of the peace process as substantive actors from the outset, with their independent political agency and organised structures recognised and respected.




- Enabling the meaningful participation of young people, victims, different peoples and faith communities, civil society and the diaspora in decision-making and implementation processes.




- Advancing work on truth, justice, collective memory and dealing with the past without unnecessary delay.




- Establishing credible, transparent and inclusive mechanisms capable of monitoring the implementation of a peace process.




- Establishing an independent UK-based observation delegation to Türkiye, in consultation with relevant authorities and stakeholders, to follow developments, engage with relevant parties and civil society, and contribute to confidence-building and dialogue.




- Drawing on relevant international experiences, including Northern Ireland and Sri Lanka, to develop independent observation and facilitation mechanisms capable of supporting dialogue and the implementation of peace processes where requested or accepted by the relevant parties.




- Encouraging the UK Government to establish appropriate channels for sustained engagement with and constructive support for the integration process in Syria.




- Supporting inclusive dialogue on lawful and sustainable security-sector arrangements concerning the YPJ and other relevant forces within Syria’s emerging institutional framework, while safeguarding meaningful participation, rights and institutional gains achieved by women.




- Preparing observation reports on developments in Türkiye and Syria, based on transparent methodology and engagement with a broad range of relevant stakeholders.




- Convening a follow-up conference in 2027 to consider the observation reports, assess developments since the London Conference, and identify appropriate next steps.




- Developing sustainable mechanisms for dialogue and cooperation through which knowledge and experience from international peace processes can be shared in ways that respect local realities.




- Publishing a policy report with recommendations, an edited academic publication, multilingual conference proceedings, recorded panel discussions, a short documentary, and research partnerships and postgraduate initiatives."




Conclusion




The text ends with a conclusion which reads as follows:




"At the heart of the two days of discussions at the Peace and Democratic Integration Conference was one fundamental question:




What democratic, legal and institutional arrangements can sustainably replace armed conflict?




The Conference discussions highlighted that no single institution, actor or model can provide a complete answer to this question. They nevertheless pointed towards a clear principle: lasting peace requires that the space once occupied by arms be filled by the rule of law, democratic politics, local democracy, equal citizenship, rights and freedoms, truth and justice, and an inclusive, organised and participatory civic and political sphere.




Peace is not simply the end of a conflict.




Peace means building a democratic order in which people can live together without being required to relinquish their identities, languages, cultures or political agency.




Peace also requires acknowledgement of the suffering associated with the past and appropriate mechanisms through which truth, justice and reconciliation can be pursued.




Peace means ensuring that women, young people, diverse communities, faith communities and social groups are not merely affected by decisions concerning their lives, but are able to participate actively in shaping them.




Peace also means ensuring that the political space opened by the end of armed struggle is sustained through democratic institutions and meaningful societal participation.




The central question following this Conference is therefore not only how a conflict can be brought to an end, but what kind of shared future can be built once the conflict has ended.




A lasting peace is most likely to be sustained within a political order in which all sections of society are able to participate, rights are protected by law, political disagreements are addressed through accountable democratic institutions, and diversity is recognised as an integral part of a shared future.




If society bears the consequences of war, it should also have a meaningful voice in building peace.




The Peace and Democratic Integration Conference, held in London, therefore affirms the importance of continuing efforts to strengthen dialogue, comparative learning, democratic politics, and meaningful societal participation in pursuit of a peaceful and democratic future.




The Centre for Kurdish Affairs stands ready to contribute to this work. Through policy development, institutional dialogue, capacity-building and international exchange, we will seek to support the knowledge, relationships and practical expertise required for a peaceful transition and for the fuller democratic participation and inclusion of Kurdish political and civic actors."

title: ABD'li Kongre üyesi "minnettar": Mekke Anlaşması, Ortadoğu'nun NATO'su
content:
ABD'li Temsilciler Meclisi üyesi Joe Wilson, Mekke Ortak Savunma Anlaşması'nın Ortadoğu'nun NATO'su olma potansiyeline sahip olduğunu söyledi.

Cumhuriyetçi Parti üyesi Wilson, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada "Husilerin İran destekli saldırganlığı karşısında ittifakı harekete geçirdikleri için müttefiklerimiz Türkiye, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan'a minnettarım" sözlerine yer verdi.

Pazartesi günü Riyad'da düzenlenen toplantıda Türkiye ve Pakistan, Mekke Anlaşması uyarınca Suudi Arabistan'a "askeri kuvvet ve kabiliyetlerin sağlanması ve hızla konuşlandırılması" kararı almıştı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Valerie Anne
title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. It is just fascinating to me that despite the fact that she has been in folklore for centuries, no new media has come out about her in years, and now these two instances pop up in the same year. Three, if you count the experimental film Báthory by Carlos Atanes. Something seems to be in the (bloody) water.

Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps The Blood Countess isn’t quite as gay as it could be. Then again, apparently Ottinger wrote the screenplay in 1998, almost 30 years ago, so that could potentially account for that. But still, I won’t say no to a lesbian vampire film so I’ll probably still check it out when it makes its North American theatrical release in spring 2027.
