title: South Kurdistan after the Coalition: Kurdish national unity is crucial
content:
The mission of the International Coalition against ISIS in Iraq officially ended on 30 September after 12 years. The date marked not only the end of a military mission, but also the conclusion of the US military presence that had continued since the 2003 invasion and of the air defence system from which South Kurdistan (Bashur) had indirectly benefited. The withdrawal, announced by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi, was welcomed as a victory in Baghdad and among Iran-aligned Shia groups, while it has been met with concern in Southern Kurdistan and among Sunni communities.




South Kurdistan, which has been targeted by more than a thousand drone and ballistic missile attacks since the US-Israel-Iran war began on 28 February, is entering a new period without air defences. Peshmerga forces have been unified on paper but remain affiliated with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) on the ground. The Coalition’s financial support for the Peshmerga has also ended. Twenty-three months after the elections, a government has still not been formed in the Kurdistan Region.




The weakness of a common political will has now been compounded by the reality of a Kurdistan Region increasingly exposed to attacks.




23 years from invasion to withdrawal




US forces entered Iraq in 2003 to overthrow Saddam Hussein’s regime. US troop numbers peaked at 170,000, and approximately 4,500 US soldiers were killed. The US withdrew from the country in 2011 but returned in 2014 following the rise of ISIS. The International Coalition against ISIS was established that same year, and its forces were deployed to the country at the formal invitation of the Iraqi government.




In recent years, around 2,500 US troops have been stationed in Iraq, mainly in Erbil (Hewlêr) and near Baghdad Airport. Their number stood at around 2,000 in July before falling to several hundred as the phased withdrawal proceeded. As major bases across Iraq were evacuated, hundreds of troops and air defence systems were concentrated around Erbil. The withdrawal has seen hundreds of troops and military equipment redeployed to Jordan and other countries in the region.




The timetable for the withdrawal was finalised following Prime Minister Zeydi’s first visit to Washington in July, where he met US President Donald Trump.




Security, economic and political gaps in the Kurdistan Region




The most tangible impact of the withdrawal on Southern Kurdistan has emerged in air defence. Iraqi National Security Adviser Qasim al-Araji said the withdrawal also covered defence systems in the Kurdistan Region, explaining that the process was being carried out under an agreement signed between the previous government and the Coalition: “The US side has also made it clear that it is ready to implement the agreement and withdraw within the agreed timeframe. This withdrawal covers all defence forces and systems previously agreed upon.”




As a result, air defence systems deployed particularly in and around Erbil, including Patriot batteries and C-RAM systems, were also removed from the region.




Although Southern Kurdistan was not a party to the war between the US/Israel and Iran that began on 28 February 2026, it became one of the regions most heavily targeted by attacks. According to Community Peacemaker Teams (CPT), 196 drone and missile attacks struck the region between the beginning of the war and 8 March. Forty-three of these targeted bases belonging to Kurdish parties from Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat). The targets also included Erbil International Airport and the 70th Forces Command in Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî).




CPT also recorded 751 attacks during the three months between 28 February and 28 May, in which 22 people were killed and 112 others injured.




At the end of July, the Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Region said the number of attacks had exceeded 900, with 30 people killed and 140 injured. Figures released by the Peshmerga Ministry at the end of September put the number of drone and ballistic missile attacks at more than 1,000.




Most attacks targeting Erbil had been intercepted by US air defence systems deployed to protect American assets, while Sulaymaniyah did not have comparable protection.




The Peshmerga Ministry described the US withdrawal at such a critical time, without another air defence system being put in place, as “concerning”. The ministry recalled that the Kurdistan Region’s airspace formed part of Iraqi airspace and said: “The federal government must assume responsibility for protecting the airspace of the Kurdistan Region when necessary.”




The KDP President, Masoud Barzani, and other officials in the Kurdistan Region recalled the rise of ISIS in 2014 following the US withdrawal in 2011 and warned that a similar security vacuum could emerge.




South Kurdistan is facing a significant gap not only in air defence but also in its budget. The Peshmerga Ministry announced that financial assistance provided to the Peshmerga by the Coalition under a four-year memorandum of understanding that came into effect on 21 September 2022 had ended. The ministry said the final payment was distributed on 24 September and called on the federal government to cover the resulting shortfall in salaries.




According to US budget documents, the US provided $135 million in salary support for Peshmerga forces in 2024 under the Counter-ISIS Train and Equip Fund (CTEF). The figure fell to $60 million in 2025, before the assistance ended entirely in September 2026.




The security and economic gaps accompanying the US withdrawal have coincided with a political deadlock in the Kurdistan Region. Twenty-three months after the elections held on 20 October 2024, a new government has still not been formed.




The KDP and the PUK, the two parties that together hold a parliamentary majority, have been unable to agree on the distribution of government posts, leaving parliament unable to become fully operational. The parties have met dozens of times in an effort to break the deadlock. The talks have failed to produce an agreement, however, and both sides have said they do not know how much longer the impasse will continue.




The resulting vacuum in governance is therefore being felt directly by citizens through serious shortcomings in public services and economic instability.




Those who see the withdrawal as a victory and those who are concerned




The Popular Mobilisation Forces (Hashd al-Shaabi) and Iran-aligned groups are celebrating 30 September, the date of the formal US withdrawal, as a day of victory. Abu Mujtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in Hashd al-Shaabi, said: “On 30 September, we will celebrate the closing of a dark chapter in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation’s attempt to impose itself on our country.”




Sunni communities, however, remain concerned, believing that Iraq is not yet fully prepared to assume responsibility for the country’s security. They say a potential security vacuum is something feared by Iraqis across the country.




Kurds also have serious concerns about the Kurdistan Region, which has been left vulnerable to possible attacks by Iran and armed groups. Kurdistan Region officials have pointed to the continuing threat posed by ISIS following the withdrawal of US forces. The removal of air defence systems has also caused concern among a population living under the persistent threat of attack.




The need for a professional and unified security force has become more apparent than ever.




Disarmament deadline postponed




The Zeydi government wants the Coalition’s withdrawal to proceed alongside efforts to bring weapons under state control. The approach has been summarised by the formula: “No foreign troops, weapons in the hands of the state.”




Prime Minister Zeydi, however, extended the deadline for armed groups from 30 September 2026 to 30 June 2027 following meetings with Trump and US officials in New York on 23 September. The plan envisages an initial 90-day phase beginning on 30 September. The government has stressed that the programme is “not optional, but mandatory”, signalling its determination to proceed.




The government’s programme to bring weapons under state control also directly concerns the Peshmerga. Kata'ib Hezbollah in Iraq set out three conditions on 18 August for laying down its arms: the complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraqi territory and airspace, the withdrawal of Turkish forces from Iraq, and the dissolution of the Peshmerga forces. Kata'ib Hezbollah described the Peshmerga as a threat to Iraq’s territorial integrity.




Sixty years of division and the drive for Peshmerga unity




The most structural weakness facing Southern Kurdistan is that its defence forces have yet to become fully independent of party control. The roots of the division between the KDP and the PUK date back to 1964, while the PUK was founded in 1975. The regional administration was established in 1992. Law No. 17, adopted in 1993, prohibited political parties from maintaining armed wings. Despite this, the two parties entered into a civil war in 1994. The agreement reached at the end of the conflict led to a power-sharing arrangement, with the Kurdistan Region effectively divided between the KDP’s “yellow” zone and the PUK’s “green” zone. The two areas remain separated by the Dêgele checkpoint today.




The 2006 administrative unification agreement, the establishment of a unified Peshmerga Ministry in 2009, the incorporation of 42,000 Peshmerga into brigades between 2010 and 2013, and the reform project drawn up with the Coalition in 2018 all failed to eliminate this dual structure.




Masrour Barzani signed Decree No. 703 on 26 February 2026, placing the KDP-affiliated 80th Unit and the PUK-affiliated 70th Unit under the Peshmerga Ministry. The unification was formally announced at a ceremony in Erbil (Hewlêr) on 21 September 2026.




Under the new structure, the former 80th Unit became the 1st Regional Command, comprising approximately 58,000 personnel under the command of Major General Nejat Ali Fatim. Its area of responsibility covers Erbil, Duhok, Mosul and north-western Kirkuk. The former 70th Unit became the 2nd Regional Command, with approximately 56,000 personnel under Major General Omar Salih. Its area of responsibility covers Sulaymaniyah, Halabja (Helebce), Kirkuk, Khanaqin (Xaneqîn) and Tuz Khurmatu (Xurmatû). The forces are being organised into 11 light infantry divisions.




Peshmerga Minister Shoresh Ismail said at the ceremony that the forces were now directly under the authority of the ministry, the government and the presidency. The Peshmerga Ministry said the process, launched in 2022 at the request of the US, could only be completed in September 2026 because of disagreements between the KDP and PUK.




Unity on paper, party divisions on the ground




The unification has largely remained nominal, with party authority continuing beyond the ministry’s control. A substantial part of the security apparatus also remains outside the reform process. There are 152,182 Peshmerga personnel in total, while 87,505 personnel under the Interior Ministry and 42,896 members of the Asayish security forces remain outside the scope of the unification. The approximately 45,000-strong KDP-affiliated Zeravani force and the 16,000-strong PUK-affiliated force also remain under the Interior Ministry.




The KDP’s Parastin intelligence organisation and the PUK’s Zanyari intelligence organisation also continue to operate along party lines. US oversight reports have likewise documented continuing party influence within units formally under the Peshmerga Ministry.




Shengal on the negotiating table




The Coalition’s withdrawal has also brought other unresolved issues in and around Southern Kurdistan back onto the agenda. Shengal stands out as one of the most critical issues concerning the gains of the Yazidi Kurds, while the future of the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Yazidi security forces remains uncertain.




As discussions continue over the integration of Yazidi security and defence forces into the Iraqi army, a military delegation headed by Iraqi Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Yarallah visited the region on 22 September. Neither side, however, issued an official statement on the outcome of the visit.




Shengal is also part of negotiations between the Turkish state and Baghdad. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Zeydi met in New York on 23 September on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Their joint statement said Iraqi state authority would be fully established in Shengal and that the presence of “banned foreign armed elements” would be brought to an end.




Turkish military bases remain in place




According to the same statement, Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan Base to the Iraqi Federal Government, in line with an agreed mechanism and timetable and depending on Iraq’s progress in the security sphere. No date has been announced for the handover.




The transfer of Bashiqa does not mean the end of the Turkish state’s military presence in Iraq and Southern Kurdistan. Around 600 Turkish troops are stationed at the Bashiqa Military Base, which was established in December 2015. The Turkish state has a total of five main bases, more than 2,000 troops and nearly 100 deployment points in Iraq. According to some figures, around 5,000 Turkish troops have occupied a 20-kilometre-wide strip along the border since 1997.




Zeydi told the New York Times on 22 September that talks with Ankara were continuing over the withdrawal of Turkish forces from Iraqi territory. A two-day visit by National Intelligence Organisation (MİT) Director İbrahim Kalın to Baghdad, Kirkuk, Erbil and Sulaymaniyah also prompted discussions about the security architecture of the Development Road Project.




The way forward: Democratic unity and collective defence




For years, the administration of Southern Kurdistan entrusted its security to external powers rather than building a defence system based on its own strength. The Peshmerga’s salaries, training and weapons, as well as the protection of the Kurdistan Region’s airspace, all became dependent on outside powers. Southern Kurdistan’s airspace being left unprotected today is therefore not simply the result of the Coalition’s departure, but of this dependency. Security that depends on an external power ends when that power withdraws.




The same dependency is now being transferred to Baghdad. Expecting the federal government to protect the region’s airspace amounts to replacing one external guarantee with another. Given Baghdad’s moves towards centralisation, this carries new risks for the status of Southern Kurdistan.




Fragmentation is undoubtedly another factor behind the current situation. The failure to achieve national unity and the persistence of a dual administration remain fundamental obstacles to Southern Kurdistan organising its own strength. Parties pursuing separate external alliances have been unable to establish a common defence structure.




Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan’s call on the political forces of Southern Kurdistan to establish a “Democratic Unity Government” therefore goes beyond a formula for forming a cabinet. The call seeks to build a common political will and a collective defence based on the region’s own strength.




The unification of the Peshmerga forces under a single structure on 21 September represents a critical step in this direction. A unification that remains only on paper, however, will not be enough to protect Southern Kurdistan. Neither Washington nor Baghdad can provide the guarantee Southern Kurdistan needs. That guarantee lies in Kurdish unity, self-defence rooted in the people and national unity. The Coalition’s departure may provide an opportunity to recognise this reality.

title: Journalist Hemrînî: Baghdad seeks a model for solution in Shengal
content:
The withdrawal of US and International Coalition forces from Iraq, Baghdad’s efforts to bring armed groups under state control and strengthen the central army are reshaping the country’s security architecture. As Iraq seeks a new security balance, Shengal, which developed its own defense and governance mechanisms in the wake of DAESH attacks, has emerged as one of the key issues in this transformation.




The status of Shengal, the security of the Yazidis and the future of their self-defence forces are closely tied not only to Baghdad’s evolving security policies but also to the balance of power among regional actors. Journalist Hîwa Hemrînî said the demands of the Yazidis went beyond administrative or political arrangements: “The Yazidis are demanding a system that will protect their existence and enable them to develop it.”




Hemrînî stressed that Shengal’s future must be addressed on the basis of a solution that guarantees the continued existence of the Yazidis. He spoke to ANF about the talks between Shengal and Baghdad, the demands of the Yazidis, negotiations between Ankara and Baghdad over Bashiqa, and Iraq’s evolving security architecture.




Recent talks between Shengal and Baghdad, particularly the 11 September meeting between Prime Minister Ali Zeydi, the YBŞ and Yazidi representatives, appear to mark a new phase for Shengal’s future. What concrete issues were agreed upon during these talks?




To properly assess the content and outcome of the meeting you mentioned, two fundamental points need to be recalled. First, the Yazidi community has long sought to develop democratic negotiations with Baghdad. Dozens of meetings were held with governments preceding the Ali Zeydi government, and numerous proposals for a solution were presented. The Iraqi government, however, consistently treated Shengal’s status and the existential issues facing the Yazidi community as a military and intelligence matter. It regarded an ancient community such as the Yazidis as a “security problem”.




Pressure and blackmail by the Turkish state and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) against the Iraqi central government further deepened this approach. We are now seeing a partial shift in this policy, which has developed under the influence of the “Peace and Democratic Society Process” initiated by Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan.




Second, the Baghdad-Shengal talks are important not only for Shengal’s future but also for Baghdad’s. Iraq is being restructured under the Ali Zeydi government, and one of the most critical issues facing the government is the presence of non-state armed groups. Iraq has yet to develop a model for resolving this issue, and the matter remains open-ended. This is precisely where the Baghdad-Shengal talks take on greater significance: will Shengal produce a model for a solution, or a model for conflict? Baghdad essentially wants to develop a model for a solution and present it to the whole of Iraq. According to information we have obtained, Prime Minister Ali Zeydi also expressed this during his latest meeting with the Shengal delegation.




The central issue at the meeting was undoubtedly the status and future of the Yazidi defence forces in Shengal, namely the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ), Shengal Women’s Units (YJŞ) and Êzidxan Asayish forces. Before the meeting with Ali Zeydi, the Shengal delegation held several days of talks with Iraq’s security bureaucracy. The final meeting with the prime minister indicated that this series of talks had produced a positive outcome.




The Shengal delegation maintained that a self-defence force was essential to protect the social existence of the Yazidis and that this force should be positioned in a way that enables it to protect the Yazidi community, while a joint mechanism could also be developed with the Iraqi army. The meeting concluded without any serious objection from the Iraqi side to this position. It was jointly agreed that the details of how Shengal’s self-defence forces would be integrated with the Iraqi army would be determined through fieldwork carried out by a joint committee.




Does integration in Shengal mean incorporating the YBŞ and YJŞ into Iraqi security institutions while preserving their own command and organisational structures, or is individual incorporation into Iraqi security institutions envisaged?




Democratic integration has a different and particular meaning for Shengal compared with other areas, as the Yazidi community frequently stresses. The Yazidis are a people whose very existence has lived under the threat of genocide. Integration must therefore be understood not within a narrow military, political or administrative framework, but on historical, social and cultural grounds.




The Yazidi community’s defence forces are structures that pledged to protect the existence of the Yazidis, emerged amid the hell of ISIS attacks and took on meaning through the experience of Yazidi women who were sold in slave markets. Such a defence force cannot preserve the meaning of its existence simply by becoming individual soldiers or police officers. The Shengal delegation also raised this point during its talks with Baghdad. A common understanding emerged that these forces should be integrated with the Iraqi army and other security institutions in a way that preserves their own organisational structure and identity.




Neither Shengal’s defence forces nor the Yazidi community would accept any other approach. The precise methods, mechanisms and procedures for this integration, however, will be determined through fieldwork by the joint security committee.




Was the future of the Shengal Autonomous Administration model also discussed in the talks? What do the Yazidis and other communities in Shengal actually want? What are their expectations and demands?




As far as we have been able to follow and according to the information we have obtained, the autonomous administration model was not discussed as a central issue. The Shengal delegation did, however, stress that the institutions established by the Yazidi community over the past 12 years, since the period of the Ferman (Shengal genocide), should continue to exist.




There is an important point worth recalling here. The Iraqi Constitution does, in fact, grant certain rights to autonomous local administrations. In particular, it provides a constitutional basis for a degree of autonomy that enables cultural and religious communities to preserve their existence. Over the past 10 years, the Yazidi community has drawn up all of its proposals for a solution with reference to these constitutional rights. The fundamental rights set out in the Iraqi Constitution, however, have so far not been recognised for the Yazidi community and Shengal. Articles 122 and 123 of the Iraqi Constitution, in particular, provide for broad local autonomy without requiring the establishment of a federal region.




Both the Yazidi community and other peoples and religious communities living in Shengal say that Shengal should have a recognised status based on the exercise of this constitutional right. The Yazidis do not frame this merely as a demand for an administrative or political structure. They see it as a vital issue in ending the history of Fermans and writing a new history of free existence.




In short, the Yazidis are demanding and struggling for a system that will protect their existence and enable them to develop it.




Baghdad’s plans to bring weapons under the state’s monopoly and centralise security decisions are a major issue on the country’s agenda. Shengal, however, is in a different position because it established its own defence and security mechanisms following the ISIS genocide. Do you think Baghdad sufficiently takes this historical and social dimension into account?




The short and clear answer is no. It is worth examining this reality in greater depth, however. From the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and the establishment of Iraq as a modern nation-state to the present day, Baghdad’s approach towards Shengal and the Yazidis has been based on denial and assimilation.




From the early 1930s, attempts were made to bring the Yazidis under control through compulsory military service. Arabisation and Islamisation policies intensified under Baathist nationalism in the 1960s. In the 1970s, the Yazidis were uprooted from the sacred Mount Shengal and resettled on the plains in camps resembling village-town projects. The genocide carried out by ISIS in 2014 was, in fact, a consequence of this century-long policy.




For a century, Iraq has consistently viewed Shengal as a military zone and the Yazidi community as a population “to be disciplined and assimilated”. For Baghdad to properly understand Shengal and the Yazidis and develop a policy grounded in their historical and social reality, it must first reassess a century of modern Iraqi history and redefine its relationship with the Yazidis on the basis of democratic unity. Although a framework for a solution is currently being discussed, it is largely based on present-day circumstances, and it must also be recognised that this framework risks changing depending on the course of military and political developments.




Why is the 2020 Shengal Agreement rejected by the Yazidis? Is the model Baghdad is proposing for Shengal’s future today genuinely different from that agreement, or is it a new version of the same approach?




Much has been said about the 9 October 2020 Agreement. The agreement was signed between Baghdad and Erbil (Hewlêr), with the Turkish state also involved, and was concluded under the encouragement and supervision of international powers. It effectively transformed the 2014 Ferman into a political agreement. The Yazidis therefore regarded the agreement as a continuation of the Ferman.




The agreement was followed by severe attacks against the Yazidis and Shengal. Dozens of leading Yazidi figures were targeted in joint attacks by the KDP and the Turkish state. The sacred Mount Shengal was bombed dozens of times by warplanes. Baghdad also subjected Shengal to a severe military, political, economic and social blockade throughout this period. That blockade continues today, even as a solution is being discussed.




The talks now being held with Baghdad are intended to move beyond the 9 October 2020 Agreement. That can be said from the perspective of Shengal and the Yazidis. Whether Baghdad actually has a model to propose for Shengal’s future, however, remains a serious question.




Baghdad is facing a number of urgent and serious issues and crises, and the models it is considering are largely focused on immediate solutions. Can Baghdad view the Yazidis through a historical and social lens and bring about a change in its mentality? That remains a major question. The Yazidis want to develop a new relationship with the Iraqi state on the basis of democratic unity. Iraq, meanwhile, wants to close one of the many accumulated military and political files before it. At least for now, that is the situation.




Amid these discussions, a decision was announced to transfer Turkey’s Bashiqa-Zilkan Base to Iraq following the meeting between Erdoğan and Ali Zeydi during the UN General Assembly. Why does Turkey want to hand over this base now, and what is it demanding in return?




Turkey has hundreds of military bases and outposts in Southern Kurdistan. The Bashiqa Base is particularly significant for several reasons. It is a base where thousands of Salafist-jihadist mercenaries have been trained, posing a threat to the Yazidis of Shengal, Mosul and the Shekhan (Şêxan) region. The closure of this base is undoubtedly important. The Bashiqa Base, however, was raised during the New York talks you mentioned as a means of exerting pressure on Iraq.




First, the Turkish state does not want the talks between Shengal and Baghdad to proceed solely on a bilateral basis. It wants to maintain a role for itself in the issue and is seeking a place at the negotiating table in this way.




Second, the Turkish state has hundreds of bases and military checkpoints in Southern Kurdistan that it should evacuate. There is not a single indication on the ground that it intends to withdraw from them. By bargaining over an important base such as Bashiqa, it seeks to soften its broader occupation of the region and remove it from the agenda. In other words, it is attempting to narrow the discussion of its position as an occupying power in this way.




In the context of the Shengal-Baghdad talks, Turkey is also seeking, as far as it can, to restrict and weaken the position of the Yazidi defence forces.




The handover of Bashiqa is being presented to the public as “strengthening Iraq’s sovereignty”. The same agreement, however, has also prompted discussion of a possible “Shengal in exchange for Bashiqa” bargain. What kind of understanding do you think has emerged between Ankara and Baghdad?




Relations between Ankara and Baghdad shifted increasingly in Ankara’s favour, particularly under the Kadhimi and Sudani governments. Ankara used a number of strategic levers, especially water and energy resources, to pressure Baghdad and bring it into line with its regional policy. Relations between Baghdad and Ankara are therefore shaped less by a democratic understanding than by Ankara’s policy of blackmail and threats.




It is not yet clear whether this relationship will change under the Ali Zeydi government. The alleged “Shengal in exchange for Bashiqa” bargain is, in fact, one example of Turkey’s broader policy of pressure and blackmail across multiple areas. Turkey continues to use issues for which it bears clear responsibilities and obligations, the most obvious example being water, as leverage to exert pressure on Baghdad.




This process also coincides with the US withdrawal from Iraq, the restructuring of the Peshmerga forces and plans to bring armed groups under state control. What kind of security system is being built in Iraq, and where is Shengal intended to fit within this new equation?




This is a very broad issue. The entire military and political architecture of both Iraq and Southern Kurdistan is changing. This is undoubtedly connected to the current stage of the Third World War. Although Iraq portrays this process as “establishing national sovereignty”, it remains unclear what Iraq will ultimately face.




Iraq has long maintained a security architecture that relied on militia structures. There is now talk of moving beyond this model and strengthening the central army. The central army, however, remains considerably weak both in terms of the quality of its personnel and its military technology, and it lacks air defence and strike systems. At a time when new military doctrines supported by artificial intelligence are being discussed, space warfare is on the agenda and the region is engulfed in intense conflict, it remains highly uncertain whether Iraq can build an effective security system.




The situation is even more serious for Southern Kurdistan. The 35-year military and political architecture that emerged after the 1991 Gulf War is changing. The issue is not simply the removal of a few Patriot air defence systems from Erbil. The US and the International Coalition are withdrawing the security umbrella they have provided over Southern Kurdistan for 35 years. Although political forces in Southern Kurdistan are attempting to respond through the project to unify the Peshmerga forces, they need to take this process further and develop a new defence strategy based on national unity.




Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan has also made historic calls on this issue.




Shengal, as is known, is administratively part of Mosul and falls within the scope of Article 140. It is therefore an area claimed by both the Iraqi central government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), with both seeking to bring it under their administrative authority.




Had the KDP not left the Yazidis to face genocide alone during the Ferman, and had it not subsequently taken part alongside the Turkish state in attacks in which dozens of leading Yazidi figures lost their lives, Shengal might now have been negotiating with the KRG rather than Baghdad. Through its policies before, during and after the Ferman, the KDP weakened Shengal’s ties with Southern Kurdistan.




Whether this situation will change in the future remains unclear. For now, however, Shengal is seeking to resolve its fundamental problems through negotiations with Baghdad.

title: JINNEWS: 27 women and 6 children were murdered in September
content:
According to the September report compiled by JINNEWS, at least 27 women and 6 children were murdered, while 10 women and 6 children died under suspicious circumstances.




Twelve of the women were murdered by their spouses, 3 by men they were in the process of divorcing, 4 by men they had divorced, 1 by a man they had reportedly previously been in a relationship with, 1 by a family member, 1 by her son-in-law, 1 by the man her sister was married to, and 1 by her tenant. The relationship between 3 of the women and the perpetrators has not been clarified.




The cities where the women were murdered were: “3 in Manisa, 2 in Amed (Diyarbakır), 2 in Antalya, 2 in Sakarya, 1 in Adana, 1 in Ankara, 1 in Çorum, 1 in Denizli, 1 in Antep (Dîlok), 1 in Batman (Êlih), 1 in Hatay, 1 in Isparta, 1 in Istanbul, 1 in Kocaeli, 1 in Konya, 1 in Kütahya, 1 in Maraş, 1 in Mersin, 1 in Muğla, 1 in Osmaniye, 1 in Tekirdağ, and 1 woman in Elazığ (Xarpêt).”

author: Unknown
title: Activist allowed final meeting with his mother has been executed in Iran
content:
In a statement posted on social media, Sepahi’s lawyer, Şehrzad Şehbazi, announced that her client had been executed and said, “I will not forget him.”




Sepahi was allowed to meet with his mother, Somaya Afşar, who is also imprisoned, for the last time at Dastgerd Prison on Sunday, October 4 — in other words, shortly before his execution.




Arrests and executions in the country are increasing in connection with the protests that took place at the beginning of the year.




According to the NGOs Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty, Iran executed at least 1,639 people in 2025. This figure was described as the highest number recorded since 1989.




According to Amnesty International, Iran is the country with the second-highest number of executions, after China.

author: Unknown
title: Hıdır Öztürk demands investigation into the murder of his daughter Ayten in 1992
content:
Thirty-four years after the abduction, torture and killing of Ayten Öztürk, her father, Hıdır Öztürk, is calling for the case, which was closed due to the statute of limitations, to be reopened. Particularly at a time when peace and a resolution of the Kurdish question are being discussed, the state must investigate and clarify the crimes of the past, Öztürk said.




His daughter’s case is among the grave human rights violations of the 1990s in Northern Kurdistan, when people were abducted, forcibly disappeared and extrajudicially executed by state and paramilitary structures. According to the Human Rights Association (İHD), at least 1,388 people disappeared while in state custody between 1980 and 2001.




Ayten Öztürk’s eyes were gouged out




Ayten Öztürk was 27 years old and worked at a state-owned flour factory in the district of Mazgirt in Dersim (Tunceli) province. On the evening of July 27, 1992, witnesses saw four men drag her into a white Land Rover and abduct her after she left work. Twelve days later, on August 8, her body was found near Kartaltepe in Elazığ. She had been hastily buried, with one hand protruding from the ground.




Öztürk had been so severely tortured and mutilated that her family was able to identify her only by her clothing. Among other injuries, her eyes had been gouged out. Nevertheless, no comprehensive autopsy was carried out, the signs of torture were not adequately documented, and the investigation was closed.






















“Yeşil” had previously interrogated the family




The abduction had been preceded by threats against the family. Hıdır Öztürk, who at the time was himself a civil servant in the provincial administration, had been summoned together with his daughters on the orders of then-Gendarmerie Commander Mustafa Sabri Yazgankıran. There, the sisters were questioned by a man who recorded their personal details. It later emerged that the man was Mahmut Yıldırım, known by the codename “Yeşil.” The intelligence operative has been linked to numerous political killings and abductions during the 1990s.




Two of Ayten Öztürk’s sisters were subsequently transferred as a punitive measure to posts in western Turkey. Ayten remained in Dersim. A few weeks later, she was abducted. Later statements from individuals associated with the military intelligence organization JITEM strengthened suspicions that the operation had been organized by state actors. Former JITEM commander Cem Ersever and former intelligence operative Abdülkadir Aygan publicly stated that Öztürk had been abducted by Mahmut Yıldırım and his team. They said a vehicle provided by the emergency rule administration at the time had been used in the operation.




According to their accounts, the young woman was taken to a JITEM interrogation center in Amed (Diyarbakır), where she was tortured and eventually executed. Although these statements became public, they did not result in those responsible being subjected to penalty.




Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to life




After decades of unsuccessful efforts to obtain justice, Ayten Öztürk’s family applied to Turkey’s Constitutional Court in 2013. On April 21, 2016, the court found a violation of the right to life, citing in particular the failure to adequately establish the facts and the shortcomings in the investigation. The ruling ultimately led to criminal proceedings being opened.




The case was later merged with the proceedings concerning the killing of Kurdish intellectual Musa Anter. Nevertheless, no one was convicted. On September 21, 2022, the proceedings concerning the abduction and killing of Ayten Öztürk, like those in the Anter case, were also dismissed on statute-of-limitations grounds. Decades of delayed and inadequate efforts to investigate the case thus once again ended in impunity.




Öztürk: Our only wish is for the truth to be uncovered




Hıdır Öztürk is now calling for the case to be revisited in light of the current political developments. He said he requested an appointment with Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek on August 10 but has yet to receive a response. His demand concerns not only his own daughter, but also the many unresolved killings and cases of enforced disappearance involving state actors.




“Our wish, our only wish as grieving fathers and mothers, is for the unresolved killings to be investigated and clarified during this period of peace. We hope that the interior minister and the justice minister will grant us an appointment, listen to our demands, and enable these crimes to be fully investigated.”




“This dark stain must not go down in history”




Öztürk recalled the brutality with which his daughter was killed. The truth about what happened to her, he said, must no longer remain concealed. “My wish is for these case files to be reopened and the truth uncovered during this period of peace, so that this dark stain does not go down in history. Gouging out a person’s eyes and mutilating their body—the fact that an innocent young woman was subjected to such treatment is a dark stain on this history.”




Öztürk said that what should go down in history is the truth. He therefore expects the state to reinvestigate his daughter’s case and bring the proceedings to a conclusion.

title: Protest in Ranya Against environmental destruction and Turkish military presence
content:
Numerous people in Ranya protested against the destruction of Kurdistan’s natural environment and the continued Turkish military presence in Southern Kurdistan. The rally, held in front of the city’s People’s Garden, was organized by the Koşan Group under the slogan “Êdî bes e dagirkerî û xirabkirina jîngeha Kurdistanê” — “Enough with the occupation and destruction of Kurdistan’s environment.”




Speaking on behalf of the group, Şadiye Samed said that for years the Turkish state had militarily occupied large areas of Behdînan under the pretext of waging war against the guerrillas of the Kurdish freedom movement. In addition to the deaths of numerous civilians, she said, the war had caused severe damage to the environment, nature and infrastructure of Southern Kurdistan.




















With the peace and democratic society process launched in February 2025, there was no longer any justification for continuing the war and military occupation in Southern Kurdistan, the Koşan Group stated. Nevertheless, it said, the destruction of the natural environment and the Turkish military presence have continued. “Protecting the borders and forests of Southern Kurdistan is not merely an environmental issue. It is also part of protecting our land, our culture and our identity,” the statement said.




Criticism was also directed at the government of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI). Its silence in the face of the destruction of the forests was described as part of the problem. In conclusion, the Koşan Group called on citizens, institutions, activists and environmental movements both inside and outside Kurdistan to take a stand against the destruction of nature and the Turkish military presence. The group demanded the withdrawal of the Turkish army from Southern Kurdistan and an end to interventions in the region.

title: Iran steps up military presence in Eastern Kurdistan
content:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has deployed heavy military equipment in the Şaho Mountains near Rewanser in Eastern Kurdistan and closed parts of the region to civilians. At the same time, artillery fire is targeting mountain ridges under the pretext of a military exercise.




According to the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN), citing a resident of a village at the foot of the Şaho Mountains, the Revolutionary Guards have deployed a convoy carrying heavy military equipment to the region in recent days.




Residents were informed through village councils that certain areas of the Şaho Mountains are off-limits until October 7. According to a notice issued by the Şiwankar village council, the restrictions apply to the mountain ridges stretching from Bedrawa through Pir-Xidir to the Goliçî Pass. The area around Pir-Xidir, among others, is being subjected to artillery fire.




The Şaho Mountains and the adjacent Kosalan Mountains were officially designated as a protected area by Iran’s Supreme Environmental Council in 2009. Nevertheless, the Revolutionary Guards have been expanding their military infrastructure there for years. At the end of August, the Revolutionary Guards heavily shelled the ridges of the Şaho Mountains in the Kamyaran area with artillery. Footage published by the KHRN subsequently documented extensive fires across the mountainous area.




According to environmental activists, the Revolutionary Guards have been establishing military bases in the Şaho-Kosalan protected area since 2007 under the pretext of combating Kurdish opposition forces. Parts of the forests and grazing lands have reportedly been destroyed during the construction of the bases and military access roads. The activists also say that vegetation and pastureland around some military posts are deliberately set on fire. The Revolutionary Guards justify this by saying they aim to prevent Kurdish forces from using the vegetation as cover for attacks.

author: Unknown
title: ISIS member arrested in Sulaymaniyah
content:
Counter-terrorism units have arrested a wanted member of the “Islamic State” (ISIS) in Sulaymaniyah. The man is said to have moved to Sulaymaniyah following the military collapse of ISIS and continued his activities for the organization there.




According to the Kurdish Counter-Terrorism Group Lexoman-Parastin (CTG), the arrest followed an extended period of surveillance and the analysis of detailed intelligence. The detainee reportedly belonged to a unit designated by ISIS as the “210th Division.”




Following the collapse of the jihadist group, the man settled in Sulaymaniyah. According to the security forces, however, he remained active as an ISIS member within the province until he was tracked down and arrested by counter-terrorism units.




His father had also held senior positions within ISIS. He initially served as commander of a military unit in the so-called “North Baghdad Province” and was later appointed ISIS “governor” of Fallujah. He was killed in an airstrike in the Abu Ghraib district.




A brother of the detainee, who was also a member of ISIS, was killed in the an-Nibāʿī area northwest of Baghdad, according to the security forces. No further information was provided about the detainee’s identity or his specific activities for ISIS in Sulaymaniyah.

author: Unknown
title: Syrian Federation for Human Rights calls for constitutional right to mother-tongue education
content:
The Syrian Federation for Human Rights Organizations and Bodies has called for the linguistic and cultural rights of all communities in Syria to be guaranteed by law and the constitution. The right to education in one’s mother tongue, it said, must not depend on temporary political or administrative decisions.




In a statement issued by its Executive Council, the federation described linguistic and cultural diversity as an integral part of fundamental human rights. Language, it said, is directly linked to identity and culture, the right to education, and equal participation in social life. The rights of Kurds, Syriacs, Armenians, Circassians and other communities must therefore be protected, the federation underlined.




Mother-tongue education does not mean division




According to the federation, the recognition of different languages does not contradict either Syria’s unity or the status of Arabic as the official language. The existence of an official state language must not be used as a justification for excluding other languages from education, culture and social life, it said.




“Protecting and learning one’s mother tongue means neither division nor isolation. On the contrary, it can strengthen a sense of belonging, participation and equality when the shared rights of all citizens are respected. Multilingual education can help preserve cultural diversity, promote mutual understanding and strengthen social coexistence.”




Legal recognition instead of temporary decisions




The federation referred to the 2025 Constitutional Declaration, which establishes Arabic as the official language while also recognizing the cultural diversity of Syrian society and the linguistic and cultural rights of the population. Decision No. 13 of 2026 also designates Kurdish as a national language and provides for Kurdish-language instruction in state schools, particularly in predominantly Kurdish areas. However, implementation by the Syrian Ministry of Education falls far short of the right to mother-tongue education: Kurdish is not recognized as a language of instruction, but is permitted only as a school subject and limited to three hours per week.




Against this backdrop, the human rights federation called for linguistic rights that have already been won not to be rolled back through new education policies. The right to mother-tongue education must be permanently guaranteed by law and the constitution, it demanded.




Recognition must be implemented in practice




The statement continued: “Kurdish, Syriac and Assyrian must be recognized as national languages, and corresponding educational opportunities must be established. Formal recognition alone is not sufficient. Curricula, textbooks and teaching materials must be developed, along with the training of qualified teachers.”




At the same time, the statement added, laws and administrative regulations that discriminate against people on the basis of their language or cultural and national identity must be reviewed. The federation called for institutional mechanisms to monitor the implementation of linguistic rights and ensure their application within the education system. “Changes to the language of instruction must not result in students having to interrupt their education or facing greater barriers to accessing education,” it noted.




“Protecting one’s mother tongue is not a privilege, but part of protecting identity and culture, the right to education, and the principles of equality and non-discrimination,” the statement said.




“For Syria to have a future based on citizenship rights, equality and human rights, all communities must be guaranteed the right to learn their languages, use them in education and pass them on to future generations,” the statement concluded.

author: Unknown
title: Baluken: Öcalan’s status is linked to the status of the Kurdish people
content:
Kurdish politician Idris Baluken has warned against viewing the peace and democratic society process solely through the lens of the current balance of power in Turkey. Speaking at an event in Besançon, France, he said the Kurdish question must be considered in the context of the restructuring of the Middle East and the shifting balance of power in the region.




Baluken referred to dialogue and negotiation efforts over the past decades and emphasized that the search for a political solution is by no means new: “The leadership of the Kurdish people and the Kurdish movement was already seeking an interlocutor 30 years ago in order to resolve this issue and intervene in the course of developments during this historic period,” the former HDP MP said, referring to Abdullah Öcalan.






















“The issue goes far beyond the current government”




Baluken described the mistrust toward the Turkish government and criticism of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the AKP and the position of MHP Chair Devlet Bahçeli as largely justified. However, he said that focusing solely on these actors is not sufficient to assess the current developments.




“The issue goes far beyond Erdoğan, Bahçeli, the AKP or the MHP. It goes far beyond the current political government in Turkey.”




The decisive factor, he said, is the restructuring of the Middle East. “At a time when regional powers are repositioning themselves, the Kurdish side seeks to overcome the factors that have weakened its position and enabled attacks against it. As a people numbering 50 to 60 million, Kurds must take their place at the political negotiating table. A Kurdish reality that no longer fits within the narrow organizational confines of the past has entered the stage of history. In the emerging balance of power, the aim is to act as a political subject and a force capable of shaping developments,” Baluken said.




"Kurdish rights must be guaranteed by law and the constitution"




According to Baluken, a lasting solution is inseparable from the recognition of Kurdish rights: “Just as this problem was created by denying the rights of the Kurdish people for a hundred years, it must be resolved in the new century by recognizing those rights and guaranteeing them both legally and constitutionally.”




The Kurdish side, he said, does not want to prolong the current process unnecessarily, but seeks to bring it to a lasting peace. To achieve this, he added, the political counterpart must now also take the necessary steps.




“Öcalan’s status is linked to the status of the Kurdish people”




Baluken pointed out that the legal status of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan, who is imprisoned on the Turkish prison island of Imrali, plays a key role. He rejected attempts to treat Öcalan’s situation as an individual matter, saying: “If Mr. Öcalan’s status on Imrali is placed on a legal footing, this will at the same time amount to legal recognition of the status of the Kurdish people, which has been denied for a hundred years.”




During the 2013–2015 resolution process, Baluken was among the key politicians involved in the dialogue with the Turkish state. He recalled that Öcalan’s position had already been treated at the time as an important component of a resolution in talks with both the government and the opposition. Today, however, Öcalan’s status is sometimes portrayed as though it concerned him alone, Baluken said. He stressed that Öcalan represents the largest politically and organizationally structured Kurdish force across all four parts of Kurdistan.




Four goals for the new phase




For the coming phase, Baluken identified four fundamental goals of the Kurdish movement: strategic renewal, ideological reorientation, organizational restructuring and lasting peace. The movement, he said, can achieve the first three objectives through its own efforts. “Lasting peace, however, also depends on steps taken by the state. The state must not obstruct the path toward a political resolution.”




Warning of plans for attacks




Baluken also linked the urgency of a political resolution to the dangers arising from the current restructuring of the Middle East. He said a process aimed at eliminating non-state forces was underway in the region. “While this process is underway, very serious plans for massacres targeting the most highly organized structures of the Kurdish movement are on the table.”




The Kurds, he said, have maintained their existence through decades of resistance. “The task now is to secure an appropriate position under the changed political conditions,” he added.




Following Baluken’s presentation, participants discussed the peace and democratic society process as well as current political developments.

author: Béla
title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.




The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.




About the session




Date & time:

 

15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 Trans communities and activists 










Register here










What the session will cover 




Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.




The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? What community networks and resources are already available? What might help or hinder efforts to build similar community-led care?










Register here










Your support makes change possible




We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

title: Kaşif Kozinoğlu soruşturması: Mezarından alınan örnekler geri konuldu
content:
Silivri Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığının talebi üzerine 2011 yılında hayatını kaybeden eski MİT görevlisi Kaşif Kozinoğlu'nun kesin ölüm sebebinin ve ölümünde üçüncü kişilerin müdahalesi bulunup bulunmadığının belirlenmesi amacıyla alınan feth-i kabir kararı kapsamında, mezardan alınan örneklerin incelenmesi tamamlandı.

Örnekler, Kozinoğlu'nun mezarının bulunduğu Ümraniye'deki Kocatepe Mezarlığına getirilerek, uzman heyetin çalışmasıyla defnedildi. Ardından mezar kapatıldı.

Adalet Bakanı Akın Gürlek, sosyal hesabından Kozinoğlu'nun ölümüne ilişkin soruşturmaya yönelik açıklama yapmıştı.

Bakan Gürlek, Faili Meçhul Suçları Araştırma Daire Başkanlığınca dosyanın yeniden incelendiğini belirterek yeni soruşturma kapsamında gizlilik kararı alındığını, özel bir soruşturma ekibi oluşturularak olayın tüm yönleriyle yeniden aydınlatılmasına yönelik kapsamlı çalışmalara başlandığını ifade etmişti.

Soruşturmadaki ilk operasyonda olay tarihinde ceza infaz kurumunda görev yapan 10 kişi gözaltına alınmış, 1 kişinin ise “FETÖ” kapsamında firari olarak yurt dışında bulunduğu tespit edilmişti. Gözaltına alınan 10 kişiden 1'i tutuklanmış, 7'si adli kontrol şartıyla olmak üzere 9'u serbest bırakılmıştı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Natalia Viana
title: Flávio Bolsonaro e o risco de um presidente com esqueletos no armário
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Xeque na Democracia, enviada toda segunda-feira, 12h. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui.







O Brasil que sai do primeiro turno está flertando com uma crise institucional permanente. Flávio Bolsonaro teve 2,2 milhões de votos a mais que Lula, ficando em 47% dos votos versus 45,1% do atual presidente. 

Se eleito, Flávio teria uma bancada de 28 nomes no Senado e 121 na Câmara dos Deputados apenas do PL, seu partido, um desempenho histórico. 




Mas 

Flávio Bolsonaro é um candidato com muitos esqueletos no armário. Está enredado em vários escândalos e corrupção

 dos quais, hoje, conseguimos ter apenas um vislumbre, mas que vão se aprofundar nos próximos meses. E 

isso levará necessariamente a um governo maculado por revelações do seu primeiro ao seu último dia. 




A jornalista Flávia de Oliveira 

chamou

 a atenção para o fato de que, 

por conta da ação de

 

André Mendonça

 

de manter sigilo do caso Master, Flávio é o único candidato investigado por corrupção, lavagem de dinheiro e evasão de divisas – e o eleitor não foi informado disso a tempo. 




Mesmo que você esteja acompanhando as notícias, é possível que tenha perdido as revelações mais recentes.  




Pois vamos a elas. 




Primeiro, as rachadinhas, esquema de desvio de verba pública dos mandatos de Jair Bolsonaro e seus filhos através de saques em dinheiro vivo de funcionários, que depois repassavam à família, das quais Flávio sempre foi figura central.

 O resultado foi demonstrado há alguns anos pelos jornalistas Juliana Dal Piva e Thiago Herdy: 51 imóveis dos Bolsonaro foram pagos parcialmente em dinheiro vivo. O processo judicial das rachadinhas foi extinto pelo STJ, que questionou a quebra de sigilo fiscal, mas as evidências existem e podem gerar novas investigações.  




Segundo, vamos ao caso Master. Ainda hoje sabe-se apenas parcialmente sobre a relação entre Flávio e Daniel Vorcaro. Além do financiamento generoso do filme

 

Dark Horse

 

e dos muitos diálogos resgatados do celular de Vorcaro

, não sabemos qual o valor real dos depósitos, que tipo de dinheiro criminoso foi usado para o pagamento pela empresa Entre Investimentos, que 

lavava

 inclusive dinheiro para o crime organizado, e nem para que fim o dinheiro foi usado nos EUA. 

Não se sabe, ainda, que outros favores e apoios foram prestados pelo banqueiro para Flávio – com quem ele tinha uma relação de amizade

, 

segundo demonstram os diálogos completos publicados pela revista

 

piauí

: são 50 mensagens de Flávio, 46 de Vorcaro e 14 ligações – oito delas atendidas.

 Sempre se tratando como “irmãos”, Flávio chegou a oferecer a Vorcaro uma reunião com Eduardo Bolsonaro em Dubai em novembro do ano passado: “Tá precisando de algo lá? Peço pra ele te encontrar”. Além disso, jantares, cafés da manhã e muitas ligações organizadas entre os dois. 




A mesma revista 

revelou

, ainda, que Flávio e Vorcaro viajaram para Fort Lauderdale, na Flórida, no feriado prolongado de 1º de maio de 2025, tendo passado 3 dias ao mesmo tempo no balneário, apenas dias depois do primeiro depósito de Vorcaro para o filme Dark Horse. É provável que tenham passado e celebrado juntos em uma das famosas festas de Vorcaro nestes três dias. Ainda não sabemos até onde foi essa relação. 




Terceiro, a ligação próxima com o “Careca de INSS”. Como

 

revelou

 

o ICL, Flávio tem uma empresa de capacetes que está registrada no mesmo lugar de empresas do operador financeiro do esquema que desviava verba dos aposentados e causou prejuízo de R$ 2 bilhões aos cofres públicos.

 Além de usar o mesmo escritório, a empresa de Flávio usava a mesma contabilidade de Antonio Carlos Camilo Antunes, mais conhecido como “Careca do INSS”, atualmente preso.




Quarto, os indícios de corrupção na gestão de hospitais públicos no Rio de Janeiro, inclusive durante a pandemia de Covid.

 Em uma reportagem 

bastante detalhada

  aqui na 

Agência Pública

, mostramos como Flávio comandava as decisões administrativas e indicações para a gestão dos hospitais federais durante a epidemia. Há diversos indícios de superfaturamento e má conduta em diversos destes hospitais, segundo investigações do TCU e outros órgãos. Esta história está só no começo.  




Quinto, a figura do advogado Willer Tomáz começa a aparecer como uma sombra sobre o passado de Flávio. O advogado já foi descrito como amigo de Flávio pelo próprio

, viajou com ele para um safári na África do Sul e usou o jatinho de Willer em sociedade com Daniel Vorcaro. Willer Tomaz atualmente é 

investigado

 pela PF depois de iniciar um processo judicial no qual alega que apostou R$ 6,6 bilhões na bet Blaze por “ludopatia” e tenta recuperar R$ 163 milhões.  




Sexto, possível lobby junto ao ministro do STF Kassio Nunes

, um expediente descrito por Rodrigo Rangel na sua 

reportagem

 sobre a relação de Flávio Bolsonaro com Alexandre Ferreira Dias Santini, ex-sócio seu na fábrica da Kopenhagen, publicado no site Platô. Nas palavras do jornalista, 

Flávio era um “resolvedor-geral da República” durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro e teria recebido mimos por isso, incluindo um rolex de 300 mil reais.

 Rangel é uma das pessoas em Brasília que tem muito mais documentos sobre a relação de Flávio e o ex-sócio, mas não o único. Dentre o material descrito na reportagem estão notas fiscais, relatos, fotos “impublicáveis” de Flávio em orgias com o ex-sócio, segundo descrito na reportagem. Mais gente tem esses documentos – eles vão acabar vindo à tona.




Se for eleito, Flávio Bolsonaro terá as investigações do caso Master suspensas

, segundo 

análise do Jota

. Mas o jornalismo investigativo continuará a fazer o seu papel. 




Temos um presidente maculado por corrupção e escândalos variados antes mesmo de pisar no Palácio do Planalto.

 Não há bancada forte que segure o impacto disto sobre a opinião pública. Além disso, vale lembrar, a liderança de Flávio é contestada mesmo dentro das fileiras do Bolsonarismo. A bancada eleita tem sua agenda própria e desafetos variados que não vão tardar a aparecer.     




Portanto, esta coluna é um aviso. 

Se o Brasil eleger Flávio Bolsonaro, não estamos flertando apenas com um governo de viés autoritário, mas com um governo que será maculado por escândalos e turbulências,

 assombrado por ex-sócios, fotos e vídeos “impublicáveis”, e que para se manter no poder só terá o caminho de chafurdar-se mais ainda na lama e perseguir a imprensa e os oponentes – como fez Trump nos EUA. 




Para quem busca “estabilidade”, “previsibilidade” e “segurança fiscal”: está dado o recado.

title: Fransa’da daha iyi eğitim için 413 okulda eylem
content:
Fransa’da eğitim koşullarının iyileştirilmesi talebiyle düzenlenen lise eylemleri devam ediyor. Fransa Eğitim Bakanlığı bugün ülke genelinde 413 okulda eylemler olduğunu açıkladı. Eylemlere yönelik polis şiddeti de devam ediyor.

Fransa'da öğrenciler niye eylem yapıyor, ne talep ediyor?

Ülkenin önde gelen lise sendikalarından USL Genel Sekreteri Marius Mesnil, katıldığı bir televizyon yayınında, hükümetin liselilerin taleplerine ilişkin adımlarını yeterli bulmadıklarını yineledi. Mesnil, lise kuşatma eylemlerinin kararlılıkla sürdürülmesi çağrısı yaptı.

Fransa'da daha iyi eğitim koşulları talebiyle başlatılan lise eylemleri büyüyor. Ülke genelinde 413 okulda protestolar sürerken, Fransa'nın en büyük işçi sendikası CGT de öğrencilere destek vererek iş bırakma çağrısında bulundu @RevPermanente/X https://t.co/eSlFa4u7Xe https://t.co/2TqmWX4Z2G

Ülkenin en büyük sendikası CGT Genel Sekreteri Sophie Binet de liselilerin eylemlerine destek vereceklerini açıkladı. CGT ve diğer işçi sendikaları bugün iş bırakma ve lise öğrencileriyle birlikte protesto gösterilerine katılma çağrısı yapmışlardı.

Fransa’da 6 Ekim çağrısı: İşçiler gençlerin yanında olacak

Lise öğrencilerinin 17 Eylül’de Créteil’deki Saint-Exupéry Lisesi’nde başlattığı eylem, kısa sürede Paris banliyölerinden ülke geneline yayıldı.

Öğrenciler öğretmen ve personel eksikliği, kalabalık sınıflar, aşırı yoğun ders programları, bakımsız okul binaları ve bazı dersliklerde masa gibi temel ihtiyaçların dahi bulunmamasını protesto ediyor.

Öğretmen açığının kapatılması, daha fazla personel, daha az kalabalık sınıflar, yenilenmiş okul binaları ve daha iyi öğrenme koşulları için somut adımlar atılması isteniyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

content:

Free breakfasts to continue for students across Kivalliq and Kitikmeot

.







ᒫᓃᐸᓗᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ 22 ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᓂ ᒫᓂ ᑭᕙᓪᓕᖅᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᕿᑎᕐᒥᐅᓂ ᐅᓪᓛᕈᒻᒥᑕᖅᑎᑕᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᑭᖃᙱᑦᑐᓂ ᑎᑭᓪᓗᒍ 2031, ᖁᔭᓐᓇᒦ ᐊᒡᓂᑯ ᐄᒍᓪ ᐅᔭᕋᒃᓯᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᑐᓂᓚᐅᕐᑕᖓᓐᓂ $5 ᒥᓕᐊᓐ ᑕᓚᐃ.




ᐅᓇ ᐅᓪᓛᕈᒻᒥᑕᖅᑎᑦᑎᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᖅ, ᑕᐃᔭᐅᓯᒪᖕᒥᔪᖅ ᐃᓄᙳᐃᓂᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ, ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᓪᓛᕈᒻᒥᑕᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ, ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᖅᑐᓂ ᓂᕿᖃᙱᓗᐊᔭᓐᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ.




“ᑕᑯᓯᒪᒐᑦᑕ ᐅᓇ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᖑᔪᖅ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᓂᖓᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓄᑦ, ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓄᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᒫᒃ-ᐅᓕᕕᐃ ᕙᓵᓐ, ᐊᐅᓚᑎᔨᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐊᒡᓂᑯ ᐄᒍᓪ ᒥᓕᐊᑏᓐ ᒎᓗᒧᑦ ᐅᔭᕋᒃᓯᐅᖅᕕᒃᒥ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 23-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑭᕙᓪᓕᖅᒥ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᓄᑦ ᓴᖅᑭᔮᖅᑎᑦᑎᔪᑦ ᑲᑎᖃᑎᒌᒃᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ.




ᐊᒡᓂᑯ ᐄᒍᓪ ᑐᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ $2.5 ᒥᓕᐊᓐ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᑦ ᐊᔾᔨᒋᓂᕋᖅᖢᓂᒋᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ ᓴᖅᑭᔮᖅᑎᑦᑎᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ 2023-ᒥ.




ᐃᓄᙳᐃᓂᖅ ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ ᑐᑭᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᔭᑐᖃᖏᓐᓂ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᖅ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓅᓂᕐᒥ.

author: Unknown
title: Perché opporci al dilagare dei data center? Opuscolo informativo con focus sulla regione Piemonte
content:
Per avvicinarsi all’iniziativa 

“La vera faccia dei data center: cosa succede in Piemonte?”

 che si terrà al Dipartimento di Fisica di Torino mercoledì 21 ottobre alle ore 17.30, abbiamo scritto un primo opuscolo informativo (

scaricabile in formato pdf al fondo

) che riporta alcuni ragionamenti collettivi sugli impatti e sulle ragioni per opporsi al dilagare dei data center. 




L’opuscolo propone poi

 

un focus sulla regione Piemonte e i progetti al momento individuati: 

per mettersi in rete ed entrare in contatto con i comitati o i cittadini che si stanno attivando su questo tema sui territori coinvolti in Piemonte scrivi a confluenza.info@gmail.com 










INTRODUZIONE: PERCHÉ OPPORCI AL DILAGARE DEI DATA CENTER 







La dispensa verso “La vera faccia dei data center: cosa succede in Piemonte?” è organizzata su due livelli-obiettivi: 1) un’iniziale mappatura dei progetti di data center rivolti al territorio piemontese che, sulla scorta del prezioso lavoro fatto dai comitati lombardi che per primi si sono trovati a fronteggiare questo fenomeno, sia fondamento per la costruzione di strumenti in grado di anticipare le dinamiche di sfruttamento; 2) la sistematizzazione dei casi puntuali, non solo piemontesi, in un quadro interpretativo generale in grado di leggere la portata di questa “rivoluzione industriale”, da cui riemerge il triangolo industriale Milano-Genova-Torino in connessione con la guerra mondiale a pezzi e l’espropriazione capitalista della natura.




La guerra e l’innovazione tecnologica




Oggi abbiamo l’urgenza di comprendere meglio e più a fondo quanto sta accadendo ai nostri territori quando si parla di nuovi data center. Nello scenario di guerra globale i territori sono obiettivo di trasformazione in funzione strategica per gli interessi dei governi che vogliono mandarci in guerra. Torino e il Piemonte, per la loro collocazione geografica, per gli interessi che si giocano e i capitali in circolo, diventano, così, luogo centrale in questo processo. 

Torino è la città dell’aerospazio: lo spazio oggi è diventato un dominio di guerra a seguito della svolta americana in questo senso.

 Il controllo spaziale diventa un’ulteriore dimensione per il controllo sulle infrastrutture e altri 

asset

 strategici. 

La militarizzazione dello spazio necessita di un’infrastruttura concreta, di corridoi energetici e dimensioni materiali: in base a tale logica  il nord-ovest rappresenta un territorio fondamentale

. A Settimo Torinese la mega industria di satelliti, visitata anche dalla Ministra Anna Maria Bernini (accompagnata dal rettore del Politecnico Corgnati e della rettrice di UniTo Cristina Prandi, a dimostrazione del 

ruolo delle università

 in questo quadro ), è un polo strategico fondamentale e fa parte di un triangolo che collega Milano e Genova. I satelliti nello spazio infatti producono moltissime informazioni. A Genova approdano i cavi sottomarini ad alta capacità per la fibra ottica mentre Lombardia e Piemonte  sono i due poli per l’innovazione computazionale e dispongono di ampie aree e infrastrutture per accogliere questa produzione importante di dati. 

Per questa ragione  servono data center soprattutto sull’asse Torino-Milano

. “L’accentramento dei dati della Pubblica Amministrazione, dei servizi finanziari e della difesa all’interno di questi centri crea un punto critico di vulnerabilità strategica, trasformando la loro tutela fisica e informatica in una priorità assoluta di sicurezza nazionale

1

.” 




L’energia non è una merce




La domanda di energia per il funzionamento di questo insieme di server, costante e imponente, produrrà costi e pressione sulla società che gestisce l’infrastruttura elettrica nazionale ossia Terna.

 Da Terna dipende l’accesso all’energia per i consumi delle città e i consumi domestici di ciascuno di noi.

Cosa sono i data center?

 




 

I data center sono infrastrutture che ospitano 

server

 e apparecchiature, impiegate prevalentemente per la 

potenza di calcolo necessaria al funzionamento della cosiddetta “intelligenza artificiale”, alla digitalizzazione, all’

ecommerce

 

e a finalità di difesa, militari e di competizione economica internazionale.

 L’Italia è coinvolta nello sviluppo dei data center in modo enorme: le richieste di nuovi progetti e nuove costruzioni di data center sono centinaia e a esse si legano molti problemi, di diversi ordini e livelli, che a oggi ci sembrano poco o per nulla affrontati. 







L’Italia come

 

hub

 

del Mediterraneo: le mosse del governo 




Il Governo Meloni ha scelto di aprire a massicci investimenti esteri per la costruzione di nuovi data center. 

L’Italia si trova inoltre al centro dei progetti per il passaggio di grandi corridoi digitali, destinati a collegare l’Europa con Israele, i Paesi arabi e l’India.

 Queste infrastrutture hanno però bisogno di grandi capacità di stoccaggio ed elaborazione dei dati, oltre che di strutture per il loro trattamento e controllo. 




A livello nazionale non esiste ancora una legislazione organica sui data center.

 Nel frattempo, il Governo sta introducendo, attraverso provvedimenti e decreti d’urgenza, strumenti finalizzati ad accelerarne la realizzazione. 

L’introduzione dell’autorizzazione unica rischia di modificare profondamente il sistema delle valutazioni ambientali, accorpando in un unico procedimento valutazioni e autorizzazioni che hanno funzioni differenti.

 Siamo quindi di fronte al rischio di una progressiva deroga alla legislazione ambientale, costruita nel corso di decenni anche attraverso la normativa europea. 

Il paradigma che si sta affermando sembra essere quello dell’eccezione e della sospensione delle regole ordinarie, ogni volta che un’opera viene definita strategica o ogni volta che viene adottata l’autorizzazione unica.

 




LA RETE ELETTRICA




L’aumento esponenziale delle richieste pone anche una domanda sulla 

capacità della rete nazionale di reggere questa trasformazione

. La rete elettrica italiana arriva a questo appuntamento dopo anni di investimenti insufficienti e deve già affrontare: 




• infrastrutture obsolete; 




• aumento della domanda elettrica; 




• eventi climatici estremi; 




• ondate di calore sempre più frequenti; 




• aumento dell’utilizzo dei sistemi di climatizzazione; 




• episodi di sovraccarico e interruzioni dell’alimentazione. 




Nonostante queste criticità, Terna sta sviluppando piani di potenziamento della rete principalmente in funzione dell’alimentazione dei nuovi data center. 




OPERE IMPATTANTI, COSTI SUI TERRITORI

 




Mentre i data center diventano infrastrutture sempre più grandi e impattanti, numerosi studi internazionali ne evidenziano le conseguenze ambientali. I costi territoriali e ambientali ricadono innanzitutto sulle comunità che ospitano questi impianti. 




I data center richiedono infatti enormi quantità di: 




• energia; 




• acqua; 




• suolo; 




• infrastrutture; 




• materiali; 




• sistemi di raffreddamento.




 A questo si aggiungono impatti ambientali e sanitari e spesso aumento dei costi in bolletta.




ALTRI RISCHI

 Esistono inoltre rischi tecnologici e di sicurezza che devono essere valutati attentamente. 




I data center possono ospitare: 




• grandi quantità di carburante per i generatori di emergenza; 




• sistemi UPS e grandi batterie; 




• impianti elettrici ad alta potenza; 




• sistemi di raffreddamento complessi.

content:
Feminist ve queer teori alanındaki çalışmalarıyla tanınan Judith Butler, Türkiye’de LGBTİ+’lara yönelik son dönemdeki baskıların ele alınacağı çevrimiçi etkinliğe katılacak.




Kaos GL’nin duyurusuna göre, 12 Ekim’de düzenlenecek webinarda Butler ile Kaos GL Genel Yayın Yönetmeni Yıldız Tar konuşacak. Etkinlikte, “Ailem Güvende” adı altında yürütülen operasyonların başlamasından bu yana geçen bir aylık süreç, yaşanan hak ihlalleri ve uluslararası dayanışmanın güçlendirilmesi ele alınacak.




Webinar; Kaos GL, Özgürlük İstiyoruz Kampanyası, Uluslararası Af Örgütü, PEN Norveç, Turkey Litigation Support Project ve Human Rights Watch ortaklığında düzenleniyor.




Kaos GL, etkinliğin Türkiye’de LGBTİ+’ları hedef alan baskılara ve hedef göstermelere karşı uluslararası dayanışmayı büyütmeyi amaçladığını belirtti. Duyuruda Butler’ın da Türkiye’deki hak mücadelesiyle dayanışma amacıyla küresel bir çağrıda bulunacağı ifade edildi.
