author: anred
title: Juicio por el transfemicidio de Azul Semeñenko: una vida atravesada por el odio a la identidad
content:
El juicio por el transfemicidio de Azul Mía Natasha Semeñenko comenzó en Neuquén mientras afuera del tribunal permanecía una pregunta que excede la responsabilidad penal de un acusado: ¿qué significa vivir siendo una mujer trans en una sociedad que todavía expone a esas vidas a la discriminación, la violencia y la precariedad? Por Manuela Wilhelm (ANRed).




 




Durante la primera jornada del juicio por jurados, la Fiscalía, la querella y la defensa presentaron sus teorías sobre lo ocurrido durante la madrugada del 25 de septiembre de 2025. Para las partes acusadoras, 

Roberto Daniel Sánchez asesinó a Azul Semeñenko

 en un ataque de extrema violencia y la Fiscalía buscará acreditar un 

homicidio triplemente agravado por ensañamiento, violencia de género y odio hacia su identidad de género

.




La defensa sostiene otra hipótesis: que la muerte ocurrió durante un episodio de violencia en el que Sánchez reaccionó bajo un estado de emoción violenta. Cabe destacar que el abogado contratado por el acusado, Ezequiel Leanza intentó pasar como prueba un “informe médico” que fue rechazado por el juez de garantias por considerarlo “inexistente” debido a que la mujer que lo firmaba tenía tres condenas por estafas en torno a un título trucho.







Gentileza




Además, el debate continuó con la prueba y el jurado popular escuchó a la primera testigo, Romina Millapán, hermana de Azul, quien reconstruyó una vida marcada por la violencia hacia su identidad que había comenzado mucho antes de aquella madrugada.




Azul Semeñenko fue discriminada y abusada en la infancia




Romina contó que Azul nació en Uruguay y que a los seis años llegó a Neuquén junto a su madre y sus hermanos. Según relató, desde pequeña manifestó que quería ser una niña. Sin embargo, comenzó la escuela con un nombre y una identidad que no eran los que reconocía como propios.




En la Escuela 61, recordó su hermana, era apartada y molestada porque prefería relacionarse con las niñas. Los insultos y las burlas continuaron durante la primaria y la secundaria. “Los compañeros consideraban que no era normal, que era un raro”, relató Romina ante el jurado.




La violencia tampoco quedó encerrada en las paredes de la escuela. Cuando Azul tenía alrededor de nueve o diez años, según el relato de su hermana, sufrió un abuso sexual dentro del hogar. Su madre lo denunció y el hombre que Romina señaló como responsable estuvo tres años preso. Sin embargo, posteriormente regresó a la familia y, según contó la testigo, continuó ejerciendo violencia y rechazando la identidad de Azul.“Mi mamá recuerda que si bien no lo volvió a tocar siempre le reprochó que no era su hijo y que en su familia no tenía un hijo maricón”, relató Romina.




Ese rechazo familiar se superponía con la violencia social. Durante su declaración, la hermana contó que Azul sufrió agresiones físicas y verbales en distintos momentos de su vida. En una ocasión, cuando había conseguido un trabajo nocturno en un puesto de panchos, un grupo de jóvenes la esperó a la salida, la golpeó, le rompió el teléfono y le fracturó un brazo.







“Yo me voy a matar porque soy un fracasado”




Uno de los momentos más duros del testimonio de Romina apareció cuando reconstruyó las consecuencias que tuvieron sobre Azul los años de discriminación, rechazo y dificultades para acceder a un trabajo.




Contó que cuando tenía 14 años encontró a Daniel —como todavía era llamada entonces— con una gillette en la mano y heridas en uno de sus brazos. Semanas después, atravesando nuevamente un período sin trabajo, le dijo que quería quitarse la vida.




“Yo me voy a matar porque soy un fracasado de mierda, nadie me quiere y nadie me va a dar una oportunidad. Yo me voy a tirar al río”, recordó Romina que le dijo.




La hermana lo siguió hasta el río y logró convencerlo de regresar a la casa. Una vez allí, Azul le pidió ayuda. “Ro, por favor ayudame porque yo así no puedo seguir. Necesito que me ayudes”, recordó.




Su madre buscó asistencia y, según el relato de Romina, comenzó un tratamiento psicológico que duró aproximadamente tres años. Después tuvo que interrumpirlo porque, al tratarse de atención en el sistema público, la falta de especialistas hizo imposible continuar.




Esos episodios fueron incorporados al juicio como parte de la historia de vida de Azul. La defensa cuestionó que se incluyeran hechos de su infancia y adolescencia que no estaban vinculados directamente con el homicidio. El juez Luciano Hermosilla, sin embargo, permitió que continuara el interrogatorio al considerar que podían servir para contextualizar la vida de la víctima.




La identidad como conquista




Con el paso de los años, Azul comenzó su transición. Romina contó que después de atravesar períodos de depresión y de alejarse de la casa familiar comenzó a regresar con otra apariencia: llevaba el pelo más largo, usaba rubor y comenzaba a presentarse de una manera diferente.




Tiempo después consiguió un trabajo estable y pudo alquilar una vivienda. Un día llamó a su hermana y le pidió que fuera a verla. Quería contarle una buena noticia.Sacó de su bolsillo su DNI. Allí aparecía su nuevo nombre: Azul Mía Natasha Semeñenko. “Estaba chocha, era feliz”, recordó Romina.




La familia comenzó a acompañar su proceso. Azul hablaba de futuras operaciones y de las dificultades económicas que tenía para acceder a ellas. Inicialmente pidió que su cambio de identidad quedara entre ellas, pero luego se lo contó a su madre y a sus hermanos. “No teníamos nada que discutir. Ella se hacía notar”, dijo Romina.







Trabajo, precariedad y supervivencia




Uno de los puntos que apareció tanto en el juicio como en la marcha realizada a un año del crimen fue la relación entre identidad, trabajo y precariedad.




Azul había conseguido un empleo formal como auxiliar en el Centro de Atención a la Víctima que depende de la provincia de Neuquén. Sus compañeras la recordaron como una trabajadora comprometida, humilde y valiente. Sin embargo, ese ingreso no alcanzaba para cubrir todas sus necesidades.




Romina contó que Azul le había hablado de las dificultades económicas y de la necesidad de reunir dinero para una operación vinculada con su transición. En ese contexto, había comenzado a realizar trabajo sexual y le había contado a su hermana que en algunas ocasiones aceptaba situaciones que normalmente no habría aceptado por necesidad económica.




Romina mostró su angustia y recordó que le dijo “te estás exponiendo”, en relación a lo que ella miraba en las noticias de los femicidios. También recordando una salida al recital de Babasònicos en la Fiesta de la Confluencia donde sufrieron un ataque de odio por parte de un grupo de jóvenes.







Newen Kvyen




“El Cupo Laboral Trans en Neuquén no existe”




Ese dato adquirió una dimensión colectiva durante la marcha realizada el 25 de septiembre de 2026, cuando se cumplió un año del crimen. Frente a la Casa de Gobierno, las organizaciones que participaron de la movilización leyeron un documento que cuestionó las condiciones de vida de las personas travestis y trans y sostuvo que el acceso a una vivienda, a la salud y al trabajo formal continúa siendo una deuda.El documento puso especial énfasis en que Azul había conseguido ingresar al trabajo estatal por sus propios medios y no como resultado de una política de cupo laboral trans.




“El cupo laboral trans no existe”, denunciaron las organizaciones, que reclamaron políticas públicas que garanticen derechos y reduzcan la situación de vulnerabilidad de las personas trans.




La historia de Azul aparecía así como una vida particular, pero también como parte de una realidad colectiva.







“Cuando Azul desapareció, no se la buscó”




La marcha por el primer aniversario del transfemicidio también permitió reconstruir otra parte de la historia: la búsqueda.




Familiares, compañeras de trabajo y organizaciones salieron a buscar a Azul cuando desapareció. El documento leído frente a Gobernación cuestionó el accionar inicial del Estado y sostuvo: “Cuando Azul desapareció, no se la buscó”.




La frase fue acompañada por un reconocimiento a la red que se organizó alrededor de su ausencia: las compañeras del Centro de Atención a la Víctima, la familia y las organizaciones que sostuvieron la búsqueda y reclamaron que se investigara qué había ocurrido.




Semanas después, el cuerpo de Azul fue encontrado dentro de un desagüe en el límite entre Neuquén y Plottier por una pareja que paseaba con sus perros.Para la querella, ese desenlace también debe ser leído en relación con la violencia estructural que atraviesa a las personas trans. Durante el alegato de apertura, el abogado Fernando Gómez pidió al jurado que no transformara la vida de Azul en un juicio moral sobre la víctima.




“No venimos a rendir examen moral”, fue uno de los planteos de la querella. La acusación pidió mirar a Azul como una mujer que había atravesado discriminaciones durante décadas, que había conseguido construir una identidad, acceder a un trabajo y desarrollar una vida a pesar de esas dificultades. Y sostuvo que esa historia no es un dato secundario para comprender el caso.







Newen Kvyen




El cuerpo de Azul habla de un crimen de odio




La Fiscalía presentó ante el jurado una reconstrucción de la madrugada del 25 de septiembre de 2025. Según su hipótesis, Sánchez se contactó con Azul en la zona del bajo neuquino para un servicio sexual y ambos se trasladaron hasta la vivienda del acusado.




Allí, sostuvo la acusación, ocurrió el ataque. El fiscal jefe Agustín García anticipó que los médicos forenses explicarán las múltiples lesiones que presentaba el cuerpo de Azul, entre ellas heridas producidas con elementos contundentes y lesiones compatibles con un arma blanca, además de fracturas en distintas partes del cuerpo y lesiones defensivas.




La Fiscalía sostiene que esas evidencias permitirán demostrar un homicidio triplemente agravado. La querella agregó una lectura particular: planteó que determinadas zonas del cuerpo de Azul fueron especialmente atacadas y que esa violencia debe ser analizada en relación con su identidad de género.




“El cuerpo de una mujer trans habla por sí mismo”, sostuvo la acusación. Será el jurado popular el que, después de escuchar a los testigos, peritos y especialistas y analizar la evidencia producida durante las once jornadas previstas, deberá determinar qué ocurrió y cuál es la responsabilidad penal de Sánchez.




No fue solamente una marcha por una condena




La movilización del primer aniversario tuvo como consigna central el pedido de justicia, pero también puso en palabras algo que atravesó todo el juicio: el 

derecho de las personas trans a construir una vida sin que esa identidad se convierta en una condena anticipada

.




Cinco cuadras de personas marcharon desde el Centro de Atención a la Víctima hasta la Casa de Gobierno. Hubo trabajadores estatales, organizaciones feministas, agrupaciones LGBTIQ+, familiares, compañeras de Azul y activistas.







Una bandera multicolor de cinco metros recorrió las calles de Neuquén. También hubo una canción. “No es mi despedida”, de Gilda, la misma que había sonado durante el velatorio de Azul, fue cantada durante la movilización.




La marcha no solo recordó a una mujer asesinada. También puso en discusión las vidas que permanecen en riesgo antes de convertirse en una estadística.




En las calles apareció el reclamo por el trabajo, por el acceso a la vivienda, por la salud, por políticas para las infancias trans y contra los discursos de odio

.




Una madre de Plottier llegó a la movilización con un pañuelo blanco atravesado por los colores de la bandera trans y la frase: “Niñeces libres, juventudes felices y adultxs plenxs”. Su hijo había sufrido una agresión en la vía pública y la familia reclamaba medidas de protección, así como medidas contra el agresor, que según denuncian está libre.




El mensaje se conectaba con el de las organizaciones frente a Gobernación: la violencia contra las personas trans no comienza con un asesinato. Empieza mucho antes, cuando una niña es expulsada de una escuela, cuando una adolescente es insultada en la calle, cuando una persona no consigue trabajo por su identidad, cuando debe aceptar situaciones de violencia para sobrevivir o cuando el Estado no garantiza las condiciones para que pueda construir una vida autónoma.

author: Unknown
title: Spencer Beswick - Building the American Anarchist Movement
content:
Author

: Spencer Beswick

Title

: Building the American Anarchist Movement

Subtitle

: Radical Collectives and Continental Convergences in the 1980s

Date

: 2026

Notes

: Journal for the Study of Radicalism (2026) 20 (1): 29–51. https://doi.org/10.14321/jstudradi.20.1.0029 

Source

: Retrieved on October 4, 2026 from https://anarchistnews.org/content/building-american-anarchist-movement




 “Bowl a strike, not a spare—Revolution everywhere!” Members of the Revolutionary Anarchist Bowling League (RABL) chanted bowling-themed slogans as they marched against President Ronald Reagan's threat to invade Nicaragua in 1988. Acting within a broad progressive coalition, RABL helped shut down major sections of downtown Minneapolis for three days in an outpouring of rebellion against the Reagan administration's covert wars in Central America. Events reached a dramatic climax when a masked protester threw a bowling ball through the window of a military recruitment office.

[1]

 The crash of the broken glass marked the beginning of a new era of anarchist militancy in the United States. The rage of a generation of young people raised in Reagan's America threatened to explode. 




 Reflecting this mood, the pilot edition of what became the 

Love and Rage

 anarchist newspaper (published from 1990 to 1998) was simply called 

RAGE!

 The pilot, which was distributed at an action at the Pentagon in 1988, reflected growing anger at the Reagan administration's wars at home and abroad, including the war on drugs. Promised a “new morning in America,” a generation of disaffected young people raised in the alienation of the suburbs found themselves shut out of political life. Many of their parents lost their unionized factory jobs to neoliberal outsourcing or were kicked off welfare. They grappled with the reality of skyrocketing inequality, precarious jobs, and violent policing. The hopes of social democracy—not to mention the liberatory movements of the 1960s and 1970s—appeared dead, and mainstream society seemingly offered little worth saving. Meanwhile, Reagan crushed the dreams of a better world in Central America by funding and training Guatemalan death squads, Nicaraguan Contras, and violent Salvadoran elites. 




 But dissidents emerged out of the cracks of the new society. A rising generation of young people encountered anarchism in mosh pits at punk shows and in street fights against fascists and police. A core group of anarchists across the country began to build a continental revolutionary movement. This article explores how several key collectives—including the Revolutionary Anarchist Bowling League, the Revolutionary Socialist League, the Youth Greens, and the Vermont Family—revitalized US anarchist theory and practice in the 1980s. Together, they formed a pole around which the diffuse anarchist scene began to cohere into a movement capable of coordinating strategic action across the country. Activists coming from these diverse groups (and many more) would expand the anarchist milieu in the 1990s and shape the turn-of-the-century antiglobalization movement.

[2]

 Members of each group became involved with Love and Rage, an organization that used its widely distributed newspaper as a catalyst to build first an anarchist network and then a membership-based Revolutionary Anarchist Federation that shaped the movement's direction. But first, local anarchist groups needed to encounter each other, exchange ideas, and build connections across North America. 




 This encounter occurred in large part through a series of four continental convergences that took place from 1986 to 1989 in Chicago, Minneapolis, Toronto, and San Francisco. Very little has been written about these gatherings. Sociologist Lesley Wood posits that social movement theorists tend to ignore these kinds of convergences in part because the disciplinary norms of what counts as social movement activity reduce them to the level of cultural background to the “real” organizing.

[3]

 Beyond the gatherings, historians have written little about anarchism in the late twentieth century. Anarchist history typically focuses on earlier periods, and the burgeoning history of the United States in the late twentieth century has generally dealt much more with the rise of the Right than the evolution of anarchism and the Left.

[4]

 Yet it was in this period that anarchism was reborn as a major tendency on the American Left since marginalization in the early twentieth century.

[5]

 This article argues that the series of continental convergences in the late 1980s was crucial to the revitalization of North American anarchism as a revolutionary movement in the late twentieth century. In the pre-internet era, these gatherings provided essential spaces for anarchists from different backgrounds to encounter each other, engage in political debates, and take collective action in the streets. Through this process, anarchists transformed what had been a diffuse milieu characterized by small-group action and countercultural institutions into something approaching a coordinated continental movement. 




Convergence #1: Chicago “Haymarket Remembered” (1986)




 Chicago sparked global outrage in 1887 by executing several anarchists for alleged involvement in throwing dynamite at a labor rally for the eight-hour day in May 1886.

[6]

 These men became known as the Haymarket Martyrs, who are remembered around the world each year on May First, International Workers’ Day. A century later, in May of 1986, a range of progressive groups came together to organize a labor celebration in Chicago. The Haymarket Centennial Committee included liberals, socialists, communists, and union officials—but not anarchists. The latter feared that the martyrs would be shorn of their revolutionary anti-state politics and turned into toothless progressive labor forerunners. A small group simply called “Some Chicago Anarchists” thus decided to organize a competing anarchist remembrance of the Haymarket Affair.

author: Clare Hymer
title: Greens Pass ‘Zionism Is Racism’ Motion at Party Conference
content:
Green party members have voted to back a motion stating that Zionism is racism, making the Greens the first explicitly anti-Zionist mainstream political party in the UK.




The motion, which was heard at the party’s largest ever conference in Brighton and passed by 1,022 votes to 813, also called on the party to back a single, democratic Palestinian state, to demand freedom for Palestinian political prisoners, oppose the Palestine Action ban and affirm Palestinians’ right to resistance. 




An amendment to mitigate the risk that the motion could be used to target Jewish members affiliated with Zionist institutions was voted down. Supporters claim it wasn’t necessary, as the motion already separates Judaism from Zionism, and it will have no disciplinary impact as it is a political policy motion rather than one to do with internal party procedures.




Gully, a Green party member whose father is Palestinian and whose mother is an Israeli Jew, told Novara Media: “Zionism is racism. It is a racist ideology… Look back at history. Look at the thinking behind Zionism and tell me it is not an ethnonationalist project.




“Every time you confuse Zionism with Judaism, you increase the risk that people think being Jewish means you support the ethnic cleansing and genocide, the checkpoints and the humiliation that my father and millions of Palestinians are subject to everyday.”




The vote followed a conference weekend in which the motion was a controversial issue, with tensions running high.




On Saturday, dozens of pro-Israel demonstraters shouted at party members as they entered the conference centre. Chants included “There is no Palestine, there is no Palestine”, with some protesters holding signs reading “Anti Zionism = terrorism” and handing out leaflets claiming “The Green party is now the most racist party in Britain”.




Senior Green figures were split on the motion. While co-deputy leader Mothin Ali spoke in favour of it on Sunday, former leader Caroline Lucas spoke against, with co-deputy leader Rachel Millward telling Sky News it was “problematic” earlier in the weekend. 




Green leader Zack Polanski did not vote, as he was campaigning in Holborn and St Pancras, central London, where he is standing in a byelection on Thursday in the hope of becoming the party’s sixth MP.




Green party policy already describes Israeli conduct as apartheid and genocide, backs a full arms embargo, sanctions and an end to occupation and illegal settlements, as well as a ban on the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) as a terror group.




Motions voted for by members at conferences set the Green party’s long-term vision and policy platform. They do not determine election manifestos.

author: Taina Da Silva
title: Near Grassy Narrows, an Elder shows us how using the land also protects it
content:
Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s Land Back Garden on the outskirts of the Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva




I’m thinking about the power of my treaty rights as I drive to meet with Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich — Roberta Keesick — on a late summer day on the outskirts of Grassy Narrows.




Gwawich is an activist and trapper who has substantial experience of being on the land and creating land-based learning systems for our community. She grew up in our territory with a traditional Anishinaabek family, and she works to restore our traditional ways. 




As I pull into the site, Gwawich offers me some ripe vegetables — a squash, green beans and tomatoes — that she’s harvested from an extensive garden nearby. 




Gwawich and I are ten minutes outside of the reserve line of Grassy Narrows First Nation, a small and semi-remote community in northwestern Ontario. We sit at an off-grid campsite and community garden which Gwawich started by herself to host her Seven Grandfathers Teachings Program.




The Seven Grandfather Teachings — love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility, and wisdom — are what Gwawich’s social program follows, and she hopes her program will impact Grassy in a way that will bring us Anishinaabek back to the land and culture. 




“Colonization has changed our ways of thinking,” she says. 




A lake in the traditional homelands of Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva




As the lake glistens in the background, Gwawich talks about how she is determined to decolonize our community from decades of learned behaviour — stemming from the reserve system that relocated people in our community, to the residential “school” system and 

devastating mercury pollution

, which have all been an upheaval to our traditional ways.




Her campsite is available for any band members who want to get away from the reserve, and the garden is another free resource where members are often invited to pick fresh food.




“Land Back Garden” is painted on a wooden sign and it sits front-and-centre of the garden. Another sign near the campsite greets visitors to the “Seven Grandfather Teachings Program — Land Based Family Healing Initiative.”

This program is how families from Grassy are now able to access different opportunities designed to bring land based learning to the community, and it is what our aboriginal land title permits us to do in our territories. 




Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s program is helping Grassy Narrows members return to their traditional ways. Photo by Taina Da Silva




What started as a community-wide gardening initiative in 2020 has grown into the off-grid garden and campsite, a monthly food program in the community, and a small sewing building right in the reserve — all operating through outside funding.




Children from the reserve are able to experience what it might have been like for the older generations to gather traditionally, share food, and play games like the old days — and with some contemporary additions.




Today, there are community events with bungee trampolines, rock climbing, horse rides and even a zipline, Gwawich tells me with true pride. 




Gwawich speaks excitedly about a farmers’ market coming up, where she will be taking vegetables from the Land Back Garden to give away to Grassy families. 




She reminds me that “being out on the land makes our rights stronger,” and that running the site is a way to protect the land — and our rights under Treaty 3.




This is an area of land which I mistakenly used to associate as a settler hunting camp on so-called “Crown land,” before I learned about traditional land use areas and our history of ancient rock paintings, burial grounds and artifacts found across our territory. 




It takes community members like Gwawich to figure out ways to navigate the colonial systems that have been imposed on us, and decolonize our ways of thinking.




Gwawich remembers a time when the entirety of Grassy Narrows spoke our language and lived off trapping and fishing incomes when she was a child in the 1960s and 70s. 




“Even my siblings were helping with trapping and fishing when they were nine and ten years old,” she said, and we laughed at the idea of that happening now — because that is a lost tradition for Anishinaabek families.




Residential “schools” — an intentional violation of our human rights — and the resulting language and culture loss are not easily forgotten about in our communities. Repairing the losses and devastation is not a simple feat; however, colonization will never deter people like Gwawich who are challenging the idea of total culture loss. 




Grassy Narrows has a history of blockading our lands to stop logging, and finding our voice when it comes to 

holding people accountable

 for the mercury pollution that has harmed our community.




Ribbon ties near the garden. Photo taken and edited by Taina Da Silva




Treaty 3 guarantees our rights to hunt, trap and fish on our homelands. But those rights are often twisted — and this led to Gwawich getting charged by the Ministry of Natural Resources back in 2009 for building a small cabin on her trapline near Red Lake.




Red Lake is five hours away from Grassy, and Gwawich explains how it is part of our traditional homeland; however, since the 1970s there has been a shift in Grassy members using our territories. 




Trappers are often people who are simply following what the government allows them to do, but Gwawich is a trapper activist who understands that we have treaty rights before trapper rights when we are out there on the land. The Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) enforces a quota for trappers, but First Nations do not have these quotas if we choose to practice our treaty rights. 




Unfortunately, there are some settlers that seem to muddy the system and confuse land rights with trapping or “Crown” rights. 




A complaint was sent to the MNR about Gwawich’s off-reserve camp, but MNR realized it was Gwawich exercising her treaty rights which allows us to add shelters to our traditional territory — whether it is a trapline or not.




Obviously, our people have treaty rights. But in 2009 there was a legal dispute between the MNR and another Indigenous family in the province.




Gwawich’s case was eventually dropped when the other case won in court which proved First Nations peoples have the right to shelter and practice our rights. This made Gwawich truly realize how powerful our treaty rights are — and what it means for land protection and cultural revitalization. 




“We have the right to be out there and we should protect it,” says Gwawich.




“We don’t need permits to build our shelters.”




Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s Land Back Garden is a demonstration of our sovereignty to utilize our lands — as guaranteed under Treaty 3. Photo by Taina Da Silva




Our right to use the land goes beyond what a trappers’ license permits because we are from this land, and we have been here surviving as best as we can. 




“MNR doesn’t do anything because we are on our land,” Gwawich confirms. 




Indigenous futurism can look like a lot of things, and in this case it means there is an Elder kwe (woman) who uses her treaty rights to garden and provide land based activities for community members. 




More off-grid gardens are just one of the ideas that Gwawich wishes to pursue because it will mean our treaty rights are actively being accessed throughout our territory.




“Why not anywhere?” Gwawich asks, and we further discuss the idea of “culture back.”




Reintegrating food sovereignty through gardening seems like the most simple solution for culture back, but the act of using our land freely is what truly empowers our people. 




Adding more off-grid campsites or shelters would be another solution. Also, land based activities are part of Indigenous futurism and culture back, which Gwawich hopes to continue as an Elder who wants to revitalize our community.




Gwawich is confident that regrowing our identity will emerge through programs like hers, while finding ways to promote land and culture back. The old ways seem replaceable in a way that does not look like the past of our ancestors, and due to the displacement from our traditional ways there are loopholes we need to discover to bring back some of the old ways. 




Encouraging families to use the off-grid campsite and Land Back Garden will emulate what our ancestors were living like for hundreds of thousands of years.




Decolonizing can be as simple as taking a swim in our traditional waters, or eating food from the land. Photo by Taina Da Silva




Eating food from the land, swimming in the clear lake, and disconnecting from the online world are all small steps that us Anishinaabek can take to decolonize.




Talking to Gwawich about land rights brought out a refreshing sense of reality that treaty rights matter — outside the box of the Indian Act.

The Seven Grandfather Teachings Program plays a large role in repairing trauma within our community, and starting the process of decolonization.

Remembering what we lost through colonialism is crucial for us to understand how to cheat-code our way out of colonial ways of thinking. Trapping is one way Gwawich connects to the land, but after the charges against her were relinquished there was a spark in her to start using the land off-reserve and protect it. 




Gwawich wishes to continue to promote the idea of land back and culture back through gardening and off-grid camps where community members grow their love for using the land again.




The future is a daunting topic because sometimes it feels hopeless to talk about our rights as Anishinaabek, but this conversation with Gwawich has brought up feelings of inspiration as she continues land based initiatives of her own and supports the initiatives of community members. 




Her work has helped me to envision a future where everyone has some sort of off-reserve shelter in our territory, where we use the land similarly to the past, and continue community gatherings and events. 




Vegetables sprout in the Land Back Garden. Photo taken and edited by Taina Da Silva




Using our treaty rights rather than ignoring our right to use the land will help us to reject colonial systems that tell us we are wrong for being who we are, and rebuild a future where we are able to continue to use our traditional territories without harassment from colonial forces.




I look around the territory surrounding us — with dense pine forests, sprawling blue sky and tall rock faces. The occasional blue jay flies by, and a chipmunk runs through the garden.




As we wrap up our conversation, Gwawich returns to tend to the garden which made me stop and think about the simplicity of taking care of our land.




We take care of this Land Back Garden, and in return it takes care of us.

Near Grassy Narrows, an Elder shows us how using the land also protects it

 appeared first on

author: Mohammed Altaj
title: Israel Above the Law … Palestine Beyond Justice
content:
The world did not lack knowledge of what was happening to Palestinians.

It knew that a people had been living under occupation for decades; that land was being confiscated, settlements expanding, homes demolished, and checkpoints cutting cities and villages off from one another.

The United Nations knew. Governments knew. Parliaments and international courts knew.

The shift now visible across significant parts of Western public opinion did not begin because the world suddenly discovered new facts about Palestine.

What changed was the distance between the news and the human being.

People saw what war means when a child is trapped beneath rubble, what displacement means when a family carries whatever it can and walks away without knowing where it will go.

And the numbers began to acquire names, faces and voices.

One of those names was Hind Rajab.

I do not mention Hind because her story encompasses everything that happened in Gaza. I mention her because some tragedies become windows through which people see what numbers alone cannot reveal.

Hind was trapped inside a car in Gaza in January 2024 after members of her family had been killed. She called for help. Twelve days later, she was found dead inside the car. The two paramedics sent to rescue her were also found dead.

But Hind was no longer a number.

The world also saw seven World Central Kitchen aid workers killed in Israeli strikes while carrying out humanitarian work. And even after the ceasefire announced in October 2025, the killing did not end. According to Palestinian Ministry of Health figures cited by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, by September 23, 2026, 1,402 Palestinians had been killed and 4,881 injured since the ceasefire announcement.

Bodies remained beneath the rubble, while families waited to reach loved ones not to save them this time, but to bury them.

But Palestinian history did not begin in Gaza.

And it did not begin on October 7, 2023.

In 1994, Baruch Goldstein, an Israeli settler and member of the Kach movement, opened fire on Muslim worshippers in the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron, killing at least twenty-nine people. In 2014, sixteen-year-old Mohammed Abu Khdeir was abducted from Shuafat, beaten and burned alive. A year later, the Dawabsheh family home in Duma was set on fire while the family slept; toddler Ali and later both his parents died.

So when a Palestinian is asked to begin the story on the morning of October 7, he is effectively being asked to erase what came before.

None of this makes the targeting of civilians acceptable, whoever they are.

Justice cannot begin halfway through history.

By September 14, 2026, the United Nations had documented more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties, property damage, or both, across 275 Palestinian communities since the beginning of the year. More than 1,500 Palestinians had been displaced because of demolitions of structures lacking Israeli-issued permits, while more than 2,600 had been displaced in the context of settler violence and related access restrictions.

Between September 15 and 21 alone, the UN documented 51 settler attacks resulting in casualties, property damage, or both. At least 800 olive, fruit and palm trees were damaged, uprooted or burned. In the same week, demolitions displaced 147 Palestinians, including 73 children.

These are not isolated incidents.

This is land being transformed, communities disappearing, families being pushed out.

And this is where the phrase “extremist settlers” is no longer enough.

Who plans the settlements? Who allocates the land? Who builds the roads, extends the infrastructure and provides the protection?

At what point does settler violence cease to be merely the act of an individual and become a problem within the system itself?

In September 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that settlement expansion was accelerating, outposts were proliferating and settler violence was rising to alarming levels. He also warned that advancing the E1 settlement plan would deal a “deathblow” to the prospect of a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.

How, then, can the world continue to declare its support for a two-state solution while the geography on which one of those states is supposed to exist is being transformed?

The problem is not confined to land.

In Jerusalem, Christian clergy have repeatedly reported being spat at, insulted and harassed. In April 2026, a Catholic nun was violently assaulted in the Old City. A Jerusalem court later found that the defendant had committed the acts described in the indictment but acquitted him on grounds of mental illness and ordered his psychiatric hospitalization.

One incident cannot define an entire society.

But neither should repeated incidents of hostility be dismissed without asking what political and social currents allow intolerance to grow.

It is easy to say: the problem is Netanyahu. Or Ben-Gvir. Or Smotrich.

But what if the problem runs deeper?

In 2018, Israel enacted the Nation-State Law, a Basic Law declaring that the exercise of national self-determination in the State of Israel is exclusive to the Jewish people and that the state views Jewish settlement as a national value.

In the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index, 71.5 percent of Jewish respondents opposed the inclusion of Arab parties in the government.

My subject is not Judaism, nor Jews around the world. My subject is the Israeli system, its laws, its policies and the political currents that allow this reality to continue.

There are Israelis who oppose occupation, settlement and racism.

But the question is not whether dissent exists.

The question is: Which ideas become laws? And which laws become policy?

When extremism moves from the margins to parliament, from parliament into government, from government into law, and from law onto the land, we are no longer talking only about individuals.

We are facing a question about the system itself.

And here, too, Gaza changed something.

What once reached the world as scattered incidents is now seen every day on a screen people carry in their pockets. The effect can be measured in public opinion.

In a Pew Research Center survey conducted in spring 2026, unfavorable views of Israel stood at 79 percent in Australia, 78 percent in Spain and Sweden, 76 percent in the Netherlands, 75 percent in Italy, 73 percent in Germany, 65 percent in Canada and 60 percent in the United States.

Perhaps Gaza did not change the values of millions of people.

Perhaps it made them realize that the values they already believed in were not being applied equally.

I do not ask the West to love Palestine.

Nor do I ask it to hate Israel.

I ask it to apply the principles it says it believes in.

If taking land by force is unacceptable, let it be unacceptable here too. If self-determination is a right, do not make the Palestinian the exception.

On July 19, 2024, the International Court of Justice concluded that Israel’s continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory was unlawful, that it was obliged to bring that presence to an end as rapidly as possible, and that it must immediately cease all new settlement activity.

The Court also said that states must not recognize as legal the situation arising from that unlawful presence, nor render aid or assistance in maintaining it.

On September 18, 2024, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution by 124 votes to 14, with 43 abstentions, demanding that Israel end its unlawful presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory within twelve months.

The unlawful presence did not end.

More than two years after the Court’s opinion, international warnings have become more direct.

On September 22, 2026, as world leaders gathered in New York, the UN Secretary-General said that the conditions for an independent, democratic, contiguous, viable and sovereign Palestinian state were being “systematically erased.” He said support for two states must go beyond words and be reflected in policies, decisions and actions.

Two days later, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said that the steps taken by the international community were clearly not enough and called on states to apply real political pressure to prevent the entrenchment of Israel’s unlawful presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

The General Assembly’s high-level week has ended.

International warnings have grown sharper.

Yet the reality on the ground continues to move in the opposite direction.

So when do words become action?

Some states have taken measures against individual settlers and settlements. But if the settler alone is the problem, who built the settlement, planned it, allocated the land and protected it?

If the problem is institutional, an individual response is not enough.

I call for peaceful and lawful international pressure on the policies and institutions responsible for perpetuating occupation and settlement, and for political, diplomatic, economic and military relations to be reviewed if non-compliance with international law continues, in accordance with the law and the obligations of each state.

That is my political position. I do not attribute it to the International Court of Justice.

I am asking a different question:

If the law determines that a situation is unlawful, and that situation continues anyway, what is the value of law if defying it carries no consequences?

This is not a call for war. It is not a call to punish someone for being Israeli, nor to target a Jew for being Jewish.

It is a call to use peaceful and lawful means to end an unlawful reality.

Palestinians waited for negotiations, for a final-status agreement, for the state they were told would come.

And while they waited, settlements grew, the land changed, and communities were displaced.

How much longer can they be asked to wait while the land meant for a future solution is transformed beneath their feet?

That is why the title of this article is not a slogan:

Israel Above the Law… Palestine Beyond Justice.

The problem is not the absence of law.

It is the distance between a ruling and its enforcement, between a principle and its application, between condemnation and consequence.

I do not ask the West to become Palestinian.

I ask only that Palestinians not be made an exception to its humanity—or to its law.

That the life of Hind Rajab be treated as a human life.

That the life of Mohammed Abu Khdeir be treated as a human life.

That the life of Ali Dawabsheh be treated as a human life.

That the lives of the twenty-nine worshippers in the Ibrahimi Mosque be treated as human lives.

Because a justice that must first know the identity of the body before deciding its worth is not justice.

If occupation is unlawful, its continuation cannot be allowed to carry no consequences.

If human rights are universal, they cannot stop at the borders of Palestine.

And when the facts are clear, when the law is clear, and when the Court has spoken, the question becomes larger than Palestine and Israel:

Can any state remain above the law?

why does Palestine remain, to this day, beyond justice?

Mohammed Altaj is a Palestinian writer, researcher and political analyst, and the founder of The Witness Stone, an independent humanitarian initiative behind the global appeal “Let Gaza Bury Its Dead.” His writing focuses on Palestinian affairs, Gaza and the human consequences of conflict.

author: Novara Media
title: Trauma Farming: the New Politics of Public Suffering
content:
Are we in the era of trauma Top Trumps? ‘Lived Experience’ has become a byword for standpoint authority and progressive politics. It has allowed people from marginalised groups to speak and be heard, and forced us to confront how power plays out in interpersonal dynamics. But it has also become a way for people to brand themselves online, and excuse antisocial or even downright nasty behaviours. Has ‘lived experience’ helped the left, or turned us into self-obsessed therapy-speakers, incapable of communicating with the majority of people?




At the latest Downstream IRL, Ash Sarkar sat down with Catherine Liu – cultural theorist, professor and author of Virtue Hoarders – to discuss her new book, Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering. Liu argues that as class politics has declined, the language of psychology has stepped in to explain problems rooted in capitalism. But what happens when trauma becomes content and politics gives way to what Liu calls the ‘gentrification of pain’? Is ‘lived experience’ a prerequisite for legitimate political analysis? Why do movements so often end up policing each other rather than confronting power? And if politics becomes about who’s hurting most, who benefits?

author: Paul Buhle
title: The Communitarian Mind of Michael Albert
content:
Somewhere, in the complex and often confused history of anarchist and communitarian movements of the US, Michael Albert resides, now almost 80, a veteran of endless campaigns but still eager to make his familiar points. Communitarianism of some kind can work, can create a substitute for the miserable economic arrangements of the present, and engage ordinary people in the process of changing themselves as they endeavor to change the world.

This sentiment has a more than honorable history even in the US, historically known for its weak and fragile Left institutions. Its origins should properly be placed well before the rise of the Marxist-related movements, mostly German immigrants, during the 1860s-70s. Indeed, the communitarian experiments of the 1820s-40s engaged some of the great figures of the age, from Shakers to Bohemians, and even produced a remarkable literature, including Nathaniel Hawthorne’s rather satirical Blithedale Romance.

The ideas of dress reform (mainly for women), healthy foods, and even freer sexual relations flowed into Abolitionist and Women’s Rights movements. The Civil War swallowed a large chunk of utopianism, but enough survived to prompt a rebirth in successive generations. Edward Bellamy’s best-selling novel, Looking Backward , published in 1887, seemed, by example, to make small-scale cooperative living imaginable, even if colonies nearly always failed in their first (under-capitalization and too few agricultural skills counted heavily). Hope is ever-born or perhaps never really goes away. Skinny-dipping and open curricula for children’s education, known in the 1910s, also found their way into the hippie mini-societies of the 1960s-70s.

It would be hard to say how deeply anarchist and communitarian ideas penetrated the “Counter Culture”—a phrase so dated and imprecise that we now set it off— but the sentiment was sincere and deep. “Share the Land” by the Canadian group Guess Who still resonates on YouTube with a confidence of “Brothers and Sisters Who Care” sharing valuables in common. It just didn’t work out in life.

To his credit, Michael Albert never gave up. Student activist, antiwar protester, launched South End Press in Boston of the 1970s, and the avowedly anarchist/libertarian Z Magazine in 1989. Thereafter, Albert and various collaborators, notably Robin Hahnel, worked out theories of alternatives to the market economy along lines that Prince Peter Kropotkin surely would have approved. At what might be called a literary highpoint, he published Parecon: Life After Capitalism (2003), a book translated into a couple dozen languages. Albert took his message to the world. The specifics of the furious debates over whether his proposal would work in practical economic terms, are now long past and largely forgotten—but the debate inevitably goes on. Beneath the specifics could be found a deeper plan, a vision based more on ethics than practical details.

And here we are twenty-some years later. And, no doubt, with the enriching personal experience of establishing, through an extended Z Media Institute, a world of training for the next generations of media and grassroots activists, now emphatically including podcasters, including Michael and the Z folks.

The conceit of this fat volume is that the Revolution has been successful, as related by an aged activist and SDS veteran to an oral historian. Like the most rigorous of oral histories, it encompasses a life story or rather a number of life stories. These mostly lack—according to me, an experienced oral historian and director of a couple of oral history programs—the deep family and community background that is most useful. But it emphatically includes details of the process of participation and learning, from a couple dozen imagined participants of widely different backgrounds, through lives of many struggles.

A little backstory from my end is useful. Oral history, the practical use of oral history, fell upon me in the 1970s as I realized that the vital living memories of the 1920s-40s Left—what they believed and what they did, far from the centers of Leftwing national leadership—were slipping away fast. The field had emerged around this time, more activist than academic, with some thousands of activists. Amongst these, the Oral History of the American Left archive (NYU), my veritable brain-child. And later more oral history on Rhode Island working people; still later teaching oral history for a decade at Brown.

I mention these personal details because, in my own experience as a field worker, administrator and teacher, oral history is valuable especially as a probing of personal life, that is to say personal life from childhood (usually also family and setting). That is: how the child grows into man or woman, developing beliefs and behaviors that often last a lifetime.

Not that there is one standard by which all oral histories can or should be judged. Michael Albert’s gambit is to construct oral histories out of his imagination, at dates largely in the future. His oral history interviewees, some of them participants in SDS a lifetime ago, seem less than likely to have childhoods or family memories useful to them. Mostly younger folks, their experiences began, logically, with 2015-16, the Bernie Campaign, or a little earlier, in Occupy.

None of them appeared to have experienced the hyper-intense working-class movement parallel to Occupy, that is the Wisconsin Uprising (2011-13). That the experience tested the capacity of perhaps a half-million participants, notably women unionists in teaching and care professions, would have been useful, even in drastic failure, thanks in no part to the unwillingness of leading Democrats or labor officials outside the state to lend a hand.

But perhaps I have exaggerated the difficulties of oral history because the speakers in The Wind Cries Freedom experience so much in their own lives from about 2010 onward. Some are inevitably more compelling than others. The personal conversion to RPS or Revolutionary Participatory Society has more than a little in common with other “conversion” experiences, but in a good way. As one participant makes clear—but is present in the thoughts of others—“We don’t just need smart policy proposals—we had those. What we needed was to share those proposals with each other across our movements.” (p.51)

The central and driving idea is that excitement and engagement in different struggles—say, for affordable housing in US cities and against the ongoing slaughter in Gaza—should or could prompt something more coherent. That coherence, in turn, could lead to a conversation and a movement around a different kind of society. The devilish details would follow

I wish to be persuaded by this line of argument because, after all, “participatory” brings back theorganic 1960s notion of “participtory democracy.” The famous two-word phrase got lost amidst the violence (99% by the government) and confusion (that we all shared).

The reader of this book can decide best, looking through it, what appeals, what makes sense, and how it may be used.

author: Mahdi Niksefat Motlagh
title: Ending the war requires accepting Iran in the Middle East
content:
The hardest question about ending the war with Iran belongs in Washington. What place can Iran occupy after the fighting stops? A country left economically excluded, unable to rebuild and exposed to renewed attack has little reason to regard a ceasefire as a durable ending. The war cannot be politically settled while Iranian recovery remains an unacceptable outcome.

The latest diplomacy leaves that question unresolved. Tehran has received US feedback, through Qatar, on a seven-day trust-building proposal. Yet on 1 October, the US Treasury expanded sanctions against Iran’s automotive and rail sectors, alongside manufacturing and steel networks. Talks about ending the confrontation are proceeding alongside measures that further restrict Iran’s capacity to sustain its economy.

The Islamic Republic connects these claims to a revolutionary and religious account of its purpose. Ali Khamenei’s 2019 Second Phase statement, with its emphasis on building an Islamic civilisation, expressed that connection explicitly. Security, within this understanding, includes the capacity to continue a political project.

Israel also brings historical and theological claims to its modern statehood. Netanyahu has described it as the Middle East’s sole true democracy. In his September UN address, he invoked the Jewish people’s three-thousand-year history and biblical attachment to the land while anticipating the Iranian government’s fall.

Different understandings of statehood do not make war inevitable. The contradiction arises when Israeli security is defined through the dismantling of Iran’s capacity to remain an independent regional power. Under that definition, even Iranian reconstruction can appear threatening because recovery restores the resources through which Iran can act. Iran’s continued existence and Israel’s preferred regional order then become politically incompatible.

This gives the war its ontological dimension. For Iran, survival involves retaining the ability to decide its future and sustain its place in the region. For Netanyahu’s government, an Iran capable of recovering may signify the return of an existential threat. Military operations can damage Iranian capabilities. They cannot resolve this dispute over what Iran is allowed to become after the bombing.

The June 2025 war and the present confrontation make a distinction between surviving an attack and securing a durable ending especially consequential.

Its strategic implication is nevertheless clear: economic recovery itself can become a reason to preserve pressure.

A settlement built on permanent Iranian weakness would therefore contain the grounds for renewed confrontation. Iran needs the capacity to rebuild. An Israeli government that treats this capacity as intolerable would retain an incentive to obstruct it. More accurate weapons or more sophisticated surveillance cannot reconcile these positions.

Washington must confront that contradiction because the costs of the war reach beyond Israel’s objectives. Energy markets, shipping through Hormuz and the security of American partners make indefinite confrontation costly. An American exit requires persuading Israel to accept the survival of an independent Iran with an economic future in the region. It also requires Washington to accept that outcome itself.

Trump’s interview with TIME, published on 1 October, exposes the difficulty. Explaining why he had continued the campaign, he said he did not want Iran to return “in some different form”. An ending that depends on preventing Iranian reconstitution keeps the political purpose of the war open even after military objectives are declared achieved.

The tension also appears in the 2025 US National Security Strategy. It advocates accepting Middle Eastern countries’ historical forms of government while prioritising Israel’s security and the expansion of the Abraham Accords. The practical question is whether such acceptance extends to Iran, or whether Iran must remain the exception against which the region’s political and economic integration is organised.

Other regional states have a decisive role here. Their political acceptance of Iran need not involve adopting its institutions or sharing its revolutionary commitments. It means recognising that Iran’s historical and political form has a legitimate place alongside their own. Regional stability requires room for different states to pursue development without making one state’s permanent exclusion the condition of another’s security.

The 2023 Saudi-Iranian agreement offers a limited precedent. Brokered by China, it connected restored diplomatic relations to sovereignty and non-interference, and reaffirmed earlier economic cooperation commitments. It did not dissolve rivalry. It demonstrated that accommodation could begin by recognising the existing states as counterparts, without requiring either to abandon its political identity.

For an ending to endure, that recognition needs practical expression in trade, financial access and regional projects. Neighbouring governments can make Iranian reconstruction part of their own vision of regional development. This would give political acceptance consequences that diplomatic declarations alone cannot provide.

author: Abe Walker
title: The Battle for the Soul of the UAW: Union Democracy and the Seductions of Power
content:
After years of struggling in relative obscurity, democratic socialists were jubilant to have elected one of their own to high-profile office. With bold rhetoric and meme-friendly soundbites, their candidate captured the hearts and minds of a working-class base eager for an alternative to the establishment’s caustic brand of demagoguery. Ignoring calls for moderation, the campaign took on a defiant, openly confrontational tone. Its outcome shocked the old guard, upended the status quo, and served as a warning to entrenched interests everywhere.

The year was 2023, and Shawn Fain had just won the presidency of the United Auto Workers union. Fain quickly became the public face of a resurgent workers movement that seemed poised to usher in a new wave of labor militancy. But there would be little time for celebration once the weight of the task ahead set in. Indeed – like a certain big city mayor – Fain would quickly discover that his election fight was only a preview of the battles to come.

Fain is now standing for reelection, with ballots set to be tallied next month. Three years ago, few could imagine that Fain would face a viable challenger as he eyed a second term. Yet today, his star has long since dimmed, and his fate now hangs in balance. The upcoming vote will serve as a referendum on his tenure, and while he remains the clear favorite, there is considerably less enthusiasm behind his current bid.

Fain’s dramatic rise and fall can only be understood in the context of the reform movement that propelled him to power. Fain traces his lineage to a long history of rank-and-file agitators who challenged the 74-year reign of the incumbent Administration Caucus from below. In the 1960s, the Revolutionary Union Movement organized Black militants to combat the union’s complicity in de facto factory segregation. In the 1980s, the New Directions caucus fought against the introduction of lean production and concessionary bargaining. These efforts scored some victories in local elections, but the possibility of taking power on a grand stage remained elusive. The established powers proved remarkably resilient, using their vast patronage network to absorb dissidents and marginalize challengers. Dissent was managed, co-opted, or crushed.

Meanwhile, union leaders embraced “jointness” and labor-management cooperation, seeking to align workers’ interests with corporate competitiveness. A series of concessions in the 2000s culminated in two-tier contracts that subjected new hires to substandard wages and reduced benefits, creating artificial hierarchies that fractured shop-floor solidarity. Givebacks at Detroit automakers were compounded by organizing challenges in the South, where the union failed to make inroads at the German and Japanese plants that were overtaking the sector. As membership plummeted, union officials oversaw a managed decline, presiding over plant closures and outsourcing. Insulated from rank-and-file agitation and accountable to no one, it was a short step from sweetheart deals and graft to outright corruption. The breaking point arrived in the late 2010s with the exposure of a scandal involving the misuse of union funds for personal expenses, and officials accepting bribes from the very auto executives they were supposed to bargain against. Two former presidents were sent to prison, and a federal monitor was appointed to oversee the union’s operations under a consent decree. But this legitimacy crisis came with a silver lining, shattering the old guard’s aura of invincibility and creating an opening for change.

Amidst the wreckage, a coalition of frustrated auto workers founded Unite All Workers for Democracy (UAWD). Drawing tactical inspiration and support from broader labor-left networks, including Labor Notes and the Democratic Socialists of America, UAWD presented democracy as an antidote to corruption. Through painstaking grassroots organizing (and an assist from the federal Monitor), UAWD successfully forced a referendum on direct elections in 2021, which passed with 63% of the vote.

After breaking the old guard’s monopoly on power, candidates had to tailor their messaging to appeal directly to the militant rank-and-file base. Shawn Fain ran on the strength of his populist, class-conscious rhetoric. He framed the election as an existential battle between the working class and the billionaire owners, while promising an end to concessionary bargaining and cozy labor-management partnerships.

Following a close run-off, Fain took the presidency, and UAWD also captured the Executive Board, winning all 6 of the seats it had contested (plus a UAWD-aligned independent). Before caucus supporters had time to catch their breath, its long-shot candidates were running the union. Fain immediately set about implementing his vision. Within months of his victory, he was leading workers in a historic strike against the Big Three that paralyzed the industry. Abandoning the union’s decades-old tradition of pattern bargaining, Fain’s Stand Up Strike kept the Big Three automakers perpetually off-balance with a targeted, escalating strategy. The resulting contracts yielded significant wage gains, eliminated lower-wage tiers, and granted the right to strike over plant closures. Fain started showing up everywhere, from the cover of MotorTrend to a featured spot at the Democratic National Convention – and was even briefly floated as a vice-presidential candidate.

But even as Fain reveled in his newfound celebrity, the union’s culture had begun to change in deeper ways. In a sign of democratic vibrancy, members were quick to note when the administration failed to deliver. Indeed, following the Stand-Up strike, several important plants rejected the contract, and it passed by a razor-thin, 56% margin at GM. Encouraged by the strike, newly emboldened workers at Mack Truck turned down a tentative contract agreement, vowing to fight for a better deal. By trumpeting democracy, Fain had inflated expectations and unleashed a movement that now exceeded his control. Having tasted real power, members were no longer content to settle for compromise.

Immediately on the heels of the strike, Fain announced “Stand-Up 2.0”: a national campaign to organize multiple non-union auto plants across the country, including Japanese and European transplants as well as non-union electric-vehicle makers like Tesla and Rivian. Fain’s chief of staff, Chris Brooks, had championed a mass organizing strategy rooted in high-profile actions. If the UAW could seize the momentum from the Stand-Up strike, he argued, it would produce a domino effect, rippling across job sites and jumpstarting a series of organizing drives in rapid succession. By organizing multiple employers simultaneously and linking their demands to the Big Three master agreement, the union aimed to take wages out of competition.

At first, the strategy seemed to work. Momentum from the strike carried into April 2024, when workers at Volkswagen’s assembly plant in Chattanooga, Tennessee, overwhelmingly voted to join the UAW, marking the first time a Southern transplant had been unionized via an NLRB election since the 1940s. Though UAWD had no organized presence in Chattanooga, workers consistently cited its influence as a source of inspiration and an indication of the union’s forward trajectory. The UAW seemed unstoppable, and expectations were high that the union fever would continue to spread.

But this was to be the high-water mark of Fain’s power. A subsequent organizing drive at Mercedes-Benz in Alabama ended in a humiliating defeat (albeit against stiffer odds). The UAW later won a narrow election at BlueOval SK – only for the company to announce the facility’s closure and the termination of all 1,600 employees amid soft demand for EVs. Even at Volkswagen, winning the election was to be merely the preamble to a brutal, 500-day war of attrition at the bargaining table, during which management deployed classic delay tactics, stalling negotiations in a calculated effort to demoralize the newly minted members.

These organizing challenges mirrored problems within Fain’s own administration. With its handpicked candidate now in the seat of power, UAWD was forced to navigate the inherent tension between the anti-establishment passions that fueled its rise and the solemn responsibility of managing a massive institution. Long consigned to outsider status, union reformers struggled to adapt to their new role. The surface-level consensus that had united the caucus against the corruption masked deep ideological and demographic fissures. The breaking point centered on the issue of Palestinian liberation and the war in Gaza. A militant faction pushed UAWD to pass resolutions demanding that the UAW divest its assets from Israeli bonds. Moderates viewed these demands as “ultra-left” distractions that paralyzed the caucus in insular debates, alienated the manufacturing base, and derailed the practical work of building union power. Meetings devolved into an endless stream of performative parliamentary debates focused on ideological purity and caucus discipline. The internal culture became toxic, recruitment plummeted, and the UAWD’s core manufacturing base began to disengage. By late 2025, the caucus could no longer function effectively, and UAWD split under the weight of deep ideological divisions. A majority of the steering committee voted to formally dissolve the caucus and to launch a new organization, UAW Member Action, even as a minority faction vowed to continue operating under the UAWD banner despite losing access to the group’s digital infrastructure. When the dust settled, the reform movement was a shadow of its former self. The reconstituted UAWD had an explicit class-struggle orientation, but found itself relegated to the fringes. The larger Member Action tendency had broader support but effectively pledged its loyalty to the administration, ceasing to be a truly independent force.

This split coincided with a series of moves by Fain to consolidate his power and fortify his position ahead of the 2026 reelection cycle. Fain formed a “United UAW Slate,” which critics viewed as a vehicle to mute the rank-and-file and insulate the leadership from accountability. Compounding the crisis, the Fain administration refused to release the official minutes of International Executive Board meetings throughout his tenure. But the most glaring sign of institutional creep emerged from a bombshell report issued in February 2026 by Neil Barofsky, the court-appointed federal Monitor overseeing the UAW. In early 2024, the IEB had voted to strip Secretary-Treasurer Margaret Mock of her primary responsibilities, citing financial improprieties. Mock immediately alleged retaliation, prompting Barofsky to investigate. The Monitor’s report charged that Fain’s Chief of Staff, Chris Brooks, and Communications Director, Jonah Furman, had conspired to oust Mock for insisting on enforcing financial safeguards. Fain countered that the Monitor had been motivated by animus over Fain’s condemnation of the war on Gaza and early support for a ceasefire—a position championed by UAWD. The fallout was swift and humiliating for the reform administration: Furman was demoted and suspended, Brooks was forced to resign, and the union was ordered to reinstate Mock.

Accusations and recriminations abound, but Fain’s lack of transparency has only given his opponents more ammunition. To critics, it appears as though the Fain administration has adopted the same mechanisms of opacity and retaliation it once condemned. While the details are still being sorted out, the irony is profound: the very federal Monitor who had paved the way for Fain’s rise to power now threatens his legitimacy, highlighting the risks of government meddling in union affairs.

Desperate for a win to break the cycle of negative press, in February 2026 the UAW presented Volkswagen’s tentative agreement to its members. The union had rejected a strikingly similar deal just months earlier, even calling a strike authorization vote to increase pressure on the firm. But workers were eager to consummate their election victory, and 500+ days of negotiations were beginning to test their patience. They ratified the contract by an overwhelming 96% margin.

A close analysis of the contract reveals both how much has been achieved and how much ground is left to cover. Under the terms of the deal, workers received a 20% wage increase over the four-year contract – a significant boost but still below the 24% increase achieved by Detroit automakers. Job security and layoff protections were mixed. Volkswagen committed not to close or liquidate the plant during the contract term, but allowed itself an escape clause for ”impossible conditions.” Scheduling PTO and dependent-care issues were another major priority, but again, the contract fell short. Healthcare costs failed to match the Big Three’s coveted no-premium, no-deductible plans–though premiums and deductibles dropped significantly. Whatever its achievements, the contract did not achieve full parity with the Big Three, diminishing but not ending the regional differential that has long served as a check on workers’ aspirations.

But perhaps the biggest disappointment was the contract’s expiration date. The union had wanted the contract to expire in May 2028 to align with the Big Three. Synchronization would enable coordinated action, up to and including an industry-wide strike, and help the union fulfill its promise to equalize wages and working conditions across the sector. But Volkswagen balked at this demand and agreed only to a 2030 expiration date, postponing the fight for full parity for at least another four years.

On the international front, Fain and company have seemingly retreated from the bold calls for cross-border solidarity that marked his administration’s early days. Fain surprised even his apologists by declaring he was “ready to work with Trump” just weeks after calling him a “scab,” and then offering a full-throated defense of Trump’s tariff regime. UAW members know the dangers of economic nationalism all too well, making Fain’s eager embrace of protectionist trade policy unsettling, to say the least.

How might the reform movement be assessed three years into Fain’s presidency? UAWD can take credit for setting in motion the chain of events that led to the first contract with a foreign automaker. UAWD-backed leaders achieved in a single year what the previous regime had failed to do over multiple decades. Still, when translating the bluster and swagger of campaign talking points into the unforgiving calculus of annual budgets and payroll ledgers, some degree of disappointment is perhaps inevitable. Operating in a climate of austerity while facing off against some of the world’s largest and wealthiest firms necessitates a certain pragmatism. Even the most naïve political operative knows better than to take campaign promises at face value. But the distance that remains between Volkswagen’s contract and that of the Big Three — and indeed, the gap between Fain’s boldest proclamations and his track record — suggests that democratic proceduralism must be accompanied by an unrelenting insistence on accountability. A vibrant reform movement is necessary to backstop the administration’s inevitable drift toward compromise.

The Fain administration’s efforts to consolidate its hold on power reveal the difficulty of sustaining a cohesive vision once the immediate enemy has been vanquished. Fain now finds himself grappling with the same oligarchic tendencies he was elected to eradicate. But those who accuse Fain and company of betrayal might be reminded that union democracy cannot rely on the benevolent intentions of elected leaders. Power, by its very nature, seeks to insulate itself from the chaotic demands of the rank-and-file. Will the rebel caucuses continue to assert their autonomy, or will they be crushed in the name of a unity that erases difference, like so many Kronstadt sailors? It remains to be seen whether the loyalist Members Action tendency or the reconstituted UAWD will prove capable of holding Fain and company accountable. UAWD 2.0 has drawn some support – even achieving its long-awaited goal of Israeli divestment at the recent convention – but the defections were costly, and there are already signs that remnants of the old guard are mounting a comeback.

As labor historians have long noted, few rank-and-file caucuses survive the transition from the streets to the boardroom. History shows that insurgent groups often cannibalize themselves once their leaders take office, leaving the rank-and-file without an independent vehicle for accountability. To Fain’s harshest critics, the incumbent administration now exhibits the very bureaucratic behaviors it was elected to dismantle. Yet ultimately, the future of the UAW does not rest on the shoulders of Shawn Fain, nor will it be secured by the opaque maneuverings of the International Executive Board in Solidarity House. It depends instead on continued pressure from an independent rank-and-file that forces the bureaucracy to perform.

Democracy is an inherently destabilizing, agonistic process. It requires a permanent state of tension: a mobilized, educated membership that unrelentingly demands transparency, contests elections, and resists the seductions of power.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: A general demobilisation
content:
“The Worker” by Vladimir Serov, 1964







In 1932, Ernst Jünger published 

Der Arbeiter

 [

The Worker

], a work in which this new figure of humanity pointed to the new world order. The centrality of work corresponds to the dominance of technology. Expanding on concepts he had expressed in his book of two years prior, 

Total Mobilization

, Jünger writes: “Technology is the way in which the worker form mobilises the world.” This diagnosis, which revisited Marx’s analyses from an entirely different perspective, exerted considerable influence on both the right and the left of the political spectrum.




It is therefore all the more surprising that this decisive figure of the era has disappeared for some decades now. Technology continues to govern the world and has certainly increased its power everywhere, but it is no longer “the way in which the worker form mobilises the world.” On the contrary, in the form of artificial intelligence, it seems to imply rather the decline of the centrality of work that Jünger had in mind. Instead of the servitude linked to exploitation and mobilisation, technology, by progressively blurring the identities of social classes and estates, seems today to be heading towards an unprecedented form of subjugation through a kind of general demobilisation.




Quodlibet

, 01/10/2026

title: Συνέντευξη Τύπου για την Απεργία Πείνας του Πολιτικού Πρόσφυγα Soner İnanç
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης: 

Συνέντευξη Τύπου για την Απεργία Πείνας του Πολιτικού Πρόσφυγα Soner İnanç




Η συνέντευξη Τύπου καλείται από τη συνέλευση 

Solidarity with Migrants

.










Η συνέντευξη Τύπου θα μεταδοθεί ζωντανά:







YouTube




PeerTube




Facebook
















Ο Soner İnanç, πολιτικός αγωνιστής για τα εργατικά δικαιώματα και τις δημοκρατικές ελευθερίες, είναι από τις 27 Αυγούστου σε απεργία πείνας σε καθεστώς κράτησης, ενώ 

κινδυνεύει με άμεση απέλαση

 λόγω της ενδεχόμενης απόρριψης της αίτησής του για άσυλο.




O πολιτικός πρόσφυγας Soner İnanç αναγκάστηκε να εγκαταλείψει την Τουρκία καθώς έχει στοχοποιηθεί για τη δράση του από το τουρκικό κράτος και ήδη έχει φυλακιστεί στο παρελθόν για τη συμμετοχή του στο κίνημα του Gezi Park.




Μετά την απορριπτική απόφαση ως προς το αρχικό αίτημα ασύλου του, Soner İnanç κατέθεσε αίτημα ακύρωσης και ακολούθησε όλες τις σχετικές διαδικασίες. Τέλη Ιουλίου, συνελήφθη και βρέθηκε σε διοικητική κράτησης στο ΑΤ Λαυρίου.




Ένα μήνα μετά, μεταφέρθηκε στη Θεσσαλονίκη με σκοπό την απέλαση του. Μετά από τέσσερις εβδομάδες στέρησης βιταμινών, αναγκαίων για την μη ύπαρξη μόνιμων επιπτώσεων, το αίτημα αυτό άρχισε να καλύπτεται όπως όφειλε εξαρχής μετά από συνεχή πολιτική κινητοποίηση και δημοσιογραφική κάλυψη για τον κίνδυνο τον οποίο διατρέχει αν δεν του χορηγηθούν. 




Το ΠΡΟΚΕΚΑ Παρανεστίου οφείλει, παράλληλα, ως απεργός πείνας, ο Soner İnanç να παρακολουθείται από ανεξάρτητη ιατρική επιτροπή για να διασφαλιστεί η απρόσκοπτη άσκηση της ως πολιτική δράση με συγκεκριμένα αιτήματα: τη συνέχιση της διαδικασίας απόδοση ασύλου, την μη απέλαση του στην Τουρκία και την απελευθέρωσή του. 




Ο Soner δηλώνει αποφασισμένος να συνεχίσει στον αγώνα του, αφού κρατείται άδικα, περιμένοντας νέα απόφαση για το άσυλό του.




Ως 

Solidarity with Migrants

, γνωρίσαμε τον Soner στο στρατόπεδο προσφύγων Οινοφύτων όπου πάντα προσπαθούσε με όλα τα δυνατά μέσα να υποστηρίζει τα δικαιώματα όλων των προσφύγων με μια βαθιά διεθνιστική προσήλωση. Η “λογική” των αποφάσεων της υπηρεσίας ασύλου καταδεικνύει τις συνέπειες των μεγάλων αλλαγών που έχουν επέλθει στο καθεστώς ασύλου τα τελευταία έτη καθώς έχουμε να κάνουμε με την καταστρατήγηση της έννοιας του πολιτικού ασύλου.




Γι’αυτό και ο αγώνας του Soner είναι και αγώνας για το πολιτικό άσυλο γενικότερα και χρειάζεται τη στήριξη όλων μας.
