author: Jesse Hagopian
title: Authoritarianism Leads Teachers to Self-Censor. Solidarity Lets Us Teach Truth.
content:
A Zinn Education Project survey reveals how collective struggle helps educators resist political intimidation.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Sixth-grade history teacher Sarah Inama was told by administrators in Idaho’s West Ada School District to remove a poster from her classroom that carried a simple but profound message: “Everyone Is Welcome Here.” Beneath the words were hands of many different skin tones.

Although upset about the directive, Inama initially complied. But the decision weighed on her. She began asking herself what message removing the poster would send to her students. She ultimately defied the order and put it back up. Her fight over a poster might seem like an isolated local dispute — the kind of conflict easily dismissed as the actions of one administrator or one conservative district. But it isn’t. It is part of a national struggle over what truths teachers are allowed to communicate to their students — on the walls, in the curriculum, and in the messages students receive about who belongs.

Over the past year, the Zinn Education Project’s (ZEP) Freedom to Teach and Learn Surveys asked classroom teachers, librarians, administrators, teacher educators, and other school staff how anti-history laws, executive orders, funding threats, and the broader political climate were affecting what they taught, what students experienced, and whether their schools and districts were defending the freedom to teach and learn. We collected responses from 610 educators in 43 states and Washington, D.C.

Their testimony reveals something larger — and harder to measure — than the books formally banned, lessons explicitly prohibited, or teachers publicly punished: the chilling effect of those attacks on classrooms across the country. Some educators gave us permission to use their names. Others, in this climate of heightened attacks on teachers, understandably asked to remain anonymous.

Our findings reinforce the findings of a nationwide 2024 RAND study examining how state restrictions and the broader political environment shape teachers’ willingness to address social and political topics in their classrooms. The ZEP survey shows that this chilling effect has not subsided and provides a clear picture of how it is shaping classrooms today. Teachers told us what fear was pushing out of their classrooms: discussions of systemic racism, gender and sexuality, LGBTQIA+ history, Palestine, immigration, U.S. imperialism, and movements for social justice. They described dropping books from their syllabus, softening lessons, avoiding discussions, and second-guessing whether teaching honestly might provoke retaliation or threaten their jobs.

The ZEP survey demonstrates how the government does not have to formally censor every classroom if it can frighten teachers into censoring themselves. That’s exactly how anti-history laws banning honest education — what I call truthcrime laws — work: They teach educators to anticipate punishment and students to mistake submission for education.

The nation has seen this before. During the McCarthy era, educators were a primary target of anticommunist loyalty investigations and blacklists, and political repression helped establish boundaries around what teachers and professors could safely say and teach.

Today, the same politics of intimidation is being organized from the highest levels of government. While Inama taught that everyone is welcome here, Trump is using federal power to advance an authoritarian, white supremacist vision of education — one that declares that people of color, LGBTQIA+ people, immigrants, Muslims, and other marginalized communities are not welcome here. A January 2025 executive order, “Ending Radical Indoctrination in K–12 Schooling,” directed agencies to eliminate federal funding for schools that support teaching the administration labels “gender ideology” or “discriminatory equity ideology” — effectively threatening to defund schools that defy its restrictions on curriculum. Since then, the administration has formally scrapped Title IX rules that expanded protections for LGBTQIA+ students, dismantled major parts of federal civil rights enforcement and racial-harassment oversight in schools, and pursued an immigration crackdown that has left children and families fearful about going to school.

Our survey shows what can help turn fear into resistance: solidarity.

The message from the Trump administration is clear: Students are to be taught sanitized U.S. history stripped of systemic racism, gender oppression, and the movements that have fought for social justice.

The stories educators shared with us show how that message travels from executive orders, state laws, school board fights, and highly publicized punishments into everyday decisions about what happens — and what no longer happens — inside a classroom.

One of the clearest findings from our survey is that censorship often works without anyone issuing a direct order.

Amanda Simpson, a high school social studies teacher in Arkansas, described how this happens:

I have found myself second-guessing lesson plans and removing materials that might be considered “controversial,” not because they are inaccurate, but because I fear professional repercussions or backlash from parents and community members.

A veteran government teacher in Fountain Valley, California, told ZEP how far that fear can reach:

I teach government, and I feel as if I have to bite my tongue teaching about the executive orders being presented and state laws enacted.

After more than 20 years in the classroom, the teacher said there had never before been such hesitation about questioning government policy. Now, they worry “that some students may take my comments and report to their parents or some authority.”

The fear this teacher had was not that the topic falls outside the curriculum, but that the curriculum itself was a liability. An American Government teacher was beginning to feel professionally at risk for teaching directly about executive orders and state laws.

Abby Lanfear, a middle school teacher in Vermont, described a version of the same retreat.

Teachers are quietly choosing less “controversial” books to teach with because they don’t want to deal with any potential pushback.

The teacher explained that the result is a less diverse curriculum, “silencing the voices and representation of a broad swath of the human experience.”

Taken together, these responses reveal a profound shift in how teachers are being forced to think about their work.

There are a lot of questions teachers should be asking: Is this historically accurate? Will this help my students understand the world and make it better? Whose perspectives have been excluded? What questions will this lesson help young people ask?

Instead, fear increasingly forces educators to ask a different set of questions: Will someone accuse me of corrupting young minds for simply teaching my subject? Will a clip of my lesson be posted online? Will I be doxed? Could I be investigated? Will my principal defend me? Could I lose my job?

This is how the chilling effect transforms education without leaving behind an official censorship order. A teacher does not have to be told, You may not teach this. They learn to anticipate what might trigger a complaint, an investigation, or a threat to their livelihood — and adjust before anyone has to command them.

There is no list somewhere recording the books quietly dropped from classrooms. No school board necessarily voted to remove them. They simply disappear.

That is why counting formal book bans and censorship laws, although important, cannot tell us the full story of this political moment.

How do you count a book that was never assigned? How do you tally a lesson that was never taught? How do you record a question a student never had the opportunity to ask?

The chilling effect is not accidental. In many communities, it is the product of an organized backlash. National right-wing groups such as Moms for Liberty, Defending Education, Citizens Defending Freedom, No Left Turn in Education, and Turning Point USA — backed by wealthy donors and billionaire-linked foundations — have worked alongside MAGA politicians to turn complaints about race, gender, books, and curriculum into coordinated campaigns against educators and schools.

A Missouri educator told us their district has spent the past year battling pressure from the federal Department of Education and Department of Justice. The teacher said the conflict intensified this summer after “contentious, unfounded allegations” from a church they described as supported by Turning Point USA. The educator described a broader backslide in the district’s equity efforts over the past year and a half: Its DEI work was dismantled and a school board equity policy was removed from the district website. Meanwhile, the educator said, the Department of Education and Department of Justice are pursuing a lawsuit accusing district staff of “disregarding parents’ rights” and helping to “hide/transition” transgender students.

“We are working on a way forward,” the educator wrote, “but things are very uncertain right now.”

It would be wrong to imagine that these attacks on honest education are only happening in states with notorious anti-history laws, like Florida or Texas. The survey suggests otherwise.

One California high school social studies teacher wrote, “My students and I felt smugly impervious since we live in California, but that smugness is disappearing.”

The same educator described undocumented students becoming afraid to go on field trips or draw attention to themselves and transgender students saying, “Well, I guess we don’t exist anymore.”

Even in states with legal protections for teachers, local politics can make classrooms precarious. A middle school social studies teacher in Illinois wrote:

While I am in a “blue state,” I am in a very conservative part of the state. The laws protect me, but I have had parents — including a now state representative — question the topics that I cover in my social studies class. My administration doesn’t support me, so I have had to learn the state laws and standards to protect myself.

The geography matters. Federal pressure, state legislation, hostile school boards, organized parent campaigns, and fear generated by highly publicized attacks can reinforce one another. A teacher does not need to live in Florida or Arkansas to anticipate whether a lesson on racism, immigration, gender, or Palestine will bring trouble.

The chilling effect doesn’t stop at state lines or borders.

Our survey also makes clear that the attack on education does not only stem from the censorship laws whitewashing the curriculum. A middle school social studies teacher in New Haven, Connecticut, described how immigration enforcement has transformed something as routine as taking attendance:

There are many days where a student isn’t in school and — more often than not, recently — my mindset has gone from “oh, they must be sick, I hope they get well soon” to “oh my god, I hope they are still here.”

I teach 11- and 12-year-olds. This is not a fear I should ever have based on a government’s actions.

In Southern California, a middle school teacher reported:

The executive orders are keeping kids from school on a daily basis. Students are afraid to come to school or leave home in fear of ICE.

Near the San Diego-Tijuana border, a high school history teacher said the presence of Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement had become “a deep concern for our staff.” Teachers responded by developing lessons explaining students’ constitutional rights and how to identify legal and illegal warrants. At another high school five miles from the border, an educator described Border Patrol vehicles and helicopters circling the neighborhood around her campus “on a daily basis.”

A Washington, D.C., middle school math teacher told us,

I have had students traumatized by their parents being picked up by ICE and deported — students who are kind, respectful, and hard-working.

Transgender students face another front of the same assault. Jason Curry, a Maine high school social studies teacher, described a transgender student who won a statewide athletic competition and was then publicly identified by a state legislator. The teacher reported that the school subsequently received “threats and intimidating calls and letters” for defending the student.

These are not separate crises. A student cannot freely participate in a discussion about immigration while wondering whether a parent will still be home that evening. A transgender student cannot simply focus on an assignment while politicians debate whether their identity deserves respect.

The attack on what schools teach is increasingly inseparable from the attack on the students whom schools are supposed to protect.

Palestine emerged in the responses as another subject that educators fear can bring consequences.

A California middle school substitute teacher wrote: “We are not able to freely discuss the genocide occurring in Palestine.” A social studies teacher in a Philadelphia high school said that while their district generally defended the freedom to learn, “there have been some repressive actions in response to Palestinian activism.”

That matters because repression around Palestine has moved the attack on social justice teaching into places where the anti-critical race theory campaigns of 2021 often failed to gain the same foothold. In cities like Philadelphia and Seattle, educators have faced intense scrutiny and backlash when they teach about Palestine.

What began as a right-wing campaign to police race, gender, and history in K–12 classrooms is increasingly shaping how Palestine and U.S. foreign policy are taught and discussed — narrowing the boundaries of acceptable speech and making educators and students alike calculate the risks of speaking openly.

Although some forms of political expression are being suppressed, others — particularly those aligned with MAGA, militarism, and American exceptionalist myths — are being emboldened.

A Colorado high school social studies teacher said colleagues were already self-censoring to avoid complaints from students or parents. Yet at the same school, Marine Corps JROTC instructors who were strong Trump supporters had “gotten much bolder in pushing their agenda.”

Matthew Finn, an educator at a high school outside Chicago, described a similar double standard:

Personally, I was reprimanded for telling students that college kids were being illegally swept off the streets and sent to super max prisons in other countries. They said it was political, I said it was human rights.

At the same time, the educator said colleagues were allowed to “show PragerU content.”

PragerU is not a university. It is a far right media and advocacy organization that produces ideological videos and classroom materials promoting American exceptionalism, climate denial, and sanitized accounts of slavery and racism. Its rise was fueled in part by billionaire fracking brothers Farris and Dan Wilks, who provided millions of dollars in early funding. As of April 2026, some PragerU materials had been officially approved for classroom use in a dozen states, including Texas, Florida, and Arizona.

The irony is difficult to miss. While teachers across the country are accused of “indoctrination” for teaching about systemic racism, gender, or other subjects targeted by the right, PragerU’s own leadership has openly embraced the term. At a Moms for Liberty gathering, founder Dennis Prager responded to accusations that his organization indoctrinates children by saying, “It’s true.” PragerU CEO Marissa Streit went further: “I do believe that we should indoctrinate kids to appreciate their country.”

The Illinois educator also described another teacher who displayed portraits of every president “but completely skipped Biden’s picture.” They concluded:

The school is in Illinois outside of Chicago, so we are pretty safe — but these little lies and omissions are how it starts.

Taken together, these accounts suggest that the current campaign is not simply removing politics from classrooms. It is helping determine which points of view are punished and which are encouraged.

For some educators, the pressure becomes intolerable.

Georgia high school AP Psychology teacher Sally Stanhope told us she had left the school she once attended as a student — the school from which she had imagined eventually retiring:

Statistically, no one will ever count me as a teacher who left because of Georgia’s divisive concept law, formally called the Protect Students First Act. Yet, that’s why I left.

Most likely, thousands like me have left because their values and personality have become divisive concepts.

To understand the current landscape of education, we have to distinguish between educators whose departures become public controversies and those who simply disappear from the profession. We already know that the visible toll is substantial. A 2022 Washington Post analysis identified more than 160 educators who had resigned or lost their jobs over two academic years amid political conflicts over race, history, LGBTQIA+ issues, and classroom instruction. The Post cautioned that its count was likely an undercount, because many such departures never become public.

But the Georgia teacher’s testimony points to an even larger problem: the people those statistics cannot capture.

We can count a teacher who is formally fired or publicly pushed out, or who goes public with their resignation. But how do we count the teacher who quietly leaves because they can no longer teach with integrity?

I teach truth every day in my classroom. Therefore, I have decided to leave Arizona for the upcoming school year to a progressive state.

Amber Corrales in Hawaii said the pressure was pushing her out of teaching U.S. history altogether. Corrales wrote:

I am transferring to an ELA [English Language Arts] position.

She explained that the political climate had become so exhausting that she is “changing jobs and schools.”

One educator leaves the school they hoped to retire from; another leaves the state; another leaves the history classroom altogether. These departures take different forms, but they point in the same direction.

When these kinds of educators leave, schools lose more than employees. Students lose teachers willing to confront difficult history, challenge pacifying myths, and make space for young people whose lives have too often been excluded from the curriculum.

The chilling effect, then, shapes not only what gets taught. It can determine who remains to teach it, and who is deprived of learning.

Repression does not produce only silence and resignation. Our survey is also filled with educators resisting — and their responses offer an important clue about what makes resistance possible. Chicago high school science teacher Juan Pablo Esquivel acknowledged the fear surrounding race, gender, and supposedly controversial history, but wrote, “I’m proud to say our district is trying to stand up for the freedom to learn.” Then came a telling sentence: “It’s not easy, but knowing we’re not alone makes a big difference.” It’s clear that educators are more willing to defend honest teaching when they know others are standing with them.

Oceanside, California, high school social studies teacher Kris Hawkins said:

We have had haters come to our school board meetings trying to ban books from our libraries, but we as teachers and a district have stood strong to keep books available to all.

Our school district is defending the freedom to learn. We are not caving by removing DEI from our teaching.

These responses point toward an essential distinction. Individual courage matters, but telling teachers simply to be brave while leaving them isolated is not a strategy.

Courage grows when it is organized — and revisiting Idaho educators offers a powerful example.

Educators in an Idaho Teaching for Black Lives study group (organized by the Zinn Education Project) described how meeting and learning together changed what they believed was possible. One educator in the group said the experience helped them move from “Something should be done about this!” to “I’m going to do something about this!” Another said teaching students to better understand people different from themselves “gave me the strength to take on anyone who might have thought I should have taught a more ‘white’ curriculum.”

The group was meeting in a state where educators were already feeling the political pressure. One study group participant noted that a high school social studies teacher had to obtain parent permission slips to teach some content. Another described their continued organizing as an act of defiance:

We kept on working and meeting even though our legislation is working on taking away what books we can read to students, what we can teach students, and what we can hang on our walls.

That collective defiance brings us back to Sarah Inama’s Idaho district.

A high school English teacher in the same district where Inama fought to keep her “Everyone Is Welcome Here” poster described a colleague at another school in the district being ordered to remove books; a poster of Amanda Gorman, the youngest poet to perform at a U.S. presidential inauguration; country flags; and even a classroom map because it still said “Gulf of Mexico” rather than “Gulf of America,” the name Trump ordered federal agencies to adopt in January 2025. That same teacher ultimately decided to leave the state.

“We must teach the truth to our students,” said Alberto Otero, an elementary school teacher in Washington, D.C., “so that they can be brave in the face of tyranny.”

But the respondent’s own school had a different culture. Administrators were supportive, the English department was “full of activists,” and the teacher praised a union president who attended district meetings and spoke out on educators’ behalf.

“I have made a promise to myself,” the educator wrote, “that I will teach the full truth of history in my classroom until I am fired for it.”

Other educators echoed that determination. The Connecticut middle school teacher who worried that an absent student might have been taken by immigration authorities wrote:

The president and his cronies can come and get me if they have a problem with that. My kids deserve the truth, and that is what they will get in my class every day.

Collin R., a Virginia high school social studies teacher, vowed to “NEVER stop teaching the realities of U.S. history,” even if doing so cost them their job.

And in Florida, middle school history teacher and Air Force veteran John Meeks captured the contradiction at the heart of the campaign to censor honest teaching about race, history, and inequality: “I took an oath to defend the very freedoms that our state claims to support. We should do whatever we can,” Meeks concluded, “to resist the rise of fascism in our state and nation.”

Educators are told they live in the freest nation on earth while watching books disappear, immigrant families terrorized, transgender students attacked, Palestinian history silenced, and teachers threatened for telling the truth.

Our survey shows what can help turn fear into resistance: solidarity. When colleagues organize together, educators learn in community, unions defend their members, administrators refuse to capitulate, and school boards protect the freedom to learn, teachers have more room to allow students to learn history and ideas that don’t conform to the current federal administration’s political views.

That is the spirit of the Zinn Education Project’s Teach Truth campaign. What began as an annual Day of Action has expanded into something broader: Throughout the year, educators, parents, students, and community members bring the Teach Truth message into rallies, school board meetings, protests, and public gatherings across the country. In 2026 alone, the Zinn Education Project documented the Teach Truth message appearing at No Kings protests, May Day events, immigrant rights rallies, Pride celebrations, Juneteenth events, and other gatherings for justice.

The forces attacking public education want every teacher wondering whether one complaint, one book, or one honest lesson could leave them on their own.

Our task is to make sure they never are.

Every time educators collectively defend a banned book, protect an immigrant or transgender student, teach the history of Palestine, organize a struggle for justice in their union, or band together before a school board, they make it easier for another educator to do the same. And every time the Teach Truth message appears at a rally or protest, it sends a message to educators everywhere: You are not alone, and you do not have to censor the truth.

“We must teach the truth to our students,” said Alberto Otero, an elementary school teacher in Washington, D.C., “so that they can be brave in the face of tyranny.”

The chilling effect is real. So is the movement generating the heat to thaw it.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

Our work is possible thanks to reader support. Help Truthout catalyze change and social justice — make a tax-deductible monthly or one-time donation today.

author: Reddebrek
title: 1983 Red Monarch
content:
Red Monarch is a 1983 British television film, starring Colin Blakely as Joseph Stalin. It is directed by Jack Gold and features David Suchet as Lavrentiy Beria and David Threlfall as Stalin's son Vasily.




Red Monarch is a black comedy based on The Red Monarch: Scenes from the Life of Stalin, a collection of short critical essays by the Russian dissident and former KGB agent Yuri Krotkov. The film depicts Soviet politics and the interplay between Stalin and his lieutenants, particularly Beria, during the last years of Stalin's rule. The reading of Yevgeny Yevtushenko's "The Heirs of Stalin" in the final scene supposedly warns that the threat of totalitarianism is constantly present.




Throughout the film, Stalin and Beria's accents are Irish, intended to single them out as Georgian. This is the natural accent of Colin Blakely and is put on by David Suchet. Most of the others actors have northern English accents, seen as stereotypically working class.

title: KNK Conference in Brussels: Kurdish international representation must be strengthened
content:
The conference organized by the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) in Brussels to discuss Kurdish representation at the United Nations (UN) and the demand for international status continues with presentations by experts in international law and human rights.




Barry A. Fisher, an international law expert, delivered the first presentation at a panel discussion that also featured Prof. Miloon Kothari and former Iraqi Human Rights Minister Bakhtiyar Amin. Fisher, who has been involved in constitution and legislation drafting as well as legal reform efforts in various countries, offered assessments on the international status of the Kurds, their representation at the UN, and regional developments.




Fisher: It is now time to rectify the injustice experienced by the Kurds




In his presentation titled “For the Rebirth of the Kurdish Nation,” Barry A. Fisher said that recognition of the Kurds at the UN and obtaining observer status were among the central objectives of the international campaign. Fisher addressed a wide range of issues, from Turkey’s military presence in Syria and Iraq and regional alliances to Kurdish international representation and diaspora efforts.




Fisher said that the Kurds have lived in the northern part of ancient Mesopotamia for more than 2,000 years, noting that the political order changed following the First World War and the collapse of the Ottoman Empire. Referring to the processes surrounding the Treaties of Sèvres and Lausanne, Fisher said that the Kurds were left within the borders of four states and have faced the consequences of this division for 103 years. “It is now time to rectify this injustice and restore to more than 60 million Kurds—the world’s largest stateless nation—the united national homeland that was promised to them during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.”




Comparison of the current period with the aftermath of the First World War




Fisher said that competition among major powers is creating new spheres of influence, comparing the current period with the aftermath of the First World War. According to Fisher, US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are seeking to expand their spheres of influence in different regions, while Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is also seeking greater room for maneuver in Syria and elsewhere within these shifting power dynamics.




Turkey’s Kurdish policy and military presence




Fisher also addressed Turkey’s policy toward the Kurds, offering assessments on the arrest of Kurdish politicians, pressure on political parties, and policies toward different communities. He said that Turkey has more than 100 military bases, outposts and checkpoints in the Kurdistan Region, and drew attention to Ankara’s military presence in Northern Cyprus, Libya, Lebanon, Somalia and Iraq.




Remarking that Turkey has maintained a military presence in northern Syria since 2016, he highlighted its implications for Rojava and the political role of the Kurds in Syria.




Referring to the Euphrates Shield and Afrin operations, Fisher said that the demographic composition of the region had been altered, Kurds had been displaced, and properties had been seized. He added that Turkey’s influence in Syria had increased following the fall of Assad in December 2024, drawing attention to Ankara’s developing military and political relations with the new administration in Damascus.




Fisher also addressed the “Countries Neighboring Syria” mechanism, the Turkey-Syria defense agreement, the “Regional Quartet” or “R4,” which emerged on the agenda in 2026, and the “Mecca Alliance” between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. He said these structures should be assessed in the context of Turkey’s expanding military and political influence in the Middle East. He also discussed Turkey’s presence in Somalia and the Red Sea within this framework.




Recognition of the Kurds at the UN is key to the international campaign




Outlining his recommendations regarding the KNK’s international efforts, Fisher described recognition of the Kurds at the UN and obtaining observer status as “the key to the campaign.” He said the KNK should expand its opportunities for representation and consultative status at the Council of Europe, the UN, in the United States and within other regional organizations. He also called for the Kurdish diaspora to be included in these efforts and recommended strengthening relations with organizations such as the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the African Union. He added that contacts with the Chaldean Church and the Vatican should also be increased.




‘KURDGRASS’ PROPOSAL IN NASHVILLE




Fisher announced that he is holding talks about an event called “Kurdgrass” in Nashville, US, which would bring together Kurdish music and bluegrass. Stating that Ferhat Tunç and other Kurdish artists could also take part in the project, he said that cultural initiatives could contribute to promoting Kurdish identity internationally.




Referring to the 103-year division of the Kurds, Fisher said: “After 103 years of ancient Kurdistan, with its history spanning thousands of years, being fragmented and left isolated in the middle of a desert, the time has come for it to reunite.”




Kothari: The Kurds’ right to self-determination is long overdue




In the second session of the conference addressing Kurdish representation at the United Nations (UN) and the demand for status, Prof. Miloon Kothari took the floor. His speech focused on international recognition of the Kurds, the right to self-determination, and initiatives that could be pursued through the UN’s human rights mechanisms.




Kothari drew attention to the reference to the “equal rights of nations large and small” in the preamble to the UN Charter, as well as Article 1 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR). He noted that Article 1 of the Covenant states: “All peoples have the right of self-determination. By virtue of that right they freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development.”




“The internal right to self-determination of the Kurdish peoples should have been recognized globally long ago,” he added.




Kothari stated that the failure to recognize the Kurds’ right to self-determination has created an obstacle not only to the full realization of their human rights but also to their integration into the international community and the UN system.




He noted that the right to internal self-determination, which is enshrined in Article 1 of the ICESCR, is also expressed through the concept of “democratic confederalism” in the works of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. Kothari described the objective of this approach as ensuring the full and democratic participation of Kurds in national political processes, securing legal recognition of Kurds as a distinct people, and enabling a form of autonomy within this framework.




Kothari said that Öcalan’s works address an internationalized approach, coexistence, and moving beyond the determining role of borders. He stated that alternative political models could take local, urban, regional and multinational forms and could correspond to the concept of a shared homeland.




Observer status at the UN and human rights mechanisms




Kothari stated that, alongside efforts to secure observer status for the Kurds at the UN General Assembly, work should also be pursued through the UN’s independent human rights mechanisms.




He explained that the independent mechanisms within the UN human rights system include UN treaty bodies, special procedures, international commissions of inquiry and fact-finding missions. He also drew attention to the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) mechanism.




Noting that these mechanisms periodically review the human rights situations in Syria, Turkey, Iraq and Iran, he said that the issues faced by Kurds could be addressed more comprehensively through these processes.




Kurdish institutions can submit reports to UN mechanisms




Kothari stated that Kurdish institutions, civil society organizations, semi-autonomous administrations, academic circles and independent organizations can submit information and reports to the relevant UN mechanisms.




In this context, he said that stakeholder reports can be submitted as part of the Universal Periodic Review process, shadow reports can be presented to treaty bodies, information can be provided to commissions of inquiry and fact-finding mechanisms, and contributions can be made to the thematic and country reports of special rapporteurs.




Kothari noted that Kurdish engagement with the UN should not be conducted solely at the institutional level but should involve participation from different sections of society. Human rights education and awareness-raising efforts should also form part of this process, he added.




‘A long-term strategy is needed’




Kothari stated that all these efforts would contribute to the recognition of the Kurds as a distinct people and to presenting their demand for observer status on the basis of international human rights instruments.




Emphasizing that efforts to secure observer status for the Kurds at the UN should be pursued as part of a long-term strategy spanning many years, Kothari wished the conference success in its work.




Amin: Kurdish identity has maintained its existence throughout a long historical process




Bakhtiyar Amin, an expert on human rights and democracy in Iraq, also addressed the debate over Kurdish international status and representation, examining it through the historical evolution of states and borders.




Amin noted that states and borders around the world have changed significantly from the first half of the 20th century to the present day. He said that there were approximately 20 independent states in the world in 1924, while around 50 states were represented at the United Nations in 1946.




Political borders around the world have never been immutable, he said, noting that from the Islamic empires and the Roman and Byzantine periods to political formations in Europe and the modern state system, borders have repeatedly been redrawn through wars, treaties and political change.




Referring to the system of states that took shape following the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, Amin said that Europe’s political map continued to change many times in subsequent periods. He noted that wars, dynastic changes and shifts in the balance of political power reshaped the borders of states, and therefore today’s borders cannot be regarded as historically immutable realities.




Addressing the historical background of the Kurds, Amin said that Kurds have participated in various political formations and experiences of statehood at different points in history. Noting that there are different historical approaches and studies concerning Kurdish history, he emphasized that Kurdish identity has maintained its existence throughout a long historical process.




'International representation and status among the fundamental issues facing the Kurds'




Amin stated that one of the fundamental issues facing the Kurds today is their international representation and status. He said there is a disparity between the Kurdish population and historical presence on the one hand, and their level of representation in international institutions on the other. For this reason, he said, different forms of representation within the UN system, particularly observer status, should be discussed.




'International mechanisms must be used effectively'




Amin noted that, alongside states, entities with different statuses can also participate in various institutions within the international system. He emphasized that the Kurds should examine existing international mechanisms and assess which avenues could be utilized for their own representation.




Amin also addressed constitutional arrangements in the countries where Kurds live. Noting that Articles 15 and 19 of the Iranian Constitution contain provisions related to language, culture and the equality of citizens, he pointed out that there can be a gap between such constitutional provisions and their implementation in practice.




Amin stated that the ability of different peoples and communities to maintain their existence with their own languages, cultures and identities is one of the key issues in international human rights discussions.




‘Kurds should establish a common platform for cooperation’




Devoting a significant part of his speech to Kurdish efforts in the field of international diplomacy, Amin said that Kurdish political organizations, institutions and civil society organizations should establish a common platform for cooperation. He stressed that differences in political views and structures among Kurds should not constitute an obstacle to joint diplomatic initiatives, adding that common ground could be built on the basis of the existence and rights of the Kurdish people.




Amin stated that the Kurds should engage not only with institutions in Europe but also with various regional and international bodies across the Americas, the Islamic world and Africa.




Alongside European institutions, he said, the participation and consultative mechanisms of other international organizations should also be utilized. Amin stressed the need to examine the statuses under which Kurdish institutions could participate in these bodies and to make more effective use of existing application and participation procedures.




Drawing attention to regional organizations in the Americas, Amin said that the Kurds have so far not made sufficient use of the Organization of American States. Similarly, relations with the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation should be strengthened, he suggested.




Diplomatic and political institutions on the African continent should be taken into consideration in Kurdish international efforts, Amin stated, citing the African Union as an example.




Emphasizing that Kurdish international efforts should not be limited to a single institution or region, he stressed the need to explore all available opportunities for representation and participation within regional organizations in Europe, the Americas, the Islamic world and Africa.




Amin pointed to the importance of Kurdish institutions operating in different countries and regions developing a common diplomatic approach rather than acting independently of one another.




Stating that the historical presence and population of the Kurds, their linguistic and cultural rights, and the issue of international representation should be addressed together, Amin emphasized the importance of pursuing coordinated diplomatic and lobbying efforts within this framework.

title: Zübeyir Aydar at KNK Conference: Kurds must have a presence on international platforms
content:
The conference organized by the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) in Brussels to discuss Kurdish representation at the United Nations (UN) and the demand for international status is continuing. Discussions at the conference focus on Kurdish representation in the international arena, diplomatic initiatives and efforts to secure status at the UN. Representatives of political parties and other figures attending the conference took the floor to express their views.




‘We will do everything we can to support Kurdish representation at the UN’




Former Icelandic Foreign Minister Ögmundur Jónasson said in his speech:




“I bring greetings from Iceland, from the Kurds in Iceland, and from the friends of the Kurds in Iceland. I am one of them. I came here to support this very important initiative that you have launched. We will do everything we can to support the Kurds in obtaining observer status at the United Nations.




I would like to thank you for a very informative morning. The speeches delivered by representatives of the Kurdistan Regional Government and by experts were highly informative for me, particularly regarding the historical context of the Kurds, the geopolitical situation, and the functioning of the United Nations. I thank you for that.




I am not going to say anything particularly important now, but I would like to begin by telling you about something that happened to me earlier this week. I was asked to take part in a Gallup opinion poll. First, they asked me about my health and whether I was satisfied and happy. I scored quite highly on the happiness scale.




Then they asked me what I thought about certain states. They wanted to know how I felt about the United States, China, Russia and the European Union. When the questions turned to the future, however, this positive person—that is, me—became critical and even pessimistic. The reason, of course, was the way the questions were framed.




If I had been asked what I thought about Americans, Chinese people, Russians and people living in the European Union in general, I would have been on the positive side. The problem is states, not people. Of course, some individuals can be a problem, but peoples in general are not.




People’s well-being is largely determined by states, and this is where states differ from one another. The Kurds have been denied the right to a state. More than 60 million Kurds are also being denied the right to voice their grievances at the United Nations, the international forum of state power.




Moreover, the United Nations itself is under attack. The rules-based international order is being systematically weakened and is increasingly coming under the influence of the military-industrial complex that US President Dwight D. Eisenhower warned about when leaving office in 1961.




This is where I come to the Kurds and why I believe it is necessary for them to have a voice at the United Nations.”






















PUK: An important step toward the unity of the Kurdish people




Speaking on behalf of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), Şêx Şemal stated that the Kurds need strong and unified representation in the international arena. Highlighting the importance of a Kurdish National Congress encompassing all four parts of Kurdistan, Şemal said that such a congress would be significant in bringing the social and national will of the Kurds together on a common platform.




Şemal stated that the Kurds’ right to self-determination is a legitimate one and that the struggle for this right must continue. Emphasizing the importance of Kurds being represented internationally under their own identity and name, Şemal said that Kurds living within the borders of different countries are a people who have maintained their existence while preserving their language, culture and identity.




Pointing out that more than 60 million Kurds live across the geography inhabited by the Kurdish people, Şemal said that this shared social presence should be represented more strongly in the international arena. He emphasized that Kurds should not only be represented in international institutions but should also actively participate in their work, stressing the importance of making more effective use of existing international mechanisms to safeguard Kurdish rights.




Şemal stated that mechanisms capable of bringing the common will and demands of the Kurds to the international arena should be developed, adding that the Kurdish National Congress could play an important role in this regard.




The beginning of a long-term struggle




Dr. Abdulkerim Omar, who attended the conference on behalf of Rojava, described the conference as a historic day for the Kurdish people, saying that the meeting marked the beginning and the first step of a long-term struggle.




Omar stated that Kurds must bring their own issues to the international arena themselves, noting that the Rojava Revolution and the Kobanê resistance brought global recognition of the Kurdish people to a new level. He said that millions of people became friends of the Kurdish people during this period and stressed the significance of holding the conference at such a historic juncture.




Omar stated that all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora should be represented collectively at the conference and in similar initiatives, emphasizing that all major political parties should also participate in these efforts. He highlighted the importance of establishing a delegation composed of experts in international law, saying that the legal dimensions of Kurdish international status and representation should remain continuously on the agenda and be closely followed.




Omar also called for diplomatic activities to be further intensified and for efforts to be expanded with institutions and states that play an influential role in global politics.




Omar emphasized the importance of Kurds from all four parts of Kurdistan and those living abroad acting with a common will and a shared approach to representation in order to preserve the gains achieved and strengthen Kurdish representation in the international arena.




‘We must also recognize our own shortcomings’




Fehmi Vergili, representative of the European Syriac Union, who attended the conference on behalf of the Syriacs, stated that they must also examine their own responsibilities when addressing the lack of Kurdish representation in the international arena.




“We must first ask ourselves about the problem,” Vergili said, emphasizing the importance of peoples such as Kurds, Armenians and Yazidis acting together. He noted that the lack of mechanisms capable of adequately representing their peoples worldwide is a significant problem and said that these peoples need to establish stronger international representation regarding their future and their rights.




Vergili stressed that rather than viewing today’s problems as being caused solely by others, they must also recognize their own shortcomings, while cooperation and solidarity should be strengthened.




KDP-I: Unity among Kurds must be strengthened




Speaking on behalf of the KDP-Iran, Bahai Kakai emphasized the importance of developing a common approach among Kurds across all four parts of Kurdistan and within the diaspora. He stated that divisions among Kurdish political structures and parties must be overcome, noting that such unity could also serve as a model abroad.




Bahai said that the fragmented structure of the Kurdish community abroad, divided among different political parties and groups, creates an obstacle to joint efforts. He stressed that Kurdish political structures in each part of Kurdistan should strengthen unity among themselves.




He stated that stronger cooperation among Kurdish political parties could pave the way for broader unity encompassing all Kurds, emphasizing that this process could be further strengthened with the support of Kurdish society and the diaspora. Bahai also stressed that joint action among Kurds is important for efforts in the international arena and called for stronger unity and solidarity among Kurds in all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora.






















Aydar: We will continue our struggle until our people are free in our own lands




KCK Executive Council Member Zübeyir Aydar stated that the struggle for freedom must be pursued not only within the country but also in the international arena, saying that the purpose of the conference was to seek an answer to the question of how Kurds can establish a presence on all international platforms. Aydar further stated the following:




“We exist in our country, and we will have a presence on every platform. We go to international institutions, but we enter only as guests; we are not members of these institutions. This is a wound for us, a deep wound for our people. Today, we are here to resolve this and to establish our presence in these institutions. As the KCK, we support this process with all our strength. We will continue this struggle until Kurdish representation is secured.




Turks, Arabs and Persians cannot represent us; they can represent their own nations. We did not become partners in these states. We experienced this at Lausanne, and we have suffered its consequences for 100 years. Today, we are beginning this work here to bring that to an end.




I propose establishing a committee to carry out this struggle. I also propose launching a petition campaign to bring all Kurds together around this cause. We are determined, and we will continue this struggle until our people are free in our own lands.




We appeal to all parties: this struggle can only succeed through unity. If we achieve unity, we can bring this process to a conclusion. On behalf of the KCK, I call on all parties: Let us convene our national conference as soon as possible, make decisions on these efforts there, and conduct the struggle in a unified manner.”






















Abubakir: The demand for status is an important step’




Addressing the issue of Kurdish international status and representation at the United Nations, Sulaymaniyah Governor Dr. Heval Abubakir drew attention to the distinction between the demand for statehood and existing forms of international representation. Abubakir stated that the Kurds have so far lacked sufficient status in their own name in the international arena, describing the demand for observer status as an important step in this regard.




Noting that this could mark the beginning of a much broader process, Abubakir said that Kurds continue to face the issue of status within the international system today. Referring to developments since the Treaty of Lausanne, he emphasized that Kurds should have a place in the international arena under their own name.




















Pêrî Ehmet also delivered a speech on behalf of GORRAN (Change Movement).




Taşçıer: Kurdish unity must be achieved




Speaking on behalf of the DEM Party, İmam Taşçıer stated that there is no other people with a population of more than 60 million that lacks representation in the international arena. Saying that the Kurds have been deprived of fundamental rights, Taşçıer noted that the Kurdish people have an ancient history and culture and governed themselves until the First World War.




Taşçıer stated that the changes taking place in the Middle East cannot occur without the Kurds, describing them as a dynamic actor in the region’s transformation and arguing that no change taking place without Kurdish involvement would produce lasting results.




He said that the technical proposals presented at the conference were valuable, but that political structures and institutions must take the lead in putting them into practice. He stressed the need to focus on how diplomacy and international efforts could be coordinated through a unified mechanism.




Taşçıer said that politicians and diplomats should take part in these efforts and that Kurdish institutions and political structures should support the process, emphasizing the need for Kurds to establish a common diplomatic mechanism among themselves. Describing this as one of the most difficult issues, he stressed that the primary objective of these efforts should be to achieve Kurdish unity.




“No matter how difficult it may be for the Kurds, we know that it is possible,” Taşçıer said. “If we had unity today, we would be in a completely different position.”






















Boz: Women’s liberationist perspective must be placed at the center




DEM Party MP Sümeyye Boz, speaking on behalf of the Free Women’s Movement (TJA), said the following:




“When we look back over the past hundred years, we encounter a very important reality that must be taken into account in the geography inhabited by the Kurdish people. Throughout this century-long period of fragmentation, Kurds have been forced to live under different state structures, political regimes and social systems. However, this experience has also produced a multilayered body of social knowledge and experience. Living within different systems has given rise to new ideas, different perspectives and rich cultural diversity.




This is precisely why the unity and solidarity we seek today must not be built on a uniform approach that forces everyone into a single mold. On the contrary, it must be based on an understanding that embraces these differences and this richness. Our diversity is not a cause for division; it is the strength and richness of our shared future.




Another vital element that has emerged in this process is the position of Kurdish women and their role in politics. Kurdish women have not merely been part of the social struggle; through their distinctive stance, political will and leadership, they have become a driving force of social transformation.




No model of unity or solution can be lasting if it ignores women’s position and way of engaging in politics, or if it is built without taking their leadership and will into account.




In conclusion, an approach that recognizes the differences produced by a century of accumulated experience as a source of richness and places women’s liberationist perspective at its center provides the strongest foundation for what we need today.”

author: Unknown
title: Final declaration at KNK conference: Committee to be established for Kurdish representation at UN
content:
The final declaration of the Conference on the Representation of the Kurdish Nation at the United Nations, hosted by the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) in Brussels, has been released.




The declaration calls for the Kurds to be recognized as a nation at the UN and represented as observers in UN-affiliated institutions. It also states that a long-term effort should be undertaken to secure representation for the Kurds at the United Nations.







 







The final declaration reads as follows:




“Upon the invitation of the KNK, we, representatives of parties, organizations, and Kurdish institutions from the four parts of Kurdistan and abroad, together with independent individuals from various professions and some friends of the Kurdish people, gathered in Brussels, Belgium, on October 3, 2026, and held a conference under the name Conference on the Representation of the Kurdish Nation at the United Nations. Following extensive discussions, we present this final declaration to the public.




Kurdistan is located in Western Asia, between Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria, and the geography of Kurdistan covers an area of approximately five hundred thousand (500,000) square kilometers. The Kurdish people are one of the ancient peoples of this geography. They have lived in this geography for thousands of years, given their name to this geography, and the name of this geography has been Kurdistan for more than a thousand years.




The population of the people of Kurdistan is approximately sixty million (60,000,000). Despite this large population, the Kurds are not recognized or represented as a nation in international institutions. Particularly at the United Nations, where almost all nations have the right to representation in this organization, the name of the Kurdish nation is absent from the institution, the Kurds are not recognized as a nation, and there is no representative at the UN acting on behalf of the Kurdish nation.




This situation constitutes a major deficiency in the lives of the Kurdish nation and all the peoples of Kurdistan and lies at the root of many questions and problems. For this reason, the KNK placed this issue on the agenda of its 24th General Assembly (June 6–7, 2026). Following extensive discussions, a decision was made to apply to the United Nations so that the Kurds, like other nations, would be recognized and represented as observers in UN-affiliated institutions, in a status similar to that of the Palestinians. Within this framework, meetings were held with experts and their views were sought. Based on these views, a letter was submitted on behalf of the KNK to UN Secretary-General Mr. António Guterres.




However, this is a major and difficult issue; it cannot be resolved through a few narrowly focused meetings and the submission of a few letters. The KNK cannot undertake this effort alone. National and international cooperation is needed. Regardless of the perspective from which it is considered, there is a great need for leaders, administrators, representatives, and all components and sections of Kurdish society with a role in society to come together at the highest level, establish committees, discuss this issue, and make decisions. The people of Kurdistan must be mobilized through meetings, actions, and strong campaigns. Through this conference, we are bringing this important issue to the agenda of Kurdistan and the world. We are beginning a long-term effort. In this work, we will use all diplomatic methods and conduct comprehensive campaigns.




Within this framework, as participants in the Conference on the Representation of the Kurdish Nation at the United Nations, we announce the following to the public:




- The conference considers and supports the KNK’s work, decision, and application in this field as important.




- The conference considers securing representation for the Kurdish nation at the United Nations to be one of the fundamental tasks of Kurdish diplomacy and places this effort before all relevant parties, organizations, institutions, and individuals.




- The conference regards the efforts to secure representation for the Kurdish nation at the United Nations as a long-term undertaking and states that this is not the work of a single organization, but a national and patriotic effort.




- The conference is establishing a working committee called the “Committee for Achieving Representation of the Kurdish Nation at the United Nations” for the purpose of carrying out this work, and calls on all parties, organizations, institutions, and Kurds to participate in this effort and support the committee.




- The Committee for Achieving Representation of the Kurdish Nation at the United Nations is an independent committee. It consists of representatives of parties, organizations, and Kurdish institutions, as well as independent individuals, and works in coordination with all Kurdish parties, organizations, and institutions.




- The conference has decided to launch a wide-ranging signature campaign for the purpose of carrying out this work; millions of signatures will be collected in the four parts of Kurdistan and abroad and submitted to the United Nations.




- The conference calls on all Kurds to take part in this effort and participate in this campaign.




- The conference regards the representation of the Kurdish nation at the United Nations as a national and patriotic effort. This work can only be achieved through strong national unity. Therefore, the conference calls on parties, organizations, institutions, individuals, and all components of Kurdistan to organize a National Conference as soon as possible and strengthen national unity.




- The conference calls on the United Nations to accept the application of the people of Kurdistan, recognize the Kurds as a nation, and accept the Kurds as observers in UN-affiliated institutions.




- The conference calls on all UN member states, particularly the five countries with veto power at the UN, to respond positively to the Kurds’ application, place this issue on the UN agenda, and vote in favor during votes.




- The resolution of the Kurdish issue and the representation of the Kurdish nation at the United Nations are not contrary to the interests of Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria; there are common interests concerning equality and a solution. The conference calls on the governments of Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria not to regard this effort concerning Kurdish representation at the UN as an initiative directed against their respective states and not to obstruct it.

author: Mada Masr
title: Dozens join syndicate demonstration to call for Matsda2sh journalists’ release
content:
Dozens of journalists participated on Saturday in a symbolic sit-in inside the Journalists Syndicate to call for the release of the Matsda2sh journalists, whose whereabouts remain unknown after security forces launched an arrest campaign targeting six of the independent fact-checking platform’s staff on Monday.




While the sit-in was scheduled to end at 5 pm, several members of the syndicate’s general assembly announced that they would remain inside the syndicate, keeping the sit-in open-ended until the Matsda2sh journalists are released.




The syndicate’s board also announced that an emergency meeting would be convened on Monday with a single clause on the agenda: how to respond to the arrest of the six journalists.




Syndicate head Khaled al-Balshy told attendees that the Supreme State Security Prosecution informed the syndicate’s lawyer that the detained journalists have not yet been investigated by the prosecution.




This was confirmed to 

Mada Masr

 on Saturday by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ head, Hossam Bahgat, who said that the prosecution head had denied a 

report

 published by the privately owned Al-Masry Al-Youm claiming that the prosecution had issued a decision to detain the journalists for 15 days.




In its 

statement

, Matsda2sh called upon journalists to take action in the wake of the campaign against them, describing the arrest campaign as a “grave event in the history of Egyptian journalism.” The platform also indicated an ongoing smear campaign against them leveling what it called “flimsy, baseless accusations” against their professional reputations and personal lives.




Accusations against Matsda2sh have circulated in the media since 

Friday

, largely reproducing the allegations first made by the Interior Ministry that the journalists are affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood.




It took the Interior Ministry over 48 hours since it initiated the campaign to announce its arrests of the Matsda2sh journalists — Abdallah Qadry, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud, Mohamed Adel and Omar Helal.




Lawyers representing the six proceeded directly to the Supreme State Security Prosecution headquarters upon the ministry’s announcement and submitted notifications to the prosecution to ensure they could attend interrogation sessions with the journalists.




The journalists had not been formally brought before the prosecution as of time of publishing.

The post 

Dozens join syndicate demonstration to call for Matsda2sh journalists’ release

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Novara Media
title: Secrets of the Chinese Internet
content:
Welcome to Series 2 of Do Your Own Research. Until the end of the year, I will be focusing on the most important and interesting country in the world: China.




We’re starting with Tianyu Fang, an editor of Chaoyang Trap, a newsletter all about the Chinese internet.




We’re starting with the internet because that’s so much of what we see of China: fragments of life online. What’s the reality behind them, and how do we square these beguiling, details with the vast story of China’s rise?




What is happening online in China is often reduced to a few memes or movements. We see the dazzling skyline and we stop thinking, and start gawping: that’s what I call the gawp-zone. How do we get out of it?




In this conversation, we go far deeper, into the circuits and technology of the Chinese internet, from its earliest utopian moments to the hemisphere-spanning computing stack we see today.




And we’ll be making our map of everything that has ever mattered and ever will: this new edition focused on China, available here: novaramedia.com/dyor

author: anred
title: Diputados mendocinos aprobaron el nuevo Régimen Penal Juvenil: más mano dura contra los pibes para no cambiar nada
content:
El miércoles 30 de septiembre la Cámara de Diputados de Mendoza sancionó el nuevo Régimen Penal Juvenil. La nueva ley baja la edad de imputabilidad de 16 a 14 años. La aprobación fue por amplia mayoría: 32 votos a favor, 10 en contra y 0 abstenciones. El nuevo Régimen Penal Juvenil de Mendoza pone en la mira a las principales víctimas del ajuste de Javier Milei y Alfredo Cornejo. En lugar de invertir en educación y asistencia para tratar los problemas de salud mental y consumos problemáticos, el gobierno va a destinar más dinero en cárceles y represión. Por Francisco Ayala*.




 




Bajar la edad de imputabilidad no reduce el delito




Cornejo y la ministra de Seguridad Mercedes Rus se suman al coro de mentiras de Milei y Patricia Bullrich. Quieren presentar a las infancias y adolescencias como responsables de una inseguridad que crece al calor del brutal ajuste del gobierno nacional, provincial y el FMI.




Sin embargo, las estadísticas internacionales son contundentes. UNICEF, la Comisión Interamericana de Derechos Humanos y la propia Convención sobre los Derechos del Niño de la ONU muestran que reducir la edad de imputabilidad no baja el delito, sino que lo aumenta.




En Ecuador, donde la edad de punibilidad es de 12 años, el índice de delitos pasó de 6 a 46 cada 100 mil habitantes. En Brasil y Uruguay, donde la punibilidad comienza a los 12 y 13 años respectivamente, los niveles de violencia no disminuyeron. Dinamarca y Georgia incluso dieron marcha atrás luego de comprobar los efectos regresivos de estas políticas.







¿Qué muestran los datos en Mendoza?




En nuestra provincia, según el último censo, alrededor del 8% de la población tiene entre 13 y 17 años, de los cuales el 45,2% son pobres y el 10,9% se encuentra en la indigencia, según datos del INDEC. En el último tiempo, la principal causa de muertes en jóvenes es por suicidio, superando incluso a los accidentes viales.




La campaña punitivista de Cornejo y Rus se monta sobre la falsedad de que la delincuencia en adolescentes es mayoritaria. Pero según UNICEF, solo el 0,45% de las chicas y chicos de entre 12 y 17 años cometió algún delito. El gobierno oculta esta realidad para poner el foco donde no está el problema.




Políticas integrales, no cárceles




Por más que el gobierno provincial prometa políticas de reinserción, lo cierto es que el encarcelamiento temprano no «recuperó» a nadie. El gobernador en más de una oportunidad se jactó de haber subido la cantidad de personas privadas de su libertad en la provincia. Si la delincuencia crece es precisamente por las políticas de ajuste, exclusión social y connivencia con el narcotráfico y las mafias. ¿De qué se jacta Cornejo? Más cárceles y represión es precisamente el reflejo de un gobierno pésimo para el pueblo trabajador.




Sabemos que la inseguridad es un flagelo que nos golpea principalmente a las y los trabajadores y sectores populares que vivimos en los barrios. Pero decir que se va a solucionar el problema con violencia contra pibas y pibes pobres es tomarnos por tontos.




Para terminar con la inseguridad, desde Izquierda Socialista y el Frente de Izquierda Unidad sabemos lo que hay que hacer. Lo primero es que los salarios sean, como mínimo, iguales a la canasta familiar. Nada alienta más a la delincuencia que saber que trabajando honestamente se vive cada vez peor.




Hay que terminar con la connivencia de las mafias y redes de narcotráfico con la policía y los gobiernos. Es imposible que operen a la vista de todo el mundo y solo caiga cada tanto algún «perejil» y nunca un «peso pesado».




Por último, y lo más importante, hay que subir los presupuestos para educación y asistencia a los problemas de salud mental y consumos problemáticos. Con asistencia a las infancias y adolescencias se ahorra el sufrimiento de las familias y dinero del Estado. Se gasta mucho más en cárceles y represión que en educación y salud. ¿O será que hay gente a la que le es muy redituable no solucionar el problema de verdad y echarle la culpa a las y los pibes pobres?.




 




*Ayala es parte de Izquiuera Socialista.

content:
كيف ندير الحزب اليوم يعكس كيف سندير المجتمع غدا


أنطلق في هذا النص من قناعة بأن الحزب اليساري صورة مصغرة للمجتمع الذي يسعى إلى بنائه وإدارته، وأن نظامه الداخلي يعكس بصورة مبكرة شكل الإدارة التي سيقدمها إذا تولى القيادة في الدولة. فالطريقة التي تتخذ بها القرارات داخل الحزب، وموقع القاعدة فيها، وحدود صلاحيات القيادة، ومدى احترام الرأي المختلف وغيرها، كلها تقدم للجماهير إجابة عملية عن سؤال جوهري: هل تكون السلطة في المجتمع الذي ننشده بيد الجماهير نفسها وتحت رقابتها المستمرة، أم تتركز في يد هيئات محدودة مهما حسنت نواياها؟ ومن هنا تأتي أهمية أن يجسد النظام الداخلي منذ اليوم قيم الديمقراطية والمشاركة والشفافية والتداول التي نعد بها المجتمع غدا.


































Author







رزكار عقراوي




Rezgar Akrawi
