title: The Revolutionary Legacy of the Balkans: Yavor Tarinski’s Balkan Federation and Communes
content:
A forgotten history of Balkan federalism, communes and internationalist struggle


By Giorgos Chatzinakos, human geographer, researcher and writer on the commons, self-government and emancipatory politics


































Author







Giorgos Chatzinakos


























    Submitted by 

free_demos

 on October 2, 2026
  
















































































































































































































The social and political history of the Balkans




The socio-political history of the peoples of the Balkans has always been multifaceted and interconnected: a complex world shaped by affinities as much as by contradictions. During the nineteenth century, the ideas of the French Revolution travelled like seeds of freedom on the winds of history, searching for fertile ground across the already turbulent Balkan Peninsula.




The Balkans were never a timeless landscape of harmony, but they were a deeply plural space in which linguistic, religious and cultural communities had lived beside one another for centuries. As Ottoman rule receded, the intervention of the Great Powers and the advance of competing imperial and national projects transformed that world. The nation-state offered a powerful language of emancipation, but it also hardened borders, rival territorial claims and exclusive national histories. The result was not simply liberation from empire, but new hierarchies, new antagonisms and, at times, the violent purification of populations in the name of the nation.




This is the history through which the Balkans are still too often imagined: nationalism, violence, ethnic antagonism and fragmentation. The very word “Balkanisation” entered political language as a synonym for disintegration. Yet this familiar narrative obscures another political inheritance, one that was equally present in the struggles of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.




Against this teleology of inevitable nation-states stands what Andrej Grubačić, in 

Don’t Mourn, Balkanize!

[1], calls “the persistent vision of a surprisingly consistent utopia”. The Paris Commune of 1871 became one of the great reference points for this political imagination. Its fire reappeared in the Bosnian uprising of 1875 and survived the geopolitical settlement imposed by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878. In 1903, the Ilinden–Preobrazhenie Uprising, the short-lived Kruševo Republic and the Strandzha Commune offered further glimpses of a different Balkan future: not a landscape ordered only by kings, governments and armies, but one of peoples, communes and federations struggling to organise life from below.







Figure 1. Group of revolutionaries with a red flag in Kruševo, July 1903. The horseman in fustanella at the far left is the local commander Pitu Guli, a leading figure in the Macedonian-Adrianople revolutionary movement. A few  days later, he fell fighting the Ottoman army on the outskirts of the town.




Yavor Tarinski’s 

Balkan Federation and Communes: Revolutionary Projects in Bulgaria of the 19th & 20th Centuries

[2] returns to this buried revolutionary inheritance. First published in Greek by Aftoleksi in 2023[3] and now being published in English by PM Press, the book examines revolutionary projects in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Bulgaria that cultivated the ideas of the Balkan Federation and the commune. Tarinski’s central intervention is historiographical as much as political: he asks what becomes visible when Balkan history is read not from the standpoint of victorious states, but from the defeated possibilities of autonomy, federation and social revolution.




A history from below, against nationalist memory




This is where the book is at its strongest. It does not simply add several forgotten episodes to an established national story; it unsettles the story itself. In a region where historical memory remains heavily organised through the nation-state, recovering suppressed traditions of cooperation and self-government becomes a way of reopening the political imagination. An unrealised past was once a possible future.




Tarinski’s genealogy reaches further back than the nineteenth-century revolutionary movements. He points to earlier communal forms and dissident traditions, including Slavic assemblies, the Bogomils and the Commune of Zealots in fourteenth-century Thessaloniki. These episodes are very different from one another and should not be collapsed into a single continuous lineage. Their significance in the book is rather to challenge the assumption that centralised statehood is the natural or only political grammar of Balkan history.







Figure 2. Armed fighters in the mountains of North Macedonia, August 1903. DEA / Biblioteca Ambrosiana via Getty Images.




The same counter-history continues into the modern period. It is a history of communal property,  assemblies, federative schemes and experiments in popular self-direction. Read in this way, the Balkans appear not simply as a region fragmented by nationalism, but also as a laboratory of repeatedly defeated alternatives to it.




Rigas and the internationalist horizon of the Balkans




At the centre of this earlier internationalist horizon stands Rigas Velestinlis [4]. Tarinski reads Rigas as a pivotal figure who tried to combine the radical republicanism of the French Revolution with the multi-ethnic reality of the Ottoman Balkans. Rather than projecting a narrowly ethnic state, Rigas imagined a democratic political community of equal citizens across the region. His Charta of Greece was therefore more than a map: it gave cartographic form to a political horizon that exceeded the national borders which would later divide the peninsula.







Figure 3. Rigas Velestinlis, Charta of Greece (1797).




Tarinski also turns to the Serbian socialist Svetozar Marković and his engagement with the South Slav 

zadruga

, a communal form that Marković treated as a basis for common property and local self-government. The point is not to romanticise pre-modern social forms, but to recover the ways in which communal institutions could be reworked into modern projects of emancipation.




From Rigas, Tarinski follows the federalist thread through figures such as Georgi Rakovski, Vasil Levski, Hristo Botev and Lyuben Karavelov. Their positions were not identical, but they shared a distrust of liberation delivered from above by imperial patrons. Levski put the point starkly: “We already have a Sultan. We do not need a master, but freedom and human equality.” Karavelov, for his part, argued that cooperation among the peoples of the region was necessary if liberation was not simply to end under a new yoke[1].




Botev is particularly revealing because his revolutionary politics connected the Bulgarian liberation struggle to a wider social and internationalist horizon. His 1871 defence of the Paris Commune, 

Ridiculous Weep

[5], makes clear that emancipation meant more than transferring sovereignty from one ruling group to another: it concerned the capacity of ordinary people to become authors of their own collective life.




Tarinski also draws attention to the way revolutionary figures have later been absorbed into competing national canons. Yane Sandanski and Gotse Delchev, for example, have repeatedly been claimed by rival state narratives. The result is a familiar paradox: people whose political worlds crossed borders are remembered through histories that retrospectively police those borders. Recovering the federalist and internationalist elements of these traditions is therefore also a struggle over collective memory.




The commune in practice




The argument becomes most concrete when the book turns from programmes to attempts at communal self-government. Tarinski had already developed this history in a 2022 essay for Freedom, 

The Commune and the Balkans: The Case of Bulgaria

[6], which provides a useful English-language account of the experiments discussed here.




During the April Uprising of 1876, insurgents in Panagyurishte attempted to organise social life along communal lines. Contemporary accounts describe common management of essential goods, the suspension of money in important areas of everyday life and plans for communes that would remain in contact with one another. The experiment lasted only days before Ottoman forces crushed the uprising, but its political significance lies in the fact that liberation was being imagined not only as independence, but also as a transformation of social relations.




The Ilinden–Preobrazhenie Uprising of 1903 produced different experiments. In Kruševo, insurgents proclaimed a short-lived republic. In Strandzha, rebels associated with the Internal Macedonian-Adrianople Revolutionary Organisation established a more explicitly communal order. For several weeks, public affairs were organised locally, resources were shared and the old authority of the state was displaced. The Strandzha experiment also sought cooperation between Bulgarian and Greek communities in the liberated territory, resisting the idea that the uprising should simply reproduce another national empire.




These experiments were brief and violently defeated. That brevity, however, does not make them politically insignificant. Revolutionary moments matter not because they hand us finished institutional blueprints, but because they reveal possibilities that the established order works to make unthinkable.




Tarinski also revisits Ada Kaleh[7], the Danube island whose ambiguous relationship to surrounding states created, for a time, unusual space for local self-organisation. Table 1 reproduces a wider chronology of communal experiments and related milestones.




Table 1. Selected communes and revolutionary experiments in the Balkans, 1871–1925


Year - Milestone


1871 - Commune in the Romanian city of Galați (Galacz)


1876 - Panagyurishte Commune in central Bulgaria


1878 - Ada Kaleh: the submerged Balkan island where people once lived without a state


1903 - Strandzha Commune in south-eastern Bulgaria


1906 - Tolstoyan commune in Burgas on the Bulgarian Black Sea coast


1919 - The newspaper The Commune in Burgas


1920 - Ruse Commune in north-eastern Bulgaria


1923 - Kilifarevo Commune in northern Bulgaria


1925 - Tolstoyan commune in Ruzhintsi in north-western Bulgaria




Why the Balkan Federation still matters




The contemporary force of Tarinski’s book lies in its refusal to treat these histories as museum pieces. Nationalism, militarism and authoritarian politics are once again gaining ground across Europe, while borders and geopolitical camps are presented as the only serious language of politics. Against this supposed realism, the Balkan federalist tradition reminds us that cooperation across ethnic, linguistic and religious differences has itself been a practical political project, pursued repeatedly under extraordinarily difficult conditions.




This is also why the distinction between national memory and revolutionary memory matters. Decades later, the Bulgarian anarchist Georgi Grigoriev, known as Georgi Balkansk[8], would describe the commune as the enduring social form through which a common popular will could express itself directly. Whether revolutions called such bodies soviets, committees or communes, he argued, their underlying principle was self-direction and federation from below.




Murray Bookchin later formulated the same anti-nationalist horizon with characteristic clarity: “When at length free communes replace the nation and confederal forms of organization replace the state, humanity will have rid itself of nationalism.”[9] The point is not that one historical model can simply be transplanted into the present. It is that decentralisation, municipal self-government and confederation remain part of the political vocabulary through which domination by the centralised nation-state can be challenged.




There is also a more immediate lesson. Natural disasters do not recognise borders, and solidarity remains one of the strongest forces for crossing them. Rebuilding connections among Balkan societies means resisting the national isolation through which neighbouring peoples are so often taught to see one another. Cultural exchange, mutual aid and shared political struggles can water the historical seeds left by earlier revolutions and connect them to contemporary movements for social justice.




As Tarinski concludes, this reading of history matters because horizontal social movements can use it as a root from which new projects of internationalism, federalism, universal equality and justice might grow across the peninsula. The revolutionary inheritance of the Balkans does not ask us to return to a lost past. It asks us to recover the futures that were defeated before they could fully exist.




So let us plant new revolutionary seeds for a new Balkan Federation — and remember that we also belong to places we have not yet known, against the bourgeois state, capitalism, nationalism and war.




Footnotes


[1] https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/andrej-grubacic-don-t-mourn-balkanize


[2] https://pmpress.org/product/balkan-federation-and-communes-revolutionary-projects-in-bulgaria-of-the-19th-20th-centuries


[3] https://www.aftoleksi.gr/2023/11/24/valkaniki-omospondia-kommoynes-epanastatika-protagmata-sti-voylgaria-19oy-amp-20oy-aiona/


[4] https://www.openarchives.gr/aggregator-openarchives/edm/helios/000024-10442_4104?language=en


[5] https://libcom.org/article/ridiculous-weep-hristo-botev-paris-commune


[6] https://freedompress.org.uk/2022/06/06/the-commune-and-the-balkans-the-case-of-bulgaria/


[7] https://libcom.org/article/ada-kaleh-balkan-island-where-people-once-lived-no-state-or-masters


[8] https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/anarchist-communist-federation-obituary-georgi-grigoriev-balkanski-1906-1996


[9] https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/murray-bookchin-nationalism-and-the-national-question

author: Amy Goodman
title: Christa Pike Hospitalized in Critical Condition After Botched Execution
content:
“I’ve never seen anything like what we saw Wednesday night,” said one reporter who witnessed the execution attempt.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Tennessee’s Governor Bill Lee has halted executions for the remainder of the year after a death row prisoner survived two lethal injections on Wednesday. According to her lawyers, Christa Pike was still breathing after she was strapped to a gurney and injected with two syringes of pentobarbital in a botched execution that spanned more than two hours. Prior to the scheduled execution, Pike and her lawyers argued a single-dose lethal injection could be tantamount to torture due to Pike’s small veins. Pike was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder she committed when she was 18. Now in the hospital in critical condition, she is the first person to ever survive lethal injection in the United States.

“I have seen five executions in Tennessee,” says Steven Hale, a criminal justice reporter for the Nashville Banner, who witnessed Christa Pike’s botched execution. “And I’ve never seen anything like what we saw Wednesday night.”

Christa Pike “has just experienced the most agonizing attempt at lethal injection in the country’s history,” says Sandra Babcock, director of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide. Babcock says Pike should have never been sentenced to death, because she was an “immature 18-year-old” with a history of severe childhood and sexual trauma who “was not receiving medication for post-traumatic stress disorder and bipolar disorder at the time of [the murder], which she committed with her abusive boyfriend at the time.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

Tennessee’s Governor Bill Lee has halted all remaining executions this year after a death row prisoner survived two lethal injections Wednesday night. According to her lawyers, Christa Pike was still breathing after she was strapped to a gurney and injected with two syringes of pentobarbital in a botched execution that spanned more than two hours. Witnesses say Pike described a burning spot in her arm that felt like it was going to burst. She smiled and laughed, then gasped repeatedly and began snoring, but continued to breathe. She was later taken to the hospital.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review of the botched execution, but Christa Pike’s attorneys say he should go further and commute her sentence. On Thursday, Christa Pike’s attorney, Randy Spivey, addressed reporters during a news conference.

RANDY SPIVEY: Christa is alive right now. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving lifesaving medical care.

The state of Tennessee has shown us again that they are not capable of carrying out an execution consistent with basic human dignity. Last night was not just inefficient; it was cruel, and it was torturous. It was also predictable. Christa’s legal team told the state of Tennessee and the court that her medical conditions would cause her to suffer an agonizing death. The state and the court dismiss Christa’s concerns.

The governor’s call for an independent review does not go far enough. After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty.

AMY GOODMAN: Christa Pike’s lawyers revealed the execution team went through at least seven needles trying to find a vein, including one that appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm. Medical experts say the blistering and burning around the IV insertion sites suggest the pentobarbital may have leaked into the surrounding tissue rather than entering Pike’s bloodstream, potentially causing chemical burns. Some experts have raised the possibility the pentobarbital may have degraded or expired, which could have made it less effective.

Christa Pike was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder she committed when she was 18 years old. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years. Wednesday night’s attempted execution went forward only after the U.S. Supreme Court lifted a stay by an appeals court, which had paused her execution to consider whether her sentencing had fully weighed mitigating evidence, including severe childhood trauma and neglect, including rape and sexual abuse and mental illness.

Weeks before her botched execution, Pike and her lawyers argued a single-dose lethal injection could be tantamount to torture due to Pike’s small veins. This is an unedited audio recording shared by her lawyers with The New York Times.

CHRISTA PIKE: The concerns I have on our lethal injection method are simply that I do not have good veins. Tony Carruthers lived out my worst nightmare, detail for detail, and I don’t want to go through that. The drug is — supposedly burns very bad, and so that sounds scary to me, because they use the word “Drano” in speaking about this drug. And the thought of suffocating and drowning on my own bodily fluid and blood isn’t very appealing to me.

I’m very remorseful now. I wasn’t in the beginning when I first caught this charge. I didn’t care what I had done or who I had done it to. The horror of the pain that I caused her family, my family, my co-defendants’ families, I have affected this world in such a negative way. When all I ever wanted to do was care for people and leave love, I have done the opposite of that, and that pains me.

AMY GOODMAN: Those were the words of Christa Pike, speaking weeks ahead of her botched execution. She was referring to the case of Tennessee death row prisoner Tony Carruthers, who was issued a one-year stay of execution in May after prison officials were unable to find a backup injection vein in another botched execution attempt that left Carruthers suffering and in pain for over an hour.

Pike’s lawyers said, quote, “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy,” they say.

Well, for more, we’re joined by two guests. In Nashville, Tennessee, we’re joined by Steven Hale, criminal justice reporter at the Nashville Banner, author of Death Row Welcomes You: Visiting Hours in the Shadow of the Execution Chamber. He witnessed Christa Pike’s botched execution on Wednesday evening. In Orleans, Massachusetts, we’re joined by Sandra Babcock, clinical professor at Cornell Law School, director of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide. She recently co-wrote an article headlined “Tennessee failed Christa Pike long before her execution date.”

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! Let’s begin in Nashville. Steven Hale, you witnessed the attempted execution of Christa Pike. Can you explain what happened?

STEVEN HALE: Well, thanks for having me, Amy.

I guess the answer is yes and no. I can tell you what I saw. One of the continuing frustrations of this situation, from our perspective as reporters, is that we can’t explain as much as we’d like to be able to. But I can tell you that, yes, what you described there in your intro is correct.

Christa Pike, we understand, was given two rounds of lethal injection drug pentobarbital. I have seen five executions in Tennessee, including the aborted one that you mentioned of Tony Carruthers back in May, and I’ve never seen anything like what we saw Wednesday night. And a number of the witnesses who were there with me have also seen a number of other lethal injections in this state and others, and it was new to all of us.

It was pretty clear early on that things were going wrong, but even then, we didn’t know they would go quite as wrong as they did. And it’s all — it’s all been quite disturbing, as you can imagine.

AMY GOODMAN: Describe what you heard and saw.

STEVEN HALE: So, you mentioned that Christa Pike was talking and kind of smiling even at times. She was in conversation with her spiritual adviser, who was in the room with her. And they, in the early stages of this attempted execution, were repeating a kind of prayer mantra. They were saying, “May you be at peace. May you be at peace. May you be kind and gentle to yourself.” At one point, she looked over in our direction at the window that we were sitting behind, and she said to the people behind the glass, and she repeated that again, “May you be at peace.” But it wasn’t long after that that the drugs were administered, and even at a certain point, we saw what we understand to be a signal in the execution chamber that the drugs had been fully administered. And even after that point, she was still moving her body. She was still talking to her spiritual adviser. And that continued long after we expected it to.

What then happened was obviously a very long process, but the curtain was drawn twice. And for your viewers to understand, that’s normally only done right before the person is declared dead. In this case, it was the curtain was closed while we all knew she was still alive, and we could still hear her breathing, snoring, kind of struggling. And it was then her spiritual adviser was pulled out of the execution chamber. We waited there in the dark for a bit, and then the prison officials came and brought the spiritual adviser back into the execution chamber so that they could try again. And that’s when they gave her a second round of pentobarbital. We continued to hear her snoring at times, saw her, you know, kind of opening her mouth wide, almost as if gasping, but without making a sound. And then, at a certain point, the curtain was closed again. And I repeat, it was closed while we could still hear her and knew she was alive. And we sat there for around 50 minutes, listening to the sound of her snoring quite loudly, breathing, you know, in strained breaths, but with no information about what was or wasn’t going on behind the curtain.

AMY GOODMAN: As we watched the news conference, Sandra Babcock — you’re one of the attorneys for Christa Pike — the attorneys called for the governor to commute Christa’s sentence. The governor’s announced independent review is described as “insufficient without greater transparency and preservation of records.” Can you talk about the legal recourse you have right now? I mean, my understanding is Christa [Pike] is in the hospital in critical condition. They’re trying to keep her alive. And if they succeed and she’s sent back to the prison, they will try to kill her again?

SANDRA BABCOCK: [inaudible] The most important thing right now is that Christa pulls —

AMY GOODMAN: Sandra Babcock, can you hear me?

SANDRA BABCOCK: I can hear you. Can you hear me?

AMY GOODMAN: Yes, I can. Go ahead.

SANDRA BABCOCK: I can hear you. Can you hear me? OK.

The most important thing right now is that Christa pulls through this. We still don’t know what her prognosis is, and we are all waiting to see. And that is the primary concern. But in the meantime, the governor must immediately commute her death sentence. Christa Pike, as Mr. Spivey said a few minutes ago, has just experienced the most agonizing attempt at lethal injection in the country’s history.

And it’s important to remember that Christa should never have been in this position. She should never have been sentenced to death in the first place. She was an 18-year-old kid, an immature 18-year-old, who was just a year after a violent rape, which was the last of three different men who — three different men who had raped her in the course of her childhood and adolescence. She was not receiving medication for post-traumatic stress disorder and bipolar disorder at the time of this crime, which she committed with her abusive boyfriend at the time. There are so many reasons why she never should have been in that execution chamber in the first place.

And on top of that, the state of Tennessee had always accused her of fabricating these accounts of childhood sexual abuse and rape. They called her a liar, a pathological liar. They said that she was promiscuous. They said that — basically, that she had invited it or invented it. In fact, her sexual assaults were documented by police reports, court records, hospital records. She actually reported them, unlike most rape victims. And after decades of denying the truth of her suffering, the state just last month finally admitted that she had — that it did not dispute her history as a survivor of unimaginable sexual violence.

We tried to get the courts to stop her execution, and the 6th Circuit agreed, and they halted it. And the state immediately appealed, and the Supreme Court vacated that stay over the dissents of three justices, who said we we must recognize that we are not infallible and that there is a risk of irretrievable harm if this execution goes forward. Their concerns were ignored. The state of Tennessee plowed ahead. As you said at the top of the hour and as Mr. Spivey explained, the state was on notice about her medical condition. All of these facts were known to the courts. This case represents a colossal failure, not only of the lethal injection process, but of the legal architecture that is supposed to ensure that people do not suffer a torturous death at the hands of the state.

AMY GOODMAN: Sandra Babcock, Tennessee’s Governor Bill Lee has halted all remaining executions this year. You’re having a governor’s election this year, and one of the candidates, the Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who’s running for governor, has said many times on the campaign trail she wants executions to happen quicker, and she wants to use the electric chair. Can you respond?

SANDRA BABCOCK: Well, I’m not a Tennessean, and I will not be voting in the election. But what I think about that statement is that it is typical of politicians who are seeking to appeal to a common thirst for vengeance when people hear about violent crime. It is a black-and-white way of viewing the world that does not reflect the complexities of crime, that does not reflect the complexities of women’s histories of violence and the experiences that pave the pathway to incarceration. It’s what they perceive as something that will appeal to the electorate. It’s a cop-out, is what it is.

And people who have worked in the system — and that includes prison officials and guards who have worked alongside, supervising people on death row — recognize that these are full human beings and that you cannot execute someone under the conditions that Tennessee just attempted to do, without recognizing that what Tennessee did was an act of cold and calculated homicide that was far crueler in its way, because of its premeditated, deliberate nature, than the act that Christa Pike was committed of — was convicted of committing at a time when she was in the grip of a mental illness that was unmedicated, coming off of the trauma of a violent rape.

AMY GOODMAN: Sandra Babcock, can you say whether Christa Pike is conscious in the hospital in critical condition?

SANDRA BABCOCK: We do not know. We have no information. None of the information that we have heard — most of it is rumors — is reliable. We are waiting to hear any official word from the medical team. She is now receiving medical assistance from doctors who respect the Hippocratic Oath, unlike the doctor who was present in the execution chamber with her, who we know is incompetent and who is also responsible for the botched execution of Tony Carruthers in May.

AMY GOODMAN: And finally, I want to go back to Steven Hale in Nashville. You not only witnessed the attempted execution of Christa Pike, you witnessed the attempted execution of Tony Carruthers in May. Your final comments on what happened there, leading to him being granted a stay of execution?

STEVEN HALE: Yeah, Amy, as you say, and I spoke to you in May, and we do need to find a much better way of getting in touch, but I — or a much better reason for doing so. That was also a horrifying attempt at execution in its own way. A difference was that this one went much further. That execution, as you remember, was called off, from our perspective as witnesses, before the curtain was open, and so before it had sort of fully begun, from our vantage point. Of course, on Tony Carruthers’ end, they had been trying and struggling to get IV access for a long time.

I think, overall, I would just emphasize to your viewers that we have been here before in Tennessee, not just in terms of there being a botched execution earlier this year, but in terms of the governor calling for a pause on execution so that the protocol can be reviewed. That happened in 2022 when an execution was called off at the last minute because of problems with the protocol. An outside legal review found that the department had not been following its protocol on numerous occasions, and a new protocol was created. That’s the one we’re using now. And this year, there have been, as we’ve been discussing, two botched executions under that protocol. We did not know until yesterday, after hearing from Christa Pike’s attorneys, the degree of struggle that there had been to get IV access for her. So that was new information to us because, as reporters and witnesses, we don’t see that part during an execution. But that, obviously, it appears, was a problem yet again in this process. And so, what will happen going forward is very unclear. But this is — the experience that we all had Wednesday night and that Christa Pike had is unique in some ways, but also not new here.

AMY GOODMAN: Steven Hale, I want to thank you for being with us, criminal justice reporter at the Nashville Banner, author of the book Death Row Welcomes You: Visiting Hours in the Shadow of the Execution Chamber, speaking to us from Nashville, and Sandra Babcock, clinical professor at Cornell Law School, director of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide. We’ll link to your piece that you co-wrote, “Tennessee failed Christa Pike long before her execution [date].”

Coming up, “Massacre at Minab: The School That Became a Grave.” We’ll speak to Jeremy Scahill of Drop Site News. Back in 15 seconds.

AMY GOODMAN: “The World’s on Fire” by Feral Foster.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

author: Sam Rosenthal
title: Progressives Saw Wins in DNC, But Battle for the Future of the Party Continues
content:
Resolutions calling to abolish ICE and pushing to block arms sales are laying a progressive groundwork for 2028.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

This summer, attendees who were punctual enough to make it into the 9:00 am Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) resolutions meeting at its August convening in Texas were treated to an unusual display: In a humdrum corner of the Austin Marriott Downtown, the DNC resolutions committee voted to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And, in a move that went against the DNC’s habit of blocking any resolution viewed as critical of Israel, the committee also voted to reaffirm its commitment to the Leahy Laws, which bar the U.S. government from supplying weapons to governments violating human rights abroad.

The resolutions committee is largely known for bland resolutions with titles like “Resolution Recognizing the Work and Contributions of the California Young Democrats” or “Resolution Reclaiming the American Promise.” That is, they are statements, sometimes grand and sometimes small, that are meant to be read as aspirational; paragraphs devoted to nice-to-haves in a world where Democrats could wave a magic wand and make it just-so.

Recently, though, the DNC resolutions committee has become a site of contention between the party’s corporate-friendly establishment and its progressive wing. While some left-leaning activists have contested the party establishment’s power in Democratic primaries around the country, others have advanced on the DNC itself in a quest to reform the party apparatus to be more accommodating toward (and maybe even supportive of) progressive policy.

This tension was on full display at this year’s summer meeting in Austin, Texas. Progressive DNC members, many of whom have organized in ad hoc formations for years within the DNC, put forward two measures intended to put the party on the record about two of the biggest hot-button issues for progressives today: the genocide in Gaza and abolishing ICE.

This was not the first time that progressives have advanced resolutions to address these issues. In recent sessions, DNC members have introduced resolutions explicitly calling for an end to AIPAC funding in Democratic primaries and resolutions calling for conditions on military aid to Israel. These, however, have routinely failed to secure enough votes on the resolutions committee, and have occasionally been blocked or procedurally undermined by DNC Chair Ken Martin.

Resolutions condemning the U.S.-Israel relationship have been especially opposed by the DNC’s establishment-friendly majority. A year ago, at the DNC’s 2025 summer meeting, the resolutions committee blocked a measure that would have called for an arms embargo against Israel, opting instead for a watered-down alternative pushed by Martin that called only for unrestricted humanitarian aid into Gaza and a vague commitment to a two-state solution.

Progressive DNC members put forward two measures intended to put the party on the record about two of the biggest hot-button issues for progressives today: the genocide in Gaza and abolishing ICE.

In that instance, Martin used a maneuver that he has deployed more than once to frustrate progressive activists’ attempts to pass more left-leaning resolutions: He authored and introduced a resolution that appeared to address the same issue, but which committed the DNC to a substantially less radical course of action than the original resolution. Martin’s resolution was agendized earlier in the committee meeting and passed by unanimous consent. Then, when the more radical resolution came up for a vote, committee members rebuked the body for taking up an issue that had already been addressed by Martin’s resolution, even though the two committed the DNC to very different courses of action.

Progressive victories during this summer’s meeting in Austin were all the more remarkable because Martin again leaned on this tactic, but unsuccessfully. A “Resolution Condemning the Trump Administration’s Reckless and Deadly Approach to Immigration Enforcement” was the third agendized item in the resolutions committee and was passed again by a unanimous voice vote. This resolution, notably, stopped short of calling for a permanent end to ICE.

When the resolution calling for ICE’s abolition came up much later in the committee session, a few members argued for voting against the resolution on the basis that the issue had already been settled by the body. A majority of committee members, though, pressed the issue, leading to a rare display of open disagreement on the resolutions committee. In the end, the vote was tallied individually and the resolution was adopted, with 25 members in favor and 12 opposed.

Elsewhere on the agenda, progressives scored a more modest victory, with the body unanimously passing a resolution calling for the Democratic Party to reaffirm its commitment to the Leahy Laws. The Leahy Laws, named for former Vermont Sen. Patrick Leahy, bar U.S. arms sales to foreign security forces that commit human rights abuses. The laws have been applied numerous times by Congress since their adoption in 1997, but have never been invoked to block military aid to Israel. Critics of Israel’s conduct have long argued that the myriad, exhaustively documented cases of human rights abuses by Israel clearly disqualify the country from receiving U.S. aid under the Leahy Laws. However, the U.S. has never blocked arms sales to Israel under the Leahy laws.

The Leahy Laws resolution, submitted by Michele Johnson of Louisiana, did not explicitly name Israel in its text. In her motivating speech on the floor, Johnson recalled an experience she had in Equatorial Guinea to justify the importance of upholding the Leahy Laws and did not mention Israel. This represents a new strategic tack for progressives inside the DNC, who have long been frustrated in their attempts to pass resolutions more overtly critical of the U.S.-Israel relationship. While resolutions that have cited Israel or AIPAC by name in the past have been blocked by the larger DNC, progressives within the party may have hit on an indirect route to eventually come to a more full throated critique of the U.S.-Israel relationship. The unanimous passage of the Leahy Laws resolution sets progressive activists up to raise the issue again in forthcoming DNC meetings.

The policy that the DNC promulgates is part of how the Democratic Party communicates its ideals to voters, especially in the years between presidential cycles.

While the passage of these resolutions marks a clear win for progressive activists inside the party, it’s important to zoom out from the DNC’s procedural arcana and ask whether these battles inside the DNC have the power to truly push the party itself to the left. For much of 2026, the progressive and corporatist wings of the Democratic Party have been in open conflict. Victories by progressive and democratic socialist candidates in a slew of state primaries have set up critical tests for the left flank of the party in November, where left-leaning candidates will have to prove their mettle against Republicans. Some within the Democratic establishment have been vocal about their concerns that progressive Democrats have hampered the party’s chances to take back the House or Senate in the midterms by adopting what they deem “radical” policy positions. Others in the Democratic Party have gone even further, condemning the avowed ideology of their fellow caucus members, in an apparent attempt to outflank their Republican colleagues on the right.

There isn’t much evidence for a causal relationship between what the DNC committee votes to support and the policies that Democratic candidates actually champion, nor is there much proof that DNC resolutions are an effective lever for pressuring the party’s risk-averse leaders into encouraging elected Democrats to embrace progressive policy.

Efforts by progressive activists within the party, then, should be seen less as an effort aimed at directly compelling lawmakers to change course, and more as another front in the battle for the soul of the Democratic Party. The DNC is one of the few bodies that purports to stand for the party as a whole, and the policy that the DNC promulgates is part of how the Democratic Party communicates its ideals to voters, especially in the years between presidential cycles. Winning these fights now, while the media gaze is on the midterms and the coming 2028 presidential horse race, could still shore up progressives’ position as the presidential primary approaches.

By then, any Democrat running for president who wants to stake out a position to the right of what the DNC itself has adopted on the Leahy Laws and immigration may have to explain why they’re out of step with their own party committee. In this sense, activists inside the DNC are contributing in a small way to larger reform efforts within the Democratic Party.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

author: Joe Mullin
title: Congress Has Another Site-Blocking Bill, And This One Targets VPNs
content:
Congress is taking another run at site-blocking, a deeply flawed concept that would undermine basic internet infrastructure. Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) has introduced the American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA), 

H.R. 10364

, a bill that would give copyright owners a new legal tool to block Americans’ access to foreign websites accused of copyright infringement. 




The basic idea is 

all too

 

familiar

, and it’s still dangerous. A copyright owner first asks a court to label a foreign website a “foreign piracy site.” Once that happens, the copyright owner could seek orders requiring internet service providers, DNS providers, and—new and explicit in this bill—VPN providers to take “commercially reasonable steps” to stop their users in the United States from accessing those sites. The decision to label a website as a “foreign piracy site” can happen without the accused site even showing up in court to defend itself. 




ACPA Goes Further Than Other Site-Blocking Proposals 




In some ways, the ACPA is even worse than a 

site-blocking legislation introduced last year

, the

 

Foreign Anti-Digital Piracy Act (FADPA)

, which EFF also opposed. That bill at least excluded companies that provide only VPN services, as well as providers that offer DNS resolution exclusively through encrypted DNS protocols. The ACPA drops those protections. In fact, the bill explicitly includes VPNs among the service providers that can be ordered to block access to a website. 




The bill also broadens the definition of a “piracy site.” Last year’s 

site blocking bill

 covered sites with “no commercially significant purpose or use” other than infringement. ACPA changes that to sites with “only limited commercially significant purpose or use” beyond infringement. In other words, under ACPA, even a website with legitimate commerce going on could still be labeled a “foreign piracy site” and ultimately blocked for all Americans. 




Better Process Still Doesn’t Fix The Problem 




The ACPA includes some procedural protections, such as requiring service providers that could be subject to a blocking order to receive legal notice and an opportunity to respond. The bill also requires courts to consider the potential harm to other websites and internet users before ordering intermediaries to block websites. It further requires the copyright owner to post a bond, in an amount determined by the court, sufficient to cover the costs and damages incurred by any service provider found to have been wrongfully enjoined. The bill also provides a mechanism for operators or users of third-party online services affected by erroneous blocking to seek compensation after the fact in certain circumstances.

 

Finally, a site operator can ask a court to rescind its designation as a “foreign piracy site.”




These safeguards are significant and positive changes, but they don’t solve the basic, and severe, due process problem. The initial decision to label a website a “foreign piracy site” can still be made without the site operator appearing to defend itself. The court can appoint a “special master,” which is an independent expert who helps the judge evaluate evidence, to review the copyright owner’s case—but that step is not required. In any case, a special master  is not a lawyer who actually represents the accused website, nor the users whose access to information and speech may be affected. 




We know what site-blocking looks like when it’s put into practice. Supporters of site-blocking like to point to its use in other countries. But what we’re seeing in other countries is serious collateral damage to lawful websites. In Italy, 

510 benign, non-streaming websites

, including a Catholic convent and a telehealth platform, were blocked by the country’s “Piracy Shield” program. In Spain, 

a site-blocking system blocked more than 550,000 domains

 during soccer broadcasts, including sites belonging to Greenpeace and Harvard University.




Congress Should Reject Site-Blocking Proposals




More than a decade ago, Congress abandoned SOPA and PIPA after internet users pushed back against site-blocking and other threats to the open internet. We shouldn't start building that infrastructure now.




ACPA adds some safeguards, but those don’t fundamentally change what Congress is being asked to create: a system for blocking Americans’ access to entire websites at the request of copyright owners. By explicitly bringing VPNs into that system, the bill also reaches into basic tools that people use to access the internet safely and privately. Adding somewhat better procedures to a bad idea doesn’t turn it into a good idea.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump DOJ Considers Reframing Watergate as “Deep State” Plot Against Nixon
content:
JD Vance has previously suggested the administration views both Trump and Nixon as victims of the “deep state.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump’s Justice Department has entertained the idea of reframing former President Richard Nixon as a victim of “deep state” persecution in the Watergate scandal, with allies likening Nixon to Trump as an unfairly maligned figure.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility — an internal watchdog that was created in response to Watergate — recently heard a presentation from a revisionist Watergate historian, Geoff Shepard, on his theory that the nation’s most infamous presidential corruption scandal was actually a result of “deep state” actors conspiring to take Nixon down.

Shepard conducted a two-hour talk, accompanied by a 78-page slide deck entitled “Watergate As Lawfare.” Shepard, a former Nixon aide, has been trying to promote this theory for decades with little buy-in by mainstream historians. He thinks that Watergate was a ploy to install Edward “Teddy” Kennedy as president, and has likened the wide-ranging Nixon plot — which was uncovered by a mixture of lawsuits, congressional hearings, and investigative journalism — to a “legal pogrom.”

Among other things, Shepard argues that the special prosecutor who investigated the 1972 Watergate break-in committed misconduct in relation to the case. One of his primary complaints is that Nixon is “loathed” and that his detractors “want to give him no credit for anything,” he told the publication for Harvard Law School, of which he is an alumnus, in 2016.

In 2022, Shepard asked to present his findings to the Biden administration, but the DOJ refused. Last month, however, he was invited to speak at the department’s headquarters by a senior DOJ official, according to the Journal.

“Given his expertise and scholarship on Watergate, he was recently invited to give a presentation, but that presentation does not constitute an investigation,” a DOJ spokesperson said.

Even if Shepard’s arguments were legitimate — and legal scholars have debunked many of them — there is a massive amount of evidence incriminating Nixon in Watergate, between testimonies of his involvement in the Democratic National Committee break-in and his thousands of hours of secret audio recordings.

However, Nixon has experienced somewhat of a renaissance on the right in recent years. Many conservatives view the famously anti-communist figure as a historical proxy to Trump, who they also view as unfairly maligned by “deep state” actors trying to take him down.

In June, Vice President JD Vance likened the two figures.

“If Watergate happened tomorrow, it would be like a 12-hour news story. The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy,” he said. “If you look at the story of how the deep state took down Richard Nixon, it’s not all that different from what the same groups of people, the same institutions tried to do to Donald Trump in the first Trump administration.”

Evidently, Trump himself has repeatedly asked former Nixon aides why he resigned instead of staying in office, even though he was facing robust impeachment proceedings against him at the time.

Indeed, there are similarities between Nixon and Trump, with both presidents facing prosecutions in massive corruption plots, fiercely attacking the media and perceived opponents, perpetuating brutal wars replete with shady side deals, attempting to obstruct public access to information, and issuing or receiving politically-motivated presidential pardons. Trump, like Nixon, constantly expresses paranoia that the media establishment and members of Congress are trying to take him down.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has undermined protections put in after Watergate in order to allow an even wider breadth of corrupt activity, with less oversight, in the executive branch amid his second term.

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

 

here

.




Sudan’s government is taking a long hard look in the mirror, and they don’t like what they see, sources close to Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the Transitional Sovereignty Council 

told

 Mada Masr this week.

 




Ushered in on a promise of hope a year ago, Idris’s government has faced significant issues. Some of those come down to war-time trials, but infighting and attempts to delimit the remit of a civilian government backed by a powerful and intrusive military council have been persistent issues. 




Now the government is considering a reshuffle of ministerial and gubernatorial appointments to address executive imbalances and shortfalls, particularly on economic and service-related issues, according to a source in Idris’s office.




While Idris and the TSC may see an administrative reshuffle as a way to address war-time woes, the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement insist that any bureaucratic rearrangement must not change the power-sharing agreement inked in the South Sudanese capital. 




For now, the reshuffle is all just talk. But the movements do not view it in isolation from the larger reshaping of the political landscape of recent months, a leader in one of the Juba armed movements told Mada Masr, particularly as the planned national dialogue will have to address their relationship with the government.

Sudan turns to China for Red Sea port after scrapped UAE deal




Two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with a UAE-led consortium to build Sudan’s 

Abu Amama port

, the government is reviving the project with a major Chinese port company, Hassan Gaafar, the deputy head of the state-owned 

Sea Ports Corporation and head of its Higher Committee for the International Conference on Seaports, 

told Mada Masr.




Sudan has begun taking practical steps toward building the port, Gaafar said. Studies are expected to be completed and construction to begin by the end of 2027, he said.




The move is part of a broader expansion of Sudan’s economic ties with China, as the government looks to Beijing for investment in ports, energy and infrastructure, according to Sudanese government and diplomatic sources.




China Harbour Engineering Company

 signed an agreement with Sudan in July to develop existing ports and build new ones, while other Chinese companies are in talks over electricity and infrastructure projects, a Foreign Ministry source said.




Abu Amama lies about 200 km north of Port Sudan, near the Mohamed Qol and Marsa Oseif port localities, along the Red Sea coast and close to major shipping routes. The area has deep waters, reducing the need for extensive dredging and allowing it to accommodate large vessels and cargo ships.




The details of the proposed arrangement with China, including financing, the length of any concession and who would operate the port, have yet to be formally announced.




The Chinese-backed version of the project is being developed as part of a different government approach to Sudan’s ports, according to a Finance Ministry source informed of the ports file. Rather than being part of a single, large investment package, Abu Amama is now being presented as part of a government push to expand Sudan’s port capacity and improve its ability to move imports and exports. The government is exploring an investment model that would link the port more closely to Sudanese trade and exports, the source said.




The UAE deal, 

signed

 in December 2022, was considerably broader. Under the agreement, a consortium comprising AD Ports Group and Invictus Investment was to develop, operate and manage Abu Amama, with announced investments of up to US$6 billion. The package included a free trade zone, an agricultural project and a $300 million deposit at the Central Bank of Sudan, according to the Sudanese government announcement at the time.




For the UAE investors, Abu Amama’s location was a central part of the appeal, the Finance Ministry source said. The port could serve as an outlet for Sudanese exports and imports and connect the coast to agricultural and mining production areas and overland transport networks, he added. 




The project would have given Sudan another port alongside the Port Sudan complex, while giving the UAE-led consortium a long-term role in developing and operating a facility on a major global shipping route, the source said.




The government cancelled the agreement in November 2024, as relations between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi deteriorated after Sudan accused the UAE of backing the RSF in the war.




At the time, Finance Minister and JEM leader Gibril Ibrahim 

told

 reporters that, following the UAE’s support for the RSF, “there is no [Sudanese] entity that could even think about giving a port to the UAE, not even a single centimeter of land.”




A Sudanese government source told Mada Masr that the cancellation was part of a broader reassessment of the country’s economic relationship with the UAE since the war. Ports, the source said, have since become part of Sudan’s political and security calculations in its foreign relations, alongside their role as commercial infrastructure.




A diplomatic source informed of Sudan-UAE relations said Abu Dhabi may view the transfer of Abu Amama to a Chinese partner as part of Sudan’s wider economic realignment following the political crisis between the two countries. The main question for the UAE, the source said, would be whether the new arrangement will reproduce any of the rights granted to the UAE-led consortium under the original agreement, including long-term operating rights or ownership of related assets.




The project comes as Sudan’s economic ties with China expand. Chinese cooperation has increasingly extended into infrastructure, energy and ports in recent months, while Sudan is looking for long-term investment to rebuild infrastructure damaged by the war and sees its ports as a key route back into foreign trade, a Sudanese diplomatic source and the government source said.




Under the potential Chinese model, the first phase could focus on building the port’s basic infrastructure, followed by expanding its operating capacity and connecting it to transport networks and areas producing goods for export, the government source said.




But much of the project’s success will depend on what happens beyond the port itself. A maritime transport expert told Mada Masr that Abu Amama could ease pressure on existing facilities if it were connected to roads and railways capable of moving goods from production areas to the coast. Its economic viability would depend not only on the depth of the water, the expert said, but also on the cost of building berths, container terminals, warehouses and logistics zones, as well as the transport links connecting the port to Sudan’s interior.




The port could handle agricultural exports, livestock, minerals and imports, but serving those markets would require a logistics network extending well beyond the construction of the quay itself, the expert said.




That broader challenge is part of why the government is looking at the ports sector as a pillar of post-war economic reconstruction. 

The International Conference on Sudanese Ports 

opened in Port Sudan on September 27, bringing together experts and institutions from Sudan, China, Egypt, Spain and Norway to discuss investment, infrastructure, supply chains, digital transformation and public-private partnerships.




A government official participating in the conference told Mada Masr that Sudan wants to move away from reliance on its existing ports toward a more diversified network along the Red Sea, combining the expansion of current facilities with new ports capable of handling trade.




Reviving Abu Amama with a Chinese partner is part of that effort, the official said, allowing Sudan to draw on Chinese experience in building and operating maritime infrastructure.
