author: Abahlali_3
title: We Welcome the President’s Response to Femicide, but Much More Must Be Done
content:
1 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Women’s League Press Statement

We Welcome the President’s Response to Femicide, but Much More Must Be Done

On 28 September 2026, after 11 women had been murdered in Ekurhuleni since July, Abahlali baseMjondolo and other residents of Ekurhuleni marched in Kempton Park against the killing of women and the failure of the police to adequately protect women from violence. We handed a memorandum to the Kempton Park Police Station and Ekurhuleni District Management.

•⁠ ⁠A public report on the investigations into the 11 murders, presented at an open public meeting. •⁠ ⁠A well-funded and properly equipped women-led GBV task team for the townships and shack settlements of Ekurhuleni. •⁠ ⁠A 24-hour Victim Support Room at Kempton Park Police Station with properly trained female officers. •⁠ ⁠Daily visible and women-friendly policing in high-risk areas, with additional patrols at night and on weekends. •⁠ ⁠A public audit of all GBV cases reported in Ekurhuleni since July. •⁠ ⁠An open public meeting at which the police must account to the women of Ekurhuleni for failures in responding to GBV and femicide. •⁠ ⁠The election of a women’s committee to which the police must report every week on their work relating to GBV and femicide.

We therefore welcome much of what President Cyril Ramaphosa announced in his address to the nation on 29 September.

The investigation into the Ekurhuleni killings has been elevated to the national level, a specialised multidisciplinary investigation is under way and visible policing in Ekurhuleni has been increased.

The President also announced a national case-recovery operation for unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children. The commitment to audit unresolved cases, identify delays and establish recovery plans for stalled cases is in accordance with the demands that we made in Kempton Park.

He made a commitment to address forensic backlogs, give urgent priority to forensic evidence in cases involving the rape and murder of women and children, and report publicly on progress.

The President has also made it clear that women must not be turned away by the police, that protection orders must be enforced, that dockets must not disappear and that women reporting violence must be treated with dignity. These are all issues raised directly in our memorandum.

Along with all these measures we strongly welcome the announcement that every municipality must conduct a women’s safety audit. Broken streetlights, unsafe transport routes, abandoned buildings and neglected public spaces all place women in danger. In shack settlements a lack of lighting, unsafe or absent toilets and unsafe routes through our communities put women and girls at risk every day. We need safe and reliable public transport, including at night and early in the morning, and safe routes between our homes, transport stops, workplaces, schools and shops.

We strongly support the President’s recognition that harmful alcohol use is ‘a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence’, his call for the stronger enforcement of liquor laws and his instruction that a package of laws and enforcement measures to reduce alcohol-related violence be put before Cabinet within 60 days. This must include reducing the excessive concentration of alcohol outlets, restricting trading hours and enforcing clear closing times, tighter licensing controls, and much stronger regulation of alcohol advertising, promotion and sponsorship. Government must regulate the alcohol industry and resist corporate pressure to weaken, delay or block effective regulation. The long-delayed Liquor Amendment Bill should be revived and debated urgently. Serious regulation of the alcohol industry is a critical part of the struggle against violence in general.

But much more needs to be done.

Women cannot just be called to meetings to be informed about decisions that have already been taken for us without us. Women must have real power and working class and poor women, who are the majority, must have real power.

This is why our memorandum demanded an elected women’s committee to which each police station must report every week. Democratically organised women must be able to demand information about investigations, police response times, missing dockets, failures to enforce protection orders and complaints against police.

Every woman must also have the right to know who is investigating her case, how to contact them, what has been done, what still has to be done, where the evidence is, why there has been a delay and where she can go if an investigation is being obstructed.

Women’s own assessment of danger must be taken seriously. Police must respond urgently to assault, stalking, death threats, forced entry, threats with weapons and violations of protection orders.

Women reporting violence should have the right to be accompanied by someone they trust. We should not have to repeat traumatic experiences again and again to different officials. As far as possible, one properly trained person or team should take responsibility for a case.

We know from our own experience that police power can also be abused. We have seen police refuse to open cases, fail to act against politically connected people and use their powers against impoverished people and activists. Our movement has repeatedly confronted police repression and police violence, including assault, wrongful arrest, wrongful imprisonment, torture and murder. Our comrades killed by the police include Nqobile Nzuza, a seventeen-year-old woman shot in the back in Cato Crest in 2013, and Jayden Khoza, a two weeks old baby, who died after the police fired teargas into the Foreman Road settlement in 2017.

Visible policing and stronger action against gender-based violence must not become a licence to criminalise poor people, migrants, activists and other people already subjected to police abuse.

There must be genuinely independent investigation when police officers lose evidence, take bribes, protect perpetrators or obstruct investigations. This is especially important when police officers themselves are accused of domestic violence, sexual violence, abuse of sex workers or femicide. Their colleagues cannot be allowed to protect them.

There must also be more women in operational and senior leadership positions in the police, with real opportunities for advancement. Gender transformation cannot mean putting some women behind victim-support desks while the culture and leadership of policing remain unchanged.

We need stronger obligations on the police, much stronger democratic control over the police and effective independent oversight. We need policing centred on protection, service and problem-solving, not an aggressive model of policing that criminalises vulnerable people and communities.

We propose the creation of an independent and feminist Women’s Ombud for Policing. The Women’s Ombud should have the power to obtain police records, inspect police stations, investigate corruption and misconduct, publish findings and refer criminal and disciplinary matters for action. Women must be able to approach the Women’s Ombud directly, and the Women’s Ombud must work with organised women and democratic community structures.

Women’s safety goes far beyond policing. Women escaping violence need somewhere safe to stay. They need healthcare, counselling, legal assistance, transport and childcare.

Economic independence is also part of women’s safety. A woman may know that she needs to leave a violent man but have no income of her own, nowhere else to live and children who depend on her. Women need decent work, decent wages, secure housing, childcare and social protection. We support a liveable guaranteed income. No woman should have to remain with a violent man because leaving him will mean hunger and homelessness.

We must also build democratic and feminist women’s power in our own communities.

We need to support women who are in danger, accompany them when they need support, help them get somewhere safe and make sure that nobody is left alone because they do not have money or family support. We need to make sure that every woman has a space where she can speak freely about the problems she is facing and receive support.

We must confront perpetrators in our own communities. Families, communities and all kinds of organisations, including churches, can reproduce patriarchy. The struggle against violence against women must confront patriarchy everywhere, including in our homes, communities, schools, workplaces, trade unions, political organisations and churches.

We as poor women refuse to be silent. We are mothers, neighbours, comrades and leaders and we are demanding to be safe, to be heard, to be alive and to build a socialist future together.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Santa Fe: “Una de cada dos familias que asiste a comedores pasa un día sin comer”
content:
El impacto de las políticas del gobierno de Milei en el interior del país. El 70% de las personas que van a comedores no lo habían hecho antes del comienzo de su gestión en diciembre de 2023.







El espacio político Fuerza Común de Santa Fe realizó un relevamiento en los barrios de la capital santafesina. A partir de este informe demostraron que una de cada dos familias de los barrios santafesinos no puede asegurar un plato de comida diario.







Pablo Landó, referente de Fuerza Común, explicó que el relevamiento abarcó a 26 barrios de la ciudad de Santa Fe y destacó que los comedores y copas de leche son vitales para muchas familias.




“Una de cada dos familias nos responde que si no existiera ese espacio no tenía garantizado una ración de comida”.




Otro de los datos relevados por Fuerza Común muestra que la mayoría de las familias que hoy asisten a los comedores empezó a asistir luego de la llegada del gobierno libertario al país.




“El 70% de las personas fueron por primera vez desde que asumió el gobierno de Javier Milei a un comedor o una copa de leche”.




Landó destacó el trabajo de las mujeres cocineras que sostienen estos espacios y la necesidad de que la legislatura santafesina ponga en agenda una ley provincial para asegurar un salario.




“Se necesita de manera inmediata un reconocimiento a aquellas personas que sostienen ese espacio y digo reconocimiento económico, el barrio lo reconoce, la política pública absolutamente no, le da la espalda” finalizó Landó.

title: Reggio Emilia: c’era una volta Bosco Ospizio, ora è il tempo delle ruspe della Conad
content:
Ruspe e polizia nel Bosco Ospizio di Reggio Emilia, dove un progetto edilizio minaccia un’area verde ricca di biodiversità. Il quartiere resiste e il presidio incontra la lotta No Tav: esperienze diverse che si riconoscono nella difesa dei territori.




Di Nicoletta Dosio da Osservatorio Repressione




A Reggio Emilia, chiuso tra reti di cantiere e sottratto alla vista da una cinta di alti pannelli, c’era un bosco: un bosco urbano in un quartiere di periferia, “tra la via Emilia e il West”, come direbbe Guccini. E’ un meraviglioso, insostituibile polmone verde, sorto intorno ai ruderi dell’antico Ospizio comunale, da cui prende il nome: il “Bosco Ospizio” appunto.




Del passato rimangono gli alberi secolari, ai quali, oltre ad un folto, impenetrabile sottobosco, si sono aggiunte nuove varietà, figlie della natura che sa rigenerare le rovine e farne giardini.




Ci raccontano un luogo pieno di vita vegetale ed animale, ricco di biodiversità, che conserva nella sua parte più segreta una zona umida, punto di sosta per gli uccelli migratori, popolata da diverse varietà di anfibi ed abitata da salamandre e libellule.




Dunque una realtà preziosa per la città, da proteggere e difendere ad ogni costo.




Invece l’area è stata dichiarata edificabile e messa in vendita, grazie alle amministrazioni comunali succedutesi negli ultimi vent’anni, a partire dall’amministrazione Del Rio, già sindaco nei primi anni 2000: sponsor di quella cattedrale nel deserto che è la stazione del TAV con annesse superstrade a cementificare una campagna fertilissima, poi ministro delle infrastrutture e paladino del progetto TAV Torino-Lyon.




Ora il proprietario è Conad, la maggior catena italiana di supermercati. Oltre al danno, anche le beffe: nel tentativo di rendere commestibile l’amaro piatto, il gigante commerciale, in omaggio al motto pubblicitario “Persone oltre le cose” di cui si fregia, concorda con il Comune di ospitare nell’area anche edifici di pubblico interesse (una biblioteca e una Casa di Quartiere), nonché un’ampia spianata di parcheggi. Risultato? Cemento e asfalto dove c’era vita e bellezza.




Ma il quartiere non ci sta e nasce cosi 

l’Assemblea Permanente Bosco Ospizio

, che dallo scorso agosto, nell’imminenza degli annunciati lavori, occupa con un presidio il terreno a rischio e ferma le ruspe che si accingono al disboscamento. Denunciati dalla Conad per “violenza e invasione di area privata” e diffidati con ordinanza della Prefettura, gli attivisti resistono ed hanno ricostruito il presidio fuori dal perimetro del bosco, a ridosso delle barriere che ne impediscono la vista e l’accesso. Ora l’interno del parco è visibile solo attraverso gli spiragli praticati nella recinzione: attraverso quei varchi il bosco ci parla, vestendosi di tutti i colori dell’autunno: i gialli e i rossi sui quali va ad infrangersi la malinconia del pomeriggio che si fa sera.




Al presidio ci sentiamo tra compagni: la nostra storia nel movimento NO TAV si fa racconto, dialogo serrato, scambio di esperienze. I presidianti si preparano ad affrontare i rigori invernali con un piccolo campeggio di tende ed una cucina allestita sotto un gazebo.




Le loro richieste di consigli ci risvegliano nel ricordo i giorni e le notti di Venaus 2005, il presidio sotto la neve tra i bidoni roventi di fuochi accesi contro il gelo, i minestroni fumanti e una moltitudine che nel pericolo e nella lotta si ritrova e diventa comunità.




Tra le poche suppellettili del presidio c’è un piccolo scaffale-biblioteca: libri che fanno compagnia, libri per pensare e per ingannare il tempo che, di notte, non passa mai.




Mi ha colpito l’ennesima analogia con la lotta No TAV. Chiomonte 2011, Libera Repubblica della Maddalena: attesa dell’esercito del TAV, che prima o poi sarebbe arrivato con blindati, lacrimogeni e manganelli; il grande tendone attrezzato a cucina dove, tra fornelli e provviste, ha trovato spazio un piccolo scaffale di libri.




Anche in questo senso, nel presente rivive il passato e le lotte si ricompongono, sentendosi sorelle nella materialità della vita, figlie dello stesso amore e della stessa rabbia, unite nel conflitto irriducibile contro il sistema che sulla guerra e sulla devastazione sociale e ambientale fonda il proprio dominio e lo chiama pace.




………………….




E invece ieri, di buon mattino, 

al Bosco Ospizio sono arrivate le ruspe.

 Per permetterne l’accesso l’intero quartiere è stato militarizzato. Bloccata nei due sensi la via Emilia. Inseguiti dagli agenti, portati in Questura e denunciati gli attivisti che hanno cercato di opporre resistenza salendo sugli alberi.




Una delegazione si è recata in Comune, chiedendo di incontrare il Sindaco, ma non ha avuto risposta, se non dal Capo di Gabinetto. Silenzio anche da parte dell’ASL e dell’ispettorato del lavoro a cui gli attivisti hanno denunciato la totale assenza di misure di sicurezza all’interno e all’esterno del cantiere.




Nal tardo pomeriggio di ieri è stata convocata l’assemblea permanente che decidere il da farsi. Così mi ha scritto una compagna del Presidio, a commento delle foto e di un video che documentano la devastazione:




“In questa porzione di terra fino a stamattina c’erano alberi adulti, platani, tigli, pioppi, cedri del Libano. Uccelli e fauna varia avevano la propria casa.




Quello che ci resta è la possibilità di andare a fare la spesa fino alla propria morte. Ammesso che si riuscirà ancora a riempire gli scaffali e se ci saranno ancora i mezzi per acquistare qualcosa…”




E invece stamattina, proprio mentre stavo per chiudere queste note, ecco un post su Facebook che dice “i nostri hanno bloccato le ruspe…” e sollecita rinforzi. Tutta Reggio Emilia è con loro, stanno arrivando messaggi di solidarietà da tutt’Italia: Bosco Ospizio non si arrende, anche lì la lotta continua, vedremo che succede nelle prossime ore.




Alcuni appresentanti dell’Assemblea Permanente Borgo Ospizio saranno con noi alla marcia NO TAV il 3 ottobre.

author: Redazione_web
title: “La mia famiglia è in carcere”. Turchia: repressione e resistenza dei movimenti LGBTQIAP+
content:
Nella notte tra il 12 e il 13 settembre la polizia turca entra nelle case dellə attivistə, perquisisce le sedi delle associazioni LGBTQIAP+, sequestra telefoni e computer, fa irruzione nei locali. L’operazione si estende a quindici province, coinvolge 162 persone, nove associazioni e tredici attività. Contemporaneamente viene oscurata una parte consistente dello spazio digitale del movimento: siti delle associazioni, media, account di attivistə, avvocatə e gruppi universitari. 




Nel rastrellamento vengono messe insieme realtà molto diverse: organizzazioni storiche e riconosciute internazionalmente come Kaos GL, associazioni impegnate sull’HIV, ma anche locali e luoghi della socialità e della sessualità queer. Le indagini insistono su sex work, sostanze, «oscenità» e altre ipotesi di reato. Attivistə turche con cui siamo in contatto leggono questa sovrapposizione come una precisa strategia di legittimazione della repressione davanti all’opinione pubblica: associare il movimento LGBTQIAP+ a droga, prostituzione e criminalità permette di presentare il rastrellamento non come un attacco politico alle sue strutture organizzate, ma come un’operazione a difesa della società, dei bambini e della famiglia. Una lettura che trova riscontro nello stesso linguaggio delle autorità: la Procura parla della necessità di impedire la «normalizzazione» di queste pratiche agli occhi della società, mentre il Ministero della Giustizia richiama insieme protezione dei minori, famiglia e «valori morali comuni». Il governo chiama l’operazione Ailem Güvende, “La mia famiglia è al sicuro”.




Il nome non è un dettaglio propagandistico. Dice molto di quello che sta succedendo in Turchia e, insieme, di un’offensiva reazionaria che conosciamo bene anche da questa parte d’Europa. La famiglia da difendere, i bambini da salvare, la denatalità, la “natura”, la “morale”, il gender e le persone queer e trans trasformate in una minaccia: sono parole che viaggiano da anni attraverso confini, destre, governi e movimenti anti-gender. In Turchia questa grammatica politica è diventata progressivamente politica di Stato.




La repressione del movimento viene da lontano. A Istanbul il Pride viene vietato ogni anno dal 2015, ma ogni anno il movimento prova comunque a riprendersi le strade. Divieti analoghi colpiscono Pride e iniziative LGBTQIAP+ anche in altre città e la risposta è diventata quasi rituale: cordoni di polizia, cortei dispersi, violenze e fermi. Ancora nel giugno scorso, il 24° Istanbul Pride si è tenuto a Kadıköy nonostante il divieto: 65 persone sono state fermate. Nello stesso Pride Month ci sono stati altri fermi a İzmir, Ankara e durante il Trans Pride di Istanbul. Non è quindi la presenza LGBTQIAP+ nello spazio pubblico a essere scomparsa: è diventato sempre più alto il prezzo da pagare per renderla visibile.




La svolta familista dell’attuale fase ha però un passaggio fondamentale nel 2021, quando Erdoğan ritira la Turchia dalla Convenzione di Istanbul contro la violenza sulle donne. Il governo lega apertamente quella scelta all’omosessualità, sostenendo che la Convenzione sia stata utilizzata per «normalizzarla» a danno dei valori sociali e familiari. Non è casuale che l’attacco ai diritti delle donne e quello alle persone LGBTQIAP+ si incontrino proprio qui. La famiglia viene costruita come un corpo sotto assedio, da proteggere contemporaneamente dal femminismo, dall’autodeterminazione delle donne, dalle soggettività queer e trans e da tutto ciò che incrina la naturalizzazione dei ruoli di genere.




È una costruzione che negli anni successivi diventa sempre più organica. Le campagne contro la cosiddetta “propaganda LGBT” si intrecciano con le proposte per costituzionalizzare il matrimonio eterosessuale, le politiche pronataliste e l’attacco ai percorsi di affermazione di genere. Nel 2024 arriva un passaggio decisivo: con il Family Protection and Strengthening Vision Document and Action Plan 2024–2028 la protezione e il rafforzamento della famiglia diventano un programma pluriennale dello Stato, articolato in cinque obiettivi strategici, quindici target e cento azioni e affidato a organismi nazionali e provinciali. Seguono l’“Anno della famiglia” nel 2025 e, quest’anno, il lancio del “Decennio della famiglia e della popolazione 2026–2035”.




Il collegamento con quello che sta accadendo oggi non dobbiamo costruirlo noi: è lo stesso ministro della Giustizia Akın Gürlek a collocare l’operazione “Ailem Güvende” dentro questa politica. La famiglia diventa così non soltanto l’oggetto da proteggere, ma il criterio attraverso cui stabilire quali corpi, relazioni e forme di vita siano legittime e quali possano essere sorvegliate, censurate e criminalizzate.




Non è nemmeno un’eccezione turca. Negli ultimi quindici anni reti transnazionali anti-gender come il World Congress of Families hanno fatto incontrare Christian Right statunitense, conservatorismo russo e destre europee. La Russia di Putin è stata uno dei laboratori della criminalizzazione della cosiddetta “propaganda omosessuale”; Orbán ha costruito attorno alla famiglia e alla natalità una parte centrale del proprio progetto politico; in Italia lo stesso World Congress of Families si è riunito a Verona con la partecipazione della Lega. Non abbiamo elementi per sostenere un rapporto organizzativo diretto fra questa rete e le organizzazioni familiste turche. Non serve inventarlo: la circolazione della stessa grammatica politica è già evidente.




E infatti la repressione di settembre non si ferma alle persone. Colpisce la possibilità stessa di organizzarsi. Secondo l’Ordine degli avvocati di Istanbul sono stati bloccati 11 siti di associazioni LGBTİ+ e 419 account o indirizzi social, mentre per altri 107 è stato chiesto il blocco. Vengono messi sotto accusa finanziamenti internazionali perfettamente legali, attività di advocacy, pubblicazioni e raccolte fondi. Associazioni che lavorano da decenni per i diritti LGBTQIAP+ e contro l’HIV vengono trattate come possibili strutture criminali.




E quando il movimento risponde, la repressione continua. Nei giorni successivi ai rastrellamenti si scende in strada a İzmir, Ankara e Istanbul. La polizia interviene anche contro queste manifestazioni: 125 persone vengono fermate e poi rilasciate. Davanti al tribunale di Çağlayan, a Istanbul, vengono portate via più di cento persone e viene impedita persino la lettura del comunicato. È importante distinguere questi fermi dagli arresti dell’operazione iniziale: chi è scesə in strada per chiedere la liberazione dellə compagnə è tornatə fuori; moltə di coloro per cui manifestavano no.




Al 23 settembre almeno 83 persone risultano ancora in custodia cautelare. E dentro non ci sono soltanto persone casualmente travolte da un rastrellamento. La repressione sta colpendo direttamente la memoria, le competenze e le strutture organizzative del movimento. Sette componenti degli organi direttivi e di controllo di Kaos GL, nata nel 1994 e parte fondamentale della storia LGBTQIAP+ turca, sono in carcere. È detenuta anche la giornalista Tuğba Tekerek; tra gli elementi utilizzati contro di lei compare un articolo del 2024 sul movimento LGBTQIAP+ in Georgia pubblicato da Kaos GL.




In carcere ci sono Umut Derin Eroğlan, Janset Kalan e Nedime Erdoğan. Nedime è una madre che da anni lavora perché le famiglie comprendano e sostengano lə proprə figliə LGBTQIAP+: essere incarcerata nell’operazione “La mia famiglia è al sicuro” restituisce quasi brutalmente il paradosso di questa politica. Janset Kalan, storica attivista trans, dal carcere di Sincan ha invece chiesto che l’attenzione non rimanga concentrata soltanto sulle persone più conosciute e sostenute dal movimento. Lei riceve visite, ha avvocatə, amicə, giornalistə e reti internazionali che sanno dove si trova. Molte altre persone trans detenute no. Il suo appello è semplice: «Ricordate le persone trans detenute a Sincan e in tutte le altre carceri; fate in modo che non rimangano sole».




Non è un appello astratto. Kaos GL denuncia dalle carceri perquisizioni corporali nude forzate, insulti e minacce omotransfobiche, isolamento, difficoltà nell’accesso ai farmaci e altri maltrattamenti. Circa metà dellə proprə compagnə detenutə sarebbe tenuta in isolamento. Le denunce sono state successivamente riprese anche da Amnesty International.




La risposta alla repressione ha ben presto superato i confini turchi. Il 21 settembre più di 450 organizzazioni di oltre 65 paesi hanno sottoscritto un appello comune per la liberazione dellə detenutə e contro la criminalizzazione del movimento LGBTQIAP+. Tra le firmatarie ci sono insieme reti queer, femministe, antiviolenza e per i diritti umani. L’appello denuncia esplicitamente una più ampia politica anti-gender fondata sul controllo patriarcale di corpi, identità e relazioni e il tentativo di trasformare attività legali – associazionismo, advocacy, pubblicazioni, raccolta fondi e finanziamenti internazionali – in elementi di un’inchiesta criminale. (

Appello internazionale “Stop the Criminalisation of the LGBTI+ Movement in Turkey”

)




Il 21 settembre ad Ankara il movimento ha rovesciato il nome scelto dal governo per i rastrellamenti: “La mia famiglia non è al sicuro. La mia famiglia è in carcere, la mia famiglia è in stato di fermo”.




È forse il modo più preciso per raccontare quello che sta succedendo. Perché la famiglia evocata dal governo non comprende le famiglie che sostengono figliə queer e trans, le famiglie scelte, le reti di cura e solidarietà costruite dal movimento. La repressione prova a spezzare proprio quelle relazioni: oscurando i luoghi in cui ci si incontra, arrestando chi organizza, isolando chi finisce in carcere.




Da qui, però, resta anche una domanda che riguarda noi. Sulla stampa italiana questo rastrellamento ha ricevuto finora pochissimo spazio, nonostante segni un cambio di passo nella criminalizzazione e nella repressione delle persone LGBTQIAP+ in Turchia. Perché una repressione di queste dimensioni fatica tanto a diventare notizia? Le nostre vite valgono, ma una parte dell’informazione italiana non sembra attribuire loro lo stesso peso. E anche il silenzio produce un racconto: stabilisce quali vite meritano attenzione, quali violenze diventano notizia e quali possono restare invisibili. Anche questo silenzio assordante è propaganda.




Babs Mazzotti




NdA: In questo articolo ho scelto di utilizzare la sigla LGBTQIAP+ perché si parla di soggettività e mobilitazioni diverse. Nei comunicati e negli appelli diffusi in questi giorni dal movimento turco ricorrono invece soprattutto le sigle più ridotte LGBTI+ e LGBT, che ho mantenuto quando riprendo direttamente le loro formulazioni.




L'articolo 

“La mia famiglia è in carcere”. Turchia: repressione e resistenza dei movimenti LGBTQIAP+

 proviene da 

.

author: Gustavo Faleiros
title: Religião nas eleições com pitadas de meio ambiente
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Ligando os pontos, enviada toda quinta-feira. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui

.







Não tenho boas pesquisas de opinião para provar o argumento. Tenho uma percepção. Pode ser até mesmo uma crença, uma questão de fé…




Eu acredito que o tema do meio ambiente nos une. Não importa a coloração política ou a religião que você professa; em princípio, estamos irmanados na preocupação com a água que vamos beber, o ar que respiramos e a boa comida em nossos pratos.




A polêmica sobre 

Nossa Senhora Aparecida

, que agora domina o debate eleitoral, me fez lembrar de um exemplo em que a questão ambiental ajuda a unir mundos diferentes. Existe uma 

iniciativa inter religiosa para a proteção das florestas

. Criada há sete anos por várias organizações não governamentais e a seção de meio ambiente das Nações Unidas, esta aliança tem colocado lado-a-lado pastores, padres, rabinos, pais-de-santo e pajés para discutir a proteção do meio ambiente, em especial da Amazônia.




Quem me contou os resultados desta iniciativa foi seu facilitador no Brasil, Carlos Vicente, engenheiro florestal acreano que por muitos anos foi um dos assessores mais próximos da ex-ministra do Meio Ambiente e atual candidata ao Senado por São Paulo, Marina Silva. Em muitas conferências nas quais nos encontramos, ele me relatou com um brilho nos olhos como estes líderes religiosos aparentemente tão distantes em seu dia-a-dia convergiam em uma visão sobre a importância de respeitar a vida e a sacralidade da natureza.




Algo que Carlos destacou foi o profundo impacto que uma visita ao Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (INPE) causou a um pastor evangélico. A viagem à sede da instituição, em São José dos Campos, no interior de São Paulo, ocorreu na época em que Bolsonaro e membros de seu governo, como o General Heleno e o então ministro do Meio Ambiente, Ricardo Salles, atacavam o INPE. Os cientistas apenas faziam seu trabalho ao divulgar os dados que mostravam aumento do desmatamento. Depois de entender como funcionavam os sistemas de monitoramento, o pastor defendeu a proteção da Amazônia em um de seus sermões.




A lembrança do que me contou Carlos Vicente em meio a este turbilhão que mistura Nossa Senhora com eleições me deu um pouco de esperança. Me confirmou algo que eu já havia sentido nas eleições de 2018 e logo no início do governo Bolsonaro, quando houve a crise das queimadas. O tema da Amazônia e do combate ao desmatamento é um caminho de diálogo com indecisos. Em conversas casuais, é difícil encontrar alguém que defenda abertamente derrubadas, poluição e maus-tratos aos animais.




Minha impressão se tornou então mais forte com o que aconteceu em 2019, logo após o fatídico dia 18 de agosto, quando a fumaça das queimadas na Amazônia transformou em noite uma tarde de São Paulo. Aquelas imagens, seguidas por investigações jornalísticas que mostraram uma articulação de produtores rurais para celebrarem um Dia do Fogo, geraram uma mobilização nacional e internacional frente aos descalabros da política anti-ambiental de Bolsonaro.




Esta pressão da opinião pública fez com que Bolsonaro tivesse que recuar. Lembrem-se que o vice-presidente Hamilton Mourão foi designado para apaziguar os ânimos, fazendo a interlocução com parceiros históricos do Brasil nos investimentos em conservação, como a Alemanha e a Noruega. 




Enquanto o mundo estava cobrando o governo Bolsonaro, a questão ambiental e a Amazônia estavam também no centro da Igreja Católica. O Papa Francisco fez das mudanças climáticas e da proteção à Amazônia uma das principais marcas de seu pontificado.

 Realizou o primeiro encontro de bispos para propor uma ação conjunta com os povos indígenas, 

o Sínodo da Amazônia.

 Estendeu os braços aos melhores cientistas do mundo no tema. Os brasileiros Carlos Nobre, do INPE, e Ima Vieira, do Museu Emílio Goeldi, foram alguns dos que tiveram o ouvido atento de Francisco.




Por isso, não me parece aleatório que Flávio Bolsonaro tenha resolvido atacar a Confederação Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil (CNBB) para achar um culpado ao dano que lhe faz a polêmica da Nossa Senhora. Os bispos sempre estiveram antenados com a questão ambiental e suas campanhas, ao longo dos anos, destacaram temas como o direito à terra, a proteção das terras indígenas e contra a estatização do acesso à água. A CNBB sempre foi uma defensora do meio ambiente como algo primordial na conduta de uma instituição religiosa.




Durante a presidência de Bolsonaro foram muitos os embates com a CNBB e outras alas da Igreja Católica, como a Comissão Pastoral da Terra e o Conselho Indigenista Missionário. Estes braços da igreja foram fiéis à sua missão e apontaram os desmantelamentos que estavam sendo promovidos por Bolsonaro. Assim como fez seu pai, Flávio ataca a CNBB pois sabe que ela será uma instituição que não deixará ocultas as maldades planejadas contra os territórios.




Cientes de seu papel em defender “a Casa Comum”, os bispos da Região Norte 1 da CNBB, que inclui as dioceses do Amazonas e de Roraima, divulgaram no último dia 23 um comunicado para conclamar aos brasileiros que levem em consideração as questões socioambientais no momento do voto. “O cardeal Leonardo Steiner, Arcebispo Metropolitano de Manaus e presidente do Regional Norte 1, nos recorda que na Carta encíclica Laudato Sí, publicada em 2015, Papa Francisco defende que o cuidado com o meio ambiente é inseparável da justiça social, da dignidade humana e da vida em sociedade”, diz um dos trechos 

da carta aberta

.




Eu arrisco dizer que a Amazônia é tão icônica como uma santa. E não só para os brasileiros: o mundo venera a Amazônia. Infelizmente, e isso não é fake news, há muitos dispostos a destruir essa maravilha da natureza. Divina? Não sei. Aí, vai de cada um.

author: Faisal Ali, Hassan Alnaser, Hazem Tharwat, Kidus Lemma
title: How a war in Tigray could set off a more complex fight
content:
For much of the past year, tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region had been steadily escalating toward confrontation.




The threat for those in Tigray, as much as for those in the wider region, was that the area could tip back into the kind of war that devastated the state between 2020 and 2022, but, this time, with a supercharged regional dimension. Officials in Addis Ababa and Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, have traded increasingly hostile accusations as the peace established at Pretoria frayed, while intermittent clashes and drone strikes produced episodes of serious violence. 




From the sidelines, Eritrea, Egypt, Somalia and Sudan — a pragmatic, loosely aligned anti-Ethiopia coalition — looked on. Then, on September 20, a drone struck a truck carrying more than 41 tons of food aid for displaced people in northwestern Tigray, setting the vehicle and its cargo ablaze.




Aftermath of a drone strike on a humanitarian aid truck in northwestern Tigray, September 22. Courtesy: @JoeTseGy on X




Three days later, Tigrayan forces seized three airports across the region. Fighting then spread beyond Tigray into neighboring Afar and Amhara. The federal government accused the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) of launching an offensive, while Tigrayan authorities said their forces were responding to federal attacks involving aircraft, drones, artillery and ground troops. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Tigray after the airports were taken, while a Tigrayan official told Mada Masr that the confrontation has now become a “full war.”




The fighting broke out only days after the TPLF joined six other armed organizations in the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival. The members have pledged to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration. The coalition brought the TPLF together with the Amhara Fano National Movement, whose fighters had fought alongside federal forces against Tigray during the previous war, as well as the Oromo Liberation Army and movements from Ethiopia’s Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. 




Tigrayan and Amhara forces remain divided by unresolved claims over western and southern Tigray, making their decision to enter the same alliance one of the clearest signs of how Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts have been realigning since the end of the previous war.




An Ethiopian political source who was close to the early discussions between several of the groups tells Mada Masr that contacts had been developing for roughly a year. The source says he lost interest as some of the participants established closer relationships with Sudan and what he had initially understood as a more political process moved, in his view, toward military coordination. 




Whatever the precise role played by those external relationships in bringing the alliance together, Ethiopian officials had already begun treating contacts between domestic armed opponents and neighboring states as parts of the same security problem. 




That concern had become increasingly public by May. After Ethiopian opposition figures and Eritrean officials met in Port Sudan under the banner of Tsimdo, army chief Berhanu Jula described what was taking shape as a “combined convergence” of Ethiopia’s adversaries. 




In June, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, predicted that an Eritrean-backed TPLF attack would come during the rainy season, while Abiy declared that, despite coordination between Sudan, Eritrea and Ethiopia’s armed groups, Ethiopia had “not an iota of fear.”




In July, Abiy described an “axe politics” in which the TPLF formed the blade, Eritrea the wooden handle and an unnamed external actor the hand wielding it. The metaphor was polemical, but it reflected a security view in which domestic armed opposition, neighboring governments and contested borderlands were increasingly being read together.




With the outbreak of fighting, which has shown no signs of abating since the end of last week, the question now is will the fighting remain confined to the Ethiopian interior or will the convergence of the last six months turn Ethiopia’s war into a new, complex regional fight to remake the Horn of Africa?




…




The significance of that convergence lies partly in the weakening of a regional hierarchy that for almost three decades gave Ethiopia greater freedom than most of its neighbors to operate across the Horn’s porous borders. After the upheavals of 1989-1991, Ethiopia emerged with the region’s strongest state and security apparatus and the greatest capacity to project influence into neighboring countries. Somalia collapsed and fragmented as its military regime came apart. Sudan retained a functioning center despite repeated peripheral wars. Eritrea became increasingly isolated since the mid-2000s, while Egypt’s 

direct role in the Horn diminished

. Addis Ababa was consequently better placed than most of its neighbors to operate through their internal divisions without exposing its own to the same degree.




That advantage has narrowed, while the means through which Addis Ababa seeks to preserve it have changed. Sudan’s political center has fractured into civil war, and Ethiopia itself has come to face armed movements across several regions. Eritrea has returned to active regional balancing, while Egypt has rebuilt relationships with states around Ethiopia, including deeper military and security cooperation with Somalia and closer ties with Eritrea and the Sudanese military-led authorities. Gulf states and other outside powers, meanwhile, operate not only through recognized governments but through ports, air routes, companies, armed groups and regional administrations. These relationships have not settled into stable blocs, and their participants can cooperate in one theater while competing in another, but they have made it easier for conflicts that once belonged to separate political arenas to feed into one another.




“The region as it currently exists will not hold and should not hold,” Abiy recently told one foreign interlocutor.




Many of those pressures intersect around Ethiopia. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) ties Addis Ababa to Egypt and Sudan through the Nile, while Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign maritime access has strained relations with Somalia and sharpened Eritrean concerns over the Red Sea. Tigray’s western frontier opens into Sudan, and the Fano insurgency runs through Amhara toward many of the same borderlands. Benishangul-Gumuz contains the GERD and faces Sudan’s Blue Nile State, where the civil war has moved toward Ethiopian territory, while Ethiopia’s agreement with Somaliland connected its search for the sea to Somali sovereignty disputes and Egyptian security policy in the Horn.




Over the last six months, as the beat of the drum for an all out regional war has grown louder and louder, Mada Masr has spoken with Ethiopian military, intelligence and government officials, Sudanese officers and former diplomats, Tigrayan commanders and political figures, Eritrean sources close to decision-making circles and Egyptian officials, all of whom speak of how these theaters are being pulled together through Ethiopia’s changing regional position and vision for what the region should look like. 




What is clear is that Abiy does not see the status quo as a thing that is worth holding onto. “The region as it currently exists will not hold and should not hold,” he recently told one foreign interlocutor, who relayed the exchange to Mada Masr. 




That outlook has increasingly translated into an effort to use the Horn’s fragmented political geography to expand Ethiopia’s room for maneuver. Along the Sudanese frontier, that means treating territory beyond Ethiopia’s borders as strategic depth, from which threats to the federal state can be contained before they reach the center. On the Red Sea, it has meant dealing directly with Somaliland in pursuit of a maritime outlet, even when doing so cuts across Somalia’s claim to sovereignty. Tensions with Eritrea have brought the same ambition into the question of Assab, where Ethiopian demands for access to the sea increasingly collide with Eritrean concerns over sovereignty. 




From the signing of the memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland in 2024.




Those moves have developed alongside a much closer relationship with the United Arab Emirates, which has given Addis Ababa access to investment, transport infrastructure and military technology at a time when Ethiopia’s own state capacity has been strained by internal war. Former Ethiopian officials describe that relationship as increasingly important not only to Abiy’s regional ambitions but to his effort to consolidate power at home. They also describe the search for Red Sea access as carrying a more personal political weight for the prime minister, who is looking for a defining achievement that can stand apart from the towering political legacy of former Ethiopian ruler Meles Zenawi. 




…




The calculations now taking shape along Ethiopia’s borders reflect a change in the basis of the regional power Addis Ababa had accumulated after the upheavals of 1989–1991. During that period, Ethiopia was better placed to use the political divisions of neighboring states than its neighbors were to exploit Ethiopia’s own. The state Abiy inherited in 2018 had built that advantage through a powerful security apparatus and regional diplomatic clout under the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front, the coalition in which the TPLF had held the dominant position. That reach was reinforced by a post-September 11 international role that made Ethiopia a central partner for Washington during the so-called War on Terror. By the time Abiy took office, however, the domestic political settlement supporting that system was already coming apart.




The Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a TPLF-led coalition, ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. 

Political scientists Harry Verhoeven and Michael Woldemariam, who interviewed a dozen senior Western and regional officials for a 2022 academic paper, 

described

 Ethiopia’s place in United States strategy during that period as that of an African “anchor state.”

 That meant an internationally backed role as regional enforcer and developmental leader, combined with an ability to influence political outcomes beyond its borders. The relationship did not create Ethiopia’s regional power, but it reinforced a system in which Addis Ababa’s diplomatic and security reach extended well beyond its immediate territory.




The GERD added another dimension to that position, after construction began under Meles in 2011 in Benishangul-Gumuz, close to Sudan, placing an enormous Ethiopian infrastructure project on the river that supplies most of Egypt’s fresh water. Ethiopia presented the dam as a development project and an expression of its right to use Nile waters originating in its territory, while Cairo and Addis Ababa became locked in a dispute over its filling and operation and the implications for downstream water security. The project made a central part of its domestic development strategy inseparable from its regional position.




The Blue Nile passes through the GERD, near Guba, Ethiopia, on December 26, 2019. Courtesy: Eduardo Soteras/AFP




Abiy therefore came to power in April 2018 at the head of a state that still possessed much of this regional reach, even as the domestic political arrangement that had sustained it was breaking down. The EPRDF remained in government, but the internal hierarchy through which the TPLF had dominated the coalition was fraying after years of protest and repression. Abiy inherited the institutions and relationships of the old order but not the same political cohesion that had held them together.




“I would fight and die for America.”




Abiy’s familiarity with Washington predated his rise to the premiership. He had spent part of his earlier career inside Ethiopia’s intelligence and cyber-security apparatus, where his work brought him into contact with US security agencies. 

Reflecting on that period in a 2022 interview with The New Yorker, he 

said

: “I was the one who would send intelligence from this part of the world to the N.S.A., on Sudan and Yemen and Somalia.

 The N.S.A. knows me. I would fight and die for America.” 




Verhoeven and Woldemariam argued that Washington consequently saw Abiy’s arrival in 2018 as an opportunity to reinvent its relationship with an indispensable regional partner, giving strong political support to a transition in which his domestic position remained much less settled. Abiy, in turn, presented himself as unusually compatible with Washington’s political and strategic preferences. He was more overtly religious than his secular left-wing predecessors, cultivated relationships with US political figures and signalled that Ethiopia under his leadership would be less dependent on China. 




Abiy Ahmed meets with former US Vice President Mike Pence. July 27, 2018




For Verhoeven and Woldemariam, that enthusiasm did more than legitimize Abiy’s transition. Washington’s strong backing, while Abiy’s position at home was still unsettled, made a more uncompromising effort to consolidate power seem less risky. In their account, the attempt to rebuild the US relationship with its Ethiopian anchor helped weaken the political settlement on which that relationship had depended.




His first year brought substantial changes as the government released political prisoners, loosened restrictions on political and media activity, welcomed opposition figures back into the country and promised competitive elections, while also beginning to shift economic policy away from parts of the EPRDF’s state-led development model. Foreign governments responded enthusiastically, and Gulf states, with Washington’s encouragement, moved quickly to support the new leadership..




Abiy’s 

reconciliation

 with Eritrea appeared to extend that political opening across the region. Ethiopia and Eritrea had remained locked for almost two decades in the “no war, no peace” order that followed their 1998–2000 border war, until Abiy accepted the boundary ruling his predecessors had resisted and traveled to Asmara in July 2018 to restore relations with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki. 

The Norwegian Nobel Committee 

awarded

 him the Peace Prize the following year for his initiative in ending the stalemate with Eritrea and for broader efforts toward peace and international cooperation.




For a period, those changes appeared to offer a way to renew Ethiopian regional leadership while rebuilding the political center at home, but the domestic project exposed a deeper disagreement over what should replace the old order. 




Most of the EPRDF and its allied regional parties were brought into the new Prosperity Party in late 2019, which Abiy and his supporters presented as a way to create a broader national political organization and weaken divisions embedded in the old coalition structure. The TPLF refused to join. Supporters regarded the new party as a means of strengthening national unity, while opponents feared greater centralization would come at the expense of regional autonomy and the multinational logic of Ethiopia’s federal system.




The merger did not by itself cause the confrontation that followed, but it made the political rupture increasingly visible, as Tigray remained under the TPLF while its former coalition partners reorganized around Abiy in Addis Ababa. The dispute widened in 2020 after national elections were postponed during the COVID-19 pandemic and Tigray proceeded with its own regional vote, which the federal government rejected. By then, each side increasingly regarded the other as acting outside the constitutional order.




War began in November 2020 and quickly drew in the Eritrean government, which had its own score to settle with the TPLF. Eritrean forces fought alongside the Ethiopian federal military and Amhara armed formations against a TPLF that Isaias had regarded as his principal regional enemy since the 1998–2000 war. Sudanese forces meanwhile moved into parts of disputed Fashaga as the fighting unfolded, while tens of thousands of refugees crossed into eastern Sudan.




The Pretoria agreement, 

signed

 by the federal government, and the TPLF in November 2022 ended the principal war between them, providing for a cessation of hostilities, humanitarian access and a process of disarmament and restoration of federal authority.

 It did not reconstruct the political order that had preceded the conflict, and Eritrea was not a party to the agreement. Territorial disputes, the pace and terms of disarmament as well as Tigray’s relationship with the center remained contested, while tactical alliances produced by the war began to shift again.




Ethiopian government representative Redwan Hussien and Tigray delegate Getachew Reda attend signing of the AU-led negotiations to resolve the conflict in northern Ethiopia, in Pretoria, South Africa, November 2, 2022. Courtesy: REUTERS/Siphiwe Sibeko




Ethiopia emerged from the conflict with a diminished international position and a more fragmented domestic security environment, weakening the institutional basis of the regional role it had occupied during the EPRDF period, without necessarily eliminating its ability to project power beyond its borders. What had been damaged was the particular combination of domestic cohesion, Western backing and regional security relationships that had underpinned that position.




The deterioration in Addis Ababa’s relationship with Washington was one measure of that loss. 

A former Kenyan ambassador tells Mada Masr that the US deepened its security ties with Nairobi during the same period, eventually making Kenya the first sub-Saharan African country to be 

designated

 a major non-NATO ally in 2024.

 

Addis Ababa’s relationship with Washington, by contrast, deteriorated sharply during the Tigray war, including through restrictions on military cooperation and weapons-related sanctions that were only 

lifted

 in September.




“Addis Ababa regards the restoration of military cooperation with Washington as part of a wider effort to rebuild state and military capacity.”




A source in Ethiopia’s National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) tells Mada Masr that Addis Ababa regards the restoration of military cooperation with Washington and the reopening of defense channels that were restricted during the Tigray war as part of a wider effort to rebuild state and military capacity. 




In the source’s account, the value of renewed cooperation extends beyond weapons to training, communications, reconnaissance, surveillance and logistical systems degraded by years of internal conflict. Reconstructing the institutional security relationship with Washington, the source says, is therefore seen in Addis Ababa as one means of recovering the ability to maneuver beyond Ethiopia’s borders rather than remain absorbed by internal wars.




…




Rebuilding the old relationship with Washington is only one part of that effort. Abiy has also sought to compensate for the erosion of the EPRDF-era architecture through a different set of relationships, relying more heavily on direct ties with foreign leaders, Gulf capital and military technology, and access to regional infrastructure that does not depend on the institutional channels through which Ethiopia exercised influence in the past.




Abiy is haunted by the shadow of Meles Zenawi, a former senior Ethiopian official says.




That search for a new basis of power has also become bound up with Abiy’s effort to distinguish his own political legacy from the era he inherited. “He is haunted by the shadow of Meles Zenawi,” a former senior Ethiopian official tells Mada Masr. He knows that the dam is, ultimately, Meles’s achievement, the official adds, arguing that Abiy is on a quest to find his own defining legacy.




Crowds gather in mourning following the death of former Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi. August 22, 2012. Courtesy: AFP




This quest has led the prime minister to embark on a brand of highly personalized politics, marked by distrust of traditional Ethiopian institutions, another former Ethiopian government official who spoke to Mada Masr in 2024 says.  




In the second former official’s account, major decisions have become concentrated around the prime minister and shaped through his relationships with individual foreign leaders, with the Foreign Ministry playing a smaller role in matters that would once have passed through established diplomatic channels. 




“Ethiopia’s relationship with the UAE increasingly brought Addis Ababa into a sphere where infrastructure carried security as well as commercial value.”




The official argues that this made policy more dependent on personal relationships and more liable to abrupt shifts as Abiy sought investment, diplomatic backing and military capacity.




The UAE has become one of the most important pillars of that newer architecture. Financial support from Abu Dhabi during the opening years of Abiy’s premiership developed alongside a much wider network of commercial, military and strategic interests across the Horn. The former Ethiopian official points particularly to Berbera and the transport connections running inland from Somaliland, arguing that Ethiopia’s relationship with the UAE increasingly brought Addis Ababa into a regional infrastructure in which ports, roads and investment carried security as well as commercial value.




The attraction of maritime infrastructure grew as Abiy made Ethiopia’s lack of direct access to the sea an increasingly prominent national-security issue.




For the first former Ethiopian official, returning Ethiopia’s direct access to the Red Sea was to be Abiy’s way of differentiating himself from his predecessor. 




In an October 2023 speech, he described the country as trapped in a “geographical prison” and argued that its growing population and economy could not remain indefinitely dependent on arrangements made through neighboring states.




The memorandum signed with Somaliland on January 1, 2024 put that ambition into territorial form. Somaliland said the agreement would give Ethiopia access to 20 km of coastline while opening a path toward possible Ethiopian recognition of the territory’s claim to independence. A Somaliland read out 

said

 the agreement would hold for 50 years, while Ethiopia’s version said the agreement was permanent. Somalia rejected the arrangement as a violation of its sovereignty, while Ethiopia said its objective was to secure access to the sea rather than initiate a confrontation.




Turkey-mediated talks later 

reduced

 the immediate confrontation between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu without resolving the strategic question that had produced it.

 Berbera remained important not only because it offered Ethiopia an alternative commercial and possible naval outlet, but because the port sits inside a wider UAE-linked network of infrastructure and security relationships across the Horn.




Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan poses with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed following a press conference in Ankara, Turkey, December 11, 2024. Courtesy: Reuters




The Ethiopian NISS source says the government treats the search for a durable route to the sea as part of the same effort to rebuild Ethiopia’s regional position, with Addis Ababa seeking a long-term arrangement that would give it a stable maritime and commercial presence rather than leave access dependent on short-term political bargains. 




The source says Ethiopian institutions are also closely following emerging Red Sea security arrangements and want the country to move from being a landlocked state affected by decisions taken around the sea toward one that participates in shaping them. They add that discussions with regional and international actors have focused on ensuring Ethiopian interests in ports and trade routes are taken into account, while any eventual security role would center on coordination, information-sharing and the protection of commercial interests, rather than direct involvement in Yemen.




…




The regional importance of ports such as Berbera extends beyond Ethiopia’s own search for access to the sea. A former Sudanese diplomat who served in Addis Ababa describes large investments in ports, agriculture and transport as capable of acquiring “quasi-sovereign” characteristics where central governments exercise limited control, because the states and companies financing infrastructure can influence which routes function, where resources move and which local authorities benefit from them. 




In borderlands where formal authority already overlaps with armed groups, regional administrations and commercial networks, control over logistical and agricultural systems can therefore carry strategic weight alongside a conventional military presence.




Alex de Waal, an author and veteran regional expert, places that process inside a wider transformation in the political geography of the Horn, which he tells Mada Masr has increasingly been integrated into the “commercial, security and political perimeter of the wider Middle East.” Arab states are central to that expansion, but Turkey, Israel and Iran also operate within it, bringing forms of competition developed across the Red Sea into political systems where authority has long extended unevenly beyond recognized capitals and borders.




Sovereignty in the Horn is increasingly “sliced” territorially and “diced” into functions that were conventionally held together by a single state, de Waal says.




The UAE, de Waal argues, has gone further than most in adapting to that environment. He describes Abu Dhabi as the region’s most developed “political marketplace” operator, building networks of patronage and influence according to the political and strategic value of particular actors, rather than the formal architecture of the states to which they belong. 




Abu Dhabi crown prince Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan walks with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed during Abiy’s visit to Abu Dhabi. January 29, 2022. Courtesy: Abdalla Al Neyadi/Ministry of Presidential Affairs/WAM via AP




That strategy depends on the fragmentation of sovereignty itself in states that have historically struggled to exercise it across the full extent of their jurisdiction. De Waal describes sovereignty as increasingly “sliced” territorially, and “diced” into functions that were conventionally held together by a single state, allowing authority over defense, foreign relations, commerce or particular pieces of territory to be dealt with separately. The actors within that ecosystem built by the UAE can include recognized governments, such as Ethiopia, regional administrations, such as Puntland and Somaliland, and armed actors operating outside conventional state chains of command, like the Rapid Support Forces. 




They do not all serve the same function or operate in the same way, de Waal tells Mada Masr, but they are connected through logistics corridors, cash and personal relationships from which they all benefit. The commercial corridors built through those relationships can also carry military value because ports generate roads, warehouses, customs arrangements and transport systems that can move weapons, personnel and military technology as well as ordinary trade, he adds. 




The former Sudanese diplomat describes a regional geography increasingly organized around those systems, in which ostensibly commercial infrastructure can become one of the means through which military and geopolitical goals are pursued.




When Ethiopia needed to mobilize this alternate geography for a specific goal, it was able stitch together roads, people and ports of different stripes. 




“Significant parts of the military leadership were kept unaware as the Assosa operation was built up,” says an Ethiopian military source.




This is exactly what happened when Addis Ababa made the decision to throw its hat more decisively into the Sudan war.




An Ethiopian military source tells Mada Masr that Somaliland’s Berbera Port has become a principal entry point for supplies destined for the RSF, with material moving overland through Ethiopia toward the Benishangul-Gumuz region. 




Berbera Port. Courtesy: Shutterstock




An official at Ethiopian Shipping and Logistics and another at the Ethiopian Transport Ministry separately tell Mada Masr that a designated group of 10 company trucks had been used to move weapons through the country, while two Ethiopian military sources place the other end of the route around Assosa, close to Sudan’s Blue Nile frontier.




The two military sources describe Assosa and the surrounding areas as part of a logistical system serving the RSF. 




The first Ethiopian military source says the Mao-Komo special district has been used for logistics and medical facilities. 




The source tells Mada Masr that the Ethiopian National Defense Forces base at Assosa supplied heavily armed vehicles to the RSF and forces allied with Abdel Aziz al-Hilu’s Sudan People’s Liberation Movement–North (SPLM-N) in their push to take the Sudanese city of Kurmuk. 




The development of that infrastructure also reflects the increasingly personalized security decision-making described by the second former Ethiopian government official. 




The second Ethiopian military source tells Mada Masr that significant parts of the military leadership were kept unaware as the Assosa operation was built up. The camp was developed secretly under Getachew Gudina, a senior intelligence commander, with close supervision from Abiy, the source says, adding that the military chief-of-staff did not become aware of the operation until the deployment stage, when equipment and logistical supplies began moving into place.




In February, Reuters 

reported

 that Ethiopia was hosting a large camp in Benishangul-Gumuz where around 4,300 fighters were training for the RSF, drawing on satellite imagery, an Ethiopian security document and interviews with 15 sources.

 Several of those sources accused the UAE of financing the camp’s construction and said the recruits were expected to deploy toward Blue Nile, while the news agency also documented expansion at Assosa airport associated with drone operations. Ethiopia did not respond to Reuters’ questions about the camp, while the UAE denied financing or supporting the RSF.




Across the border, Blue Nile was becoming more closely integrated into Sudan’s civil war as the RSF and Hilu’s SPLM-N faction pushed against Sudanese army positions around Yabus, Bau and Kurmuk. Hilu’s faction joined the RSF-aligned Tasis coalition after spending much of the earlier war outside the principal confrontation between the Sudanese military and the RSF, giving the latter experienced local forces in terrain adjoining Ethiopia and South Sudan. Sudanese officials have accused drones operating from the Ethiopian side of supporting those operations, allegations Addis Ababa has denied.




The geography helps explain why activity around Assosa carries consequences beyond Blue Nile itself. 




Kurmuk, which has regularly 

changed

 

hands

 between the RSF and the army, sits directly against the Ethiopian frontier, immediately west of Benishangul-Gumuz, while the GERD lies a short distance to the east.

 Farther north, the same frontier runs toward Fashaga and western Tigray, while roads and communities to the south connect Blue Nile to South Sudan. The route described by the Ethiopian transport and military sources runs from Berbera across Ethiopian transport networks toward Assosa and onward to the Sudanese border. 




The RSF was unusually well placed to operate through such a system because its own growth had occurred partly outside the conventional chain of state authority. 




It emerged from the Janjaweed militias used by the Sudanese government in Darfur before receiving formal recognition in 2013 and greater legal autonomy in 2017. Khartoum repeatedly assigned the force responsibilities in peripheral territories where the state had limited reach, while RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo  later positioned the group inside the European Union-backed architecture for controlling migration along Sudan’s borders and deployed fighters to Yemen as part of the Saudi and Emirati-led coalition.




Sudan researcher Sarra Majdoub 

described

 Hemedti in 2019 as a “governor” of the country’s margins, whose responsibilities across Darfur, Blue Nile and South Kordofan allowed him to accumulate political and economic power alongside his military role.

 She also called the RSF a “Frankenstein’s monster,” warning that the order that had empowered the force might eventually find itself threatened by it. By the time then-Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir was removed that year, Hemedti had already converted power accumulated on Sudan’s peripheries into an independent position with substantial foreign relationships of his own. Four years later, the RSF turned its weapons against the Sudanese army.




The war greatly expanded those relationships into a logistical system stretching across neighboring states and commercial jurisdictions, making Assosa one component of a much larger network rather than a self-contained supply route. 




***




Ethiopia’s place within these relations is particularly consequential because the same permeability that can give the RSF access into Sudan can also give Ethiopian armed movements access to territory beyond the federal state’s control.




A group of Tigrayan fighters, known as Army 70, operates from the Sudanese border. 

The force is made up of thousands of fighters and officers of Tigrayan origin who once served in Ethiopia’s federal armed forces before defecting or fleeing into Sudan after the outbreak of the Tigray war, a Sudanese source informed of the fighters movements previously 

told

 Mada Masr.

 




In early August, Army 70 crossed from Sudan into Ethiopia and targeted Ethiopian military forces near the border area of Shererina. 




Earlier this year, when a Sudanese security attaché in Ethiopia spoke to Mada Masr, renewed war in the region remained a possibility rather than the reality it became in September. He described Tigray as a continuing vulnerability for the Ethiopian state because another political or military mobilization could draw on territory outside Ethiopian control, giving particular importance to the Sudan-facing crossings that could provide Tigrayan forces with external “logistical depth” in another confrontation with the center.




“Ethiopia recognizes we’re no longer facing a fleeting disruption, but a comprehensive process of dismantling and reassembling the Sudanese state.” 




Several Sudanese sources describe the frontier from a different perspective, in which the breakdown of authority inside Sudan has created a vacuum for neighboring states and armed actors to operate through territories Khartoum can no longer regulate in the same way. 




“If you ask me what Ethiopia wants from Sudan at this defining moment and why it has intervened with all its weight [in the Sudan war],” a former senior Sudanese security and intelligence officer told Mada Masr earlier this year, “the answer lies in the fact that Addis Ababa, more than any other country, recognizes that we are no longer facing a fleeting disruption, but rather what I would call a comprehensive process of dismantling and reassembling the Sudanese state.” 




The era in which borders carried “the weight of rigid sovereignty,” he continued, was giving way to “a world of fluid borders and spaces.”




In his account, that fragmentation has increased the leverage available to Addis Ababa around longstanding disputes over the Fashaga triangle and the GERD because influence can increasingly be exercised through local balances of power that Sudan’s central state is less able to manage. 




A former senior officer in Sudan’s eastern zone describes Fashaga, in more practical terms, as an area in which control is accumulated through cultivation of land, roads, rural infrastructure and security presence. During the Bashir era, an arrangement allowed Amhara farmers to cultivate land inside Sudan and return seasonally, but it broke down during the Tigray war when Sudan moved to halt incursions by Amhara militias accompanying Ethiopian farmers. Formal claims to sovereignty remain important, but the cost of reversing arrangements on the ground grows as communities, production and military positions become embedded in them, narrowing the distinction between economic activity and security control.




For Tigrayan actors, the federal government’s concern over external “logistical depth” therefore appears in reverse. 




Access to Sudan is a “matter of life and death that transcends the calculations of temporary governments.”




A prominent TPLF commander tells Mada Masr that weak central authority on the Sudanese side presented less of a threat to Tigray than an opening that could prevent the region from being sealed off. He argues that the Ethiopian government’s attempts to establish a lasting security cordon around Fashaga and Gadarif ran against much older social and logistical relationships crossing the frontier, and he describes Sudanese territory as Tigray’s principal source of strategic depth outside Ethiopia.




Those relationships predate the present crisis by decades. During the struggle against the Derg in the 1970s and 1980s, Sudan provided Tigrayan fighters with refuge and served as a corridor for humanitarian and military supplies. The networks involved eastern Sudanese communities as well as regional governments, making them harder to eliminate through the closure of formal crossings alone.




Federal security officials consequently regarded an open route into Sudan as one of the ways a renewed Tigrayan mobilization could acquire supplies and room for maneuver. The TPLF commander describes the same geography as protection against isolation, calling access to Sudan a “matter of life and death that transcends the calculations of temporary governments.” Those competing views of the frontier were recorded before the September fighting again turned the question of Tigray’s external access from a contingency into an immediate security concern.




…




Ethiopia’s effort to acquire maritime access produced another series of reactions to the east. 




Somalia treated the 2024 memorandum between Ethiopia and Somaliland as a challenge to its territorial integrity and deepened its relationship with Cairo as its dispute with Addis Ababa intensified. Egypt and Somalia signed a military cooperation protocol in August 2024, after which Egyptian military aircraft delivered weapons and ammunition to Mogadishu, while Cairo later offered forces for the African Union mission that succeeded the African Union Transmission Mission in Somalia (ATMIS).




Ethiopian officials increasingly interpreted those relationships less as support for Somalia and more as an attempt to constrain Ethiopia. 

Redwan Hussein, Ethiopia’s intelligence chief, 

accused

 Cairo of acting from “animosity toward Ethiopia,” while Ethiopia’s ambassador to Somalia later described Egypt’s regional posture in the language of “encirclement.”

 




Cairo describes its expansion of regional relationships through a different security logic, in which the Horn has become increasingly important because the issues of Nile water security, Red Sea navigation and approaches to the Suez Canal intersect there.




“Cairo treats the region as a form of strategic depth to protect interests that can no longer be addressed through the Nile dispute alone.”




An Egyptian official responsible for the Horn file tells Mada Masr that Cairo consequently treats the region as a form of strategic depth, with relationships in Somalia, Eritrea, Sudan and Djibouti intended to protect interests that can no longer be addressed through the Nile dispute alone. 




The official describes Ethiopia as the principal state-level challenge to Egyptian interests within that system, while acknowledging that Egypt has fewer financial resources than Gulf states capable of using investment, infrastructure and patronage across the region on a much larger scale. Cairo’s effort has therefore relied heavily on state-to-state security relationships, military cooperation and diplomatic coordination with governments whose own disputes with Addis Ababa have intensified.




Somaliland’s former president, Muse Bihi, who signed the recognition-for-sea-access agreement with Ethiopia, later 

identified

 Egypt as the principal external actor behind efforts that ultimately thwarted the arrangement.

 Whatever weight is given to Bihi’s account, the dispute demonstrated how quickly Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions could become entangled with the much older Egyptian-Ethiopian confrontation over regional power and the Nile.




And once the sea-access agreement with Somaliland was pushed to the side, Ethiopia turned its sights to Eritrea. 




In a September 2025 speech near the GERD, Abiy described the loss of access to Assab as a mistake made three decades ago, referring to Eritrea’s 1993 independence from Ethiopia. 

“The mistake took place yesterday and will be corrected tomorrow,” Abiy 

told

 the gathered crowd.

 




“Well, the question of Eritrea’s independence isn’t really settled yet, is it?”




While the prime minister later publicly 

backed

 away from the suggestion that he would “reclaim” Assab, a Western diplomatic source says the messaging coming from Ethiopian officials over the past two years has been: “well, the question of Eritrea’s independence isn’t really settled yet, is it?”




For Asmara, this line of talk in public and behind closed doors has raised concerns. 




“We view Ethiopia’s declared and implicit rhetoric and ambitions to secure a sovereign maritime outlet, particularly the repeated hints regarding Eritrea’s Port of Assab, as an existential threat and a direct infringement on Eritrean sovereignty that can’t be tolerated. We consider it a broad red line, and crossing it or any unilateral Ethiopian military move toward Eritrean borders would ignite a direct and full-scale confrontation,” an Eritrean source close to decision-making says.




The increasingly tense Eritrean-Ethiopian relations created an opening for Egypt. 




Eritrea occupies a particularly important place in Cairo’s calculations because, as the Egyptian official puts it, its geography connects the Nile, the Red Sea and the Horn, and its long coastline gives it importance to Red Sea navigation, while its border with Ethiopia gives it direct strategic relevance to a state with which Egypt remains divided over the GERD. The official describes closer relations with Asmara as part of a wider effort to prevent any one regional actor from acquiring overwhelming influence across both the Nile Basin and the Horn.




Those relationships had acquired a public diplomatic structure by October 2024, when President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Afwerki and Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud met in Asmara. 

The 

declaration

 that came out of their meeting emphasized sovereignty and territorial integrity and established a tripartite foreign-ministerial committee for strategic cooperation.

 Following the summit, a 

separate

 Egyptian-Somali declaration reaffirmed support for Somalia’s territorial unity and closer cooperation with its state institutions. The summit did not announce an alliance against Ethiopia, but it brought together three governments whose relations with Addis Ababa had all become more difficult as Ethiopia pressed its maritime claims and its dispute with Cairo over the Nile continued.




President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud meet in Asmara. October 10, 2024




The Eritrean source close to decision-making circles describes the rapprochement with Egypt in more explicitly security-focused terms, calling it a “comprehensive strategic restructuring” intended to adjust the balance of power in the Horn and Red Sea. 




The source says Eritrea sought Egyptian assistance to improve military readiness and technical capacity after concluding that the Sudan war, Ethiopia’s internal conflicts and renewed tensions over maritime access were becoming increasingly difficult to treat as separate threats. Sudan also forms part of that relationship, in the source’s account, with security and intelligence coordination among Asmara, Cairo and the Sudanese military-led authorities developing alongside Eritrean support for forces aligned with the Sudanese military.




Accounts differ over the extent of Egypt’s physical military presence in Eritrea. The Eritrean source says cooperation is concentrated on training, military modernization and intelligence coordination. 




“The idea is not to fight. The idea is to send a message to Ethiopia and the UAE.”




Cairo is working to improve its military position in the area, an informed Egyptian state official says.




“The idea is not to fight. The idea is to send a message to Ethiopia and the UAE that we have a strong presence around Ethiopia,” they add. 




The first Egyptian official echoes the flexible contours of the cooperation, saying that military and security coordination operates through understandings between the leaderships and the agencies involved.
