Several Egyptian officials who spoke to Mada Masr in recent months downplayed the possibility that Egyptian troops would become involved in the fight. However, one Egyptian state official underlined that logistical and military support is already being set in motion and would continue. 




…




As those state-level pressures have accumulated, Ethiopia’s domestic armed movements have acquired greater regional value without ceasing to be products of conflicts rooted inside Ethiopia.




But that growing regional value has not made those armed movements mere products of the governments seeking relationships with them. 




Tigray’s confrontation with the federal government grew out of the collapse of the political order that had governed Ethiopia since 1991 and the war that began in 2020, while Fano’s mobilization followed a different history rooted in Amhara protest politics, insecurity, territorial claims and a wartime alliance with the federal government that later broke down. 

The two movements arrived at their present confrontation with Addis Ababa through different political trajectories and retain disagreements that the 

alliance

 announced in September has not resolved as a starting point.




Tigray People’s Liberation Front forces. Courtesy: AFP/Yasuyoshi Chiba




Tigrayan politics itself had fractured in the years after the Pretoria agreement, as rival political camps sought accommodation with governments that had fought against the region during the previous war. A faction associated with TPLF head Debretsion Gebremichael rebuilt contacts with Eritrea, while figures associated with Getachew Reda, the former head of Tigray’s interim regional administration and current minister advisor to Abiy on East African affairs, pursued a more accommodating relationship with Addis Ababa. The realignments were particularly striking because Eritrean forces had bitterly fought the TPLF during the war, while Amhara forces fought alongside the federal government and took control of territories claimed by Tigrayan political forces.




Fano had meanwhile become one of the principal armed challengers to the same federal government alongside which its fighters had acquired much of their expanded military capacity. 




After Pretoria, Addis Ababa moved to dismantle regional and irregular armed structures, while Amhara actors feared that disarmament would weaken their position in territories captured during the conflict. The wartime reliance on Amhara armed formations had strengthened organizations outside the regular federal chain of command before the alliance between them and Addis Ababa collapsed. 




“More than 85 percent of Amhara Regional State’s territory is controlled by Fano, while government forces are highly squeezed in the zonal cities,” Eyob Tilahun, an Ethiopian academic with close contacts with the Fano fighters, tells Mada Masr. “Fano forces frequently attack even major zonal cities and the regional capital.”




The process through which Fano became a force bears some resemblance to the trajectory through which the Sudanese state empowered the RSF, although the organizations emerged from very different political and institutional histories. Bashir’s government formally built up the RSF over years and granted it autonomous coercive, economic and political capacity, while Fano remained considerably more dispersed and less institutionalized. In both cases, however, governments struggling to exercise coercive control across contested peripheral territories helped strengthen armed actors that later pursued increasingly autonomous goals.




Their subsequent search for outside relationships does not make either Fano or Tigrayan factions simple proxies for neighboring governments. Fano’s territorial demands and claims of insecurity predate the current regional alignment, while Tigrayan actors understand access to Sudan through a history stretching back to the struggle against the Derg. What has changed is the strategic value those conflicts can acquire for governments seeking leverage over Addis Ababa, since an armed movement capable of opening another internal Ethiopian front can become useful to an external actor even where their political projects remain incompatible.




The contacts that eventually developed into the alliance announced in September moved through several channels without resolving those incompatibilities. An Ethiopian source close to the Fano armed group tells Mada Masr that one purpose of the Tsimdo initiative hosted in Port Sudan in May was to facilitate contacts between Tigrayan and Eritrean actors through Sudanese mediation. 

By August, Fano commander Zemene Kassie was publicly 

describing

 relations with several Ethiopian opposition movements, including Tigrayan actors, as the beginnings of wider cooperation.




By September 21, seven armed organizations had formalized that cooperation in the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival. Their common opposition to Addis Ababa did not resolve disputes carried over from the previous war. Wolqayt and other parts of western and southern Tigray remain claimed by Amhara and Tigrayan political forces, leaving one of the conflict’s most consequential territorial questions inside the alliance itself.




A senior Somali official tells Mada Masr that this kind of political order is better understood through overlapping networks whose participants can cooperate in one theater while competing in another. Turkey has defended Somali territorial sovereignty and developed deep military ties with Mogadishu while maintaining important economic and military relations with Addis Ababa. Somali officials were able to use Ankara’s relationships on both sides to help defuse their dispute with Ethiopia. But those same overlapping ties also place limits on how far Mogadishu can push the confrontation, the source says. Despite broader concern about Ethiopia’s rapidly changing regional posture, Somalia’s own security relationship with Addis Ababa due to mutual concerns about Al-Shabab makes a more aggressive stance difficult to sustain.




…




And while all these overlapping networks can take on an air of abstraction — through diplomatic gossip of who is talking to whom as all sides try to adopt the right posture — nothing better establishes how this comes to a head than the border area itself.




In late August, Hemedti traveled quietly to Addis Ababa as fighting intensified in Blue Nile State. 

A source in the RSF leadership and an Ethiopian official 

told

 Mada Masr at the time that operations and troop movements along the border were among the subjects discussed during the visit.

 




Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed receives RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo at a restaurant in Addis Ababa. Courtesy: Ethiopian Prime Minister on X




An ENDF source and a Benishangul-Gumuz security source tell Mada Masr that Hemedti traveled onward to Assosa, where he consulted RSF and Ethiopian military officers at the Bamboo Hotel. Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, General Abebaw Tadesse and military intelligence chief Getachew Gudina traveled to Assosa several weeks earlier for meetings with regional security officials and ENDF commanders, the sources add.




RSF presence has become more entrenched around an ENDF site near Fana Mountain, where they are developing a drone operations center.




Those meetings took place amid a broader military buildup around Assosa. The Benishangul-Gumuz security source says that the RSF presence had become more entrenched around an ENDF site near Fana Mountain, where they are developing a drone operations center alongside facilities capable of handling military aircraft. The source describes foreign personnel and local irregular forces operating around the site. 




Airports at Assosa and Bahir Dar are also being used to stage drone operations, a high-ranking Ethiopian Air Force official tells Mada Masr. At the Ethiopian Air Force Headquarters in Debre Zeit, Emirati colonels are stationed under special security protection to oversee drone operations, the source adds, while close to 30 Ethiopian military personnel have been sent to the UAE to train in drone operation. 




While the equipment that been flown and shipped into northern Ethiopia in the last month ahead of Hemedti’s visit to the base will be made available in part to the RSF, the Ethiopian Air Force source says that the focus on drone capacity has mostly been in preparation for war with Tigray and ongoing fighting with Fano. 




…




The Sudanese military-led authorities were building relationships of their own as military activity around the Ethiopian frontier increased. Burhan traveled to Asmara on September 4 for talks with Afwerki, describing the visit as part of continuing consultations between Sudan and Eritrea and thanking Asmara for what he called its “consistent stance.” The visit placed the leader of the Sudanese military in Eritrea only days after the head of the force fighting him had reportedly been in Ethiopia.




On September 17, Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council Deputy Chair Malik Agar, originally from Blue Nile State, said Khartoum does not want to enter a war with Ethiopia, even as senior Sudanese military officers were accusing Addis Ababa of allowing RSF drones to operate from Ethiopian territory. Two days earlier, Sudanese military chief-of-staff Yasser al-Atta accused Ethiopia of exploiting Sudan’s civil war to take border territory and permitting RSF drone launches as attacks struck Blue Nile. Ethiopia had rejected earlier Sudanese allegations of involvement as baseless. 




Hemedti’s movement toward Addis Ababa and Assosa, Burhan’s visits to Asmara and the sharpening dispute between Sudan and Ethiopia gave visible form to alignments that still fell short of two disciplined military blocs. Eritrea and the Sudanese military-led authorities have reasons to avoid a wider interstate conflict, while the extent of Egyptian military involvement remains calibrated, and, in some areas, ambiguous. The Ethiopian opposition alliance is itself held together across political and territorial disagreements capable of resurfacing even as its members confront a common federal adversary.




The events of late September nevertheless showed that those contradictions do not prevent tactical relationships from acquiring military consequences. Two days after the alliance was announced, the confrontation in northern Ethiopia expanded across Tigray, Afar and Amhara as Tigrayan forces seized the airports that had connected the region to the rest of the country. The renewed conflict therefore began at a moment when the actors around Ethiopia were more densely connected to one another than they had been when the Pretoria agreement ended the previous war.




The permeability through which those relationships operate belongs to a much longer history of the Horn. 




De Waal has compared the states of the region to trees whose branches grow across one another because the effective political reach of governments and armed movements has rarely ended at recognized borders. The upheavals around 1989–1991 were themselves produced partly through insurgencies, governments and external patrons operating across those boundaries, and the regional order that followed did not eliminate those practices so much as arrange them around a hierarchy in which Ethiopia enjoyed greater capacity than most of its neighbors to manage them.




What has changed is less the existence of cross-border alliances and proxy relationships and more the infrastructure available to sustain them. The branches extending across the Horn now carry drones and air bridges, commercial ports and transport companies, foreign contractors, financial networks and sub-state authorities alongside the rebel movements and intelligence services familiar from earlier periods. Geographic permeability is old, while the density and technological capacity of the systems operating through it are newer.

The post 

How a war in Tigray could set off a more complex fight

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Charlotte Reck
title: Stop Helping Saudi Arabia Bomb Yemen, Rights Experts Tell Burnham
content:
Rights experts have urged prime minister Andy Burnham to reverse a decision to refuel Saudi Arabian warplanes as they bomb Yemen.




An open letter to Burnham and foreign secretary Ed Miliband said the UK risks being “complicit in further war crimes” after the government announced last week it would support the Saudi dictatorship’s latest attacks. 




The 

letter is signed by NGOs

 including Shadow World Investigations UK and Campaign Against Arms Trade, as well as eleven human rights and international relations experts. 




It notes the Saudi-led coalition, which the UK first joined in 2015, “stands credibly accused of using starvation as a war tactic” against Yemen and of “widespread attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.” 




The UN estimates 377,000 were killed in the war on Yemen – which involved 25,000 Saudi-led air raids – between 2015 and 2022, when a ceasefire was announced. 




The new Saudi bombing campaign began after the Houthis seized large areas of land along the Red Sea coast, giving them more leverage over a crucial global shipping route.  




Recent escalation by the Houthis, the letter argues, has been driven by Israel’s UK-backed genocide in Gaza – which saw the Houthis enforce a naval blockade against Israel from 2023 – as well as the illegal US-Israeli war on Iran, a key Houthi ally. 




The latest bombings, like previous attacks, are unlikely to “weaken or dislodge the Houthis”, the letter adds. “There is a real risk that further UK military support for Saudi Arabia will not achieve the desired outcome and could make the UK complicit in further war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law,” it says. 




Earlier this week, ten union leaders 

wrote to Burnham

 urging him to end military collaboration with Saudi Arabia and UK support for the war on Iran. 




“Britain should not collaborate with a military that has repeatedly violated international law and has been central to creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises in Yemen,” said the letter, signed by Unison general secretary Andrea Egan and the National Education Union’s Daniel Kebede, among others. 




“Providing military support to Saudi Arabia inflames the war started by the US and Israel against Iran in February, which has expanded across the region,” it added. “The more this war expands, the more expensive our bills will get. The only way out is a diplomatic settlement to the regional war.”

author: Nahuel Lag
title: Cuando producir alimentos se convierte en una deuda
content:
Por Agustín Suárez* 




El endeudamiento se instaló en la vida cotidiana de las familias productoras. El acceso al crédito puede ser una herramienta positiva para el sector productivo, para iniciar una nueva campaña, ampliar la superficie de producción o cambiar una máquina. Pero, en la actualidad, una parte de ese endeudamiento tiene otro destino. Se toma deuda para llegar a fin de mes, pagar deudas anteriores o comprar alimentos para llenar la olla.




Un relevamiento realizado por el Centro de Estudios de la Tierra (CET) de la Unión de Trabajadores de la Tierra (UTT) a 

340 productores y productoras del cinturón hortícola de La Plata

 muestra la magnitud del problema. El 

92,3 por ciento

 de las personas consultadas 

tiene alguna deuda o crédito pendiente de pago

. Y se trata de un proceso reciente. El 

87 por ciento contrajo sus deudas durante los últimos dos años

.




Uno de los datos más preocupantes aparece cuando se observa para qué se endeudan las familias. 

El 37 por ciento tomó créditos para comprar alimentos, afrontar gastos del hogar y cubrir necesidades básicas

. La paradoja es fuerte. Familias que trabajan todos los días produciendo alimentos tienen que endeudarse para poder comprarlos.




A esto se suma una dinámica de endeudamiento que se retroalimenta. 

El 65,9 por ciento tuvo que contraer una nueva deuda para pagar una anterior

. La deuda deja de ser una herramienta para invertir o mejorar la producción y pasa a formar parte de las estrategias cotidianas para sostener la quinta y la vida familiar.




Foto: Municipalidad de La Plata




“No se vende”




Detrás del endeudamiento aparece una frase que se escucha todos los días entre las quintas: “No se vende”. Y cuando se vende, muchas veces los precios recibidos están por debajo de los costos de producción.




En el relevamiento, 

los bajos precios a los que se vende la producción aparecen como el principal obstáculo para pagar las deudas

. Entre quienes se endeudaron exclusivamente para sostener la producción, el 56 por ciento señaló este problema como la principal dificultad para cancelar sus compromisos.







Los datos recientes acompañan ese diagnóstico. Durante agosto, el Mercado Central registró bajas interanuales en los precios de distintas hortalizas. Al mismo tiempo, entre enero y agosto de 2026 los costos del transporte aumentaron un 27% y el combustible un 34,5%.







Semillas, plantines, insumos, alquiler, electricidad y combustible deben pagarse antes de iniciar cada ciclo productivo. 

Con costos que aumentan y precios de venta que muchas veces quedan por debajo de esos costos, cada nueva plantación implica asumir un riesgo mayor

.




La situación se observa con fuerza en el cinturón hortícola de La Plata, pero atraviesa también otras zonas hortícolas del país y distintas producciones regionales.




Foto: Plaga colectiva




Menos superficie para reducir el riesgo




Una de las primeras respuestas frente a este escenario es achicar la producción. El productor que trabajaba dos hectáreas pasa a cultivar una. El que producía una hectárea reduce la superficie a media. Se produce menos porque hay menos margen para perder.




Las decisiones económicas y las políticas del gobierno arrastraron a un sector a que se endeude. 

El aumento de los costos, la caída de las ventas y los bajos precios que reciben por su producción se combinan con problemas estructurales que llevan años sin resolverse

. El alquiler de la tierra, las condiciones habitacionales y los altos niveles de informalidad forman parte de esa realidad. Para muchas familias, endeudarse empieza a ser una de las formas de sostener la producción y la vida cotidiana.




El achicamiento de la producción también modifica la organización de las familias. Integrantes que históricamente trabajaban la tierra comienzan a buscar changas y otras fuentes de ingreso. Se reduce la superficie cultivada, disminuye el trabajo familiar dedicado a la producción y aumenta la necesidad de conseguir ingresos por fuera de la quinta.




Foto: Plaga colectiva




La crisis reduce la capacidad de elegir cómo producir




La crisis también empieza a impactar sobre los procesos de transición agroecológica

. Durante los últimos años, numerosas familias avanzaron en experiencias de producción agroecológica, incorporando bioinsumos, diversificando cultivos y desarrollando nuevas formas de manejo del suelo, las plagas y las enfermedades. Son procesos construidos durante años a partir del conocimiento, la experimentación y el acompañamiento técnico y organizativo.




Pero producir con deudas, alquileres cada vez más altos, altos costos de energía y combustible y precios de venta que muchas veces quedan por debajo de los costos reduce cada vez más el margen para decidir cómo producir.




Ante la necesidad de asegurar ingresos, algunos productores vuelven a las formas de producción que conocen desde hace años y que perciben como una manera de reducir el riesgo inmediato. Procesos de transición agroecológica que llevaron varias temporadas pueden frenarse o retroceder en pocos meses.




La agroecología también necesita condiciones materiales para sostenerse. 

Las familias necesitan poder planificar, experimentar y atravesar los procesos de transición sin que cada nueva campaña ponga en juego su subsistencia

.




Producir cada vez menos




El problema ya no pasa solamente por cómo financiar la producción. También pasa por las condiciones que tienen los pequeños productores para seguir produciendo alimentos.




Cuando una familia pasa de dos hectáreas a una, o de una hectárea a media, está tomando una decisión para reducir el riesgo y poder sostenerse.

 Pero cuando esa decisión comienza a repetirse entre cientos de productores, deja de ser solamente una estrategia familiar frente a la crisis. Lo que 

empieza a reducirse es la superficie destinada a producir alimentos y la cantidad de familias que pueden vivir de esa producción

.




El endeudamiento es hoy una de las expresiones más visibles de un problema más profundo. Si producir significa endeudarse, achicar la quinta y buscar ingresos por fuera para poder continuar, lo que 

está en riesgo no es solamente la economía de cada familia, sino la continuidad de los pequeños productores que todos los días producen alimentos

.




Cuando una familia deja de producir, las consecuencias también se extienden más allá de esa familia. 

Se pierden fuentes de trabajo y la producción de alimentos queda cada vez más concentrada en menos manos

. Detrás de cada quinta que se achica hay menos tierra produciendo, menos familias viviendo de la actividad y menos pequeños productores produciendo los alimentos que llegan todos los días a la mesa de las ciudades argentinas.







*Ingeniero agrónomo, integrante de la Unión de Trabajadores de la Tierra (UTT) y el Centro de Estudios de la Tierra (CET – UTT). 







La entrada 

Cuando producir alimentos se convierte en una deuda

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Amélie Béchard hopes to maintain CAQ hold on Ungava
content:
Nunatsiaq News reached out to each candidate running in the Ungava riding ahead of Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election. Here’s what Coalition avenir Québec candidate Amélie Béchard had to share with us.




Amélie Béchard isn’t a career politician. She says she decided to run for office in Ungava with the Coalition avenir Québec because she wants to make a difference.




“I’m here for the people,” said Béchard, speaking to Nunatsiaq News from her hometown of Matagami.




The candidate hopes to replace former Coalition avenir Québec member Denis Lamothe, who held the seat for two terms, from 2018 to 2026.




“I could be a strong voice in Quebec City — bringing our issues to the forefront, defending them, and helping our region grow,” said Béchard, who visited Whapmagoostui and Kuujjuarapik last week.




She owns a forestry consulting company in Matagami that specializes in operations management and has worked alongside the provincial government and Cree communities — experiences she says make her fit to lead economic development in northern Quebec.




She has also sat on boards of directors, such as the economic development society of Baie-James and Matagami’s business development society.
















She has also sat on the board of Femmes Essor de la Jamésie, an organization that promotes entrepreneurship among women.




She said the cost of living for Cree and Inuit is especially high and that she wants to reduce the amount of transportation costs on essential items like food that are being passed onto consumers.




To address the cost of living, she mentioned that the party’s promising to increase tax credits for seniors over 65 as well as for first-time homebuyers. It has also promised to triple the amount it currently gives to local business in remote areas, through a regional economic fund.




Béchard said the party also wants to ensure royalties from mining are re-invested into critical infrastructure and services that nearby communities rely on. The party previously projected those royalties could generate as much as $78 million a year.




Béchard is among five candidates running for Ungava in Quebec’s provincial election. Advance polls have been open since Saturday and will stay open until Wednesday. Election day is on Monday, Oct. 5.

author: L214
title: Marche pour la fermeture des abattoirs
content:
Chaque année, des milliards d’animaux sont tués pour l’alimentation : environ 69 milliards d’animaux terrestres et plus de 1 000 milliards de poissons dans le monde. Derrière ces chiffres se trouvent des individus sensibles, capables de ressentir la douleur, la peur et la détresse.

La Marche pour la fermeture des abattoirs est un appel à mettre fin à cette hécatombe. L’élevage, la pêche et l’abattage condamnent des êtres sensibles à une vie d’exploitation, puis à une mort violente et prématurée, alors même que nous n’avons pas besoin de produits d’origine animale pour vivre en bonne santé.

C’est dans ce contexte qu’aura lieu la nouvelle édition de la Marche pour la fermeture des abattoirs à Paris le 3 octobre 2026. Une Vegan Place (village associatif et commerçant) sera organisée le même jour pour apporter une touche gourmande et festive à l’événement.

ouverte au public de 12h à 18h, sera composée d’une quarantaine de stands

author: Unknown
title: Kataib Hezbollah suspends military activities in Iraq
content:
Kataib Hezbollah, one of the Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq, announced that it has suspended its military activities in the country following the complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraq.




Kataib Hezbollah leader Ahmed al-Hamidawi instructed the group’s fighters to halt military activities in Iraq. However, the statement said that operations targeting “enemy aircraft” violating Iraqi airspace would continue.




The decision came after the United States withdrew its remaining troops from Iraq. With US Central Command (CENTCOM) completing the evacuation of personnel and equipment from Erbil Air Base, Washington’s military mission in Iraq under Operation Inherent Resolve officially came to an end.




A new period following the US withdrawal




The United States and Iraq agreed in 2024 to end the mission of the International Coalition in Iraq. The US-led coalition was deployed to the country in 2014 after ISIS seized large areas of Iraqi territory.




The Pentagon says that despite the end of the military mission, training and intelligence support for Iraq will continue. The Coalition’s command structure is expected to continue operating from outside Iraq.




The US withdrawal is also viewed as the beginning of a new phase in the Iraqi government’s efforts to bring the weapons of Iran-aligned armed groups in the country under state control.




Some powerful groups, particularly Kataib Hezbollah, had previously made the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq a condition for laying down their weapons. However, the suspension of military activities does not mean that the group has disarmed. Indeed, groups operating under the umbrella of the “Islamic Resistance” in Iraq have stated that no agreement has yet been reached with the government in talks over the regulation of weapons and that they do not consider themselves bound by the timelines announced by the government.




Al-Sadr announces dissolution of armed groups




On September 30, Iraqi Shiite leader Muqtada al-Sadr announced that the armed groups affiliated with him had been dissolved and that one of them would be transformed into a civilian foundation. According to Sadr’s statement, Saraya al-Salam (Peace Brigades) was dissolved, while the Imam Mahdi Army, which had previously been among Sadr’s armed formations, would be transformed into a civilian organization under the name “Ansar al-Imam al-Mahdi Foundation.”




Sadr also announced the dissolution of the armed group Liwa al-Yawm al-Mawud (Promised Day Brigade).

author: anred
title: Abajo la «Facho Week»: manifestación en rechazo a la visita de Javier Milei a París
content:
Foto: Claudio Casparrino (Página/12).




El Colectivo Argentina en Lucha París convoca a una manifestación pública para expresar su rechazo a la visita del presidente argentino Javier Milei a París, en el marco de la denominada «Argentina Week». La movilización tendrá lugar este viernes 2 de octubre, de 18 a 21, en la Place de la République, y adoptará el formato de una manifestación-performance artística. La expresión artística será el corazón de la jornada, acompañada por una presentación musical e intervenciones de participantes. Será una manifestación contra el ajuste, el saqueo y la represión. 

Por Colectivo Argentina en Lucha París.







Javier Milei

 visitará 

París

 entre el 

30 de septiembre y el 2 de octubre

, en el marco de la denominada 

Argentina Week

. La misma tiene por objetivo “explorar las oportunidades denegocios e inversión de la Argentina”. En este viaje estará acompañado por una delegación integrada por gobernadores de 13 provincias argentinas, miembros del gabinete argentino, empresarios y dirigentes de organizaciones patronales.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Colectivo Argentina en Lucha Paris (@argentina.en.lucha.paris)













La movilización busca denunciar la visita de Javier Milei y de su comitiva como parte de la 

ofensiva para profundizar el modelo extractivista y el saqueo del territorio argentino

, así como las 

consecuencias sociales y económicas de las políticas de ajuste del gobierno argentino y la represión

 contra quienes se movilizan y se organizan para rechazarlas.




El Colectivo denuncia también la 

complicidad de Macron y del gobierno francés

, que, en su afán por facilitar el acceso de los capitales franceses a los negocios en Argentina, le tiende la mano a un gobierno de extrema derecha. Esta complicidad resulta aún más grave en un contexto de avance de las extremas derechas en Francia y en Europa.




El Colectivo Argentina en Lucha París participará también de la manifestación convocada por la 

Asamblea de Ciudadanos Argentinos en Francia (ACAF)

 el miércoles 30 de septiembre en Trocadéro en París, en el marco de la visita presidencial. La movilización del 2 de octubre buscará ampliar esta expresión colectiva mediante una jornada que combine protesta, arte, música y palabra pública.




Milei llega a París en medio del rechazo y la movilización




La llegada de Milei a París se produce en un contexto de creciente rechazo a sus políticas en Argentina, marcado por el aumento de la movilización social y por el cuestionamiento de su gestión y sus desastrosos resultados (aumento de la pobreza, del desempleo, de la precarización laboral, del endeudamiento, de la tasa de suicidio, etc.).




En Francia, la visita tiene lugar pocos días después de que el gobierno de Milei se viera obligado a desplazar a Santiago Muzio de la dirección de la Casa Argentina de la Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris, tras meses de fuertes cuestionamientos a su gestión.




Residentes, ex residentes y organizaciones denunciaron persecución y medidas contra estudiantes, trabajadoras y trabajadores, el retiro de una placa conmemorativa en homenaje a las víctimas de la última dictadura cívico-militar y la utilización de las instalaciones de la Casa Argentina para actividades vinculadas a sectores de la extrema derecha.




Estas denuncias dieron lugar a una amplia movilización en Francia, impulsada por residentes y exresidentes junto al Colectivo Argentina en Lucha, y respaldada por organizaciones sociales, sindicatos, partidos políticos, intelectuales y artistas. La situación también generó el cuestionamiento de autoridades parisinas y tuvo repercusión en medios argentinos y franceses.




Sobre el Colectivo




El Colectivo Argentina en Lucha París fue creado en enero de 2024, pocos días después de la llegada de Javier Milei a la presidencia argentina, y reúne a argentinas y argentinos residentes en Francia.




Desde su creación, el colectivo se moviliza contra las políticas de ajuste, represión y regresión social impulsadas por el gobierno argentino y busca visibilizar en Francia las consecuencias de estas políticas. Asimismo, desde una perspectiva internacionalista, se plantea generar puentes con organizaciones locales en Francia y otros países con el fin de combatir el avance de las extremas derechas en el resto del mundo.




El colectivo forma parte además de la 

Red Internacional Argentina No Se Vende

, que articula organizaciones de migrantes de Argentina en distintas ciudades y países, entre los cuales se encuentran Toulouse, Berlín, Madrid, Barcelona, Bilbao, Londres, Portugal, Italia y Río de Janeiro.

author: Nadia Salem
title: Interior Ministry accuses Matsda2sh of belonging to Muslim Brotherhood in claim founder says ‘authorities know is untrue’
content:
Over 48 hours since authorities initiated the arrest and forced disappearance of six Matsda2sh journalists, the Interior Ministry acknowledged on Thursday morning that it had detained the independent fact-checking platform’s staff. 




The journalists’ whereabouts remain unknown, according to their legal representatives at the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, and they have not been presented for investigation before prosecuting authorities.




The ministry accused the journalists of belonging to the Muslim Brotherhood, a claim the founder of the independent fact-checking platform said authorities know to be untrue in comments to Mada Masr.




In the statement published Thursday morning, the Interior Ministry 

said

 Matsda2sh aims to undermine the country’s stability by “fabricating lies and spreading rumors.” The statement added that it is an unlicensed page, managed from abroad to broadcast false news and distort facts. It also accused the platform’s founder, Abdel Rahman Mansour, of being a “fugitive member of the Brotherhood” and that he is working in cooperation with “a number of  Brotherhood elements in other countries, in exchange for funding they receive from abroad.”




EIPR lawyer Islam Salama said that the six journalists have still not been brought before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, which handles terrorism investigations, and said authorities are yet to inform the journalists’ families and lawyers of their place of detention. He added that lawyers have submitted requests to authorities to ensure they are able to attend investigations with the detainees, and that they have gone to wait at the prosecution headquarters for the journalists to be brought there, though authorities have not yet permitted them into the building. 




Mansour told Mada Masr that authorities know that Matsda2sh is not affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood and that it is a professional journalism platform. He pointed to the prior summoning of one of the platform’s journalists for investigation in 2023. The journalist was released shortly after the summons. “Why are they now saying that they are Brotherhood?” he asked. 




“We know that there are voices who support us from within the state because they know us, and because they are committed to sound governance and believe that not all voices should be silenced,” Mansour added. His personal priority, he continued, is “human dignity and defending the right to hold on to the ideas one wishes to hold on to, and to adopt one’s own causes in a peaceful manner.” 




Authorities 

arrested

 several members of Matsda2sh’s team three years ago following their 

coverage of a case involving the arrest of Egyptian nationals in Zambia who were 

onboard a 

private 

jet carrying cash, counterfeit gold and weapons

. They were forced to erase the coverage from their pages, and the journalists were 

released

 after two days and allowed to continue their work. 




In the aftermath of the 2023 campaign, 

Matsda2sh proposed to security authorities that they legalize their status as an official journalistic platform and establish headquarters to gather the team together inside Egypt, as other journalistic organizations are allowed to do. This initiative was ignored by security authorities, according to an informed source who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity.




A source from the Journalists Syndicate informed of the ongoing mediation between the syndicate and authorities since the arrests confirmed the initiatives had taken place, adding that the same proposal “and more” is currently being put forward, but that security authorities are not engaging with the suggestions. 




The same source, alongside another source from the syndicate, clarified that security authorities, during the course of mediation, have pointed to a letter the syndicate had previously sent to all official entities, including the Interior Ministry, to say that state officials should only speak to  journalists registered with the syndicate, trainees at syndicate-accredited newspapers or trainees with media websites and agencies licensed by, or who have applied for a license, from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council.




Security authorities used that letter to repudiate the syndicate’s attempts at mediation for the six Matsda2sh journalists, claiming the platform is a social media page operating without a license from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council and that it has not applied for one. 




“I had said you should not deal with them, not that you should arrest them,” Journalists Syndicate head Khaled al-Balshy told Mada Masr, commenting on authorities’ misuse of the syndicate’s letter. 




The first syndicate source said 

mediation efforts had witnessed authorities expressing readiness to escalate the situation by levelling accusations 

of belonging to the Muslim Brotherhood at the journalists.




A third syndicate source said that, in communications with the syndicate, there has been a divide in how security bodies have proposed to handle the fallout from the arrests. While one has shown a willingness toward de-escalation, conveying a sense that the arrests were an exaggerated move, the other has taken a more hardline approach. This hardline approach has maintained the argument that Matsda2sh was planning to critique the state ahead of 

Egypt Forum 2026

, an event scheduled for October to display the government’s achievements, which comes with an invitation from the Cabinet for public feedback and commentary. The hardline stance has argued that letting the six journalists out now would show that security bodies are willing to fold as soon as there is an online campaign and would be an invitation for people to be bold in their criticism, the source added.




By Thursday morning, however, it was clear that authorities were moving toward further escalation against the detained journalists, the first and second syndicate sources said. 




The Interior Ministry referred to the Matsda2sh journalists as members of a Muslim Brotherhood “media committee,” and indicated that only one of the six is a registered member of the Journalists Syndicate, adding that the head of the syndicate was informed both of the arrest of the registered journalist and the circumstances surrounding it. 




For the third syndicate source, the move toward labeling the journalists as Muslim Brotherhood members is meant to halt further mediation, for, per the state’s logic, if they are considered members of the group, they should be treated harshly like all members of the organization, which is legally classified as a terrorist organization in Egypt.




After the ministry’s Thursday statement, one of the syndicate sources said a call was issued by the syndicate’s general assembly for journalists to gather inside the union’s Cairo headquarters on Thursday afternoon to discuss the crisis and decide on the appropriate response. 




The arrested journalists are Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal. According to 

EIPR

, Abu Emaira and Qadry were arrested from their homes on Monday night while the remaining four journalists were detained the following evening, with Barakat and Helal also being taken in raids on their homes. Mahmoud and Adel were arrested on a Cairo street. 

The post 

Interior Ministry accuses Matsda2sh of belonging to Muslim Brotherhood in claim founder says ‘authorities know is untrue’

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

author: Khyl Ramos, Ben Radford
title: Gen Z protests, Pax Silica and fighting for an ecosocialist future
content:
Khyl Ramos works on climate justice, labour rights and grassroots organising in the Philippines. He is the deputy project manager at Transform Asia Gender and Labor Institute and youth coordinator for the Party of the Labouring Masses (PLM).

Ramos was a guest speaker at the recent Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, where he sat down with Green Left’s Ben Radford to discuss last year’s Gen Z protests, recent opposition to the United States-led Pax Silica initiative and the need for ecosocialist alternatives.

How would you characterise the Gen Z protests in the Philippines last year?

The Gen Z uprising in the Philippines last year was simultaneous with the protests in Indonesia, Nepal and Bangladesh.

The president revealed in July that there was a flood control scandal, in which congresspeople, along with other senior government officials and contractors had corrupted billions of pesos in public funds.

The funds were supposed to go to disaster preparedness and disaster risk reduction management, because we’re a very flood-prone country. But the people in charge of the Department of Public Works and Highways, as well as lawmakers — since they deliberate on the budget in Congress — pocketed the money.

That was the start [of the protests] — students were really enraged about that, especially university students, since there are many universities in Manila situated in flood-prone areas, and they see this as a broader systemic issue of corruption.

In terms of the [Gen Z] movement, it’s very spontaneous. [PLM] tried to maximise on organising around that spontaneity. We’ve revived our youth and student groups; however, not just university students — we are trying to expand to senior high school students — 16- to 17-year-olds — as a new force in the movement.

We’ve been explaining the issue through a number of youth and students’ assemblies against corruption and political dynasties we held in November, 2025. We related it to issues that students can easily understand, for example, around education funding, [and what it would mean] if funds were allocated to education instead of being corrupted.

We’ve been centring our argument to fuel the movement — [explaining] how corruption is really affecting not just grassroots communities, but also students.

We are building an independent youth movement, separate from parents as well, because some of the youth are quite shy when their parents are around. As people in the party say: “Don’t let the parents get involved, let the students do the organising.”

How do the recent Pax Silica protests tie in with struggles for climate justice and resisting green colonialism?

Pax Silica is a US-led economic and technological security initiative, with the US trying to gather allies from around the region. Australia is also part of that alliance, along with Japan and more than 20 other countries, including the Philippines. [The US] has been trying to move its allies away from China, since China is one of the leading countries in the critical minerals and semiconductor industries.

Now, we are being targeted as one of the centres for the Pax Silica initiative. They’re trying to build AI data centres and a manufacturing and semiconductor processing hub in New Clark City [in Central Luzon, about 100 kilometres northwest of the capital, Manila], which will occupy around 1600 hectares of land, which indigenous communities are living on. It is their ancestral lands, which they will face displacement from.

When we started the campaign around April this year, it wasn’t well known... But the campaign against Pax Silica has really boomed in the past two months, because they’ve been trying to fast-track it.

There are different progressive movements making solidarity visits to the area to see the situation and put forward a campaign.

[Pax Silica] also has a geopolitical agenda because of the US conflict with China. We’re in the middle of it, especially with the continuous installation of US presence [through the] Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement (EDCA). We had five [EDCA sites] in 2023, and it’s increased to nine now.

Filipino and US troops are doing [joint] military exercises ... firing guns and detonating bombs. Last May 2026, in Leyte, Eastern Visayas, a US Tomahawk cruise missile was launched as part of the Balikatan [military] exercises, and struck a designated target area in Nueva Ecija. The impact on the ground is really being felt by our communities.

They’re planning to build a new capital [in the New Clark City area]. They plan to transfer the industrial-commercial hub there and extend that hub... It is also being targeted as a staging platform for war, since AI is also being used for militarisation. It will be used to intensify the genocide in Palestine and the war with Iran. Their imperialist tendencies will be strengthened because of this initiative.

As an environmental and climate justice issue, we all know that AI uses tonnes of water, and, if my data is correct, [the AI and semiconductor hub in new Clark City] will use 65-90 million litres of water every day (39 billion litres annually). This initiative will feed the global demand for the country’s natural resources already undergoing decades of massive colonial extraction.

The president is pushing it under a “green transition” — their agenda for green capitalism... But it’s also opening tendencies towards nuclear energy. The Bataan nuclear power plant was built by the dictator [Ferdinand] Marcos Snr, but never operated commercially because of safety hazards and environmental risks. Now, they’re reconsidering nuclear power as a national energy policy because of the Pax Silica initiative. These are really interconnected issues.

Then, there’s the economic impact. They say it is going to provide jobs … but we all know that it will all be automated in the end. Filipino workers will just contribute during the construction of the site, but after that? It’s really not sustainable.

Our national sovereignty is being eroded because [under Pax Silica, the government] is planning to give land to the US for free for two years. Surrounding that, there was a law (Republic Act No.12252) passed a year ago, that we can lease our land to foreign “investors” for 99 years ... basically, that is foreign ownership of land — which our organisers are explaining to the communities.

They are completely lying to our faces ... They’re giving our land away to these imperialist powers; not for our benefit, but for their benefit, especially with the US’ war strategies and tactics around the Asian region.

They’re also planning to use the Pax Silica initiative for cyber warfare, since the fight now is not only physical, but digital.

They’re already destroying the environment in the Philippines — it’s been a ground for resource extraction, which will intensify under the Pax Silica initiative. They’ve already been mining in other parts of the country as part of the unjust transition that we’re seeing: the fight for nickel, lithium, cobalt and other “critical minerals”.

In November, a US representative is coming to the Philippines to formalise the agreement. They’ve been holding pre-conferences in the Philippines. There have been protests already, and alarmingly, there have been arrests of activists for protesting Pax Silica.

There was also recent news that the government is appealing to activists to refrain from holding protests during the ASEAN summit, which is absurd and an unacceptable attempt to silence the people.

Hopefully, we can sustain the momentum, since the general public is also against Pax Silica. It is easy to explain how it will affect the environment and how it will doom us.

The Central Luzon region, where the data centres will be built, is scarce in water resources because of local corporations mishandling access and prioritising profit. On social media, there have been campaigns, not just by the left, but also the general public, [demanding] “no to Pax Silica, shut the Pax down”. That’s a great opening for us to continue the campaign.

We’ve talked about defensive struggles, but how, as ecosocialists, are you putting forward alternatives?

An ecosocialist alternative is critical at this point because of the worsening capitalist system in the Philippines. The corporations and businesspeople are controlling the government. The government is working with the corporations.

That’s why we’ve been advocating for democratic planning and democratic consultation with communities as part of an ecosocialist transition.

In terms of resources, public utilities should be in public ownership. An ecosocialist alternative must pursue planned, sovereign industrialisation by investing in Filipino-owned industries, local supply chains, research and scientific capacity.

As part of the PLM’s campaign, we’ve been putting forward the [demand for a] “government of the masses”, because the masses are the ones who really know what the situation on the ground is and what we really need from the government.

We’ve been advocating for workers’ control of resources — water, energy, transportation. Our transportation systems have been sold off to local corporations. We’ve also been campaigning for energy prices to go down because it is also controlled by private corporations, as well as water.

PLM is one of the leading groups at the forefront of the ecosocialist movement. We’ve been trying hard to extend the message to more movements in the Philippines. There are many climate justice movements, but some people in the movement still need convincing on the idea of ecosocialism.

We’ve been trying to put forward public education through a socialist school ... since we’ve also had a new wave of young comrades [join PLM]. It’s great for advancing and explaining what an ecosocialist transition will look like.

Since the disaster in Nepal ... [it is clear that] the capitalist-induced disasters we are facing are not separated. We have borders, but it is felt across countries.

Recently, we had the haze in Manila from [the wildfires in] Indonesia. Some of our Indonesian colleagues and comrades said to us, “you should sue our government”. I tell them we need Asian solidarity with the left parties and movements as well, on how we can make our own governments accountable.

With the disaster in Nepal and the global race for a just energy transition, we must have a regional plan through democratic planning — [for] how we can move as a region in terms of these just energy transition initiatives, and how can we put forward an ecosocialist alternative.

The PLM has grown, particularly in the past year or so. What are the reasons for this?

We have a presence in eight regions and beyond, and each community has different local mass struggles around housing, access to water and resistance to corporations building environmentally destructive infrastructure.

We’ve been maximising the opportunities to organise grassroots communities, since they’ve been looking for organisations or people to help them to file cases, to talk to the government agencies — since we’re in dialogue with the government to register our demands, especially with the housing issues in the urban poor communities in Manila.

People are looking for alternatives, because the politics in the Philippines is ridiculous right now — the elites are fighting each other, which people are seeing on social media and in the news. That’s why we’ve been maximising that opportunity and opening ... it’s the political situation and the need for a socialist alternative [driving the PLM’s growth].

What impact does the PLM’s election work have on drawing people into socialist politics?

We see it as a positive development — we’ve been building the left and socialist movement in the Philippines [through elections]. We’ve been moving forward with how we can expand and extend our message beyond our own networks, especially [in the context of] the connotations and the propaganda against socialist movements. In the Philippines, socialism as a word is still viewed with skepticism and is not widely accepted.

The election has been an instrumental part of this change in the wave of people coming to the left, especially, since in 2022 we were not as visible. The momentum started when we first appeared on mainstream television for debates. I think that’s one of the turning points; when our candidates, Leody de Guzman and Luke Espiritu, really showcased our platform to a wider audience.

The youth campaigning for our candidates is also a significant development, because they’ve been talking to their parents ... [and] campaigning on social media.

When we were participating in the elections, people were telling us, “You won’t win”. But our first goal is to establish our presence, and we’ve achieved that.

author: Feven Merid
title: Where the mouse eats the cat
content:
“Welcome to the Central Prison of Douala,” La PJ, an inmate and a star of the documentary 

Jail Time Records

, says in an opening scene of the film. “The place where the mouse eats the cat.” Dione Roach, one of the film’s directors, offered me an interpretation: “The world is upside down in prison; the mouse can be more shrewd,” she said. The intimate glimpse into the Central Prison of Douala, also known as New Bell Prison, does indeed reveal an upside-down world. Like many prisons, its inmates recreate the contours of outside life on the inside, but in New Bell it’s taken to another level. There are actual neighborhoods like the Latin Quarter, home to the Emperor and his gang known as the Latinos, and the Base, where the prisoners who make up the quasi police squad reside. There’s a marketplace for people to sell fried foods and taxis, except these taxis are inmates who swiftly run through the congested prison to hand-deliver messages. They even have a “homeless” population, those who must sleep outside in the courtyard because there aren’t enough beds. Their neighborhood is dubbed House of the Penguins.

This all comes into focus when you learn New Bell is notoriously overcrowded — it was built for 800 people but currently holds almost 6,000. Thus, the prison has been transformed into a mini city, colloquially referred to by inmates as the 11th province of Cameroon (there are officially 10). La PJ, a lanky and charismatic man dressed in his uniform of a conductor’s hat, blazer, and tie, steps in as mayor to give us the lay of the land. “Our jewel of jewels,” he says, as he approaches his final stop on this tour — a recording studio. Specifically, it’s the Jail Time Records studio, for which the film is named and the reason for its making.

Jail Time Records, the recording studio, is the first to be put in an African prison, according to the film’s directors and the studio’s founders Dione Roach and Steve Happi. The two run it as a nonprofit music label for inmates and those who are readjusting to life outside of prison. From its start in 2018, the duo has been documenting the studio’s impact; first, inadvertently, through shooting music videos and then with the intention to make a documentary. Roach, who is from Italy and has been based in Cameroon since 2017, has served as the studio’s artistic director, and Happi, who is from Cameroon, as its lead producer (Happi was incarcerated at New Bell for two years, during which time he met Roach and helped get the studio up and running). Shot over six years, they’ve created a film that captures the curiosities of New Bell remarkably well (

Jail Time Records

 won top prizes at Tribeca Film Festival in New York). A few weeks ago, I spoke to the two directors over Zoom about what it’s like documenting New Bell, the music of their main characters, and how the film let them show a fuller picture of life in prison. This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Feven Merid

How did you start Jail Time Records and when did you realize you wanted to make a film about it?

Dione Roach

I was volunteering, doing art courses, and I came across a group of really talented musicians. They were incarcerated, and I just had the idea to do an album with them. And then I was even like, why just an album? Why don’t we actually build something that can stay and be used by many people? And so I proposed the recording studio to the prison, and they accepted, and we got it built. And then that’s when I met Steve, who was incarcerated at the time, and he was already a music producer and sound engineer. Someone introduced us, and I was finished volunteering, so I left him the keys of the studio. I came back a few months after, and they’d been doing like so much work and recording, and it had really become this like place of like extreme creativity and outlet.

Steve Happi

Before even starting the movie, I was already doing music videos and having access with the camera inside prison when I was still incarcerated. So as she said, it was just a natural process, and having access with the camera and such intimate moments of our life and our journey, we started recording everything.

Feven Merid

What was it like to film inside such a crowded place?

Dione Roach

At the start, we went with a friend who had like a gigantic camera, and he didn’t already work in prison as well, like so they didn’t know him, and so it just wasn’t really the right setup, you know, for that kind of space and situation. You need something very discreet, and it’s better the closer you are to the people, the more they know you, the more you know them, the better it is, obviously. So then we just shot with a very small little camera, a handheld camera. It’s a very hot place, and yeah, I mean it’s overcrowded; it’s hard. Like, you really have to think if you want to have deeper, more confessional moments with the guys. You really have to think around sound, noise and like where you’re gonna go to shoot and for the place to be quiet for the parts that were kind of more directed. A lot of what we did was just spontaneous and following life, and we’re in prison a lot just doing the work for Jail Time Records, so beyond the film, so we just always had the camera with us.

Feven Merid

Steve, you were in Douala for two years, and now you continue to do work with the prison through Jail Time Records and the film that requires you to return often. What’s that experience like?

Steve Happi

As soon as I went out, like the day after, I was already back there, in the studio as a free man. But I went back there straight to record with the guys and continue projects. So I’m just feeling like it’s part of the journey, and you know we are trying to pull out the best part of each other and see how we can lift our project, how we can push it to the max.

I don’t think of myself as a film director. Naturally, I started being involved in filming, in sharing ideas with Dione, brainstorming, like pushing the narrative where the film’s going to go, so that’s how I end up being a director. But it wasn’t intentional; I just want to be the director of doing music. As she said, it’s really a collaborative project, and that’s even with the guys inside; we taught them how to record with the [sound] boom. So it’s really participative; it’s like a family business.

Even recently, going to Tribeca, we were just there to share the movie with people, and we ended up winning trophies, and from my point of view, it wasn’t really intentional. Like, we started this journey little by little, and we were discovering ourselves. I’m discovering myself.

Feven Merid

In addition to La PJ, there are three main characters you follow in the film: Transporter, Emperor, and Stone. What stood out to me was that they made three distinct-sounding types of music; Stone was reflective and serious, Transporter was more electronic-dance, and Emperor’s sound was very hard. How did they come to be the main three?

La PJ, the charismatic guide to New Bell Prison in 

Jail Time Records

, surrounded by fellow inmates. Photo: Jail Time Records/Dione Roach.

Dione Roach

I think the three of them, it was always clear that they would be like the main characters, but there were other ones that we would have loved to show more of, but it just had to be reduced. As you said, they just have three different energies. They represent three different parts of masculinity, of humanity, of reasons for being in prison, of different ethnic groups in Cameroon, different music. It just made sense. Stone is this rock and is the person that’s, I think, for a normal person or the public, more easy to identify with. He’s got a daughter outside. Transporter is just this kind of incredible Trickster character, and Emperor is like a force of nature, and they’re also the guys that often we were closer to for many periods.

Steve Happi

Emperor was my best friend in prison. My cell and his cell were neighbors, as you say. A character like Transporter, he really wanted to be in the movie. At the beginning, he wasn’t too interested about the music, but he was really interested in the movie. He was always around and made sure to be in every frame, and he started revealing himself.

Feven Merid

How did everybody else around them feel about being filmed? Because you see people like Transporter, La PJ, who were very comfortable on camera and had a lot of energy, but then you see other people, and you’re reminded that this is a hard place to be and this is a low point for people. So how did other people feel about being on camera?

Steve Happi

Generally speaking, they loved it. We’ve been working there for so many years. They are used to the camera already. That’s why you have people doing their normal life, their daily routine. You might see some of them maybe hiding themselves, but people really love to be part of the project, and they love being filmed. This attention that is mostly coming from outside, the energy from the outside, and being seen like in music videos or the film- they don’t know where the project is going to land, but from my observation, they’re always ready for the camera to be there. Most of the time, people are people surrounding us.

Feven Merid

The film won several awards at Tribeca this year, including Best Documentary Feature. How did everyone feel about the film’s success?

Dione Roach

We rang them immediately, Stone and Transporter, and they were super happy, but then the best moment for them was a few weeks ago. It took a bit of time, but it became viral in Cameroon because the BBC did an article, and then all the Cameroonian media started doing articles, and they were like, “we won the Oscar!

”

Transporter, one of the three incarcerated artists at the center of 

Jail Time Records

, inside New Bell Prison in Douala. Photo: Jail Time Records/Dione Roach.

Steve Happi

That’s how we call everything related to films. We call it “Oscar”. We called all the guys, and they were screaming, “We won the Oscar!”

Feven Merid

Why do you think rap is the sound, the musical form that people gravitate to the most inside?

Steve Happi

Right now in Africa, to be honest, we don’t listen that much to hip hop anymore. It’s more about Afrobeat, Afro rhythm. So what is really more popular right now is Mbolé and Coupé-Décalé, like what Transporter is doing in some of his songs: fast-paced rhythm beats, rapping fast on top of that. People are listening to hip hop less and less, maybe more melodic and auto-tune type of hip hop, but less and less. With Emperor, we created this new breed [of music]. I have many tracks we didn’t release, but he really represents the sounds of Jail Time.

Feven Merid

Dione, what was your experience like as a woman filming in a crowded, all-men prison?

A scene from 

Jail Time Records

, filmed over six years inside New Bell Prison in Douala. Photo: Jail Time Records/Dione Roach.

Dione Roach

I think because usually it’s always like men filming men and men getting perspectives on men, or like women talking about women, I think there’s very little of women talking about men, and especially prison, it’s such a male world. So I think the fact that I was a woman did help with the guys opening up. Most of the confessions they told me before [filming], even. And then I would ask them how they felt while on camera, and I think because I was a woman, it allowed them to feel they could be more vulnerable.

I never really had issues. I’m quite tough in there as well, quite a tomboy. When you work in the prison, you have to be very ironical, and in Cameroon in general, when someone speaks to you, you have to answer in like a funny and shrewd way, and they like it, and so once you get the hang of that, they really respect you and you’re joking with them, and it kind of brings down barriers.

There are things they might have done that are really difficult to hear because you know these people and you’re friends, you love them, you’ve been together for years with them. When you’re working in prison, it’s expected that a lot of people are there because they have committed acts, but you get to see all sides of people that, if you only read in the news about them, you’d be judging them really negatively. Here you get to see the 360, and that’s the beauty. That’s humanity because I think we are all such a mixture of good and bad and of circumstances, so you definitely become less judgmental.

title: Docentes bonaerenses: la bronca en las escuelas les impuso un paro a las conducciones sindicales aliadas de Kicillof
content:
Este miércoles, luego de un nuevo hecho de violencia en el distrito de Trenque Lauquen, las conducciones del Frente de Unidad Docente se vieron obligadas a convocar al paro para el 1° de octubre. La lista Multicolor ya había convocado a la medida, a partir de asambleas y mandatos de escuela. Es necesario imponer un plan de lucha frente a la miseria salarial y falta de respuesta del gobierno provincial de Kicillof en las paritarias, el endeudamiento y las situaciones de violencia en las escuelas. 

Opinan: 

Paula Akerfeld (miembro de la Directiva de SUTEBA Tigre) y María Díaz Reck (docente y congresal de Suteba La Plata), para La Izquierda Diario.







Las y los trabajadores de la educación vienen protagonizando importantes muestras de descontento y movilización frente a una situación salarial y educativa

 que se vuelve cada vez más difícil de sostener.




La marcha de la bronca

, donde asistieron más de 50 mil personas, demostró que hay fuerzas para pelear contra el ajuste tanto del gobierno nacional de Milei y sus cómplices, como de los gobiernos provinciales.




Los paros y las convocatorias impulsadas por la Multicolor son un canal de expresión de un descontento que también aparece por diferentes vías en los distritos. 

En La Plata se realizó una importante movilización al Banco Provincia

 contra el creciente endeudamiento docente y las tasas que golpean nuestros salarios.




Mientras tanto, distintas situaciones de violencia en las escuelas dieron lugar a medidas de fuerza y movilizaciones en Ensenada, San Miguel, Hurlingham, Almirante Brown y Florencio Varela.




Ensenada: más de 400 docentes en asambleas zonales




Luego de los graves hechos de violencia contra los docentes de la EP Nº 13, la exigencia de asambleas y de una medida de fuerza se impuso desde abajo. Tras el paro de 36 horas, y en el marco de una movilización de más de 300 maestras y profesores, la lista Multicolor que es segunda minoría en el distrito y cuenta con la fuerza de los delegados en las escuelas, realizó una asamblea en la que quedó planteado que la respuesta no podía terminar allí.




Por eso, el lunes pasado desde la Multicolor y ante la ausencia de convocatoria por parte de la conducción Sudeste se impulsaron asambleas zonales abiertas a la comunidad educativa con más de 400 compañeros, con suspensión de clases, para debatir colectivamente las demandas necesarias frente a estas situaciones: presupuesto, creación de cargos, jornadas institucionales y protocolos efectivos de resguardo para docentes y estudiantes. No alcanza con actuar después de cada hecho de violencia. Necesitamos recursos y políticas que permitan intervenir integralmente antes que las situaciones lleguen a esos extremos.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Multicolor (@multicolorensenada)













El salario y los descuentos también pesan




Frente a la masividad de las medidas que se vienen sosteniendo durante todo el año, convocadas con mandatos de escuelas, impulsados por las seccionales de conducción Multicolor y la oposición en casi cien distritos; la respuesta del gobierno Provincial en lugar de hacerse eco de los reclamos y la insostenible situación de miseria salarial y falta de recursos en las escuelas, responde castigando a la docencia con descuento que promediaron $85mil en los últimos recibos. Según el relevamiento impulsado desde la Multicolor sobre 9327 casos, los descuentos podrían haber representado 2,5 veces el “aumento” otorgado en el mes de Agosto.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por SUTEBA.Tigre (@sutebadetigre)













Más del 80% de la docencia, somos mujeres, muchas sostén de hogar, por lo que los descuentos tienen un impacto directo en el marco de magros salarios

, a lo que responde el efecto disciplinador que pretende tener esta medida del gobierno provincial. En momentos en los que el gobierno nacional se embandera atacando el derecho a huelga, Kicillof elige seguir ese camino.Por eso necesitamos fortalecer la organización desde abajo y construir medidas cada vez más masivas.




La lucha es ahora




Este escenario se desarrolla mientras el gobernador Axel Kicillof busca proyectarse políticamente a nivel nacional. Su reciente viaje a Nueva York incluyó reuniones con empresarios y representantes de fondos de inversión. Busca mostrarse potable para el establishment.




Mientras tanto, 

los trabajadores de Fate enfrentaban una orden de desalojo

, que se suspendió temporariamente producto de la resistencia . El gobernador Kicillof y su fuerza política deberían tratar el proyecto de ocupación temporaria presentado hace meses.




En la Provincia de Buenos Aires la miseria salarial, la precarización son moneda corriente.Mientras una maestra tiene que endeudarse para llegar a fin de mes y en muchas familias se decide qué gasto básico se puede pagar y cuál debe postergarse, no podemos aceptar que la respuesta sea esperar al 2027.




La reciente autoconvocatoria nacional de la Marcha de la Bronca volvió a mostrar que existe disposición para enfrentar las políticas de ajuste.

 La docencia que la tomó en sus manos y también se movilizó el 6A contra la ley de tierras, tiene planteado ahora retomar las calles contra el escandaloso fallo de la corte que habilita la venta indiscriminada de tierras

.




Para enfrentar las políticas del gobierno nacional de Javier Milei y, al mismo tiempo, reclamar al gobierno provincial de Kicillof respuestas en salarios, presupuesto educativo y condiciones de trabajo, necesitamos fortalecer la organización de las escuelas y la coordinación provincial.




Las y los docentes no podemos esperar un recambio electoral mientras nuestros salarios pierden poder adquisitivo, aumenta el endeudamiento y las condiciones en las escuelas son cada vez peores. Tenemos la posibilidad de llevar esta pelea a cada escuela y barrio, organizando asambleas o comisiones junto con familias, estudiantes y auxiliares que también viene sufriendo la miseria salarial y van al paro el próximo 7 de octubre que será en los hechos la continuación del paro del 1/10. Urge unificar las peleas.




La fuerza está en las escuelas. Organicemos esa bronca, transformémosla en mandatos y construyamos desde abajo un nuevo paro provincial.
