author: Meli Newen
title: Opinión: Asesinos de Palestina, asesinos de América Latina
content:
Los asesinos de Palestina ahora vienen por América Latina. Vienen por el agua para intensificar el capital de la gran agricultura en contra de los pequeños, para nutrir de armas a las Fuerzas Armadas e involucrarnos en sus guerras; para abastecer de ciberseguridad a las proliferantes empresas de seguridad e intensificar los dispositivos de control para que miles de Cerimedos sean posibles y así las repúblicas latinoamericanas sean destruidas y sustituyan al sujeto pueblo por el sujeto algoritmo.

FUENTE: La Voz de los que Sobran

25 de septiembre, 2026 – Palestina al olvido -tal y como el sueño sionista aspira. Palestina recluida, nuevamente, a ser negada. Los medios no son neutrales respecto de la nakba, constituyen parte de ella, de su maquinaria de borramiento, precisamente en el instante en que docilizan al espectador con un genocidio en vivo en orden a normalizar las pasiones y despotenciar el horror que experimentamos. La idea sionista de colonización de Palestina no consistió jamás en la simple “ocupación” sobre el territorio para vaciarlo, expulsando enteramente a su población. Su apuesta fue siempre más allá: no solo expulsar población, sino negar completamente su existencia.

Todo el proyecto de colonización sionista no solo implicó la sustitución de la población nativa por la población colona sino también, la negación de que dicha población nativa realmente existía. Bien decían Elías Sanbar y Gilles Deleuze a principios de los años 80: el proyecto sionista sobre Palestina consistió en la producción de un vacío. Sin embargo, este proceso de borramiento ya no es solo un proyecto circunscrito a Palestina. Es, sobre todo, una apuesta desplegada a nivel global: los medios no solo niegan la existencia de Palestina y, con ello, colaboran todos los días, con la empresa de la nakba perpetrada por Israel y el imperialismo occidental, sino también a las multitudes que resisten la imposición de su dominio.

Los asesinos de Palestina ahora vienen por América Latina. Vienen por el agua para intensificar el capital de la gran agricultura en contra de los pequeños, para nutrir de armas a las Fuerzas Armadas e involucrarnos en sus guerras; para abastecer de ciberseguridad a las proliferantes empresas de seguridad e intensificar los dispositivos de control para que miles de Cerimedos sean posibles y así las repúblicas latinoamericanas sean destruidas y sustituyan al sujeto pueblo por el sujeto algoritmo.

Pero, sobre todo, la penetración estadounidense-israelí (el sionismo, al fin y al cabo) en América Latina va sobre los recursos naturales: agua y las “tierras raras” que ofrece el territorio nacional, dado que China tiene alrededor del 80% de ellas, el desarrollo de la industria de Inteligencia Artificial por parte de Estados Unidos e Israel, así lo demanda. Es clave, en este sentido, el hecho de que hoy asistimos a una palestinización de América Latina: no sólo Estados Unidos ha sometido al continente a partir del Escudo de las Américas sino conjuntamente con Israel que, a partir de los Acuerdos de Issac que ha firmado con Argentina, intenta proyectarse en el continente en función de la sangrienta competencia por la industria de la Inteligencia Artificial. En este marco, la sionización de las oligarquías latinoamericanas y la palestinización de sus pueblos es ya una realidad: el gobierno de Kast es el primer gobierno sionista de la República de Chile.

Ahora bien, la palestinización del mundo y la sionización del imperialismo no constituye una novedad para la historia. En 1492 mientras las naves de Cristóbal Colón llegaban a las imaginarias “Indias” para encontrar un atajo a China, los Reyes Católicos terminaban la conquista de Al Andalus obligando al último reino musulmán de Granada a su capitulación. Todos los métodos que los católicos usaron contra los musulmanes y judíos en orden a la conquista de la península ibérica fueron utilizados, posteriormente, en la conquista de las tierras americanas. Por eso, la palestinización del mundo no es una anomalía al funcionamiento del orden imperial, sino su regla. Al igual que la experiencia andalusí, todas las tecnologías de despojamiento que Israel aplica contra los palestinos lo vende globalmente en sus empresas de armas, seguridad y aguas.

Ahora bien, detengámonos en el nombre dado a los acuerdos reservados para América Latina: Isaac. Ante todo, tenemos que leer bajo la rúbrica de la teología política sionista que traduce el relato bíblico en una narrativa de la muerte que proyecta su vocación hacia el dominio planetario. Se trata de una expropiación del vocabulario de la teología judía para ponerla al servicio perverso de un léxico neofascista que, en el nombre de la “libertad”, apuesta por el dominio totalitario. En estos términos, Isaac condensa la idea de “elección”, del “hijo” y del “territorio”.

En primer lugar, bajo mandato divino, fue originalmente llevado al cadalso para ser sacrificado por Abraham pero que, la irrupción del ángel permitió a su padre soltar el cuchillo con el que lo ejecutaría. Desde este punto de vista, Isaac es ya un “elegido” de Dios que fue salvado del sacrificio situándose así, por fuera de los sacrificados, más allá de los sometidos en el terreno de los vencedores que inviste a los firmantes de los Acuerdos en la posición de los “elegidos”.

En segundo lugar, es relevante que Abraham sea el padre de Isaac precisamente porque estos acuerdos se presentan como una réplica o, si se quiere, el “hijo” de aquellos consumados por Israel y los Emiratos Árabes Unidos que la primera administración promovió. “Hijo” que, por serlo, deberá depender del legado “paterno” en la que se escenifica la relación de absoluta “dependencia”.

En tercer lugar, Isaac, según el relato bíblico, habría sido el único de los patriarcas en permanecer en la “Tierra de Israel” al no trasladarse a Canaán. Bajo la hermenéutica de la teología política que aquí está en juego, Isaac constituye el nombre de aquél que permanece en el territorio, que indica la vocación conquistadora del imperialismo sionista (estadounidense e israelí a la vez), el salto mortal para apropiarse de los territorios de América Latina.

De esta forma, Isaac es el nombre que condensa al “elegido”, al “hijo” que se apropia y permanece en un “territorio”. Tres características de la modalidad imperialista por la que Estados Unidos e Israel se aferran al “hemisferio occidental”. Así, la sionización de la política latinoamericana nos muestra un asunto decisivo: por más que pretendan hacernos olvidar Palestina, Palestina está necesariamente aquí donde los asesinos de Palestina pretenden ahora apropiarse de América Latina.

Por supuesto, nada tiene que ver todo esto con el famoso “Plan Andinia” -un supuesto plan inventado por los nazis latinoamericanos (del que habló alguna vez Miguel Serrano) de corte antisemita que acusaba a Israel de pretender colonizar la Patagonia. Es mucho peor que dicho ingenuo y conspirativo plan. Es la forma de dominio imperial impulsado por el sionismo estadounidense e israelí para incrustar sus intereses sobre el continente y convertir a los países en simples centros de datos consumiendo sus recursos naturales para engrandecer las fortunas de Peter Thiel y los oligarcas tecnológicos.

¿Qué lugar ocupa Israel, con su lectura perversa de la misma biblia hebrea, en la asonada geopolítica estadounidense sobre América Latina? Ante todo, Israel es al sacerdote como Estados Unidos al príncipe. El primero bendice la guerra de conquista y la vuelve “justa”, el segundo la ejecuta gracias a la legitimación promovida por el primero. Entre ambos articulan la máquina “moral” del último reducto de cristianismo imperial que, desesperado y agónico, intensifica su fuerza mortal, acelera incondicionalmente el capital justamente, y al igual que Colón, busca un atajo a China.

– Acusan a Israel por calificar volantines como “armas de guerra”, la nueva excusa para atacar a niños

– Jorge Nawel: “Los acuerdos de Milei con Israel también son una amenaza para nosotros”

author: Chris Walker
title: Paxton Caught on Tape Saying Trump’s Midterm Convention Dragged Republicans Down
content:
“Everybody’s numbers dropped” after Trump’s midterm convention event, the Senate candidate from Texas was heard saying.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

An audio recording of a private conversation between U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton (R-Texas) and conservative donors last week reveals that he may view President Donald Trump as a “drag” on his and other Republicans’ campaigns.

It’s unclear whether the discussion in the recording is directly about Trump, and parts of it are difficult to hear or understand. In the recording, a donor asks Paxton, who is the current Texas attorney general, whether the candidate feels “like he’s a little bit of a drag,” without explicitly stating who “he” is.

Paxton responds by discussing the recently held GOP midterm convention, which was heavily promoted by Trump.

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” Paxton says in the recording.

The conversation occurred during a GOP fundraising event last week. The New York Times obtained audio of the discussion from a source who attended the event, who describes themselves as opposed to Paxton’s campaign.

Leaked audio of Ken Paxton:Q: Do you think Trump is a bit of a drag?Paxton: To be honest with you, when we did that midterm convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Yeah. Not good.

The conversation — whether Trump was the subject or not — is likely to upset the president, who called for as many Republicans as possible to attend the midterm convention. The event, held in Paxton’s home state of Texas, was billed as a means to promote GOP candidates throughout the country, though many in the party were skeptical of having Trump as the headliner.

Trump has embarrassed Paxton, too, albeit more publicly. Earlier this month, Trump said Paxton “may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” at an event where he was attempting to promote the candidate.

Paxton may be correct that the midterm convention for the party hasn’t helped him or other Republicans. According to an average of polling data collected by FiftyPlusOne, Paxton was within 2-3 percentage points of his Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico, during the first few days of September. Currently — weeks after the convention was held — Talarico has expanded his lead slightly, leading Paxton by 3-4 points in the polls over the past several days of averages.

Republicans in general have seen their numbers slip since the convention. In an Economist/YouGov poll conducted from September 4-8 (just days before the convention began), Democrats led Republicans by 11 points among likely voters. In the most recent poll, conducted September 25-28, that lead has widened to 15 points.

Other surveys have indicated that Republicans’ continued fealty to Trump is dragging them down, making it more likely that Democrats will win control of the House and potentially even the Senate in the midterms. According to a recent NPR/PBS NewsHour/Marist poll, 45 percent of Americans said they wanted their vote to be viewed as symbolic opposition to the Trump administration, while only 24 percent said they wanted it to be seen as a vote in support of Trump.

author: Kelcie Moseley-Morris
title: Republican Attorneys General Sue Abortion “Shield Law” States in Supreme Court
content:
The AGs also filed a separate lawsuit in a Louisiana district court against individual providers in three states.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and the attorneys general in Arkansas and Alabama filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. Supreme Court, suing California, Massachusetts and New York to invalidate the so-called “shield laws” that have allowed providers in those states to send abortion medication to people in states with abortion bans.

The state officials, all Republicans, also filed a lawsuit in federal district court against individual abortion providers in the same three states.

“We will not allow activist states, activist providers or distributors profiting from killing babies to threaten Louisiana’s sovereignty, violate Louisiana’s laws and endanger Louisiana women and Louisiana babies,” Murrill said at a news conference on Tuesday. Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin and Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall of Alabama also were present.

The lawsuit filed in the Western District of Louisiana seeks to stop the individual providers named from being able to prescribe and send abortion medication to those states, while the Supreme Court complaint asks the justices to find the shield laws are a constitutional violation of state sovereignty..

“Today, plaintiff states filed a lawsuit against as many organizations and individuals as they have been able to identify notwithstanding the shield laws intended to thwart such litigation,” the Supreme Court complaint reads. “To fully obtain relief, however, they must also eliminate other contributing causes for the harm that they are suffering, including … the shield laws.”

The district court suit names 30 defendants, including the Massachusetts Medication Abortion Access Project and its founder, Angel Foster, Dr. Remy Coeytaux in California and other telehealth providers around the country.

The complaint compares the mailing of abortion medication to anthrax, mail bombs and chemical weapons, despite studies since 2000 showing that abortion medication is safe and effective to use.

“(Defendants) think themselves invincible because their agents swear to never step foot in plaintiff states (thereby avoiding arrest), and their home states have enacted so-called ‘shield laws’ intended to thwart legal liability for individuals perpetrating this interstate abortion scheme,” the complaint says.

Following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in 2022 allowing states to ban abortion at any stage of pregnancy, 13 states now have near-total bans, while others have expanded abortion access. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration allowed the drug mifepristone, one of two commonly used to terminate a pregnancy in the first trimester or to treat miscarriages, to be dispensed without a visit to an in-person provider in 2023, after years of safety studies.

Providers in states with access can prescribe and mail the medication to states with bans, and Murrill, along with other state AGs, has tried to extradite those providers to Louisiana to face legal charges for violating the ban. One of the providers Murrill tried to extradite in January was Coeytoux in California. Governors in those states have refused to comply with the extradition requests.

To protect those providers, California, Massachusetts and New York were among the 22 states and the District of Columbia that passed shield laws to block out-of-state investigations and prosecutions against providers dispensing for abortion medications to patients in other states.

Murrill is also leading a lawsuit against the FDA to reverse the 2023 provision allowing telehealth access to mifepristone, and two other lawsuits of a similar nature are ongoing in Missouri and Texas. The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Louisiana’s case earlier this month and is expected to issue a decision in the coming weeks about the future of nationwide access to the drug.

Louisiana Illuminator reporter Piper Hutchinson contributed to this report.

author: Redazione_web
title: Iniziato l’abbattimento di Bosco Ospizio a Reggio Emilia
content:
Oggi 30 settembre le ruspe hanno iniziato ad abbattere gli alberi del Bosco Ospizio.  




Le ruspe sono entrate dopo più di una settimana di serrato tamtam sulle testate locali della stampa serva -televisiva e cartacea- e sui social, in cui conad illustrava la bontà e la bellezza del suo progetto, ponendosi quasi come un ente no profit dedito alla cura e salvaguardia dell’ambiente e non come una comune azienda capitalista affamata di profitto.   




A proteggere le ruspe c’erano decine di poliziotti in tenuta antisommossa e parecchi altri in borghese, nonché varie pattuglie di vigili urbani armati di taser, pronti ad affrontare chissà quali minacce. 




Ma non c’erano solo loro: erano -e mentre scrivo sono ancora- presenti anche tante di quelle persone che in questi mesi hanno portato avanti il presidio permanente in difesa del bosco, e tante altre che sono passate a testimoniare l’ennesimo scempio della natura in favore del cemento. Scempio ben rappresentato dall’abbattimento di un acero di circa vent’anni e sei metri di altezza, contro il quale una ruspa si è accanita per una buona mezz’ora prima di riuscire a spezzarlo. Sì, perché nemmeno l’onore della motosega è stato riservato alla vegetazione: forse per “dimostrare” che non era un bosco si sono usati mezzi più adatti a estirpare dei cespugli. Una tristezza infinita. Tante persone presenti avevano le lacrime agli occhi, altre erano decisamente incazzate.  




La violenza del capitale sta già distruggendo il Bosco Ospizio. Per evitare altri crimini contro l’ambiente, in questa città e ovunque, servirà una mobilitazione più generale e permanente. 




J.Scaltriti

author: Sharon Zhang
title: White House Openly Brags About Islamophobic Efforts to Cut Legal Immigration
content:
The White House’s bigotry was celebrated by many on the right, who called for further cuts.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The Trump administration bragged about reductions in legal immigration from majority-Muslim countries in a post on social media on Tuesday, touting its discriminatory and white supremacist policies as it moves to increase immigration from white populations.

Sharing information from an analysis by libertarian think tank Cato Institute, the White House posted a graph showing that legal immigration and refugee admissions from majority-Muslim countries have been cut nearly entirely – by 96 percent – since December 2024 until February 2026.

The Trump administration has implemented sweeping travel and immigration bans against many countries with large Muslim populations. The State Department has slashed legal immigration by refusing most visas and all refugees from nearly every majority-Muslim country in the world, the Cato Institute’s analysis noted, while annual immigration levels from such nations are projected to reach their lowest point in 30 years.

These policies are openly Islamophobic, coming from a president whose first major action in office during his first term was to implement a “Muslim Ban” that was later overturned in court. This term, his administration has deepened its embrace of racism and Islamophobia both in policy and in rhetoric, with Trump repeatedly calling Somalis “garbage” and attempting to outright ban visa issuances to immigrants from 75 Muslim-majority countries.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin shared the White House’s post, saying that the decline is a result of “tougher vetting” from “high-risk countries,” without specifying what “risk” the immigrants would pose.

The White House’s post was celebrated by Republican lawmakers and influencers, including many of the most bigoted figures on the right.

“Absolutely incredible victory for the American people, thanks to @POTUS,” said Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas).

“4 percent to go! Thank you, President Trump,” said Rep. Randy Fine (R-Florida).

Noah Pollak, who serves as a senior adviser in the Treasury Department’s Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, said that the Trump administration’s efforts to slash immigration from majority-Muslim countries is critical to fighting antisemitism — parroting a false, hateful trope that Muslim people drive hatred against Jewish people.

“This is the single most consequential policy to combat antisemitism in the U.S. in the last decade and it’s not even close. And the Trump admin — and especially those like [White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller] who implemented it — will get no thanks or credit from legacy Jewish organizations, which is shameful,” said Pollak.

The author of the Cato Institute post whose data was shared by the White House, libertarian David J. Bier, condemned the anti-immigration policies. He noted that immigrants from majority-Muslim countries have been shown to be a boon for the local, state, and federal economies, being on average more highly educated than U.S.-born Americans.

“Thanks for citing my work. You are violating the law and harming Americans while making the country less safe, less free, and less prosperous,” said Bier.

author: Anjali Kamat
title: Mahmoud Khalil’s New Memoir, No Land to Stand On, Looks Beyond His Own Case
content:
The Palestinian activist discusses his book, his lawsuit against Columbia University, and fighting deportation.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

We speak with Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil about his new memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention. It details his 104 days of detention inside a Louisiana ICE jail after he was targeted for arrest and deportation by the Trump administration over his pro-Palestine campus advocacy at Columbia University. Khalil missed the birth of his first child, Deen, while he was separated from his wife, Noor Abdalla, who is a U.S. citizen. The administration is still trying to deport Khalil, who has launched civil rights lawsuits against the government and Columbia University over his treatment.

“Eighteen months after my arrest, this administration has never charged me with any crime or even presented any evidence that I committed any crimes, yet they are able to get away with this because I’m Palestinian,” Mahmoud tells Democracy Now!

Khalil’s memoir also looks beyond his own case, recounting the people he met behind bars and what their stories taught him about the broader human cost of the U.S. immigration detention system. “This book is about a story of so many incredible men, fathers and workers who came here seeking safety and a better future, only to be snatched off the street,” he says.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

ANJALI KAMAT: No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention. That’s the title of a searing new memoir by the first pro-Palestinian campus protester to be jailed by the Trump administration: Columbia University graduate and Palestinian student protest leader Mahmoud Khalil. On March 8th, 2025, Mahmoud was detained by plainclothes police officers who did not identify themselves in the lobby of his apartment building in Columbia University housing. His wife, Noor Abdalla, who was eight months pregnant at the time, filmed this video of his arrest as Mahmoud was being taken away. Her voice is heard in the clip.

DR. NOOR ABDALLA: Can you — can you please specify what agency is taking him, please? Excuse me. They’re — nobody — they’re not talking to me. I don’t know. Excuse me, the lawyer would like to speak to somebody. Oh my god, they’re literally running away from me.

AMY GOODMAN: That was March 8th, 2025. Mahmoud was taken into immigration detention, ultimately transported more than 1,300 miles away, to Louisiana. He spent over a hundred days in jail and was denied permission to attend the birth of his first child, Deen. He could only listen on the phone.

Mahmoud Khalil’s new memoir also looks beyond his own case, recounting the people he met behind bars, including immigrants who had lived in the United States for years and parents who were separated from their children, and what their stories taught him about the broader human cost of the U.S. immigration crackdown.

Mahmoud Khalil was released in June of last year and spoke outside the detention facility, the ICE jail, in Jena, Louisiana.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: No one is illegal. No human is illegal. That’s the message. The message is: Justice will prevail, no matter what this administration may try to portray.

ANJALI KAMAT: More than a year after Mahmoud Khalil’s release, the Trump administration is still seeking to deport Khalil. The Board of Immigration Appeals has approved his removal, and this week the board denied Khalil’s request to end his removal proceedings. His lawyers are pursuing further appeals, including seeking review by the Supreme Court.

In his new memoir, Khalil takes on not only the Trump administration, but also Columbia University, which he sued earlier this month, alleging it failed to protect pro-Palestinian students, instead retaliating against them when they reported harassment. Khalil writes in his new memoir, quote, “Rather than protecting its doxxed students, Columbia leaned into the intimidation campaign.”

In his memoir, Khalil describes the moment, just days after his arrest, when he came to see himself not simply as an individual facing deportation, but as a test case. He writes about his decision to take on the Trump administration and fight for his freedom, saying, quote, “My case was the blueprint they wanted to set, and the one we had to tear up.”

AMY GOODMAN: Well, for more, we’re joined now by Mahmoud Khalil to discuss his new memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention. It was just released this week.

Mahmoud, thanks so much for being with us. Can you start off by talking about the title, No Land to Stand On? What does that mean to you?

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Thank you so much, Amy, for having me.

No Land to Stand On is really, to me, is a realization that this country, that promised me at least safety and stability, was not there, and also it talks about my experience. You know, I was born and raised in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, and then I had to flee the country at the age of 18 to Lebanon. And then I had also to leave Lebanon to come here to this country, only to be surprised that the promise that I was seeking was not there. So, it was really a realization, but also it’s my family’s story, where they are also now scattered around the world with no — with no place to go back to or, really, no land to stand on.

ANJALI KAMAT: Mahmoud, you write in your memoir, quote, “Today, Palestine is the exception to those rights the world claims as universal. In reality, it is a warning. The rights we are denied were never only ours to lose.” Can you talk about what you mean by that?

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Absolutely. You know, Palestinians are the canary in the coal mine. They start everything, the test case with Palestinians. For example, this deportation campaign, the Trump administration deportation campaign, started with me as a Palestinian to chill the speech of others. It’s not only chilling the speech of those speaking out for Palestine, but really anyone who’s speaking out against this administration, in essence. You know, when they started with me, they went right after to the universities, threatening them with federal funding, but also with journalists, you know, going after nonprofits and organizations that does anything that this — that do anything that this administration deem to be a threat, a threat to them. So, that’s why I feel why, like, when we talk about Palestine, it is really the warning.

And what happened now is a result of so many years of dehumanization against Palestinians, whether in the media or even in the political institutions or any institution in this country. That’s what made my targeting possible. You know, like, now 18 months after my arrest, this administration has never charged me with any crime or even presented any evidence that I committed any crimes, yet they are able to get away with this because I’m Palestinian, because, you know, a lot of politicians, whether they are Democrats, whether they are Republicans, they don’t care about Palestinians. So, this country, when it comes to Palestine, it’s really a one-party system, that everyone is just against Palestinians.

ANJALI KAMAT: You write, “I am Palestinian. That is not a complication of the story, it is the story. Everything else follows from it.” And this remarkable memoir, it’s not just, you know, your experiences. It’s an indictment of the entire system of American democracy. And you compare the failures of American democracy to growing up under the Assad regime in Syria.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Yeah, exactly, because what happened to me, you know, I fled forced disappearance and arbitrary detention in Syria, only to be surprised that this happens to me here in a country that supposedly champions human rights, liberty and justice, rule of law. So, I wrote this book really to raise the alarm. You know, what’s happening behind ICE detention walls is a stain on the U.S. consciousness. So is the Palestine exception, the fact or the idea that free speech, rule of law and basic dignities are denied to Palestinians.

AMY GOODMAN: Mahmoud Khalil, if you can share your experience growing up in Syria? You were, in fact, shot. You lost your friends. Explain what happened and how you ended up coming to the United States.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Absolutely. You know, in 2011, when the Syrian people revolted against the Assad regime, and Egyptians and Tunisians, as well, the Arab Spring, Palestinians felt also the urge and the earn to their homeland. So, we decided to march to Palestine, to the borders. And I was one of thousands of Palestinians who wanted to march back to Palestine. And while, you know, we peacefully marched to Palestine, I was shot by Israeli soldiers while trying to cross the border.

And then, you know, when also in in Syria, I was helping out with relief, and also I couldn’t just stay silent while my Syrian neighbors were being killed and kidnapped by the Assad regime. So we started to organize, as well, to help out our Syrian brothers and sisters. And that’s when, you know, Assad cracked down on any sort of civil organizing and kidnapped two of my friends on January 9, 2013. And in a day, I had to leave the country to flee to Lebanon. So, I only had that one day really to flee the country to Lebanon.

And in Lebanon, I lived, you know, in Shatila camp, one of the largest Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon, where the situation was also so, so bad in there. But I got to teach myself English there, get into school, and eventually get work in Lebanon. And that’s how sort of like my journey from Syria to Lebanon, and eventually to the United States.

But my story is only one story of the Palestinian story, really, how, you know, it’s all a result or a consequence of the Nakba of the 1948 that we had to go through all of this. You know, my grandparents had to live in tents. They had to upgrade it to mud houses, and my father was born into a tent. And then, when we built houses, you know, the Syrian revolution happened, and my family had to leave everything behind and leave.

ANJALI KAMAT: Mahmoud, you were a green card holder, and you write about how, you know, for many immigrants, the green card is the promise and the finish line. And yet you were detained. You know, all these months later, as you’re still fighting this case in the courts, you know, give us an update on what’s happening with your case and why you believe you were chosen to have — you know, to be detained, why you’re going through all of this.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Yeah, so, you know, this case or this fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country. It is really about whether anyone in this country get to speak out for Palestine, against this administration, and not punished for it.

Right now the Trump administration is really putting the full weight of the Justice Department to deport me. They’re trying it through the immigration system, as you’ve mentioned in your introduction. The Immigration Board of Appeals, which is fully controlled by the Trump administration, refused to open, or reopen, my case, because — you know, New York Times reported that there were a lot of, I would say, like, a lot of corruption, really, like, in my case, where a judge was appointed to look into my case, and that judge was the chief judge, but also over — many other individuals also intervened to make sure that there is a certain outcome in my case. So, we know that we wouldn’t get justice from the immigration kangaroo courts in this country. That’s why we’re turning to the federal court.

But also there, the Trump administration is blocking us from seeking — from seeking a neutral judge or a federal judge, Article III judge, from there. So, they are claiming that we should first go to the immigration court, and once it’s that done, we can go to a federal court in Louisiana, which is known to be one of the most right-wing or, you know, favorable to this administration in particular.

And for that, we’re going to the Supreme Court. We hope that next month — or, this month, in the 19th of October, we are petitioning to the Supreme Court to take my case, because, you know, our ask is very simple, that no federal agent or no government should have the power to detain anyone over constitutional claims or over their freedom of speech. So, it’s very simple.

And if you could remind me of the last question? I know there was a part of that question.

ANJALI KAMAT: Oh, you know, you write about how, you know, there was a moment in detention when you realized your detention wasn’t arbitrary or a mistake or accidental, and, you know, the president himself was tweeting about you.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Exactly. I think that was the moment. You know, the first couple of days in detention, it felt to me that this was a mistake, that there’s no way they would come after me. I was a permanent resident — I’m still a permanent resident — never committed a crime. But when I saw that the president was actually tweeting about me, and the language of that tweet or even of the officials, it seemed to me that this is — this was way bigger than me, that that was a very calculated measure or a very calculated, I would say, targeting to chill the speech of others. They wanted someone who they can make an example out of, so that the hundreds and millions of American citizens and non-American citizens would fear speaking out against the U.S. support to Israel. So, that was the point where I was like, you know, to me, this is way bigger than just like me, my ability to stay in this country. It is really about the ability of so many people to speak out for Palestine.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re talking to Mahmoud Khalil. His book is just out this week. It’s called No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention. Mahmoud, I want to go back to that day that you were detained. It was actually International Women’s Day, March 8th, 2025. Just before your detention, you wrote to Columbia’s interim president at the time, Katrina Armstrong, appealing directly to her and to the university for protection. You wrote, quote, “Interim President Armstrong, Since yesterday, I have been subject to a vicious, coordinated, and dehumanizing doxxing campaign … they have falsely labeled me a security threat and called for my deportation. Their attacks have incited a wave of hate, including calls for my deportation and death threats. I have outlined the wider context below, yet Columbia has not provided any meaningful support or resources in response to this escalating threat. I haven’t been able to sleep, fearing that ICE or a dangerous individual might come to my home. I urgently need legal support, and I urge you to intervene and provide the necessary protections to prevent further harm,” unquote.

Again, that letter on the day that you ultimately were detained, just before. You were then held by ICE for 104 days. And earlier this month, you filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against Columbia University, accusing the school of failing to protect you and other pro-Palestine student activists from harassment. You’ve denounced Columbia’s, quote, “deliberate indifference” and “discrimination aimed at intimidating Palestinian students.” Can you explain exactly what this lawsuit is about?

MAHMOUD KHALIL: You know, Amy, Columbia laid the groundwork for my targeting by the Trump administration by their not only, you know, indifference to our pleas, but also for participating in vilifying us as a movement. As you’ve mentioned, Columbia did not reply or answer any of my emails. Instead, you know, Columbia fueled a very dangerous rhetoric against Palestinian students and their allies on campus. They harbored these actors who smeared and doxxed me and other Palestinian students, as well. And in fact, just recently, they settled with some of these students, and giving them money for harming — for harming us.

And I was very shocked when I joined Columbia by the level of anti-Palestinian bigotry that’s institutionalized within every department in that school. You know, I was in the School of International and Public Affairs, SIPA, and its dean, Dean Yarhi-Milo, was also very indifferent to Palestinian concerns, and her only, really, concern was how to — how to protect Israel, how to do more events and more events about Israel. Like a day after October 7, she immediately called for a webinar, inviting Hillary Clinton, to assess Israel’s next steps. And these next steps, of course, included the killing and genociding of the Palestinian, the Palestinian people.

So, Columbia was not only an idle actor in this, or that they did not do anything; they, in fact, helped fuel this campaign against me. And in one of our cases, or the cases of these students who were detained by the Trump administration, the Rubio determination, in fact, quotes what Columbia said about the protests — falsely said about these protests, because the ideologues on the Board of Trustees, it was more important for them to protect Israel than actually protecting freedom of speech, than protecting academic freedom, than protecting the students.

You know, Columbia missed an opportunity to be an institution that would respect the human rights law, that would respect just basic dignities and would, you know, be a place to have a difficult conversation. Instead, it chose to surveil its students, to bring the police more than four times to brutalize its own students, expel and suspend over 100 students. Just imagine 100 students, over 100 students, between the ages of 17 and 20, whose their future now in limbo just because they dared to protest a genocide. So, that’s why I’m bringing this lawsuit, because no student, regardless of their background, regardless whether they were Palestinians or anything — no students should go through the hell that Columbia put us through over the past three years.

ANJALI KAMAT: Mahmoud, you write, “Had Columbia possessed the power to deport me, I have little doubt it would have done so.” I want to ask you about another lawsuit you filed in July, a federal lawsuit against several top Trump administration officials, two pro-Israel groups and a conservative think tank, accused of conspiring to suppress your criticism of Israel and constitutional rights to free speech. Can you talk about this lawsuit?

MAHMOUD KHALIL: So, you know, the White House, when they arrested me, they touted about a blueprint. They said this arrest would be a blueprint to go after everyone who speaks for Palestine. And that blueprint is called Esther, the Esther Project. It’s a document or a policy document produced by the Heritage Foundation, and in that — it was produced in 2024. And what they said, that to implement this project, we need an administration that’s favorable to us, that would work with us. And as part of that project, it was detaining and deporting international students to chill the speech of other students who dare to speak out about Palestine.

So, we’re suing now government officials also in their personal capacity, because that’s — we’re suing them under the KKK Act. It’s a civil rights act that was, you know, brought during the Reconstruction era to really — you know, after the abolition of slavery and to protect the rights of Black Americans, this law was brought because there were actors conspiring together to deprive Black people from their rights. So, we’re bringing this lawsuit under that law. And, you know, a judge in Massachusetts, a Reagan appointee, confirmed what we are alleging right now, which is that government officials conspired with themselves to deprive these noncitizen students, so they can — to make an example out of them. And that judge, you know, like, in his proceeding, said, “I’ve never seen such a flagrant, just, like, assault on the Constitution or assault on the — just the rule of law.”

And I’m suing because I’m seeking accountability. I’m suing because no one should go through this, whether — you know, if they were able to deport a Palestinian for his views, they would be able to deport anyone else for their views, whether this administration or any other administration.

AMY GOODMAN: Mahmoud Khalil, you were in that Jena ICE jail for 104 days, during which time your son Deen was born. In your audio book, you do not read that chapter; you have someone else read it. And I’m wondering if you can talk about why and talk about what that meant. And you tell the story not only of missing your own baby’s birth, but of other people in that jail, another man in the same situation. And that’s also part of the power of this book, the other stories that you tell, Mahmoud.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: You know, missing the birth of my child, of Deen, was one of the most difficult times in detention. And it’s something I really — you know, it brings so many emotions to me that I was stripped that very, I would say, divine moment, like to be with my wife Noor at a moment where every couple, like, wish to be together. And as you’ve mentioned, this is not only about me. This book is about a story of so many incredible men, fathers and workers who came here seeking safety and a better future, only to be snatched off the street.

You know, I write about Alexander, the young man who was begging for safety in this country, only to be deported, only to be denied the ability to stay in safety here. And then I learn a few months later that he was killed when deported to Honduras.

I talk about the — you know, my fellow inmates, who also were not able to see their families. You know, I would go — when I would go to the visitation room in Jena, Louisiana — the detention center housed over 1,200 detainees. But when I go to the visitation room, it’s empty, because their families were frightened to come and visit them, because it was in the middle of nowhere, that — it’s in the middle of a swamp. So, their families would fear. Like, I had to tell someone that your mom shouldn’t come visit you, because she’s also undocumented. So, just imagine that you have to tell that to an 18-year-old, that your mother shouldn’t visit you because they may arrest her.

So, that was the terror, the cruelty in these detention centers. And they were designed also, like, to make people give up immediately. So, the conditions, the bad conditions in these detention centers, like the constant light, the low temperature, the bad food, it’s all designed so that you give up your case and sign your deportation order immediately, because if you want to fight, you need to be able to stay in that detention center for minimum of six months, but that could go up like a few years. You know, in only 104 days, I lost over 15 pounds. So imagine, like, staying for a year there.

AMY GOODMAN: Mahmoud Khalil, we want to thank you so much for being with us, author of the new memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention. All safety as you travel the country talking about your book. You’ll be in Somerville, Massachusetts, tonight. You’re going to be at Seattle Town Hall and all over the country.

Coming up, German human rights lawyer Wolfgang Kaleck of the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights. He’s usually here in Berlin, but he’s in New York, and we’re going to talk to him there. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “World Keeps Spinnin’” by Sol Reliqs.

author: Thiago Domenici
title: iFood passa R$ 3 milhões para pesquisa científica após acordo para encerrar inquéritos
content:
Em 16 de abril de 2021, um homem de colete preto circulava entre os entregadores do iFood que faziam greve em frente ao estádio do Pacaembu, em São Paulo. Tinha um adesivo no boné, outro no face shield, além de uma faixa de três metros de comprimento e pacotes de adesivos para distribuir. Todos diziam a mesma coisa: “vacina pros entregadores de aplicativo já”.




Parecia mais um motoboy, mas segundo a 

Agência Pública

 revelou, 

era um funcionário de uma agência de monitoramento digital a serviço de uma campanha contratada pelo iFood. A ideia da empresa era levantar a pauta das vacinas para esvaziar a reivindicação da greve.

 Funcionou: naquele dia, parte da imprensa 

noticiou

 que os entregadores pediam vacinas.




A cena abre “A máquina oculta de propaganda do iFood”, 

reportagem

 de Clarissa Levy para a 

Pública

, de abril de 2022. Com base em mais de 30 documentos e em relatos de quem trabalhou no projeto, a apuração descreveu como as agências Benjamim Comunicação e Social QI (SQi) teriam operado, entre 2020 e 2021, uma propaganda “lado B” contra os “Breques dos Apps”.







Um documento de orientação resumia a regra: “NUNCA assinado como iFood para que ninguém desconfie”. 

Numa reunião gravada, obtida pela reportagem, publicitários da Benjamim avaliaram que a Não Breca Meu Trampo “cumpriu uma missão” ao enfraquecer Paulo Lima, o Galo, líder dos Entregadores Antifascistas.

 O iFood negou qualquer relação com a SQi e disse que não compactua com perfis falsos. As agências contestaram a reportagem à época.




iFood não pode interferir em greves de entregadores




Nesta semana, o caso chegou a uma nova etapa, conforme 

informou

 o Ministério Público Federal (MPF), nesta terça-feira, 29 de setembro. 

O iFood repassou R$ 3 milhões ao Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico (CNPq) para financiar pesquisas como parte de um Termo de Ajustamento de Conduta (TAC) que a empresa, a Benjamim e a SQi assinaram em 7 de julho de 2023 com o MPF e o Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT) para encerrar três inquéritos abertos a partir da denúncia da 

Pública

.




Apesar de ter aceitado o acordo, o iFood não reconhece as condutas e repete isso na 

página que mantém sobre o TAC

: afirma que “não cometeu qualquer uma das condutas investigadas” e que assinou o TAC para evitar um processo “longo e desgastante”.




O TAC se divide em três eixos: satisfação, não repetição e compensação. Os dois primeiros, segundo o MPF, foram cumpridos “em larga medida”.




A declaração pública conjunta veio primeiro. Pelo registro do próprio iFood, saiu no site da empresa em 10 de julho de 2023, na página inicial da 

Folha de S.Paulo

 no dia 16 e, entre 18 de julho e 5 de agosto, em dias alternados, no Instagram, no Facebook e no Twitter.




Depois, veio a campanha sobre o direito à informação e a liberdade de expressão dos entregadores, com três meses de peças semanais nos perfis oficiais do iFood, criadas com a Benjamim e com alcance medido pela SQi. A proposta foi entregue aos procuradores em setembro de 2023. O MPF informa que a campanha foi realizada.




No eixo de não repetição, o iFood indicou três consultorias em direitos humanos em agosto de 2023. O MPF escolheu uma em outubro, e a contratação foi concluída em dezembro. Cabe à consultoria elaborar um programa interno para identificar riscos à transparência e à liberdade de expressão nas atividades da empresa, com relatórios semestrais ao MPF por dois anos. O MPF diz que a medida é inédita em TACs e que o programa segue “sob acompanhamento”. Por seis meses, o iFood também ficou proibido de anunciar suas próprias medidas de respeito ao direito de greve.




Outras obrigações não têm prazo para serem cumpridas. 

Perante o MPT, o iFood se comprometeu a não bloquear, suspender ou descredenciar entregadores por participação em greves ou sindicatos, a não usar “prepostos ou instrumentos tecnológicos” para interferir em manifestações e a não premiar quem deixar de aderir a paralisações.

 Benjamim e SQi assumiram compromissos semelhantes. Cada obrigação descumprida gera multa de R$ 50 mil por mês, até o limite de R$ 500 mil por ano.




Dinheiro vai para pesquisas sobre trabalho de entregadores e responsabilidade de plataformas




O eixo de compensação é o que se movimenta mais lentamente. 

O TAC fixou em R$ 6 milhões o valor que o iFood deve investir em pesquisas sobre três temas: relações de trabalho dos entregadores, mercado publicitário e responsabilidade das plataformas.

 O acordo não fixou prazo para a escolha de quem administraria o dinheiro, mas determinou que, feita a escolha, a transferência ocorreria em até 15 dias úteis. O primeiro repasse chegou três anos e dois meses após a assinatura e corresponde à metade do total.




O CNPq deve lançar, ainda neste semestre, a chamada pública para selecionar pesquisadores. Os projetos se dividem em duas frentes: regulação da publicidade e do marketing digital, e responsabilidade das plataformas diante de conteúdos falsos sobre saúde pública, meio ambiente e democracia. As pesquisas devem terminar até julho de 2030, com resultados públicos.

author: Jonathan Rosenblum
title: Amazon Is Deploying AI to Spy on Its Workers and Bust Unions Before They Form
content:
Internal company documents obtained by a Canadian labor board show how Amazon is tracking workers’ every move.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The 18th-century notion of the panopticon — a circular prison design with a guard station in the middle, allowing a single officer to enforce discipline by keeping watch over all the prisoners — has become real in the 21st century through AI-driven surveillance against workers: It’s the Amazon warehouse.

It should be no surprise that the company that harnessed technology to create a vast, $2.7 trillion empire would employ the same sophistication to enforce workplace discipline and tamp down insurgent unionization efforts. A recent disclosure of Amazon’s internal “employee relations” documents reveals just how extreme Amazon’s methods of warehouse surveillance and control have become.

Amazon employs what it calls the “Atlas” model, inputting into a computerized model a staggering amount of information on workers, their thoughts and behaviors, the workplace environment, and myriad other factors — “hundreds of data points,” according to the company. Atlas produces not just a granular measurement of ongoing worker unrest, worksite by worksite around the world, but also a prediction model for future organizing. It’s like the “precrime” police in the film Minority Report who use psychic powers to identify and apprehend would-be criminals before they act — except in this case, it’s an AI-driven tool used by the billionaire owners of one of the richest companies in history to head off rebellion among its low-wage workforce. And this is not Tom Cruise play-acting; it’s very real.

Workers anywhere who have endured anti-union campaigns can relate to stories of overbearing surveillance by management; the Atlas model, however, takes the spying to an entirely new level.

Details of the Atlas model came to light recently as a result of a legal dispute between Amazon and Unifor, the Canadian private sector union. Last year, British Columbia’s Labour Relations Board awarded union certification to Unifor at Amazon’s YVR2 warehouse outside Vancouver, finding that the company had broadly interfered in the union drive. It was the second union certification at Amazon in North America — the other being the 2022 union win at JFK8 in Staten Island, New York. But in contrast to the U.S., where Amazon has managed to stall bargaining for four and a half years because of weak labor laws, the B.C. Labour Relations Board ordered Amazon to recognize the union and negotiate. Contract bargaining commenced last December.

Not surprisingly, Amazon has dragged its feet in negotiations, prompting the union to file unfair labor practice charges with the Labour Board. Following a series of hearings earlier this year, the Labour Board found that Amazon violated provincial law. In August it ordered a remarkable step — first-contract arbitration at YVR2. That fight remains in play, but as a result of the legal proceedings, Amazon was required to turn over documents to the Labour Board and Unifor. Unifor has shared them with Truthout, and they can be viewed here.

Atlas produces not just a granular measurement of ongoing worker unrest, worksite by worksite around the world, but also a prediction model for future organizing.

In addition to the Atlas model revelation (beginning on Page 19 of the document), the material includes more than 100 pages that reveal in great detail how Amazon trains its frontline managers in union-busting. My colleague at the Center for Work and Democracy, Ben Fong, has written about this other portion of the disclosed material.

“Amazon’s own documents pull back the curtain on what workers have been telling us for years,” said Justin Gniposky, Unifor’s organizing director. “Behind the friendly PR, Amazon sees workers as property and treats their fundamental right to unionize as a threat to be managed and then eliminated.”

Amazon did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment on the Atlas model.

The documents describe the Atlas model as “a labor risk framework to clarify how Amazon evaluates emerging workforce issues, labor union targets, and internal or external labor threats.” The Atlas model ingests hundreds of data points: employee trainings completed; health and safety incidents, from simple first-aid cases to serious injuries; feedback from workers on management; worker tenure and turnover; the proximity of a warehouse to another workplace experiencing union activity; local minimum wage rates and other area economic conditions; and even the temperatures inside and outside of the warehouse.

Amazon seems especially thorough about scraping data from worker communications channels to plug into the Atlas model — the company’s internal “Voice of the Associate” (VOA) electronic bulletin board, the answers to digital questions posed daily to workers, and externally, forums including Reddit — “to understand the tenor of the discussion at the site level,” according to the documents.

“Behind the friendly PR, Amazon sees workers as property and treats their fundamental right to unionize as a threat to be managed and then eliminated.”

Atlas uses AI to identify phrases and “common keywords” to allow managers to do a “deep dive into the worker population driving the discussion.” Atlas also looks at the upvotes or other responses — positive, negative, or neutral — that the comments elicit, and the volume of those worker reactions. All of these data points go into Atlas and let managers “look around corners to identify developing themes” so they can “tailor strategic responses for addressing emerging risk.”

Amazon also tracks and documents all organizing activities that managers detect, and records them under the category of “employee relations events.” Each activity is assigned a severity score. “High severity” events include employees signing union cards, delegations of workers approaching management with demands, protests, sickouts, and work stoppages.

Atlas uses mathematical modeling to create a point system for all these data points, assigning a “labor score” to each workplace. The scale is further broken down into tiers, with the Tier 5 designation applied to facilities with high scores, where there is “no immediate perceived risk,” and Tier 1 applied to facilities where “future activity is imminent.” Amazon’s union busters focus largely on Tier 1 and 2 facilities.

Atlas produces extensive spreadsheets ranking different facilities and looking not just at raw “labor scores” but also at monthly trends. In 2024, the year the documents date from, Amazon was most concerned about union activity at 16 warehouses it had ranked as Tier 1. For instance, at LDJ5, a Staten Island sortation center across the street from JFK8, Atlas noted that leading issues of worker concern were “bathroom breaks, equipment, rest breaks, leadership/management, temperature.” The spreadsheet noted that “internal activists” — workers — were organizing, and that by looking at month-over-month trends, LDJ5 was experiencing “Risk Increase,” with the phrase placed inside a bright red box. At four of these Tier 1 facilities, the spreadsheet noted, the threat of union activity was sufficiently high to justify deploying Amazon’s “rapid response” team: union busters who travel to hotspots of organizing throughout Amazon’s global network.

Union organizing at Amazon is not just a battle over economics; it’s also a fight for basic freedom and democracy.

But the main value of Atlas seems to be predictive. For the Tier 2 worksites (“future activity is highly probable”), the spreadsheet poses these questions: “Which sites are showing the most future risk that are not Tier 1 sites yet?” and “What is the risk in each business line and which has the most risk, is it increasing or decreasing? What is driving the risk?” Tier 2 spreadsheets in the document look at the number of investigations of workers that management has handled in the last month, whether that number is trending up or down, the number of worker appeals of those investigations, and — notably — the percentage of negative worker comments on internal bulletin boards.

Voice of the Associate and other internal bulletin boards are key focal points. Charts in the document track how often workers raise particular topics, like weather, time off, breakroom amenities, management treatment, and restroom cleanliness. They also analyze the “vector” of each issue: “What are the top drivers of negative Sentiment and change MoM [month over month]?” is one question posed in the document. “What Sites are spiking MoM in negative sentiment? What themes are driving the sentiment? What anecdotes can we pull?”

Atlas is not strictly a North American tool. One chart analyzes trends for warehouses globally, documenting “employee relations events” — worker organizing — and cataloguing the number of worker comments on Voice of the Associate and the percentage of those comments that were negative. Two warehouses in the English Midlands where workers have been organizing with the GMB union — both Tier 1 sites in Atlas’ taxonomy — showed high volumes of negative VOA posts. A warehouse in Melbourne, Australia, also showed mostly negative Voice of the Associate posts, while posts were mostly not negative in some of the warehouses in Poland, Germany, and Italy.

All this is surely a tiny sliver of Atlas’s output. The former head of Amazon’s HR platforms, Bud Cashatt, boasted on LinkedIn recently about how his department created “predictive site-risk ML touching every building in Amazon’s global network.” (“ML” stands for machine learning, where programmers train AI to learn patterns and build predictions based on analyzing vast quantities of data.)

Did Jeremy Bentham, the 18th-century British philosopher who dreamed up the panopticon, anticipate Atlas? Nearly 250 years ago, he imagined his panopticon as a useful tool for prisons, “madhouses,” and also “to the business of manufactories,” the industrialized manufacturing plants then just emerging in England. Speaking of his watchman in the center of the operation — the human Atlas of his time — Bentham wrote, “The concealment of his person will be of use.”

The documents uncovered at the B.C. Labour Board shine a light on Amazon’s concealed watchman. Atlas illustrates just how far Amazon will go to try to rule the warehouse floor. And its scope also underscores just how terrified Amazon’s masters are of their own workforce rising up and claiming their due.

Bentham theorized that the panopticon would facilitate social control: He imagined that incarcerated people would behave, not knowing at any moment whether they were being watched by the guard. It was, he wrote, “A new mode of obtaining power of mind over mind.”

But what happens when prisoners — or workers — resist such attempts at social control? There’s no level of AI sophistication that can erase the reality that Amazon’s workers move millions of packages every day, and without their labor, the Amazon supply chain collapses.

Peter B. Olney, the retired organizing director of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union, calls Atlas “a promethean tool for union busting and the thwarting of any employee organizing.”

To fight back against this “existential threat” to basic worker rights and unions, Olney says, “we have to get real about deploying massive resources towards organizing the workforce and finding their serious vulnerabilities and choke points.”

Today we see emerging fights everywhere against a billionaire class intent on harnessing AI and technology to undermine basic democracy and impose authoritarianism, both in the workplace and throughout society: in revolts against the algorithmically driven content we are force-fed on the internet; protests against and sabotage of the Flock cameras on neighborhood lampposts; and resistance against the replacement of workers with bots and computers. The Atlas model places Amazon workers at the center of this global fight against the AI billionaires. And it highlights that union organizing at Amazon is not just a battle over economics; it’s also a fight for basic freedom and democracy.

author: Tadeu Porto
title: Lula Shows the Power of Workers in the Final Stretch
content:
Lula is entering the final stretch of Brazil’s most contested election, showing the intelligence and energy that define the country’s leading political figure, an asset that is beyond dispute in our history and in the history of the working class.

This moment in the campaign is not just about passion. It reflects the direct result of workers’ ability to steer public debate toward the population’s real needs.

By taking a firm stand and banning online betting, the government showed authority and political courage. It confronted gambling addiction, runaway debt among working families, and money laundering head-on. In doing so, it prioritized protecting family income and family stability, which is what the overwhelming majority of the country’s working class wants.

At the same time, the increase in Bolsa Família payments reaffirms the Lulista hallmark of this project, one that puts the poorest at the center of attention and of the budget, and ensures the state fulfills its essential role of social support.

The impact of these decisions shows up in the most recent polling. According to the BTG/Nexus survey, Lula will win 44% of the vote in the first round, compared with 39% for the second place candidate. In the runoff, the race is a statistical tie, 46% to 44%, leaving no room to be triumphant in victory.

The key data point in the poll is the group of voters who say they might still change their vote. Among them, Lula has taken a clear lead as the second choice, showing that society is moving toward a message of stability. Meanwhile, the backlash against the exploitation of faith has put respect for religion and the defense of democracy back at the center of the debate.

In the end, building the election result in this final stretch cannot depend on naive optimism. It will require steady, concrete work that speaks to the working class’s immediate needs.

This is a time for mobilization and face-to-face dialogue, carried out by workers in the streets, online and in collective spaces. When the national conversation turns back to real life, the popular project reaffirms its decisive strength.

Tadeu Porto is the director of the Unified Federation of Petroleum Workers (FUP).

title: Öcalan: The YBŞ must become part of the Iraqi army and remain in Shengal
content:
The Shengal People’s Council provided information on the latest developments in the region during an assembly. Representatives of Yazidi civil society organizations, the local population, and Yazidi security forces took part in the meeting on Wednesday. A message from Abdullah Öcalan was read out during the assembly.




In the message, the Kurdish leader focuses in particular on the future of the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and the protection of Yazidi society. He advocates integrating the YBŞ into the Iraqi army while allowing it to remain in Shengal as a local force. “The YBŞ must remain in Shengal,” Öcalan states, describing the Yazidis’ own self-defense forces as necessary.




Öcalan also addresses the talks between the YBŞ and the Iraqi government. According to the information available to him, an agreement has already been drafted but has not yet been signed by the Iraqi prime minister. Reports indicate that the agreement is being blocked by Turkey. Öcalan calls on Ankara not to obstruct it and emphasizes that the Yazidis are not demanding an autonomous region, but local democracy.




Abdullah Öcalan's message to the Yazidi community reads as follows:




“Do Yazidi women have a strong stance in the face of ISIS attacks? This needs to be understood. Yazidi culture alone is also not sufficient for freedom. I say this, and I have also told the state the same thing, and I repeat it: In view of the threat of attacks against the Yazidis in general, we will protect them through armed means. Even if everything goes well here, we will shift more of our focus there and protect them. The state must understand this as well.




My message to this young woman is this: What has happened to you must make you stronger. You must develop your personality. A common language must be created that will carry the line forward. If you know Kurdish, you should also learn to write it and use the language extensively. You should write down what you have experienced and preserve it for history. I hope that we will see each other soon.




The YBŞ must remain in Shengal. If this does not happen, neither Barzani nor the Arabs will grant them the right to live. If the YBŞ becomes part of the Iraqi army, they must remain where they are. A decision has been made to eliminate them. The Yazidis must have their own self-defense forces. The Yazidi people are currently undergoing a process of genocide and have no legal protection.




According to the statements that have been made, talks are taking place between the YBŞ and the Iraqi government. An agreement is even said to have already been drafted. However, the prime minister has not signed it. It is said that the Turkish state is blocking the agreement. The Turkish state must not obstruct it. Because the Yazidis are not talking about an autonomous region. They want local democracy. We will discuss all of this with the High Committee. I assume that our demands will be readily accepted. It is the KDP that seeks discrimination and division. We will also discuss this at our committee meeting.




For Shengal, a model similar to the one in Turkey should be developed. That is why I removed the obstacle posed by the PKK. The PKK is no longer an obstacle to resolving the problems. In other words, the PKK has completed its time and fulfilled its role. However, if action is not taken in accordance with this reality, it will become incapable of acting during this process. Ultimately, I decided to dissolve the PKK, and I take responsibility for that decision. There may be some shortcomings, but this approach is correct.




Self-defense is a necessity in Shengal. The YBŞ must take its place within the Iraqi army. According to what has been reported, Iraq has agreed to this. If that is the case, it is a good thing. It is still unclear who is behind ISIS. Arab nationalism is strong. Even if this nationalism is pushed back, they will eliminate the Yazidi people as soon as they have the opportunity. Arab nationalism subjected the Turkmens in Kirkuk to a massacre. Local security is necessary to prevent this from happening again.




In Iraq, this applies to almost every tribe. The system that exists in Turkey does not exist in Iraq. Such protection is also necessary for the Turkmens and Yazidis. The problems of the Yazidis must also be resolved. A close relationship must be established with Shengal.”
