author: Rizomatica
title: Ante la amenaza de la instalación de torres de alta tensión comunidades recurrirán a la justicia contra el proyecto Itahue-Hualqui
content:
La iniciativa contempla una línea de transmisión de 407 kilómetros entre el Maule y Biobío, y ha sido cuestionada por los efectos que generaría sobre ecosistemas, actividades productivas y formas de vida locales, así como por la falta de una evaluación integral de sus impactos acumulativos relacionados con otras iniciativas extractivas que se proyectan para estas regiones, tanto energéticas como vinculadas a la minería de tierras raras.




La acción judicial será presentada ante el Segundo Tribunal Ambiental para solicitar la revisión de la decisión que mantuvo vigente la aprobación ambiental del proyecto Sistema de Transmisión Zonal Grupo 3 S/E Itahue – S/E Hualqui, luego del rechazo del recurso administrativo de invalidación.




Con esta acción se inicia una nueva etapa en la judicialización del proyecto, luego de que el Comité de Ministros resolviera mantener su aprobación ambiental. La reclamación cuestionará tanto aspectos de forma como de fondo de la decisión adoptada durante el procedimiento de evaluación ambiental.




La iniciativa, presentada por el consorcio español CELEO Redes, a través de su empresa Mataquito Transmisora de Energía, contempla una línea de 407 kilómetros entre el Maule y Biobío, amenazando los ecosistemas y la calidad de vida de los habitantes de 20 comunas. Expertos advierten vacíos técnicos en la evaluación ambiental y riesgos acumulativos por la concentración de infraestructura eléctrica.




Los argumentos




Entre los principales argumentos que serán presentados ante el Tribunal se encuentra la falta de fundamentación técnica para revertir los pronunciamientos desfavorables de organismos sectoriales, particularmente aquellos formulados por CONAF y otros organismos con competencia ambiental.




La acción también cuestiona las deficiencias de la línea de base en materia de flora y vegetación, incluyendo la caracterización de especies en categoría de conservación, ecosistemas críticos y bosque nativo remanente en sectores próximos al área de amortiguación e influencia del Parque Nacional Nonguén.




En materia de fauna, se señala que la evaluación ambiental no habría considerado adecuadamente la pérdida y fragmentación de hábitats, los impactos acústicos asociados a las líneas de transmisión y los riesgos de colisión y electrocución para aves migratorias, rapaces y especies amenazadas o endémicas.




La reclamación también aborda deficiencias relacionadas con recursos hídricos y suelos, particularmente por la construcción de torres, caminos e instalaciones en sectores de ladera, junto con los posibles efectos de erosión y arrastre de sedimentos y la afectación de humedales, vegas y cursos de agua.




Consulta indígena y participación ciudadana




Otro de los ejes de la acción judicial es la falta de consulta indígena, en relación con los efectos que el proyecto tendría sobre territorios ancestrales, sitios de significación cultural y ceremonial, espacios de recolección de 

lawen

 y prácticas tradicionales de comunidades y asociaciones indígenas de las comunas involucradas.




Asimismo, se cuestiona la evaluación de los impactos sobre los sistemas de vida y costumbres de las comunidades locales, considerando actividades agrícolas, apícolas, ganaderas y de subsistencia, además de aspectos como la división de terrenos, pérdida de valor predial, ruido, contaminación electromagnética y riesgos asociados a incendios forestales.




Para Marioles Quevedo, vecina de Maqueuto Sur, la instalación de las torres representa una amenaza para un territorio donde se desarrollan actividades agrícolas, apícolas y ganaderas.




“Defendiendo mi territorio, defendiendo mi naturaleza y los animales silvestres de Maqueuto Sur, donde quieren instalar doce hectáreas de torres produciendo un gran daño al ecosistema, un impacto ambiental. Nuestro entorno es apícola, agrícola y ganadero. Todos mis vecinos y mi familia no queremos este tipo de torres de transmisión eléctrica, debido a su alto impacto a nuestro ecosistema y su entorno natural”.







A ello se suma el cuestionamiento a los procesos de participación ciudadana, respecto de los cuales se alegará la exclusión de organizaciones comunitarias e indígenas y la insuficiencia de las instancias desarrolladas durante la evaluación ambiental.




Para Macarena Lagos, integrante de la agrupación Toconey No Se Toca, de la región del Maule, la decisión de recurrir a tribunales responde a la necesidad de continuar defendiendo el territorio frente a los efectos negativos que la comunidad atribuye al proyecto.




“Como comunidad de Toconey estamos defendiendo nuestro territorio. Aquí nacieron nuestros abuelos, aquí crecimos y aquí queremos que crezcan nuestros hijos. Es por eso que nos hacemos parte de este recurso”.




Lagos agrega que, durante la presentación del proyecto, la propia empresa habría reconocido que la iniciativa no generaría beneficios para la localidad.




“Cuando vino la empresa, sus representantes reconocieron que este proyecto no traería ningún beneficio a nuestra localidad. Ninguno. Es por esta razón que asumimos este desafío y llegaremos hasta el final. Porque rendirse no es una opción. Es entregar nuestro territorio en bandeja. Es abrir la puerta a todo lo que pueda venir asociado a él y a otros megaproyectos que quieran instalarse”.







Impactos acumulativos y relación con otros proyectos




La reclamación también plantea cuestionamientos respecto del fraccionamiento y la evaluación de impactos sinérgicos y acumulativos.




En particular, se argumentará que determinadas obras del proyecto, como la Subestación Las Delicias, podrían cumplir una función habilitante para otros proyectos energéticos que se desarrollan o proyectan en el territorio, entre ellos el Parque Eólico Quirihue Poniente.




Desde esta perspectiva, la acción sostiene que la evaluación debió considerar de manera integral los efectos que podrían producirse por la concurrencia de distintas iniciativas, incluyendo ruido, tránsito pesado, sombra intermitente y transformación de sectores rurales vinculados actualmente a actividades agrícolas y ganaderas.




El abogado de la ONG Defensa Ambiental, Francisco Astorga, señaló que la presentación ante el Tribunal Ambiental constituye el siguiente paso luego del rechazo del recurso administrativo.




“Dado el rechazo de nuestro recurso de invalidación por parte del Comité de Ministros, vamos a recurrir ante el Tribunal Ambiental para que sea éste quien acoja los Recursos de Invalidación y Reclamación de Observaciones Ciudadanas.”







Dos procesos judiciales que continuarán en paralelo




La nueva reclamación se suma a los recursos derivados de las observaciones ciudadanas que ya se encuentran en tramitación ante el Segundo Tribunal Ambiental.




Ambos procedimientos tienen orígenes y fundamentos distintos: mientras la nueva acción busca impugnar la decisión del Comité de Ministros respecto del recurso de invalidación, las reclamaciones de observaciones ciudadanas se relacionan con cuestionamientos formulados durante el proceso de participación ciudadana.




Una vez admitida a trámite la nueva reclamación, se espera que el Tribunal continúe con la revisión de ambos procesos. De acuerdo con la tramitación prevista, los alegatos correspondientes a ambas causas serán conocidos conjuntamente en una misma audiencia, en la fecha que determine el Tribunal, instancia que será transmitida públicamente.




De esta manera, la aprobación ambiental del proyecto 

Sistema de Transmisión Zonal Grupo 3 S/E Itahue – S/E Hualqui

 continuará siendo discutida ante la justicia ambiental, mientras las comunidades y la ONG Defensa Ambiental mantienen las acciones destinadas a cuestionar su legalidad y los impactos que atribuyen a su ejecución en los territorios involucrados.



















Por: 

ONG Defensa Ambiental




Esta información se publicó en 

Radio Kurruf

.

author: Unknown
title: We can definitely use the words estrogen and testosterone (though ‘get curvy HRT’ might also involve…
content:
trackerkitsune

:

queeranarchism

:

nico-thenecromancer

:

mx-macintosh

:

they are estrogen and testosterone

. 

they are estrogenizing and androgenizing hrt.

 stop fucking calling them transfem and transmasc hrt. stop fucking calling them mtf and ftm hrt. stop fucking calling them feminizing and masculinizing hrt. 

stop going out of your way to exclude non-binary and intersex people.

As a non-binary person on hrt (and in the process of getting off it) I approve this message!

Honestly I have mixed feelings about this, because I encounter a lot of trans people who didn’t stay in school long enough to learn to read, or who don’t have English as their first language, or have a disability that impacts language, for whom learning the words ‘estrogenizing and androgenizing’ are not easy tasks.

Communicating in this ways would alienate them from the spaces in which I am trying to talk about HRT. & those spaces are already far too dominated by college educated white middle class trans kids. 

Like, I could see myself explaining all the effects of both options and then calling it 'get curvy HRT’ and 'grow hair everywhere’ HRT’. But I would not go for words that make it qall sound even more complicated.   

As a nonbinary person, have we tried just calling them estrogen and testosterone??? And not infantilising whole people who can, in fact, learn to say words with a bit of patience and grace given to them?

Can we stop dumbing down language?




We can definitely use the words estrogen and testosterone (though 'get curvy HRT’ might also involve progesterone and one of 6 different kinds of blockers) but we still have to explain what they are and what they do. 

Because people do. not. know. I’ve done a lot of trans-on-trans education and people with language-barriers often lack the most basic knowledge about what hrt does and doesn’t do. I’ve met people who thought they could grow fully functional penis and balls on T and could get women pregnant with sperm from those new balls. I’ve met people who thought it was impossible to grow boobs on E. 

People don’t know and they can not 'just google it’ because that requires access to written text or being able to navigate complicated text-to-speech software. It’s overwhelming and asking for help is scary because ignorance and illiteracy gets shamed a lot. So when they do ask for help, they need someone to explain HRT to them in words that they already know. 

There is nothing 'infantilising’ about meeting people where they’re at and including the whole spectrum of disabilities in our spaces without expecting them to first learn enough to meet our communication standards. Simple language is a basic accessibility issue for a lot of people. So yeah, we 

need

 to dumb down language if we actually want 

all

 trans people to have access to care and community.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Libro: Entrenamiento, Bases y Militarización en América Latina
content:
Por Álvaro Ramis







(Prólogo) El presente libro, Entrenamiento, Bases y Militarización en América Latina: La OTAN y Estados Unidos en América Latina, compilado por Pablo Ruiz Espinoza, llega en un momento histórico de profunda reconfiguración geopolítica mundial. Su objetivo es tan claro como urgente: evidenciar las múltiples formas en que el militarismo global —articulado principalmente por los Estados Unidos y la OTAN— continúa reproduciendo estructuras de dominación en nuestra región bajo nuevos rostros, discursos y tecnologías.




A lo largo de estas páginas, un destacado conjunto de autores y autoras —entre ellos Alicia Lira Matus, Renán Vega Cantor, Paola Gallo, Olga Pinheiro, W.T. Whitney, Gabriel Aguirre, Alfonso Insuasty Rodríguez, Andrés Escobar Vásquez, David Barrios Rodríguez, Félix Madariaga, Hervi Lara Bravo, Vijay Prashad y Pablo Ruiz— ofrece un análisis colectivo y plural sobre un mismo fenómeno: la expansión del poder militar occidental y sus consecuencias sobre la soberanía, la paz y los derechos humanos en América Latina y el Caribe.




El texto no se limita a la denuncia, sino que propone un marco interpretativo para comprender las continuidades históricas de la política imperial estadounidense, desde la Doctrina Monroe hasta la actual configuración de alianzas estratégicas, bases militares y acuerdos de “cooperación en defensa”. Las más de 800 bases distribuidas por el planeta, muchas de ellas en territorio latinoamericano, son expresión material de una lógica de control que combina injerencia política, condicionamientos económicos y dominación cultural. En este contexto, la OTAN aparece como un instrumento de expansión global del poder euroatlántico, cuyo interés por la región se reactiva en un escenario de crisis energética, disputa por los recursos naturales y competencia con potencias emergentes.




El libro también aborda los efectos internos de esta militarización. En países donde el discurso de la “seguridad nacional” se impone como dogma, se normaliza la presencia del ejército en tareas de orden interno, el espionaje sobre movimientos sociales y la criminalización de la protesta.




América Latina corre el riesgo de convertirse, una vez más, en el laboratorio de una guerra sin fronteras: una guerra que no se libra solo con armas, sino también con sanciones económicas, bloqueos financieros, campañas mediáticas y manipulación de la opinión pública.




Cada capítulo aporta una mirada crítica sobre hechos concretos: la ocupación ilegal de Guantánamo, la impunidad de las violaciones a los derechos humanos en ese enclave; el resurgimiento del racismo y la xenofobia institucional en la política migratoria de Estados Unidos; las agresiones sistemáticas contra Venezuela, Cuba, Nicaragua y Haití; y el papel de los grandes medios de comunicación en la guerra informativa contra los procesos de emancipación regional.




Pero el libro no se queda en la denuncia: formula propuestas de acción y articulación internacionalista. Entre ellas, la exigencia de convertir a América Latina y el Caribe en una “Zona de Paz”, en consonancia con la Proclama adoptada por la CELAC en 2014. Este horizonte supone fortalecer la solidaridad entre los pueblos, promover la educación para la paz, y construir un modelo de desarrollo basado en la justicia social, la equidad ecológica y la autodeterminación.




En estas páginas se entrelazan, además, las luchas de los pueblos palestino, saharaui, haitiano, indígena y afrodescendiente, entendidas no como causas ajenas, sino como parte de una misma resistencia al orden imperial. El libro recuerda que la paz no puede construirse desde la subordinación ni desde la exclusión: requiere soberanía, memoria histórica y voluntad de transformación colectiva.




Entrenamiento, Bases y Militarización en América Latina es, en definitiva, una invitación a mirar críticamente el mapa militar del continente, a interpelar los discursos que justifican la injerencia y a reconocer que la verdadera defensa no se mide en número de tanques o bases, sino en la capacidad de los pueblos para sostener su independencia, cuidar sus territorios y garantizar vidas dignas.




Como advierte uno de los autores, “la paz no es ausencia de conflicto, sino presencia de justicia”. Este volumen, al reunir voces diversas de nuestro continente y más allá, constituye una contribución fundamental a esa justicia pendiente. Leerlo es un acto de conciencia, pero también de compromiso: un llamado a resistir la normalización del militarismo y a reimaginar una América Latina libre, soberana y solidaria.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Farsacracia Argentina: el infame recorrido de los traidores
content:
La historia reciente de la Argentina parece escrita por manos que confunden poder con impunidad. El artículo 154 del inconstitucional DNU 70/2023 marcó el inicio de una ofensiva contra la soberanía nacional: al permitir la venta ilimitada de tierras a extranjeros, se abrió la puerta a la entrega del territorio, disfrazada de “modernización” y “libertad económica”. Fue el primer acto de una farsa institucional que hoy alcanza su clímax.




La reacción popular no tardó. Las movilizaciones ciudadanas, las organizaciones sociales y los centros de excombatientes denunciaron el atropello y lograron que la justicia declarara la 

inconstitucionalidad del decreto

, recordando que ningún gobierno puede disponer del suelo argentino como si fuera mercancía. Ese fallo fue una victoria de la ciudadanía, un recordatorio de que la soberanía no se negocia.




Pero los intereses espurios no descansan. El siguiente intento llegó bajo otro nombre: el proyecto de 

“Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada”

, una maniobra legislativa que buscaba reinstalar el mismo espíritu entreguista, esta vez con ropaje jurídico. El Senado, presionado por la movilización popular, rechazó el proyecto. Otra vez, la calle impuso su voz frente al poder.




Sin embargo, la trama no terminó allí. La reciente decisión de la 

Corte Suprema de Justicia

 de revocar el fallo que había frenado la derogación de la Ley de Tierras y restablecer el artículo 154 del DNU 70/2023 representa el último capítulo de esta farsacracia: un sistema donde las instituciones parecen servir más a los intereses del capital extranjero que al pueblo argentino. La Corte, escudada en tecnicismos, evitó pronunciarse sobre el fondo, pero su silencio es cómplice. Con su fallo, deja nuevamente abierta la puerta a la extranjerización del territorio.




Cada intento de entrega fue frenado por la movilización ciudadana. Cada vez, el pueblo salió a defender lo que es suyo. Pero los poderes económicos, los lobbies y los jueces funcionales al modelo de dependencia han demostrado que pueden imponerse incluso contra la voluntad popular.




Hoy, más que nunca, 

la soberanía está en peligro

. No por invasiones externas, sino por traiciones internas. Por quienes, desde los despachos, venden el país pedazo a pedazo mientras hablan de progreso.




La historia no se repite: se profundiza. Si el pueblo no vuelve a ocupar las calles, si no defiende su tierra, su agua y su futuro, la Argentina quedará reducida a un territorio administrado por intereses ajenos. Es hora de despertar, de organizarse, de resistir. Porque 

la soberanía no se mendiga: se defiende.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Jorge Macri redobla la apuesta represiva en CABA
content:
El gobierno de CABA busca avanzar con la implementación y el uso de sistemas de reconocimiento facial en el espacio público. Nuevo desalojo. Las escuelas asociadas al sistema penal. Contra la Marcha del Orgullo







Por Mario Hernandez




El gobierno de la Ciudad está intentando reactivar el sistema de reconocimiento facial mediante cámaras instaladas por todo Buenos Aires. El viernes pasado se celebró una audiencia judicial para revisar el nuevo proceso de licitación impulsado por el gobierno. ¿Por qué una audiencia judicial? Porque existe una causa legal en curso que ha mantenido suspendido el sistema de reconocimiento facial durante cuatro años. En abril de 2019, la ciudad activó el sistema de reconocimiento facial, cuyo objetivo declarado era identificar a prófugos y personas con órdenes de captura pendientes.


El sistema no se utilizaba para localizar a prófugos; por el contrario, terminaron incluyendo indiscriminadamente a 10 millones de personas. Elaboraban listas arbitrarias y actuaban a partir de ahí. Todo esto salió a la luz gracias a la labor del CELS, ODIA, Ceprodh y diversas organizaciones de Derechos Humanos dedicadas a estas cuestiones. En 2022, la justicia declaró inconstitucional la implementación del sistema y, en 2023, la Cámara de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires ratificó dicho fallo.




“Ley y Orden”, dejó a 60 personas en la calle




Durante la mañana del martes, bajo la lluvia, un operativo de la Policía de la Ciudad desalojó a 60 personas de un edificio del barrio porteño de Constitución. En el inmueble ubicado de la calle Luis Sáenz Peña 1700, donde antiguamente funcionaba un hotel, vivían desde hace 21 años familias con niños, incluso.


Tres camiones, un vallado y varios efectivos fueron dispuestos para llevar adelante la medida. La orden judicial fue dispuesta por el Juzgado de Primera Instancia en lo Contencioso Administrativo y Tributario N°9.


Desde el Gobierno porteño señalaron que el inmueble no reúne condiciones de seguridad para ser habitado debido a su deterioro edilicio y a la falta de mantenimiento. Sin embargo, como se ha advertido, es la modalidad utilizada por la justicia porteña servil a los intereses del PRO para avanzar con esta verdadera expulsión de personas.




Denuncian que Jorge Macri convierte a las escuelas en una puerta de entrada al sistema penal




El Gobierno de la Ciudad avanza con la implementación del Régimen Penal Juvenil dentro de las escuelas porteñas. Un nuevo protocolo establece que las autoridades educativas tienen el “deber de denunciar” ante situaciones que pudieran constituir delitos y dispone mecanismos para la intervención de la Policía y la Justicia. La medida se aplica en el marco del nuevo régimen que establece la responsabilidad penal desde los 14 años.


Entrevistado en 

AM750

, Federico Puy, secretario general adjunto de Ademys, denunció el nuevo protocolo del Gobierno porteño que obliga a las autoridades escolares a denunciar hechos que pudieran constituir delitos e incorpora la intervención policial y judicial en las escuelas. “Es parte de una política de criminalización de las juventudes”, señaló.


La normativa alcanza a las situaciones que ocurran dentro de los establecimientos educativos, pero también contempla hechos que involucren a estudiantes y estén vinculados con la comunidad educativa. Frente a determinadas situaciones, los directivos deberán dar intervención al 911, al SAME y a organismos de protección de derechos. En otros casos, deberán realizar la denuncia ante el Ministerio Público Fiscal. De esta manera, conflictos que hasta ahora podían abordarse mediante herramientas de convivencia escolar quedan bajo la posibilidad de una intervención penal.


“La escuela pasa a ser un lugar donde se denuncia a los pibes”, cuestionó Federico Puy, al referirse al nuevo protocolo. El dirigente docente señaló que la medida debe ser leída en conjunto con el avance del Régimen Penal Juvenil y advirtió sobre el peligro de transformar a las instituciones educativas en espacios atravesados por la lógica policial y judicial.


El protocolo también habilita la presencia policial dentro de las escuelas en determinadas circunstancias. Para los docentes, esto supone un cambio profundo en el funcionamiento de las instituciones: frente a situaciones de conflicto, en lugar de fortalecer los equipos de orientación, trabajadores sociales y herramientas pedagógicas, el Gobierno incorpora como respuesta la denuncia, la Policía y el Ministerio Público Fiscal. La lógica punitiva se introduce así en un ámbito que debería garantizar derechos y acompañar las trayectorias educativas.


Esta avanzada punitivista que intentan penetrarla dentro del sistema educativo debe ser enmarcada en toda una ola de persecuciones, represiones y judicialización de los sectores populares. Desde los más hollywoodenses como los operativo Tormenta Negra sobre los barrios populares o los desalojos violentos hasta la persecución sistemática contra los vendedores ambulantes.


Desde Ademys cuestionan que el Gobierno porteño coloque sobre los equipos directivos la responsabilidad de denunciar situaciones que “pudieran” constituir delitos y advierten que esto puede profundizar la criminalización de estudiantes, particularmente de adolescentes. La denuncia docente apunta a una política que, mientras recorta recursos para abordar las problemáticas sociales y educativas, refuerza los mecanismos de control y persecución sobre las juventudes.




Macri contra la Marcha del Orgullo




Jorge Macri intenta correr la Marcha del Orgullo el próximo 7N por la visita del Papa. Una vez más la discusión sobre el papel retrógrado de las iglesias frente a los derechos de las diversidades y la necesidad de no subordinar las luchas a ningún gobierno.


La decisión del Gobierno de Jorge Macri de restringir los eventos en el espacio público entre el 6 y el 13 de noviembre, con motivo de la visita del papa León XIV, puso en discusión la realización de la Marcha del Orgullo prevista para el 7 de noviembre.


La Comisión Organizadora rechazó la posibilidad de postergarla y ratificó la convocatoria. El canciller Pablo Quirno, por su parte, afirmó que la movilización está contemplada dentro del operativo de seguridad previsto para la visita papal.


El conflicto por el 7N vuelve a poner en primer plano la necesidad de que el movimiento LGBTIQ+ mantenga su independencia política frente a los gobiernos, los partidos y las iglesias.


El intento de mover la Marcha del Orgullo también vuelve a poner bajo la lupa el vínculo entre el Estado y las instituciones religiosas. La visita de León XIV llega en un contexto en el que distintos sectores religiosos, incluidos grupos evangélicos conservadores, buscan intervenir en debates sobre ESI, derechos sexuales y reproductivos y diversidad.


La discusión no pasa por las creencias personales sino por el papel político de las instituciones religiosas. Frente a esto, la independencia del movimiento implica que sus demandas no queden subordinadas a acuerdos entre gobiernos e iglesias.

Jorge Macri redobla la apuesta represiva en CABA

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Activists Are Targeting One of ICE’s Key Staging Grounds — Parking Spots
content:
Protesters say they are “throwing sand in the gears” of the agency’s deportation and abduction machine.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.

In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson, and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, have issued executive orders banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from using city-owned parking lots and properties.

But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency posted a notice seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu released a public letter to local parking garage and lot owners, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”

“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,” she wrote. “In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity.”

In the Boston suburb of Burlington, Massachusetts, Bearing Witness New England has been holding weekly protests outside ICE’s Boston Field Office, where people are held for days in inhumane conditions. Activists say ICE has been keeping its vehicles in a nearby parking lot owned by local developer National Development.

According to a report by NPR affiliate WBUR, the company sent a letter to local activists in February, stating that ICE vehicles were being “improperly parked” in its parking spaces, and that it had “reached an arrangement with ICE that they would no longer park their vehicles on our property.”

However, the company also said that the government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has rights to use the garage and the company does not have authority over how the FAA parcels out parking spaces to other federal agencies, according to WBUR’s report.

Nathan Phillips, a Boston University professor who organizes with the Burlington-area coalition Building Up Resilience Networks (B.U.R.N.), says ICE has continued to park in sections of lots National Development leases to the FAA that exceed what the lease allows.

Protests that target parking garages are “throwing sand in the gears” of ICE’s deportation and abduction machine, he says.

“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel … It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”

“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel,” Phillips told Truthout. “It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”

Fellow B.U.R.N. activist Josh Model says National Development’s recent actions contradict its public image as a philanthropic company committed to improving communities.

“National Development Corporation, which, as a local developer, likes to promote that they’re cognizant of community needs and give to charity and all these nice things,” but they’re “letting ICE stage kidnappings” from their property, said Model.

While the government spending website, usaspending.gov, only lists 12 active contracts for parking spaces, as of September 28, the true number of parking lots that ICE uses is likely much higher, said Model. It’s difficult to untangle where ICE is parking, in part, because many of the contracts are not with ICE, but through another federal agency, the General Services Administration (GSA), he said. The GSA manages government buildings and real estate, and owns or leases space in more than 8,300 buildings, according to an explainer on the agency published by the Congressional Research Service.

In the case of National Development, ICE is using parking leased by the GSA for the FAA, according to Model.

Of the 12 contracts found on usaspending.gov, two were with the Philadelphia Parking Authority (PPA). The PPA website states that, among other responsibilities, it coordinates “the efforts of public agencies concerning parking” and establishes and operates public parking facilities. Its operations are governed by a six-member state-appointed board appointed by the governor of Pennsylvania.

Earlier this year, Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker signed a package of bills to protect city residents from ICE, including legislation that prohibits ICE from using city-owned properties as staging locations for raids and prohibits employees from granting ICE access to city-owned spaces without a judicial warrant. Over its history, the PPA has had a complicated relationship between state and city governance. It is currently controlled by a state-appointed board. The Parking Authority did not respond to a request for comment.

One contract with the PPA “provides Homeland Security Investigations with sixteen leased parking spaces in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.” It runs from Sept. 30, 2026 to Sept. 29, 2027, with a potential end date of Sept. 29, 2031. A separate contract ran from Sept. 30, 2025 to Sept. 29, 2026, and was for “the rental of indoor parking garage spaces required for government vehicles for ICE Homeland Security Investigations Philadelphia.”

“City Council’s ICE OUT package of legislation is one of the most comprehensive measures in the country that used every tool available within City Council’s authority to limit collaboration between ICE and City government, including protecting our data, protecting residents from intimidation and discrimination, and limiting the use of City owned spaces for staging,” Councilmember At-Large Rue Landau said in a statement to Truthout.

Landau and Minority Leader Kendra Brooks introduced the ICE OUT legislation.

“As ICE continues to instill fear and perpetrate violence against our neighbors and in our communities, I think PPA should take a hard look at this federal government contract and what their options are as the independent agency running those spaces to limit ICE’s use,” Rue said.

Protesters in New York have uncovered what they say are ICE vehicles parked in an Icon parking garage in downtown Manhattan’s Tribeca neighborhood. Earlier this month, activists in New York protested outside the parking garage. Icon did not respond to emails requesting comment.

“The neighbors downtown don’t know that their neighborhoods, their communities, are being used as staging ground for ruthless assaults on our neighbors in more vulnerable neighborhoods,” said Julie DeLaurier, an activist with Rise and Resist. “People are walking around oblivious to the threat that these thugs present to our neighbors.”

Rise and Resist, along with Hands OFF NYC, are part of the NO PARKING FOR ICE coalition.

New York City Councilmember Christopher Marté, whose district includes Tribeca, was one of the approximately hundred people who attended a protest outside the Icon parking garage in September.

“What we’ve been seeing all throughout the city is a really drastic uptick of ICE abductions of our neighbors,” Marté told Truthout in a phone interview. “They use these parking lots as staging locations, and so I believe if we disrupt, evict them from these parking lots, then they would have no place to start their process of abducting our neighbors.”

“We will do whatever we can to protect our neighbors. One thing we can do is let ICE know that they will have no peace trying to park on our streets in downtown Manhattan to terrorize our neighbors.”

Earlier this year, activists demanded that Hudson River Park Trust, which manages the Hudson River Park in Manhattan, cut its contract with ICE for parking spaces at Pier 40 at the park. After widespread outcry, the company did not renew its contract when it expired on June 30.

However, community members say they saw what appeared to be ICE vehicles park on the property in July, according to amNewYork. The news outlet reported that a company spokesperson said they would look into the situation and noted that the Trust has federal parking contracts with other agencies, including the GSA.

DeLaurier says New Yorkers will continue to fight to get ICE off their streets.

“New Yorkers protect New Yorkers from ICE,” said DeLaurier. “We will do whatever we can to protect our neighbors. One thing we can do is let ICE know that they will have no peace trying to park on our streets in downtown Manhattan to terrorize our neighbors.”

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

title: MARFIN Απορρίφθηκε η προσφυγή της 46χρονης
content:
Με το υπ. αριθμ. 

3763/2026 βούλευμα του Συμβουλίου

 Πλημμελειοδικών Αθηνών 

απορρίφθηκε ηπροσφυγή 

της 46χρονης κατηγορούμενης για την υπόθεση Μarfin

 εναντίον του εντάλματος προσωρινής κράτησης

, που προφυλακίστηκε χωρίς η ανακρίτρια και ο εισαγγελέας που την αποφάσισαν να λάβουν υπ όψη τους το απαλλακτικό δεδικασμένο του 2022, την ομολογημένη από τη ΔΕΕ/ΕΛΑΣ έλλειψη ταυτοποίησης της με το πρόσωπο που εικονίζεται ως ύποπτο και την τεράστια 

καταστροφή στη ζωή της ίδιας και της πεντάχρονης κόρης της

 που προξενείται.




Η εισαγγελική πρόταση που είχε προηγηθεί ήταν

απορριπτική για την προσφυγή,

 κάτι που ήταν αναμενόμενο αφού επιλογές ανωτέρων της είναι εκείνες που έχουν αναλάβει την νομική ευθύνη για την ανάσυρση της δικογραφίας και την άσκηση της ποινικής δίωξης. Τα επιχειρήματά της 

απαντήθηκαν αναλυτικά με υπόμνημα

 που κατατέθηκε στις 2.9.2026 υπ όψη του Συμβουλίου, αλλά δεν προκύπτει από το περιεχόμενο του βουλεύματος ότι ελήφθη υπ όψη.




Αξιοσημείωτη είναι η καθυστέρηση ανάμεσα στην ημερομηνία διάσκεψης (10.9.2026) και την ημερομηνία έκδοσης του βουλεύματος (25.9.2026). Και ακόμα περισσότερο το ότι με 

διαφορετική επιχειρηματολογία και επίκληση νομικών διατάξεων από την εισαγγελέα 

το συμβούλιο επιχειρεί να  παρακάμψει την ύπαρξη δεδικασμένου. Η διαφοροποίηση από την εισαγγελική πρόταση επιβεβαιώνει την αβεβαιότητα και τη σύγχυση για τη νομιμότητα της δίωξης και παρά το δυσμενές διατακτικό δικαιώνει και μόνο εξ αυτού τις αντιρρήσεις μας. Σχετικά με την έλλειψη ταυτοποίησης το Συμβούλιο δεν διατυπώνει ιδιαίτερες κρίσεις. Επαφίεται στην εισαγγελική πρόταση και σιωπά στα εναντίον της επιχειρήματα του υπομνήματός μας και της τεχνικής έκθεσης του κ. Καραθανάση, την ύπαρξη των οποίων ούτε καν αναφέρει.




Τελικό συμπέρασμα είναι ότι τα αρμόδια δικαστικά όργανα δεν έχουν ακόμα ξεπεράσει το σοκ από τον πρόσφατο επικοινωνιακό βομβαρδισμό κυβέρνησης και Μ.Μ.Ε. και την περιρρέουσα ατμόσφαιρα, που αργεί ακόμα να διαλυθείπαρά το γεγονός ότι όλον αυτόν τον καιρό

δεν υπήρξε κάποιος

 από την κυβέρνηση η την αστυνομία 

για να διαψεύσει

 όσα έχουμε καταγγείλει.




Ετσι η 46χρονη παραμένει θύμα της κατάστασης αυτής, 

προφυλακισμένη άδικα, χωρίς στοιχεία εναντίον της, χωρίς ταυτοποίηση και κατά παράβαση δεδικασμένου

και αντιμετωπίζει την 

καταστροφή της ζωής της και την αποκοπή της από την πεντάχρονη κόρη της

 μέχρι νεωτέρας. Ενώ η ανάκριση δεν έχει προχωρήσει 

ούτε καν στην ανεύρεση του αποστολέα του ανώνυμου μέηλ

 που προκάλεσε τη δίωξη. Μόνο στις προφυλακίσεις !




Είναι αυτονόητο ότι θα εξαντλήσουμε κάθε νόμιμο μέσο μέχρι τη δικαίωση.




Αθήνα, 

30.9.2026




Κώστας Παπαδάκης




συνήγορος υπεράσπισης

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.




The root cause




According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.




The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.




“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.




Lives of patients at risk




The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”




The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.




The nurse also told 

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.




Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told 

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.




It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.




Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Admin101
title: “A Dense Web of Solidarity”: How Chicago Public School Workers Defend Students Against ICE
content:
ICE’s invasion of Chicago during Operation Midway Blitz sparked a range of organized community responses, from rapid response teams

 

to fighting detentions at Broadview ICE Facility.

 

In this interview, Heather, a teacher with Chicago Public Schools (CPS) and the Chicago Teachers Union (CTU), reflects on their organizing experiences during that wave of struggle. Drawing on their work in school and supporting a picket line in the Little Village neighborhood, they describe building and mobilizing sanctuary teams while connecting immigrant defense to worker struggle.




This ground-floor recollection shows self-organization in the face of fear, few options for durable collective infrastructure, and uncertainty as to what the deportation siege might bring. It practically outlines the importance of solidarity and connecting struggles across sectors and sites. As the leadership of ICE/Border Patrol continues to change,

 

bringing a lower-key (and successful

) tactical shift, we must revisit our approach. This interview provides insights to apply to future struggles against ICE, Border Patrol, and whatever other forms of domination capital and the State throws at us.







Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): Tell us how you learned about 

Operation Midway Blitz

. What was the sense at your school site and in your district?




Heather:

 Even before Midway Blitz, immigrant rights organizers in our union had run a training series, during the first Trump administration, about building sanctuary teams in the workplace. Our union also won “sanctuary” language in our contract during a strike in 2019, which set an institutional precedent to turn away ICE whenever legally possible. So, smaller groups of more active members were preparing, even before the surge began. 




After, there was a long lead up of news stories where the Trump administration was threatening and attempting to deploy the National Guard, threatening more ICE activity, etc. Our union was already seeing how the National Guard was harassing Black youth in Washington, D.C., and how ICE racially profiled people so blatantly, so among the more active members of our union, we were interpreting this as a direct threat to basically every student and family of color in our school district. During this lead-up, some federal agents showed up at a public elementary school wanting to see a student, and the workers and administrators successfully turned them away, which put the threat and the possibility of defeating it in everyone’s minds. It later came out that it was actually Secret Service agents trying to question the elementary schooler about social media posts, but that didn’t change anything for anyone. So when Midway Blitz began, parents and workers I knew were already fired up to do something about it.




BRRN:

 

How did you and other public school workers prepare for the potential of ICE deployments to your sites?




Heather: 

At my school, we pulled together a “sanctuary team” that included myself, a security guard, the English Learner Program Teacher (ELPT), and other interested teachers and support staff. I took point on gathering all the resources and examples from my union’s trainings to share with the team. The ELPT had relationships with some of our most vulnerable families, so she was on distributing know-your-rights information to them, and other interested staff were going to do the same to families they had connections with. The security guard is responsible for watching our school’s entrance and he was the only one looped in with our administrators’ implementation of district-wide guidance. At times when the administration delayed implementing the district’s guidance at our school, the security guard was able to push them along, as well as fill in the sanctuary team on any gaps in their plan.




As a sanctuary team, we never had a set plan about how exactly we would respond if ICE showed up. Based on if ICE showed up during recess, drop-off, normal class, after-school, the front or back entrance, etc. our response would have to be completely different. We followed the advice from case studies we got at union trainings: go over general best practices, distribute know-your-rights and rapid response hotline information as widely as possible, think of different response options, and be prepared to communicate quickly if ICE shows up.




Some coworkers and I also flyered parents after school a few times with legal resources, info on the district policy’s protections for immigrant students, and know-your-rights info that applied to interactions with ICE, the National Guard, and the Chicago Police Department. We also worked with our clerks and other parent-facing roles to make sure they knew the full scope of district policies protecting immigrant students. 




Throughout all this, we had to combat some misconceptions about which students were vulnerable. Some coworkers thought only our students whose families were seeking asylum from Venezuela were going to be targeted. Many of those students had moved schools over the summer, so they thought we had nothing to worry about. We had to have conversations to explain how many of those families had legal status at the time, but a huge portion of our students might have someone undocumented in their family or they could just be profiled, including not only Latine students but Asian, Arab, and Black students.




BRRN:

 

You also helped with ICE watch at a nearby picket line. Set the scene of the struggle for us and how defense against ICE figured into it.




Heather:

 A bit over 100 mainly Black and Latine workers at a multinational packaging plant in Little Village called Mauser were striking over dangerous conditions, inadequate protective equipment, low pay, and management’s refusal to incorporate anti-ICE language in their contract. It was a grueling strike; it had already been going on for 3 months when I heard about the ICE watch effort through my union’s communication channels.By then, Mauser was threatening to close the plant because they refused to pay for the repairs needed to make the workplace a safe environment, and the battle was shifting to trying to secure a strong severance package.




By the time I got there, the whole of Little Village was basically under siege as part of Midway Blitz. During some stretches, there were intensive ICE or Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) operations starting early in the morning every day for a week or two weeks in the same neighborhood. “ICE not welcome here” signs were on every block, local restaurants would bring food to the ICE watch volunteers, and more horrifying scenes came out on the news every day. It was just interwoven into daily existence in that area. 




To defend the strike, a local workers’ center led an ICE watch effort on the picket line. When I was being trained, the union had secured a location nearby where all the workers would go that they could lock up to buy time as they get the word out and people mobilize to support them and hopefully make ICE back down. As ICE watchers, our job was to stay posted at the intersections with greater visibility so we could warn the workers  if ICE showed up. We also tracked some local rapid response channels so we knew what cars to be on the look out for that day and when ICE was heading our direction.




BRRN:

 

Were there issues with ICE or other federal agents surveilling or harassing the picket?




Heather: 

Once, a CBP or ICE team of 2-3 cars was driving just a block away from the picket, and neighbors were tailing them honking and driving slowly in front of them. At one point an agent pointed a gun or a taser at a driver to make them get out of the way, and ICE/CBP was driving and swerving absurdly dangerously of course. When I saw them, I alerted the workers and they went through with the emergency plan, but CBP or ICE just continued on, so it was a false alarm, which was pretty common. 




Agents also showed up to the picket another time when I wasn’t on shift, including Gregory Bovino, who was the public face of Midway Blitz, but they didn’t detain anybody. It seemed like it was more an intimidation or PR move–and a failed one at that since it didn’t break the strike and the picket continued. 




Ultimately, the strike ended after several months with the plant getting closed down, but through their collective action, workers secured a pretty good severance deal. The workers, including Mauser truckers who had joined the strike despite not being part of the bargaining unit, also won protections from retaliation for supporting the strike.




BRRN: Drawing from these experiences, what lessons would you like to leave for other education workers who want to protect students and each other?




Heather: 

The main thing picket line support taught me was the importance of having a plan for turning out public pressure or confrontation with ICE. In a lot of scenarios both there and at my school, ICE/CBP could be outside and you’re kind of trapped inside for some time while agents are trying to get in, which isn’t an ironclad plan. The next step for organizing both at school and the picket line was to help form a tangible plan for how to spread the word publicly or to rapid response networks so that we could mobilize folks ASAP, like a phone tree. That can be especially tricky if you’re worried about ICE activity early in the morning. We started moving in that direction, but never created a plan that would have met the need of those situations.




I would also just say try to organize as early and as broadly as possible. No agents ever showed up at our school. However, the school community is still a powerful place to organize community resistance to ICE. In our school community, that looked like getting know-your-rights information out to as many parents and families as possible, including but not limited to our most vulnerable families. At other schools, that looked like ‘walking buses’ of parents and neighbors walking students to school in large groups, ‘solidarity strolls’ by school workers to watch for any ICE or CBP activity during pick-up and drop-off, and collaborations or mobilizations with neighborhood-based response groups. You want to have a dense web of solidarity — the more people who know what to do when ICE shows up and are organized to communicate, the stronger your entire school community is, whether someone is targeted at school, at home, or in between.







If you enjoyed this article, we also recommend

: 

Healthcare Workers Freed a Patient From ICE – You Can Do the Same

 

and

 

How Teachers, Students, and Parents are Organizing to Keep ICE Out of Durham Schools

.

“A Dense Web of Solidarity”: How Chicago Public School Workers Defend Students Against ICE

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation

author: David Swanson
title: 10 Reasons to Oppose the “Arc de Trump”
content:
Culture of Peace, North America

By Medea Benjamin, September 30, 2026

There was already widespread opposition to Trump’s proposed arch at Memorial Circle in Arlington, Virginia—a 250-foot structure, roughly the height of a 20-story building and 50 percent taller than Paris’s Arc de Triomphe. Now the controversy has intensified: Trump says the arch, which originally included plans for an observation deck, a café, a gift shop and exhibition space, would also function as a military complex, housing drones, snipers and ammunition.

Here are 10 reasons (really 9 plus your own) to oppose the “Arc de Trump.”

1. It would overwhelm one of America’s most important historic landscapes. The giant arch would sit directly on the ceremonial axis connecting Arlington House, Arlington National Cemetery, Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, dramatically altering this historic view and dwarfing the surrounding monuments rather than complementing them.

2. It clashes with the very meaning of the site. Arlington Memorial Bridge and the surrounding landscape were conceived as symbols of national reconciliation after the Civil War. And Arlington National Cemetery is a solemn resting place for hundreds of thousands of service members. Inserting a gigantic triumphal arch into this setting would transform a landscape devoted to reconciliation, remembrance and sacrifice into a monument celebrating triumph and power.

3. Congress never authorized it, and veterans are taking Trump to court. Three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian have filed a federal lawsuit arguing that Trump cannot unilaterally erect such a monumental structure without congressional authorization and the legally required reviews. A federal judge has already imposed restrictions on work at the site while the legal challenge proceeds. The question is simple: Does a president have the right to build whatever monument he wants on public land without congressional approval?

4. Construction would disrupt commuters and military funerals. Building a 250-foot monument at this location could mean years of construction along a major commuter artery connecting Washington, DC, and Virginia. Excavation, heavy equipment, traffic disruptions, noise and dust would also affect the area immediately outside Arlington National Cemetery, where military funerals and burials take place.

5. Trump now proposes turning the arch into an armed military complex. Trump has said the arch would house large numbers of drones and sniper ammunition, with positions for snipers on the roof and plaza. Why in the world would we want to militarize this historic site when the Pentagon is just two miles away? And what exactly is the purpose of stationing snipers and drones at a ceremonial monument?

6. Drones, snipers and ammunition raise serious safety concerns. The proposed location is only about 3,000 feet from Reagan National Airport and lies near its approach and departure corridors. Adding drone operations, ammunition storage and armed positions to an already heavily traveled location raises obvious aviation and public safety questions. Drone flights in the Washington area are already subject to exceptionally strict restrictions. What additional risks would this new military complex create?

7. The price could be enormous. Estimates for the arch were already running above $100 million before Trump announced his military ambitions for the project. Adding drone facilities, ammunition storage, sniper positions, communications equipment and security infrastructure could drive the cost substantially higher. At a time when Americans are struggling to afford housing, healthcare and other basic necessities, why should taxpayers foot the bill for Trump’s monumental ambitions?

8. National security could become an excuse to circumvent the law. Trump originally promoted the project as a ceremonial triumphal arch. His announcement that it would also serve as a military complex raises a new set of questions about how the administration intends to justify the project. Critics, including Rep. Don Beyer, whose district includes the proposed site, have questioned whether national security is being invoked to overcome legal and preservation obstacles. Will the administration use security claims to evade the normal approval process?

9. It is a monument to Trump’s colossal ego. Trump has repeatedly treated beloved national spaces as extensions of his personal brand—from his $400 million White House ballroom project to his insistence on putting his name on the Kennedy Center. When asked about the purpose of the arch, Trump told reporters it is meant to honor him! The nation’s capital is not supposed to be a playground for presidential self-glorification. These monuments and landscapes belong to the public, not to one man with an ego that knows no bounds.

10. Add your own. What am I missing?

The administration is pushing ahead despite all these unresolved objections. But opponents are fighting back through lawsuits, public testimony and protests. If you want to get involved, join Third Act DC’s organizing and demonstrations, follow the National Capital Planning Commission’s review and public-comment process, contact your members of Congress and sign the MoveOn petition opposing the arch.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Rejects AI Regulation as Tech CEOs Sign Voluntary “Self-Policing” Accord
content:
Critics warn that self-regulation isn’t enough to prevent AI models from making disastrous mistakes in the future.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced that several tech firm executives had signed an accord agreeing to self-regulate their artificial intelligence (AI) ventures amid growing concerns about the technology’s rapid expansion.

Before the accord was signed, Trump said that “self-regulation is very important” — dismissing calls for formal government regulation, even as industry experts warn that AI’s unfettered expansion could lead to catastrophic outcomes.

In remarks to reporters after the accord was signed, Trump touted the unenforceable measure as a positive move.

“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump insisted.

But when questioned over a hypothetical scenario about an AI bot going rogue and committing a crime — and who should be held responsible for such an event — Trump ignored the query altogether, instead ranting about how he no longer calls the technology AI but instead “SI,” or “super intelligence.”

“We changed the name officially today to ‘SI.’ You know what that means? Super intelligence. The name has been officially changed,” Trump said.

Q: Who should be held accountable when the AI agents commit a crime?TRUMP: It's not AI. That's the other thing. We changed the name officially today to SI. Like sigh.

Trump signed an order on Tuesday changing the name in all executive branch documents.

The accord was signed by multiple tech barons, including X’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman. Notably, Palantir’s Alex Karp did not sign the accord.

The document, entitled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” calls on companies to “implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment” of their AI models. It also calls for “an internal team” within the companies “to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended,” and to partner with external auditors to “carry out independent assessments.”

These measures are entirely voluntary, with no requirement for the signatories of the document to abide by them.

The document features Trump’s signature above the tech moguls’, listing him as “President of the Unites States,” misspelling the word “United” in his title.

Interestingly, the document contradicts what Trump has said regarding government-imposed regulation, recognizing that, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws.”

Several critics of AI, including former workers at tech firms, have demanded that more be done by the federal government, and internationally, to curtail the expansion of AI.

“We can and should be demanding that our governments protect us from the catastrophe of out-of-control AI. … Today’s AIs appear to occasionally lie or cheat, even when they know better,” Alex Turner, a former research scientist at Google DeepMind, wrote in an op-ed for The Guardian earlier this month.

“AI billionaires have shown us that they’re willing to chase a dollar bill off the side of a cliff if it makes them a dollar richer. But Donald Trump doesn’t give a damn if AI puts us in harm’s way, as long as he can make himself richer in the process,” read a statement from Maurice Mitchell, national director of the Working Families Party. “We cannot trust a multi-billion dollar AI industry to regulate itself.”

author: Laura Hernández
title: Clinton-Era Laws Passed 30 Years Ago Enabled Trump’s Anti-Immigrant Agenda.
content:
Clinton’s ‘96 laws provided the legal foundation for mass detention, rapid deportations, and the evasion of due process.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The more the American public sees of President Donald Trump’s hardline, anti-immigrant policies in action — the deaths, military-style invasions of neighborhoods, and mass detention and deportations — the more his approval on the issue drops.

If this trend sounds familiar, it’s because a similar wave of disapproval played out in Trump’s first term. Despite that backlash, Trump returned to office embracing even more extreme measures.

We must finally confront and uproot the core of the U.S.’s anti-immigrant underbelly, which is largely reflected in the racially motivated notion of criminalization.

Trump was not the first politician to exploit the concept of criminality, and he certainly won’t be the last. Criminalizing narratives are deeply planted in the American psyche, and they have commonly acted as the vessel through which white supremacist rhetoric and policy are ingrained into our culture and laws.

In the late 1980’s, criminalization went mainstream in the form of racist dog whistles, particularly those hinging on vile anti-Blackness deployed by politicians seeking to activate white voters. In the decades since, conservative and liberal leaders alike more purposefully extended this criminality framework to immigration — so much so that it’s now perhaps the primary driver of the public immigration debate.

Consider how Americans of all political stripes are often presented with the binary choice of supporting the “right” type of immigrant. In this oversimplification, immigrants fall into categories like “good” or “bad,” “legal” or “illegal,” “deserving” or “undeserving.”

Trump did not invent these narratives. They’ve underpinned both major parties’ politics of immigration for several decades, despite their basis in fiction and fear-mongering rather than evidence and compassion, or the fact these narratives are weaponized against non-white immigrants who for centuries have disproportionately faced restrictive and punitive policies for the act of seeking relief in this country.

But Trump’s partisan opposition, despite its massive opportunities in the face of unpopular, hardline policies, has repeatedly failed to capture the public’s long-term support on immigration. Too often, Democrats repackage the same old criminalizing narratives — often in softer terms, but always in line with the oversimplified good-or-bad thinking. This lack of imagination is reflected in the nearly annual bipartisan votes to increase funding for federal enforcement agencies like Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, as well as Democratic leaders’ messaging and policies.

Take, for example, former President Barack Obama’s push to deport “felons, not families”; Joe Biden squandering his mandate to reverse the cruelty of Trump’s first term by continuing many Trump policies, like Title 42 and the backing of for-profit immigrant detention; or Kamala Harris, in her presidential bid, focusing much of her immigration rhetoric on “securing” the border.

It’s a toxic cycle: The public rightfully disapproves of the atrocities of anti-immigrant policies; in response, liberals roll out unimaginative plans hinged on outdated narratives; and finally, in the vacuum created by the lack of any tangible, pro-immigrant vision, the right recaptures the public’s attention with fear mongering and a sensationalist focus on crime and the border.

To break this cycle, we must imagine a pro-immigrant future in which our communities, not politicians and pundits, get to define safety.

We can start with recognizing that the modern-day legal basis for the criminalization of immigrants largely rests on a pair of anti-immigrant bills signed into law by Bill Clinton 30 years ago. Building upon the U.S. legacy of racialized immigration control, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) further entrenched mass incarceration and laid the blueprint for the detention and deportation machine we have today.

These laws drastically expanded the government’s ability to automatically detain and deport people without due process and without consideration for their current circumstances.

IIRIRA, in particular, dramatically expanded who can be deported, made detention mandatory, created fast-track deportations, and stripped immigration judges of much of their discretion.

The numbers show just how much these laws have supercharged the mass incarceration and deportation of immigrants over the past 30 years. In 1995, 50,924 people were deported and fewer than 7,500 people were held in immigration detention. By 1997, the number of people deported more than doubled to 114,432, and by 2001, 20,500 people were held in detention. Thirty years later, the devastation has only climbed higher, with nearly 330,000 people deported in 2025 and roughly 70,000 people in ICE detention today.

Once mandatory detention created the demand, private prison companies cashed in and played an integral role in building what is now the world’s largest immigration detention system. Today, approximately 90 percent of people detained in ICE custody are held in prisons owned or operated by private corporations.

The bills also provided the blueprint to turbocharge detention and deportation by further entangling the criminal legal and immigration systems. In what is known as the prison-to-ICE pipeline, immigrants are subject to double punishment; many face the loss of their freedom twice for the same conviction. Because ICE can arrest people as they’re released from prison (despite that individual serving their time and completing their sentence) many are re-incarcerated on the very day they would otherwise go home to their families.

This double standard disproportionately punishes Black people and reinforces systemic racism by propagating existing racial disparities — like those found in conviction rates and policing practices like profiling — into the immigration system.

Today, the ’96 laws continue to be key tools the Trump administration uses to carry out its immigration agenda. As the administration’s enforcement net widens to target and arrest political dissidents, families, and even U.S. citizens, we must recognize the role criminalizing narratives have played in leading us to our present slide into authoritarianism. Criminalization is the primary justification used to make these cruel policies all the more entrenched and widespread.

Here lies the danger of not fighting the root of the problem: When we concede fundamental rights like due process for some, we begin to concede those rights for all. When we fight only for those immigrants who have not yet been labeled “criminal,” we’ll find ourselves unprepared when authoritarians inevitably stamp that label on more and more of us.

All people are worthy of human dignity, due process, and the right to live in safety, no matter where we were born. Those who have been previously ensnared in the U.S. carceral system — including those who have committed harm in their past — are not disposable. They’re people, often with full lives established in the U.S., who are worthy of redemption and second chances like anyone else.

To build toward this vision, we must rally around bold proposals that affirm these values. We must reject the toxic “good immigrant/bad immigrant” narrative once and for all and champion a vision in which freedom, human rights, and basic human dignity are the floor for our demands, not merely concessions or carveouts for some.

Legislatively, we must repeal laws like the IIRIRA and AEDPA bills of 1996, and their modern-day counterparts like the Laken Riley Act, which expands mandatory detention. The New Way Forward Act offers a concrete start to fixing much of the damage of the ‘96 laws. And at the border, it won’t be enough to restore the U.S. asylum system to its pre-Trump state. Instead, we must decriminalize the act of seeking safety or economic security.

At the state and local level, communities can chip away at the interconnected carceral and deportation dragnet by fighting for legislation that blocks local law enforcement’s collaboration with ICE, including the transfer of people from local jails and prisons to the agency.

Ultimately, to turn the tide, it’s going to take all of us. In each of our lives, we must resist the urge — at work, the dinner table, online, and in our opposition to Trumpism — to tie one’s worth and humanity to however they’ve been labeled. In fighting for everyone, we’ll advance our struggle for fairness, justice, and family unity. And we’ll just so happen to build a winning coalition along the way.

author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament approves last-minute delay to Criminal Procedures Code enactment
content:
The Criminal Procedures Code’s enactment was 

postponed

 for one year, after Parliament gave their final approval to an amendment during an emergency session on Wednesday morning.




The law, which has been 

likened

 to “a second constitution” in terms of its foundational importance to Egypt’s legal system, was due to come into effect less than 24 hours after the session, on October 1.




Parliamentary Affairs Minister Hany Hanna 

attended

 the session to argue in favor of the postponement, which he said had been called for by over 60 MPs — the required quorum for a proposal’s presentation to the plenary session.




Hanna, whose comments were relayed in a Cabinet 

statement

 on Wednesday evening, expressed the government’s backing for the postponement, adding that it would ensure the law’s provisions can be implemented without obstacles. He specifically highlighted the benefit this extra time would grant in allowing for the completion of the new digital system — to be used for judicial notifications and remote court proceedings — while also ensuring that it can be properly tested.




The government’s request was preceded by calls for the law’s postponement from legal rights advocates who voiced concerns that the new law would do more to threaten defendants’ access to fair terms of investigation, detention and trial than it would to improve the workings of the criminal justice system.




A delay would “allow time to address the contentious issues raised concerning the law, which civil society organizations, legal scholars and United Nations rapporteurs believe significantly undermine procedural guarantees, violate the right to defense and compromise the standards of fair and equitable trials,” the Arab Center for Independence of the Judiciary and the Legal Profession said in a September 

statement

.




The law is one of the most important texts determining the function of criminal justice and law enforcement as enacted by security, investigative and judicial authorities. Its provisions govern criminal prosecution, trial and appeals systems; investigation and arrest terms; criminal sentencing; law enforcement and judicial cooperation with other countries.




The law that was amended Wednesday 

surfaced

 in bill form in July 2024, when the House Constitutional and Legislative Affairs Committee announced plans to discuss the draft during the House recess that summer.




The step immediately sparked anger among former prisoners, civil society figures and rights advocates who were participating in a parallel, state-led process set up to brainstorm ideas for the criminal justice system’s reform — particularly with regard to the use of remand detention to hold people for extended periods without trial. While the law does reduce the time a defendant can be held in remand, it comes 

short

 of addressing the practice of charging defendants with multiple similar charges, which can result in them being held for many consecutive remand periods.




Criticism has also been 

levied

 at other elements of the law, such as its establishment of remote hearings as a standard practice, which rights experts believe will weaken defendants’ access to a fair trial as well as  allowing the seizure and monitoring of electronic devices, belongings and online accounts — an inclusion which some believe threatens constitutional privacy protections.




Participants in the National Dialogue forum at the time expressed consternation that a draft law had already been formulated and submitted for parliamentary review without their knowledge. Similar grievances were expressed by the lawyers and 

journalists

 syndicates.




The draft nevertheless progressed rapidly through Parliament, with less than a year’s passage all in all between the draft’s submission and its final approval in April, 2025.

The post 

Parliament approves last-minute delay to Criminal Procedures Code enactment

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Redazione_web
title: Assemblea internazionale FICEDL
content:
Si è svolta a Bologna, lo scorso 11-13 settembre, l’assemblea della Federazione Internazionale dei Centri di Studio e Documentazione Libertari. La precedente assemblea generale si era tenuta esattamente 10 anni or sono ancora a Bologna sempre al Circolo Anarchico C. Berneri.




L’incontro ha registrato una grande partecipazione. Oltre 40 archivi, biblioteche, centri di studio e documentazione erano presenti, altri hanno inviato comunicati e saluti. Di questi, circa la metà erano italiani ed erano presenti compagne e compagni da Francia, Spagna, Svizzera, Austria, Inghilterra, Romania, Brasile e Cile. Le relazioni di presentazione hanno manifestato la diffusione ed il radicamento del movimento anarchico e libertario legato alla conservazione della documentazione delle attività del movimento, ma anche alle attività contemporanee, svolgendo un’importante attività culturale e sociale.




Al sito 

https://ficedl2026.bida.im/

 potete trovare maggiori dettagli dell’incontro.




A questo link 

https://tubocatodico.bida.im/c/ficedl_2026__berneri/videos

 trovate le registrazioni di tutti gli incontri.




Al sito 

https://ficedl.info/

 la storia della Federazione.




L’intervento di Lorenzo Pezzica, svoltosi venerdì nel tardo pomeriggio, ha rimarcato il carattere “non museale” dell’attività dei nostri archivi e delle nostre biblioteche. Se è pur necessario un approccio “tecnico” alla conservazione, catalogazione, diffusione dei materiali, questa attività non deve essere avulsa dalla relazione con i movimenti che si danno nella società contemporanea. Impostazione che è stata ripresa e confermata da moltissimi degli interventi presenti, sia nei workshop del pomeriggio di sabato che nella carrellata di presentazioni della mattina, come già accennato.




Durante i workshop sono emerse diverse esperienze in atto che propongono e già in parte realizzano piattaforme di scambio e federazione degli archivi e del materiale. 




La disponibilità per l’organizzazione del prossimo incontro della rete FICEDL (2027) è arrivata dalle compagne e dai compagni di Anarhiva e si dovrebbe tenere a Cluj-Napoca in Romania. In tempi brevi arriverà da parte loro la conferma ufficiale.




Per il 2029 si sono resti disponibili invece le compagne e i compagni della Biblioteca Terra Livre di Sao Paolo e dell’Archivo La Revuelta di Santiago del Cile. Entrambi compiono vent’anni, sarà dunque l’occasione per festeggiare a dovere. 




Nello spirito di coinvolgimento di realtà attive e affini alla FICEDL, all’incontro hanno partecipato anche alcuni archivi che non fanno ancora parte della rete. Molti di loro hanno chiesto di aderire.




Si sono poi messi in cantiere una serie di gruppi di lavoro per coadiuvare la gestione del sito ufficiale della Federazione, per la redazione di un “annuario”, per la realizzazione di una cassa di mutuo appoggio (che permetta di coprire i costi organizzativi e di spostamento per i prossimi incontri), per organizzare una lista di traduttrici/tori in simultanea o in consecutiva che agevolino i prossimi incontri.




Infine l’assemblea ha approvato una mozione di solidarietà ad Autistici/Inventati e di denuncia dei provvedimenti sempre più autoritari contro i movimenti. Qui il testo della mozione 

https://ficedl2026.bida.im/mozione/

.




Non sono mancati i momenti conviviali come in ogni convegno di compagne e compagni. Cena, pranzo e cena al Berneri con concerto di Mars on Pluto il venerdì sera e la cantata con il Coro delle Mondine di Bentivoglio il sabato sera e il partecipatissimo pranzo della domenica al VAG, in via Paolo Fabbri, dove si era svolta l’assemblea della Federazione nella mattinata. Qui si svolgeva un’iniziativa di solidarietà con grande pranzo popolare per sostenere le spese legali della famiglia di Abderrahim Fakir, cittadino bolognese ucciso dalla polizia nel luglio scorso in città.
