author: Njeri Wangarĩ
title: The Fallacy that is the CBE Arts Pathway
content:
“So CBC is designed for short-term training of workers. In Europe, it is used among refugee and immigrant communities who need to be integrated into the community as fast as possible with skills they can use to earn a living. In other words, the adults are assumed to have basic human abilities of cultural identity, values, communication, and social skills, and all CBC is doing is giving workers tools for the workplace.” ~ 

Dr Wandia Njoya 




When Hannah*, our firstborn daughter, sat for her KJSEA exams last year, she was among the thousands of pioneers transitioning to Grade 10 in the newly established Kenyan Education Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC), since rebranded to Competency-Based Education (CBE).




Like many parents, I was drunk on the PR and the political rhetoric 

strungi

 that extolled the new curriculum above the 8-4-4 system, which we – a millennial generation still grappling with the side effects of exams, cramming, the Big 4 career options – blamed for our miserable lives stuck in jobs we hate but can’t quit. Not in this Kasongo economy.




We, the products of a system we felt seemed hell-bent on judging a fish based on its ability to climb a tree, together with the Ministry of Education, wanted to do away with exams completely. We had also swallowed the “talent carrot” that was dangled in front of us, whose hook – careers beyond being a doctor, lawyer, pilot, aeronautical engineer – was but a mirage for a majority of the learning population attending public schools.




Grade 10s and the indigestion of the CBE strungi




For nine years, the strong 

strungi

 was given to us like prescribed medication three times a year. Take two tablets of expectations: “Below”, “Approaching”, “Meeting”, and “Exceeding Expectations”; two tablets of practical-based learning (I see you all who also spent nights making 

wandindis

, printing portfolio photos, late evenings hunting for “locally available materials” and accompanying your young ones to the market for evidence photos of activities). 




This CBE has had us doing all manner of acrobatic exercises, which I found increasingly impractical. CBE has turned us all – parents and our children into local DIY scavengers. For any learner living in an urban area, some project activities border on the absurd. Take, for instance, the assignment that our son was given to make a 

wandidi

 or 

orutu

 (traditional musical instrument) using tin cans. And don’t even get me started on what the children in the rural areas are subjected to. How do you learn swimming lessons in fields or atop tables? 




We were sold a pipe dream for nine years, only to wake up to a nightmare early this year.




Hannah did exceptionally well and earned herself a place at a girls’ national school in Kiambu. But she was adamant about the pathway she wanted to take: Arts & Sports Science – a subject combination of fine arts, literature, French, music, and dance. This came as no surprise to us. We had spotted her affinity for the arts from as early as five years old when she began drawing characters from her favourite cartoon shows.




While Hannah had not been accepted at any of the schools of her choice, we, in our naive faith in the system, had believed that the national public school assigned to us by the ministry would indeed offer both the chosen subject combination and a conducive environment for her. 




An educator and a fierce critic of CBC, Dr Wandia Njoya had warned us for years. In 

a 2019 article

, she said,




“Pathways mean that the arts will always be treated as an appendage, as something for children who do not perform well in academics or science. And those children will invariably be those attending poorly equipped schools. And that attitude towards the arts implies ALL KNOWLEDGE, not just the arts. It means we remain mediocre, uncreative, and unimaginative. It means that Kenyans will remain blocked from inventing, innovating, and creating, even as institutions perform innovation by creating ‘hubs’ and ‘innovation funds’.




As a product of public high school education, I knew that this school was no private school. I anticipated that it would be devoid of the bells and whistles that Hannah had enjoyed. Similarly, I had no illusions about the kind of culture and rigour Hannah would be exposed to. Her father and I wanted that for her. A public boarding school setting where discipline, individual and collective responsibility, and academic excellence, with infrastructure to support the Arts & Sports Science pathway, would mould her.




We were shocked to learn that the school was not offering fine art – had no amenities, no faculty – and that the administration had no interest in supporting the over 30 students it had admitted for this pathway.




Perpetuation of traditional prejudice against the arts




When Dr Njoya 

predicted

 that there would be hardly any fine arts teachers and that few parents would encourage their children to pursue that pathway, she was branded an enemy of progress who sought every possible opportunity to malign this wonderful curriculum which, according to the Ministry of Education, recognized, encouraged, and supported the talent pathway.




“Right now, we are bracing for a fight over the pathways which Grade 10 children will be entering next year. I can almost predict with certainty that few parents will want their children to pursue the talent pathway. There are hardly any fine arts teachers anyway, because the colleges are not training them, because the fine arts are not an examinable subject in the outgoing 8.4.4 system.”




By Hannah’s own account, corroborated by numerous other students in the arts pathway who confided to their parents, they began experiencing systemic bullying which, according to her, was instigated by the teachers and emulated by the other students. 




Disparaging remarks like, “You are all academic dwarfs”, 

“Msifikiri mlikuja hapa tu kuimba”

 (Don’t think you came here just to sing) became normalized, thrown around casually any time the arts class was caught making noise or whenever there were altercations between the students and the teachers.




As a creative whose career and life’s purpose are centred around the arts, this was phlegm-filled spit in my face.




The whole “talent” pathway is a veneer. Once you scratch the surface, there’s nothing but hot air.




Last year, Dr Njoya found that 

only 14 public schools in Kenya offer art at the KCSE level

, meaning that the Teachers Service Commission does not have teachers in sufficient numbers to teach fine art under the new curriculum. Thus, despite all the PR from the Ministry of Education, despite their arm-twisting all national schools to offer all three pathways, including arts and sports science, the ministry only had 14 trained art teachers. Let’s chew on that for a minute.




News reports

 indicate that during the first Grade 10 intake in January, most public high schools that had been earmarked to teach the arts dropped subjects such as fine art, film, and theatre. A principal I spoke to during my search for a school for Hannah disclosed that the school had to use the English, Kiswahili, or music teachers to teach subjects under the arts pathway.




By the second term half-term break, it had fully dawned on us that the only alternative for Hannah was a private school.  




Perpetuating the view of the arts as elitist




Although relieved to have finally found a private school where the arts are accorded equal regard as the sciences, we are aware that this is an option that very few parents can afford. 




Parents are now grappling with the reality that the ministry has removed the pedestal on which we had placed our prestigious national high schools. According 

to news reports

, many schools are understaffed, underfunded, and overpopulated, accommodating between 10 and 15 streams with between 50 and 60 pupils per class within much the same infrastructure left behind by the schools’ colonial founders. 




Is artistic expression a luxury or a fundamental human right?




Our education system has forced us to unwittingly continue to perpetuate the arts as something only the elite can pursue. By treating artistic expression as a luxury rather than a fundamental human right, our education system quietly executes a cultural heist – convincing us that creative legacy is reserved solely for the privileged. But creativity is not an elite commodity to be rationed; it is our collective heritage, our memory, and our primary engine for critical thought. 




Early this year, as my family and the art fraternity 

mourned the death of Patrick Mukabi, one of Kenya’s most distinguished visual artists, my thoughts and memories of him kept returning to the Dust Depo Studio where he inspired, moulded, and imprinted his legacy on the minds, hearts, and hands of a new generation of children, including Hannah and her siblings. 




Uncle Suppu – as Mukabi was known to the children he taught – treated his artistic expression as a historian with nothing but a brush, paint, and canvas would. His artistic rendering of women in the marketplace tells our collective story of what beauty there is even in the mundane simplicity of the everyday moments at Marigiti.




When we allow schools to strip the arts from the classroom, we actively participate in erasing our own stories and stripping ourselves of the only language we have to convey our deep human emotions, experiences, and reflections of the world around us. We must reject this erasure narrative of artificial scarcity. It is time for parents, educators, and community creators to aggressively advocate for a curriculum that recognises and supports the teaching of the arts to be as essential as the teaching of STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects. 




The post 

The Fallacy that is the CBE Arts Pathway

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

author: Andrea
title: ᑭᓕᒃᕙᒃ ᑲᓪᓘᓇ ᐃᓚᐅᓕᕐᐳᖅ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓂ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see 

Kilikvak Kabloona joins National Council for Reconciliation

.







ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖑᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᕕᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᑕᐃᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᒪᓐ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᖅᑐᓂ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᓇᑕ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕆᐊᖃᖅᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᑐᕋᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑕ




ᑭᓕᒃᕙᒃ ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐃᓚᐅᓂᐊᓯᔪᖅ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ




“ᐱᒃᑯᓇᑦᑎᐊᕐᑐᖅ,” ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 17-ᒥ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᓚᐅᖅᑎᓐᓇᒍ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᓐᓂ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓄ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᒥᓂᔅᑕᓄ ᑐᒡᓕᕆᔭᐅᔪᓄᑦ, ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᖃᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥᓐ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐃᒻᒥᓃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ.




ᑕᐃᑲᓂᓕ ᐃᑲᔪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᒃᓴᖅᑖᕋᓱᖕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᐊᖅᑯᓴᕆᐊᖅ ᒪᒥᓴᕐᕕᒃᒧᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂᑦ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᒪᓕᒃᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᓱᓕᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯ ᐊᑐᖁᓯᒪᔭᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᒪᒥᓴᖅᐸᓪᓕᐅᔾᔪᑎᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ.




“ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖃᕐᓂᓐᓂ ᑕᑯᓯᒪᕗᖓ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᖃᓄᐃᙱᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᒪᐅᓇ ᐊᑐᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᒃᑯ  ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂ,” ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.
















ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᖅᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᒃᑲᓐᓂᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᓐ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. ᐅᓄᕐᓂᕐᓴᐃᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑖᒃᑯᓇᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᕐᕕᒃᓴᓂ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓗᓂ, ᑖᓐᓇᑦᑕᐅᖅ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᓴᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᑲᐅᑎᒋᔪᓐᓇᔾᔮᙱᑦᑐᑦ, ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑰᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒥᒃ, ᐅᓇ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᔫᓴᕝ ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ, ᐃᓚᐅᓕᕐᓂ ᐱᒋᐊᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔩᑦ ᒫᔅᓯ 2025-ᒥ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑉᓘᓇᒎ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᑦᑎᐊᕐᓇᕐᒪᓐ ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᕐᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ ᐅᖃᐅᔾᔪᐃᔨᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᓕᒪᓂᕐᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᒻᒥᓃᖅᑎᑦᑎᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥᒃ.




“ᐱᓇᓱᑦᑎᐊᒻᒪᕆᖕᒪᓐ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᓕᖕᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒧᑦ. ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓯᒪᓂᖃᕐᒪᓐ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᑯᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑕᒪᑐᒧᖓ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ.




ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔩᑦ ᐱᑕᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᑲᓇᑕ ᒪᓕᒃᑲᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑦ 94-ᓂ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖁᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᑎᒍᑦ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᓱᓕᓂᕐᒧᓐ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂ, ᑖᒃᑯᐊᓗ 2015-ᒥ ᑎᑎᕋᐅᓯᖃᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᕕᓂᕐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓯᒪᔾᔪᑎᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕆᐊᕕᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᑯᓄᑦ.




ᐃᒻᒥᒃᑰᖓᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖅᑐᑦ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐅᖃᑦᑕᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᙳᕌᖓᑦ. ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ 2025-ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᔭᖅ ᑐᓂᓯᑕᐃᓐᓇᖅᖢᑎᒃ.
















ᑕᕝᕙᓂᓕ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓂ ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᓇᑕ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᖓᓂᒃ ᐊᑐᖁᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᒪᐅᓇ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᐅᑎᒃᑰᖓᔪᓂ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥ, ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓄᑦ ᐱᑦᑎᐊᖅᑕᐅᙱᔾᔪᑎᕕᓂᕐᓄᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᓯᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᐃᑲᔫᑎᖃᒃᑲᓐᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᖏᒡᓕᕚᓪᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥᒃ.




ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ, ᓇᓕᒧᒌᒃᑎᑦᑎᓂᖃᙱᓐᓂᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕈᑎᑎᒍᑦ, ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᖅᑕᐃᓕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᓱᓕ ᐱᑕᖃᕐᒪᑕ, ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᖕᒥᔪᖅ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᑦ.




ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐅᓄᕐᑐᐃᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᖅᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᓖᑦ ᓱᓕ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᑕ. ᐅᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᐃᓐᓇᖅᑐᖃᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂᒃ, ᐊᑯᓂᒍᓗᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒧᑦ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᒃᓴᖃᙱᓐᓂ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ.




“ᖃᐅᔨᒪᖕᒥᔪᒍᑦ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᙱᓐᓂᕋᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ,” ᐅᖃᕐᒥᔪᖅ.




ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᓄᑖᓂ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᓂᐊᓕᖅᑐᓂ ᑖᒃᑯᓇᓂ, ᑖᒃᑯᐊᓗ ᐱᑕᖃᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᐊᓕᖅᖢᑎᒃ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᒃᓯᕙᐅᑕᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᔫᓕ ᐋᓐ ᐅᕆᔅᑕ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᑎᒍᑦ.
















“ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᓂᖅ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᒻᒪᕆᐅᔪᖅ. ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑉᐸᕗᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᒪᒋᑦᑎᐊᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᐊᖅᖢᑎᒍᑦ,” ᐅᕆᔅᑕᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐃᓚᐅᖃᑕᐅᓕᕐᒥᔪᖅ ᐅᓇ ᐹᐳᕋ ᕕᓕᐊᓐ, ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᓄ ᓄᓇᖏᓐᓂ ᒪᔅᑎᐅᐊᔅ ᐅᕙᓂ ᓵᒐᓂ-ᓛᒃ-ᓴᐃᓐ-ᔮᓐ (Innu Nation of Mashteuiatsh in Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean) ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ UNESCO, ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᑯᓗᐊᓐ ᐋᑕᒥᒃ-ᐋᓐᔨᑯᓐᓂ (Kluane Adamek–Aagé), ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᓂᑯᑦ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᐊᓪᓚᓄᑦ ᔫᑲᓐᒥ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖅ ᐅᕙᙵᑦ ᑯᓗᐊᓐ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᓪᓚᓂ.

author: Olive Kobusingye
title: Medical Ethics and the State’s Security Interests
content:
I grew up on a staple of detective novels. Agatha Christie, Ian Fleming, P.D. James, Colin Dexter… there was always the smart forensics team that ultimately cracked the case. The dried blood stain nobody had noticed, the single hair on the comb, the fingerprints on the backdoor doorknob… I wanted to become a forensics expert when I grew up. Either that, or a psychiatrist. There was something fascinating about being able to read people’s minds, and to set them right if they were disturbed. I carried these thoughts with me into medical school.




The psychiatrist option suffered a rude jolt during the three weeks I spent on the psychiatry rotation as a junior clerk. It seemed as though the patients never got well. Most patients we met had been there before, several times. There were three, at most four, drugs that were used to treat all conditions. And then there was the electroconvulsive therapy, which left me persuaded that I did not want to return to that unit if I had the choice. I am glad things have changed tremendously since.




I went into internship with an open mind. Two weeks in, I was told I was on medico-legal duty. The assigned doctor did post-mortems and could be called upon to examine inmates at the municipal prison. These were usually convicts whose sentences included corporal punishment – caning. Thankfully, it has been outlawed as a form of punishment. 




Anyway, I was asked to go and examine a couple of inmates who were coming up for the cane. I was required to ascertain that they were fit to withstand the trauma, and afterwards, to confirm that they had survived. As fate would have it, that day’s inmates were small-bodied men in their fifties. When you are in your early twenties, you think anyone on the other side of fifty has one foot in the grave. I examined the men and, based purely on the physical exam, found them to be in good health. I recorded my findings in their files and appended my signature to the report.




Then I went to the office, only a few feet away from where the corporal punishment was to be administered, and waited to re-examine them post-trauma.




Before I had settled in the chair, I heard what sounded like a cross between a muffled gunshot and a loud door bang… punctuated by an “uughhh” from deep in a human being’s throat. This went on for several minutes – or so it seemed. Then a second name was called, and a repeat. With each strike there was a tightening in my chest. Then it was over. The prison staff who had administered the punishment came and invited me to go and ascertain that the men were alive. I cannot recall how I got through that part. I only remember thinking afterwards that if this was the path to becoming a forensic expert then I was going to have to find another way to become famous.




I suppose as long as there have been health workers taking care of prisoners, there has been that conflict – the dual loyalty bind. The medical worker’s professional duty to the patient on one hand, and the requirement by the state for medical workers to provide information, cooperation, or compliance on the other.




Doctors may be expected to disclose information about patients, to permit security officials access to patients or their records, or to downplay conditions whose mention would get in the way of the state’s objectives concerning the patients.




As a young doctor, I was only vaguely aware of this universal dilemma. My medical ethics classes had taken place in lecture rooms far removed from the reality of the harsh prison yard. Apartheid was still the official policy of South Africa. Steve Biko had been dead for ten years, having died in custody, in circumstances that came to light through the t South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) hearings. 




Generations of doctors have studied Biko’s case in medical ethics, yet the dilemma is as real today as it was then. And in some ways, it has become more entrenched, with the thin line becoming more tenuous by the day. 




Often, the state’s requests of health workers looking after prisoners may come across as reasonable. They are often made of doctors who take pride in their profession, and who look at requests for information as purely objective, and delinked from any background “political noise”. Sometimes they do not ask the simple question: What is this information going to be used for? Is this in the best interests of my patient? Is it neutral? 




It rarely is. 




In apartheid South Africa, medical workers were found to have facilitated the mistreatment of prisoners in various ways. Former detainees reported instances in which medical files were handed to the security police; doctors and nurses failed to properly document injuries; doctors declared detainees medically fit for further interrogation or torture; psychologists breached patient confidentiality for security reasons;  doctors examined detainees in the presence of police or prison warders, making confidential disclosure of torture or other complaints virtually impossible. 




In all those cases, the results of these actions hurt patients and strengthened the already powerful arm of the state against the vulnerable patient.




Let us look at Steve Biko in particular. He died in police custody in 1977. He had sustained severe head injuries while in detention. Doctors examined him while he was under police control. Despite evidence of serious neurological injury, they accepted the police’s refusal to transfer him to hospital and eventually permitted him to remain in police custody. The TRC found failures, including failure to maintain confidentiality, failure to properly examine him, failure to record injuries accurately, and failure to provide appropriate treatment. 




But there is more. The TRC heard evidence that a medical certificate and medical record had been falsified at the request of the security police. 




The significance of Biko is that the doctors did not necessarily have to be enthusiastic supporters of torture. The system could work through institutional pressure, subordination to police authority, fear of repercussions, and gradual normalization of abuses.




Apartheid South Africa’s medical ethics problems might sound extreme, but they were neither unique to South Africa nor limited to the few well-known names. They were systemic.




South African district surgeons were employed within a system in which they had responsibilities both to the patient and to the prison/security authorities. The TRC described these as “dual obligations”. Doctors had statutory duties to examine prisoners and ensure appropriate health care – but they were operating within an institution whose primary objective was incarceration and security. 




The TRC’s evidence showed that the most common failing was not necessarily actively torturing people, but failing to perform ordinary medical duties because the security system took precedence.




That distinction is important. A doctor could become complicit in abuse simply by examining but not documenting the injury; documenting but not reporting it; reporting but accepting the security officer’s decision; or treating a patient in a way that allowed the security operation to continue.




This is a classic example of how an authoritarian system can compromise medical ethics without requiring every doctor to become an active perpetrator.




History is replete with examples of medical workers failing to protect, defend, and advocate for their patients, primarily because of “security interests”. 




In Nazi Germany, doctors and health officials became integrated into the machinery of racial persecution. 




In the Soviet Union, psychiatrists – mental health practitioners – were sometimes used as an instrument of political repression. Some psychiatrists cooperated voluntarily; others gave in to coercion. 




During Argentina’s military dictatorship of 1976–1983, political prisoners and people suspected of being subversives were tortured and disappeared. Medical personnel worked within detention and military institutions, and there were documented instances of medical professionals participating in or facilitating the treatment of detainees in ways that served the security apparatus rather than the patient’s interests. Here again the fundamental ethical conflict was between the doctor as protector of the patient and the doctor as an agent within a state-controlled detention system.




Research shows that there is a clear pattern of progression, from something that appears benign, to something definitely sinister. 




First comes the state’s asking for patient information: “What is his/her problem? What are they complaining of?” Then medical workers are asked to disclose information that should ordinarily be confidential – diagnoses, medication, test results, medical records. It then progresses to doctors being asked or expected to examine patients in the presence of security personnel. If the breach was subtle before, at this point a red flag should shoot up. 




But it gets worse. Modification of care: treatment, transfer or investigation is delayed or denied because it would interfere with the state’s objectives. Documentation failure: complaints, symptoms, test results that might be inconvenient to the state’s case are omitted from the records. Finally comes normalization: what initially appears exceptional becomes routine practice.




The lesson these cases contribute to modern medical ethics is that a doctor does not cease to have a duty to the patient because the patient has become a prisoner, political suspect, protester, or even an enemy of the government.




So – how is all this relevant to Uganda today? What has the state done to people in custody, and how have medical workers responded? 




We have medical workers employed by the armed forces – military, police, and prisons. They have statutory duties to examine prisoners, and ensure appropriate health care, yet they operate within institutions whose primary objectives (regarding inmates) are incarceration and security. 




We have seen repeatedly that when the two obligations collide, security almost always carries the day. Patients such as Eddie Mutwe are brought to court with obvious signs of torture, from institutions where doctors and nurses are on staff.




On 17 June 2026, Erias Lukwago was brought to court via Kira police station, where it was reported that a police doctor examined him. He found him to have a blood pressure reading that, under normal circumstances, would warrant an emergency admission to a health facility. The doctor administered some first aid and allowed security operatives to cart him off to court. (To their credit, when Mulago Hospital doctors finally saw Lukwago, their report was unequivocal – he needed to be in hospital and not in prison. Their recommendations have been summarily ignored by the state.) 




Kizza Besigye’s saga between the courts, prison, and health facilities is still unfolding, but it is clear that at almost every stage the state has expected medical workers to put security concerns above medical priorities. Prisons staff have normalized being present during examinations, and demands for patient information are without regard for doctor – patient confidentiality.




These might be considered small steps by some, but they are a slippery slope to disaster – for vulnerable patients in custody, and for health workers who have to live with the knowledge that they could have done better for their patients.




The World Medical Association’s post-war formulation captures the fundamental ethical principle: medical knowledge must not be used contrary to humanity. The ethical problem of “dual loyalty” arises precisely when a physician is simultaneously being asked to serve the patient and the interests of the state. 




A government may sometimes legitimately require medical information – for example, in public-health situations or through lawful judicial processes. But that is very different from compelling a doctor to disclose information because it will facilitate the persecution, interrogation, detention or harm of the patient.




The post 

Medical Ethics and the State’s Security Interests

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

author: Soraya Kishtwari
title: UK Universities Set to Strike in ‘Last-Ditch Fight Over Existential Cuts’
content:
University lecturers are set to walk out over “existential” cuts and course closures, as thousands of students face major disruptions as the new academic year begins.




At least eight universities have announced industrial action for the coming year, including three Russell Group institutions.




At Edinburgh, staff are striking for five weeks to protest £140m of cuts, 1,800 potential job losses and management’s refusal to rule out compulsory redundancies.




The university has also announced that 90 degree programmes will be scrapped from 2027.







The kind of cuts many universities are proposing “will fundamentally reshape higher education in the UK”, Emile Chabal professor of contemporary history at Edinburgh University, told Novara Media. He added there was a risk of university contraction leading to a 

“second deindustrialisation”, given the outsized contribution universities make to local economies.  




Peter Mathieson, Edinburgh University’s principal and vice-chancellor received 

£422,000 in total remuneration in 2023/24

 – equivalent to more than 10 times the university’s 

median staff pay

. As part of his package, 

Mathieson lives rent-free in a university-owned mansion

 on one of Edinburgh’s premier streets, where maintenance costs are also borne by the university.




 




Since Mathieson took up the role in February 2018, the university has acquired more than 

£1bn

 in capital assets. Staff at the university have described its financial woes as “

manufactured

”. 







Writing on X, Chabal, said: “I am not given to hyperbole when it comes to university industrial relations, but this feels like an existential event. The heart of the university is being torn out, with long-lasting consequences. These strikes are a last-ditch attempt to stop that. Will anyone listen?”







91% of union members at the University of Exeter voted in favour of industrial action, although dates have yet to be set for the walkout. As many as 

500 jobs are at risk

, with the University and College Union (UCU) warning that more than 80% of arts and humanities staff were at risk of losing their jobs.




Starting today, staff at Nottingham University, are also set to strike for 67 days this

 

autumn, amid plans to restructure departments and potentially close courses.







In Scotland, the universities of Dundee, Glasgow Caledonian and Heriot-Watt have also voted to strike, as have the universities of Essex, Exeter and Sussex in England. 







Lopa Leach, professor of vascular biology and former president of Nottingham’s UCU branch, 

told the Guardian

: “The word is carnage, it is carnage what they are doing now – at the local level and also at the national, senior management level in the UK. Why are they thinking about the destruction of higher education?”

author: Unknown
title: Mazloum Abdi issues message on Kurdish-language education
content:
Syrian Presidential Adviser Mazloum Abdi delivered a video message through ANHA on Kurdish-language education, the situation of schools, Rojava University and Kobanê University.




The message was as follows:




“Dear people, the Kurdish language is our identity. Protecting and developing Kurdish has always been a fundamental objective of the struggle we have waged to this day. Learning and receiving an education in one’s mother tongue is a natural right of all peoples, and education in Kurdish is likewise a fundamental and natural right of the Kurdish people. Over the past 14 years, during the Rojava Revolution, tremendous efforts have been made to provide Kurdish-language education and establish an education system despite the conditions of war. Although it has had shortcomings and weaknesses, it was something new and represented a historic step in the history of Rojava.




I would like to take this opportunity to salute all the families who sent their children to Kurdish-language schools despite the war, difficulties and obstacles. I also congratulate all the teachers and staff who have contributed to the teaching and study of the Kurdish language over the past 14 years.




It has been one year and eight months since the fall of the Baath regime. Our efforts to make Kurdish an official part of Syria’s education system are continuing. Numerous meetings, initiatives and discussions have taken place towards this goal. As a result, the Ministry of Education issued a decision concerning the Kurdish language. Our people and students did not consider this decision sufficient and organised demonstrations, expressed their position and continued their struggle. We regard this as a right of our students and stand with them in this process.




However, as the new academic year has begun and we are in a transitional period, we need to ensure that the education system continues successfully through to the end of the year. Necessary measures have been taken to ensure that children attending Kurdish schools do not face difficulties. The children will not be disadvantaged; they will learn Arabic while continuing their education in Kurdish.




We expect families and students to continue sending their children to schools where Kurdish is the primary language of instruction. This will allow us to successfully complete the new academic year during this transitional period and secure greater rights for the Kurdish language next year. This will provide a foundation for achieving all our rights concerning the Kurdish language in full.




This year, ninth-grade and baccalaureate education will continue under the Autonomous Administration’s education system.




I therefore ask all students in these two grades to continue their studies under the existing Kurdish-language education system in order to better safeguard their future.




Discussions and negotiations are still continuing over the official recognition of Rojava University and Kobanê University. Although no final decision has yet been reached, we hope that an appropriate decision will be made in the interests of our students at both universities.




For the new academic year at both universities, we ask students who completed their education in Kurdish to submit their preferences in accordance with the system published by the Ministry of Higher Education so that they can secure their places at these universities.




Finally, I congratulate everyone on the new academic year and wish you all success.”

author: Unknown
title: Mother of NATO prisoner: We are now victims of the judiciary too
content:
Twenty-nine-year-old earthquake survivor Halil Yakut was among those imprisoned in what was described as a witch-hunt against opposition groups ahead of the NATO Summit on 7–8 July 2026. Yakut, whose family home in Antakya was destroyed in the Maraş-centred earthquakes, was detained on 23 June 2026 in Muğla, hundreds of kilometres from Ankara, on the assumption that he was planning to stage a protest, and was subsequently imprisoned. An indictment prepared months later included anti-NATO articles published in Halk Okulu magazine and social media posts by Halkın Sesi TV concerning NATO bases as evidence relating to the alleged preparations for a protest ahead of the summit. It also referred to previous cases in which Yakut had been tried, including cases in which he had been acquitted. The indictment was submitted to the Istanbul 14th High Criminal Court, which ruled that it lacked jurisdiction over the case. Halil Yakut’s mother, Gülten Yakut, spoke to ANF and said: “We are earthquake survivors, but the injustice inflicted on my son has now made us victims of the judicial system as well.”




Gülten Yakut, whose family home in Antakya was destroyed in the Maraş-centred earthquakes, said she had not even had time to recover from the devastation because of what she described as the systematic use of hostile law against her son. She said Halil had repeatedly been imprisoned because of his struggle against injustice and unlawful practices. Yakut said, “We are earthquake survivors, but now we have also been made victims of the judiciary,” and expressing her anger at what her family had endured over the years. She said her son had been repeatedly targeted because he had been flagged by the police. Yakut recalled that Halil had previously been imprisoned in connection with the 6 February attack at Çağlayan Courthouse and said he had now been held for three months on the assumption that he was planning a protest ahead of the NATO Summit.




He was detained at the bus station before he could even set foot in Muğla




Yakut said her son was detained on 23 June 2026 in Muğla, hundreds of kilometres from Ankara, where the NATO Summit was due to take place. Yakut also said: “Halil was detained at the bus station before he could even set foot in Muğla. He had gone to Datça for a holiday. As soon as he got off the bus, the police detained him and held him in custody for three days. They asked whether he was preparing any action related to the NATO Summit and whether he knew anything about statements against NATO published on Halkın Sesi TV’s social media accounts. Although he said he had nothing to do with them, he was hastily imprisoned.” Yakut said that on the same day her son was detained, police simultaneously raided both the container home where the family was staying and the house they were renting in Hatay. Yakut added that her husband, who has Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, was at home during the raid but could not remember what had happened.




Halil’s imprisonment disrupted both our affairs and his treatment




Yakut said her son was initially held in a solitary isolation cell at Muğla E-Type Prison before being transferred to İzmir Şakran T-Type Prison. She said: “Halil had submitted a petition asking to be transferred to a prison in Adana so that he could be closer to us, but that did not happen. They transferred him to İzmir Şakran instead.” Yakut recalled that her son had also previously been imprisoned in what she described as unlawful circumstances and said: “Halil had previously been imprisoned on the pretext of the attack on Çağlayan Courthouse on 6 February. My son was forcibly transferred from Silivri Prison to Kırşehir Pit-Type Prison, where he began an indefinite hunger strike to protest against the isolation conditions imposed on prisoners. He was released on the 100th day of his hunger strike. Afterwards, he was working on a documentary about the earthquake, helping us with the sale of our land and also receiving medical treatment. His imprisonment once again on the pretext of the NATO Summit has disrupted both our affairs and his treatment.”




They keep putting my son’s old case files in front of him




Yakut said the indictment was issued in the third month of her son’s imprisonment. She pointed out that the indictment, which alleged preparations for a protest ahead of the NATO Summit, once again relied on accusations made by the same witnesses whose statements had been used to justify his imprisonment following the 6 February attack. Yakut said Istanbul 14th High Criminal Court, where the indictment was submitted, ruled that it lacked jurisdiction and transferred the case to Muğla. Yakut said: “Three months have passed, but my son is still in prison and it is still unclear what he is being held for. The indictment against Halil once again includes false statements by informants from previous cases in which he was tried and acquitted. My son has no connection with any organisation. They always find some excuse to imprison him, and every time they do, they keep bringing up his old case files. They arrest him on the same accusations, then release him, and while those proceedings are still continuing, they detain him again and use the same cases against him all over again. They wear people down and never leave them alone. It is as if they are deliberately trying to push him into trouble. This unjust system makes people angry.” 




Years later, his right to education is being denied again




Yakut stressed that her son was also being denied his right to education. She said Halil’s studies had previously been interrupted because of what she described as his unlawful imprisonment. He later benefited from an amnesty that allowed him to re-enrol at university, only to be imprisoned once again.




Yakut said, “My son will not be able to go to university again.” Halil is studying International Trade and Logistics at Tarsus University. His university enrolment had previously been cancelled because of his imprisonment, but he later re-enrolled under a subsequent legal arrangement. His classes began on 28 September. Yakut criticised the continued deprivation of her son’s freedom, saying there was no basis for his imprisonment and that he was being targeted simply because he had been flagged by the authorities. Yakut continued: “The NATO Summit ended three months ago, but my son is still being held hostage in prison. Applications by his lawyers for his release have also been rejected. His father has a 90 per cent disability and has Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease. Halil used to take care of his father and take him to the doctor. His father is not doing well now, and I have to rely on other people to help me take him to the doctor. We also have a plot of land that we were trying to sell, and Halil was handling that. The sale has also been left unfinished. In other words, their unlawful actions are victimising an entire family.”




The book was confiscated, but no notice was served




Yakut said she learned after her son was imprisoned that a confiscation order had also been issued for his book Beton Sizin, Vatan Bizim (The Concrete Is Yours, the Homeland Is Ours), which he wrote following the earthquake, on the grounds that it was considered “objectionable”. Yakut also said: “Halil asked me to bring his books Liseliler and Beton Sizin, Vatan Bizim to the prison. When I took them there, they did not give him Beton Sizin, Vatan Bizim. That was when Halil learned that a confiscation order had been issued for the book. He had not received any notification about it.”




Yakut called for her son’s immediate release and said: “If they are going to act fairly and genuinely uphold the law, they should release my son without waiting for the trial, because there is no crime. They should release him as soon as possible so that he can return to university. They have already caused him enough suffering. They should not prolong it any further.”

author: Unknown
title: Against male violence and male domination
content:
An extremely interesting march will take place in Amed today, 30 September. Perhaps it would be more accurate to call it a march without precedent, or one of very few of its kind. Men will march against male violence. Through this march, they will protest the dominant male violence directed against women. Until now, women have organized marches and rallies to protest male violence against women. Some men who had educated themselves on the basis of women's freedom would occasionally participate in these demonstrations and marches. Now, however, men themselves are organizing and carrying out a march to protest male violence against women. And beginning in Amed, which is known as the “capital of democracy.” In this way, the spirits of the many Gülistan Doku, Rojin Kabaiş and little Narin Güran, who were murdered by dominant masculinity, may find at least some consolation.




Undoubtedly, the fact that such a historically significant action is taking place in Amed also carries great meaning. This action demonstrates the level of development and strength attained by the Kurdish Freedom Revolution. It reveals that the essence of this revolution is, in fact, a Women's Freedom Revolution. Once again, it proclaims to the entire country and the world that Amed is a pioneering city of such a revolution. It calls on everyone to join the social revolution based on women's freedom and directed against dominant masculinity.




Some people who are sworn enemies of Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] and the PKK, which have spearheaded the Kurdish identity and freedom revolution, claim that this struggle, which has continued uninterrupted for 50 years, “has achieved nothing.” It is particularly noticeable that such statements have increased since Leader Apo's 27 February 2025, Peace and Democratic Society Process. According to them, the war waged for 50 years was supposedly for nothing, and all the blood, sweat and suffering were wasted! Yet the march scheduled to take place in Amed on September 30 clearly demonstrates that the struggle waged over the past 50 years, the blood shed and the suffering endured have enabled the Kurds to experience one of the greatest and most meaningful freedom revolutions in history. It has transformed Kurdish society, where patriarchy and feudal relations were among the most deeply entrenched, into a pioneer of the Women's Freedom Revolution. So much so that Kurdish men, who under reactionary notions of honor and custom once considered every form of oppression, violence and murder against women acceptable, are now marching against all of this so that women can live freely and equally. Can there be a greater or more meaningful development in the cause of freedom? Can there be a more profound and meaningful transformation toward liberation? If these people are not sworn enemies of freedom, why have they been attacking this development and transformation for decades?




One might argue that if men had to march against male violence in Amed, then male oppression and violence against women is still continuing. Undoubtedly, this argument is correct in one respect. The consequences of dominant male violence in Amed and other cities appear in the news every day. Women struggle every day against this dominant male violence and the massacres it produces. Indeed, on the very day the planned action was announced, the DEM Party's Women's Spokesperson's Office also issued a statement condemning this male violence. Of course, all of this is one side of the matter. The other side is that people are refusing to submit to this dominant male oppression and violence. The struggle being waged by women in Kurdish cities, particularly Amed, against dominant male violence and killings is now being joined by a men's movement that is beginning in Amed. Yes, dominant masculinity still exercises oppression and violence, but women and men are also engaged in a highly conscious and organized struggle for freedom against it. This struggle is what offers hope for a free and equal life in the future.




Of course, we cannot simply dismiss what is happening as “a march” and move on. Yes, on September 30, men will march for women's freedom, but this is part of the historic Women's Freedom Revolution that is advancing with tremendous force, and it is one of its most meaningful aspects. Looking back at recent history, one can see with the naked eye how far things have come. Let us not forget that this protest march by men against male violence toward women is taking place in a society where, until very recently, women were being murdered by men for the most trivial excuses. Beyond that, let us consider the real-world experience of recent socialist history.




We all know very well that even the most optimistic position was that the women's question would be resolved after the socialist revolution. Those who spoke of “male violence” were immediately accused of engaging in gender discrimination and making the class struggle invisible. In this context, the Kurdistan Freedom Revolution has undergone two major revolutionary stages in addressing the women's question. In the first, women became conscious and entered into a major revolutionary struggle against male domination in particular, alongside women's enslavement. It appears that in the second stage, men are also becoming conscious and are now entering into a major revolutionary struggle against every form of male domination in the name of women's freedom and equality.




Of course, this major development has a very significant history. It is well known that it has taken place on the basis of the creative theoretical and practical efforts of Leader Abdullah Öcalan. The theories of “breaking away, killing the man, and the struggle between the sexes,” developed by Leader Apo as early as the mid-1990s, together with the “Women's Liberation Ideology” he proclaimed in March 1998, provide the theoretical foundation for today's developments. The concept of “Jineoloji,” developed in his defenses, and the historical thesis based on the “caste-killer system,” presented in the Manifesto, now provide a foundation and direction for all emancipatory searches and aspirations. Undoubtedly, while Leader Abdullah Öcalan develops the theory and ideology, the courageous and self-sacrificing women's movement, which continues to grow and spread, puts them into practice. This great revolutionary struggle has a deeply meaningful and instructive history, as well as thousands of heroic martyrs, as the many Sara and Zilan. In other words, nothing develops by itself; on the contrary, everything emerges as the result of immense intellectual and physical labor.




Of course, reducing male domination over women to violence alone, and defining it exclusively in those terms, would be insufficient. Male domination over women is the first form of domination to have emerged in history and to have shaped those that followed. This domination is a system and a mentality. Violence is one of its faces, clearly its visible face. There are also invisible dimensions of this domination, which involve exercising control over women from their emotions and spirit to their thoughts. Male violence against women is therefore a consequence and a visible manifestation of male domination over women. Naturally, struggling against this violence is both necessary and important, and it must be pursued at all times and everywhere. But to eliminate this violence, a comprehensive struggle against the dominant masculinity that produces it is essential. In Leader Apo's words, dominant masculinity must be killed.




Of course, the march that men will hold in Amed today against male violence toward women is a beginning, and it is important. But it is clear that not everything can be achieved through a single march, nor can the problems created by dominant male violence be resolved by one action. The most fundamental problem of today's global society is the dominant male mentality and system, and the resolution of all other problems will also depend on resolving this one. In this respect, first and foremost, everyone—women and men alike—must educate themselves sufficiently and continuously on this issue, and become organized and equipped with the necessary knowledge and capabilities. At the same time, a multifaceted struggle must be developed in every sphere to overcome and transform the dominant male mentality and system, and to create a man who is free from dominant masculinity and has achieved a free and equal life. This is a struggle between the sexes and a struggle against the ego. Therefore, it is the most important and greatest struggle of all. Good luck to everyone who says they want to live in genuine freedom and equality based on women's freedom and respect for differences!




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

author: Unknown
title: Öcalan must be able to carry out his work as Coordinator for Peace and Political Transition
content:
As a well-known saying goes, there can be no proper treatment without a correct diagnosis. Whatever anyone may say, the main issue on Turkey’s agenda today is the Peace and Democratic Society process, which began with Abdullah Öcalan’s call for the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). The President of Turkey and the Speaker of Parliament have said that the process is important and progressing well. Yet recent developments raise doubts about how accurately the state understands the process. If there is a problem and a process aimed at resolving it, it can only be addressed with the parties directly concerned. The leadership of the Kurdish Freedom Movement, one of the principal parties to the issue, says that the process is not progressing well. Doubts inevitably grow when one side says things are not going well while the other insists that they are.




On the day the so-called framework law was passed, Justice and Development Party (AKP) Deputy Parliamentary Group Chair Abdullah Güler said that Abdullah Öcalan’s status would change and that he would subsequently meet with many different groups. Two months have passed, yet there has been no tangible outcome from those remarks. Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli and some government officials also said months ago that Öcalan would become the Coordinator for Peace and Political Transition, but those words have likewise remained unfulfilled. Anyone who now claims that the issue can be resolved without Öcalan assuming an open and official role is deceiving themselves. The leadership of the Communalist Movement is surely not issuing statements and assessments for the sake of it. The issue to which this movement is most sensitive is its leadership. Its cadres and fighters will therefore take no action unless what they say concerning their leadership is taken into account.




There is now a debate over disarmament. The very fact that the issue is being treated solely as a matter of disarmament shows that it has not been properly understood. It also suggests that a movement which has waged an extremely difficult struggle for 50 years has not been properly understood either. Its cadres and fighters say that unless their leadership is openly and officially involved in the process, there will be no laying down of arms and no return to Turkey. If the AKP government fails to take this seriously, it will run into a major obstacle. The government can therefore no longer conduct this process behind closed doors. Some aspects may not be made public, but the parties to the process must be able to act openly. Öcalan must now be able to carry out his work openly. Without this, there can be no progress in the process, because the Movement’s leadership wants Öcalan to be able to work openly and freely.




Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan must, of course, be able to meet frequently with his own organisation for the process to move forward. If he cannot meet with the organisation’s leadership and cadres over such a difficult issue, the process cannot develop properly. Failure to understand this would justify doubts about whether the state is serious about the process. The urgent priority, therefore, is for Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan to immediately begin carrying out his work as Coordinator for Peace and Political Transition. According to information we have received, if there is no development on this issue in the first week of October, the process could face its first genuine deadlock. Everything that happened before the law was passed was part of the discussion. The process has now entered the implementation phase. If Abdullah Öcalan, the chief negotiator of the Kurdish people, cannot work freely and fulfil his role, how can there be any talk of a process? The Kurdish people and democratic forces expect political actors to take steps towards democratisation. If the guerrillas are to lay down their arms and engage in politics, then democratic conditions must be created in which they can freely participate in political life.




Democratic politics cannot be pursued under the current legal and judicial conditions in Turkey. If parties operating within the existing political system cannot freely engage in politics and political groups are subjected to operations every day, then it is impossible to pursue a democratic political struggle that also encompasses the Kurdish people’s demand for a free and democratic life. Under such circumstances, how can the guerrillas lay down their arms?




Far from introducing democratic legislation, the space available to existing opposition forces to engage in politics is being narrowed. How can society be prepared for such a process under these circumstances? How can the Peace and Democratic Society Process advance unless the prevailing political approach changes and public support for democratisation is secured?




All these problems can only be resolved if the Kurdish People’s Leader is able to live and work freely. Expecting the guerrillas to lay down their arms and return before this happens would mean that the problem is still not being diagnosed correctly.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: PQ’s Sonia Caron looks to switch from education to politics
content:
Nunatsiaq News reached out to each candidate running in the Ungava riding ahead of Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election. Here’s what Parti Québecois candidate Sonia Caron had to share.




Sonia Caron said she never saw herself going into politics. Her decision to run for MNA in the Ungava riding came after four parties approached her.




“After a very long reflection, I decided to make the jump,” the Parti Québécois candidate said in an interview from Lebel-sur-Quévillon.




A lifelong supporter of the party from Chibougamau, Caron has spent the last 25 years working in education. She serves as the director of professional development at the Centre de services scolaire de la Baie-James, which oversees trades programs in northern Quebec.




She said her priorities are the lack of frontline health services and clean drinking water in many remote communities, issues that need to be treated with urgency.




“I told myself, ‘We have to do something,’ because our region is undergoing major upheavals, and public services are constantly deteriorating,” Caron said.




The current opposition party has promised to double the budget for medical travel reimbursements and a massive increase in funding for frontline care to be offered at community clinics.
















Caron has long worked alongside economic leaders in Quebec as a member of the Société du Plan Nord, which advises the provincial government on economic and social development in the north, and as a board member of Quebec’s mining industry institute.




She is also the president of the Conseil régional des Partenaires du Marché du travail de la Jamésie, which advises the province on labour supply and demand.




She said that the party wants to work hand in hand with Cree and Inuit on economic and social development and that it wants communities to benefit from royalties from the mining industry.




“I’ve always cared deeply about the Inuit villages,” Caron said, adding that she worked as a high school French teacher in Inukjuak in 2003.




Caron is among five candidates running for Ungava in Quebec’s provincial election. Advance polls have been open since Saturday and will close Wednesday. Election day is set for Oct. 5.

author: Kay Pacha / Equipo Pueblos Originarios del SERPAJ
title: El pueblo Mbyá resiste y lucha
content:
La resistencia y lucha de los pueblos originarios, hoy en día se lleva a cabo de diversas formas y con distintas estrategias, por eso queremos hacer notar los esfuerzos que desde diferentes espacios se suman a lo que ya se viene haciendo desde hace un tiempo.










https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MBYA-KAY-PACHA.mp3




https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MBYA-KAY-PACHA.mp3




Descargar audio




Y en este caso nos referimos al pueblo Mbyá guaraní de Misiones, que además de las movilizaciones, y las distintas gestiones para enfrentar las amenazas contra sus derechos y territorios, encontramos a jóvenes comunicadores que se ocupan de difundir, explicar y reflexionar sobre los diferentes temas que tienen como protagonistas a distintas comunidades de su pueblo.  Nos referimos al joven William Ayala conocido como Wilicho.







También destacamos la resistencia de la comunidad Puente Quemado II, que a pesar del desalojo, detención de algunos hermanos y amenazas del empresario forestal Alfredo Ruff, volvieron a su tierra y en forma pacífica pero segura, se instalaron nuevamente en el lugar de donde no debieron haber salido nunca.







Al mismo tiempo no dejamos de reconocer la importancia de la organización  del pueblo Mbyá, que a través del Aty Ñechiró viene discutiendo y tomando decisiones que acompañan a las comunidades en la defensa de sus territorios.







Por eso decimos que son diferentes formas de resistencia y lucha, pero las tres son válidas y necesarias, y por eso queremos destacarlas, haciendo conocerlas.







Escucharemos a un joven Mbyá que participó en la reunión del Aty Ñechiró, a Wilicho y a Santiago Ramos, cacique de la Comunidad Puente Quemado II.







El Micro Kay Pacha se realiza con el apoyo de la organización Otto per Mille-Chiessa Valdense.

author: Ezra
title: Paris ermöglicht Auslieferung des Antifaschisten Gino an Deutschland: No Extradition!
content:
Paris ermöglicht Auslieferung des Antifaschisten Gino an Deutschland: No Extradition!




Gino wird beschuldigt, sich zusammen mit anderen Antifaschist*innen im Februar 2023 in Budapest an körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen mit Nazis beteiligt zu haben. Damals fand der 

NS

-verherrlichende „Tag der Ehre“ statt, das jährlich stattfindende europaweit größte Nazi-Vernetzungstreffen, wogegen es antifaschistische Proteste gab. Die Vorfälle nahm Ungarn zum Anlass für eine internationale Kriminalisierungswelle gegen Antifaschist*innen, wobei sich vor allem die deutschen und 

US

-amerikanischen Behörden der Repressionsoffensive engagiert anschlossen.

Auch in Deutschland laufen Prozesse im Budapest-Komplex, wobei Ende September 2025 als erste die Nürnberger Antifaschistin Hanna zu fünf Jahren Haft verurteilt wurde – ohne jede Beweise. Seit Anfang 2026 läuft in Düsseldorf das Budapest-Großverfahren gegen sechs Antifaschist*innen, und auch im Dresdner Antifa-Großprozess wird mehreren Angeklagten eine Beteiligung an den Vorfällen in Ungarn vorgeworfen. Die meisten in Deutschland Beschuldigten sind schon seit Jahren in Untersuchungshaft. Parallel dazu wurde heute in Budapest das Strafverfahren gegen Maja T., Gabriele M. und Anna M. beendet und vom Revisionsgericht der Schuldspruch und die grotesk hohen Haft- und Geldstrafen im Wesentlichen bestätigt.

Zu den international verfolgten Antifaschist*innen gehört auch Gino, der in Mailand aufwuchs, aber einen albanischen Pass hat. Er lebte zuletzt jahrelang in Finnland und floh vor den Verfolgungen im Budapest-Komplex nach Frankreich, wo er im November 2024 für mehrere Monate in Haft genommen wurde, weil Ungarn per Europäischem Haftbefehl seine Auslieferung verlangte. Angesichts der katastrophalen Menschenrechtslage, insbesondere der drohenden Folter, und mit Verweis auf die fehlende Rechtsstaatlichkeit in Ungarn lehnte es die Auslieferungskammer des Pariser Berufungsgerichts im April 2025 ab, Gino an Budapest zu überstellen.

Als enge Bündnispartnerinnen bei der ungarisch-deutschen Verfolgungsjagd gegen Antifaschist*innen erließen daraufhin die deutschen Behörden Ende 2025 einen eigenen Europäischen Haftbefehl gegen Gino und verlangten seine Auslieferung, um ihn in Deutschland anzuklagen. Zur Begründung verweist die Bundesanwaltschaft darauf, dass zwei der Nazis, die in Budapest verletzt worden sein sollen, die deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit besitzen. Im Fall von Deutschland fiel es der Pariser Justiz deutlich schwerer, die offen politische Verfolgung und die unübersehbaren Rechtsbrüche im Umgang mit Antifaschist*innen zu benennen, die einer Auslieferung im Wege stehen. Dabei besteht das hohe Risiko, dass die deutschen Behörden anschließend Gino an Ungarn ausliefern und das Pariser Urteil von 2025 auf diese Art rechtswidrig umgehen. Eine Auslieferung könnte entweder direkt nach der Ankunft erfolgen oder aber nach einem Prozess und mehrjähriger Haft in Deutschland. Die Gefahr ist umso größer, als der Antifaschist weder Deutscher noch 

EU

-Bürger ist. Aber der politische Druck aus Deutschland ist enorm, und am 18. September 2026 hatte deshalb bereits das Berufungsgericht Ginos Auslieferung beschlossen, wogegen die Verteidigung vor das Kassationsgericht zog. Die heutige Sitzung des Kassationsgerichts bestätigte die Auslieferung an Deutschland endgültig.

Die Entscheidung war ein Schock und löste unmittelbar starke Proteste vor allem in Paris aus. In den letzten Wochen hatte sich eine internationale Solidaritätskampagne formiert, die besonders in Frankreich und Italien zu Massenprotesten und breiter gesellschaftlicher Unterstützung für Gino führte. Hunderte Prominente unterzeichneten eine Petition, die die drohende Auslieferung scharf ablehnte und die Verfolgung von Antifaschist*innen im Budapest-Komplex anprangerte. Für heute Abend sind zudem mehrere Proteste im ganzen Land angekündigt.

„Die heutige Entscheidung des Pariser Kassationsgerichts, Gino nach Deutschland auszuliefern, ist ein Skandal und zeigt, dass auch in Frankreich Grund- und Menschenrechte nicht länger für Antifaschist*innen gelten. Schließlich muss Gino nicht nur mit schwerer politischer Verfolgung und langer Haft in Deutschland rechnen, sondern auch die rechtswidrige Auslieferung an Ungarn fürchten“, erklärte Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Wir stehen an der Seite von Gino und allen anderen verfolgten Antifas. Wir rufen zu Protesten gegen die drohende Auslieferung an Deutschland auf. Und vor allem müssen wir dagegen ankämpfen, dass Gino von hier aus an Ungarn ausgeliefert wird. Wir sind alle Antifa – no extradition!“

Pressemitteilung













Am heutigen Mittwoch, 30. September 2026, hat das Pariser Kassationsgericht mit einem empörenden Urteil den Weg für die Auslieferung von Gino an Deutschland freigemacht. Budapest-Komplex beschuldigt wird, droht jetzt unmittelbar die Überstellung an Deutschland. Zudem ist aber auch nicht auszuschließen, dass die deutschen Behörden Gino direkt weiter an Ungarn überstellen, wo ihm unmenschliche Haftbedingungen, Folter und eine Strafe von bis zu 24 Jahren drohen.

title: Yılmaz: Visually impaired people face barriers to sport
content:
Sport is one of the key areas that strengthens individuals’ participation in physical and social life, yet barriers preventing visually impaired people from accessing sport persist. Inaccessible sports facilities, limited opportunities for different sports and training, transport difficulties and economic constraints make it harder for visually impaired people to participate in sporting activities regularly and independently.




The lack of accessibility at sports facilities, particularly in urban areas, makes it difficult for visually impaired people to reach them independently and participate regularly in sporting activities.




Abdülmecit Yılmaz, President of the Amed Visually Impaired Sports Club and the Amed Federation of People with Disabilities, spoke to ANF about the difficulties visually impaired people face in accessing sport.




The biggest barriers are the lack of facilities and infrastructure




Yılmaz said people with disabilities were unable to participate freely in sport in the city and that the most fundamental problem was the lack of facilities where they could train and compete.




Yılmaz drew attention to goalball, a sport specifically designed for visually impaired people and said: “We face enormous difficulties in accessing sporting activities, particularly as visually impaired people. There is a sport for visually impaired people called goalball, but we do not have a court where we can play it. We do not have anywhere to train. This is one of the main problems we face. Because we have no court, we cannot train properly or go into our matches adequately prepared. When we travel to tournaments in western provinces, unfortunately we can find ourselves effectively defeated before we even arrive because we have not been able to train.”




We face serious barriers to participating in social life




Yılmaz said that, in addition to difficulties participating in sport, visually impaired people also faced serious barriers in accessing stadium stands and taking part in social life.




He said: “We can face a number of accessibility problems when we go to Amedspor matches. There is a great deal of interest in the city and in sport, but we have problems accessing tickets. Take the Passo app, for example. It was not designed to be accessible to visually impaired people. We use screen readers on our phones, and when apps are not designed to work with them, we cannot easily buy tickets. If we cannot get an e-ticket, we are effectively unable to exercise that right.




There is also an internet problem at the stadium. As a visually impaired person, when I go to a match, I want to experience the atmosphere but also know what is happening on the pitch. Since I cannot expect someone to describe everything to me, I need to follow the match on the radio or through an online broadcast. When there is no internet connection, we cannot access the broadcast and are left with nothing but the noise of the crowd. So, we cannot fully experience the atmosphere.”




Practices used in other cities should also be introduced locally




Yılmaz recalled the queues of people with disabilities waiting for tickets outside Amed Stadium and continued: “Last week, there was a queue of people with disabilities waiting for tickets outside Amed Stadium. These people encounter this situation simply because they want to watch an Amedspor match. You go to the match full of enthusiasm, but when you cannot watch it or encounter an upsetting situation, it takes all the enjoyment out of the experience.




The Federation, the Ministry of Youth and Sports and the Amedspor management need to find a joint solution to the ticketing problem. There are different practices at other clubs: people can obtain tickets online, or when they make a request, club officials can allocate tickets to people with disabilities. So why should people with disabilities in our city have to wait in ticket queues? We expect these problems to be resolved.”




Our athletes face serious financial difficulties




Abdülmecit Yılmaz said the proportion of people with disabilities and the potential pool of athletes in the region were above the average in Turkey. 




He said: “Research conducted in Turkey put the proportion of people with disabilities at 12.29 per cent, while the figure in Diyarbakır (Amed) is higher, at 15 per cent. Inevitably, this is also reflected in sport. Sports organisations working with visually impaired people carry out these activities on a voluntary basis, but we cannot access funding. We face serious financial difficulties when taking our athletes to tournaments.




We have highly successful visually impaired athletes in our region, but we cannot keep them here. When they cannot access the opportunities they need, they inevitably have to move to western provinces, and we end up losing our strongest athletes.”

title: Iraqi Prime Minister: International Coalition’s mission has officially ended
content:
A ceremony was held today in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, to mark Sovereignty Day and the end of the International Coalition’s mission against ISIS. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi attended the ceremony alongside commanders of the coalition forces and the Iraqi military.




Speaking at the ceremony, Ali al-Zaidi said: “We officially announce the end of the International Coalition forces’ mission in Iraq. Today, Iraq is reaping the fruits of the sacrifices and heroism demonstrated over many years. Our security forces, with all their components, have established security and operational control across all regions of Iraq.”




Stating that the fight “against terrorism” would continue, the Prime Minister added: “The end of the International Coalition’s mission does not mean that our war against terrorism is over. On the contrary, it marks the transition to a stage in which Iraq assumes full responsibility for its own defense, security, and stability.”

author: Unknown
title: Cebar Yaver: KDP-PUK dispute leaves the door open to threats
content:
In an exclusive interview with Fırat News Agency (ANF), military and security expert Cebar Yaver assessed the security situation in Iraq and the Kurdistan Region, the end of the mission of the International Coalition forces, and the process of unifying the Peshmerga forces of the KDP (Kurdistan Democratic Party) and PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan).




‘Coalition forces were established to protect US interests’ 




Yaver noted that the end of the mission of the anti-ISIS International Coalition forces in Iraq was an expected development, noting that the force had been deployed for a specific purpose.




Yaver said: “This coalition was established at a time when ISIS had gained control in Iraq and Syria, occupied a quarter of Iraqi territory, and become a serious threat to Baghdad, Saudi Arabia, and Jordan. Taking its own interests into account, the United States formed this coalition of more than 70 countries.”




Regarding the withdrawal process, Yaver said that two years ago a joint military committee comprising representatives from Iraq, the Kurdistan Region, and the United States assessed the ISIS threat and concluded that the organization’s military and financial capabilities had diminished and that it had lost territory.




The agreement stipulated that the departure would take place in two phases; withdrawal from central and southern Iraq by the end of September 2025 in the first phase, and from the Kurdistan Region by the end of September 2026 in the second.




Addressing differing approaches on the withdrawal of coalition forces, Cebar Yaver said: “Masoud Barzani and Masrour Barzani emphasize that the coalition’s withdrawal is premature and that there is a risk of ISIS returning. In contrast, Qubad Talabani and the Iraqi government stress that local forces are prepared and capable of handling the security portfolio.”




‘The ISIS threat has not been completely eliminated’




Sharing his assessment of the process as a military expert, Yaver stated: “The ISIS threat has not yet been completely eliminated. The organization continues its propaganda activities by actively using digital media. Indeed, just a few days ago, it clashed with the Iraqi army and killed two civilians. However, it is a fact that its forces have weakened. On the other hand, the end of the International Coalition’s mission does not mean that these countries’ influence in the region has come to an end. Iraq has bilateral military and economic agreements with the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. The Kurdistan Region can also benefit from these agreements and from air defense capabilities through the Iraqi Ministry of Defense.”




‘The greatest threat is the dispute between the KDP and PUK’




Regarding the greatest threat facing the Kurdistan Region, Yaver said: “The most dangerous issue is the dispute between the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP). The greatest risk is the inability to form a government and the fact that parliament has remained dysfunctional for two years. Nothing could be more dangerous than this. If we want to fight armed groups and ISIS and demand our legal rights from Baghdad, we must first reach an agreement among ourselves.”




Yaver emphasized that the first step should be to form a government and provide public services, followed by the normalization of relations with Baghdad so that the armed forces of the Kurdistan Region and Iraq can work together to fill the security vacuum.




‘We hope that the parties’ control over the Peshmerga will come to an end’




Cebar Yaver, former Secretary-General of the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, also recalled previous unsuccessful attempts to unify the Peshmerga forces: “In 1992, the PUK, KDP, Islamic Movement, Socialist Party, and Communist Party came together for the first time under the umbrella of the ‘Kurdistan Army.’ However, the civil war in 1994 derailed these efforts, and the forces once again came under the control of the political parties. In 2009, another attempt at reorganization was made within the framework of Units 70 and 80, but they were unable to free themselves from the parties’ dominance. They are currently organized under the ‘First Regional Command’ and ‘Second Regional Command.’ We hope that this time the parties’ control over the Peshmerga forces will come to an end.”




‘A High Political Council should be established’




Regarding the unity of Kurdish military and political forces across the four parts of Kurdistan, Cebar Yaver said: “Since Kurdistan is divided among four different states, establishing a unified military command is not easy. However, a High Political Council should be established so that the Kurdish question can be presented to the world as a single dossier. Only after that can further steps be taken.”

title: Muqtada al-Sadr announces dissolution of his armed structures
content:
Iraqi Shiite leader Muqtada al-Sadr announced that the armed structures affiliated with him have been dissolved and that one of them has been transformed into a civilian foundation.




According to Sadr’s statement, Saraya al-Salam (Peace Brigades) has been dissolved, while the Imam Mahdi Army, which had previously been among Sadr’s armed formations, will be transformed into a civilian organization under the name “Ansar al-Imam al-Mahdi Foundation.”




Sadr also announced the dissolution of the armed group Liwa al-Yawm al-Mawud (Promised Day Brigade).




In his statement, Sadr emphasized Iraq’s sovereignty and independence, saying that weapons in the country should be brought under state control.




Sadr’s move came on the same day that the US-led International Coalition ended its military mission in Iraq and US forces completed their withdrawal from the country.




The Iraqi government had previously called on armed groups in the country to place their weapons under state control and identified September 30 as an important milestone. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government had stated that weapons held outside state control would face legal consequences. However, the government was later reported to have treated this date as the beginning of a process of regulation and integration rather than a deadline for the complete surrender of weapons.




Sadr-affiliated Saraya al-Salam was among the groups that took steps in May toward dissolving its armed structure and coming under state control. In June, the group was reported to have held a ceremony in Samarra related to the process of handing over its weapons.




However, not all armed groups in Iraq have adopted the same position. Powerful groups such as Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, in particular, oppose laying down their arms and describe their weapons as “weapons of resistance.”




Sadr also described the end of the US military presence in Iraq as “the end of the occupation” and called on Washington to pay compensation for its past military interventions. He also warned that foreign interference in Iraq’s internal affairs could draw the country into new regional conflicts.
