title: Besê Hozat: Women are the vanguard of this process and its defining force
content:
Besê Hozat, co-chair of the KCK Executive Council, said in an interview with Medya Haber that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot succeed in Turkey without democratization.




The first part of the interview can be read 

here

.




A campaign has been launched by a number of writers, intellectuals, and politicians in this regard – taking responsibility within this process – called “1001 Signatures.” Presuming that you are aware of this campaign, how do you assess it?




This, for example, is truly a meaningful and valuable initiative. It needs to be expanded further and make it more widespread. What is Turkey’s fundamental impasse? In Turkey, many groups are waging their struggles in their own separate spheres. These struggles do not converge, do not unite, and do not transform into synergy. The women’s movement is waging a struggle on its own front, the youth on theirs, the ecological and environmental movements on theirs, workers on theirs, peasants on theirs, and the democratic forces on theirs – everyone is waging a struggle in their own neighborhood, on their own periphery, in their own lane. If we think of each of these as a river, every river flows from a different place and flows to a different destination. If these rivers were to merge, if these dynamics of struggle were to come together and transform into a common, united struggle, this would give rise to a very powerful democratic movement in Turkey – a very powerful democratic dynamic – and this process would also foster a strong sense of ownership. It would play a decisive role in the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




This newly launched initiative, developed primarily by intellectuals, is very valuable and meaningful. But if it remains limited to intellectuals alone – and if it is confined solely to a petition drive with a thousand or so signatures, or a stance that barely goes beyond that – it certainly has meaning and value, however, in terms of the results it will produce, its impact would remain limited.




There was also a decision by autonomous women’s organizations. They will organize a conference – involving artists, politicians, intellectuals, and academics – to discuss women’s role in the Peace and Democratic Society process and to create a common front against male and state violence.




Correct. Women have also launched a process under the name “Side by Side,” a process of struggle. I believe they will hold a meeting in late October or early November, where they will develop a joint plan for their struggle. And it will be a united and collective struggle. This is very important. So, this struggle led by women unites all workers, environmental and ecological movements, and all democratic forces in Turkey into a single pot if it transforms into a common struggle, and if the central demand of all those at the heart of this struggle is, after all, democracy, freedom, equality, justice, and a shared, democratic life – then this will give serious rise to a very powerful democratic movement in Turkey. It will also play a decisive role in the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, and I am convinced that it will accelerate this process.




It will also create serious pressure on the government. It will compel both the government and the state to take democratic, political, and legal steps more quickly, without dragging their feet. This can only happen through struggle. Sitting back and watching, waiting, or having everyone continue this limited struggle only in their own neighborhoods will not lead this process to success in the short term. I reiterate that these struggles do have meaning, but we need to bring them together in a joint effort, transforming them into a common struggle and a shared synergy. This will bring to the fore a very strong democratic will, power, and movement and will compel the state and the government to take democratic steps. It will facilitate the swift advancement of this process. We need to develop this further.




The same applies to women. Women are the pioneers of this process. They are its vanguard and its defining force. They are the driving force behind the construction of a democratic society – its fundamental building block. This process will develop under women’s leadership, with their significant and active participation and struggle. Women must be able to bring their struggle together with other democratic dynamics in society and unite them. They must succeed in becoming the driving force and the vanguard of all these struggles. If this develops, it will translate into significant pressure on the government and the state, and these efforts – which will bring about the taking of democratic steps – are extremely valuable.




There was a march for the protection of land and water in Giyadîn the other day. It is of great importance. There is widespread environmental destruction in Kurdistan, in Turkey, and everywhere. Ecological movements are gradually gaining momentum. Serious awareness is emerging on this issue. In the Black Sea region and in the villages of the Aegean, a serious peasant movement is also emerging – one that stands up for its land, trees, olive groves, forests, and water. Women are leading the way in this movement. This is very valuable. For months, almost a year now, there has been a struggle in Varto (Gimgim), in Dersim, and in Şırnak. There is a lot of environmental destruction in Kurdistan. An ecocide is going on. It has been carried out for years as part of the genocide policy, and it has not yet come to an end. There is awareness of this issue. This awareness needs to expand and become more widespread. An absolutely serious struggle on this issue must be waged everywhere.




Then again, there is the “Şiyar Be” campaign against drugs. This is also raising significant awareness. A serious policy of 

sociocide

, specifically targeting children and young people, is being carried out through drugs, prostitution, and violence against women. As I said, if all of these struggles against this progress become widespread and converge in a common effort, they will generate a powerful synergy and give rise to a very strong social democratic movement. This will play an absolutely decisive role in the success of the process. It is necessary to work on this, focus on it, and strive for this.




Recently, there have also been positive developments in South Kurdistan. The Peshmerga forces of the KDP and the PUK have come together and united under a single ministry. What impact will this have on the ongoing developments?




The situation in South Kurdistan is important. And the unification of the Peshmerga forces under a single ministry is a positive development. There are also discussions about forming a government, because as is known, so far no government has been formed since the election. It is, of course, important that these discussions lead to a conclusion. We attach great importance to the establishment of a democratic government in South Kurdistan. In South Kurdistan, too, the era of rule based on party or family dominance must be left behind. A democratic unity government must be formed in which all representatives of the people, organized structures, and political entities can express themselves and be represented in a democratic manner. Gradually, both the federal structure in South Kurdistan must transform into a democratic federal structure and system, and the administration must evolve into a democratic government and administration.




A system and administration that have established democracy and internal peace will play a significant role and serve as a decisive force in the democratization of both Iraq and the region. If this happens, the democratic struggle waged by the Kurds as a whole – in Turkey, South Kurdistan, Syria, and Iran – will play a significant role in the democratization of the Middle East and will democratize the region as well. South Kurdistan’s role in this regard will also be important. A democratic federal South Kurdistan and a democratic unity government, along with the Peshmerga as a unified military force, are of the utmost importance. We believe that South Kurdistan’s contribution to the democratization of both South Kurdistan and Iraq will be immense.




An integration process has also begun in Rojava, with various appointments made and certain decisions taken regarding mother tongue. However, there appears to be serious discontent within society regarding this. Furthermore, the unfolding events in Kobanê highlight the situation of pressure. How do you assess this situation? How do you evaluate the policies of the Sharaa administration?




It is simply not possible to speak of a democratic state, government, or administration in Syria. There is currently a centralized, authoritarian, fascist system in Damascus. Democratic integration is hardly possible within a centralized, fascist system. Under the current circumstances, it is clear that the democratic integration efforts underway in Rojava are not progressing in accordance with the essence and spirit of the process and that integration is not developing properly. It appears that democratic integration has not yet been fully understood or grasped. Yet democratic integration is possible only with a democratic state. Without a democratic state – a democratic republic – democratic integration cannot be achieved. What is democratic integration? Democratic integration means the state’s recognition of local democracy, self-governance, and democratic autonomy. And in this sense, it also means that the state must change itself. It means it must become sensitive to democracy. It means it must develop a process based on the construction of a democratic republic. It means the state must also participate in establishing a democratic constitutional order. Do these things exist in Syria? No, they do not. So what is currently understood by “integration”? It is understood as a sort of transfer of the democratic autonomous administrative institutions – which have been in place for 14 years – to Damascus. In a sense, it is understood as the administration of the Rojava region and the province of Hesekê according to the state system. This is a mistaken way of understanding the issue. It is a deeply flawed way of understanding and conceptualizing democratic integration. The process of democratic integration is not one that will unfold easily. It is a process that will develop in parallel, in coordination, and intertwined with the democratization of the state, the democratization of Syria, and the construction of a democratic Syria. This requires a serious struggle for democracy and hard work.




The mindset in Damascus has become clear throughout the developments. An extremely anti-democratic, fascist mindset still prevails. In this sense, it will be a tense process. Nor is it a process that will unfold easily. A struggle for democracy must, of course, be waged with this in mind. Indeed, the reduction of mother-tongue education to three hours – as an elective course – is a result of the mindset in Damascus. Now, if there is no democratic system in Damascus, if there is no form of governance, then, of course, that mindset will not accept education in the mother tongue. At most, it will accept three hours of elective courses. Rojava has been governed under democratic autonomy for 14 years.




The paradigm of the democratic nation has taken shape there. For 14 years in Rojava – and throughout north and east Syria – the peoples have lived together in a democratic and free manner. Every people, with the Kurds foremost among them, received education in their native language. The Kurds received education in their native language, and the Assyrian-Syriac people received education in their native language. Rojava has developed a multilingual identity encompassing all groups living in northeastern Syria, including the Arabs. Now, however, we are seeing an approach that ignores, rejects, and denies this reality. This approach, this mindset, will not bring democracy, peace, or freedom to Syria. It will not bring about a situation where peoples can live together freely and as brothers and sisters. If this mindset is not overcome, Syria – whether today, tomorrow, or the day after – will never be free from war. It will never be free from tension or instability. This is clear. No one can accept receiving Kurdish-language education as just three hours of elective classes per week; they cannot accept this. And they have made it clear that they do not accept it.




Every day, children, young people, and the elderly – the entire people of Rojava, from the age of 7 to 70 – are on their feet. Serious protests are unfolding. This will clearly continue. It has sparked immense anger. If you do not accept a people’s language or education in their mother tongue, it means you do not accept that people’s very existence. To recognize a people’s existence means to accept their right to education in their mother tongue. What does it mean to ban education in the mother tongue? This people has waged a great struggle and paid a heavy price. These sacrifices were made for the sake of education in their mother tongue, for the sake of administrating themselves freely, for the sake of self-governance, and for the sake of self-defense. To disregard these sacrifices now is to throw the door wide open to instability in Syria. There is a serious need for a shift in mindset on this issue. Without a shift in mindset in Damascus, a healthy, proper democratic integration process cannot develop; it is simply not possible.




The anniversary of the Jin, Jiyan, Azadî Uprisings was recently observed. Crises and problems continue in Iran. No steps have been taken regarding the end of oppression against women, the issue of executions, or towards democratization. What roadmap would you suggest the Kurds here follow?




Iran is in the midst of a major war. Although things have calmed down somewhat, relatively speaking at the moment, this war is in fact still ongoing. Sanctions and attacks against Iran continue in every form. Iran has suffered a serious weakening. And the regime has imposed intense pressure on society. Execution policies have continued to escalate. Massacres have been carried out on a widespread basis. Society has been subjected to attempts of intimidation and suppression. A state of relative silence has thus developed within society. However, this by no means implies that the public’s anger against the regime and the government has subsided or that its demands have disappeared. We believe that both the Iranian regime and the government recognize this reality. There is a great deal of pent-up anger within society. The Jin, Jiyan, Azadî Uprisings were the eruption of this anger.




The entire Iranian society, from the age of 7 to 70 – not just the poor, but the middle class and many sectors of the bureaucracy within the state – took part in this uprising. They voiced their opposition and put forward their demands. Women led the way in these uprisings. A truly magnificent women’s struggle unfolded. The Jin, Jiyan, Azadî Revolution sparked a social revolution in Iran and Rojhilat. It led to very significant social change and transformation. This is irreversible. Sociologically speaking, there is a significant shift taking place in Iranian society – a shift toward democratization. Demands for democracy, freedom, equality, and justice have increased tremendously within society. If Iran turns a blind eye to this, turns a deaf ear to it, it will lose everything. It is facing external intervention, and there is such serious unrest within the country as well.




The current administration and the regime have already lost their legitimacy. It is impossible for a government that does not have the consent of the people to remain in power. Perhaps it can prolong its existence slightly through repression, oppression, executions, intimidation, and suppression. But that is only a brief respite. It cannot sustain itself for long. Legitimacy is a crucial matter. Right now, we are dealing with a regime and a government that have lost their legitimacy. It naturally faces two options. Either it undertakes serious reforms and takes democratic steps. Iran can weather and overcome this process by democratizing and responding to the demands of women and society as a whole, or it will collapse. There is no other path or option before it. The right course is to take democratic steps.




The role of the Kurds is again very important in this regard. From the very beginning, PJAK in particular has followed a sound strategy. It has pursued a policy aimed at and grounded in the democratization of Iran based on local democracy. It has worked and struggled on this basis. This is the correct policy. Recognizing the identity and freedoms of the Kurds and others, acknowledging their rights, and accepting local democracy is what will truly democratize Iran. Throughout history, Iran has always been governed in a federal manner. It has a history consistent with this. Its sociology and historical reality are also quite conducive to democratic governance. It has a wealth of accumulated experience in this regard. However, its province system today lacks substance and is not functional. But it could be revitalized.




A democratic, federal Iran; a Rojhilat based on democratic, self-governing local democracies – if all peoples and faiths living in Iran freely express themselves and organize on this basis, and if Iran becomes democratized on this foundation, it can emerge from this situation. It can also successfully navigate this process. The Kurds’ struggle, as well as the strategies and policies they have developed, serve as an important example. It also serves as a model for other organizations and for other democratic dynamics in Iran and Rojhilat. On this basis, the alliance for democracy in Iran is also valuable. There are many dynamics within Iran as well. There are various circles that support the democratization of Iran. If they come together around this alliance, unite, and demonstrate a common fighting force and will, this movement will play a decisive role in the democratization of Iran.




A campaign has been going on against the continued executions. KJAR has been carrying out this campaign for years. This has now turned into a campaign of the whole PJAK. These executions are truly barbaric practices. Especially in this day and age, it is an execution policy that is simply unacceptable. It is therefore very important to elevate this campaign to the level of a full-scale movement and ensure that everyone takes ownership of this campaign and this movement. It is crucial that all circles, and forces – including those across all four parts of Kurdistan and abroad, as well as those opposed to the death penalty and all forms of undemocratic practices, who defend democracy, freedom, and equality in Iran, and who are fighting for a democratic Iran – join this campaign and this initiative against the death penalty. It is vital that they raise their voices. It is vital that they expand and unite their struggles. We must also wage a very strong struggle against this.




There was a news report the other day. Twenty-eight executions took place in Iran within a single week. This is horrific. There has been a very significant increase, especially over the past year or year and a half. A society cannot be subdued with such execution policies. Any government that fails to see this is blind. This is fueling even more anger. It is fostering even greater resistance. As I’ve said, the Jin, Jiyan, Azadî Uprisings are the result of years, even decades of suppression. It continues even in the current situation. It is necessary to wage a strong struggle against the death penalty. And alongside the organizations in Rojhilat – and in this sense, alongside the initiative they have developed—everyone from all sectors who stands for democracy, freedom, and equality must take their place alongside them and join this struggle.

author: winter oak
title: Never Accidentally Offer Luxury Recycled Cream Cakes to Portuguese Vegan Punks!
content:
This is the fifth and final chapter from the book 

King of the Squatters

 by jaybo which we are delighted to be able to share on Winter Oak. The whole text can be found as a pdf 

here

.










I had enjoyed going for food at the social centre twice weekly. But it became tiresome for me to recognise blatant hierarchies and leaders when their on-line blurb claimed that they were anarchists against leaders, organised along horizontal lines, not vertical, top-down power structures. But my relationship with the social centre was completely destroyed one afternoon, after I had just recycled some expensive, fancy cream cakes.




In front of our house, a fiesta had been happening all weekend, so lots of drunken revellers engulfed our usually quiet home. Our squat had been under siege for the three days, being attacked by young adults who threw stones and came into our building looking for trouble. I had not been sleeping well and was very tired one day as I ate some luxury recycled cream cakes in the city centre. Then the social centre’s leader passed me and stopped to speak. We had only ever seen each other previously at the centre, never in public. I offered yer man a fancy cake, without thinking that they were patently not vegan.




He refused and asked me exactly where our squat was. I innocently told him directions to our home. Then he left to go on a demonstration against workers’ exploitation. That night as I walked home, I was stopped dead in my tracks by fresh graffiti on the bridge just before our squat. In big white letters it simply stated, “vegan limit!!!” I had no doubt that the vegan punk anarchist leader had just sprayed the graffiti as some kind of attempted bullshit intimidation directed at me. Because I had offered to share my hard-earned cakes with him.










I never went back to the social centre after that. I was so angry that I knew if I had returned then I would have certainly made trouble and probably have given the leader an excuse to ban me anyway. I hate egos and authoritarians. However, as always, I tried to turn a negative into a positive. That incident inspired one of my most popular signs for The Whimsical Atrocity Theatre (TWAT): “I only eat vegans”.




The next day, TWAT proudly unveiled its new message to the world. It worked immediately. The show was good. I was a little bit worried that one or more of the social centre vegan punks would pass by, see the sign and beat me up. I was probably safe in my theatre, as I usually had a police escort at one side, looking out for the tourists’ safety. But they knew where I lived.




Some brave souls came and spoke to me during or after my cardboard shenanigans. But things reached dizzying heights for TWAT when an American woman came up to me and asked me how much my signs were. I was absolutely flabbergasted. Someone wanted to buy my recycled carton signs. I replied to her spontaneously that, if she wanted to buy a sign, then she had to tell me how much it was. She put four euros into my hat for “I only eat vegans”. Black permanent marker pen on quality recycled cardboard.










Women were flirting with me almost every day when I performed, but I was caught completely off guard when an extremely attractive, well-dressed young French woman came up to me with her friends, picked up the condoms and said, “OK, let’s go!” She was absolutely serious and in a pathetic response, I replied, “You’re wearing a wedding ring.” She countered with, “It’s only an engagement ring. This is my last chance. Are you coming?” Her friends’ looks assured me that she was absolutely serious. I did not go. One of her friends looked at me as though I must have been insane. One of several potentially delicious sexual opportunities that I missed in life.




As the summer really heated up, it felt as though all of Portugal’s crazy folk were coming out of the woodwork and heading for fun in Lisbon. As I worked one day, a sun-drenched, handsome, young man swaggered up the steps towards me. He wore rags as clothes, had matted, unkempt hair flopping all over his face and had a long stick over his shoulder, with a cloth bundle tied up at the other end. He asked if he could write something on one of my signs. I told him he could, so he picked up “this sign was my bed” and wrote on it, “but I washed it in my jacuzzi first”, which killed me and the audience. Then he shouted for all to hear, “We are homeless because we choose to be.”




Before his departure, he asked me if he could take a condom because he might meet a girl on the way up the steps. Again, his question cracked me up. I said yes, admiring his confidence and forgetting to tell him that they were out of date. As he walked up the steps, I witnessed him stop half-way and start talking to a young woman. Immediately, they were lost in each other’s eyes. He slept in his hammock, which he tied to two trees right in the middle of the busy poetry district of the city, for the following two weeks.










I rarely had sad stories gleaned from TWAT’s daily performances. But when a young girl of six or so years of age saw my few unoriginal signs, “free hugs”, she asked her parent or guardian, a man, “What are hugs?” He responded by extending his arms wide, whilst still standing, towering over her. I was gob-smacked and heartbroken at the same time. They were English speaking. I believe they were English. The only thing I could do was to try to describe the situation in a long sign, which I did. My only sad sign.




It did not take me long before I had created twenty-five signs, saying things like, “the only constant is change”, “smile please you are on holiday, or get a divorce”, “footballers v dung beetles. Who are more talented?”, “there is no authority but yourself” (inspired by the punk band Crass), “clamp the homeless” (inspired by the comedian Chris Morris) and “all this was forest and everything was free” (inspired by Crimethinc).




The wind, which I called my boss, had been an occasional issue in my theatre. A few times, my condoms blew down the busy main street and helpful young children would run after them and gleefully give me back a handful of condoms, sometimes thinking that they were recovering sweets. Their parents were rarely impressed.




After a few weeks, I think some tourists complained about me. I enjoyed incorporating any possible slapstick into my silent theatre. But perhaps making a sign that read “Do not step on signs. Fine ten euros”, and then sliding it underneath the feet of unsuspecting tourists as they walked up the steps past me, was not my greatest idea. I had not endangered anybody, but many average people live in constant fear of everything. People may have complained merely due to the content of some of my signs. Every day, some people looked at me like they might attack me. I had always felt, whilst working the streets, that if people did not look at me like they wanted to kill me, then I was not doing good work.










As the glorious Lisbon summer really heated up and the tourists flooded the city, the police, for whatever reason, finally decided that they had had enough of my carton shenanigans. They closed TWAT’s theatre down. I simply moved around to the back of the elevator shaft. This meant that I lost my main captive audience, the hundred or so people shuffling along slowly. At the back of the lift, my audience was the tail-end of the queue and passing punters. Some would stop to read all of my signs and chat with me. Some bought me new sets of pens with many colours so I could make my signs really colourful.




My takings were drastically reduced in my new theatre, which became more of a gallery on an entirely flat surface. However, the wind was much more of an issue, and sometimes my whole performance would consist of playfully trying, against the wind’s desires, just to get all of my thirty signs standing up at the same time and not blowing away completely.




I was deeply touched when a Portuguese mother and her two daughters, aged about ten and twelve, asked if they could buy two signs, one for each little girl. I told them they had to name their price, and then the girls took ages choosing very carefully which sign they each preferred. The youngest chose “Bob Marley…”, and the older chose “the only constant is change”. I felt flattered. They were obviously very poor, and they were so pleased with their signs. It did not matter how much money they gave me. It never did. Money is not in the same dimension as being rendered speechless by children.










Another day, a young man gently asked me if he could make a sign. I had recently been bought a big set of pens and always had spare cardboard, so replied sure. He went to work, and I left him to it. After some time, I was intrigued as to what he would write. What he wrote touched me deeply and made me belly laugh at the same time. In many colours he had written, “I am the only elevator around here”. I thanked him and used his sign often, propped up against the enormous elevator shaft.




My last story about signs in Portugal happened when a young Swiss woman stepped up to me and asked how much my signs were. I told her that, if she wanted to buy one, then she had to tell me how much it was. For “You are a universe” she paid me twenty euros! The most I ever received for a sign.




In the summer, two young street kids moved into our squat in the room next to me. That meant that I was not the only person on the floor that any intruders could walk straight into. Zwal and his girlfriend had a big dog, which also helped us all feel safer. There were no other dogs in the house. Zwal spoke the most English in the house, and we got on well. The guys were very poor and very generous. They shared the end of their weed with me frequently, always living for the day.










The new guys were punky streetwise squatters, and I had no doubt about their class background. They were survivors, and we enjoyed hanging out together at home and out on the streets. They came to life on the streets, where they turned into a two-person spontaneous circus, winging it all the way. It was when hanging out with Zwal and co that I witnessed my first beggar ‘fishing’ for money.




A man was sitting on a busy city-centre street, with a woven basket hanging off the end of his wooden walking stick. He was extending it out into the passing shoppers and calling them all angel, whilst asking for money in strong Mancunian accent. Under his bright blond, floppy hair, he had piercing blue eyes, and in his own way he had angelic qualities. His energy really caught my attention, and when he heard me speak to Zwal he shouted with delight “Scouser! Can you help me open these bottles of wine? I’ve been trying for three days!” I knew that he was serious. Steve really had been trying to open three bottles of wine for three long days.




He told me that he had been invited to a wedding in the countryside, outside Lisbon, that had happened five days previously. He had gotten utterly wasted at the wedding, which had lasted for two days, and then he had spent three days trying to get back to Lisbon. Three days to cover not such a large distance had not bothered Steve at all. But three days of not being able to open any of his wine had left him absolutely desperate.










I wanted to help him and felt sure that I could, then a waiter from a nearby restaurant stepped outside to smoke a cigarette. “Get him to do it for me! Please, scouse!” Steve begged. I got the waiter to open all three bottles of wine, and Steve and I started drinking together on the street close to the train station. We would not stop for the next two weeks.




Sintra is only thirty minutes’ train ride from central Lisbon. I had heard that it was a stunningly beautiful place and that there were permaculture projects located there. We got enough money for two train tickets, and Steve took me off to show me where he lived. I was drunk by the time we arrived in Sintra, and it was dark. Steve took me straight to the best bar in town, where we met his wild crew, Dougie and his young Portuguese girlfriend named Marney. Dougie was a crazy Glaswegian alcoholic, and Marney was very sweet. I wondered how she had ended up with two middle-aged chaos merchants. I never found out, but she obviously loved Dougie and was very patient with him. We all got on like a house on fire.




After a few beers in the sleazy little bar, we all stumbled back to their farm. Situated on the outskirts of the small town of Sintra, there was an abandoned-looking, old farmhouse with extremely overgrown land surrounding it. I could not appreciate its full beauty in the dark. The guys took me inside, lit a big open fire and cooked us all food.




Next morning in glorious sunlight, I saw the derelict paradise that my new pals called home. The buildings and land were spectacular. Some of the trees looked old enough to have had dinosaurs urinate on them. There were the biggest palm trees that I had ever had the good fortune to witness and laze under. When I asked the guys how they came to live, there they smiled cunningly.










Dougie explained the situation. The owner was in jail a long way away, for shooting a guy in the neck. He told me that he was a nice guy as long as you did not get on the wrong side of him. The owner, in his wisdom, had recognised that Dougie, Steve and Marney were the wildest folk in Sintra, and he had offered the property to them to look after in the knowledge that nobody else would be mad enough to go there, whilst they occupied the place. They explained that the only crucial condition had been not to dig anywhere in the surrounding grounds. Then they said I could stay for as long as I wanted. Much as I loved gardening, I was not going to risk being shot in the neck. But it was hard not to wonder just what was buried there. Treasure, or bodies?




I came to love all of those guys and recognised that Steve struggled a bit with schizophrenia and that Dougie also seemed to have it in a milder form. Like some of my other schizophrenic friends, they had no interest in the medication on offer from the men in white. They self-medicated with heavy alcohol consumption instead. Every day that they survived was another little victory.




Dougie told me a little about his childhood on some of Glasgow’s meanest streets. He had been surrounded by heroin from a young age and had started using the gear early. He described how, by seventeen years of age, he and his pals had used to shoot up in stereo. That meant using a needle in each arm at the same time.










We ate breakfast in the farm, drank some wine and headed out onto the streets of touristic Sintra, to earn more money and buy more cheap wine. I explored Sintra’s beautiful mountain and forest, and the guys showed me their favourite places to drink, smoke and ‘work’. We were rarely troubled by the police or anyone else. Sleepy little Sintra had its own lawless wild bunch. Completely out of control, but ultimately darlings of the streets. In our own individual crazy ways, we loved the street life; Dougie and Steve played guitar, whilst Marney and I made percussion, and she sometimes sang. We met some interesting folk who were brave enough to speak to us, and life was good. Nothing else mattered.




One day as we played on the High Street, we found ourselves faced by a large group of Korean tourists, maybe thirty-plus in total. They stared at us from across the street, looking absolutely amazed. Appearing more like bland conformists than rebels in their average tourist clothing, we all sensed immediately that they loved us.




One of them crossed the High Street to speak with us. He asked if it would be OK for them to take photos of us all doing our thing. We agreed no problem. They smiled huge smiles in return and took some pictures. Then the original guy asked if he could get a picture with me, to which I agreed. We put our arms around each other’s shoulders, and he seemed immensely proud to get that photograph. I imagined that they were all rebels at heart, and they respected our absolute rejection of all authority and norms. And they loved us for it.
















Dougie could play guitar and sing really well when he wanted to. As we sat inebriated on our favourite High Street pitch one afternoon, with the street bustling with tourists and locals, he launched into my favourite song by John Lennon, ‘Working Class Hero’. Dougie played and sang the spine-tingling song better than anyone else I had ever heard try. It is a song that takes no prisoners, and when Dougie gave his heart and soul to his performance it seemed perfect. The perfect song in the perfect moment. Sintra froze in time. The hairs all over my body stood on end. It felt as though the whole of Sintra knew what was being sung, and why. My heart nearly burst out of my chest.




Steve was an avid recycler, unable to pass a bin without exploring inside. He did not walk very easily, after an incident that had resulted in him having his leg run over by a small truck. On purpose. He had upset some local wanna-be gangstas and, as a result, they had driven over his leg! Anyway, he was a very quirky character, always dressing up in unusual clothes that he had recycled. Although he had the energy of an angel, which turned out to be how he addressed everybody that he spoke to, he could certainly become difficult after too much alcohol. So, he did not live at the farm full-time after many fights with Dougie, but actually had his own secret hideaway.




One night after I had earned his complete trust, he took me to his home in the woods. In an over-grown field on the edge of town, he had set up camp, with the owner’s reluctant agreement. He had been told that he was the only person allowed to live there, and he took a risk taking me to stay for a while. He had made a nice bedroom, with a lovely open but covered kitchen area. I only stayed one night in the end, because I would have been gutted had my presence brought him any difficulties with the land-owner.




Sintra had a nice little cafe where they actually gave free food to the homeless and destitute on a daily basis. I had never heard of such generosity before and was eager to go. One afternoon, I went and found all the staff to be punky-looking, with many tattoos and piercings. I could not believe my luck. I was alone the first time, and I enjoyed the soup and coffee.




The next time I went, I was treated like shit. I was with my crazy gang, and it was obvious that they were not welcome at the café, which was mostly filled with tourists. Every time I went subsequently, I purposefully went alone. But it was too late. I was associated with the wild bunch, and it felt like some of the staff hated us. After terrorising the town for a while, I felt like the cafe could possibly lose all its custom and close, just because our gang lived in Sintra in our own ungovernable way.










Two weeks flew by, and then the shit hit the fan. We were doing our thing on the streets when four American women stopped and asked us where they could buy some marijuana. Dougie told them that he could sell them some, and at that moment a Portuguese guy stopped, after hearing the girls’ request. As Dougie went into his backpack for herbs, the Portuguese guy tried to muscle in and sell his weed to the Americans. Within seconds, the Portuguese guy was waving a knife at Dougie, and Dougie was shouting that he was getting his knife out from his bag.




The girls decided that there were safer ways of buying weed and ran away screaming. We heard distant police sirens, and the guy with the knife also ran away. Another Portuguese guy who had witnessed the incident came over to inform us that the guy with the knife had only just been released from prison after a long time inside, for killing a cop. We decided it was time to leave the high street for the day. I decided it was time to leave Sintra for good.




It was so hard saying goodbye to my dysfunctional Sintra family. I felt for Marney, so much. Dougie could be difficult for her at times, but she could not leave him. And Steve really was an angel. Just before I left, we met some people fresh from the Rainbow Gathering. Steve took us all to a lovely garden to smoke a few spliffs. Within minutes, the rainbow people were discussing how Steve and I were actually angels, but they informed us, in their wisdom, we were dark angels. Steve and I could live with that.










I left Sintra absolutely penniless and had to beg for three euros outside the train station to pay for the ticket fare home. When I got back to the Lisbon squat, all was as before. The last three weeks in our squat were strange because our building was on its count-down to a grossly premature ending. One Monday morning at eleven am, several contractors broke the front door lock, which none of us had a key to, and entered the building with the police. The police were actually OK, but the contractors looked scared, yet ready to kill us if necessary.




We were told to leave, so we gathered our belongings and left through the front door. The contractors put a new lock on the door that was never used and left with the police. We all stored our few belongings in the bushes in the park at the back of the house, near to our drawbridge entrance, which had been left intact. In their wisdom, the authorities had left our entrance way just as normal, so we could still get in and out without any problem.




Sometimes, differences between countries, not necessarily far apart, can be glaringly obvious. If the eviction I just described in Portugal had have happened in England. the contractors and police would have been racing each other to destroy our means of entry into the building. They would have, at the very least, thrown our drawbridge down, out of reach. More likely, they would have taken it away and sealed the open doorway into the squat. In Portugal, one policeman seemed very concerned that I had forgotten a pair of shoes. It took a while to explain to him that I had not forgotten them, but that they were in fact broken.




Every night for the following week, seven of us got our stuff out of the bushes in the park and re-entered the squat, to sleep inside. Each morning, we put all of our belongings back into the bushes in the park. Then, exactly one week later, again at eleven am on Monday, police and contractors entered the building through the front door, using their new key. The second time we were evicted, the police were a little aggressive, and the contractors looked scared of us.










Exactly the same thing happened on our next eviction. It seemed like an exercise in futility, but the contractors put another new lock on the unused front door and left our rear entrance untouched. My first Portuguese eviction became surreal on week two. Would you believe that the same thing happened again the following week? It did.




But when our eviction had stretched to three long weeks, something more sinister happened. Two huge demolition vehicles appeared and were parked at either side of our beautiful old home. Then, we really felt threatened. Most of the residents moved out, to sleep in the park. It was summer and warm enough. But Roni and I decided that we would stay until the bitter end.




Perhaps stupidly, Roni and I slept in the building for another two nights. It certainly went through my mind that I was in Portugal and not England, and that I might have woken up being buried alive in rubble, and no one would have ever known how or where I had died. But Roni and I lived to tell the tale, after sleeping in the squat on those Monday and Tuesday nights.




On the Wednesday, I was relaxing in central Lisbon’s main park after work, when I sensed that someone was very close to me. I sat up and opened my eyes, to see a beautiful, young woman sat on her blanket, which was almost on my feet. She patted the blanket next to her, motioning me to join her, so I did. Her energy was extremely magnetic.










In her slow, sultry, Spanish accent, she told me that her name was Carmen. I found her very attractive, and she was fascinated by my alternative beliefs and lifestyle. We chatted easily, for hours. She was into photography and took photos of my signs. As I had never taken a single photo of one squat that I had lived in, I asked Carmen if she would be interested in taking any shots of the house. She was, so we agreed to meet that evening, after she finished work.




Upon arrival at our squat, as the sun was slowly setting in the background, we were greeted by a pile of rubble that was in excess of two stories high! Carmen almost burst into tears. Although I had fully explained our predicament to her, I guess neither of us were really prepared for what we saw. I did my best to reassure her that at least our three weeks in limbo were over and we then knew where we all stood. Homeless.




That did not do much to reassure her, and then the alcoholic couple from the house appeared, very drunk. They burst into tears, and I really struggled not to cry, for a magnificent, old building in perfectly fine structural and cosmetic order had been prematurely destroyed. We had had some of the best views in Lisbon, from the edge of the city out to the green mountains beyond. The area was being gentrified. It was far too valuable to allow poor people to live there, rent free.










The mountain of rubble that had been home to seven desperate people stood to the ceiling height of the second floor. By a bizarre twist of demolition fate, my double glass doors were stood exactly in their usual position. The only thing in the entire building that had not moved. The rubble backed up behind the doors had supported them perfectly in place, leaving them looking like they still worked.




I joked with Carmen, saying that we could have opened my doors and all of the rubble would have just poured out, comedy style. She could not laugh, but we got photos of my doors and what was our house. Attempting to lighten the mood, we crossed the street to a field full of sunflowers, which were in full bloom. We frolicked in the field and got some nice pictures.




I enjoyed hanging out with Carmen whenever possible. She was splitting up with her boyfriend, and I felt as though I was falling in love, when I received some devastating news from Liverpool. One of my dearest friends, lovingly known as Stanarchist, had passed away. I knew I had to go to his funeral, and, after sleeping rough in the park, Carmen kindly let me spend my last night in Lisbon at her place.




After cooking us some good food, we drank some wine, and I found it difficult to keep my hands off her. The next morning, I needed to leave early for one last TWAT performance. I had to earn the money for the bus fare to the airport. Under pressure, I made twice what I needed in the time that I had, bought some nice hashish, smoked a phat last spliff and rode the bus to the airport.










Stan had reached the ripe old age of eighty-six. He had told me many stories of his war-time experiences as a child. Most importantly, Stan had been a vocal anarchist for decades and was an anti-hero celebrity on Liverpool’s underground. He was also the longest-running BBC Radio Merseyside DJ, who had created and broadcast his show ‘Folk Scene’ for more than forty years. I had hoped that he would outlive me and had agonising anxieties about not being there for him at the end. But, he knew, as well as I did, that Liverpool had been killing me, and my international life had been a life-saver for me.




The previous funeral that I had not attended, my dad’s, had gone horribly wrong, even though I was not there. I had no suspicions that anything could go wrong at the funeral of Stanarchist. How wrong I was. Flying into Liverpool had never excited me, but I would see everyone I knew at the funeral of the much-loved man. Or so I thought.




A mutual friend Anna, in Liverpool, had been communicating with me about the ceremony. Anna and I had been Stan’s closest friends, over many years. I was the only person who had ever been in Stan’s home, to my knowledge. And I know I had the only spare key to Stan’s house, where I slept occasionally. I wanted to recycle his many years’ worth of hoarded stuff and clean up, but he would never let me and got angry at such suggestions. Three of the large rooms in his big house were completely unusable, crammed to the ceilings full of things.




For some reason there was a delay before the funeral. I sent several messages requesting the actual details for the ceremony. Stan had previously said to me, “If they ever try and put me in a nursing home, I will get a gun!” He had also told me that he wanted nothing to do with the church when he died. He said that he just wanted to fall into the vegetation in Otterspool woods, before transcending to nature. He had also told me that he wanted his house to go to the two people that he loved. Anna and me. Not his sister or nephew, who he said did not need it. He had, on the rare occasions that he mentioned his two relatives, told me that you choose your friends not your relatives. They were straight, conformists, and he did not like them. Sadly, none of his wishes were kept.










I kept waiting for responses to my requests for details, but to my astonishment none came. Not wanting to push such sensitive matters, I waited, and waited, and waited. I heard of other ceremonies that had been planned for the Sunday and during the week. The funeral was on Saturday, but on Saturday morning I still had no idea where the venue was to be. Saturday came and went. I was terribly upset.




I messaged Anna early on Sunday, and she finally replied. Her message dumbfounded me. She informed me that the funeral had been a small private affair arranged by Stan’s nephew, held in a church outside the city. Crushingly, she informed me that only Stan’s friends who had been in the city before he had died were invited. I was not invited to my dear friend’s funeral, because I had been out of the country when he died.




On the Sunday, I went to the celebration of Stan’s life that was held in his beloved Palm House in Sefton Park. I cannot describe how difficult it was for me to face Anna, and Stan’s nephew. It took all of my strength not to crack in the circumstances. For Stan had made a special trip to visit me when I lived in Wales, twelve hours of public transport, to tell me something that he said he had never told anybody, but he had to tell me. Which he did. A secret that had chewed away at him inside for over sixty years. Then he told me he wanted to give his house to me and Anna, with no fuss.




I had never told Anna that information. I never wanted to think of Stan dying and actually thought that I would die before him. And the opportunity had never arisen. I thought that he would probably have made a will, but certainly would never have asked. That was early September 2012. By that December, he told me that he was beginning to get dementia.




At the Sunday ceremony, when I met Stan’s nephew, introduced by Anna, she said something that was entirely unexpected. She steamed right in and told the nephew that Stan had paid for my book to be published. Several years before, I had written a small book called 

Man Cry

, which Stan loved, and he had offered to contribute towards the printing cost. He gave me three hundred pounds, because he wanted my book to be ‘out there’. Immediately, I realised that the sentence was all Stan’s nephew needed to hear. I became absolutely irrelevant at the moment Anna spoke. They all just walked away from me. Anna and I both lost half a house, perhaps one hundred thousand pounds’ worth, each!




I had to focus on being positive and strong, knowing that Stan would want me to laugh in the face of other people’s bullshit. Luckily, I had a plan for TWAT to play the Edinburgh Fringe Festival. And my life-time mission was unbreakable. As long as there was a world to change, I had a lot of work to try to do, in my own little way.







Previously:




Discovering Anarchism




Reclaim the Streets




The Love Activists




Anti-Fascist Always




Jaybo is currently living in a cave in southern Spain. If you would like to contact him, please write to winteroak@greenmail.net and we will forward your email to him.

title: Affaire du 8/12 : justice d'exception, procès d'intention [radio]
content:
Les Amis d'Orwell / 

RL

 89.4. Émission du 18 septembre 2026 - Discussion après le verdict de la cour d'appel de Paris dans l'affaire du 8 décembre.




La justice antiterroriste s'est encore illustrée le 10 septembre, lorsque la Cour d'appel de Paris a rendu son délibéré dans le procès d'appel de mai 2026 qui jugeait 6 personnes dans l'affaire dite du 8 décembre, c'était en 2020. Le principal enseignement de cette affaire, c'est que deux tribunaux ont donc condamné des personnes pour «

 

association de malfaiteurs à caractère terroriste

 

», sans qu'aucun début de projet n'ait été démontré, sans but ni cible, confirmant le caractère uniquement «

 

intentionnel

 

» des instructions pour «

 

terrorisme

 

». L'état actuel du droit français se sert de l'antiterro pour instruire des procès politiques.




L'émission 

Les Amis d'Orwell

 revient sur ce théâtre judiciaire dans son émission du 18 septembre

. Deux invités pour en parler : 

Svink

, l'un des 7 prévenus de cette affaire, qui était à l'époque artificier de métier (ce qui donnera aux enquêteurs la conviction d'être tombé sur une cellule clandestine préparant des attentats à l'explosif...). Et 

Max

, l'un de leurs soutiens, qui a assisté à quasi toutes les audiences de ce procès en 2 actes. Nous aurons également l'occasion d'entendre 

Bastien

, un autre inculpé, qui s'est exprimé dans l'émission Tapage de Canal Sud a Toulouse, animée par l'équipe de la Sellette (émission de novembre 2025).




 

 

 

 

Les Amis d'Orwell (Radio Libertaire) / Verdict procès des inculpés du 8/12

 

 

 

 

 

 

 




 




musiques : titres «

 

Black Bloc Terroriste

 

» et «

 

Des flics porcs assassins

 

» du groupe Pekatralatak, tiré de l'album «

 

Djiad de Classe

 

» (2008) - 

toute leur disco sur Pirate-punk

title: Trump’ın İran açıklamasının ardından petrol fiyatları yükseldi: Brent yeniden 103 doların üzerine çıktı
content:
Petrol fiyatları, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump’ın İran’a yönelik yaptırımların hafifletilebileceğine ilişkin haberi yalanlamasının ardından yükseldi. Brent petrol yüzde 1,11 artışla 103,73 dolara, ABD ham petrolü (WTI) ise yüzde 0,38 artışla 89,72 dolara çıktı.

Bloomberg HT’nin derlediği habere göre petrol fiyatları, Ortadoğu’dan arzın toparlanmasının etkisiyle önceki seansta gerilerken, Trump’ın İran açıklaması ve Katar’ın ABD ile İran arasında yürüttüğü diplomatik temaslar piyasaların odağında yer aldı.

Brent petrolün eylül ayını yaklaşık yüzde 14 yükselişle tamamlaması bekleniyor. Bu, temmuzdan bu yana en güçlü aylık artış olacak. WTI ise mayıstan bu yana ilk kez 106 doların üzerine çıkmasının ardından aylık bazda yaklaşık yüzde 4 artışa yöneldi. İki petrol türü arasındaki fiyat farkı da eylül ayında son dört ayın en yüksek seviyesine ulaştı.

Piyasalarda ABD’nin dizel ihracatına yönelik atabileceği adımlar da izleniyor. İhracatın kısıtlanmasının ABD iç piyasasında arz fazlasına yol açabileceği ve rafinerilerin ham petrol işleme miktarını azaltabileceği değerlendiriliyor.

Trump yönetiminin, kasım ayında yapılacak ara seçimler öncesinde akaryakıt fiyatlarını düşürmek amacıyla dizel ihracatını yasaklamak yerine kırmızı renkli dizelin satışına izin verilmesini değerlendirdiği belirtiliyor.

MST Marquee Enerji Araştırmaları Başkanı Saul Kavonic, Hürmüz Boğazı’ndan petrol akışının toparlandığına ilişkin işaretler, ABD’nin dizel ihracatına yönelik olası kısıtlamalarına alternatif arayışları ve İran kaynaklı yeni bir gerilimin yaşanmamasının fiyatlar üzerinde etkili olduğunu söyledi.

Kavonic, piyasalardaki durumun halen oynak olduğunu, petrol lojistiğinin ise pahalı ve kısıtlı kalmaya devam ettiğini belirtti.

Katar, İran ile ABD arasındaki temaslarda ilerleme sağlanmasını umduğunu açıkladı. Katar Dışişleri Bakanlığı Sözcüsü Majed al-Ansari, taraflar arasında mesaj taşıdıklarını belirterek, çatışmanın sonuçlarından bölgeyi koruyacak bir anlaşma için ortak zemin oluşturmaya çalıştıklarını söyledi.

Trump ise ABD’li yetkililere dayandırılan ve İran’ın nükleer programına ilişkin adımlar atması karşılığında yaptırımların hafifletilmesi ile dondurulmuş İran fonlarının serbest bırakılmasının gündemde olduğunu öne süren haberi yalanladı.

Trump, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada, “Bu doğru değil. Onlara hiçbir şey teklif etmedim” dedi.

Suudi Arabistan, Doğu-Batı Boru Hattı’ndaki faaliyetlerin yeniden başlamasının ardından Kızıldeniz kıyısındaki Yanbu Limanı’ndan tankerlere petrol yüklemeye yeniden başladı.

Ortadoğu’daki üreticilerin ham petrol ihracatı eylülde günlük 16 milyon 328 bin varile yükseldi. Bu miktar, ABD ve İsrail’in İran’la savaşının şubat sonunda başlamasından bu yana kaydedilen en yüksek seviye oldu.

ABD’de ise 25 Eylül’de sona eren haftada ham petrol stoklarının 1,02 milyon varil arttığı bildirildi. Benzin stokları da yükselirken distilat stokları geriledi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Balmain meeting calls for public housing in Bays West, opposes Labor’s plan
content:
Bays West includes public land at Glebe Island, White Bay and parts of Rozelle and Lilyfield. Labor’ wants to hand this to developers to build high-rise apartments; it proposes only 10% be reserved for “affordable” or “essential worker” housing.

The 150-strong meeting was organised by the Better Future Coalition (BFC), comprising resident groups which oppose NSW Labor and the Labor-dominated Inner West Council’s (IWC) pro-developer planning schemes.

Many community and housing groups supported the meeting including Leichhardt Matters, Save Dully, Action for Public Housing, Save Marrickville, Hands off Glebe, Friends of Erskineville, Doing Density Better, Mosman Matters and others.

Judy Mundey, a long-time activist and barrister set the framework for discussion by outlining the historic decline in public housing across NSW and the consequent rise in homelessness, housing insecurity and expensive rents and house prices.

“It’s not as if the government is not aware we have a housing crisis; there is no shortage of announcements and promises … but almost all proposals involve the private sector.”

Mundey said there are “almost daily” reports on dodgy developers, to whom Minns is handing over public land.

“If we’re going to address the housing crisis, we need less privatisation of public land and more well designed public housing,” Mundey said.

“In opposition, Labor said any surplus land would be subject to a mandatory requirement for 30% of social, affordable and universal housing. But now in government, at Bays West, it has reduced that to 10% for affordable and essential worker housing.

“There is no commitment for public housing to be any part of the plan. This is a failure to utilise public assets to address the social injustice inflicted on so many, a failure to ensure a decent, safe, secure home, essential for health and wellbeing.”

Architect and urban designer Eddie Ma gave details about what is known about the Bays West plan. He said Minns had commissioned international architecture firms to make proposals.

Ma emphasised that the plans could be changed — for better or for worse. “It should be the community that decides what we do with Bays West, not the government and certainly not architects.”

Former independent Inner West councillor John Stamolis said that the inner west was one of the country’s highest density areas and that it was ridiculous for Labor to accuse people who want better planning of opposing any development. He said there needed to be more public housing now because of the security it brings.

Greens MP for Balmain Kobi Shetty said it was hard to know a lot about Labor’s plan as it has been vague. She said the Greens welcome Labor’s commitment to delivering the Glebe Island Bridge as an essential walking and cycling link.

Ben Radford, a town planner and Green Left journalist, MCed the meeting, which voted overwhelmingly to adopt a resolution opposing Labor’s plan, calling for community consultation and to add a sixth point calling for any housing at Bays West to be public.

BFC had invited Philippa Scott, Labor’s candidate for Balmain and deputy mayor of IWC, to come and listen to the concerns. She did not reply.

[Isaac Nellist is a member of the Better Future Coalition and is the Socialist Alliance candidate for Balmain in the NSW elections.]

author: Unknown
title: Suudi Arabistan’dan Türkiye ile vize muafiyeti anlaşmasına onay
content:
Fotoğraf: Kit (formerly ConvertKit)/Unsplash

Suudi Arabistan, Türkiye ile diplomatik ve hususi pasaport sahiplerinin karşılıklı olarak vizeden muaf tutulmasını öngören anlaşmayı onayladı.

Suudi Arabistan resmi haber ajansı SPA’nın aktardığına göre, Bakanlar Kurulu başkent Riyad’da Veliaht Prens Muhammed bin Selman başkanlığında toplandı.

Toplantıda, Türkiye ile Suudi Arabistan arasında diplomatik ve hususi pasaport sahiplerine yönelik vize muafiyeti anlaşmasına onay verildi.

İki ülke, 6 Mayıs 2026’da Ankara’da düzenlenen Türkiye-Suudi Arabistan Koordinasyon Konseyi toplantısının ardından söz konusu anlaşmayı imzalamıştı.

Anlaşmanın Türkiye tarafından onaylanmasına ilişkin Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı da daha önce Resmi Gazete’de yayımlanmıştı.

Karara göre diplomatik ve hususi pasaport sahipleri, her 180 günlük süre içinde 90 günü aşmamak kaydıyla diğer ülkeye giriş, çıkış, transit geçiş ve geçici kalışlarda vizeden muaf olacak.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: MGK bugün toplanıyor: Masada hangi başlıklar var?
content:
MGK Erdoğan başkanlığında toplandı

Milli Güvenlik Kurulu (MGK), Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan başkanlığında bugün Beştepe’de toplanacak. Toplantının gündeminde çözüm süreci kapsamında PKK’nin silah bırakmasına ilişkin gelişmeler ile bölgesel gelişmelerin yer alması bekleniyor.

Kamuoyunda “çerçeve yasa” olarak anılan Milli Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmenin Güçlendirilmesine Dair Kanun, 10 Ağustos’ta TBMM’de kabul edilmesinin ardından 18 Ağustos’ta Resmî Gazete’de yayımlandı.

Kanuna göre PKK/KCK ve bağlantılı yapıların fiili varlığına son verdiğinin ve kontrolündeki silah ve mühimmatı teslim ettiğinin güvenlik kurumlarınca tespit edilmesi gerekiyor. Bu tespitin MGK kararıyla teyit edilmesi ve kararın Resmî Gazete’de yayımlanmasının ardından kanunda öngörülen soruşturma, kovuşturma ve infaz ertelemelerine ilişkin mekanizmalar işletilecek.

MGK toplantısında bu kapsamda sahadan gelen bilgilerin değerlendirilmesi bekleniyor. Kurulun alacağı karar, kanunda öngörülen sürecin işletilmesi açısından önem taşıyor.

Toplantıda Sincar başta olmak üzere PKK’nin çekildiği belirtilen bölgelerdeki durumun yanı sıra Irak Merkezi Hükümeti ve Irak Kürt Bölgesel Yönetimi (IKBY) ile yürütülen temasların da ele alınması bekleniyor.

MGK’nin diğer gündem başlıkları arasında Rusya-Ukrayna savaşı ve Karadeniz’de seyir güvenliği ile ABD-İran hattındaki gelişmelerin yer alacağı belirtiliyor. Yemen’deki gelişmeler ile Babülmendep Boğazı’nda deniz ticareti ve seyir güvenliğinin de toplantıda değerlendirilmesi bekleniyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 30 septembre
content:
Dans l'éphéméride des luttes du 30 septembre, la belle ville de Naples nous met sur une voie intéressante pour penser l'avenir, et peut-être bien le présent : l'insurrection populaire, antifasciste et radicale.




1943 :

 Fin des quatre journées de Naples : l'occupant nazi est définitivement chassé de la ville par la population napolitaine après quatre jours d'insurrection.




 

 

 

 




1964 :

 En Colombie, création des FARC, qui existent toujours aujourd'hui et ont récemment annoncé le cessez-le-feu définitif.




1970 :

 A Puerto Rico, des manifestant-e-s brûlent plus de 1400 formulaires de conscription au service militaire.




1971 :

 En Irlande du Nord, deux membres de l'IRA 'Officielle' (OIRA) meurent dans l'explosion prématurée d'explosifs qu'ils confectionnaient.




1977 :

 - Arrestation à Paris de Klaus Croissant, ancien avocat des membres de la Fraction Armée Rouge allemande.




 A Rome, le militant de Lotta Continua Walter Rossi est assassiné par des fascistes, sous les yeux de la police : un groupe d'une quinzaine de fascistes avance dissimulé derrière un fourgon de police vers un groupe de jeunes d'extrême-gauche et commencent à tirer en arrivant à leur hauteur, touchant Rossi à la nuque. Le fourgon de police tourne à l'angle et part sans intervenir. Une manifestation sera ensuite organisée contre la présence des fascistes dans le quartier et leur protection par la police, qui sera réprimée par cette même police, tandis qu'un bar de fascistes est attaqué, un autre brûlé, et que des voitures personnelles de militants d'extrême-droite sont incendiés. Un début d'incendie se déclare également devant le local du MSI, le parti fasciste d'où étaient venus les tueurs.


 

 

 

 




 

 

 

 




1981 :

 A Carmaux, le groupe libertaire '

Les Artilleurs du Grand Soir

' fait sauter la statue de Jean Jaurès en soutien à la grève de la faim de prisonniers.







1999 :

 Au Japon, accident nucléaire dans l'usine de traitement d'uranium de Tokaimura.




2009 :

 En Suisse, près de Zurich, un groupe signant 'Azione Rivoluzionaria' incendie un véhicule de luxe en soutien au prisonnier anarchiste Marco Camenisch.




2014 :

 A Mexico, plusieurs véhicules du corps de sécurité de l'université sont incendiés pour leur rôle dans la surveillance qu'ils exercent pour le système judiciaire et en solidarité avec les prisonniers anarchistes.




2017 :

 A Göteborg en Suède, de violents affrontements ont lieu quand une contre-manifestation antifasciste s'est opposée à des néonazis qui tentaient d'organiser une manifestation dans la ville, ces derniers étant protégés par la police.




 Au Kurdistan Turc, près du village de Ziyaret (région de Lice et Diyarbakir), un sergent et un sergent-chef de l'armée turque sont enlevés après avoir été arrêtés à un barrage du PKK.

 A Assemini en Sardaigne, une grue d'une entreprise qui collabore activement aux chantiers de l'armée sur l'île 

est incendiée

.




Voir 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 30 septembre.

author: Unknown
title: Gülistan Doku’nun aile avukatından Sonel ailesine 5 soru: İki büyük bavulda ne taşındı?
content:
Gülistan Doku soruşturması kapsamında tutuklanan eski Tunceli Valisi Tuncay Sonel’in 2024 yılında yaptığı Japonya tatiline ilişkin dosyaya yeni bir ifade girdi. Tutuklu Albay Ali Kahraman’ın evli olduğu Burçin Kahraman, tatil ve alışveriş masraflarının Ordulu bir iş insanı tarafından karşılandığını öne sürdü. Doku ailesinin avukatı Ali Çimen ise Sonel ve kızına yanıtlamaları istemiyle 5 soru yöneltti.

Tunceli’de 5 Ocak 2020’de kaybolan Gülistan Doku’ya ilişkin yürütülen soruşturmada, tutuklu eski Tunceli Valisi Tuncay Sonel ile tutuklu Jandarma Komutanı Albay Ali Kahraman hakkında yeni bir ifade dosyaya girdi.

Erzurum Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığında ifade veren Ali Kahraman’ın evli olduğu Burçin Kahraman, 2024 yılında Tuncay Sonel ve kızıyla birlikte gerçekleştirdikleri Japonya gezisine ilişkin iddialarda bulundu.

Sabah’ın haberine göre Kahraman, kızıyla planladıkları seyahat sırasında Tuncay Sonel ve kızının da Japonya’ya geldiğini söyledi. Kahraman, Sonel ve kızını burada Ordulu bir iş insanının karşıladığını öne sürdü.

Kahraman, tatilin son gününde Tuncay Sonel ve kızının iki büyük bavul satın aldığını, bu alışverişin yanı sıra konaklama giderlerinin de söz konusu iş insanı tarafından karşılandığına tanık olduğunu iddia etti. Kahraman, yaşananların ardından Sonel ailesiyle arasına mesafe koyduğunu belirtti.

İfadenin ortaya çıkmasının ardından Doku ailesinin avukatı Ali Çimen, iddialara ilişkin tutuklu Tuncay Sonel ve kızı Hanzade Sonel’in yanıtlaması istemiyle şu 5 soruyu kamuoyuyla paylaştı:

Tatil masraflarını karşıladığı öne sürülen Ordulu iş insanı kimdir?

İki büyük bavulun içerisinde ne bulunmaktaydı ve ne taşınmak üzere Sonel ailesine verildi?

Tuncay Sonel’e ait Adana’daki Sonel İş Merkezi’nin 2022-2024 yılları arasındaki yapımını üstlenen müteahhit firma ile tatil masraflarını karşıladığı iddia edilen kişi aynı iş insanı mıdır?

Sonel İş Merkezi’nin yapım işi neden Ordulu bir iş insanına verilmiştir?

Tuncay Sonel’in o dönem Ordu Valisi olması ile projede yer alan iş insanlarının Ordulu olması arasında nasıl bir bağ bulunmaktadır?

Soruşturma kapsamında incelemeler sürüyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Elecciones Brasil 2026, una batalla contra el imperialismo
content:
Las amplias elecciones que el próximo 4 de octubre tendrán lugar en Brasil, en las que se elegirán presidente, gobernadores y legisladores, son de importancia estratégica para nuestra Abya Yala y para todo el globo terráqueo. Brasil es el 5to país más extenso, está entre las 10 economías más grandes y demográficamente ocupa el séptimo lugar en el mundo.




Por otra parte, el Brasil de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, del Partido de los Trabajadores (PT), forma parte de los BRICS, quienes vienen abogando por un orden mundial más justo y equilibrado; su principal socio comercial es China, con una tendencia al crecimiento en su intercambio comercial; ha hecho fuertes críticas al ente sionista que, con la ayuda de los EE. UU., está ejecutando un genocidio contra el pueblo palestino. Todo lo anterior lo convierte en el principal objetivo del presidente Trump en el hemisferio. Ya le ha impuesto a las importaciones de EE. UU. desde Brasil, entre el 12.5 % y el 50 % de aranceles, lo que ha hecho descender las exportaciones brasileñas hacia los EE. UU. a sus niveles más bajos desde 1997, lo que ha afectado negativamente su economía, expresado esto, en el bajo crecimiento de su PIB durante 2026.




Trump y su secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, se han estado pronunciando a favor de la candidatura de Flavio Bolsonaro y criticado ferozmente el juicio que se le siguió a Jair Bolsonaro, por el intento del golpe de Estado, llegando al extremo de tomar medidas coercitivas unilaterales contra el juez que llevó la causa.




La intromisión de los EE. UU. en los asuntos internos de otros países es bien conocida. En Nuestra América han derrocado decenas de gobiernos e instalado dictaduras militares, han desestabilizado gobiernos legítimos, han bloqueado e impuesto medidas ilegales e inhumanas contra pueblos enteros y han llegado a violar la soberanía de varios países con agresiones militares directas: México, Cuba, Haití, Nicaragua, República Dominicana, Panamá, Granada y Venezuela son ejemplo de ello. Han manipulado elecciones abiertamente, teniendo los últimos 18 meses los ejemplos de Honduras, Ecuador, Colombia y Perú, donde, de manera grotesca y descarada, han impulsado candidatos, amenazado a la población con bloquear el envío de remesas, amedrentado a los gobiernos y empresarios con elevar aranceles y han utilizado sus mecanismos de manipulación y desinformación contra amplios sectores de la población, utilizando técnicas como la Big Data, los algoritmos de las redes sociales y buscadores y la última tendencia que es el uso de la inteligencia artificial como una más de estas nefastas herramientas.




La injerencia de EE. UU. en los asuntos internos de decenas de países, ha quedado registrado en diversos libros, como los de William Blum (2005) y (2006), Guenther Roppel (2005) y Luis Suárez Salazar (2006) entre otros. En el caso brasileño ya en 1960 los militares, por presión de la embajada yanqui, exigieron y lograron la salida del presidente Quadros, quien pocos meses antes de ser destituido había otorgado la máxima condecoración, para autoridades extranjeras, al Che Guevara. En 1964 le darían un golpe de Estado al presidente Joao Goulart, poco después de anunciar la expropiación y redistribución de tierras privadas y la nacionalización de refinerías de petróleo y lograrían la destitución de la presidente Dilma Rousseffa del PT, a través de un impeachment, en 2016.




Por otra parte, el candidato con mayores posibilidades de disputar la presidencia a Lula, es el actual senador del Partido Liberal (PL), Flávio Bolsonaro. Como digno hijo de su padre, el ex presidente Jair Bolsonaro, viajó a Washington a reunirse con el secretario de Estado, para planear la campaña en contra de Lula, lo que resultó en la aplicación de aranceles del 50 % a importantes productos provenientes de Brasil, pretendiendo afectar a todo el pueblo de Brasil, con la intención de robarle apoyo al gobierno de Lula. Pocos días después de esta visita, llegó Rubio a declarar que, “Brasil no es amigo de Estados Unidos”, lo cual fue dirigido a genera malestar y angustia en las clases medias y altas del país.




Flavio Bolsonaro también visitó Tel Aviv, buscando el apoyo de Netanyahu y ofreció cambiar la embajada de Brasil a Jerusalem, en caso de ganar las elecciones. El apoyo sionista es muy importante, ya que tienen relaciones muy importantes con los grandes grupos económico-financieros que manejan la economía brasileña y mundial. También son un apoyo importante en el área tecnológica, poseen recursos muy sofisticados para la manipulación de la población y para el espionaje de todo tipo. Por contraste, hay que recordar que Lula fue declarado persona non grata en 2024 por el gobierno sionista y retiró su embajador de Tel Aviv.




El tema de Jerusalem también toca a las iglesias protestantes, muchas de las cuales tienen financiamiento sionista y, por ende, están influenciadas directamente por el sionismo, lo que incide en millones de votantes brasileños. Como si fuera poco, una cantidad importante de cuadros del PL y otras agrupaciones políticas que apoyan a Flávio Bolsonaro son definida y claramente seguidores del fascismo, militantes de derecha y militares negacionistas de los asesinatos, desapariciones y torturas hechos por las dictaduras, llegan a auto definirse fascistas.




También es obligatorio recordar que los pueblos, sobre todo los más humildes, se cansan de posturas indefinidas. Querer estar bien con los poderosos y también con los desposeídos, querer estar bien con dios y con el diablo, generalmente no deja buen rédito electoral. Su posición de confrontación con Trump le ha válido para recuperar parte del electorado que se había alejado. Brasil es uno de los países con mayor desigualdad económica en el planeta y el PT y el mismo Lula deben retornar a sus raíces y confrontar con los opresores, con los hacendados terrófagos, con los contratistas corruptos y volver decidida y contundentemente al lado de los obreros, de los campesinos, de los indígenas, de las clases medias bajas y de los pobres, y con seguridad logrará recuperar una muy buena parte de la mayor masa de votantes.




Al presidente Lula hay que reconocerle que ha sacado de la pobreza a millones de ciudadanos brasileños, tiene ascendencia en las clases populares y en los trabajadores organizados, entre los indígenas y en los campesinos sin tierra. Comentan que ahora está trabajando los sectores evangélicos populares, también a la juventud y a los trabajadores más deprimidos, que suman una buena parte del electorado.




Es muy poco probable que alguno de los candidatos gane la elección en la primera vuelta del 4 de octubre, por lo que los apoyos para la segunda vuelta son vitales. Los militantes decentes del llamado “centrao”, la gente de izquierda moderada que está desencantada y la ultra izquierda que no quiere a Lula por no hacer mayores cambios, deben hacer un esfuerzo para ayudar a derrotar a la derecha fascista, sionista y pro imperialista, deben apartar las consideraciones mezquinas y personalistas y ayudar a Lula a ganar con mayor margen.




Aunque Lula vetó a Venezuela en su ingreso al BRICS, desconoció al presidente Maduro en 2024 y actuó excesivamente tibio ante su secuestro; aunque Lula no ha apoyado a Cuba con combustible y petróleo crudo, acciones que no le atrajo seguidores, sino por el contrario se los restó, lo que está a tiempo de revertir, corrigiendo su postura y asumiendo su responsabilidad en estos aspectos.




Lula debe ganar. Lo contrario significaría un gran retroceso sobre todo para Brasil, el continente y para el mundo. Brasil debe contener el avance de la Doctrina Monroe y su corolario Trump, que implica neo-colonialismo e imperialismo del más brutal. Brasil debe ser parte importante de los polos de poder que se deben conformar en Nuestra América. El fascismo no es democrático, el neo-colonialismo no es democrático, el imperialismo es explotador, supremacista y solo vela por sus intereses y debe ser contenido y derrotado.




Esperamos que el pueblo brasileño y sus actores políticos sepan elegir el mejor destino para todos sus habitantes actuales y por venir.




Los pueblos son sabios y valientes, el pueblo brasileño y sus líderes sabrán demostrarlo en el próximo proceso electoral.

Date

Notes

The Master’s Tools Will Never Dismantle The Master’s House

 

Comments at “The Personal and the Political” Panel 

[Second Sex Conference, October 29, 1979]

THIS BRIDGE CALLED MY BACK

Published in the United States by Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press, Post Office Box 908, Latham, New York 12110–0908. Originally published by Peresphone Press, Inc.
