title: Conference in London discusses international experiences of peace and political settlement
content:
The Centre for Kurdish Affairs (CKA) convenes the Peace and Democratic Integration Conference in London on 29–30 September 2026, bringing together Kurdish political and civic figures, parliamentarians, policymakers, academics, peace-process practitioners, journalists, researchers and representatives of civil society.




The conference provides a structured and non-partisan forum for examining the prospects for peace, democratic participation and political settlement in relation to the Kurdish question, with particular attention to the evolving process in Turkey and its wider regional and international implications.




The conference is taking place at a significant stage in the current political process. In August 2026, the Turkish Parliament adopted the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion, establishing a legal framework for certain procedures connected with the disarmament, dissolution and reintegration process, subject to the conditions set out in the legislation. The law was approved by Parliament on 10 August and published in the Official Gazette on 18 August 2026.




This development represents an important institutional stage in a process that now raises questions extending beyond the cessation of armed conflict. These include the future of democratic politics, political participation, local governance, legal guarantees, institutional reform, social reconciliation, rights and the reintegration of individuals and communities affected by decades of conflict.




The conference therefore seeks to examine how a political opening can develop into a sustainable, peaceful and democratic settlement, drawing both on international experience and on Kurdish perspectives from Turkey, the wider region and the diaspora.




Peace processes rarely conclude with a single agreement or legislative act. International experience demonstrates that the transition from armed conflict to sustainable peace involves a longer process of political, legal, institutional and social transformation.




The conference will therefore consider questions including:




● How can a political opening be transformed into a durable peace?




● What legal and institutional guarantees are required for confidence between political actors?




● How can former participants in armed conflict be reintegrated into political and civilian life?




● What forms of democratic participation can support a transition from conflict politics to democratic politics?




● How can constitutional and institutional arrangements accommodate political, territorial, linguistic and cultural diversity?




● What role can local and regional governments play in a sustainable settlement?




● How can women, minorities, civil society and the media participate meaningfully in peacebuilding?




● What can be learned from international peace processes, including experiences in Northern Ireland, Colombia, South Africa, the Basque Country and elsewhere?




● How might the Kurdish question evolve within the changing political and strategic environment of Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Iran and the wider region?




● What role can international actors, including the United Kingdom and European institutions, play in supporting peaceful and democratic political processes?




The conference is intended not simply as a discussion of the past, but as an opportunity to consider the political and institutional choices that will shape the next stage of the process.




Panel I - Why Peace Processes Succeed or Fail




The first panel examined the conditions that allow peace processes to move beyond an initial political opening and develop the resilience necessary for a durable settlement.




Drawing on comparative experience from cases including Colombia, South Africa, Cyprus and other international processes, the discussion considered the importance of political commitment, sequencing, implementation, institutional guarantees and public legitimacy.




It also examined why peace processes can become vulnerable to delay, reversal or renewed confrontation, and what lessons may be relevant to the Kurdish peace process.




The contributors of the first panel included Mahmoud Patel (Online); Radha D'Souza; Dr Andrei Gomez-Suarez; Mariela Kohon; Prof. Vasileios Fouskas; Victoria Sandino (Video Intervention). The panel was moderated by Mustafa Gündoğdu, a Kurdish author, editor and human rights practitioner with over two decades of experience in conflict resolution, peace processes and international legal advocacy.






















Gündoğdu: Experiences are different but there are lessons that can be learned




Moderator Gündoğdu stated the following: “Our session today asks a difficult but essential question: why do peace processes succeed or fail? This is important not only because of what happens during negotiations, but because of what comes afterwards: how political agreements are implemented, how trust is built, and how societies move from conflict towards a sustainable political settlement.




Today, we have the opportunity to explore these questions through experiences from different parts of the world, including Colombia and South Africa. These experiences allow us to examine different approaches, institutional structures, and challenges in transforming conflict through political processes.




The Colombian experience, in particular, raises important questions about negotiating with armed groups, political participation, the role of victims and survivors, transitional justice, and the difficult process of translating a negotiated agreement into meaningful political and social change.




These experiences also encourage us to ask some fundamental questions:




What was actually negotiated between the parties?




How important was trust, and how was trust built?




What made the process resilient when it faced serious challenges?




And perhaps most importantly, how does a peace process move from an agreement on paper to an agreement that can actually deliver change in people's lives? This is particularly important when we consider the developments we are witnessing today and the future of the peace process.




One of the central questions of this session, therefore, is how political agreements are implemented and sustained over time.




Ultimately, a peace process cannot be measured only by whether the parties reach an agreement. It must also be considered in terms of whether that agreement can survive political change, maintain public confidence, address the concerns of those affected by conflict, and create the conditions for lasting democratic participation.




At the same time, we are not here to suggest that every conflict, every society, or every negotiation can be treated in exactly the same way. The circumstances are different, the actors are different, and the political and institutional contexts are different. But there are lessons that can be learned.




We can ask: What worked? What failed? Why did certain approaches succeed in one context and encounter difficulties in another? And what can these experiences teach us about the challenges facing peace processes today?




These questions are particularly relevant when we look at the role of political actors, civil society, international institutions, transitional justice, and the broader international community.




Our panel brings together people with direct experience and expertise in these areas, and I hope today’s discussion will allow us to move beyond general statements about peace and instead examine the practical realities of making peace processes work.




With that, let me welcome our speakers and invite them to share their experiences and perspectives on why peace processes succeed or fail, and what is required to build a sustainable political settlement.”




Victoria Sandino:

 

Peace has to become a policy of the state




The panel continued with a video message from Victoria Sandino Simanca Herrera, who is a Colombian peacebuilder, social leader and former Senator of the Republic of Colombia (2018–2022). She served as a plenipotentiary negotiator in the Havana peace talks that culminated in the 2016 Final Peace Agreement between the Colombian Government and the FARC-EP. As coordinator of the Gender Subcommission, she played a key role in incorporating gender, differential and ethnic perspectives into the agreement.




As a senator, Sandino worked on rural equality, women’s rights and implementation of the peace agreement. In 2023, she served as a senior adviser to the Colombian Government’s Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, contributing to gender-inclusive approaches within the “Total Peace” dialogue. A sociologist and journalist by training, her work spans victims’ rights, reparations, rural development, conflict resolution and political reintegration.




In her message to the conference, Victoria Sandino stated the following:




“I speak not only from the perspective of the Peace Agreement itself, but from my own experience as a negotiator and signatory to the peace agreement.




Ten years later, I can say that a negotiation does not end when an agreement is signed. That is where perhaps the most difficult stage begins: building the political, legal, social and cultural guarantees that make returning to armed conflict no longer a viable option. The first political lesson is that the safeguards for a peace process must begin to be constructed before the agreement is signed. They must be built into the agreements themselves.




During the negotiations, we developed an intensive international agenda. Guaranteeing countries such as Cuba and Norway, accompanying countries, governments across Europe and Latin America, the European Union, the United Nations, international organisations and experts all contributed to building confidence.




We learned from successful experiences, but also from the failures of other peace processes. This helped us understand that peace needed an architecture of guarantees that went beyond the two delegations sitting across from each other in Havana.




After the agreement was signed, that architecture became stronger. The agreement established mechanisms for implementation, monitoring and verification, including the commission responsible for this process, as well as broad international accompaniment. The United Nations assumed fundamental responsibilities for verification. The agreement also provided for special accompaniment by the European Union, the United Nations, Switzerland, Sweden and other institutions and countries.




We also constructed legal safeguards. Legislative Act 02 of 2017 established constitutional obligations for good-faith compliance and made provisions of the agreement relating to fundamental rights and international humanitarian law parameters for interpreting its implementation.




The agreement was also concluded as a special agreement under Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, with an original copy deposited with the Swiss Federal Council in Bern.




The lesson is that an agreement will be more resilient to political change when it depends less on the will of one individual and rests more firmly on an architecture involving the state, society and international institutions.




As we learned in Colombia, peace has to become a policy of the state. On opposition to the negotiations and the results of the 2016 referendum, Colombia learned this lesson very quickly. We lost the referendum on 2 October 2016. It was a huge blow, but our response was not to walk away from the negotiating table.




The government opened conversations with those who had voted No and listened to their concerns and proposals. Those observations were brought back into the negotiations, the agreement was revised, and a new text was eventually signed on 24 November and subsequently endorsed by Congress, alongside the legislation created for its implementation.




The fundamental lesson is: listening to the opposition does not mean giving the opposition a veto over peace.




Democratic opposition must have guarantees to express its concerns, challenge agreements and participate politically. It can even help identify weaknesses. But fundamental rights cannot be sacrificed, and disinformation cannot be allowed to replace the democratic deliberation required to build peace.




We experienced this particularly in relation to the gender perspective. Conservative sectors mounted a strong campaign around what they called “gender ideology.”




Defending the gender perspective was not easy, even within the negotiating table. Initially, there was not enough support for it from either the government delegation or the guerrilla leadership.




It was fundamentally women, both inside and outside the negotiations, who managed to defend and sustain the gender approach in the agreement.”




Sandino said the Colombian process ultimately incorporated more than 100 gender-sensitive provisions, which she described as a historic achievement in a peace agreement.




She stated that she would distinguish between legitimate opposition and opposition that seeks to undermine the process or rights themselves. The first should be incorporated into democratic debate; the second cannot be allowed to become an obstacle to building peace, destroying rights or returning a society to war.




On the transition from disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) towards democratic political reintegration, she said the FARC opposed the idea that the transition should simply follow the traditional formula of the DDR. They did not consider themselves simply to be a group of individuals who needed to be disarmed, demobilised and reintegrated.




From the Colombian experience, she argued that when deaths decrease, an extraordinarily valuable political space opens up, and that space must be protected. Every person who is no longer killed is not simply a statistic in a security report. It means a family that does not have to receive a body, a community that does not accumulate more grief and hatred, and a generation beginning to imagine its future outside of conflict.




Sandino said it is important to preserve the political opening that currently exists and transform the reduction in confrontation into political, legal and institutional guarantees.




“Colombia teaches that periods of transition are also periods of enormous fragility. The absence of gunfire is not yet peace. It is only the opportunity to build peace. The greatest mistake would be to assume that because violence has decreased, the political problem has already been resolved. Precisely when the guns fall silent, politics, peace and democracy must begin to speak more strongly.”




On the principal Colombian lesson for transforming a reduction in violence into a comprehensive and durable democratic agreement, she said: “The negotiation of weapons cannot be the endpoint of a peace process. It must be the starting point for a new architecture of guarantees.”




Sandino pointed out that: “Handing over a weapon is a relatively concrete and straightforward act. Building the conditions in which nobody feels that they need to use that weapon again is much more difficult.”




She identified five essential guarantees:




1. Legal guarantees, so that agreements do not depend on the government of the day or its political priorities, but are protected through constitutional and institutional guarantees and become a policy of peace.




2. Security guarantees, so those who have abandoned armed struggle can live safely and participate in political life.




3. Political guarantees, so they can organise, defend their ideas and participate democratically.




4. Social and territorial guarantees, to transform the conditions that contributed to and sustained the conflict.




5. International guarantees, to accompany, verify and help preserve peace during difficult moments and political crises.




Sandino added another guarantee: preserving the political dignity of those making the transition from armed struggle to democracy. A sustainable negotiation, she said, cannot be built around the idea of winner and loser.




She continued: “The message cannot be: ‘Hand over your weapons, and afterwards we will decide which rights you will be given.’ That makes it difficult to build trust. Instead: ‘We abandon the weapons so that our differences can be contested politically and democratically.’




Perhaps the central lesson is that the success of a peace process should not be measured by the number of weapons that were handed over, but by the strength of the guarantees that ensure those weapons will never again be considered necessary.




Colombia demonstrates that signing a peace agreement does not immediately eliminate distrust, inequality or the wounds within a nation. But it also demonstrates that it is possible to transform an armed organisation into political actors, legally recognised organisations, social organisations, cooperatives, women's movements and community organisations.”




Ten years later, she said, that transformation remains one of the most important dimensions of the Colombian experience.






















Radha D’Souza addresses the Kurdish and Tamil experiences




The panel discussion continued with the assessment offered by Radha D’Souza, a critical scholar, barrister, social justice activist and writer from India, and Professor of International Law, Development and Conflict Studies at the University of Westminster. Her interdisciplinary work spans international law, development, conflict, colonialism, social movements and global justice. She previously practised as a barrister in the High Court of Mumbai and has taught and conducted research in India, Aotearoa/New Zealand and the UK.




Radha D’Souza stated: ”I was told that the purpose of this panel, and of this conference, is for Kurdish communities to learn from other struggles. I come to this conference in that spirit, asking myself: what can we learn from each of these struggles, including from the Tamil struggle? For me, this has to be a reflective process. I do not claim to represent the Kurdish struggle. I have been on the fringes of it. I am a human rights activist and a supporter of democracy. One of the most important similarities between the Kurdish struggle and the Tamil struggle, I think, is the question of the homeland.




We are both peoples who have experienced the absence of a homeland, and the idea of a homeland means something very deep. It cannot simply be measured in material or political terms. It is something that people carry within themselves.




Both our struggles have therefore been connected to this desire for a homeland. There is a deep connection in that aspiration.




But then we come to the difficult question: How do we achieve that homeland? That is an issue that both of our peoples have struggled with for a very long time.




One of the most important starting points for understanding the difference between the Tamil struggle and the Kurdish movements is how we understand the contemporary world.




The Tamil movement has, in many ways, understood the contemporary political world as an egalitarian and pluralist civilisation.




I think the Kurdish movement has tended to understand it differently, in terms of a capitalist civilisation. That distinction is not simply an ideological or political one. It shapes the way we understand the state, because ultimately the struggle has been against the state.




When we understand the world in one way or another, that inevitably shapes how we understand the state, how we understand political power, and therefore how we understand the possibilities for resolving the conflict.




The state itself was not a completely sovereign or autonomous entity. It was also subject to manipulation and influence by imperial powers.




An important part of understanding the Tamil struggle is understanding the relationship between the state, external powers and the international system.




When we look at how the Tamil struggle developed, how it approached the question of peace, what happened during the peace process, and what has happened since, this becomes extremely important.




When we assess the state, whether we understand it as a Western state, as a protectorate, or as a state operating under the authority and influence of larger imperial powers, this shapes how we understand the international environment.




This brings us to a fundamental political question: Who are our friends, and who are our enemies?




This has always been an important question for movements engaged in political struggle. The Tamil struggle studied these questions deeply and remained closely connected to anti-imperialist movements around the world.




The Tamil movement learned a great deal from the Irish struggle, which it followed very closely.




It also followed the Palestinian struggle and the peace processes surrounding it, studying those experiences and learning from them.




The Tamil movement therefore looked beyond its immediate circumstances and closely followed other struggles for national rights, self-determination and political change. Through these connections and comparisons, it developed a broader understanding of international politics and the forces shaping peace processes.




The central political demand was for a free, sovereign and secular state. This was part of the political context in which the Tamil struggle developed during the twentieth century.




A major turning point came with the first significant unified peace process, initiated by the Indian government. India played a very significant role in the conflict and in the political process that followed. The peace process cannot be separated from the role played by external states and regional powers.”




Andrei Gómez-Suárez: The most important aspect is protecting the implementation of the peace agreement




The following speech was made by Dr Andrei Gómez-Suárez, a former peace negotiator for the Colombian Government, Associate Researcher at SOAS University of London, and co-founder of Embrace Dialogue (Rodeemos el Diálogo), a peacebuilding organisation. His work brings togetheracademic research, peacebuilding practice and direct experience of Colombia’s peace process.




Andrei Gómez-Suárez noted that although formal negotiations in Colombia began in 2012, the political history of the process goes back much further. He said that following the agreement signed in 2016, the implementation phase began, that the FARC laid down its arms in 2017, and that this process was verified by the United Nations.




Gómez-Suárez outlined five key lessons that could be drawn from the Colombian experience: agreeing on a realistic and concrete roadmap for peace, selecting credible guarantors, ensuring the participation of key political actors, establishing commissions capable of generating progress and building trust between the parties, and involving civil society in the process.




He also addressed warning signs that could indicate a peace process is heading toward failure, citing a lack of strategic alignment between the leaderships of the parties, weakening civil society support, and growing internal divisions within the parties themselves as key risks.




For negotiations to remain lasting and credible, Gómez-Suárez said that the signatories must remain committed to implementation, the agreement must be incorporated into the country’s legal framework, support from credible international actors must be secured, and civil society must be provided with the means to safeguard the implementation of the agreement.




Kohon: Challenges didn't stop the momentum of the process




The next speaker was Mariela Kohon, Assistant Director of Strategy and Delivery at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) in the United Kingdom. She previously headed the TUC’s international division, overseeing international labour rights and relations with the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) and International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC).




Kohon has extensive experience in international peacebuilding and diplomacy, including as a strategic adviser during the Colombian peace negotiations in Havana that culminated in the 2016 Final Peace Agreement. She has also advised the United Nations, the Norwegian Embassy, the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue and Colombia’s Office of the High Commissioner for Peace. As former Director of the Justice for Colombia campaign, she facilitated exchanges between Colombian peace negotiators and figures involved in the Good Friday Agreement and South African peace process.




Kohon stated that she was involved in the peace process between the FARC and the government, and also in the negotiations around the international mechanism and the international support for the agreement. She also worked with the most recent Colombian administration from the government side.




Speaking specifically about the peace agreement between the FARC and the government, she highlighted the need for commitment to meaningful work.




On the government side, she said, there were years, kind of secret, of confidential negotiations as to the agenda for the process.




Referring to the aspects of the peace process, she talked about the normalization of the community, addressing some of the causes of conflict, destruction, and confidence.




She remarked that the two key structural causes of the conflict were a lack of equality -with 1% of the population owning 80% of the land- and a lack of democratic political space, where civil society, whether trade unions or community leaders, also organized.




“So, when there were difficulties, or certain issues, they were put into freeze, which wasn't really opened again. But it meant that even if there were challenges, it didn't stop the momentum of the process,” she noted.




She noted that civil society mobilized and organized to be involved in the process, describing the initiative as important.  




Kohon also stressed the importance of having the support of international actors and the international community as a kind of guarantor that could mediate when there were difficulties.




She also talked about the specific challenge for women in peacebuilding, and their reintegration in the peace process after picking up a weapon.




Kohon further underlined the importance of creating mechanisms that hold the agreement in place for post-agreement conditions. She said international support was important to ensure that.

title: Conference in London addresses issues of power-sharing and constitutional arrangements
content:
The Centre for Kurdish Affairs (CKA) has organized a Peace and Democratic Integration Conference in London on 29 and 30 September 2026, bringing together Kurdish political and civic figures, parliamentarians, policymakers, academics, peace-process practitioners, journalists, researchers and representatives of civil society.




Today, the conference’s second panel was titled “Peace, Power-Sharing, and Constitutional Arrangements: Lessons from the United Kingdom.” The panel explored the role of constitutionalism in conflict resolution, drawing on the UK’s experience of power-sharing, devolution and differentiated forms of governance. It will examine how constitutional arrangements can provide credible guarantees, distribute political authority and accommodate distinct political and territorial claims within a stable democratic framework. The discussion will consider what these experiences can offer to the Kurdish question, particularly how constitutional reform can provide durable channels for recognition, political participation and meaningful local authority while strengthening confidence in the wider political settlement. 




Speakers were Prof. Michael Gunter, Dr. Matthew Whiting, Prof. Michael Keating, Geraint Thomas, while Matt Broomfield was the moderator.




Prof. Michael Gunter said: “In Turkey, the so-called peace process that formally began in October 2024 between the government and the PKK is looking more like a PKK surrender. Turkey frames the process as little more than PKK disarmament and dissolution, while the PKK claims that it seeks constitutional rights as Kurds and the release of its incarcerated leader Abdullah (Apo) Öcalan. The two sides appear to be inhabiting two different universes, while the entire process seems interminably slow. The long-anticipated legislation amounted to little more than a humiliating PKK capitulation.”




Prof. Gunter added: “The so-called peace process was concluded on grounds that it amounted to little more than a virtual PKK surrender. Even those minor PKK members eligible for parole were given no guarantees once they had surrendered their arms and returned to civilian life. It would be relatively easy for the government to rearrest them on any manufactured excuse. The once formidable PKK now seemed to be in decline and on very shaky ground. The fate of Rojava or the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria is arguably the most prominent example of the Kurdish decline.”




Prof. Gunter continued: “Once held as a brilliant example of Kurdish self-government, its sudden collapse in 2026 after 14 years of existence was striking, but predictable. Although the ultimate outcome remains to be completely decided and the Syrian Kurds appear headed for a more positive position than the misery they suffered from under the Assad regime, Rojava’s sudden collapse resembled a Shakespearean tragedy. Although I have shared with you my serious doubts, we must all give the new current Turkish framework law a chance, even though it is at its best, only a modest beginning. Hopefully, this law offers us an opening for Öcalan’s call for democratization to benefit all Turkish citizens, Turks and Kurds  both. Despite his pessimistic evaluation, even Cemil Bayik did vouch, the [framework] law can act as a foundation.”







 







Dr. Matthew Whiting said: “They realised at some point in the 1980s, so 15 years before they took part in the peace process, that they could achieve their aims just as well through political means as they could through violence. If not, in fact, they were more likely to achieve them. So suddenly, in this sort of long reappraisal over a 15-year period, the movement went from violence being an asset and a sine qua non to violence actually being what's holding us back from being able to advance our political demands. And so we see this gradual shift in this way. We see a rebalance from the military element to the political element and embrace of exclusively political politics.“




Dr. Whiting added: “They said, okay, well, this shift to being political is a change in our tactics but not a change in our goal. We are still pushing our ultimate aim, which is the unity of Ireland, but what we're doing now is seeing how we can pursue short-term reforms to policies and not always say Brits out and that fix everything and then move on.




We can pursue fair employment law, we can pursue educational opportunities, we can pursue housing reforms, etc. As an example of that, prior to the peace process, Sinn Féin had an average poll rating of 8 to 10% in the North of Ireland. After the peace process, they're now up the 30, and they're the largest party in the North of Ireland. In the Republic of Ireland, they polled about 2%, they're now the second-largest party in the Republic of Ireland in the high 20 percent. But that has reaped electoral rewards and it has undoubtedly improved the position of Catholics in a very discriminatory against proportion of the North of Ireland population.”




Professor Michael Keating and Geraint Thomas assessed federalism, devolution, European Union membership, and the changes brought about by Brexit through the experiences of Ireland, Scotland, the North of Ireland, and Wales.




Failure to recognize federalism had disastrous consequences in Ireland




Referring to the Irish experience, Professor Michael Keating described the failure to recognize that federalism could coexist with the recognition of nationalism as “a catastrophic failure.” Keating said: “In Ireland, the failure to recognize that federalism could combine recognition with nationalism was a catastrophic failure.”




He added that this failure resulted in separation and partition in Ireland. He added that, in subsequent years, nationalism in Scotland and national consciousness in the North of Ireland grew, leading to demands for arrangements that moved, at least in part, toward federalism.




Keating said these demands were addressed toward the end of the 20th century through what is known as devolution in Scotland and Wales. In the North of Ireland, an arrangement also emerged during the same period, although for different reasons. As a result, Keating noted, a highly asymmetrical system developed in Britain.




Keating placed particular emphasis on the fact that the devolution process in Britain took place while the country was a member of the European Union. “One of the reasons all this happened was that the United Kingdom was a member of the European Union at the time,” Keating said, explaining that the EU provided a framework that made different constitutional arrangements possible.




He identified the separation of rights from nationality as one of the framework’s important features, making the following observation about the North of Ireland: “In the North of Ireland, it doesn’t matter if you say you are Irish. You don’t get your rights from there. You get your rights from Europe. That is extremely important.”




The framework changed after Brexit




Keating said the system changed following Brexit, explaining that the repatriation of powers from the European Union also affected the devolution system in Britain. Noting that the European Union had previously served as a kind of “umbrella,” Keating said that the future of this framework had become an important question after Brexit. Addressing questions about whether Britain might move closer to Europe again in the future, Keating said the relationship between the transfer of powers upward and downward was critically important.




The debate over Scottish independence




Keating also discussed developments in Scotland, recalling that an independence referendum was held in 2014. He noted that Scottish nationalists had come to power and said that support for independence had continued in the years that followed. Keating said Brexit was closely connected to this dynamic and noted that the British experience contained both positive and negative elements. He emphasized that the guarantees provided by constitutional arrangements, and how those arrangements could subsequently be changed, were among the central issues.




Thomas: A quiet revolution is taking place in Wales




Geraint Thomas, meanwhile, based his remarks on the historical and political experience of Wales. Noting that little is known outside Wales about its current situation, Thomas said: “We are very quiet. This is a bit of a small revolution, and I’m going to talk about it today.” Thomas added that Wales had not been independent since 1282, pointing to a period of approximately 750 years. “We lost our sovereignty,” he said. He explained that, apart from a small uprising in the early 15th century, there had been no significant change in Wales’s political position for a long time.




Our natural resources flowed east




Discussing Wales’s natural resources, Thomas said that throughout history his country had been “quite generous” toward the rest of Britain, particularly England. Listing resources such as coal, steel, slate, and agricultural products, Thomas said: “Our natural resources flowed east quite willingly.” He noted that Wales’s transport routes also largely extended eastward, toward England, while Wales itself received very little in return. Thomas said the same was true of water resources. He explained that Wales had substantial water resources and that some cities in England wanted to benefit from them.




Second day to focus on the Kurdish question




The sessions planned for tomorrow, Wednesday 30 September, will focus directly on the political, legal, social, and regional dimensions of the Kurdish question.




The future of Kurdish politics, democratic representation, local government, and the role of civil society and the diaspora will be discussed, while the impact of developments in Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran on Kurds will also be assessed.




The programme will also cover the role of women in peace processes, minority participation, human rights, freedom of the press, and social reconciliation.




Speakers at the conference will include figures from Kurdish politics such as Pervin Buldan, Gültan Kışanak, Gülüstan Kılıç Koçyiğit, Serpil Kemalbay, and Osman Baydemir, as well as academics, journalists, and experts working on international peace processes.

author: Amy Goodman
title: A Year Later, Trump’s Gaza Plan Just Bought “More Time for the Genocide”
content:
Writer and analyst Muhammad Shehada notes the release of Israeli hostages is the only plan item that’s been fulfilled.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Palestinian death toll from Israel’s war on Gaza has surpassed 74,000, according to the Ministry of Health in Gaza. While this figure represents the official death toll as confirmed by local authorities, the true number could be much higher when missing people and indirect deaths are taken into account, such as from disease, exposure, denial of medical treatment and the destruction of civic infrastructure. And since the so-called ceasefire brokered by Trump last October, nearly 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks.

“The [ceasefire] plan ended up just buying more time for the genocide,” says Muhammad Shehada, a writer and analyst from Gaza speaking to Democracy Now! in Copenhagen. “Instead of suspending attacks on Gaza, Israel has been bombing Gaza every day.”

“The idea of the plan was to divide the reconstruction, rehabilitation, Israeli withdrawal, decommissioning of Hamas and Palestinian statehood into three phases,” says Shehada. “So far, only one item of the 20 items on the Trump plan has been fulfilled, and that is the release of every single Israeli hostage in Gaza.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman. We are broadcasting from Copenhagen, Denmark.

The Palestinian death toll from Israel’s war on Gaza has surpassed 74,000. According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli attacks since the so-called ceasefire last October have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians. Gaza’s Government Media Office puts the toll even higher at more than 1,400. On Sunday, two Palestinians were killed in an Israeli airstrike on downtown Gaza City. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, settler violence has killed at least 1,107 Palestinians since October 7, 2023.

On Monday, a senior U.N. official condemned what he called “the relentless expansion of Israeli settlements” in the occupied West Bank. This is U.N. Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov addressing the U.N. Security Council.

RAMIZ ALAKBAROV: I strongly condemn the relentless expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which fuels tensions, impedes access by Palestinians to their land and threatens the validity, viability of a fully independent, sovereign and contiguous Palestinian state. The rapidly expanding settlement footprint, including outposts, is taking place in conjunction with the rise in settler attacks.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, Democracy Now! is broadcasting from Denmark, which recently joined 20 other countries, as well as the European Commission, in signing a declaration opposing Israel’s planned settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Denmark, along with 11 other countries, is also backing sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. On Monday, Denmark’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Christina Markus Lassen, addressed the U.N. General Assembly.

CHRISTINA MARKUS LASSEN: In Gaza, civilians continue to pay the price. Far more must be done to secure humanitarian access and long-term peace. And in the occupied West Bank, settler violence and settlement expansion threaten the daily lives of Palestinians and undermine the prospects for a future Palestinian state. This has to stop.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Denmark’s ambassador to the United Nations, Christina Markus Lassen.

For more, we’re joined here in Copenhagen by Muhammad Shehada, writer and analyst from Gaza, visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

Muhammad Shehada, welcome back to Democracy Now! It’s wonderful to be here with you in the studio in Copenhagen. We’re usually interviewing you by Zoom. These are extremely harrowing times. It’s been almost a year since the Trump plan for Gaza was created, October 9, 2025. Can you explain what that plan is and what has been fulfilled so far?

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: Thanks so much, Amy. Great to finally see you in person, one of my favorite heroes.

So, the idea of the plan was to divide the reconstruction, rehabilitation, Israeli withdrawal, decommissioning of Hamas, and Palestinian statehood into three phases. The first one was related to early recovery, so it would see Israel suspending its attacks, allowing 600 trucks per day of food and humanitarian aid into Gaza, rehabilitating basic infrastructure — water, electricity, hospitals, roads, sanitation — and basically opening up the Rafah border crossing for people to be able to travel in and out. The second phase was the one that relates to Hamas decommissioning and Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, as well as the reconstruction, the rebuilding of the enclave. And the third one is the long-term one that relates to Palestinian statehood.

So far, only one item of the 20 items on the Trump plan has been fulfilled, and that is the release of every single Israeli hostage in Gaza and the remains of dead hostages. Nothing else was completely fulfilled. Israel either violated its obligations completely or fulfilled some of them extremely partially, to the point that it does not have any significant impact on the ground. For example, food, instead of 600 trucks of humanitarian aid per day, we are getting an average of 95 trucks per day, which is less than 20%. Instead of suspending attacks on Gaza, Israel has been bombing Gaza every day — as you mentioned, 1,400 people killed since the so-called ceasefire started.

And the idea here is that the plan ended up just buying more time for the genocide, allowing Israel to continue it with sort of low intensity, low profile, amid a facade and promises of progress. But those promises, if there is no enforcement mechanism behind them, they read mostly as a wish list. They don’t read as a plan.

AMY GOODMAN: Why did Palestinians sign this deal? You’re a Palestinian from Gaza.

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: I’ve asked Palestinian negotiators and Arab mediators, as well, what was the highest expectation behind the deal, and the answer is unanimous. Nobody expected it to be fulfilled completely. The highest ambition was three things: allowing more food to go in, at a point when Israel manufactured famine in Gaza, reducing the Israeli killing machine in Gaza as much as possible — so, before that ceasefire was put in place, Israel was killing an average of a hundred people per day. Now it’s about five people per day, which is still monstrous and atrocious. But the idea was to reduce the rate of the killing. And the third one was to prevent the mass migration or the mass ethnic cleansing in Gaza. That was the ambition from the Palestinian end and Arab side.

The other dimension is that they were blackmailed very openly by the Trump administration, that if they don’t sign onto that deal before the Nobel Peace Prize was announced on Friday in that October 2025, that Netanyahu would get a total free hand to decimate Gaza and annihilate it. So, Arab mediators told us that Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner would keep nudging them daily to say, “You need to get a deal by Wednesday. You need to get a deal by Thursday. The Nobel Peace Prize is going to be announced tomorrow, and we want to make the big guy happy.” That was the idea of the deal.

AMY GOODMAN: And, of course, President Trump was not the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize.

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: Precisely, but he managed to steal it anyways from Machado.

AMY GOODMAN: Yes, from the Venezuelan woman who won the Peace Prize. She handed her trophy to him, though the Nobel Committee said, “Doesn’t matter who hands a trophy to anyone. We give out the prize.” If you can talk about at this point what role Netanyahu is playing?

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: Well, Netanyahu is doing two things. Number one, he is using Gaza, the destruction there, the settler terrorism that we see in the West Bank, as his election campaign. So, he’s promising the Israeli public that if he’s reelected, he will finish the job in Gaza. We’re seeing him, his Minister of Defense Israel Katz, his Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich, all of them promising, one after the other, that Israel’s plan for Gaza remains resuming military operations back to full scale, doing even more destruction than what we have seen before, because now Israel doesn’t have any hostages in there, so they can accelerate the damage and destruction exponentially, and basically ethnically cleansing Gaza completely and rebuilding Jewish-only settlements in the enclave. So, that is number one.

The other thing is that Netanyahu is trying to show that he’s stronger than the United States and the international community, that he cannot be pressured by Trump. So, when the Trump plan was announced and the Trump roadmap was then announced this year, I think in July, when Hamas accepted to disarm, lay down its arms, in return for Israel’s withdrawal, Netanyahu used it for his theatrics to pretend to be stronger than Trump, to pretend to be the Winston Churchill of Israel, that he can stand on his own against a storm and not bend at all. And one of the reasons for this is because opposition parties in Israel are attacking Netanyahu from the right, not from the left. So, Gadi Eisenkot, the next premier in Israel, supposedly, the one with the highest chance of winning and becoming prime minister, has been telling the Israeli public that Netanyahu will, quote, “squander” and waste away the achievements, the military achievements, of the IDF in Gaza and capitulate to Trump and fulfill his roadmap. So, Netanyahu is stuck in the position of pretending that, “No, I am actually stronger than Trump, and I can prevent any progress.”

AMY GOODMAN: I wanted to get your response to the foreign minister of the U.K. We were just in London yesterday. Ed Miliband was in Liverpool addressing the Labour Party.

ED MILIBAND: And I want to say to the millions of people in this country, and indeed elsewhere, who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: We hear you. You were right. … We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with action. We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government says: We will not let you succeed.

AMY GOODMAN: So, that’s the British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband on Monday, saying there will be new economic sanctions on Israeli settlements. The speech came a day after police, though, arrested more than 50 protesters outside the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, with demonstrators nonviolently urging support for the banned direct action group Palestine Action in the U.K. Muhammad Shehada?

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: It’s extraordinary and very surprising to me. A few years ago, before October 7th, before the genocide in Gaza, the idea of even demanding from those governments to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements was so laughable, so impossible and unthinkable, that no one would even try to bring it up. And what we see now with Ed Miliband, it’s an extraordinary speech. It was very heartwarming to watch, especially from someone that comes from a Jewish background, that grew up in a household that was very supportive of Israel. And to see that transformation, it shows even more deeply that it’s not about Ed Miliband himself. It shows the fundamental shift in public opinion in the United Kingdom, that now those in power are trying basically to catch up with where public opinion is.

Nonetheless, what we see here is an extraordinary shift in rhetorics, but not an equally strong shift in actions. There’s still more that needs to be done: banning weapon exports to Israel, basically sanctioning Israeli government officials, Netanyahu himself, his entire Cabinet, the Israeli army. If Ed Miliband is saying that war crimes were committed in Gaza, that incriminates the chain of command.

And the last point is that I hope that Miliband’s speech is the future of the Democratic Party in the next few months.

AMY GOODMAN: The son of the imprisoned Palestinian leader Marwan Barghouti — his name is Arab Barghouti — was recently interviewed by Piers Morgan and shared his reaction to seeing National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir taunting his father in prison in a video.

ARAB BARGHOUTI: As a son, it was a shock to me to see my father in this condition. And this is important to highlight, that my father has been put in solitary confinement right after October 7th, even though, obviously, he has nothing to do with it. He has been tortured, assaulted multiple times, attacked.

PIERS MORGAN: Do you ever get to see him or speak to him?

ARAB BARGHOUTI: I haven’t been able to see him in four years. I haven’t been able to speak to him in four years. I haven’t been able to hug or even touch my father in 25 years. And this is an experience —

ARAB BARGHOUTI: Yes, and this is an experience that thousands of Palestinians go through.

AMY GOODMAN: So, that was the son of Marwan Barghouti. And for a global audience, if you can talk about Marwan Baghouti’s significance? On Saturday, you wrote on social media, quote, “Releasing Marwan Barghouti would be the most consequential event in Palestinian politics since the death of Yasser Arafat. He’s the only leader that can unify Palestinians, & that’s precisely why Netanyahu told John Kerry he’d never release him!” That’s what you wrote. Explain.

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: Absolutely. So, I remember exactly the day when the Israeli security minister, Ben-Gvir, stormed Marwan Barghouti’s prison cell, and that video showed up. And I remember being at a conference with fellow Palestinians, some of whom were very critical of Fatah, the party that Marwan Barghouti comes from. And as soon as we watched that footage, it felt like a dagger that was basically stabbing you straight to the heart, to everyone around the table. It was so shocking, because Barghouti has been established in our minds, in our collective memory, as the father of the Palestinian nation, as our own Nelson Mandela.

And basically, that legend allows him, when he comes out, to do things that other Palestinian leaders in today’s political mainstream are incapable of doing, one of which is to unify the Palestinian factions, to heal the divide and accomplish total reconciliation. We see that in every poll, Marwan Barghouti is, by a giant margin, leading against any opponent from Fatah or Hamas or any other political party, for that matter. And that’s precisely why you have people even in the Israeli lobby in the United States or in the Israeli army and the Israeli government that are in favor of releasing him, because from their perspective, the power of Barghouti allows him to take steps of reconciliation and compromise vis-à-vis Israel that no other Palestinian leader would be able to without his legitimacy coming into question. From our perspective, it’s basically we see that he would revitalize the Palestinian street. He would reestablish the connection between the leadership and the public and energize our movement again. And that’s precisely why Netanyahu told John Kerry in 2013 that he would never release him, because he’s the only one that can unify Palestinians.

Releasing him at this stage is the single most consequential event in reviving Palestinian politics, that has been long murdered by a veto from the United States, from Israel, from the international community, that heavily invested in maintaining the divide between Gaza and the West Bank, Hamas and Fatah, the diaspora and Palestinians in the occupied territory. And that’s precisely why we need to add it as an agenda item for the Democratic Party in the United States. I saw Ro Khanna already advocating for his release, and that is the right thing to do at this stage.

AMY GOODMAN: Finally, NAZA has just been released, the documentary by Yuval [Abraham] and Rachel Szor, a film that portrays the Israeli military’s use of secret AI-powered systems to deliberately and systematically target and kill civilians in Gaza, received this record ovation at the Venice Film Festival, exposing Where’s Daddy? and Lavender, something Yuval has been reporting, and others, Palestinians and Israelis, have been talking about, but all in this film — Yuval Abraham. If you can, finally, comment on the significance of this film and the Israeli — some officials in the Israeli government threatening to remove the citizenship of these filmmakers?

MUHAMMAD SHEHADA: So, the movie NAZA, it perfectly captures the distinction between disproportionate warfare, in which you are attacking an enemy and then civilians in high numbers are getting killed, and genocide, in which the civilian population is the target. If you watch the movie, you can’t help but come out with the impression that Hamas, in that instance, Hamas militants that were being targeted, were basically the excuse or the alibi or even the collateral damage, that you see Israeli soldiers that are saying that they were authorized to drop a bomb that would kill 500 civilians, most of whom are children and women, to get to one junior Hamas militant that even may or may not be there in the first place. And the idea is to use that militant as an excuse for maximum damage. That’s why we saw the chief of staff of the IDF at the start of the war, Herzi Halevi, saying that “the focus for us is on the damage, not on the accuracy.” That’s why we’re seeing Israeli politicians and military generals and commanders throughout the genocide that were telling their soldiers explicitly, “Destroy everything. Don’t leave anything standing. Maximum destruction.”

I even met Israeli soldiers here in Copenhagen. A colleague of mine brought them here to testify before European decision-makers and politicians. And when I met them, their testimony was very simple. It was three things: We were told to destroy everything in our face, we were told to kill every single person that crosses an invisible line, and we were told to use people as human shields systematically. The problem is that most decision-makers refused to even meet with those soldiers to hear the testimony, because they wanted to maintain plausible deniability. So, now having that power being captured in image, in art, it is extraordinary, and that’s why Israel feels threatened.

AMY GOODMAN: Muhammad Shehada, I want to thank you so much for being with us, writer and analyst from Gaza, visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, lives here in Copenhagen.

Next week marks the 25th anniversary of the 2001 U.S. invasion of Afghanistan. We’ll speak with the Danish Afghan journalist Nagieb Khaja. His most recent documentary on Afghanistan is titled Winning Hearts and Minds. In 2008, he was kidnapped by the Taliban, but escaped. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Ella’s Song: We Who Believe in Freedom Cannot Rest Until It Comes,” Sweet Honey in the Rock, performing at the 2025 Peace Ball.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Opposition to AI Data Centers Is Actually a “Chinese Psyop,” Mike Johnson Says
content:
“This is not a conspiracy theory,” the House speaker added.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) has dismissed popular concerns among the American public over Big Tech’s hastened buildout of data centers across the U.S. as nothing more than propaganda pushed by the Chinese government.

In an interview on AI with Fox Business on Monday, Johnson was asked how he plans to fight back against Democrats seizing on opposition to data centers to attack Republicans in the midterm elections.

“I’ve had several tech executives and lawmakers, to be clear, say that the information against data centers, that push back against data centers, that is coming from China,” said Fox host Cheryl Casone.

“Yes,” replied Johnson. “Don’t buy it. It is a Chinese psyop.”

“I really believe that. It’s not a conspiracy theory,” he went on. He then contradicted himself, claiming that “the community concerns are important” and that companies seeking to build a data center must “ensure the local community they’ll be good corporate partners.”

Johnson’s comments ignore the massive, nonpartisan anti-data center movement that’s erupted in the past months.

A mountain of polls and grassroots campaigns across the country this year have revealed a groundswell of opposition to tech companies’ massive buildout of data centers amid the explosion of AI adoption. Proposals by tech companies to build data centers in communities across the country have been met with protests and organizing campaigns.

Polls repeatedly find that the vast majority of Americans say in surveys that they oppose the construction of a data center in their community, and the very concept of them is extremely unpopular, even among Republican voters.

A New York Times/Siena University poll conducted earlier this month, for instance, found that 61 percent of voters oppose the construction of AI-supporting data centers in the U.S. entirely, including 40 percent who said they “strongly oppose” the idea. Opposing voters cited water and environmental impacts, local resource usage, and distrust of AI as their top concerns.

Still, Republican officials and tech executives have tried to spread the conspiracy theory — which cybersecurity and media experts have cast doubt on — that it is China that is behind the opposition. President Donald Trump told Fox earlier this month that it’s a “China PR thing” that people don’t want data centers in their communities, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has blamed the opposition on a “propaganda war.”

Officials have cited reports from tech firms that claim to have rooted out and banned bot-run Chinese accounts that spread anti-data center sentiment. But these reports have not found evidence of a widespread campaign. Last month, X said that it found 200 Chinese anti-data center accounts — on a platform with more than 500 million monthly active users, according to owner Elon Musk. Meanwhile, OpenAI said in June that it banned a set of Chinese accounts that were highlighting harms of data centers to local communities, but admitted that the campaign didn’t gain much traction.

“This was not a case of an influence operation creating a debate. The debate existed already. This was an influence operation from China trying to interfere in it. We didn’t see any signs that they succeeded,” said Ben Nimmo, OpenAI’s principal investigator for threats, per NPR.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) criticized Johnson’s claim for sweeping aside public opinion.

“No, Mr. Johnson. The 75 percent of Americans who oppose data centers, including a majority of Republicans, have not fallen victim to a ‘Chinese psyop,’” said Sanders on social media on Tuesday. “They are rightly concerned about AI billionaires raising their electricity bills, destroying the environment and threatening humanity.”

author: By Niko Georgiades, Unicorn Riot
title: Israel Bombs Newly Built Water Desalination Plant in Gaza
content:
Gaza, Palestine — For nearly two months, Palestinians in Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan neighborhood had access to water at any time — a welcome sense of stability in the depths of a genocidal war. On Aug. 24, that stability was disrupted by an Israeli airstrike that destroyed the newly built water desalination plant and damaged apartment buildings and tents.




Standing next to rubble and forcibly displaced from the airstrikes, Louay Al-Namnam told Unicorn Riot that at least 14 Palestinian families were now looking for “somewhere to live.”




“We were sitting safely inside the complex,” he said, “when suddenly someone approached us and told us to leave because the area was about to be bombed. A water desalination plant was struck first, and then the complex itself was hit.”



















“We are all now out on the streets. We need somewhere to live! We couldn’t salvage any of our personal belongings—we escaped with nothing but the clothes on our backs, just as you see us now. What kind of truce is this? What kind of humanity allows this to happen to us?”




Louay Al-Namnam, forcibly displaced by Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City













The water plant had provided free desalinated water to families and over a dozen shelters and collectives. The bombing worsens Gaza City’s drinking-water crisis which impacts 92% of the population.




According to 

Al Jazeera

, the owner of the desalination plant estimated his losses to be at least $500,000 with the machines half of that amount. The plant which was totally destroyed was carefully assembled with hard to obtain equipment and materials. 













Despite being condemned for war crimes Israel continues their acts of collective punishment toward all of Gaza, eradicating the infrastructure of all civil society from healthcare, education, to electricity and 

water

 plants. They now occupy over 70% of Gaza and are continuing daily attacks.




Since the U.S.-brokered ceasefire between Palestinian resistance fighters and Israeli forces in October 2025, Israel has killed over 1,400 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Officially the death toll has exceeded 74,000 Palestinians killed by Israel — with numbers likely in the hundreds of thousands — in response to the Oct. 7 attack which killed around 1,150 people.

author: Dennis Pillion
title: Trump Rollback of Fuel Economy Standards Will Deal Blows to Climate and Health
content:
“There’s nothing Trump won’t sacrifice on the altar of fealty to Big Oil and auto polluters,” said one critic.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Trump administration Monday finalized the rollback of a major fuel economy standard for cars and trucks, a move critics say will cause more climate-warming pollution, human health problems and higher fuel costs for consumers.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, a part of the Department of Transportation, published new Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards Monday, greatly reducing the fuel efficiency for new passenger cars and light trucks made between 2022 and 2031.

The Department of Transportation estimates that the new standards would correspond to an industry fleetwide average of about 34.9 miles per gallon for new vehicles in model year 2031. The previous standard, set in 2022 during the Biden administration, would have required around 50.4 miles per gallon, driving automakers to invest more heavily in gasoline-free electric vehicles.

The DOT said in a news release the move would give automakers more flexibility, reduce the average cost of a new vehicle and encourage new car sales. The Trump administration continued to call the Biden rules an EV “mandate.”

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a group that advocates on behalf of auto manufacturers, praised the new standards.

“The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand,” John Bozella the Alliance’s president and CEO, said in a news release. “Today’s final rule is an appropriate course correction.”

But the changes will likely mean that new cars produced will be less efficient and emit more greenhouse gases and harmful air pollutants that studies show are responsible for 9 million deaths per year worldwide.

“Today’s rule to weaken fuel economy standards will create more air pollution, harm health and accelerate climate change,” American Lung Association President and CEO Harold Wimmer said in a news release.

“For decades, fuel economy standards have ensured that new cars, SUVs and pickup trucks are more efficient, which saves lives and money,” Wimmer said. “There is no reason to weaken standards that are technologically feasible and have a direct benefit for the quality of the air people breathe.”

Transportation accounts for about 28 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, according to the Environmental Protection Agency, more than electric power generation (25 percent) or industry (23 percent).

Monday’s rule finalized plans Trump announced in December to reduce the fuel efficiency standards. But in between, the war in Iran has sent gas prices skyrocketing to an average of $4.48 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association.

Jason Schwartz, regulatory policy director at the Institute for Policy Integrity at New York University’s School of Law, said the repeal will result in higher fuel costs for consumers and make them more vulnerable to “price shocks” in the cost of gasoline.

“The 2024 fuel-economy standards were projected to save consumers $80 billion in fuel costs and reduce more than $125 billion in damages from climate change,” Schwartz said. “Today, [the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration] made those savings disappear, and households that are already stretched thin will pay the price.”

The Institute for Policy Integrity says more than $17 billion in projected annual consumer savings are now at risk due to regulatory rollbacks by the Trump administration.

Environmental and health groups and others say they plan to contest the new standards.

“Americans need relief from high costs, but instead Trump is giving automakers a free pass on pollution and handing families the bill — at the pump and with their health,” Katherine García, director of the Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a news release.

“The Sierra Club will fight this senseless rollback every step of the way,” Garcia said. “We’re going to continue to fight back against this administration’s dangerous and costly attacks on cleaner cars and public health.”

Dan Becker, director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s Safe Climate Transport Campaign, said in a news release that the previous standard was “the biggest single step any nation has taken to save gas, money at the pump, and auto pollution.”

“Trump is tanking sensible mileage standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who’re getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump,” Becker said. “Consumers will pay the price for these reckless rollbacks while Trump’s Big Oil and Big Auto buddies reap the short-term profits. This move spells short- and long-term disaster for people’s health, the planet, and even U.S. automakers who’ll sit on the sidelines while clean cars advance around the world.”

The rollback also comes as EVs from China are taking off around the world, including places like Argentina. Chinese EV maker BYD surpassed Tesla in 2025 as the world’s largest producer of electric vehicles.

“Trump’s creating a perfect storm to crush competitiveness of domestic car companies, drive up consumer costs and kill the climate,” said Becker. “There’s nothing Trump won’t sacrifice on the altar of fealty to Big Oil and auto polluters, whether it’s our health or our wallets. Trump’s rollbacks are speeding us toward a sicker, poorer America.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Joy and remembrance on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation schedule
content:
Joy and celebration are on the schedule for many of the events throughout Inuit Nunangat for the sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday.




“Truth and Reconciliation Day is a day where we take a good look at ourselves and we realize that we’ve made it,” said Tylie Arnatsiaq, head co-ordinator with Igloolik’s Artcirq performance troupe. 

“It’s a good reason to have a joyful event as a community.”







Also known as Orange Shirt Day, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation was established in response to Call to Action 80 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.




It called on the federal government to collaborate with Indigenous peoples to create a holiday to recognize survivors, their families, and communities while ensuring the history and legacy of residential schools are publicly remembered.




Artcirq has acrobatic acts, a clown show and a juggling routine scheduled to follow a walk and a feast at Igloolik’s community hall on Wednesday afternoon.




“We will feed the community,” said recreation coordinator Qumangaapik Arnatsiaq.




A hukki, or square dance, will cap off the day’s events, which also include survivors sharing their reflections. he added.
















Arviat residents can also look forward to a square dance that’s organized by Victims Services, the Department of Family Services and hamlet recreation staff. It’s scheduled to take place Wednesday evening at Mark Kalluak Hall,

 following a feast and an elders discussion about their experiences.




In Iqaluit, the Qikiqtani Inuit Association is hosting events at Cadet Hall, after a poor weather forecast prevented outdoor plans, said spokesperson Markoosie Qaunirq.




Staff will hand out orange T-shirts, followed by speeches and a moment of silence and prayer. 




The event will end with a parlak, or candy toss.




“We’re closing it with a candy toss so everyone can be happy that we’re there,” Qaunirq said.




Later that evening, at St. Jude’s Anglican Cathedral, the Inuksuk Drum Dancers will open for Juno-winning classical soprano Deantha Edmunds of St. John’s, N.L.
















The concert will close with the song 

Quviasuppunga

, by the late Inukjuak songwriter Charlie Adams.




“The song encourages us to meet the world with optimism, kindness, and confidence,” said dance troupe leader Mary Piercey-Lewis. 

“It’s a bright, uplifting piece that reminds us how powerful our attitude can be.”




Meanwhile, Wednesday morning on Parliament Hill, Ottawa plans to hold a more sombre flag-raising ceremony with residential school survivors.




An estimated 150,000 Indigenous children were taken, many forcibly, from their homes to attend residential schools. Canada’s last residential school closed in the mid-1990s.




Residential school survivors in need of emotional support can call the national Residential School Survivor Support Line line 24 hours a day, seven days a week, at 1-866-925-4419.

author: Chris Walker
title: AI School Praised by McMahon Reportedly Does “More Harm Than Good” for Students
content:
“Accuracy of the content provided by the [AI] is a concern,” read an internal assessment of Alpha School’s lessons.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

During a Fox Business interview on Tuesday morning, Education Secretary Linda McMahon promoted the use of artificial intelligence in schools, citing a controversial online charter school that has been criticized for utilizing inaccurate and confusing AI-generated lessons.

When asked whether she viewed AI as a “tool” or a “threat,” the former World Wrestling Entertainment CEO chose the former.

“I certainly believe AI is definitely a tool used correctly, and I’ve seen it in action,” McMahon said in the interview. “I have visited the Alpha School in Austin, Texas, where they use AI for the first two hours every single morning.”

AI is an “additional tutor” that can provide “one-on-one instruction” to students, McMahon said. “It is incredibly effective.”

Alpha School is used by online-only K-12 students as an alternative for in-person learning across the country, and McMahon frequently touts the Austin-Texas-based company as a success story. Yet some families have reported concerns about its effectiveness, with parents warning that its lessons can lead to high stress levels among students.

Evidence of the online school’s problems was obtained and published by 404 Media earlier this year. The outlet reported that internal documents from the company suggested that AI lessons generated at the school were doing “more harm than good.”

For example, lessons and tests with questions often featured multiple-choice answers that didn’t make sense.

“These questions not only fail to meet SAT standards but also fall short of the quality we promise to deliver,” one employee’s assessment of the AI-modeled lessons read. “From a student’s perspective, when answer options don’t logically fit the question, it feels like a betrayal of their effort to learn and succeed. How can we expect students to trust our assessments when the very questions meant to test their knowledge are flawed?”

“Accuracy of the content provided by the [AI] tutor is a concern,” another internal assessment stated. “There are instances where it not only delivers incorrect answers but also provides convincing yet flawed justifications. Despite raising multiple queries about a particular answer, the chatbot erroneously confirmed an incorrect option as correct.”

Former employees of the company also expressed their concerns.

“Students are being treated like guinea pigs,” one former Alpha School employee said.

“Students incoming into AP Biology the previous year were seriously lacking in their foundational skills,” another employee noted.

Disturbingly, Alpha School also collects data on the students themselves, including video recordings, and publishes it to a Google Drive online. That folder, 404 Media reported in February, was made accessible to anyone who had the link.

“We are not computers or algorithms. We are simply people who need breaks. We are people that don’t like being watched through their computers,” one student said in a company feedback form.

The company also lacks transparency, making it difficult to conduct a real analysis of its successes or failures, said Victor Lee, an associate professor at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Education.

Alpha Schools “refus[es] to allow for any independent research to evaluate the claims or to really scrutinize what’s going on from disinterested parties,” said Lee, speaking to CNN about the school in January. “That sort of behavior sort of implies there’s something to hide.”
