author: Joe Sandler Clarke
title: UN’s Israeli Settlements Blacklist Names Firms With UK Public Contracts
content:
Several companies with major British government contracts have once again been named in a 

UN database of firms

 involved in the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements.




The database names 214 companies – 61 more than the previous year – that the UN human rights office has “reasonable grounds to believe” are involved in activities linked to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.




Earlier this month, the UK government announced new sanctions targeting the settlements, including a ban on the import of goods. 




Foreign secretary Ed Miliband 

said the move

 – which will also involve action against companies that support settlement expansion – was the “beginning of a new approach”.




The firms named in the UN list include French infrastructure giant Egis, which operates the M40 motorway for National Highways; Motorola Solutions, which owns Airwave, the radio network used by British emergency services; and Heidelberg Materials, with which the UK government agreed a major carbon capture deal in 2025. 




Egis was listed for its role in planning the construction of a new light rail network in Jerusalem, which 

rights groups say

 will connect Israeli settlements in occupied East Jerusalem with each other. An Egis spokesperson said the firm “has formally expressed its disagreement with this inclusion” in the UN database. 




Norwegian pension fund KLP 

divested from Motorola

 in 2021 over the firm’s involvement in providing services for use in surveillance in the West Bank. 




Heidelberg directed us to 

a statement it issued last year

 where it said its Israeli subsidiary had ceased all operations at the Nahal Raba quarry – located in the  West Bank – in 2023, and that neither it nor its Israeli subsidiary operates “any facilities in the occupied Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem”. 




Spanish trainmaker CAF, which is involved in the Jerusalem light rail project, was also named in the UN list. The firm is in the running to build new trains for a suburban rail service in Scotland. 

Trade unions have urged

 the Scottish government to exclude CAF over its links to the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, while ScotRail drivers have said they will 

refuse to drive

 CAF trains if the deal goes ahead. 




ScotRail, which has the final say on the new train deal, told Novara Media it is “committed to a thorough evaluation” to ensure the final decision on the deal is fair. 




CAF has said

 its “operations cannot be interpreted as contributing to, facilitating, or benefiting from settlement related practices”. 




On the publication of the most recent database, Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, said: “This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses.” 




A spokesperson for the Scottish government’s transport department said its guidance holds that “firms who are exploiting assets in illegal settlements can be excluded from tender exercises for grave professional misconduct. The Scottish Government is clear that all Public Bodies should take any such evidence into account when deciding where to award public contracts.”

author: Alessandra Bergamin
title: Lebanon’s Environmental Defenders Say Israel Is Deliberately Targeting Them
content:
Israel has decimated Lebanon’s land — and is also slaughtering the people who protect it.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In late April 2025, after 41-year-old farmer Oussama Farhat was discharged from the hospital, two pieces of shrapnel still lodged in his body, he hurried to check on an injured red fox. In his southern Lebanon village of Meiss el-Jabal, Farhat, a volunteer with the environmental organization Green Southerners, had helped rescue the cub from beneath the rubble of ongoing Israeli air strikes — the same kind that has decimated southern Lebanon and its people for the past three years. Now, the young fox was curled atop a starry blanket, its outstretched leg wrapped in a blue bandage.

In a message to Hisham Younes, the founder and president of Green Southerners, Farhat wrote that the fox cub would soon be ready for release.

Concerned, Younes replied: “Oussama, where are you?”

A member of the Lebanese Civil Defense, Farhat had been injured on April 25, 2025, after he and a fellow volunteer went to check for casualties unknowingly halfway through an Israeli double-tap strike — a tactic where an attack is followed by a second in the same location. In the days following October 7, 2023, Hezbollah, an armed group and political party formed in response to Israel’s 1982 invasion of Lebanon, launched rockets and artillery into occupied Shebaa Farms as an act of solidarity with the Palestinian people. Since then, Israel has continued to attack southern Lebanon near-daily, making Farhat’s village — just 700 yards from the UN-demarcated “Blue Line” that separates the two states — a hotspot.

After Farhat was discharged from the hospital, Younes implored him to go to Nabatieh, about an hour north, and rest with his family, including his elderly mother. But, says Younes, steadfast in his commitment to the south, Farhat explained that he needed to stay in Meiss el-Jabal.

“Please Oussama, you need to leave,” Younes replied.

The next day, Farhat was killed.

For the past three years and over two ceasefire agreements, Israel has systematically and violently erased life from southern Lebanon, committing what many, including Lebanon’s environment minister, have deemed an ecocide. An agricultural borderland in the heart of the historic fertile crescent, Israel has transformed southern Lebanon from small-scale and subsistence farms of tobacco, olives, and goats to a landscape set ablaze by white phosphorus munitions, littered with unexploded ordnance, and poisoned by the pesticide glyphosate. In a region where around 70 percent of families rely on farming, explained Ghassan Makarem, an organizer with the Lebanese food sovereignty organization AgriMovement, Israel has used airstrikes, shelling, and the steady roar of bulldozers to destroy around a quarter of the country’s cultivated land, burning olive groves to ash, slaughtering flocks of livestock, and flattening entire villages.

“Nothing that lives has been spared … It’s all part of the genocide that’s occurring.”

“Nothing that lives has been spared,” said Makarem. “It’s all part of the genocide that’s occurring.”

Since 2023, that genocidal violence, as described by multiple outlets, has displaced more than 1 million people, killing nearly 9,000 and injuring more than 30,500, mostly in the south. Included within that figure, alongside a high number of emergency services workers, are southern Lebanon’s land and environmental defenders — displaced, disappeared, injured, and killed, because of their commitment to steward and protect the land.

As Julia Choucair Vizoso, a senior fellow at the Arab Reform Initiative and researcher for The Public Source who has written about environmental struggle and food sovereignty in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), explained, Israel has long had a policy, stretching from occupied Palestine to southern Lebanon, of attacking those who resist occupation by refusing to leave. Because of that, farmers, shepherds, fishers, and beekeepers have not only suffered as Israel destroys their livelihoods and land, but have been marked as a threat because of their very connection to it in the first place.

Among those environmental defenders is Farhat.

Six years ago, explained Younes, the farmer reached out to Green Southerners asking how best he could help local animals, especially those that were injured or sick. Farhat soon became part of the all-volunteer team, helping map bird habitats in the eastern Mediterranean flyway, documenting illegal logging, and photographing the region’s flora and fauna, including the iridescent Palestine sunbird. But shortly after Israel started bombing southern Lebanon, Farhat’s role changed.

As a field coordinator with Green Southerners, he began documenting the frequency and impact of Israeli white phosphorus strikes, some of which have since been deemed potential war crimes. Alongside two other volunteers, Farhat photographed the white, tentacled clouds caused by the munitions, geolocated and dated the strikes, and, whenever possible, helped quell the phosphorus fires that burned hot and long — often sustaining injuries that landed him in the hospital. From October 2023 to November 2024, volunteers with Green Southerners verified some 285 attacks, many in residential areas and above agricultural land.

While Farhat’s story, much like that of slain sea turtle conservationist Mona Khalil and former Green Southerner volunteer Mohammad Skaff, who was killed in the residential town of Abbasiya in May 2026, fits a more Western idea of activism, those who tend the land of southern Lebanon without an “activist” title, said Younes, are no less environmental defenders — and no less impacted.

“In every village, the community has environmental defenders for whom it is their culture to take care of livestock, wild animals, pets, and abundant beehives,” said Younes. “It’s not just Mona or Oussama — there are thousands of casualties that go unseen.”

On July 2, 2024, farmer Muhyiddin Abu Dalla was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Zalloutieh shortly after he finished harvesting wheat. “The land was more important than his life,” Dalla’s brother told journalist Amal Khalil, who herself was later killed in an Israeli strike in 2026.

On November 25, 2024, 91-year-old Ali Kdouh, known locally as Abou Hussein, was killed after remaining with his herd and enduring two months of attacks on the region. He was considered the last shepherd of Nabatieh.

On February 2, 2025, fisher Mohammad Juhair was abducted by Israeli soldiers while fishing with his cousin near the southern Lebanese port of Naqoura. According to the most recent reporting, he has not been seen since.

On June 17, 2025, Mohamed Abdel Salam Nasrallah, a dedicated beekeeper, was killed in an airstrike while in the fields of his home in Houla. “I am the type of person who gives from his heart to what he loves,” Nasrallah told Reuters in 2022.

“In Lebanon, a lot of the people who are on the front lines of genocidal violence are just trying to stay on the land and keep living off the land.”

“In Lebanon, a lot of the people who are on the front lines of genocidal violence are just trying to stay on the land and keep living off the land,” Vizoso said. “These are communities at large that are threatened but kind of invisibilized globally.”

Because of this, the term environmental defender can often be an imperfect one. With origins that are more institutional and individualistic, explained Vizoso, it fails to capture the collective struggle of communities operating outside of international, nongovernmental organizations. But patterns of violence and repression against those protecting the environment, the land, and the sea are often repeated around the world, from one government, one corporation, and one paramilitary to the next.

The attacks in southern Lebanon are part of that global context.

From 2012 to 2025, some 2,375 land and environmental defenders were killed or disappeared, according to data from the human rights organization Global Witness. This figure includes well-known defenders such as Indigenous Lenca leader Berta Cáceres, who was killed in her home in Honduras, to farmers, community activists, peasants, and Indigenous peoples targeted for protecting the land from extraction and development projects including mining, logging, agribusiness, renewable energy, and even tourism.

Over the years, both Israel’s public and private sectors have played a role in these attacks, too.

Both Israel’s public and private sectors have played a role in these attacks.

In 2014, private security guards from Israel’s Golan Group were hired to “protect” a Canadian mine in Guatemala. During a demonstration against the mine, the guards shot at Indigenous protesters, injuring seven people. In Indonesia, including in occupied West Papua, the country’s police and military forces use a cellphone hacking system sold by Cellebrite, an Israeli digital intelligence company. Since 2018, seven environmental defenders, including four Indigenous West Papuans, have likely been killed by state forces.

In 2018, as former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faced a preliminary examination into war crimes from the International Criminal Court, he publicly committed to solely purchasing weapons from Israel, given the country’s complete lack of human rights restrictions. An investigation I conducted in 2024 found evidence that between 2014 and 2024, the Philippine state was potentially involved in 109 out of 210 killings of environmental defenders recorded in the country.

But while killings and repression by governments, corporations, and paramilitary groups have been consistently documented globally for more than a decade, violence leveled against environmental and land defenders in the Middle East and North Africa is often underreported, in part because of ongoing conflict. Global Witness noted in its 2024 report that a lack of capacity and the challenges of research amid conflict have meant that many victims, including Farhat, are omitted from official tallies. The organization acknowledged, however, that this doesn’t diminish the importance of the victims’ work, the extent of violence and repression they face, or the fact that, in many instances, they have more than likely been targeted for their work.

“I believe the targeting is not secondary — it’s deliberate,” said Ghassan, with a reference to the killing of Khalil. “[The Israelis] say they have information about everyone which means they are saying they know who they’re targeting — they have already admitted it.”

Younes, too, believes Khalil, Skaff, and Farhat were targeted.

In the months before Farhat was injured while volunteering with the Civil Defense, he told Younes that he had appeared in a documentary. While Green Southerners volunteers regularly in coordinated interviews with journalists, the extent and destruction of Israeli aggression had made Younes more cautious. Since 2023, he has preferred that volunteers don’t show their faces on camera as he feared they might become targets. Then, on May 1, 2025, as Farhat drove in his pickup truck through Meiss el-Jabal, he narrowly escaped an Israeli airstrike, according to Younes. Within half an hour, as the farmer and environmental defender neared his home, a drone struck again. This time, before Farhat was even out of the car or in the house, he was killed.

“I think this is part of the policy to push the people out — threaten them, kill them. This is the easiest way, and the Israelis are professionals.”

“I think this is part of the policy to push the people out — threaten them, kill them,” said Younes. “This is the easiest way, and the Israelis are professionals.”

In a video from July 2018, Farhat filmed a golden jackal close to the village of Bint Jbeil. As it wanders through long, yellowed grass, the wolf-like animal notices Farhat and pauses, watching him as he watches back. Farhat’s caring relationship with wild animals is among his qualities Younes remembers best. In particular, he says, the time a female golden jackal, normally extremely protective, allowed Farhat to approach her pups.

“This was something really rare,” said Younes. “It was extraordinary.”

Since Farhat was killed, few Green Southerners volunteers have remained in the south and, for now, Younes has continued to encourage everyone to leave. But as the destruction continues, so, too, does the documentation. This year alone, the organization has recorded Israeli airstrikes near UNESCO World Heritage sites, nature reserves set ablaze, and multiple white phosphorus strikes, including several across the densely populated town of Nabatieh in June. While Younes acknowledges that, for now, Israel — supported by the U.S. — operates with impunity, he is optimistic that one day there may be a path for justice and accountability.

“The documents are there, the images are there, the faces of those who were killed — Mona, Mohammad, Oussama — are there, looking at you,” he said. “We hope that through documentation we are keeping the truth alive, we are keeping the collective memory of our land alive.”

“And we hope, one day, this world will wake up.”

author: Chris Walker
title: Alito Reverses Course, Announces Recusal From Major Corporate Fossil Fuels Case
content:
The Supreme Court associate justice had previously refused to step away from a case involving fossil fuel companies.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito is recusing himself from a climate crisis-related case before the court this year, reversing his previous announcement that he would remain on the case despite his personal financial interests in its outcome.

Clerk of Court Scott Harris sent the announcement to attorneys on both sides of the pending matter on Monday.

“I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case,” Harris wrote.

The letter gave no explanation as to why Alito came to the decision to recuse himself.

The case features ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, which are seeking to have a Colorado-based lawsuit against them dropped, citing federal law they claim supersedes state statutes. State municipalities are suing the companies, seeking to hold them financially liable for the impacts of the climate crisis.

Alito does not have any financial stakes in either company. However, the associate justice does hold stocks in other fossil fuel-based companies, which means the outcome of the case could still directly benefit him.

Earlier this year, Alito said he would not recuse himself from the case, claiming that, because he doesn’t have any stocks in those companies specifically, he doesn’t have a vested interest in the case’s outcome.

“Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party,” a statement from the court read in May.

A coalition of progressive watchdog groups pushed back against that assertion, submitting evidence to Congress that Alito could be influenced by the pending ruling and urging lawmakers to investigate.

Alexandra Nagy, organizing director for Consumer Watchdog, one of the organizations involved in that request, reacted positively to Alito’s decision to recuse.

“Justice Alito’s recusal from Suncor v. Boulder is the right decision, and one he should have made from the start,” Nagy said, noting that “the Supreme Court’s Code of Conduct says a justice should step aside when the justice has a financial interest in the subject matter of a case or another interest that could be substantially affected by its outcome.”

“The public should not have to wonder whether a justice’s personal investments could benefit from a ruling that shields the fossil-fuel industry from liability,” Nagy added.

Others reacted to the decision by calling for limits on the stocks justices are allowed to invest in — if they’re allowed to have stocks at all.

“The real question is: Why does any justice hold stock in an individual company that is part of an industry that is going to appear before the court?” asked Louis Virelli, a law professor at Stetson University and an expert on judicial recusals.

Alito’s refusal to recuse in other key cases has been highlighted in the past, including in 2024, when he refused to step aside in cases involving January 6 defendants and in other high profile cases relating to President Donald Trump.

That year, it was revealed that Alito had flown a U.S. flag upside down — a symbol adopted by Trump loyalists and the “Stop the Steal” movement — outside of his Virginia home in 2021, shortly after Trump was impeached for instigating the January 6 attack. Alito also flew an “Appeal to Heaven” flag outside his home, a symbol commonly used by Christian nationalists.

This past Supreme Court term has been viewed negatively by most Americans. According to an Economist/YouGov poll conducted in July, only 36 percent of respondents gave the high court approving marks, while 50 percent said they disapproved of the court’s job over the past year. Alito also received a negative review, garnering a -7 point net approval rating from voters.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Pressure Mounts at Labour Conference to Kick Palantir Out of NHS
content:
The NHS’s contract with Palantir has come under pressure at Labour party conference, with 20k party members backing a motion to end the service’s reliance on the US spytech firm. 




Healthcare workers and patients protested outside the venue, calling for the government not to renew a highly controversial £330m patient data contract with Palantir.




The company provides tech to the Israeli military during its genocide in Gaza, as well as custom surveillance tools to ICE in the US.. 




A majority

 of Labour voters

 

(76%) 

 believe Andy Burnham’s government should allow Palantir’s NHS contract to expire without renewal in February 2027.




Around 30 health workers dressed in scrubs attended the No Palantir in the NHS demo outside the conference in Liverpool on Tuesday, ahead of Burnham’s speech. 




NHS doctor Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a campaigner at Medact, told Novara Media: “The government has the perfect opportunity to end this contract. It can do so safely and transition over to NHS-owned infrastructure. 




“Palantir’s NHS contract is a threat to the ethics we sign up to as health workers, it’s a 

threat to our patient relationships

 and data privacy, and it’s a threat to the integrity and independence of NHS infrastructure.”




Patients cannot opt out of having their sensitive healthcare data stored on Palantir’s Federated Data Platform (FDP), and some Palantir staff are granted 

“unlimited access” 

to identifiable patient data by NHS England. 




First secretary of state Louise Haigh used her conference speech to delegates on Sunday to say Burnham’s government will refuse to “be in hock to foreign giants”, in a comment 

understood to be aimed at

 Palantir. 




The Cheltenham Constituency Labour Party (CLP) 

tabled a conference motion

 on tech sovereignty on Monday, stating that overreliance on US tech “poses unacceptable risks to the independence and security of the UK, its institutions and its people”. 




Exeter CLP called on the government to allow the NHS’s Palantir contract to expire in 2027, look to Greater Manchester’s approach as a “blueprint” and build an NHS-controlled replacement system. 




However, the motion was not chosen for debate, despite more than 

20k members

 voting for it. 




Greater Manchester, where Burnham served as mayor for nearly a decade, has repeatedly rejected Palantir’s FDP in its NHS services, using

 a UK-created alternative 

instead. 




More protests against Palantir are set to take place across England as part of an international week of action uniting health workers and unions in the US, Brazil and Europe.

title: Puerta del Sol (Μαδρίτη): Ένα κίνημα ταξικής αλληλεγγύης
content:
Εδώ και 4 μέρες, στην πλατεία Σολ στη Μαδρίτη, ένα αυθεντικό κίνημα ταξικής αλληλεγγύης έχει πάρει σάρκα και οστά. Με αφορμή την απόπειρα έξωσης της 87χρονης Μαρικάρμεν, έπειτα από αύξηση ενοικίου από τον ιδιοκτήτη του σπιτιού από 500 σε 1.650 ευρώ (!)




Η ταξική αλληλεγγύη νίκησε, και η αλληλεγγύα συλλογική δράση στάθηκε εμπόδιο απέναντι στους αδήφαγους και απάνθρωπους landlords, που με τόσο απροκάλυπτο τρόπο αναδεικνύουν την ουσία του καπιταλιστικού συστήματος: δηλαδή της κοστολόγησης της κερδοφορίας ως ατομικού δικαίωμα, έναντι του συλλογικού δικαιώματος στην ζωή με αξιοπρέπεια.




Το κίνημα σαφώς συνεχίζει δυναμικά, καθώς πραγματοποιούνται ανά μέσο όρο 70 εξώσεις την ημέρα.




Αύριο, τίθενται προς ψήφιση από το κυβερνητικό συνασπισμό οι εξής προτάσεις, μετά από τις πιέσεις του εργατικού κινήματος:




– Περιορισμός στα νομικά πρόσωπα όσον αφορά την αγορά ακινήτων.


– Πάγωμα των εξώσεων μέχρι να ρυθμιστούν τα ενοίκια.




Στο πανό, διακρίνεται το σύνθημα ” Αφεντικά και Ιδιοκτήτες, εχθροί της εργατικής τάξης” στο πανό της αναρχοσυνδικαλιστικής συνομοσπονδίας CNT, στη συγκέντρωση στη πλατεία.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “Se crean más condiciones para el ingreso al sistema de encierro juvenil y menos oportunidades de salir”
content:
La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM) presentó la sección de niñez de su Informe Anual 2026, un diagnóstico sobre los lugares de encierro y el sistema de promoción y protección de derechos que realiza en su calidad de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura. Con la presencia de funcionarios judiciales e integrantes de organizaciones por los derechos de la niñez, sindicales y políticas, se generó un espacio de diálogo y debate para pensar los desafíos en torno a las políticas destinadas a niños, niñas y jóvenes, en particular a partir de la puesta en vigencia de la nueva y regresiva ley penal juvenil. Los ejes de un debate de larga data que no parece avanzar en más oportunidades para las nuevas generaciones sino en más encierro y violencia.







Las políticas de niñez están en crisis y no pueden responder a los problemas actuales de les jóvenes. Las graves regresiones en derechos de la nueva ley penal juvenil son el último eslabón de una sistema que desde hace muchos años viene reforzando el sistema penal y punitivo en detrimento del sistema de promoción y protección de derechos. Un sistema que responde con más encierro y violencia a las y los jóvenes más vulnerables.




El diagnóstico parte de lo relevado por la Comisión Provincial por la Memoria en su calidad de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura y se pública en la sección de niñez del Informe Anual 2026, El sistema de la crueldad XX, que el organismo presentó días atrás en su edificio.




Los datos aportan claridad a la discusión: la cantidad de niños, niñas y adolescentes abordados por el sistema de promoción y protección de derechos pasó de 41.511 en 2018 a 85.907 en 2025, sin que el sistema haya sido dotado de los recursos necesarios para ese abordaje. En el otro extremo se encuentra el fuero de responsabilidad penal juvenil extendido ahora por la nueva ley, aunque las estadísticas indiquen otro cosa: en los últimos 10 años la cantidad de jóvenes imputados descendió un 55% mientras que la de detenidos se mantuvo constante.




“Se recargan las capacidades de actuaciones punitivitas por parte de los mismos operadores judiciales que antes actuaban de otra manera. No logro entender esta extensión de la mirada punitivista sin nada que lo justifique porque el delito no creció”, describió brevemente el defensor del fuero penal juvenil de La Plata Ricardo Berenguer sobre las primeras reacciones de los funcionarios judiciales ante la puesta en vigencia de la reforma de la ley penal juvenil que bajó la edad de punibilidad a los 14 años y extendió, además, la persecución a delitos leves que antes no eran abordados por la justicia penal. El funcionario, no obstante, advirtió que la ley cristalizó acciones de la justicia que ya venían ocurriendo: “A la extensión de la prisión preventiva como regla se suma la retención de los jóvenes en el sistema. No hay revisión de las penas ni medidas morigeratorias, que sí se le conceden a los adultos”.




En esa línea coincidió la jueza de garantías del joven del departamento de Moreno-General Rodríguez Mirta Guarino: “Las llaves de cualquier medida, ya sea una internación en un hogar o una de seguridad, la tenemos los jueces, pero estamos en un momento muy crítico y hay magistrados que ni siquiera responden un teléfono”. La jueza también llamó a revisar el funcionamiento del sistema de promoción y protección de derechos que funciona en una fragmentación absoluta y aún más con el penal.




Los funcionarios judiciales fueron algunos de quienes tomaron la palabra durante la presentación de la sección de niñez del Informe Anual de la CPM junto a las organizaciones y el propio organismo. “Es el triunfo de las políticas neoliberales, que pensaron con estrategias muy precisas, como endurecer el sistema penal. En la provincia de Buenos Aires desde el gobernador Ruckauf hasta acá, se profundizaron las políticas punitivistas de mano dura y no podemos seguir sosteniendo que son los resabios del patronato: el sistema de promoción y protección ha creado sus propios monstruos”, señaló Roberto Cipriano García.




De hecho uno de los datos más sobresalientes del informe es cómo la baja en la edad de punibilidad que entró en vigencia recientemente a partir de la reforma de la ley penal juvenil ya se implementaba en los hechos: el 20% de los menores de edad encerrados en la Provincia durante 2025 tenían menos de 16 años y estaban detenidos con la aplicación de una medida de seguridad determinada por la justicia.




La graves regresiones en derecho de la nueva ley penal juvenil son el último eslabón de una sistema en crisis, que desde hace muchos años viene reforzando el sistema penal y punitivo en detrimento del sistema de promoción y protección de derechos de la niñez.




“El problema en la Argentina no es el delito (no es que no haya), es que hay muchos otros problemas anteriores al delito, y el delito entendido como el delito contra la propiedad privada, inter clase. Ese no es el problema, en la Argentina tenemos el 40% de los pibes bajo la línea de la pobreza, ¿cómo que el problema es el delito y no la pobreza en la que viven los niños y adolescentes en nuestro país?”, resumió la referente del Foro de niñez Vanesa Salgado.




Ante la falta de políticas públicas dirigidas a garantizar derechos y terminar con los problemas que llevan a los jóvenes a ingresar al sistema, se recrudece el sistema de encierro en condiciones que hacen imposible la aplicación de los principios de resocialización que es el único objetivo del fuero penal juvenil. “Validar la palabra de la víctima no es una cuestión menor, reconocerlas como tales y validarlas como sujetos de derecho. Estamos hablando de una niñez vulnerada y no podemos resignarnos ni naturalizar este estado de cosas”, agregó la directora general Sandra Raggio.




En los dispositivos destinados a la protección de niños, niñas y adolescentes “falta supervisión y previsiones de estándares mínimos de atención y cuidado para promocionar y restituir derechos de esos niños que el Estado separó transitoriamente de sus familias en un medida de abrigo. Esto se combina con condiciones de discrecionalidades en cada institución con casos de semi clandestinidad respecto a la permanencia de niñas y niños en instituciones no conveniadas”, describió la directora del programa de la CPM, Sofía Porta. Otra vez, los datos del informe aportan claridad a la discusión: a diciembre de 2025 había 4.200 niños y niñas institucionalizados, más del 90% alojado en hogares no oficiales; sólo el 27% egresó porque se consideró que se habían restituidos sus derechos y un 30% egresó en guardia pre-adoptiva.




El penal por su parte -apuntó Rodrigo Pomares- “es un sistema neutralizante, lejos de los eufemismos de reinserción y educación. Y cuando los jóvenes entran al sistema, se deberían garantizar los mayores niveles de libertad posible, aun en el encierro. Pero no hay conexión con el mundo exterior, ni salud o educación; se pierden los vínculos familiares, hay requisas vejatorias permanentes… Esto es el encierro para los jóvenes en la Provincia. No exageramos: la tortura en la Provincia existe y es muy amplia sobre los jóvenes”.




El encuentro contó también con la presencia y participación del funcionario judicial Matías Ponce, la co-directora del Instituto de abogado del niño Sonia Aiscar, la integrante de la Red de consejos locales y la mesa incidencia de niñez de la Provincia Betina Perona y la referente de las organizaciones de Lxs chicxs del pueblo Manuela Mendy, entre otros militantes por los derechos de la niñez.




A partir de la experiencia de intervención, la toma de la palabra permitió construir un espacio de intercambio para pensar cómo trabajar en clave de derechos con uno de los sectores más vulnerables de la sociedad: las y los jóvenes pobres.




Las voces en diálogo coincidieron en la preocupación sobre la falta de propuestas de restitución y reparación para la niñez y la juventud. Y se abrieron preguntas sobre el papel del Estado y la necesidad de restituir lazos sociales que hagan posible una democracia que proteja a su infancia.

“Se crean más condiciones para el ingreso al sistema de encierro juvenil y menos oportunidades de salir”

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

title: Besê Hozat: The process cannot succeed without democratization
content:
Besê Hozat, co-chair of the KCK Executive Council, said in an interview with Medya Haber that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot succeed in Turkey without democratization.




This is the first part of the interview.




The discussions regarding the Peace and Democratic Society Process are ongoing. As movement, you have already taken a number of significant steps in this regard. Also, before Parliament adjourned, the framework law – which you referred to as a law that creates a foundation on which to build on – was passed. What has been done afterward, and what hasn’t? Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş stated that the process is running smoothly. Do you assess it similarly?




Before addressing your question, September 25 marked the anniversary of the martyrdom of our comrade Rıza Altun. He was commemorated extensively both in Kurdistan and abroad, and many commemorations were held. I commemorate all the martyrs of the revolution and freedom – represented by our comrade Rıza – with respect, love, and gratitude. Our comrade Rıza holds a very significant place and value within our struggle. With his theoretical, ideological, political, and practical experiences, as well as his consciousness and expertise, he has contributed greatly to this struggle. He has contributed immense value to this struggle. On the path illuminated by comrade Rıza and all our martyred comrades, we will carry out this struggle successfully – with determination, conviction, and resolve – and we will achieve success based on the principle of living up to their memory. This struggle will lead to victory. I wish to reaffirm this pledge once again on the occasion of this anniversary.




Coming to your question; we have made several statements regarding the framework law. From the very beginning, both Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] and our movement have clearly laid out our standing on this matter. We have made many assessments and statements based on the premise that this law should be a comprehensive one, that it should truly play the role of a foundational law, and that it should pave the way for a democratic solution to the Kurdish issue. This law did not fully meet these criteria, and accordingly, we have criticized it. It is an extremely flawed, internally contradictory, and paradoxical law. Implementing it as it stands – in a straightforward manner – is hardly possible anyway. This is quite clear. When we speak of the law’s comprehensiveness, it should have encompassed Rêber Apo’s physical freedom, his conditions for a free life and work, the leadership of the movement as a whole, and the entire organizational structure – from the top leadership down to every level – including Rêber Apo, who is excluded from the scope of this law.




The law should have demonstrated an approach and a commitment to taking democratic, political, and legal steps. It is known that both the emergence of the PKK and the armed struggle came about because of the lack of this. The existence of the Kurdish issue gave rise to the PKK and to the armed struggle. There is a very serious need for democratic, political, and legal steps that lay the groundwork for and pave the way toward resolving this issue. This law did not fully address this; that much is clear. It is also very, very difficult to describe it as a truly fundamental law in this regard. It is a legal text, and in that sense, it may have some significance. It is a step – a step on the legal level – that has emerged and developed within this process. However, it would not be realistic to ascribe much more meaning to it beyond that. Since the process began, we have taken very important steps as a movement. In particular, many steps were taken following the Call for Peace and Democratic Society on February 27, 2025 by Rêber Apo.




The PKK’s dissolution congress was a historic development. At this congress, the decision was made to cease armed struggle against Turkey. However, for this process to proceed, it was established as a fundamental requirement that Rêber Apo’s physical freedom be secured, allowing him to freely lead this process. This remains valid today. Numan Kurtulmuş made a statement the other day saying the process is running “like clockwork.” In reality, there is no such process running “like clockwork.” That is the truth of the matter. There is a process that is moving extremely slowly, a process driven by unilateral steps. At present, the state has not taken any democratic, political, or legal steps. The position of Rêber Apo is clear. While it is crystal clear that our leader’s freedom to work and live under decent conditions is an absolute necessity – a prerequisite for this process to proceed successfully and develop – there has been no progress on this front. It is incomprehensible how the process is supposedly “running like clockwork.” It is proceeding extremely sluggishly and slowly.




So far, this process has proceeded largely through unilateral steps. As a fundamental prerequisite for the process to move forward, it is essential that Rêber Apo be provided with the conditions to work and live freely and that our leader be in a position to directly oversee this process, both officially and in practice. People from every sector that Rêber Apo needs to be able to consult – whether they are politicians, academics, writers, artists, intellectuals, journalists, organizational leaders, political parties, or institutions – must be enabled to meet with Rêber Apo, and Rêber Apo must be able to convey its views openly and freely to the public. The success of this process depends on this. If it is to run smoothly, it must proceed in this manner. The smooth functioning of the process is contingent upon Rêber Apo freely leading this process, both officially and in practice. This process cannot proceed unilaterally; it is simply not possible.




The Turkish state has always portrayed the PKK and the armed struggle in Turkey as the fundamental obstacle to resolving the Kurdish issue. You have demonstrated your resolve through the steps you have taken to eliminate these justifications. In your assessment, what needs to be done to truly resolve the Kurdish issue, and what changes do you expect following the fundamental law? Numan Kurtulmuş also stated that a new constitution is needed. What kind of legal or constitutional changes can be anticipated in the coming period, or what kind of constitution could be developed for Turkish society and the resolution of its problems?




Without democratization, it is impossible for this process to succeed in Turkey. Turkey’s democratization – its adoption of a democratic, pluralistic, libertarian, and egalitarian constitution, and the development of a democratization process grounded in local democracy – is an absolute prerequisite for the success of this process. As I mentioned a moment ago, the emergence of the PKK is a consequence – a result of the continued existence of the Kurdish issue. This issue must be resolved on the basis of local democracy and Turkey’s democratization. A democratic, freedom-oriented constitution must grant freedom to all peoples and faiths, particularly the Kurds, and the constitution must enshrine this. On this basis, a democratic constitution is a fundamental necessity for Turkey. The September 12 Constitution – which is like a patchwork quilt – is still in effect today. Although they have made some changes over time, these changes are not quite democratic. These are various amendments made based on the needs of the ruling political power. The constitution is extremely authoritarian, centralizing, fascist in character, and denialist. Because of this, the existing constitution must be abolished, and instead a brand-new constitution must be drafted – one that is democratic, pluralistic, and accommodates and accepts all the diverse identities and beliefs. It is already late for this. The participation of all forces of society in this process is essential. Civil society organizations, political parties, democratic groups, environmental organizations, and particularly women must be included in this process. All these forces and organized democratic structures must participate in this democratic constitution-drafting process. This is crucial.




Right now, there is a fruitless debate on this issue as well. Whenever the ruling party deems it necessary, and to the extent it deems it necessary, it puts the constitution on the agenda, and debates ensue. In reality, it is demagoguery surrounding the constitution – it has gotten completely out of hand. There is no genuine, serious plan or program to draft a new constitution. It is a debate brought to the agenda only when the government deems it necessary. This, too, is actually being exploited for political purposes. The agenda of drafting a new constitution is being turned into a political tool. There is no reflection of full determination, will, or seriousness on this matter. This needs to be pointed out. And without the Kurdish issue being safeguarded by a democratic, pluralistic constitution that also recognizes Kurdish identity, one cannot speak of lasting peace, democracy, or a solution in Turkey. The drafting of a democratic constitution is of utmost importance.




In parallel with all these intertwined and coordinated discussions, democratic, political, and legal steps must be taken in Turkey. There is a critical need for a process aimed at a democratic solution to the Kurdish issue – one that recognizes local democracy and subjects the unitary and centralized system of governance and the state apparatus to serious reform. In this process, a serious agenda or framework for resolving the Kurdish issue has not yet been developed. The issue is reduced solely to the question of arms. Without discussing the root causes of this issue, without discussing local democracy, and without discussing the democratization of Turkey – a discussion that is solely focused on and reduced to the issue of arms – becomes an extremely shallow, narrow, and unproductive debate. This situation must now be addressed and overcome.




Already in earlier interviews and statements, you pointed out that certain segments in Turkey are adopting approaches that overly emphasize the perception of disarmament. You, on the other hand, focus on ensuring that Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan can work freely and that opportunities for him to meet with everyone are provided. When the framework law was enacted, AKP officials stated that from then on, anyone who requested it could visit Imrali Island and that intellectuals, writers, and academics could go there to meet with Abdullah Öcalan. However, such a situation is not currently observed. Even the Imrali delegation has been reduced to visiting only once a month. This situation is causing serious discontent among both the Kurdish people and democratic circles. How do you approach this?




There has been no change in the conditions imposed on Rêber Apo. They ease the isolation when they want to, and they tighten it when they want to. Sometimes there are periods of weeks, even up to two months, during which no meetings take place with Rêber Apo. They state every time that this is a state decision. This process is one that unfolds based on a state decision. They say they are determined to carry out this process. In that case, Rêber Apo’s conditions must be changed immediately. Rêber Apo must be able to freely lead this process. Various committees and coordinating bodies are being discussed. The other day, comrades also evaluated these in various programs. Beyond all this, Rêber Apo must be able to freely lead this process. Rêber Apo is the driving force and leader of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Rêber Apo will play a decisive role in the success of this process. Therefore, Rêber Apo must be able to work freely. The conditions under which Rêber Apo works and lives must be secured by legal guarantees and a legal framework. These matters cannot be handled de facto. If Rêber Apo is to lead the process freely, there must be a legal framework for this free leadership. There must be a legal regulation. In law, this must have a name and a status. This matter must also have an official character. From the very beginning, our leader has put in tremendous effort and made great strides to ensure the successful progress of this process. Rêber Apo devotes immense effort and energy 24 hours a day.




An appropriate approach must develop. Rêber Apo is extremely determined, persistent, and committed to advancing this process. And he naturally expects to see the same determination, the same commitment, and the same seriousness from the other party as well. As a movement, we also want to see this. If the counterpart – and the state itself – is serious, determined, and ambitious in advancing this process, then it must establish the democratic, political, and legal foundation for it and take democratic steps. It is necessary to ensure, swiftly and without further delay, that there is a legal and political foundation guaranteeing that our leader can carry out this process under free conditions.




In this context, a subcommittee has been founded in which Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan is said to be part of. Recently, Mehmet Uçum made a statement that trivialized the role of this very committee. In response, it was stated by your movement’s leadership and the DEM Party that Abdullah Öcalan would play a coordinating role in this subcommittee. What role will Abdullah Öcalan play in this subcommittee during this process?




Rêber Apo is not taking on a role in the subcommittee. As far as we know, this is a wrong perception. Rêber Apo is the coordinator of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. If we must use the term “coordinator,” then Rêber Apo is the coordinator of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. In practice, Rêber Apo has been coordinating the Peace and Democratic Society Process over the course of two years, particularly ever since the February 27 call. He is providing leadership and guidance. He is managing the process. Now, this work that he has been carrying out in practice needs to be given a legal framework, an official framework, procedure, and status. And this needs to be declared and announced to the public.




The committees that have been established are the state’s own committees. The state’s own people are part of them. Based on its own perspective and the policies it has defined, it envisions operating them in a manner appropriate to the process. Rêber Apo is the coordinator of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. He is the leader and the administrator of this process. As I have said before – and I emphasize this again – I am underscoring the importance of this process, which has been developing for nearly two years. It needs to be formalized, given a status, and given a clear name. This is what is desired and expected.




Since the beginning of the process, there have been serious attacks directed at Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement. We see that the rhetoric of certain Kurdish nationalist circles, some leftist groups, and specific Kemalist factions has become even harsher. What is the reason for these attacks?




We were quite busy during this process. I really couldn’t follow all the discussions closely. Accordingly, it is difficult for me to make a concrete assessment of this. However, we are aware that there have been many debates ever since this process began, and sometimes unfounded criticisms arise as well. Certain circles are launching ugly attacks directed at our leadership. I find the various criticisms, concerns, and anxieties expressed by democratic forces, leftist and socialist movements, and democratic forces in Turkey understandable – to a certain extent. So far, the state has not taken any democratic steps. The ruling party continues to exert intense pressure and launch attacks against society, the democratic forces, and the opposition. It is carrying out extremely anti-democratic attacks and practices. This is indeed causing serious unease and anger. If there is so little room for democratic development, there are serious concerns about the successful development of the process.




The concerns and anxieties of the democratic forces and the leftist socialist movements on this matter are well-founded. We share these concerns as well. Without democratization – without Turkey embracing local democracy and taking democratic political and legal steps – it is impossible for the Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey to succeed. This is clear. Democratization in Turkey plays a crucial and decisive role in the success of this process. Without this foundation and environment being established – and without corresponding changes in the government’s policies – it is hardly possible to expect success in this process. Various forces are now observing the government’s actions, and naturally, their faith weakens and they are becoming more pessimistic. They harbor serious concerns and anxieties, and this leads to various unhealthy debates as well as prejudices directed at Rêber Apo and the movement. Some argue as if Rêber Apo and the Kurdish Freedom Movement had made a secret deal with the AKP.




Definitely, the AKP has its own calculations regarding the maintenance of its power. It will try to use this process on that basis. This, in itself, shows a complete failure to understand Rêber Apo. To entertain such thoughts, to harbor such concerns, is to fail to understand Rêber Apo at all – and to fail to understand the Freedom Movement. In a way, it means failing to see the 53-year struggle and the results that struggle has produced. This is, therefore, a great injustice. Rêber Apo is waging an extremely principled, great struggle for democracy, freedom, and peace. If this process leads to success, Turkey will breathe a sigh of relief. Democracy will advance in Turkey; freedoms will advance; justice will advance. Turkey will enter an entirely different era. The freedom movement and Rêber Apo’s 53-year struggle are proof of this. The results it has produced are proof of this. It is entirely unwarranted to feel anxiety or concern about this matter.




If democracy is desired in Turkey, if peace is desired, if freedom, equality, and justice are desired, then all political forces must strongly champion this process. They must take responsibility. They must lead this process. Together with the Kurdish Freedom Movement and the democratic political structure, they must wage a joint struggle for democracy, freedom, and equality. At the heart of this is the freedom of Rêber Apo. Rêber Apo’s freedom is not separate from the freedom of the Kurds, nor is it separate from democracy in Turkey. Rêber Apo’s freedom truly means the freedom of the Kurds. It means Turkey must embark on a process of democratization. Now, it is crucial to devote our energy to this cause, to work toward it, to strongly champion this process, and to take the lead.

title: MAF-DAD: Reasonable grounds to suspect war crimes in North and East Syria
content:
The Association for Democracy and International Law (MAF-DAD) has published its report, International Crimes Committed by and on Behalf of the Government of the Syrian Arab Republic, examining developments in North and East Syria in January and February 2026.




MAF-DAD’s independent Fact-Finding Mission investigated violations in North and East Syria following attacks on the Sheikh Maqsoud (Şêxmeqsûd) and Ashrafiah (Eşrefiyê) neighbourhoods of Aleppo in early January 2026. Members of the mission conducted field investigations in the region between 21 February and 17 March 2026.




The report said 32 detailed qualitative interviews were conducted as part of the fieldwork, involving a total of 62 people. Those interviewed included 25 direct victims, one victim’s family and six representatives of institutions and organisations involved in documenting violations or assisting victims.




MAF-DAD said the report was based on a comparative assessment of statements from victims and witnesses, direct field observations, medical records, reports by institutions and civil society organisations, evidence collected by the Rojava Information Center (RIC) and open-source material. The report applied the standard of “reasonable grounds to believe” that a violation had occurred.




Attacks on civilians




The report said attacks on civilians in January 2026 were concentrated particularly in the Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafiah neighbourhoods of Aleppo and along routes leading out of Tabqa and Raqqa (Reqa).




The field investigation documented drone strikes, artillery fire, sniper attacks, gunfire directed at vehicles, violence at checkpoints, attacks on areas where civilians had sought shelter and direct attacks on homes.




The report also included testimony that civilians attempting to flee Tabqa and Raqqa came under fire, were stopped, searched, robbed and detained, and in some cases killed.




MAF-DAD concluded that the evidence provided reasonable grounds to believe that civilians had been deliberately and indiscriminately targeted and that these acts constituted serious violations of international humanitarian law and war crimes.




Hospitals and healthcare workers targeted




The report examined attacks on healthcare infrastructure in Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafiah in a separate section.




MAF-DAD said Xalid Fecir Hospital and Osman Hospital were targeted by artillery fire. Evidence was also collected indicating that healthcare workers had been injured, detained, disappeared and killed.




The report said attacks on healthcare infrastructure and medical personnel were not isolated incidents, but formed part of a broader pattern in which protected medical facilities and personnel were systematically endangered or directly targeted. MAF-DAD said there were reasonable grounds to believe that these acts constituted war crimes.




Detention, torture and enforced disappearances




The report said cases of detention and disappearance occurred following the capture of Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafiah and at checkpoints along routes used by fleeing civilians.




Witnesses said men were separated from women and children, detainees were held in severely overcrowded facilities and their families were given no information about them.




People interviewed by MAF-DAD reported beatings, electric shocks, blindfolding, handcuffing, forced confessions and statements, inadequate food and water, poor hygiene and denial of access to healthcare.




The report said there were reasonable grounds to believe that these practices could constitute war crimes, including arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture, enforced disappearance or hostage-taking. It added that, where the necessary legal requirements were met, they could also amount to crimes against humanity.




Mutilation and humiliation of the dead




The report also documented serious violations involving the bodies of the dead.




MAF-DAD said it had examined direct photographic and video evidence showing the mutilation of bodies, the public display of corpses, the cutting of women’s hair or braids, the removal of tattoos from bodies and the severing of certain body parts.




Witnesses also said families had been prevented from burying the dead with dignity and that bereaved relatives had been subjected to degrading treatment.




The report said these acts were accompanied by racist, sectarian and sexist insults. MAF-DAD found reasonable grounds to believe that the acts were intended to humiliate and intimidate victims, their families and their communities, and said they should be considered “outrages upon personal dignity”, constituting a war crime.




Looting and seizure of private property




The report said extensive evidence had also been gathered concerning the looting of homes and private property.




Witnesses described homes being raided, looted, occupied or marked to designate new occupants. Some people said their phones, money, identity documents and personal belongings had been confiscated.




Some displaced residents said that when they returned, they found the locks on their homes had been changed, their belongings removed and their properties under the control of armed groups or individuals affiliated with them.




MAF-DAD also documented attacks, looting and destruction targeting institutions including women’s organisations, libraries, and educational and cultural centres. The report said looting may have developed into a widespread practice involving the deliberate seizure, destruction or repurposing of property rather than merely being a consequence of the fighting.




Thousands forcibly displaced




MAF-DAD documented mass displacement from Sheikh Maqsoud, Ashrafiah, Raqqa and Tabqa.




The report said a significant proportion of those displaced were Kurdish civilians who had previously been forcibly displaced from Afrin (Efrîn) and were forced from their homes for a second time in January 2026.




MAF-DAD said the available evidence provided reasonable grounds to consider the displacement as the war crime of “forcible displacement”. Where the necessary legal requirements were met, it could also constitute the crime against humanity of “deportation or forcible transfer of population”.




Violations targeting women and women’s institutions




The report examined violations against women in a separate section.




MAF-DAD documented threats against women because of their activities in public institutions, the publication of their personal information, attacks on women’s centres and libraries, and the destruction of institutions associated with women’s political and cultural participation.




The research team interviewed 10 Kurdish and Arab women as part of its investigation into attacks on women’s institutions. Witnesses said Zenobiya women’s centres, Jineoloji institutions and libraries in Aleppo, Tabqa and Raqqa had been looted or destroyed.




The report also included testimony that women had been subjected to sexist insults and threats relating to their clothing while being detained. Women activists and women working in local government institutions reportedly received death threats, had their personal information published on social media, and had their homes and offices seized.




MAF-DAD said there were reasonable grounds to believe that the mutilation of women’s bodies, the cutting of their hair, the dissemination of images showing their mistreatment and sexist threats constituted the war crime of outrages upon personal dignity. Where the necessary legal requirements were met, the report said such acts could also constitute persecution of women as a crime against humanity.




Report highlights Turkey’s role




One of the notable sections of the MAF-DAD report focused on Turkey’s role.




The report said multiple sources indicated that non-Syrian elements were present among armed forces affiliated with the Syrian Transitional Government (STG) during the fighting in January and February 2026.




Some witnesses reported seeing fighters wearing uniforms bearing the Turkish flag and individuals making a hand gesture associated with Turkey’s far-right Grey Wolves movement.




The report also said there was evidence indicating that Turkish military personnel and equipment, as well as Turkish interrogators, had been deployed in support of the STG.




MAF-DAD concluded that this external support alone was insufficient to classify the hostilities as an international armed conflict. Based on the available evidence, the research team assessed the events of January and February 2026 primarily within the framework of a non-international armed conflict (NIAC).




Call for an independent investigation




MAF-DAD devoted a separate section of the report to Turkey and called for allegations concerning the involvement of Turkish military personnel, equipment and interrogators in potential violations to be investigated independently, effectively and impartially.




The association also called on Turkey to preserve relevant records, information and other evidence and to cooperate with competent national and international investigative and accountability mechanisms.




The report also called on Turkey, the United States, France, Germany, other EU countries and the United Kingdom, which provide military, financial or logistical support to the STG, to ensure that their assistance was not used in violations of international humanitarian law.




Call for international accountability




MAF-DAD assessed that the existing domestic legal mechanisms in Syria were not capable of ensuring effective accountability for the crimes documented in the report.




The report said local courts did not exercise effective jurisdiction over forces affiliated with the STG, while judicial institutions in STG-controlled areas were either inaccessible to victims or raised concerns about their independence.




MAF-DAD therefore called for investigations not only into the direct perpetrators, but also into those in positions of command who ordered, encouraged or facilitated the crimes, or failed to prevent or punish them.




The association called for the use of international courts and mechanisms, as well as universal jurisdiction where available. It also urged the preservation of evidence and measures to ensure the safety of witnesses.




The report further called on the UN International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism for the Syrian Arab Republic, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and other international mechanisms to follow up on the events of January and February 2026.




Among MAF-DAD’s key demands were clarification of the fate of missing and detained persons, the creation of conditions for the safe and voluntary return of those forcibly displaced, the restitution of looted property, and access for victims to effective remedies and compensation mechanisms.

title: Life of Kurdish political prisoner at risk in Tehran
content:
The Kurdistan Human Rights Network has published a report about the health of Mutelîb Ehmedyan, a Kurdish political prisoner from Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan).




Ehmedyan has been imprisoned for 16 years, and is reportedly suffering from several illnesses, including stomach cancer.




His health condition is said to be so serious that he is no longer fit to remain in prison. For this reason, Ehmedyan requested a postponement of the enforcement of his prison sentence. However, following an objection by the Tehran Prosecutor General’s Office, the political prisoner has continued to be held in the harsh conditions of Evin Prison.




According to the report, due to the negligence and indifference of the authorities, the Kurdish man was previously denied permission to receive treatment outside the prison. As a result, the cancer spread throughout his body. After his condition deteriorated, doctors reportedly had to remove his gallbladder, liver and part of his intestines in several operations. The report also states that prison authorities frequently withhold or prevent the delivery of medication obtained from outside the prison.




Ehmedyan was arrested by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on September 13, 2010. He was held in solitary confinement for eight months and subjected to severe physical torture. He was sentenced to 30 years in prison on charges of “rebellion.”




On 5 May 2025, Ehmedyan began a hunger strike in protest against the obstruction of his access to medication and medical treatment. Having lost 35 kilograms due to the lack of treatment, Ehmedyan continues to be held in prison despite his deteriorating health.

title: Öcalan: The true objective of this transformation is to build a democratic society
content:
Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan has addressed the international “Peace and Democratic Integration Conference” in London with a detailed message. The two-day conference, which begins today, focuses on international experiences from peace processes and their significance for a democratic and political solution to the Kurdistan question. In his message, Öcalan refers back to his Call for Peace and a Democratic Society of February 27, 2025, stating that the political perspective opened at that time must now be developed further in practice.




At the heart of Öcalan’s message is the concept of democratic integration. He understands this not as assimilation or the abandonment of social autonomy, but as the voluntary participation of a democratically organized society in a democratic republic on the basis of collective rights. Lasting peace, he argues, requires far more than an end to armed conflict: legal guarantees, the democratization of the republic, the free development of language and culture, strengthened local self-government, and social organization.




The message from Öcalan reads as follows:




“My Call for Peace and a Democratic Society of February 27, 2025 opened the door to a new phase. The PKK movement, democratic politics, the parties represented in the parliament of Turkey, and, more broadly, Turkey’s society have embraced this call. Now is the time to move forward through this door that has been opened. The issues you are addressing at this conference concern precisely the tasks that lie before us at this threshold. By drawing on international experiences and Kurdish perspectives and discussing how a political opening can be transformed into lasting peace, you are giving practical form to this call.




Peace cannot be completed through a single agreement or a single law. The silencing of weapons is a beginning. What is lasting is the building of a democratic society. The transition from armed conflict to sustainable peace requires a longer-term political, legal, institutional, and social transformation. The true objective of this transformation is to build a democratic society. In my view, revolution is not a transfer of power, but transformation through construction. A “freedom” achieved through violence soon turns into the opposite of the very values for which the struggle was waged. Without a dignified peace, democracy and freedom cannot endure; neither can democracy develop nor social peace take root in the shadow of weapons.




The thousand-year relationship of the Kurds with Turks, Persians, and Arabs is not based on a mutually exclusive antagonism but, despite all its ups and downs, on a reciprocal dialectic. Today, it is possible to renew these relationships through democratic integration, without assimilation and without separation. Separatist solutions do not correspond to the reality of this geography, where peoples, cultures, and faith communities live intertwined with one another. The principle of fraternity, by contrast, is rooted in historical and sociological realities.




The relationships of the Kurds with Turks, Persians, Arabs, and the other peoples of this land cannot be resolved by drawing borders. Millions of Kurds live in the major cities of the states in this region. A separation along the lines of “Kurds to the north, Turks to the south,” for example, corresponds neither to the historically developed common ground nor to the social proximity between these communities.




Integration is the opposite of assimilation: assimilation dissolves, and intensifies hostility, while integration unites, and creates peace and fraternity. This integration means the voluntary participation of a democratic society in a democratic republic within the framework of collective rights while preserving its own distinct existence.




The PKK, which I founded, emerged under the conditions of its time as a struggle for existence. It demonstrated the existence of the Kurds and broke the chain of denial. In the world of 2025, the Kurdish people are a historical reality that can no longer be denied. For this reason, the historical mission of our movement has been fulfilled. Like every revolutionary structure, it must evolve into a new form once its mission has been completed. Dissolution is neither an end nor a surrender, but a transition into a new historical phase. Insisting on maintaining the old form would harm everyone, first and foremost the Kurds.




Weapons must no longer be glorified; now society must be built. Democratic politics has replaced the strategy of national liberation struggle. Our stronger weapons are the word, the law, and organized society. Fully democratic politics is possible only under normal conditions in which not only have the weapons fallen silent, but violence and the mutual threat of war have also been eliminated.




A Turkey in which Kurds participate with their democratic consciousness will become a genuine democratic republic. In Turkey and the Middle East, the goal should not be separation, but the joint construction of a genuine democracy.




The way out of the crisis in the Middle East lies not in seeking new nation-states that would break apart existing borders, but in reviving what the peoples have in common—in other words, through an integration-oriented negotiation process and the building of local democratic networks.




Dear friends,




Transforming a political opening into lasting peace cannot be achieved through the decision of only one side. Integration requires reciprocal steps, mutual understanding, and recognition of the suffering experienced by the other side. A process that is not secured through legal arrangements cannot progress beyond a short-term period without conflict. Lasting peace, by contrast, requires democratic politics to become embedded in everyday life, in neighborhoods, cities, and institutions. At the same time, our emotional world and ways of thinking must change in accordance with the new conditions.




Without law, existence cannot attain legal status, and the democratic struggle is left without a foundation. The necessary guarantees consist of recognition of democratic society, the free development of language and culture, expanded rights to local self-government, and a framework in which constitutional citizenship and free citizens complement one another. As long as the unilateral and centralist legal order of the nation-state is not restructured through constitutional and legislative reforms, trust cannot be established. If the republic is not democratized, democratic integration cannot be realized either.




People who have been involved in the armed struggle must be given the opportunity to return to political and civilian life and assume responsibilities within democratic politics. Once the process is completed, these friends will become active participants in democratic debate, the legal sphere, and civilian life. Democratic integration means becoming part of society and an active participant in an unarmed, nonviolent phase.




The forms of participation that will sustain the transition from a politics of conflict to democratic politics are not limited to parliamentary representation and elections. Networks of local democracy, neighborhood and city councils, cooperatives, political parties, civil society, and local administrations are the lifelines of this transition. Democratic politics encompasses every form of organization and action through which society becomes politically empowered.




Constitutional and institutional arrangements must address political, regional, linguistic, and cultural diversity not through a project of a homogeneous nation, but through the concept of a democratic nation. The democratic nation is a political model in which different identities share a common right to equality, freedom, and fraternity. Differences in language, faith, culture, and regional belonging are a source of richness. The imposition of homogeneity has produced crises in this region; recognition of diversity, by contrast, provides the constitutional foundation for a solution.




Since existence takes concrete form through language and culture, recognizing it requires the removal of barriers to education and cultural development.




In a sustainable solution, local and regional administrations are not merely bodies that ease the burden on the central government, but local democratic administrations that shape social life. The organization of democratic society functions under the same political framework as the nation-state and through the direct participation of society. The foundation of the solution lies not in centrally concentrated powers, but in locally rooted and deepened democratic rights and social organization. The establishment of councils in the fields of education, health, culture, economy, and politics creates the building blocks of democratic society.




Women, minorities, civil society, and the media are not issues of peace that can be “resolved later,” but active participants in this process today. The question of women is one of the fundamental issues facing democratic society. Women’s freedom and ecological awareness form the backbone of building a democratic society. Different identities, faith communities, and social groups must be active participants in local governance. Without their effective participation, neither can legal reforms take root, nor can social reconciliation be achieved.




Dear friends,




My call to the peoples of Turkey and to this conference is this: the goal is not separation, but the joint construction of a genuine democracy. The Kurdish question has long ceased to be merely the question of a single people; it is a question concerning the shared future of Turkey and the Middle East. What is expected of you is to translate this transition and these theoretical insights into practice, and to connect and concretize international experiences with the historical foundation of fraternity in this region.




In a Middle East where the Kurdish question remains unresolved, it is not possible to build a more peaceful, secure, and livable future for everyone.




The path forward lies in reciprocal steps, legal guarantees, and democratic organization that permeates every sphere of society. At the threshold of a new era, what matters is not destroying the state, but building a free society.




This process is neither directed against any section of society nor addressed exclusively to any particular group. It is an outstretched hand to all those who stand for a solution, peace, and democratic values, and a call for joint action.




With my warm regards and respect,




Abdullah Öcalan




İmralı.”

title: DEM Party calls for parliamentary inquiry into the ‘Fund Crisis’
content:
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) Central Executive Board called for a comprehensive investigation and public scrutiny into developments it described as the “Fund Crisis” in a statement.




The statement said the developments could not be regarded merely as a technical financial problem, arguing that persistently high inflation, unemployment, the rising cost of living and poverty in Turkey had driven people to seek alternative ways to invest their savings and make ends meet. It added that financial markets had been turned into an arena for speculation and manipulation by certain groups.




The DEM Party said the issue could not be considered resolved simply through the resignation of a former minister or by holding certain fund managers responsible. It called for an investigation into why the relevant public institutions, particularly the Capital Markets Board (SPK) and the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK), had failed to intervene in a timely manner.




The party called for every stage of the process to be examined and made public, from the establishment of the funds and their investment decisions to their relationships with companies, regulatory oversight and liquidation decisions.




The DEM Party said any irregularities, manipulation and potential conflicts of interest needed to be uncovered, adding that everyone found responsible should be held accountable before the courts regardless of their political or economic position.




The party also called for a parliamentary inquiry commission to be established once Parliament reconvenes to investigate all aspects of the issue.




The statement said the rights of small investors who had suffered losses must be protected and their losses compensated. The DEM Party added that it would continue its efforts to protect the savings of low-income citizens.




The "fund crisis"




The crisis began after several investment funds that had built large positions in low-float stocks struggled to meet investors’ redemption requests. The Capital Markets Board (SPK) subsequently suspended trading on the Turkish Electronic Fund Trading Platform (TEFAS) for funds managed by seven portfolio management companies and ordered the liquidation of 131 funds.




The SPK had previously stated that funds managed by certain portfolio management companies had contributed to price movements in low-float stocks that could not be explained by the companies’ economic circumstances or financial performance.




On Aug. 28, the regulator introduced tighter rules governing fund concentration, related-party transactions, valuation methods and hedge fund operations.




Under Article 107 of Turkey’s Capital Markets Law, transactions intended to create false or misleading impressions about the price, price movements, supply or demand of capital market instruments may constitute market fraud.
